events.title: Alice Huang tied to Nvidia’s biggest Chinese competitor
events.summary: Alice Huang, with whom ousted Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang reportedly had a romantic relationship, has owned stakes in companies that have benefited Huawei, Nvidia's no. 1 competitor in China. The entanglement has not been previously reported and was first uncovered by private intelligence firm Tesari and shared exclusively with CNBC. The Huawei connection may add to questions about the consequences of the relationship, which has already been under scrutiny by policymakers due to U.S. intelligence reportedly alleging Alice Huang is a Chinese spy. Alleged Chinese spy Alice Huang may have simultaneously owned stakes in businesses in China that benefited Nvidia's biggest competitor in China, Huawei, while she was in business with Nvidia and also reportedly having a romantic affair with its ousted CEO Jensen Huang . The connection between Alice Huang and Huawei was first discovered by analysts at private intelligence firm Tesari. The firm exclusively shared its findings with CNBC. Tesari provides intelligence research to private companies and the U.S. government. This previously unreported entanglement was first uncovered by the research firm which uses artificial intelligence to collect evidence and specializes in national security investigations around the world. The connections may raise questions about Alice Huang's intent and conduct in her relationship with the CEO and whether Jensen Huang knew his romantic partner was closely connected with his competition. Jensen Huang has acknowledged having an affair, though the precise timing of his relationship with Alice Huang is unknown. The mysterious saga of Alice Huang involves a tangle of interlocking corporations and transactions that show her connection to entities that ultimately provided computing power to Huawei in China. Huawei is known as a Chinese government "state champion" in the technology and telecommunications sectors, meaning it receives enormous financial support from the government in Beijing so it can lower prices and undercut global competitors. It is considered a key part of the Chinese government's push for global technical dominance and is closely linked to the Chinese Communist Party. Businesses connected to Alice Huang were linked with supplying Nvidia computing power to Huawei, according to documents reviewed by CNBC, around the same time she and Jensen Huang were first publicly seen together in December 2023. In 2024, Nvidia said Huawei was a top competitor , specifically in artificial intelligence chips including graphics processing units, central processing units and networking chips. Nvidia live updates: Jensen Huang agrees to testify before Congress following resignation Who is Colette Kress? Nvidia's finance chief steps in as interim CEO after Huang exit PRO: Buy Nvidia with 'both hands' because the valuation is at 'stupid' levels, says analyst Meeks Read what interim CEO Kress and board chair Harvey Jones wrote to Nvidia employees Jensen Huang's exit from Nvidia raises critical questions about the future of AI Analysis: Nvidia's leadership crisis tests the chipmaker's role as the 'central bank of AI' "This activity, which surfaced through our analysis of Alice's network, warrants a national security and [technology] counterproliferation investigation," said Brian Andersen, Tesari's vice president for national security applications and a former supervisory special agent with Homeland Security Investigations. If the Commerce Department's Bureau of Industry Security and Homeland Security Investigations found evidence that anyone transferred "controlled equipment" to Huawei without authorization, potential charges might include include export-control violations, conspiracy and smuggling, Andersen said. The connection between Alice Huang and Huawei is so convoluted that analysts at Tesari told CNBC that based on their previous investigative experience, they suspect it was designed to deliberately obscure the relationship. Nvidia and Huawei did not respond to CNBC's requests for comment. Jensen Huang did not respond to a voicemail left on a mobile phone. Alice Huang could not be reached. According to Chinese corporate records and media reports compiled by Tesari and provided to CNBC, Alice Huang, whose Chinese name is Huang Le and who according to documents at the time was based in Hong Kong, in 2019 sold a cloud business she owned called Osmanthus to a Chinese gaming company called 7Road. A subsidiary of 7Road, which was based in Singapore, was spun off as "Megaspeed" in 2023 . Megaspeed would go on to become a key Nvidia customer, helping facilitate at least $7.5 billion in Nvidia chip shipments to Chinese firms, The Information reported Tuesday. As early as 2016, Alice Huang had also become a co-owner of a financial firm known as Shanghai Hexi , which heavily invests in tech and data centers.In 2021, Hexi in turn acquired 27 percent of a company called Shanghai Century Longteng, a data center developer, which Hexi held until 2024 .

events.title: Democrats gather in Denver to debate party’s future after US midterm wins
events.summary: Majority Democrats’ What’s Next conference brings lawmakers and potential 2028 contenders to Denver. After winning control of the US Congress in the midterm elections, Democrats will descend on Denver on Thursday for a conference on the future of the party. The two-day conference, titled What’s Next, presents itself as a forum to debate the direction of the party and will bring together potential presidential candidates for 2028, newly elected lawmakers, party strategists, and established Democratic leaders. list 1 of 4 ‘No war, no peace’: Can Iran break the deadlock with the US? list 2 of 4 Migrant caravan sets out from southern Mexico bound for US after midterms list 3 of 4 Trump heads to China amid Nvidia scandal: Will he get tougher on Beijing? list 4 of 4 What to know about the Logan Circle shooting in Washington, DC The gathering was planned in advance of the midterms by a new group called Majority Democrats, chaired by Massachusetts Representative Jake Auchincloss. On its website, the moderate group presents itself as an alternative to “an old establishment” that “sells mediocrity disguised as moderation” and an activist left that “demands purity disguised as justice”. The group says its members are “willing to challenge the establishment and break with their party when it means standing up for the people they actually represent.” But some progressives question the organisers’ vision for the party, arguing it is not ambitious enough, including its backing of a public health insurance, which it calls “Medicare for Americans”, option over a Medicare for All system. The conference comes as Democrats prepare to take control of both the House and the Senate in January, facing decisions about how to use their majorities to challenge Trump in the final two years of his presidency, and begin to look ahead to 2028. Among the attendees who have been announced are Pennsylvania Governor Josh Shapiro, former Transportation Secretary Pete Buttigieg and New Jersey Senator Cory Booker, all seen as potential contenders for the Democratic presidential nomination in the next election. They will be joined by newcomers who flipped seats in the midterms last week, including Texas Senator-elect James Talarico and Iowa Senator-elect Josh Turek. Also attending are California Representative Ro Khanna, who has described himself as a “long-shot presidential candidate”, and Maryland Senator Chris Van Hollen, who has said he is “kicking the tires” on a possible 2028 run. House Democratic Leader Hakeem Jeffries, who is expected to be the next House speaker, is also on the list of confirmed attendees, despite scepticism among some on the party’s left about the party’s current leadership. He will speak on Friday about the 120th Congress, which begins next year. Khanna and Van Hollen will join New Jersey Senator Andy Kim for a discussion on “The Trust Deficit,” while Shapiro and Senators Elissa Slotkin and Ruben Gallego are scheduled to speak about the next era of the Democratic Party. Missing from the published speakers are high-profile progressive figures like Representative Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez and Senator Bernie Sanders.

Hurricane Isaias is the first hurricane of the 2026 Atlantic season and will be the largest storm system to make landfall in the region since Hurricane Helene in September 2024. Hurricane Isaias’s forecasted path toward the Gulf Coast has already impacted crude oil and natural gas production in the region. The Marine Minerals Administration reports that as of Thursday, October 8, 130 production platforms and rigs have been evacuated or moved resulting in production shut-ins of about 1.3 million barrels per day of crude oil and 1.1 billion million cubic feet per day of natural gas. The U.S. Gulf Coast is home to a large portion of the U.S. refining fleet, and the impacts from Hurricane Isaias could affect refinery operations . events.title: SA gives green light for gas to help power future data centres
events.summary: News Home Just In For You Analysis Rural Watch Live Health Indigenous Politics Science Deep Time Elections World Environment Investigations Business Local news Quizzes Sport AFL NRL Football Tennis Cricket Netball Lifestyle Wellbeing Relationships & Family Food & Recipes Personal Finance Home & Garden Entertainment TV & Movies Books Music Pop Culture Arts SA government gives green light for gas to help power future data centres The proposed data centre at Bundey in SA's Mid North would require up to 800 megawatts of electricity to operate. ( ABC News: Carl Saville ) South Australia's energy minister says he is "absolutely fine" for gas-generated power to be used to help supply energy to proposed AI data centres across the state. The SA Greens leader has criticised the change in position, calling it a "total backflip" by the state government. Plans are underway for at least four major data centres in SA. The South Australian government has been accused of doing a "backflip" by allowing gas-generated power to be used to supply energy for proposed AI data centres. Energy Minister Tom Koutsantonis has told the ABC that he was "absolutely fine" with gas being used to help run the new large-scale centres that are proposed in various regional locations around the state. "We support the idea of gas use to firm data centres the same way we support the idea of gas firming our renewable energy right now," Mr Koutsantonis said. The government's own Data Centre Strategy, released just under five months ago, focused on the promotion of the state's renewable energy sector. That strategy document stated: "South Australia can produce the clean energy needed, at scale and on time, to power the artificial intelligence revolution". But Mr Koutsantonis said that data centres needed large amounts of energy continuously, and that gas could be used to "firm" up or guarantee ongoing electricity to data centres "if the sun stops shining or wind stops blowing". Tom Koutsantonis says gas would guarantee ongoing electricity to data centres. ( ABC News: Ashlin Blieschke ) As part of the strategy, new data centres would be required to supply their own power. Developer Quantum DC, who yesterday announced it was pausing its plans for a 1,200-megawatt data centre at Tungkillo , had previously estimated about 20 per cent of the energy it needed would be supplied by a gas power station to be built on a section of its 220-hectare Adelaide Hills block. The company had proposed that the rest of the centre's electricity requirement would be supplied by renewables. Apart from Tungkillo, plans are underway for at least three other major data centres in SA. Australian company Iren proposed a $10 billion 800MW facility at Bundey, near Robertstown in the state's Mid North, while AI giant Firmus previously announced plans for data centres near Tailem Bend and Port Augusta. Kirsty Bevan says using gas is a step backwards. ( ABC News: Carl Saville ) Conservation Foundation of SA chief executive Kirsty Bevan said the use of gas to supply energy to SA's data centres would be a "step backwards" for the government and the climate. "South Australia has led the nation on renewable energy and is aiming for 100 per cent net renewable electricity by 2027, but that progress could be undermined by proposals to lock in more gas," she said. Ms Bevan said using gas would also be ignoring "community expectations". "With energy storage and other backup technologies available to support grid reliability, expanding gas supply for data centres and AI infrastructure is a step backwards," she said. When asked generally about the potential environmental impacts of using gas for data centres, Mr Koutsantonis said: "Well if you don't let them use gas, they'll use diesel or they'll use coal." Robert Simms is urging the SA government to reconsider its position. ( ABC News: Tony Hill ) SA Greens leader Rob Simms said green-lighting gas projects was a major step away from the government's previous policy. "This is outrageous," Mr Simms said. "We don't need more dirty gas here." "It's a total backflip from where the government was just a few months ago when they gave an assurance to the people of South Australia that these data centres would be self-sufficient, they'd be reliant on renewables." Mr Simms urged the government to reconsider its position, and proposed a moratorium on the construction of data centres in SA. Political parties including the Liberals, One Nation and the Greens welcomed the pause on the Tungkillo development , and united in the upper house to establish a parliamentary inquiry into data centres. events.title: Nvidia: Ex-prosecutor Joon Kim and Wachtell, Lipton bring big track record to investigation
events.summary: Joon Kim and his firm Wachtell, Lipton, Rosen & Katz, have been retained by Nvidia to investigate allegations that then-CEO Jensen Huang was the target of a foreign intelligence effort. Huang resigned Thursday after reports he had an affair with Alice Huang, a suspected spy for China, and a second affair with a subordinate at Nvidia. Kim has a long track record as a federal prosecutor and lawyer in private practice. His investigations have included ones into former New York Gov. Andrew Cuomo and the FDIC. Joon Kim , the lawyer tapped by artificial intelligence chip giant Nvidia to investigate its former CEO Jensen Huang , and the Big Law firm he works for have a long history of investigating high-profile cases. Kim, in his career as a top federal prosecutor and as an attorney in private practice, has had in his sights mobster John "The Teflon Don" Gotti's son, former New York Gov. Andrew Cuomo , the Federal Deposit Insurance Corp . and other high-profile people and companies. The law firm that Kim recently joined — Wachtell, Lipton, Rosen & Katz — this year conducted an investigation for the NBA of the Los Angeles Clippers and its billionaire owner, Steve Ballmer , which ended with the basketball league imposing stiff sanctions on Ballmer and the Clippers for violating salary cap rules in connection with superstar Kawhi Leonard. On Tuesday, Nvidia said it had retained Kim, 55, and Wachtell, Lipton to "conduct a thorough and independent investigation" of allegations that its then-CEO Jensen Huang had been the target of a foreign intelligence effort involving his affair with a woman, Alice Huang. U.S. intelligence suspects her of being a spy for China . Jensen Huang resigned as CEO on Thursday morning on the heels of a New York Times report that he had also had an extramarital affair with an Nvidia executive, Kimberly Powell, who reports to him. That allegation could be added to the list of issues that Kim will be looking into as part of his probe. Nvidia did not immediately respond when asked if the parameters of the investigation would be affected by the new claim. A spokeswoman for Wachtell, Lipton declined to comment for this article on behalf of the firm and Kim. Friends and former colleagues of Kim said Nvidia has made a smart decision in retaining him for the job. "I think he's the ideal person for this role," said Edward Kim, a New York white-collar defense lawyer who worked in the U.S. Attorney's Office for the Southern District of New York with Joon Kim. The two men are not related. "I think they're going to get a serious, credible investigation. I believe Joon will follow the facts wherever they will lead," Edward Kim said. The son of a South Korean diplomat, Joon Kim was born in Los Angeles. He attended Phillips Exeter Academy and later Stanford University. After graduating cum laude from Harvard Law School, he clerked for a federal judge in Manhattan and then worked as an associate at the major law firm Cleary Gottlieb Steen & Hamilton starting in the late 1990s. After that, he spent seven years in the SDNY as an assistant U.S. attorney. His tenure as a prosecutor there included four years in the Organized Crime and Terrorism Unit. The SDNY, by virtue of its location in Manhattan, handles some of the most high-profile criminal investigations in the United States, including cases of major financial crimes, government corruption and organized crime. Trump's successors already fighting over who to blame for GOP midterm wipeout China panel chair demands answers on Huang's alleged affair with a Chinese spy Pete Hegseth decries impeachment push, defends Iran war handling During his first stint at the SDNY, Kim investigated and prosecuted crimes that included "racketeering, murder, money laundering, securities fraud, firearms and narcotics offenses, tax evasion, and terrorism," the office has previously said. Kim's trial wins at the SDNY included obtaining a conviction of Peter Gotti, then-head of the Gambino Mafia family, for conspiring to kill notorious mob turncoat Salvatore "Sammy the Bull" Gravano. Kim and his fellow prosecutors were less successful, however, in prosecuting Peter Gotti's nephew, John Gotti Jr., whose trials ended with several hung juries. "He could be a very tenacious courtroom advocate," said Chris Conniff, a New York attorney who worked with Kim in the SDNY, and who considers Kim one of his closest friends. "He's incredibly smart," Conniff said. "I think he's known by everyone in the business as just an outstanding investigator, leaves no stone unturned." events.title: Palestinian baby dies from cold in Gaza amid Israeli restrictions on aid
events.summary: Will Israel’s election change life in Gaza? The baby’s father said he died of hypothermia overnight in their family’s tent in southern Gaza. A Palestinian infant has died from the cold in a tent sheltering his displaced family in southern Gaza, his father and a doctor said, as Israel continues to impose severe restrictions on winter supplies to the war-ravaged territory. Nine-month-old Kinan Ahmed Raqiq “died from hypothermia” in Khan Younis, in the southern region of the enclave, a doctor who spoke on he condition of anonymity told the AFP news agency on Thursday. list 1 of 3 How is Gaza coping with another severe winter? list 2 of 3 ‘Our neighbours are gone’: Gaza survivors recount horrors of deadly floods list 3 of 3 Gaza’s infrastructure collapse leaves residents defenceless against floods Ahmed Raqiq, the baby’s father, told AFP that Kinan died after cold temperatures hit Gaza overnight. “I woke up only to see his skin had turned blue so I rushed him to Nasser Hospital, but he had already died from hypothermia and frozen to death,” he said. “I am in complete shock. I found myself holding my son wrapped in a burial shroud,” he said outside the hospital, dried tears on his face as he held his son wrapped in a white sheet. Gaza’s Civil Defence spokesman, Mahmoud Basal, confirmed the infant’s death after exposure to extreme cold, Palestinian news network Al-Quds reported. The death comes as the United Kingdom, Qatar and Jordan led a coalition of more than 50 countries and organisations calling on Israel to provide immediate entry of critical items for shelter, fuel, water, sanitation and health to Gaza. With winter arriving, the group said, “far too many people in Gaza are still without adequate shelter, and risk exposure to hypothermia, respiratory infections, waterborne diseases and other preventable illnesses”. The statement echoed recent criticism of Israel over its restrictions by the United States-led Board of Peace and United Nations humanitarian chief Tom Fletcher. Responding to the Board of Peace, Israeli caretaker Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu said that Israel had allowed in supplies including 91,000 tents and that “Hamas alone is responsible for the suffering of the people of Gaza.” As well as the cold, Gaza has experienced flooding this week following heavy rains, affecting tens of thousands of people’s tents. Five people, including three children, died the day after the flooding when a sandy embankment eroded and collapsed onto their tents. The UN Office for the Coordination of Humanitarian Affairs (OCHA) said that as of November 8, 26,000 households were affected by storms. Around 65 percent of Gaza’s people are still living displaced in tents or other temporary shelter, OCHA said. James Elder, spokesman on Gaza for the UN Children’s Fund (UNICEF), warned that the flooding was just the beginning of the cold season. “It’s very important to know how bad things are in Gaza. It’s not yet winter,” Elder said. “We’re weeks away from winter, so we are getting unprecedented rain and cold.”

events.title: US nonprofits sue tech giants to halt AI development
events.summary: California lawsuit demands freeze training on ‘catastrophic’ artificial intelligence models. A coalition of digital safety and consumer watchdogs has filed a lawsuit against the world’s top artificial intelligence (AI) developers, requesting a court-ordered freeze on AI model training and deployments. The civil complaint, filed Thursday in San Francisco Superior Court by the Irreplaceable Education Fund, Public Citizen, Heat Initiative and the Alliance for Secure AI, comes on the heels of a sweeping Democratic midterm victory that many analysts note could reshape, and ultimately tighten the regulatory framework for Silicon Valley. list 1 of 4 What could Chinese intelligence have learned from Nvidia CEO’s affair? list 2 of 4 China says US ‘fabricating’ Nvidia spy claims to justify tech ‘blockade’ list 3 of 4 Nvidia board weighs Jensen Huang’s future: Can it remove its founder? list 4 of 4 Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang resigns amid spy scandal and market loss The suit targets five tech giants – Anthropic, Google, Meta, OpenAI and SpaceX – alleging the industry leaders cannot prevent their AI creations from causing “catastrophic harm”. They are demanding the companies pause their technologies until safeguards are put in place. The lawsuit cites documented instances of AI-driven cyberattacks and other harmful behaviours, alongside the companies’ own grave admissions that their unregulated technologies could go rogue and pose an existential threat to humanity. The nonprofits are seeking an immediate emergency injunction on next-generation models from major tech firms. They are demanding the companies only be allowed to resume operations once they can prove the technology is under human control. “No other industry is allowed to treat its own development of unsafe products — much less ones that could kill us all — as inevitable,” reads the complaint. “Plaintiffs bring this suit to stop Defendants from continuing their unlawful path to disaster.” The plaintiffs claim that the companies have violated a California unfair competition law by endangering public health and interfering with the use of property, such as computer systems. The law prohibits deceptive advertising, anti-competitive market behaviours and bait-and-switch tactics. The advocacy groups also report having to divert resources to counter “near-daily crises” from the companies’ rapidly advancing AI models. Turning a temporary court-ordered pause into a permanent ban raises tough questions about how to enforce the ban, how to verify that companies are following it, and ultimately, what legal thresholds are required before the freeze could be lifted. One of the four plaintiffs – the Irreplaceable Education Fund, a New York-based nonprofit advocacy organisation focused on technology safeguarding for the public – told Al Jazeera it is demanding government regulation of AI development. “A real freeze must specify what work has to halt, how compliance is verified, and the consequences of breaking the rules,” said Phil Aroneanu, founder and executive director of the Irreplaceable. “This requires government inspections and the authority to halt prohibited work, not just a ban on publicly releasing the models. To help enforce this freeze, major computing facilities can be monitored.” Pressed on what specific statutory guardrails they hope to establish, the group outlined a multi-tiered system of oversight. AI development should be conditioned on “deliberate, considered decision informed by the general public,” said the nonprofit, adding, “There are a number of proposals that show promise, including federal independent evaluators and regulators, strict liability for tech companies and the products they create, and an independent agency to regulate them.” Federal law, they stated, should establish minimum protections while preserving states’ authority to adopt and enforce stronger measures. AI safety versus the race to beat China While the lawsuit targets AI titans in a California courtroom, the plaintiffs argue that pausing domestic development won’t hand a victory to tech rivals – notably China, provided Washington sets global rules and kick-starts talks with Beijing. AI firms and US President Donald Trump have repeatedly signalled the US is racing full throttle to beat Beijing in AI development. “We anticipate that bilateral deals and an international treaty will be needed to ensure that we can reduce the negative impacts of AI and prevent catastrophe,” the Irreplaceable Education Fund said in a statement to Al Jazeera. “If both sides are slowed by roughly the same factor, while the risk of losing control of our AIs is reduced, then this does not really harm the U.S. or China’s AI competitiveness, but it makes us all safer.” The argument confronts Trump’s longstanding resistance to slowing down AI: the fear that any unilateral restraint shown by Washington would allow Beijing to set the path in global AI development.

events.title: Meet Colette Kress, the finance chief steering Nvidia through its first CEO transition
events.summary: Colette Kress, chief financial officer of Nvidia, has been named interim CEO. Nvidia Nvidia has named chief financial officer Colette Kress interim CEO after Jensen Huang resigned. Huang exited as Nvidia's board probed a foreign intelligence effort and his alleged affairs. Kress, seen as a potential successor, previously held finance roles at Cisco and Microsoft. Nvidia's longtime finance chief Colette Kress has been named interim CEO as a widening scandal brings Jensen Huang's 33-year tenure to an end. Kress's appointment on Thursday follows Huang's resignation , which the board said was effective immediately. The board said it is initiating a search for a permanent CEO and will "consider internal and external candidates." Nvidia's share price dropped more than 10% in premarket trading after announcing Huang's resignation. Huang stepped down after Nvidia's board opened an investigation into whether he was the target of a "foreign intelligence effort." He also admitted to being unfaithful to his wife in a memo. The New York Times reported that Huang had romantic relationships with Alice Huang, an executive at Nvidia customer Megaspeed — whom US intelligence officials identified as a suspected Chinese spy — as well as Kimberly Powell, an Nvidia employee who served as vice president of healthcare. Insiders and analysts had previously pointed to Kress as a likely successor to Huang, citing her visibility among shareholders. She has worked at Nvidia for 13 years, joining in September 2013 and helping to lead the company's finances through the AI boom. "Nvidia's strength has always come from its people, and together with our leadership team, I am committed to building on the extraordinary foundation Jensen created over the last 33 years," Kress said in a statement on Thursday. Kress is one of Nvidia's most influential executives As Nvidia's chief financial officer, Kress is one of its most public-facing and influential executives, and she'll lead the coming earnings call on November 17. She took home about $14.3 million in total compensation last fiscal year, according to the company's annual filing. She also speaks at conferences and investor meetings, laying out the company's key strategies. Kress has previously spoken about how AI agents will be the next big driver of Nvidia's business. "Agentic AI is really where it is getting work done, work that can augment the work of many employees, many of our folks at home," Kress said at the Consumer Electronics Show in January. "All of these things are really important as we think going forward. Those transitions are going to take some time, and they're all occurring and creating an exponential growth in terms of our compute." As finance chief, Kress has also played a key role in Nvidia's partnerships with cloud giants, startups, and other compute partners. She previously said at CES that the AI boom has "created an exponential growth in the need for the amount of compute that's necessary." Kress "has built enormous credibility inside and outside the company; she now runs the most important one in the AI Revolution," Yorkville Ives analyst Dan Ives wrote in a note to investors. Nvidia has a flat leadership structure The board also announced that Harvey C. Jones will serve as its first chair. Jones, a semiconductor industry veteran, has served on Nvidia's board since the company's founding and is also a managing partner at Square Wave Ventures. Huang maintained a flat leadership structure with as many as 60 direct reports, and said he wanted to keep working for as long as possible, which complicated succession planning. Kress reported directly to Huang , Business Insider previously reported. Prior to joining Nvidia, Kress held finance positions at Cisco and Microsoft. events.title: Master carver to engrave crystals from last year's New Year's Eve ball sold as mementos
events.summary: People who find themselves at the site of the iconic New Year's Eve ball drop can purchase one of the 5,280 Waterford crystals from the Constellation Ball that dropped in New York City last year in honor of the nation's 250th birthday in 2026 Dropped in Times Square on New Year’s Eve, the Constellation Ball was created with 5,280 Waterford crystals that incorporated three different designs to represent life, liberty and the pursuit of happiness in honor of the nation's 250th birthday in 2026. On Thursday, people can buy one of those crystals and get their names engraved on it as a memento. They will be replaced with new crystals to ring in 2027 with a theme yet to be announced. It takes about three days to make each crystal by hand for the roughly 12-foot (3.7-meter) geodesic sphere that weighs 12,350 pounds (5,602 kilograms). The process involves the design, molding, kilning and the finishing of each crystal. Waterford, a longtime luxury crystal brand from Ireland, has designed the New Year’s Eve ball’s crystals for over 25 years. Some new crystals are swapped in every year. Richard White, a master cutter for Waterford, flew to New York City to engrave the crystals that vary in size from 1.5 to 4 inches in diameter. White will use a small electronic pen with a diamond tip to engrave names on the small crystal pieces Thursday. “To be actually here and to be up close, personal with it, is a real excitement for me,” White said of seeing the completed ball. Delfin Ortiz, general manager and senior vice president of One Times Square, the 26-story building from which the annual ball drops, said the crystals are part of “tomorrow's history.” Baby buried alive for 24 hours released from the hospital; father charged House tables Hegseth impeachment, effectively killing it in current Congress Wisconsin state trooper detained by ICE A New Year’s Eve ball was first dropped in Times Square in 1907. Built by a young immigrant metalworker named Jacob Starr, the 700-pound (318-kilogram), 5-foot (1.52-meter) diameter ball was made of iron and wood and featured 100 25-watt light bulbs. Nine versions of the ball have been featured in the century-plus since that first celebration. The only years no ball drop occurred were 1942 and 1943, when the city instituted a nightly “dimout” during World War II to protect itself from attacks. Crowds instead celebrated the new year with a moment of silence followed by chimes rung from the base of One Times Square. One Times Square began offering crystals for purchase last year, though Thursday marks the first time they will be engraved. The prices of the crystals range between $140 and $195, depending on the size. events.title: Only four government ministers have saved money this year. Here's who
events.summary: News Home Just In For You Analysis Rural Watch Live Health Indigenous Politics Science Deep Time Elections World Environment Investigations Business Local news Quizzes Sport AFL NRL Football Tennis Cricket Netball Lifestyle Wellbeing Relationships & Family Food & Recipes Personal Finance Home & Garden Entertainment TV & Movies Books Music Pop Culture Arts Only four ministers have achieved net savings this year, budget papers show Jim Chalmers and Katy Gallagher have flagged further savings in the mid-year budget update. ( ABC News: Callum Flinn ) Four federal ministers have achieved net savings in their portfolios this financial year, according to ABC analysis of the May budget. The most significant savings were in the infrastructure portfolio. The government is searching for savings ahead of the mid-year budget update, but has not committed to a net save. Only four out of more than 20 government ministers have managed to save more than they have spent this year, pointing to challenges across the board as the cabinet works to rein in spending. Stung by the accusation from the opposition and some commentators that the federal budget is worsening inflation and fuelling interest rate hikes, ministers have indicated they are searching for fresh savings ahead of December's budget update. Finance Minister Katy Gallagher has indicated the government is looking "across the board" for savings, but has declined to commit to a "net" saving — that is, big enough to offset any new spending. A net save of $8.2 billion was achieved in the May budget, measured over the full five years of budget forecasts. But the government failed to achieve a net save for this financial year, when inflation pressure is most acute. Looking at this year alone, the government spent $8.7 billion more than it saved. It also raised an extra $2.2 billion in revenue, meaning the budget was $6.5 worse off overall. Only Infrastructure Minister Catherine King, Education Minister Jason Clare, Agriculture Minister Julie Collins and Treasurer Jim Chalmers achieved net savings for the 2026-27 financial year, according to an ABC analysis of budget papers. Of these, only Ms King's portfolio had substantial net savings with $1.3 billion overall, mostly from the decision not to proceed with programs including Inland Rail. The largest net spend for 2026-27 was Health Minister Mark Butler, whose total includes measures the government describes as "unavoidable", including the listing of new PBS medicines and a major hospitals deal. This was despite some savings from the NDIS and the private health insurance rebate for older Australians, which is yet to win support in parliament. Defence Minister Richard Marles and Finance Minister Katy Gallagher, whose responsibilities include Services Australia, both spent in excess of $1 billion. Catherine King achieved the largest net save this year, with nearly $1 billion. ( ABC News: Matt Roberts ) The government has offered few specifics about areas it will target for mid-year budget savings, but Senator Gallagher confirmed last week the public service would be subject to "belt tightening". The Albanese government has overseen a significant expansion in public service headcount, from 173,558 before it came to office to 217,256 as of May, spread across multiple portfolios. The largest individual increases were the National Disability Insurance Agency (more than 5,000 new staff) and Services Australia (more than 4,000). Labor fought former Liberal leader Peter Dutton's bid to reverse that increase during the 2025 election campaign, but has made quiet moves of its own to contain public service spending since then. Peter Dutton campaigned unsuccessfully to return public service numbers to their pre-pandemic levels. ( ABC News: Matt Roberts ) In 2024, it opted not to give departments any extra money to cover the wage rises in a new pay agreement worth 11.2 per cent over three years. That effectively required departments to find 11.2 per cent of savings elsewhere. Several subsequently offered redundancy rounds last financial year, with at least 1,500 redundancies confirmed but an exhaustive tally not yet available. But an ABC analysis of budget papers show departmental staffing costs still increased by $792 million last year, only partly offset by a $687 million reduction in "supplier" costs, such as consultants. Annual reports indicate further cost overruns are likely. Government won't promise net savings Finance Minister Katy Gallagher says growing pressures on the federal budget mean the government cannot promise it will find overall savings in its December update, even as Australians brace for another interest rate rise amid ongoing high inflation. Earlier this year, ministers asked all departments and agencies to identify five per cent of their resourcing that was "low priority". Senator Gallagher emphasised at the time that this was meant as a savings shortlist, not as a five per cent overall cut.

events.title: ‘A dark day for Nvidia’: Here’s what analysts have been saying about Jensen Huang’s departure
events.summary: Global markets reacted to news of Jensen Huang's resignation from his role as CEO of Nvidia. The company's board convened Wednesday evening after reports emerged of Huang engaging in a second extramarital affair, this time with an employee. Before the decision, one analyst said Huang was "toast," while another described the developments as "a dark day for Nvidia." Nvidia investors are preparing for a future without Jensen Huang after the CEO's resignation was announced on Thursday. Markets were on tenterhooks ahead of the decision amid reports that the chip giant's board had convened to discuss his future with the company. By the time of the announcement, at least six analysts had downgraded the stock between Wednesday night and Thursday morning. The New York Times on Wednesday reported that Huang had engaged in a second extramarital affair with an employee. The CEO was already under scrutiny after Huang admitted to having a romantic relationship with a woman U.S. intelligence believes is a Chinese spy. Nvidia announced on Thursday morning that, following a board meeting, Huang would step down after more than 30 years at the company's helm. CFO Colette Kress has been named interim CEO. Those downgrading the stock included longtime Nvidia bull Ben Reitzes of Melius Research. Nvidia shares were seen down more than 12% shortly after the open on Wall Street, bringing losses for the last month close to 25%. Here's what analysts and investors are saying about the company and the stock. Reitzes changed his rating for Nvidia to hold from buy. His price target is now $185 — down from $315 — is 6% above the level at which shares last closed. "We thought we had experience, but nothing prepares you for what has happened at Nvidia over the last few weeks - and especially since Saturday. The only situation remotely close to this we can recall was HP in 2010. Waiting to see what that Board would do (and who they would hire) that time didn't work out. It was really cheap, too, at ~9x EPS right after its initial swoon. Nvidia is a much stronger, more important company, but its market moves far faster, and this story touches geopolitical flashpoints. In this unique crisis, we have decided (reluctantly) to step aside on Nvidia (now a Hold) after recommending it since we launched our AI platform coverage universe in July 2023," he said. Analyst Mark Lipacis downgraded Nvidia to in line from outperform. He also lowered his price target on shares to $186 from $465, implying 7% upside from Wednesday's close. "The Wall Street Journal reported Nvidia's Board was 'preparing to oust' its CEO after he had two extramarital affairs, including one with a suspected Chinese spy. The NY Times reported that Nvidia's Board hired law firm Wachtell Lipton to lead an investigation into the matter. While Nvidia's Board said that it 'has no reason to believe that either national security or Nvidia secrets were compromised,' we believe that the investigation will take time and we expect NVDA's P/E multiple will continue to compress consistent with our 'Late-Innings of the Semi Cycle' thesis, especially since Nvidia has no obvious succession plan or number 2 operational executive," he said. William Blair's Sebastien Naji downgraded Nvidia to market perform from outperform. "After a head-spinning week of news and allegations around CEO Jensen Huang, Nvidia's board is reportedly preparing to remove him, according to the Wall Street Journal. The full story will take time to emerge and may require several investigations, including the board's own independent probe and a requested U.S. House briefing. What is already clear is that Huang's likely departure and heightened scrutiny of the company will be a significant overhang on NVDA shares in the near term. Meanwhile, the potential for a slower AI buildout and more intense competition from other chipmakers will only add to execution risk...governance and regulatory pressure, the potential for more serious fallout, and a sudden change in management are likely to muddle both execution and sentiment. As a result, we are downgrading NVDA to Market Perform and will wait for the dust to settle before reassessing," he said. Analyst Rick Schafer downgraded the AI stock to perform from outperform. "We are downgrading shares of NVDA and removing our price target following reports (WSJ, NYT) of founding CEO Jensen Huang's imminent departure amidst allegations of a 2nd extramarital affair. Credible media reports circulated Wednesday evening that NVDA's board is preparing to part ways with Huang following a widely reported relationship with an alleged Chinese spy compounded by new allegations of a relationship with an NVDA executive. This 'one-two' punch appears to have forced the board's hand...While we see upside to the F3Q (Oct.) print and F4Q (Jan.) outlook, we expect fundamentals to take a backseat near term. The departure of Mr. Huang could, in our view, translate to a lingering share overhang," he said.

events.title: Why did Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang resign, and who is Colette Kress?
events.summary: Huang has stepped down amid revelations about extramarital affairs and allegations of Chinese espionage. Jensen Huang resigns as Nvidia CEO as affairs raise security concerns Nvidia chief executive Jensen Huang has resigned following revelations that he had two extramarital affairs. Nvidia’s chief financial officer, Colette Kress, has taken over as interim CEO while the company looks for a permanent replacement. list 1 of 2 Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang steps down, more affair details revealed list 2 of 2 Trump heads to China amid Nvidia scandal: Will he get tougher on Beijing? The company controls an estimated 90 percent of the market for advanced artificial intelligence (AI) chips and is one of the world’s most valuable companies. Why did Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang resign? Huang stepped down on Thursday following several days of intense scrutiny over his personal relationships and potential national security issues. On Sunday, Huang admitted to being unfaithful to his wife and apologised to his family and to Nvidia employees. Huang moved to the United States from Taiwan as a child. His wife, Lori, has been with him since before he cofounded Nvidia in 1993. Nvidia’s board initially backed Huang, saying on Sunday that it had confidence in his leadership. It also launched an independent investigation into reports that he had been targeted by Chinese intelligence. But on Wednesday, the Reuters news agency reported the board was meeting to consider whether to remove him following further revelations of a relationship with Kimberly Powell, a senior Nvidia executive who reported directly to him. The company announced his resignation on Thursday. Huang also resigned from the board, ending his 33-year tenure as chief executive. Nvidia didn’t give a reason for his departure. “Jensen’s contributions to Nvidia are profound,” the board said in a statement, thanking him for his “immeasurable contributions to the company and the industry”. What are the allegations involving Jensen Huang? The allegations were related to reported extramarital affairs. The first involved Alice Huang, a former executive at Singapore-based tech company Megaspeed, who is alleged to have worked for Chinese intelligence. The allegations have raised questions about national security, particularly given Huang’s support for allowing Nvidia to sell advanced AI chips to China. Separately, The New York Times reported on Wednesday that Huang had an affair with Powell, Nvidia’s vice president of healthcare, who reported directly to him. The second reported relationship raised concerns about a potential conflict of interest involving a senior executive. Why are there national security concerns? The controversy comes amid a debate in Washington over exporting advanced US AI chips to China. Huang, 63, spent years campaigning against the restrictions on Nvidia chip sales to China. In December 2025, President Donald Trump approved the export of Nvidia’s H200 chips to China, despite concerns that the technology could bolster Beijing’s AI capabilities. The chips are about six times more powerful than the H20 models previously available to Chinese buyers. Exports are subject to US inspections, limits on shipments, restrictions on military use and a 25 percent tariff. According to Al Jazeera’s Osama Bin Javaid, Chinese companies reportedly ordered more than two million H200 chips, potentially worth $54bn. “Worth remembering it’s orders, not completed sales,” he said. Critics are concerned the technology could help China close the AI gap with the US. The allegations raised questions about whether his personal relationships could have exposed sensitive information. “There is no established evidence he knowingly assisted Beijing or that company secrets were compromised,” Bin Javaid noted. Nvidia’s board has also said it has no reason to believe national security was compromised. Who is Colette Kress, Nvidia’s new interim CEO? Kress has served as Nvidia’s chief financial officer since September 2013 and oversaw the chipmaker’s finances during a period of growth. During her time at Nvidia, the company’s annual revenue rose from $4.13bn in fiscal 2014 to $215.9bn in fiscal 2026. Before joining Nvidia, Kress held senior finance roles at Texas Instruments, Microsoft and Cisco. She holds a bachelor’s degree in finance from the University of Arizona and an MBA from Southern Methodist University. Kress is also among America’s wealthiest self-made women, according to Forbes. In a statement following her appointment, Kress said she was committed to building on the foundation Huang had created over the past 33 years. Will Colette Kress become Nvidia’s permanent CEO? Nvidia’s board has appointed Kress as interim CEO while it searches for a permanent replacement and considers both internal and external candidates. Trump has suggested former Apple chief executive Tim Cook as Huang’s successor.

events.title: Nvidia stock pares morning losses after CEO Jensen Huang announces resignation
events.summary: Nvidia’s stock plunged after CEO Jensen Huang announced his resignation. Chief Financial Officer Colette Kress will serve as interim CEO until a new leader is appointed. Harvey C. Jones, former CEO of Synopsys, will become the first-ever chair of the board. Follow CNBC's live coverage of Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang's resignation here. Nvidia shares were trading down 5% on Thursday after Jensen Huang announced he would immediately step down as CEO and a member of the board at the chipmaker. The stock hovered just under $4 trillion in market cap, after paring steeper losses earlier in the day of as much as 14%. Nvidia has closed above the market cap benchmark since July 2025. Chief Financial Officer Colette Kress will serve as interim CEO until a new leader is appointed, Nvidia said in a Thursday statement. Harvey C. Jones, former CEO of Synopsys, will become the first-ever chair of the board. On Sunday, Huang admitted to having an affair . The CEO was romantically involved with Alice Huang, an executive at cloud company Megaspeed , according to The Financial Times , who U.S. intelligence officials believe is a spy for China. The New York Times on Wednesday reported that Huang had another extramarital relationship with Kimberly Powell, vice president of health care at Nvidia. Powell reports to Huang, according to the Times. Before Huang resigned, several Wall Street analysts told CNBC that this departure could lead the stock to fall 20%, given how critical he has been to Nvidia's success. Nvidia's stock is already down more than 20% over the last month. Bernstein on Thursday slashed its price target on Nvidia's stock by half from $400 to $200. Stacy Rasgon, a senior analyst at Bernstein, told CNBC's "Squawk Box Asia" on Thursday that Huang's alleged affair with a direct report means it is "much tougher for the board to leave him in position." Huang was central to Nvidia's rise, having co-founded the company in 1993 and was pivotal in transforming Nvidia from a gaming hardware player to the company at the center of the artificial intelligence boom. Rasgon said it is unclear who could be the "visionary" to lead Nvidia into the future as new CEO. "Jensen is Nvidia, right? He is the visionary. The reason they're in the position that they're in today is because he made decisions 10 years ago," Rasgon said. "Who is the right person now to make the decisions for the next 10 years? I don't intuitively know who that person would be." Earlier, U.S. lawmakers had called for Huang's resignation , adding further pressure to the CEO and the company. Richard Reyle, chief investment officer at Questar Capital Partners, said Nvidia's lack of a succession plan makes the stock "uninvestable." "Nvidia doesn't have that person in place, and so it's going to be either a choice of keeping Jensen and being faced with months and months of being hauled in front of probably congressional boards and things to explain themselves and all kinds of interrogations," Reyle told CNBC's "Access Middle East." "Or they're going to have to move on from him, and that's just going to make the stock uninvestable. That doesn't make the AI trade uninvestable, but it certainly makes Nvidia uninvestable." — CNBC's Caleigh Keating contributed to this report. events.title: Here's what Nvidia interim CEO Colette Kress and board chair Harvey Jones wrote to Nvidia employees
events.summary: After Jensen Huang's announced resignation, interim CEO Colette Kress and board chair Harvey Jones sent emails to Nvidia employees. Kress said she "believed deeply" in Nvidia's future. "The Board has full confidence in Colette to deliver on our commitments to shareholders, customers, partners, and to each of you," Jones wrote. On the heels of founder Jensen Huang's resignation as CEO of Nvidia , new interim CEO Colette Kress and board chair Harvey Jones sent emails to employees Thursday expressing gratitude and optimism for the future. CNBC obtained copies of the emails from a source familiar with the matter, who said Jones sent the first email and Kress replied shortly after. Follow CNBC's live coverage of Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang's resignation "The Board, Estaff and I recognize that this has been an extraordinarily difficult period and I want you to know how grateful we are for your resilience, professionalism and continued dedication," Kress wrote in her email. The term Estaff is commonly used to refer to executive staff, the group of direct reports to C-suite executives at a company. Nvidia will host a company meeting on November 18 at 9am PST, her email said. Board chair Jones took a similar tone in his email, and praised Kress as "a key architect of NVIDIA's growth and capital strategy." Below are the staff emails obtained by CNBC on Thursday. I believe deeply in this company and in its future. More than anything, I believe in each of you, in our customers and partners and in the vital role we play every day in the global economy. The Board, Estaff and I recognize that this has been an extraordinarily difficult period and I want you to know how grateful we are for your resilience, professionalism and continued dedication. Thank you. This company has achieved so much because of the work that all of you bring to it every single day. You are our greatest strength. You will hear more from leadership in the coming days about our future together, and we will host a company meeting on November 18 at 9am PT. We play a vital role in building the technology that is powering the AI revolution, and we have important work ahead of us. So let's move forward together, with the same determination and commitment that have always defined this company. I am writing to share an important update. Jensen has resigned as CEO and Board Member, and the Board has asked our Chief Financial Officer Colette Kress to serve as interim CEO while it conducts a search for a permanent successor looking at both internal and external candidates. I will serve as the first-ever Chair of the Board. As CFO for over 13 years, Colette has been a key architect of NVIDIA's growth and capital strategy. She possesses a deep understanding of this business and the markets in which we operate. The Board has full confidence in Colette to deliver on our commitments to shareholders, customers, partners, and to each of you. Jensen's contributions to NVIDIA are profound. NVIDIA is one of the most consequential technology companies in the world. We pioneered accelerated computing, defined the modern GPU, and built the platform that powered artificial intelligence. The Board takes seriously our duty as stewards of this great company. The strength of this company resides in our employees, leadership team, technical strength and partner ecosystem. I am confident that under Colette's leadership, with the full support of the Board, we will continue to grow our business, and lead the industry forward. Thank you for your focus, your professionalism, and your commitment to NVIDIA. events.title: Nvidia’s Jensen Huang to testify to US Congress amid scandal, reports say, as CFO Colette Kress replaces him as interim CEO – follow live
events.summary: Jensen Huang resigns as Nvidia CEO - at a glance Jensen Huang resigned on Thursday as chief executive of Nvidia after reports of extramarital affairs with an alleged Chinese spy and a company employee , bookending a stunning fall from grace of one of the leading figures of the AI boom. He will be replaced on an interim basis by Nvidia’s chief financial officer, Colette Kress, until a full-time successor is named. A statement from Nvidia’s board of directors confirming Huang’s departure did not mention the spying scandal and personal conduct revelations, instead paying tribute to Huang’s “profound” contributions to the company he co-founded. “Jensen’s contributions to Nvidia are profound. Nvidia is one of the most consequential technology companies in the world. The board and the company thank Jensen for his immeasurable contributions to the company and the industry,” the statement said. It added that Huang had resigned as chief executive, president and Nvidia board member “effective immediately”. Donald Trump, who had defended Huang at first as the scandal threatened to overwhelm Nvidia co-founder, quickly moved on to potential successors on Thursday, posting on social media that he should be replaced by Tim Cook, Apple’s former chief executive and current executive chair. “NOW THAT Nvidia CEO JENSEN HUANG, who has done a fantastic job, has resigned, there is only one man to take his place – TIM COOK of Apple,” Trump wrote, adding: “A Legend replaces a Legend!” Nvidia’s board directors said it would consider internal and external candidates for the chief executive role, with Cook featuring among potential runners and riders before Trump’s intervention. Rene Haas, the chief executive of Arm Holdings, a UK-based chipmaker, has also been mooted, along with Lisa Su, the chief executive of the chipmaker AMD. In the US, the Democratic House minority leader – expected to become speaker in the next Congress – Hakeem Jeffries said lawmakers should receive a classified briefing on the scandal. “We need a classified briefing made available to members of Congress as it relates to the Nvidia situation and to the extent that our national security has been compromised,” Jeffries said at his ongoing press conference. “The American people deserve answers, and we’re going to work to make sure that happens.” 2h ago Jensen Huang resigns as Nvidia CEO - at a glance 3h ago From washing dishes at Denny’s to rockstar of AI: the rise and fall of Nvidia’s Jensen Huang 4h ago Trump says former Apple CEO Cook should replace Huang at Nvidia 6h ago Nvidia's value has slumped by $888bn this week 6h ago Nvidia shares now down 10% in premarket trading 6h ago Nvidia shares plunge 10%; board pays tribute to Huang and appoints first-ever chair 6h ago Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang resigns over scandal, replaced by CFO Colette Kress on interim basis 6h ago US trade representative says US 'remains concerned' about Nvidia 7h ago Wall Street to open lower with tech shares seen sliding 7h ago Chinese AI companies rush to secure Nvidia chip capacity 7h ago Megaspeed says 'committed to working constructively and transparently with US government' 12h ago Who could potentially replace Jensen Huang if Nvidia ousts him? 13h ago Nvidia shares plunge nearly 9% in pre-market trading, reverberating across Asian markets 15h ago Opinion: Nvidia’s board needs to do some succession planning – sharpish 16h ago Why is Nvidia so important to the AI sector? 18h ago Nvidia share price plunges 8% in after-hours trade 18h ago Jensen Huang's future rests in the balance as Nvidia board reportedly meet Ousted Nvidia CEO Jensen ‌Huang had an intimate relationship with a second employee, two people familiar ​with the matter have told Reuters. The revelation follows two other extramarital ⁠affairs that led to his dramatic resignation ​today, one with Alice Huang, ​who US intelligence suspects of being a Chinese spy, and another with Kimberly Powell, Nvidia’s vice-president of health care. Reuters is not ​naming the second employee. Attempts to reach the ‌woman ⁠were not successful. Nvidia declined to comment for Reuters’ story. The Trump administration faces an investigation of its scheme to take a 15% cut from any Nvidia chip sales going to China , as part of a deal to secure export licenses for the semiconductors. Under the scheme, Nvidia chips made in Taiwan could be sold to Chinese companies if they were imported to the US first for a security review. This also made them subject to a 25% tariff under section 232 of the Trade Expansion Act of 1962, which was aimed at dealing with imports that threaten national security. The commerce secretary could then grant an export licence to sell the chips to China.

events.title: Jensen Huang's Nvidia exit casts shadow over Wall Street’s $500 billion AI financing bet
events.summary: Jensen Huang has resigned as Nvidia president, CEO and board member, the company's board said Thursday. The chip giant announced in August memorandums of understanding with six major financial firms aimed at mobilizing more than $500 billion for AI infrastructure. Huang's departure could see further scrutiny of those arrangements amid growing uncertainty over Nvidia's direction. Leadership change at Nvidia has the potential to threaten financing of the artificial intelligence boom and test Jensen Huang's $500 billion vision to turn AI chips into tradable debt securities. The Nvidia CEO's resignation was announced Thursday following revelations that he had two extramarital affairs — one with an employee and the other with a woman believed by U.S. intelligence to be a Chinese spy . Nvidia has never identified a successor to Huang, who has led the chipmaker since its founding in 1993. Colette Kress, chief financial officer, has been named interim CEO. Follow CNBC's live coverage of Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang's resignation The company has been dubbed the "central bank" of the AI build-out, with Huang seen as the "hypeman" for the sector and its chips considered the industry's gold standard. Huang's departure raises a central question: whether his successor can carry forward a financing strategy designed to transform GPUs from rapidly depreciating hardware into bankable infrastructure assets The $4.2 trillion firm's industry dominance, with Huang front and center, allowed it to sign memorandums of understanding with some of Wall Street's biggest asset managers, intended to secure third-party capital for a landmark $500 billion AI financing drive . The preliminary agreements, involving Apollo Global Management , BlackRock , Blackstone , Brookfield , Goldman Sachs, and KKR , sought to tap institutional investors and private capital to finance a range of computing infrastructure, including data centers and chip factories. The funding would involve specialized financing vehicles, with Nvidia's AI chips used as underlying collateral, in arrangements comparable to real estate or toll roads securitizations. The financing arrangements are still preliminary and subject to final agreements. BlackRock and Goldman Sachs declined to comment on today's resignation. The other firms weren't immediately available for comment. Nvidia live updates: Jensen Huang agrees to testify before Congress following resignation Who is Colette Kress? Nvidia's finance chief steps in as interim CEO after Huang exit PRO: Buy Nvidia with 'both hands' because the valuation is at 'stupid' levels, says analyst Meeks Read what interim CEO Kress and board chair Harvey Jones wrote to Nvidia employees Jensen Huang's exit from Nvidia raises critical questions about the future of AI Analysis: Nvidia's leadership crisis tests the chipmaker's role as the 'central bank of AI' The arrangements could now face heightened scrutiny in the aftermath of Huang's departure. Sunaina Sinha Haldea, global head of private capital advisory at Raymond James, said a leadership change gives every firm involved a "natural moment to pause and look at the terms again." "The best thing a new CEO can do is leave these partnerships alone in the first few months and focus on getting the final agreements signed," Haldea told CNBC via email. "Jensen brought these firms to the table with his vision, and any potential successor will keep them there by showing that the business behind that vision hasn't changed." She added: "I don't think the capital walks away, because these lenders are underwriting Nvidia's chips and the customer contracts behind them, but they could want to be paid more for the uncertainty." Charu Chanana, chief investment strategist at Saxo, said Huang's successor would need to reassure lenders that Nvidia's technology roadmap, customer relationships and strategic vision remain intact. "I wouldn't expect Nvidia's financing partnerships to unravel simply because Huang leaves, but a leadership shake-up could make Wall Street more cautious, potentially slowing commitments or tightening financing terms," Chanana told CNBC via email. "The bigger risk is a ripple effect across AI financing, particularly when rising debt, circular financing and uncertain investment returns were already under scrutiny," Chanana added. "This is not a financing crisis yet, but it could become a catalyst for a broader repricing of risk across the AI ecosystem." Haldea added that she expects to see more discipline among investors in the aftermath of the scandal. "Lenders will ask harder questions about who is really carrying the risk in these structures, and that scrutiny will spread throughout the AI infrastructure deal market."

events.title: Financial pain of outer suburbs fuelled demise of David Jones, experts say
events.summary: News Home Just In For You Analysis Rural Watch Live Health Indigenous Politics Science Deep Time Elections World Environment Investigations Business Local news Quizzes Sport AFL NRL Football Tennis Cricket Netball Lifestyle Wellbeing Relationships & Family Food & Recipes Personal Finance Home & Garden Entertainment TV & Movies Books Music Pop Culture Arts Economic pain of outer suburbs accelerated demise of David Jones, experts say Economic pain felt in outer suburban areas could have fast-tracked the problems that overtook David Jones. ( ABC News: Fletcher Yeung ) David Jones is closing 19 stores across Australia and New Zealand, with the majority to close in metropolitan outer suburbs. Property analyst Howard Penny says outer suburbs were disproportionately feeling mortgage stress. According to retail expert Gary Mortimer, a changing business model is forcing major suburban centres to adapt to survive. Acute economic pain being felt in the outer suburbs may have accelerated the demise of David Jones, according to property and retail experts. The 188-year-old shopping giant announced on Wednesday that it would close 19 stores across Australia and New Zealand, with the vast majority being in metropolitan outer suburban areas. Among those are stores in areas like Hornsby, Parramatta and Campbelltown in Sydney, Maribyrnong and Glen Waverley in Melbourne, and Robina on the Gold Coast. Howard Penny says retail challenges reflect negative consumer impacts in emerging areas. ( ABC News ) Howard Penny is the head of Real Estate and Infrastructure Research for Australia and New Zealand at Citigroup. He said that was a symptom of the financial strain in those areas after five interest rate hikes this year. S&P Global Ratings data this week revealed that households in some outer suburbs in Sydney, Melbourne and south-east Queensland are more than twice as likely to be experiencing mortgage stress than the national average. "It's new home buyers, it's young families, et cetera, and naturally the areas where these types of consumers are, are in the newer areas further out in the cities," Mr Penny said. The announcement has also raised questions about how large suburban shopping centres will fare losing a large anchor tenant. Nine of the stores that are closing are in Westfield shopping centres, owned by Scentre Group. Scentre had offered David Jones discounted rents to continue trading, after the department store stopped paying rent in September. Howard Penny said there was likely to be a short-term impact on Scentre Group, but that was unlikely to threaten the viability of its shopping centres in the outer suburbs. "Although we are, in the short term, a little concerned as to the short-term impacts on income and rent due to the disruption, in the medium term, we remain optimistic, and we believe that in 18 months, these shopping centres may actually look even stronger on the back of this," he said. After Wednesday's news, Scentre Group chief executive Eliott Rusanow was similarly confident. "Our business is practically full, with occupancy at 99.8 per cent and strong demand for space," Mr Rusanow said in a statement. "We have a unique opportunity at 17 Westfield destinations to introduce and grow local and international brands and experiences that our customers want." Gary Mortimer says the fall of David Jones comes as major suburban centres shift. ( Supplied: Gary Mortimer ) Gary Mortimer is a professor at the Queensland University of Technology who specialises in retail and marketing. He said the closures represent the changing business model of major suburban centres. "A big centre once might have included an anchor tenant, be that a department store, and possibly a discount department store and a supermarket," Professor Mortimer said. "Today, those centres have changed. Those centres are now underpinned by precincts: health precincts, services precincts, libraries, gyms, childcare, car wash facilities and a whole wide range of experiences and offers." He said the changes in the composition and socio-economic pressures in outer suburban areas require shopping centres to adapt to survive. "As the demography of those suburbs changes and the centre now is better representative of a Kmart, Target, Big W discount department store than a traditional department store, I think they'll have no problems filling that space," Dr Mortimer said.

events.title: Senegal’s wrestlers turn tradition into gold at Dakar Youth Olympics
events.summary: Senegal’s young wrestlers thrive as they adapt skills from their traditional sport to beach wrestling at Dakar’s Youth Olympics. She wasn’t even supposed to be there. Sixteen-year-old Elisabeth Diatta is from the southern Senegalese region of Casamance. Football was her sport, not wrestling. Yet, On Saturday, there she was on the sand at Saly beach, representing Senegal in beach wrestling at Dakar’s Youth Olympics , almost instinctively seizing her opponent and throwing her down. Then came the whistle, the referee’s look, the confirmation, the disbelief. She celebrated like Cristiano Ronaldo; the leap, the turn, the “Siu!” At 16, she had beaten Japan’s Reisa Kojima 5-1 in the 55kg final to win Senegal’s first Youth Olympic gold. A teenage girl had delivered a medal in a sport so often described as belonging to men. The crowd roared. Diatta danced, defiant, before wrapping herself in green, yellow and red. Beneath the Senegalese flag’s green star, a new star was born. Her path here began when her older sister Jeannine was injured and could not enter a wrestling tournament at a sport camp. Diatta took her place. She won her first bout. The footballer kept wrestling. “They said wrestling would make me less feminine,” explains Diatta – the “they” she is referring to are the adults around here. Out of teenage defiance, she persisted in the sport. Watching proudly was coach Isabelle Sambou, twice an Olympian herself. She had wanted this gold for Senegal long before her young wrestlers were old enough to compete. “I wanted to win gold for Senegal when I was an athlete,” she said. “Today, I have my reward.” She would soon have another reason to celebrate as another Senegalese teenage hopeful, 16-year-old Maguette Diop, stepped into the wrestling circle later on Saturday. Diop had been preparing for this moment long before the games, being held from October 31 to November 13 in the Senegalese capital Dakar and nearby towns of Saly and Diamniadio. Three months in an intense training camp had helped Senegal’s young wrestlers adapt to beach wrestling, where the rules differed from those of their traditional sport. In traditional Senegalese wrestling, a wrestler wins by bringing their opponent to the ground, typically onto their back, buttocks or knees, or by forcing them onto all fours. Unlike beach wrestling, there is no points system. One decisive fall can end the contest. In beach wrestling, forcing an opponent outside the circle earns one point, as does a takedown. A throw onto the back earns three and ends the contest. Bouts last up to three minutes; the first to at least three points wins. Diop had spent months preparing for this moment. On August 27, he had lost to Iran’s Reza Jalilian in the semifinals of the under-17 world championships in Baku. Barely two months later, on home ground, he was not about to let that happen again. He reached the boys’ 80kg final feeling confident despite facing Azerbaijan’s Nihad Suleymanli, a two-time under-17 world champion. Suleymani wrestled with skill, ignoring the crowd cheering for Diop. For a moment, the gold appeared to be slipping away. The referee awarded Suleymanli three points. Diop’s coaches urged a challenge. The replay reversed the decision: Those points belonged to Diop. He had won 4-0. More dancing. More flags. Another Senegalese teenager with gold. Here, wrestling runs deep. Long before the Olympic flame reached this Atlantic coastline, generations had gathered around circles of sand. Laamb, Senegal’s traditional wrestling, carries the pride of villages and neighbourhoods. It is more than a contest of strength. Wrestlers seek spiritual protection through prayers, rituals and amulets believed to ward off evil spirits. All to the rhythm of sabar drums, traditional Senegalese percussion whose beats accompany the ceremonial dances, summoning courage and stirring the crowd. In Casamance, where Diatta comes from, women have long wrestled too, even as men dominate the professional arenas. “I hope this experience will give girls courage and determination,” said Ndeye Khady Anna Diatta, who added a third Senegalese gold in the 45kg category the following day. By Thursday, Senegal stood sixth in the medal table – three of their five golds won wrestling on the sand. For Africa, hosting its first Olympic sporting event, these victories offered something the rankings could not measure: young people seeing themselves in the athletes wearing gold, a familiar sport carrying them onto a world stage. And for the girls watching Senegal’s female wrestlers, perhaps something closer still. A place inside the circle.

events.title: Visa holders are delaying purchases and tuning out the news amid immigration uncertainty
events.summary: Immigration uncertainty is influencing some visa holders' decisions about jobs, major purchases, and their futures in the US. Namas Bhojani/Bloomberg via Getty Images Government and corporate immigration policy changes have raised concerns among tech visa holders. Some worry that fewer employers will sponsor foreign workers, making future job searches harder. Workers described how immigration uncertainty is affecting their careers and long-term plans. When Ashok Kumar lost his job in 2019, the H-1B visa holder had 60 days to find a new employer willing to sponsor him. He pulled it off, but he's worried his next job search could be even harder. This week, Business Insider reported that IBM is ending visa and green card sponsorship for most roles in its consulting division. The company cited evolving skill availability and client needs as reasons for the move. Kumar, a tech lead at a large corporation, said he's concerned that more companies could follow IBM's lead. He's among several tech visa holders who told Business Insider that immigration policy uncertainty and concerns about job security are influencing their career decisions and long-term plans. Some worry about their ability to stay in the US or find new jobs, while others remain focused on the opportunities available to them. IBM's decision comes amid other developments affecting foreign tech workers. In October, the Trump administration suspended Microsoft, Adobe, and six major IT services companies from the Permanent Labor Certification program, a key step in the employment-based green card process. The move prevents the companies from submitting new applications or moving forward with pending ones. The administration said the move was aimed at stopping companies from misusing the program to favor foreign workers over American workers. The administration has also sought to impose a $100,000 fee on new H-1B visas , though federal courts have blocked the measure. Kumar's employer wasn't among the companies suspended from the PERM program, but the news added to his concerns about the future of immigration sponsorship. He said friends he discussed it with shared similar concerns. "Everyone was worried about their future," he said Jacob Zinkula writes about how workers in tech and other industries are navigating their careers. Share your story with him by filling out this form , emailing him , or reaching out via Signal at jzinkula.29. Follow his work by clicking here . 'You can do everything right' One Microsoft employee is preparing for her final attempt at the H-1B visa lottery, but she's already worried about what comes next. The worker said she initially ignored Instagram reels that friends sent her about the October PERM suspension. When she finally watched one, she was shocked to learn that Microsoft was among the companies affected. Even if she's selected in the lottery, she worries that the PERM suspension could create another obstacle to securing a green card and staying in the US long-term. "You can do everything right, build a career at a company like Microsoft, and still not feel secure about your future here," she said. Microsoft has disputed the administration's allegations that it misused the visa system. For some foreign tech workers, the uncertainty extends beyond their careers. One tech worker on an F-1 STEM OPT visa said he's delayed buying a car because he doesn't know how long he'll be able to remain in the US. He also raised the possibility of moving to another country, such as Canada or the UK. "My friends are indeed panicking and getting restless," he said. Different reactions to immigration uncertainty Not every foreign tech worker is equally concerned about their immigration future. Some pointed to the fact that the PERM suspension currently affects only a handful of companies. One Big Tech visa holder said he's not too concerned because he doesn't have long-term immigration plans in the US. Others have tried to tune out immigration news altogether. "It's exhausting to follow everything so I'm staying away from all of it," one tech visa holder said. For Aman Goyal, a product manager on an H-1B visa, the uncertainty hasn't outweighed the opportunities he sees in the US. Goyal, who came to the US in 2023, considered looking for work abroad after being laid off last year but ultimately landed a new role based in the Seattle area. He said visa challenges remain a concern as he considers his long-term future in the country, but he wants to make the most of his time in the US. "I'm definitely interested in continuing to be here, meeting and building my network as much as possible, as well as learning about the next phases of AI as much as possible," he said.
