events.title: Google’s latest Search upgrade promises better answers to your most complicated questions
events.summary: Google Search is getting better at understanding complicated questions, including those with multiple parts, highly specific requests, or confusing typos. The updates are coming via the company’s newly released Gemini 4 Hydrogen model, which Google claims is its “biggest model improvement to Search yet.” While Google’s frontier models, Gemini 4 Carbon and Gemini 4 Argon, are best at deep reasoning for hard problems, Hydrogen is designed for fast execution across a variety of agentic workflows, or tasks in which an AI carries out multiple steps on its own, the company explained in an announcement. The idea behind the model’s release is that using the most powerful model isn’t always needed — sometimes a faster, cheaper, and reasonably smart one will do. Google says Hydrogen completes tasks 2.5 times faster than Gemini 3.8 Flash, its previous fast model, but it’s still pretty smart, even beating the more powerful Gemini 4 Argon on one broad intelligence benchmark, the Artificial Analysis Intelligence Index , at its default high thinking level. In Search, Hydrogen brings several improvements, including a better understanding of user intent, the ability to offer more helpful links and visual responses, and better answers across the different languages supported by Google’s AI Mode. In terms of intent, Google says Hydrogen can handle more nuanced and complicated questions more quickly. This means people can ask their questions in their natural train of thought, including those that have multiple parts or that include highly specific requests. Hydrogen is also better at navigating hard-to-understand typos, Google says. Because of its improvements and better ability to follow instructions and call the right tools, Hydrogen is able to more precisely address each part of a user’s question. Its advanced reasoning also improves Search’s fan-out technique, which breaks down a single user’s prompt into multiple subqueries. This allows people to discover websites related to the query that they may have otherwise missed, the blog post explains. The addition of Hydrogen to Search will also mean more images, structured responses, comparison tables, and custom tools will appear as visual responses to users’ queries in AI Mode. Google also says Hydrogen can work on its own for everyday work in areas like writing code, running tests, or verifying code changes, or it can be paired with Carbon and Argon in workflows that combine several models. The model offers four thinking levels: low, medium, high (default), and a new, extra-high tier (“xhigh”), all of which are designed to complete tasks faster with fewer output tokens. On multi-step tasks like deep research, data analysis, and broad codebase navigation, Hydrogen ranks No. 5 on Agent Arena’s benchmarks, the company pointed out. In addition to Search, Gemini 4 Hydrogen is coming to all tiers of Google’s AI Studio, the Gemini API, the Gemini App, and the paid AI Pro and Ultra subscribers in Google’s Antigravity development platform. events.title: I'm a millionaire in California who supports taxing the rich. I'm disappointed Prop. 40 was rejected — people will suffer.
events.summary: Scott Ellis is a Silicon Valley-based millionaire who supports the taxation of the wealthy. Patriotic Millionaires Scott Ellis is a millionaire in Silicon Valley who supported a proposed wealth tax on billionaires . After the proposition was rejected by Californians this week, Ellis was disappointed but not surprised. He said he's glad it's started important conversations about wealth, and hopes for future efforts. This as-told-to essay is based on conversations with Scott Ellis, a 56-year-old millionaire who lives in Silicon Valley, about Proposition 40, California's proposed 5% billionaire wealth tax , which was rejected by California voters on November 9. Ellis is a member of Patriotic Millionaires, a group of wealthy Americans who advocate for a fair tax system, a livable wage, and equal access to political power. The following has been edited for length and clarity. (Editor's note: This article was first published in January 2026 and updated on November 12, 2026.) I'm disappointed, but I'm not surprised. The reality is that if people spend over $300 million opposing something and people spend about $30 million in favor, you get outspent by 10:1. That does matter. It was a big task to get it on the ballot in the first place, and I was really delighted that it was, because it at least started us on what I think is the right conversation: Let's talk about wealth. How much wealth do people have? Is there such a thing as too much? What should we do when people have too much? I've been talking about wealth and excessive wealth for a number of years. I feel like a few years ago, people were kind of humoring me. They're listening much more seriously now. There are conversations in my group chats with friends about wealth and wealth taxes. The conditions that led to this in the first place haven't suddenly gone away, and they will get worse. The massive federal funding cuts are working their way through states and local communities. There are tens of millions of voters in California who don't have a billion dollars. They're the ones who chose to do this, and I hope they're watching. I think it should be interesting for people to see how the wealthy responded. When I think about my concern about excessive wealth and how it distorts democracy and undermines our society, you couldn't ask for a clearer example than Sergey Brin spending over $100 million in one state election. The question I ask everybody is, "Are you worried?" I'm worried about the health of our economy, our society, our democracy. But I'm going to be fine — I've been very financially fortunate. events.title: Nectar launches an AI agent to automate creator discovery and outreach for brands
events.summary: Nectar , an AI-powered operating system for marketing, is launching a new AI agent designed to take a lot of the manual work out of influencer marketing, from finding the right creators to contacting them, managing partnerships, and tracking results. Founded by sisters Misbah and Farah Uraizee, both former Meta employees, Nectar came out of stealth last year and uses AI agents to help brands manage social media, customer conversations, content moderation, creator partnerships, and competitor research. Announced Thursday, its new “Creator Agent” can search for creators, check their content and brand partnerships, send personalized messages, coordinate collaborations, and monitor how campaigns perform. Instead of having marketing teams spend weeks scrolling through social media, building spreadsheets, and sending individual DMs, Nectar wants its agent to handle much of that work automatically. Nectar joins other companies introducing agentic AI assistants designed to automate influencer outreach, including Aspire and GRIN . The launch also comes as more brands turn to creators to reach customers. U.S. spending on creator advertising is expected to reach $44 billion in 2026, according to the Interactive Advertising Bureau . As companies work with hundreds or even thousands of creators, keeping track of relationships and measuring results can get pretty difficult. Nectar says its Creator Agent searches more than 300 million creator profiles to find potential partners, including smaller creators who may not yet have a large following but are gaining traction. The system analyzes videos to understand what creators post about, how their content fits a brand, and whether their previous partnerships are appropriate. It also checks brand safety by reviewing content in context rather than simply searching for specific keywords. Nectar then creates ranked lists of recommendations and adds new matches as creators become more popular. Once it finds a potential match, the agent can draft and send messages in a brand’s voice, create custom landing pages to collect creator information, and help manage contracts, product gifting, and shipping details. It also remembers previous conversations and interactions, so brands can keep track of relationships without relying on spreadsheets. “Brands can share voice guidelines in any format, and Nectar picks up the rest from their history,” CEO Misbah Uraizee tells TechCrunch. “On top of that sits a set of proprietary guardrails that keep every draft on tone and in context. Nectar understands what is being said in a video, reads the tone of the conversation, and knows the difference between a quote post on X and a TikTok comment section. A brand should not sound identical in both, and with Nectar it doesn’t.” Another feature looks for personal milestones in creators’ lives, such as an engagement, a new baby, or completing a marathon. The agent can then suggest a personalized message or gift, helping brands build relationships that feel less like one-off advertising deals. Creator Agent is available today globally and covers Instagram creators and TikTokers. The company plans to make the agent available through its Model Context Protocol (MCP), allowing teams to use it through AI assistants such as Claude, ChatGPT, Gemini, and Copilot, as well as their own custom-built agents. This past May, Nectar raised a $30 million Series A round led by Menlo Ventures and its Anthology Fund, which is a joint initiative launched with Anthropic. events.title: House Foreign Affairs chair: 'Very likely' chips restrictions make it into defense bill
events.summary: Rep. Brian Mast, R-Fla., talks with reporters outside the US Capitol. Tom Williams/CQ-Roll Call, Inc via Getty Images The chair of the House committee overseeing export controls says chip guardrails in a coming defense bill are likely. Rep. Brian Mast cast doubt on whether ousted Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang knew where his company's chips ended up. Mast is also pressing for Huang to testify soon about the scandal, Politico reported . House Foreign Affairs Chair Brian Mast said Thursday it is "very likely" a group of bills that would impose new guardrails on exports of advanced US chips to China will make it into a must-pass annual defense bill this year. The Florida Republican told reporters that the controversy involving Jensen Huang, who resigned as Nvidia's CEO earlier Thursday after revelations he had an extramarital relationship with a potential Chinese spy, has added momentum to the effort. "If he doesn't know who he's in bed with, he doesn't know where all the chips are going either, and we know that for a fact," said Mast, whose committee oversees export control policy. Lawmakers are discussing a trio of chip export control bills for the annual defense package, including the Chip Security Act , a measure that would crack down on smuggling by requiring advanced chips to contain location-verification mechanisms. Two other measures are in the mix as well. One would tighten restrictions on chip-making equipment and push foreign countries to match US restrictions. The other would give Congress a chance to review licenses for advanced sales of AI chips. President Donald Trump has been cool to the idea of tighter chip export restrictions and previously signed off on deals that allowed Nvidia to sell more of its high-end chips to China. Mast also said Thursday that he still has confidence in Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick, who is facing growing scrutiny over his handling of the Trump administration's chips policy. But he declined to say the same for a key Lutnick deputy, Jeffrey Kessler, who heads the Commerce Department bureau in charge of export controls. Asked if he has confidence in Kessler, chief of the Bureau of Industry and Security, Mast said: "I'm not going to answer that yes or no. It's something that — you know, he's been most granular on this level and a lot of things about where chips can and can't be sold to. That's been more of an argumentative dynamic." He also said he "absolutely" wants to investigate BIS' role in the Nvidia controversy. A BIS spokesperson did not immediately respond to a request for comment. Mast is pressing for Huang to testify soon about the scandal. "We want to see him basically in a week," Mast said. "Sooner rather than later." He is in talks with the former CEO's team, but didn't rule out a subpoena. Nvidia did not immediately respond to a request for comment. "If negotiations shut off and we don't think they're in good faith, OK, fine, do that," he said. "I'll just subpoena you for the next day. No big deal." events.title: In a policy switch, the Fed says its October 2027 meeting will not see a vote on interest rates
events.summary: The Federal Reserve won't vote on a potential interest-rate change at its October 2027 meeting. The Fed will have seven voting meetings next year, down from eight in 2026. The October session will be used for longer-term and bigger-picture discussions. The Federal Reserve won't vote on a potential interest-rate change at its October 2027 meeting, a departure that is part of a broader initiative from Chairman Kevin Warsh aimed at reducing the central bank's market footprint. According to an announcement Thursday, the rate-setting Federal Open Market Committee will set aside its Oct. 26-27 session for "the discussion of broad monetary policy strategy issues." Warsh announced the move at his news conference after the FOMC met in October, though he did not specify which meeting would be affected. In 2027, there will be seven voting meetings, with the October session set up as extra time for policy deliberation without a formal vote or post-meeting statement. The new calendar shows that the final meeting of the year will now take place in November. It had previously been set for December. Consumer prices rose more than expected in October, complicating Fed's inflation fight Fed Governor Waller opens door to possible half-point increase Consumers are showing signs of strain even as they keep spending 3 unexpected reasons the October jobs report was so strong "Now, what's the reasoning behind this change? To me, it's quite straightforward," the chairman said in explaining his rationale. "Getting policy right involves assessing near-term developments at timely, regular, and information-rich intervals." "But it's equally important we reserve time and space, as an intellectually diverse group, for strategic deliberations—for thinking anew about big questions, looking out over longer time horizons, focusing, as I say, on the left side of the decimal point," he said. Warsh has been critical of the Fed's prior communications strategy, saying policymakers spent too much time providing guidance on policy moves that handcuffed them when it came time to make decisions. Under typical practice, the Fed meets eight times a year, following with a vote on interest rates and then a news conference from the chair. Since Warsh took over, the post-meeting statement has been shortened dramatically. Moreover, the press question-and-answer sessions have been cut to around half an hour from their customary 45 minutes or so. Warsh said in October that the meeting schedule is another step in his plan to streamline communication. He indicated last month that the number of nonvoting meetings would increase to two in 2028. "I believe the setting of the meeting schedule and agenda is more than some administrative detail," he said. "It's an institutional choice, affecting the nature and the quality of our deliberations and, ultimately, the wisdom of our decisions. It's yet another change to get the conduct of monetary policy on the right track." The FOMC next meets Dec. 8-9. Its first meeting in 2027 will happen Jan. 26-27. events.title: Oil prices rise after Trump says no Iran deal needed: 'We've got their Strait'
events.summary: U.S. oil prices rose Thursday, as comments from President Donald Trump stoked worries that an end to the U.S.-Iran war was not in sight. Brent crude traded 1.9% higher at $94.48 per barrel. West Texas Intermediate futures were up 2% at $88.19 per barrel. "We don't need a deal with Iran. Those days have long since passed. We've got their money, Hundreds of Billions of Dollars, and we've got their Strait!" Trump said in a Truth Social post . Jeffrey Currie, founder of Real Macro and a widely followed forecaster on Wall Street, said oil prices in the near term will remain tame because there is now a substantial amount of volume coming out of the Middle East. However, he noted that sky-high insurance and tanker rates are keeping prices elevated on longer-dated oil futures contracts. "While it caps the prompt barrel, it does nothing to cheapen the next one, which is why you can't get bearish here nor can you get really bullish," said Currie to CNBC's "The Exchange." On the investing front, Currie said he still favors long-dated oil and the drilling and producer stocks. Thursday's moves come as oil prices have been under pressure after comments from Trump following the U.S. midterm elections eased fears of further strikes on Iran. WTI is down 16% in November, and Brent has lost 20%. Trump said Sunday that fresh attacks were highly unlikely as talks to end the conflict progressed, despite both ⁠countries reporting that shipping had been hit in or near the Strait of Hormuz. He also said further military action did not appear necessary "at this point," easing concerns about prolonged disruptions to Middle East oil supplies. John Kilduff, a partner at Again Capital, said investors may have been too quick to price in an end to the fighting. "The market may have gotten ahead of itself on pricing in a cessation of hostilities," Kilduff told CNBC. He warned that renewed doubts about a deal would push the security premium in oil prices higher. Trump's assertion that the U.S. controls the Strait of Hormuz could spur further Iranian attacks on shipping, increasing the risk of prolonged supply disruptions, according to Kilduff. "The President may be thinking that given enough time, the economic blockade of Iran will force them to either negotiate with the USA or result in a regime change as the Iranian economy collapses. The Iranians might have different ideas and continue to attack Middle East Infrastructure that results in higher prices and forces the President to the negotiating table," said Andy Lipow, president of Lipow Oil Associates. "In any event, it does not seem to me that either side's negotiating position has changed. Iran wants the blockade to end, sanctions to be lifted and a ceasefire including Lebanon to be declared. The USA wants Iran to get rid of its entire nuclear stockpile and allow free transit through the Strait of Hormuz," he said. —CNBC's Pippa Stevens contributed to the report.

events.title: Jensen and Lori Huang's Nvidia fortune is jointly controlled. How that makes things complicated now that he's resigned
events.summary: Huang and his wife Lori jointly own about 800 million Nvidia shares worth roughly $135 billion through a complex web of trusts and LLCs, according to SEC filings. Jensen Huang directly owns about 70 million shares valued at about $12 billion. While owning company stock through a trust is common among tech founders and CEOs, it’s less typical for a founder to have equal ownership with a spouse, tax experts say. A version of this article appeared in CNBC's Inside Wealth newsletter, a weekly guide to the high-net-worth investor and consumer. Sign up to receive future editions straight to your inbox. Jensen Huang's $140 billion stake in Nvidia is largely held by trusts that are co-owned with his wife, Lori, creating added uncertainty for the shares and his financial future following his resignation from the company, according to attorneys and SEC filings. Follow CNBC's live coverage of Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang's resignation Huang and his wife jointly own about 800 million Nvidia shares worth roughly $135 billion through a complex web of trusts and LLCs created for tax and estate planning purposes, according to SEC filings. Jensen Huang directly owns about 70 million shares valued at about $12 billion. While owning company stock through a trust is common among tech founders and CEOs, it's less typical for a founder to have equal ownership with a spouse, tax experts say. The arrangement further complicates Huang's sudden exit from the company, but could prove to be a stabilizing force for the shares, since the trusts make it more difficult for either Huang or his wife to quickly sell. "Each of Mr. Huang and his wife may be deemed to have shared beneficial ownership of, and to exercise shared voting and investment power over," according to an SEC filing. According to the filings, Jensen and Lori Huang own about 530 million shares as co-trustees of the Jen-Hsun and Lori Huang Living Trust, created in 1995. They're also co-trustees of the Huang 2012 Irrevocable Trust, which owns 31.4 million shares, and the Huang Irrevocable Remainder Trust, which owns 109 million shares. About 135 million shares are held by LLCs that have the Living Trust as the sole member, according to the filings. Nvidia live updates: Jensen Huang agrees to testify before Congress following resignation Who is Colette Kress? Nvidia's finance chief steps in as interim CEO after Huang exit PRO: Buy Nvidia with 'both hands' because the valuation is at 'stupid' levels, says analyst Meeks Read what interim CEO Kress and board chair Harvey Jones wrote to Nvidia employees Jensen Huang's exit from Nvidia raises critical questions about the future of AI Analysis: Nvidia's leadership crisis tests the chipmaker's role as the 'central bank of AI' Lori Huang is the president of the Jen-Hsun and Lori Huang Foundation, which owns 69 million shares and reported $9 billion in net assets in 2024, according to IRS filings. Each of the trust structures serves different tax or estate purposes, according to trust and estate attorneys. The living trust is likely a revocable marital trust, since it was created 10 years after the Huangs married and two years after Nvidia was founded in 1993. Attorneys say living trusts help couples avoid the potentially expensive and public probate process when one spouse dies. Many couples, for example, create living trusts for homes they purchase or other assets. The main tax benefit of living trusts is that when one spouse dies, the surviving spouse gets a step-up in basis for the entire trust's assets, rather than just their half, according to attorneys. While the rules of each living trust vary, attorneys say shares in the living trust can typically be sold or divided fairly easily in the case of a divorce. "It's like a joint checking account," said Kathleen Martone, partner at Varnum LLP. While the revocable trust would typically allow each of them to sell their shares, lawyers said it is common for executives or their trusts to have agreements with the company limiting the sale or transfer of shares to prevent large-scale liquidation. "In the event they divide shares in their revocable trust, there's probably transfer restrictions. He may have to hold them for her benefit, and she would get the monetary benefit of the shares but not voting or management rights," said Leslie Evans, partner at Withers. "He could retain the stock while Lori receives other assets or an equalization payment." The more complicated structures used by the Huangs, and the ones with the largest tax benefits, are the irrevocable trusts. The SEC filings state that "Mr Huang and his wife are co-trustees" of both trusts. With an irrevocable trust, the creator transfers ownership of an asset into the trust and the terms can't be changed without the consent of the beneficiaries or a court.

events.title: Salmon deaths at 'eye-watering' levels in Macquarie Harbour
events.summary: News Home Just In For You Analysis Rural Watch Live Health Indigenous Politics Science Deep Time Elections World Environment Investigations Business Local news Quizzes Sport AFL NRL Football Tennis Cricket Netball Lifestyle Wellbeing Relationships & Family Food & Recipes Personal Finance Home & Garden Entertainment TV & Movies Books Music Pop Culture Arts Mortality data for salmon farms in Macquarie Harbour revealed after RTI documents release Topic: Fishing and Aquaculture Industry The farmed salmon died over a 15-month period in Macquarie Harbour. ( Huon ) It's been revealed that almost 2,000 tonnes of salmon died in Macquarie Harbour over a 15-month period. Salmon Tasmania says it equates to about 8 per cent of fish farmed there during that time. The EPA is yet to issue new licences for companies to continue operating in the harbour. Almost 2,000 tonnes of farmed salmon died over a 15-month period in Macquarie Harbour on Tasmania's west coast, new data shows. The Environment Protection Authority's (EPA) mortality data was obtained by conservation group Environment Tasmania, which submitted the Right to Information (RTI) request in December last year. But it took until this week for the information to be made public after salmon companies sought reviews of the EPA's decision to release the data, as they are entitled to do under RTI laws. The EPA regulates 10 salmon leases in the harbour. ( Supplied: Tassal ) The data shows a total of 1,907 tonnes of farmed salmon died in the harbour between October 2024 and December 2025. "Salmon has no place in Macquarie Harbour," Environment Tasmania campaigner Jess Coughlan said. Industry group Salmon Tasmania said up to 9,500 tonnes of salmon can be farmed in the harbour each year under a feed cap. The mortality data was obtained by Environment Tasmania. ( Supplied: Tassal ) Environment Tasmania said this would infer about 15 per cent of the total maximum haul died over the 15-month period. But Salmon Tasmania chief executive John Whittington said the maximum tonnage could not be used to determine a "mortality rate". "Mortality is measured by counting the number of fish that died, not their weight," Dr Whittington said. The new figures come after a separate RTI in late 2024 showed a total of 1,149 tonnes of salmon had died over a seven-month period between September 2023 and March 2024. Monthly data on salmon deaths doesn't show locations Since 2025, the EPA has released monthly data showing the total tonnage of mortality among salmon farms across the state, but it is not broken down by location. Macquarie Harbour, which is the only habitat for the endangered Maugean skate , makes up only a small portion of the salmon industry's annual production across Tasmania. Dr Whittington said mortality was "unfortunately part of all livestock farming". He said there was no standard "mortality rate" for farmed salmon. Salmon Tasmania CEO John Whittington said mortality was measured by numbers of fish not weight. ( ABC News: Madeleine Rojahn ) "As with other forms of farming, survival rates or losses vary by year, location and season," Dr Whittington said. "Salmon growers employ a range of strategies to maintain fish health and maximise survivability, including selective breeding, vaccination, specialised diets and growing fish larger on land so they spend less time at sea." The new RTI data did not include details about what caused the deaths of the salmon. Salmon Tasmania said Macquarie Harbour was free of the bacterial disease that had caused other mass mortalities. ( ABC News: Sophie Zoellner ) But Dr Whittington said Macquarie Harbour was free of the bacterial disease that had caused mass mortality in salmon pens in other parts of the state. As such, he said the industry had not applied to use the antibiotic florfenicol in Macquarie Harbour. Ms Coughlan said there had been "near complete opacity surrounding operations where disease and mortality are concerned" in the harbour. The EPA regulates salmon farming at 10 leases within Macquarie Harbour. However, the environmental licences issued to the three salmon companies that operate there expired almost a year ago. A map showing the location of salmon farm licences in Macquarie Harbour. ( ABC News: Magie Khameneh ) Prior to the expiration, the companies applied for new licences, meaning they can continue to operate pending the outcome of their applications. The EPA told the ABC it was continuing to assess the environmental conditions in Macquarie Harbour to inform future regulatory decisions about salmon farming in the region. Three companies farm salmon in Macquarie Harbour. ( ABC News: Sophie Zoellner ) "The timing of a decision on the environmental licence renewals will be determined by the completion of the necessary assessment and scientific work. Tasmania's environment department is currently considering declaring the harbour a "critical habitat" for the Maugean skate.

events.title: UK mosque rebukes comission’s ‘warning’ following Palestine comments
events.summary: Will Israel’s election change life in Gaza? The Lewisham Islamic Centre accused the charity watchdog of imposing disproportionate expectations on Muslim charities. The Lewisham Islamic Centre (LIC) in London has rejected a warning issued by the UK’s independent Charity Commission, which reprimanded the mosque for comments on Palestinian suffering made by an imam during October 2023 sermons. “The matters raised by the Commission represent a troubling attempt to scrutinise, restrict and penalise legitimate religious worship” and “the expression of solidarity with the Palestinian people,” the mosque said in an official statement issued Wednesday. list 1 of 3 UK to double wait for permanent residency, with exemptions for care workers list 2 of 3 UK Supreme Court hears appeal against Palestine Action’s proscription list 3 of 3 UK jailing of Indian sailor over Russia sanctions sets off ‘perfect storm’ The statement comes after the charity watchdog accused the religious centre of including “content that was inflammatory, divisive and not in the charity’s best interests” during two separate sermons, as they issued an official warning urging the centre to “improve its handling of speakers and events hosted at the charity’s premises” on October 20. The commission warned that if the mosque fails to “remedy the misconduct”, it may be subjected to further action. The mosque also accused the commission of imposing disproportionate expectations on Muslim charities after the warning, describing them as “unnecessarily burdensome”. The religious centre explained that a sermon, or khutbah, is an integral part of Islamic worship and often speaks to the issues affecting the wellbeing of congregations and their communities. The LIC worried that the warning suggested the commission was “entitled to dictate which subjects Imams may address in their khutbahs”. LIC added that they are currently seeking legal advice as to the best way to move forward following the warning. CAGE International, a London-based human rights organisation, supported the mosque, and claimed the Charity Commission showed lenience when it came to pro-Israel charities. “The Commission’s position treats the word ‘Zionist’ as inflammatory in itself,” CAGE said on Thursday. “This merges opposition to a political ideology with hatred of a people, and places Muslim religious expression under suspicion by default.” “The Commission has told a mosque that naming who is responsible for Palestinian suffering falls outside acceptable religious practice,” a spokesperson for CAGE said. “This is the same regulator asking for the power to remove trustees for their views,” they added, referring to a recent government consultation to expand the Charity Commission’s powers.

events.title: Palantir’s Karp takes a sharp left turn, says he and the company’s products are actually ‘progressive’
events.summary: With tech CEO roles, a certain level of shamelessness comes with the job description. Yet Alex Karp, head honcho of Palantir, seems set to raise the bar with a conspicuous display of political flexibility following the Democratic wave in the US midterms. In December 2024, Karp gave $1 million to the pro-Trump super PAC MAGA Inc . But it does not take cutting-edge AI and data analytics – in which Palantir claims to have unique power – for Karp to understand on which side his bread is buttered. The man with the distinctive verbal diarrhea is now stressing his progressive credentials – and those of Palantir's products. The CEO told Politico that he is now open to voting for the Democrats come 2028. "I've been a Democrat my whole life. I grew up in a far-left environment. I know more about being a progressive than almost anybody on the planet, and I absolutely believe Palantir – all of our products are essentially progressive," Karp reportedly said. Karp's explanation for his political generosity was an apparent desire for balance. "My giving is equal, Democrat, Republican," Karp told the publication. "I can tell you, without going into things I'm not gonna disclose, I'm very balanced, and everyone in the political arena knows it. And I'll tell you what, I'm also not the village idiot." All of which raises the question of whether, in avoiding idiocy, it is necessary to eschew any principled stance whatsoever. If only the Germans of the Weimar Republic had thought to fund both sides. Apparently, all Europe needed was a more balanced political donations portfolio. Such is Karp's sensitivity towards the topic that he once claimed: "I love when I'm getting yelled at in cities in Europe... Keep yelling at me... the only reason why someone's not goose-stepping between me and you is my product. Say thank you." They have not said thank you. In fact, across Europe, governments are looking to reject Palantir , while the EU has instigated a sovereign tech and AI policy to escape the clutches of the US tech giants. Karp has a talent for holding two seemingly contradictory positions. He has talked about the need for democratic societies to exercise hard power , and, elsewhere, about founding a company that could "power the West to its obvious innate superiority ." At the same time, he has presented Palantir as a force for peace. "We see ourselves as the pioneers of a genuine and viable antiwar movement ," he wrote in his shareholder letter. It is his company's association with a longstanding customer, the controversial US Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE), that has drawn the most criticism. In Minnesota earlier this year, federal immigration officers shot and killed two American citizens, Renee Good and Alex Pretti, in incidents captured on video. It has detained US citizens, and critics argue it has shown scant regard for due process. Karp denied that Palantir's association with ICE should reflect badly on the company. He told CNBC: " If you are critical of ICE, you should be out there protesting for more Palantir . Our product, actually, in its core, requires people to conform with Fourth Amendment data protection." In the Politico interview, Karp said he was "really happy to hear" President Trump, a driving force behind ICE's expansion, acknowledge after the midterm elections that ICE deportations have been too tough . "And I'm glad he's saying in public now what I've been saying in private," Karp told the news outlet. Karp has no shortage of public opinions on goose-stepping or innate Western superiority. Why, then, reserve his concerns about deportations for private conversations? A public intervention from a Trump donor and ICE supplier might have carried some weight. Maybe he doesn't care so long as people are still writing about Alex Karp. But anyone who cares about more than that might feel the need to take a hot shower and scrub off the associated trauma. ®

events.title: I've cooked over 1,300 recipes from Ina Garten. Here are 10 of my favorites for Thanksgiving.
events.summary: Over the past few years, I've made all of Ina Garten's recipes. These are my favorite picks for a perfect Thanksgiving dinner. Trent Pheifer I've made more than 1,300 Ina Garten recipes. These are my favorite recipes for Thanksgiving .  Garten's make-ahead turkey gravy and autumn sangria are some of my favorites. Her Parmesan smashed potatoes, shaved Brussels sprouts with pancetta, and popovers are great sides. If Ina Garten's taught me anything, it's that a solid game plan is the key to a successful Thanksgiving dinner . I may go overboard by planning my dishes, timeline, and grocery list in early October, but my meal prep runs like a well-oiled machine every year. Fortunately, I have you covered when it comes to planning a menu . I've cooked all of the Barefoot Contessa's 1,300-plus recipes , and here are some of my absolute favorites for Thanksgiving dinner. Her autumn sangria packs a punch. Trent Pheifer " Cook Like a Pro ," page 24 When guests arrive, I love to kick things off with a seasonal cocktail . So many sangrias can be cloyingly sweet, but Garten's autumnal recipe is a perfectly balanced mix of cabernet sauvignon, apple cider, apple and pear brandy, and cinnamon syrup. Even better, you can make it days in advance to let the flavors meld. Be careful, though, as the Barefoot Contessa's drinks pack a punch. Making a turkey roulade is a good alternative to carving a whole bird. Trent Pheifer " Barefoot Contessa Back to Basics ," page 109 I'd always preferred dark-meat turkey until I tried this roulade. It's a deboned turkey breast packed with cranberry, sausage, and fig stuffing, then rolled, baked, and sliced. With this recipe, you don't need to carve an entire bird as your guests arrive. If you are choosing to go with a full bird, I'd suggest Ina's Accidental Turkey — the dry-brined method is a game changer! Her make-ahead turkey gravy with onions and sage is fabulous. Trent Pheifer " Make It Ahead ," page 103 I joke that I make extra of this gravy to sip on while making the rest of the Thanksgiving meal — it's that good. It can be made days in advance and then be rewarmed with turkey drippings on the day of the big meal. Even without the drippings, it's a fabulous gravy. Garten's mushroom-and-leek bread pudding is packed with flavor. Trent Pheifer " Foolproof ," page 188 For years, I never fully appreciated the appeal of dressing or stuffing. Sure, it was good, but with so many delicious Thanksgiving sides, I often only grabbed the smallest portion of it. That changed when Garten introduced me to savory bread pudding — stuffing's moister, much more flavorful cousin. This mushroom-and-leek one is my favorite. Parmesan smashed potatoes are pretty easy to make. Trent Pheifer "The Barefoot Contessa Cookbook," page 158 Garten's truffle mashed potatoes are an absolute favorite of mine, but her Parmesan smashed potatoes are my go-to when I'm planning to smother my spuds in gravy. The potatoes contain sour cream, which adds a nice tang as the Parmesan takes these to the next level. One big perk of this recipe is that it lets you skip the annoying task of peeling potatoes. Her shaved Brussels sprouts with pancetta are loaded with flavor. Trent Pheifer Food Network If you grew up in the '80s or '90s, there's a good chance you hated Brussels sprouts, which were almost always boiled and never delicious. Now, they're one of my favorite veggies, and nothing complements them better than a little bacon or pancetta and syrupy balsamic vinegar. For this recipe, I recommend using a food processor to quickly shred your sprouts. Popovers can be sweet or savory. Trent Pheifer "Parties," page 189 These popovers are impressively puffy and can skew sweet or savory — serve them with jam or gravy. The key is to get the popover pan as hot as possible before adding the batter — I usually heat the pan for 10 minutes rather than the two minutes Garten recommends. Maple-roasted butternut squash is a great side dish. Trent Pheifer " Barefoot Contessa Back to Basics ," page 158 I take back all the bad things I said about butternut squash when I was growing up. It makes for a dreamy side dish when paired with pancetta, maple syrup, and sage in this recipe. Skip pie and opt for pumpkin-mousse parfaits instead. Trent Pheifer "Barefoot Contessa at Home," page 180 Forget making pumpkin pie this year and instead prep this show-stopping, light-as-air treat. The ethereal pumpkin mousse layered with whipped cream and spicy, crunchy crumbled ginger cookies is the perfect cap to an otherwise heavy meal. Pecan squares are a good alternative to the classic pie. Trent Pheifer "The Barefoot Contessa Cookbook," page 188 Pecan pie was a must at Thanksgiving until I discovered these. Garten swaps the pie dough for a shortbread crust and tops it with a chewy, crunchy pecan mixture with a hint of orange. Go ahead and gild the lily by dipping the squares in the optional chocolate. This recipe yields a lot of bars — I usually cut it in half and make the dessert in a 9-by-13-inch casserole dish. events.title: Bowen pushes pragmatic climate deal amid pressure over fossil fuels
events.summary: News Home Just In For You Analysis Rural Watch Live Health Indigenous Politics Science Deep Time Elections World Environment Investigations Business Local news Quizzes Sport AFL NRL Football Tennis Cricket Netball Lifestyle Wellbeing Relationships & Family Food & Recipes Personal Finance Home & Garden Entertainment TV & Movies Books Music Pop Culture Arts Chris Bowen seeks pragmatic consensus heading into final COP31 talks Chris Bowen rejects suggestions Australia's role as a major fossil fuel exporter has damaged its standing in the negotiations. ( Reuters: Murad Sezer ) Chris Bowen has rejected criticism of Australia’s climate leadership over its continued coal and gas exports. The climate change and energy minister says countries must be realistic about the transition to cleaner energy. Negotiations at COP31 will intensify next week as Australia seeks agreement on electrification and climate finance. Climate Change Minister Chris Bowen has defended Australia's credibility as a global climate negotiator and signalled a pragmatic approach to securing a deal at COP31 amid pressure for a stronger international commitment to move away from fossil fuels. Mr Bowen has questioned why the Coalition sought to diminish Australia's role on the world stage and singled out Opposition Leader Angus Taylor for attacking expenses introduced during his own time as minister. "Does he want one lump of hypocrisy or two with his coffee?" Mr Bowen told the ABC in an interview on the sidelines of COP31 in Türkiye. Australia holds the presidency of negotiations at the summit, putting Mr Bowen at the centre of efforts to secure agreement between more than 190 countries on the next steps to tackle climate change. "My job is to steer consensus to the most ambitious outcome that consensus will allow," he said. Anthony Albanese (right) and Chris Bowen have defended Australia's decision to expand coal and gas production. ( ABC News: Matt Roberts ) That task has become more complicated as momentum builds behind a renewed push for a plan to transition away from fossil fuels. Fossil fuel road map lacks consensus Despite efforts by Brazil and others to advance work on a global road map for moving away from coal, oil and gas, the COP31 agenda remains predominantly focused on electrification, adaptation and climate finance. Mr Bowen described the fossil fuels transition as a "challenging issue" and noted the failure to get consensus on fossil fuels at last year's COP showed the enthusiasm of some governments was no guarantee of a collective agreement. He said there was "good spirit" around the negotiations at this year's summit before adding there was a "long way to go", with talks to ramp up next week. Mr Bowen also drew a connection between the road-map push and Australia's efforts to accelerate global electrification, arguing that reducing the use of fossil fuels would depend heavily on replacing them with electricity. Australia rejects fossil fuel hypocrisy claims Australia's role at COP31 has brought with it scrutiny of the nation's continued expansion of coal and gas production, with environment campaigners arguing the country's domestic policies undermine its climate credibility. Swedish climate activist Greta Thunberg has criticised the pace of Australia's climate policy. ( AP: Olivier Matthys ) Speaking overnight at the summit, activist Greta Thunberg said even a "snail" would agree Australia was moving too slow on climate action. But Mr Bowen emphatically rejected suggestions that Australia's role as a major fossil fuel exporter had damaged its standing in the negotiations. He said other governments understood the practical challenges of reducing dependence on fossil fuels, including their continued reliance on Australian exports. Mr Bowen said the argument Australia's exports undermined its leadership on climate was not one that "survives contact with reality in a COP negotiation". Prime Minister Anthony Albanese also defended the government's approach, arguing resource companies contributed substantial tax revenue used to fund public services. Coal and gas policies under scrutiny at COP31 Prime Minister Anthony Albanese has put the Pacific at the centre of his COP31 pitch, but Australia's continued expansion of coal and gas is drawing criticism from climate advocates. Asked why he did not directly reference fossil fuels in his speech at the opening of the COP31 leaders summit, Mr Albanese said "you could pick out any number of things" that were not in the short address. Electrification presents its own challenges Australia is championing a commitment to increase electricity's share of global energy consumption from about 23 per cent to 35 per cent by 2035. But the proposal has attracted criticism because it does not explicitly require the additional electricity to come from renewable sources. Mr Bowen said linking electrification exclusively to clean energy would be difficult to achieve.

events.title: Jensen Huang was a busted flush at Nvidia – he had to go | Nils Pratley
events.summary: Jensen Huang was a busted flush at Nvidia – he had to go CEO was viewed as ‘irreplaceable’, but recklessness of affair with a woman regarded by US officials as a Chinese spy made him a political liability H alf the tech world made up its mind before the facts could be assessed properly. Jensen Huang was “irreplaceable”, said the chorus at the start of this week. Nvidia would melt without the co-founder’s brilliance, apparently. The chipmaker’s board had to find a way to save its genius for the sake of corporate America and the entire AI universe. It was always nonsense because, after the passage of only a few days since his confession of infidelity, Huang looked less like a towering corporate titan and more like a political liability. An extramarital affair is not usually a resigning matter in itself – saintliness is not an absolute requirement of the job. But the circumstances here were different. A relationship with the Chinese boss of a Singapore-based firm suspected of smuggling Nvidia chips into China? That displayed recklessness on top of mere unfaithfulness. Get set for the working day – we'll point you to all the business news and analysis you need every morning Did he know the Megaspeed executive, Alice Huang (no relation), was regarded as a Chinese spy by US officials? It hardly matters. In the ultra-political world of in-demand AI computer chips, there were enough reasons for him to be careful in the extreme. The conflict of interest, and the risk of landing Nvidia in a quagmire of national security inquiries in Washington, would have been obvious. Reports of a second affair with a senior Nvidia employee compounded matters – US companies tend to be sensitive about such relationships. But the company’s directors might also have wondered what else could be revealed in coming weeks. Rule number one in these situations is to get all the bad news out on day one. The kneejerk reaction to Jensen Huang’s resignation was 13% off the share price. That was understandable – some investors truly believed the “irreplaceable” thesis. However, sitting in Nvidia’s boardroom, the job was not to worry about the initial stock market response but about what was best for the business. For multiple reasons, it was time to “rip off the Band-Aid and take Nvidia into its next chapter”, as Dan Ives, a senior tech analyst, put it. First, the congressional investigations will happen anyway. Democratic senators have asked administration officials to preserve all documents and communications related to the sale of Nvidia’s advanced AI chips to China. At heart, that issue is wider than Nvidia – it’s about whether US officials have themselves jeopardised the country’s lead over China in AI. But, one way or another, the company’s activities, and ties to the Trump administration , will come under scrutiny like never before. Nvidia is better placed to defend itself without Huang in the top job. Second, his personal lobbying clout on export policy had evaporated. After this week’s revelations, he had no credibility as an advocate of looser restrictions. The political demand will be entirely in the other direction – for loopholes to be closed. Third, there is the issue Nvidia’s underpowered board has dodged for too long: over-reliance on one individual. Never mind the risk of scandal, there is always a danger in concentrating too much day-to-day power in the hands of one individual. Nobody doubts Huang’s commercial talents, but even “godfathers of AI” in leather jackets don’t go on forever. Better to have a setup that can cope with change at the top. Colette Kress, the chief financial officer who will stand in as chief executive, is well regarded on Wall Street. Nvidia will not be short of outside applicants on a permanent basis. And the board has heard the governance criticism that a multitrillion-dollar company ought to have an independent chair: Harvey Jones, a former chief executive at semiconductor company Synopsys and a member of the current crew of directors, has got the gig. Then comes the task of creating some proper governance checks and balances, which may require fresh faces among the independent directors. Within a couple of hours, the fall in the share price had narrowed to 5% as investors remembered that Nvidia still has the best, and most in-demand, graphics processing units in the world and that many pioneering companies have prospered after the exit of an “irreplaceable” chief executive. Nobody pretends the management job will be easy. Nvidia will be different, not least because the political winds in the US have shifted. But there was no point trying to cling to a chief executive, however successful, who had made himself a busted flush. Huang had to go.

events.title: Unions helped Democrats win big in 2026. Now they want action
events.summary: Unions spent millions of dollars and mobilized thousands of members to get out the vote for Democrats in the midterm election. The CNBC Voter Poll showed a 22-point Democratic margin among union households in 2026, reversing a recent decline. Labor leaders say they expect newly elected Democrats to act on affordability and workers rights if they want to keep their support in the future. When Brody Rutledge wasn't working 60-hour weeks or raising his four children this year, he was busy helping secure political victories for Democrats . The 25-year-old was part of a group of Ohio union members who planned social-media blitzes in support of Amy Acton 's campaign for governor and Sherrod Brown 's effort to reclaim a Senate seat. On his lunch hour, during break times and after his kids went to sleep, the electrician created posts and videos to help raise the profiles of the two candidates among blue-collar voters. The posts attracted more than 15,000 views. Rutledge's efforts paid off: Acton and Brown won their respective races, part of the blue wave that swept Democrats to power in Washington and in state houses across America — including in many states, like Ohio, that had been considered Republican-leaning, or reliably Republican. "People are realizing that there needs to be a change," Rutledge told CNBC. "We are extremely excited with the results." Rutledge was a part of what organized labor considered one of its biggest political efforts yet. Unions spent millions of dollars and mobilized thousands of members to get out the vote for Democrats in the midterm election . Now, they expect newly elected politicians to deliver. Democrats, they say, need to get a handle on inflation, enact worker protections and deliver union jobs. The AFL-CIO launched a seven-figure paid media campaign for the election and said its members since Labor Day had engaged with nearly 15 million voters. By the AFL-CIO's count, more than 600 members of unions themselves were elected in the midterm, including dozens heading to Washington and hundreds who are bound for statehouses. The CNBC Voter Poll shows midterm voters who were union members or lived in a union household went for Democrats over Republicans by a margin of 22 percentage points, the highest of the last four election cycles. That's more than double the margin for the rest of the electorate: When looking at voters in non-union households, the gap shrunk to 10 percentage points. "We are very proud of the impact that the labor movement made on this election," said Liz Shuler, president of the AFL-CIO , a federation of unions that represents almost 15 million workers. "It was our biggest and boldest effort ever." In some cases, unions got involved before party nominees had been decided. In Michigan, the United Auto Workers organized behind Democrat Abdul El-Sayed ahead of what became a contentious primary race for U.S. Senate that he eventually won against Haley Stevens . The union believes that about one out of every 10 early voters in the August primary were UAW members. "It was incredibly impactful," Connor Farrell, a progressive fundraiser who worked with El-Sayed, said of the UAW's endorsement. "I'm not sure we would have won without them." El-Sayed and Jocelyn Benson — the Democratic nominee for Michigan governor, who also had early backing from the UAW — cruised to victory in last week's general election. It was a sharp reversal for the Wolverine state, which backed President Donald Trump in 2016 and 2024. The UAW held a rally on the eve of Election Day headlined by El-Sayed and Benson, along with other Democrats running for statewide office. The Detroit-based union said its volunteers knocked on more than 100,000 doors and made half a million phone calls for the election. The CNBC Voter Poll showed union households made up about 22% of the electorate in Michigan in the 2026 midterm, above the 16% mean nationwide. Union households in Michigan broke for El-Sayed and Benson by higher-than-average margins of 25 and 27 points, respectively. "There's a direct correlation between a ballot box and a bread box," said UAW President Shawn Fain, who described the union's 2026 political efforts as the largest in his lifetime. "What we bargain for today can be taken away in the legislative halls tomorrow." In Nevada, another swing state, members of AFL-CIO unions canvassed for a list of candidates including Aaron Ford , the Democrat who unseated Republican Gov. Joe Lombardo. Down ballot, the AFL-CIO endorsed candidates in state assembly, mayoral and city council races. Vladimir Ortega, a member of the National Association of Letter Carriers living in North Las Vegas, said displeasure with how Republicans had managed the economy led him to volunteer to canvas with the AFL-CIO for the first time. The 34-year-old met Ford and other candidates at political events, and he plans to volunteer for candidates backed by AFL-CIO again in 2028.

events.title: Pro-Palestine philanthropist faces US extradition hearing in Spain
events.summary: Will Israel’s election change life in Gaza? James ‘Fergie’ Chambers denies wrongdoing, while his wife urges PM Pedro Sanchez to grant him political asylum. Madrid, Spain – The wife of a pro-Palestine philanthropist who faces extradition to the United States has urged the Spanish prime minister to grant asylum, to save him from being sent to his own country. James “Fergie” Chambers is the first US citizen to face extradition to their own country. He is accused of supporting Hamas, an allegation apparently linked to a money laundering charge and donations that he made to support Palestinians in Gaza. list 1 of 2 US seeks extradition of wealthy pro-Palestine donor from Spain list 2 of 2 As US seeks Gaza donor’s extradition, wife warns of ‘terrifying precedent’ “I am pleading with [Spanish Prime Minister Pedro] Sanchez to use his powers to ensure Fergie’s political asylum claim is expedited for urgent consideration by the panel of ministers. This is within his gift. If he chooses not to act, he risks enabling [US President Donald] Trump to establish a precedent in Spain and across Europe which criminalises solidarity with the Palestinian people,” Stella Schnabel told Al Jazeera. Spain’s National Court will hear evidence from the US authorities on Friday, and a final decision will be made later. Chambers, a left-wing activist with a reported $250m net worth, is also facing charges of riot and conspiracy to riot relating to a protest at an Israeli arms company in 2023 in the US, for which he could face up to 30 years of imprisonment. The self-proclaimed anti-imperialist denies any wrongdoing. Chambers was arrested in July in Ibiza as he and his partner, Schnabel, an actress, searched for a school for their son, after Interpol issued a Red Notice for his detention. Since his arrest, he has claimed asylum, alleging he is the victim of political persecution. Chambers cannot be extradited until the asylum claim is resolved, and if it is successful, he cannot be extradited. The US government’s case centres on Chambers’s alleged laundering of $7.5m, which he is said to have wired several years ago from a US bank account to Tunisia, where he lived at the time, allegedly using the cash to support Hamas. Schnabel said in an earlier interview with Al Jazeera that the money was to support Club Africain, a Tunisian football club, to pay off its debts and overdue salaries, to reconstruct a training centre and build pitches for youth sides. Lawyers for Chambers said mistranslations between the US criminal charge in English and the version presented to Spanish authorities in Spanish make the allegations seem more serious. Under Spanish law, all extradition requests must be translated into Spanish. The alleged mistranslations, which relate to protests in 2003 in the United States that targeted the US-based facilities of Elbit Systems, Israel’s largest weapons manufacturer, changed “direct action” to “direct violence”. Lawyers also said there is no reference to violence in the original US criminal complaint, but the translated version submitted to Spanish authorities mentions “three fires” even though no fires are mentioned in the original text. US authorities also changed the description of protesters’ “activation” of smoke canisters to “detonation”, which, defence lawyers say, is usually used to describe an explosive device, not the release of smoke canisters. The most serious mistranslation, say defence lawyers, involved a conversation between third parties that in the original criminal complaint described Chambers as being part of a “global terrorism game”. However, in the translated version submitted to Spanish authorities, this phrase is changed to “global terrorism activities”. Chambers has not been charged with any “terrorism” offences. “It’s important to highlight that the US administration has not charged Fergie with material support for or financing terrorism or any terror-related offences, nor presented a shred of evidence that even a single cent has been used for violent or terrorist acts,” Aitor Martinez, one of the defence lawyers, told Al Jazeera. “The reason not to charge him with those offences is clear: there is no evidence.” If the court backs the US extradition request, defence lawyers for Chambers will appeal, dragging the case on longer. However, the Spanish government’s Council of Ministers may have the last word on the case and could refuse to send him to the US if they believe the case is politically motivated. The situation is complicated by the fact that Spain is holding an early election on November 29, which, according to the polls, the conservative People’s Party is likely to win, potentially requiring the support of the far-right Vox party. Both right-wing parties may be more inclined to support extraditing Chambers than Spain’s Socialist prime minister Sanchez, an outspoken critic of Trump’s support for Israel’s genocidal war in Gaza.

events.title: Jensen Huang’s exit puts Nvidia’s support for open source in question
events.summary: The open source community just lost one of its strongest advocates. Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang resigned Thursday after he admitted to an affair with an alleged Chinese spy, raising concerns about U.S. national security and the motives behind the executive’s support for softer chip export controls on China. Huang has been a staunch supporter of open source AI, framing the ecosystem as good for safety, innovation, diffusion, and sovereignty. And as frontier AI labs increasingly move to reduce their reliance on Nvidia and build their own chips, supporting open source is also a good way for the company to diversify its customer base by selling chips to nation-states, enterprises, and any organization that wants to own its own models. Still, Huang’s resignation raises questions about whether Nvidia will carry on his legacy by continuing to support the open model community. Jensen no longer being CEO would be very very bad for the open model cause in the US. Huang’s departure also comes as Nvidia has yet to finalize a deal to acquire open source platform Hugging Face for $13 billion . Hugging Face CEO Clem Delangue said in a post on X that the company would continue to fight for open source , whatever happens next. Nvidia also agreed to pay $6 billion for a non-exclusive license for open AI coding startup Poolside’s technology. Within Nvidia, Huang pushed for the development of the Nemotron family of open-weight AI models built for long-running agentic AI systems and reasoning workloads — potential competitors to closed frontier models. Huang also backed companies that would make American open models more competitive, investing in startups like Reflection AI and Thinking Machines Lab. Huang’s influence extended beyond Nvidia’s investments and product roadmap. He also emerged as one of the most prominent voices pushing back against Washington’s efforts to restrict the open AI ecosystem. Earlier this year, Huang wrote an open letter signed by 25 companies, including Microsoft, Meta, IBM, and Palantir, urging the U.S. government not to over-restrict open-weight AI models, many of which come from China. The impetus for that letter was Washington’s debate over how the U.S. should respond to allegations that Chinese AI labs are stealing intellectual property from American counterparts like Anthropic and OpenAI, both of which have reportedly appealed directly to Washington on the matter, urging stronger protections. That combination of Huang’s personal visibility and Nvidia’s market power made him the strongest counterweight to arguments from closed-model providers like Anthropic and OpenAI, which have advocated for greater restrictions on advanced AI models due to safety reasons. Without Huang, the concern among open source community members is that whoever takes over will be more cautious. Nvidia has named CFO Colette Kress as interim CEO. It’s not clear how Kress will approach the Hugging Face deal or support for the open model ecosystem, but founder-driven priorities tend to get a downgrade when leadership changes. Huang’s exit could also strengthen the arguments of those in Washington who are arguing for tougher restrictions on Chinese AI companies, particularly as the scandal surrounding his relationship with Alice Huang, the Megaspeed executive and alleged spy, puts renewed scrutiny on his efforts to loosen chip export controls. Restrictions on open-weight models from China could kneecap competition for American companies, the most powerful of which have kept their models closed. Still, supporting open source isn’t simply a passion project Huang pursued out of idealism. It’s increasingly central to Nvidia’s business strategy. As some of Nvidia’s biggest customers, including Google and OpenAI, develop their own chips, Nvidia has an incentive to cultivate a much broader ecosystem of AI developers and customers. More players training, fine-tuning, and running models mean more GPUs sold, and less dependence on a handful of frontier labs. Huang may be gone, but Nvidia still needs an open AI ecosystem. The question now is whether that commitment can survive without the man who made it a priority. TechCrunch has reached out to Nvidia for comment. events.title: ‘The plot twist’: A study of 73,000 adults found America’s richest still die sooner than most Europeans
events.summary: Americans have never earned more or lived longer. Median household income hit $87,460 in 2025, the highest since the Census Bureau began tracking it in 1967, according to Census data released in September . Life expectancy reached 79 years in 2024, also a record . Yet money still can’t buy Americans a European lifespan. A Brown University study published last year in the New England Journal of Medicine found that Americans die sooner than Europeans at every level of wealth, and that the richest Americans fare no better than the poorest people in much of Western Europe. “The plot twist is that even the wealthiest quartile of Americans does not have better outcomes than most of northern and Western Europeans,” says Sara Machado, a research scientist at Brown’s Center for Health System Sustainability. “That was unexpected and counters a lot of the narrative that we’re used to.” What the Brown study found The researchers tracked more than 73,000 adults ages 50 to 85 in the U.S. and 16 European countries, starting in 2010 and following them for about a decade, using data from the U.S. Health and Retirement Study and Europe’s SHARE survey. The wealthiest people in northern and western Europe had a mortality rate about 35% lower than the wealthiest Americans . Survival among America’s richest quartile was statistically equivalent to that of the poorest quartile in countries like France, Germany, and the Netherlands. Across the board, people in continental Europe died at rates about 40% lower than Americans over the study period, according to Brown . In southern Europe, death rates were about 30% lower. Wealth still matters within each country. “We found that where you stand in your country’s wealth distribution matters for your longevity, and where you stand in your country compared to where others stand in theirs matters, too,” Machado says. Why money doesn’t close the gap The U.S. spent an estimated $14,775 per person on health care in 2024, nearly $7,000 more than the average comparable wealthy country, according to the Peterson-KFF Health System Tracker . Those countries averaged a life expectancy of 82.7 years, 3.7 years longer than the U.S. Fortune has reported on why U.S. health care costs run about twice those of peer nations . The spending doesn’t buy universal access. About 26.7 million Americans went uninsured for all of 2025, Census data shows , and about 2.6 million fewer Americans had ACA marketplace plans in early 2026 than in early 2025. “Fixing health outcomes is not just a challenge for the most vulnerable – even those in the top quartile of wealth are affected,” says Machado. Lifestyle plays a role. Americans tend to have less healthy diets and a more sedentary lifestyle , and heart disease and cancer remain the two leading causes of death nationally. The researchers noted that smoking and rural living, both tied to poorer health, were more common in the U.S. Europe is also home to two of the so-called blue zones , Sardinia in Italy and Ikaria in Greece, where longevity is credited to activity, diet, rest, and strong social ties, though some researchers dispute the claims . When Fortune first reported on the study , senior author Irene Papanicolas pointed to higher U.S. rates of avoidable deaths from firearms, alcohol, and suicide; higher cardiovascular mortality; and a thinner social safety net, with health coverage tied more closely to employment. Inequality compounds it. The U.S. has a far wider gap between rich and poor than Europe, a divide that Creative Planning CEO Peter Mallouk recently warned is unsustainable . “Our previous work has shown that while wealth inequality narrows after 65 across the U.S. and Europe, in the U.S. it narrows because the poorest Americans die sooner and in greater proportion,” explains Papanicolas, a professor of health services, policy, and practice who directs Brown’s Center for Health System Sustainability. What researchers say comes next The recent gains in U.S. longevity came largely from the end of the pandemic, and a drop in overdose deaths and suicides also occurred in 2024, according to the CDC. Those gains have not closed the gap with Europe. “If we want to improve health in the US,” explains Papanicolas, “we need to better understand the underlying factors that contribute to these differences – particularly amongst similar socioeconomic groups – and why they translate to different health outcomes across nations.” “There is a lot of it that is a collective issue,” Machado agrees. “But I would say to individuals that you really need to think about your retirement—about when you’re going to retire, how you’re going to retire, and how you can be happy as a person that has retired.” Machado adds, “If you look at other countries, there are better outcomes, and that means we can learn from them and improve. It’s not necessarily about spending more — it’s about addressing the factors we’re overlooking, which could deliver far greater benefits than we realize.” This story was originally featured on Fortune.com

events.title: Federal Reserve Board announces pricing, effective January 1, 2027, for payment services the Federal Reserve Banks provide to banks and credit unions, and changes to streamline and adjust their check services
events.summary: The Federal Reserve Board on Thursday announced pricing, effective January 1, 2027, for payment services the Federal Reserve Banks provide to banks and credit unions, such as the clearing of checks, automated clearing house (ACH) transactions, instant payments, and wholesale payment and settlement services. By law, the Federal Reserve must establish fees to recover the costs, including imputed costs, of providing payment services over the long run. The Federal Reserve expects to recover 101.5 percent of actual and imputed expenses in 2027, including the return on equity that would have been earned if a private-sector firm provided the services. Overall, price changes for 2027 will result in an estimated 1.4 percent average price increase for established, mature services. In addition, the Federal Reserve Banks announced changes to streamline and adjust their check services. As described in the request for information on check services issued last year, the volume of checks processed by the Federal Reserve Banks is declining, but checks remain an important payment instrument for many consumers and businesses. The changes were informed by public feedback and ensure that the Federal Reserve Banks continue to provide check services efficiently. The adjustments include optimizing check processing windows during low-volume periods, increasing fees that banks and credit unions pay to process checks, and other operational updates. These changes do not impact consumers' and businesses' ability to pay with or receive checks and only impact how banks and credit unions process checks with Federal Reserve Banks. The entire 2027 fee schedule for all of the Federal Reserve's payment services is published on FRBservices.org ® . Additional information on the Federal Reserve's payments services, including service usage statistics, is available on the Board's website . events.title: Thanks to American oligarchy, Jensen Huang’s midlife crisis is a problem for all of us | Moira Donegan
events.summary: Thanks to American oligarchy, Jensen Huang’s midlife crisis is a problem for all of us At a time when individual men wield massive power, the ramifications of the Nvidia CEO’s affair could be enormous O ne of the reasons you want to distribute power and responsibility in powerful organizations and high-stakes enterprises is so that the narcissism or myopia of one man do not come to carry outsized consequences. When power is spread out across multiple people, it matters less if one of those people is prone to flattery, or in the midst of a midlife crisis, or perhaps just a bit stupid; the limits on his power become limits on the fallout of his character flaws. A broad distribution of authority also has the virtue of making any one man disposable, replaceable: if he turns out to have poor judgement or counterproductive preoccupations, he can be dispensed with, and his role can be filled anew with someone better suited to its responsibilities. But if one man becomes synonymous with a company – or a country – then untold numbers of other people live and die by that man’s decisions. And when his decisions are bad – petty, selfish, shortsighted, small-minded or dumb – then it is other people who will pay the price. And the price is often quite steep. Because we live in an era of massive inequality, tightly consolidated corporate leadership, and rule by a billionaire class with large egos and deficient dignity, the US economy is now experiencing one of the latter scenarios, in the form of Jensen Huang , a Silicon Valley billionaire who this week confessed to having an extramarital affair. This would be tacky and embarrassing for Huang on its own. But because Huang is the longtime CEO of Nvidia , one of the country’s largest companies and the manufacturer of advanced chip technology that is powering the US’s AI boom, his petty midlife crisis – the kind of small-minded narcissism that can usually be dispensed with in the form of a red sportscar, or indeed with one of the cheesy leather jackets that Huang is prone to wearing – is now a problem for the US economy, and potentially for national security. Because Huang’s mistress was not just any of the interchangeable young women that such men usually go for. This one happened to be a suspected Chinese spy. It’s unclear how much the woman, Huang Le, also known as Alice Huang – no relation – learned from her relationship with the tech billionaire, or how the information she may have gathered could undermine US economic and military interests. Alice Huang worked in television in China before becoming an executive at Megaspeed, a Singapore-based tech company and one of the largest purchasers of Nvidia’s advanced chips. Megaspeed was under investigation by the US commerce department on suspicion of smuggling the advanced chips to China, which is banned from importing them by US law. (Megaspeed said it had offered to cooperate with the US government’s investigation but those offers went unanswered.) According to the New York Times, the investigation was abruptly halted last year after the general counsel for Nvidia, Jensen Huang’s company, intervened. Among other things, Jensen Huang is known for his close relationship with Donald Trump. On Sunday, Huang issued a statement admitting to an affair, and his company announced that it would be launching an investigation into the incident. “The Board has no reason to believe that either national security or NVIDIA secrets were compromised,” which is perhaps a bit too hopeful. On Thursday, Huang stepped down as Nvidia’s CEO. But the statement itself is a reflection of the depth of Huang’s control over the country. If you or I had endangered corporate secrets and state security in a flight of reckless, narcissistic frivolity, the way Huang may have done, then our employers would not be announcing the investigation while we kept our jobs. Nvidia’s stocks were down when the markets opened on Monday. They may well go down further still. And yet the scandal is fitting for our current era of Silicon Valley, in which loyalty to Donald Trump has gone from a strategic move by major tech companies to ensure favorable contract and regulatory terms to much more full-throated embrace of the ideology and style of the far right. Following the lead of its major male executives, the tech industry has become reckless and irresponsible, proud of itself for accelerating technologies it plainly claims to be unable to control, demanding investments in datacenters and government contracts from taxpayers whom it smugly brags about putting out of jobs, and flooding our aesthetic and informational worlds with low-grade slop that is frequently factually inaccurate, often dangerous for vulnerable users, and uncanny in its unpleasantness, bearing a creepy and inhuman sheen in its images and language.
