events.title: After Jensen Huang is Howard Lutnick the prime target of national security inquiry?
events.summary: When questioning the motives of certain public leaders, the Roman orator Cicero was said to have used as a shorthand, “cui bono?” meaning, whose interests come first? That line rings true as Secretary of Commerce Howard Lutnick falls under rapidly escalating bipartisan scrutiny over his role in the flow of Nvidia chips into China. Nvidia founder and CEO Jensen Huang resigned Thursday after reports of affairs with a direct report and with Alice Huang, a suspected Chinese spy , yet the national security questions he leaves behind keep growing amidst escalating congressional investigations . Megaspeed, the Nvidia customer where Alice Huang was an executive, was suspected of funneling advanced chips to China for years, yet the U.S. government took little action. Many are now asking: Who knew what, and when? And why is this surfacing only now? We have already described Nvidia directors’ exposure to shareholder lawsuits over their own failures of oversight. Now the scrutiny is shifting to Washington. How did the U.S. government look past so grave a threat to national security for so long, and let these sales go on? As the reporting accumulates, all roads lead to one person, who by multiple accounts blocked action over the objections of fellow cabinet members and leading voices in both parties in Congress: Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick. He is now squarely on the hot seat, and it grows hotter by the day as more information comes to light. Untangling the Truth of a Muddled Timeline Megaspeed has long been a major target of U.S. government focus amidst pervasive allegations that the Singapore-based data center company helped Chinese firms evade U.S. export controls on sensitive Nvidia chips. The Department of Commerce’s own agents began investigating Megaspeed , the Singapore firm that bought billions of dollars of Nvidia chips and is suspected of diverting them to China, in 2024, under the Biden Administration. After the change of administration but amidst the ongoing probe, The New York Times reported that in 2025, Nvidia’s general counsel emailed those agents directly, citing permission from Lutnick’s export-control chief, Jeffrey Kessler, with Commerce soon pausing its work on the investigation. That sparked many concerns even within the GOP, with respected Senate Intelligence Committee Chair Tom Cotton writing to Lutnick directly , urging Commerce to investigate Megaspeed more carefully. Still, Megaspeed never landed on the entity list, the blacklist kept by the Department of Commerce that cuts suspect firms off from American technology; even though other agencies repeatedly agreed on proposing to add Megaspeed to the list, with the Financial Times reporting that the State Department, Treasury Department, Energy Department and the Pentagon were pushing particularly aggressively to add Megaspeed to the entity list. Despite these entreaties, Lutnick’s Commerce Department was unmoved, steadfastly refusing to add a single company to the entity list for more than a year . Then came the memo. This spring, the New York Times reports , Secretary of State Marco Rubio oversaw the drafting of a highly classified assessment built on electronic surveillance of Alice Huang. Its conclusion was as stark as can be: China’s Ministry of State Security had recruited her to gather intelligence on Jensen Huang and on America’s AI chips, and she had grown close to the Nvidia CEO. U.S. officials assessed that Beijing’s aims may have gone further, to steering Nvidia into pressing Washington for greater Chinese access to its most advanced chips. The memo went to a handful of senior officials before President Trump’s May trip to China, with Axios reporting that Lutnick was among those who received the memo directly. Perhaps not coincidentally, Jensen Huang was originally left off the delegation of business leaders traveling to China with Trump, before being added at the very last possible minute during an Alaska refueling stop . That same month, Reuters reported that Commerce had cleared about 10 Chinese companies to buy H200s. Perhaps even more alarmingly, but less widely known than the existence of the memo; Axios also reports that President Trump approved a crackdown on chip diversion to China no less than three times, in May, in August, and on Nov. 5, with even Elon Musk supportive, and that Lutnick and his deputies had resisted carrying out each order. As Maria Curi and Marc Caputo of Axios reported pithily , “One administration official has repeatedly stood in the way: Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick,” noting that virtually every other Administration official was supportive of these crackdowns. Just last week, after news of the Jensen Huang spy scandal broke, Axios reported that Bessent confronted Lutnick about why his department has resisted implementing the export controls, particularly on Megaspeed, the company at the center of the spy scandal, with virtually all other Admin officials siding with Bessent; yet Lutnick apparently continued to stall. Already, there has been speculation that the leaks over the last week that felled Huang came from sources within the Trump Administration, perhaps from within the National Security Council, who were frustrated at Lutnick pushing what they perceived to be pro-China policies, with many remarking about the suspicious timing of these leaks right after midterm elections, even though the original memo was circulated in May this year, six months ago. Lutnick Loses Cabinet Confidence and GOP Trust What makes this scrutiny so hot is who is turning up the temperature. Lutnick’s chief antagonists on the issue of China chip controls are almost entirely his own colleagues within the administration, ranging from Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent, Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth, U.S. Trade Representative Jamieson Greer and National Security Adviser and Secretary of State Marco Rubio, to U.S. Director of National Intelligence Jay Clayton, all of whom reportedly favor a far tougher approach than Lutnick has been willing to impose. Lutnick’s Republican detractors are plenty outside the administration as well, particularly within the GOP congressional ranks. Republican Sen. John Kennedy says Lutnick must explain himself “ in front of God and country .” Rep. Bill Huizenga has attacked Lutnick’s lack of responsiveness to Congress as “frustrating,” and the Republican chairs of the House China and Foreign Affairs committees, Rep. John Moolenaar and Rep. Brian Mast, have made their unhappiness with Lutnick just as vivid. All these intraparty critics join legions of Democratic senators who are demanding records from Lutnick, and after last week’s midterms , their party takes the committee gavels in January with detractors making clear that Lutnick is one of their top targets – for reasons extending far beyond merely his role in sensitive U.S. technology making their way to China. events.title: Jensen Huang built Nvidia into a $4 trillion AI giant but owned less than 4% of it, leaving him without the super-voting power to protect his CEO role
events.summary: Jensen Huang, the billionaire ex- Nvidia CEO who took the company from a small player in the video game graphics industry to the chipmaker at the center of the AI revolution, once made a surprising revelation: He could be fired at any time. “In a well-governed company, the CEO was always designed to report to the board of directors and the board of directors report to shareholders,” Huang said in a January podcast interview with Jodi Shelton. “If the CEO doesn’t do his job according to 12, 13, 15 board members, however sized the board is, that CEO is let go.” This reality sets Nvidia apart from other Silicon Valley companies, especially those still run by a cofounder. That includes Meta , where CEO and cofounder Mark Zuckerberg wields considerable power over the board due to its dual class share structure. On Thursday, Huang resigned from the company that he cofounded and led over the past 33 years after publicly admitting to being unfaithful to his wife. Nvidia’s board opened an independent investigation into Huang and the possibility he may have been a target of a foreign intelligence operation after reporting by the New York Times explored his close relationship with a businesswoman that U.S. intelligence identified as a Chinese spy. Huang reportedly had another affair with an Nvidia executive who reported to him, according to the New York Times . On Thursday, the board appointed CFO Colette Kress as interim CEO. Still, Huang said in that January interview any future Nvidia CEO would not measure up to him. “There will never be one like me, and the reason for that is because I was raised by the company,” he said at the time. Nvidia did not immediately respond to Fortune ’s request for comment. Why Jensen Huang’s stock ownership didn’t protect his CEO position Despite being the company’s largest individual shareholder, Huang did not have unparalleled voting control over his company or outsized control over the company’s board, like other founders. Huang owned about 870.6 million Nvidia shares, or about 3.58% of the company as of March, according to the company’s 2026 proxy statement. His holdings were far greater than that of  other executives and directors, including Kress, who held 4.4 million shares. Vanguard and BlackRock both owned more than 7% of the company each. Because of Nvidia’s one-share-one vote system, Huang’s stake doesn’t come with special privileges, despite his status as a cofounder. That means the number of votes he has directly corresponds with his number of shares.  As Huang alluded to in his January podcast interview, Nvidia’s bylaws are written in such a way that the company’s CEO can be removed by the board for any reason and at any time—still, Huang lacked enough voting power to independently elect or remove Nvidia’s directors.  While founders with majority voting control, such as Zuckerberg, can effectively determine who sits on their boards, Huang would have needed support from other Nvidia shareholders to do the same. That differs from other companies run by tech founders including Meta, Snap , and even Google.  At Meta, a dual class voting structure (it said last month it would add a third non-voting tier next year ) gives Zuckerberg outsized power over voting.  Despite owning 13.4% of the company, Zuckerberg controls about 60% of the company’s voting power because his class B shares give him 10 votes each compared to one vote for every class A share. With this voting power, Zuckerberg can effectively elect Meta’s entire board and is the deciding voice on most matters sent to shareholders. Snap, the social media company, has a similar arrangement with CEO and cofounder Evan Spiegel controlling 53% of the company’s voting power while only owning about 9.3% of the company.  Even at Google parent company Alphabet , where cofounder Sergey Brin and cofounder and former CEO Larry Page no longer run day-to-day operations, the pair still collectively retain majority voting control of the tech giant. Both still serve on the company’s board.  Nvidia’s stock plummeted by as much as 14% Thursday following the announcement of Huang’s departure, before rebounding. It was down about 4.7% as of 1:30 p.m. EST on Thursday. With a nearly $4 trillion market cap, the company makes up about 6% of the S&P 500 and about 10% of the Nasdaq 100 , meaning any reckoning it experiences will trickle through the broader market and everyday Americans’ 401(K) accounts.  Huang was key to Nvidia’s operations with a flat management structure and direct involvement in the company’s product strategy and its supplier and customer relationships. In recent months, he has also cultivated a close relationship with President Donald Trump, who has been a vocal proponent of boosting the AI industry and the infrastructure backing it in the U.S.—although Trump was quick to back ex-Apple CEO Tim Cook as Huang’s successor on Thursday. The board has now made changes to its own structure as well. It previously operated without a board chairman, opting instead to rely on lead independent director Stephen Neal to oversee management. On Thursday, it appointed Harvey C. Jones, a former semiconductor company CEO and Nvidia board member since 1993, as its chairman of the board, it said in a statement. Kress, the company’s CFO since 2013, said for her part she is planning to build on Huang’s legacy at Nvidia as interim CEO she said in a Thursday statement. In the January interview, Huang said while he didn’t love his job every day, he always tried his “mightiest” because of two reasons. “One, I’m the best person for the job. I believe that,” he said. “And, two, I have to earn being the best person for that job every day.” This story was originally featured on Fortune.com

events.title: Home sales in the US are at their lowest level since 2016
events.summary: Home sales dropped 5.5 percent in October, the lowest level since August 2010. Sales of previously owned homes in the US have hit the lowest level since 2010 as mortgage rates hover above 7 percent. The National Association of Realtors (NAR) said on Thursday that home sales dropped 5.5 percent in October to a seasonally adjusted annual rate of 3.75 million units. That was the lowest level since August 2010. list 1 of 4 Trump launches probe into Federal Reserve Governor Lisa Cook list 2 of 4 How has the cost of living changed in France, Italy, Spain and Portugal? list 3 of 4 The world is $365 trillion in debt, and the interest bill is climbing list 4 of 4 Rising costs and tight budgets strain Americans ahead of midterm elections “Home buying is difficult when mortgage rates have climbed to their highest levels since 2000, aside from a single month in 2023. As a result, home sales fell to their lowest level since August 2010,” said NAR Chief Economist Lawrence Yun. He said, “It is just a tough market for buyers and sellers.” “Sales decreased by 8.8 percent year-over-year,” the NAR report found. “Month-over-month sales declined in the Midwest, South and West and held steady in the Northeast. Year-over-year sales declined in all four regions.” The home sales used in the report are counted at the closing of a contract and are a look at previously occupied ones. October’s sales likely reflected contracts signed in August and September. “Despite fewer transactions in October, the 88 million homeowners across the country are largely in a comfortable financial position due to sizable housing wealth accumulation,” said the report. First-time buyers accounted for just 29 percent of home purchases last month, down from 31 percent in September and 32 percent in October last year, NAR said. First-time buyers have historically made up closer to 40 percent of home sales. The US housing market has been in a slump since 2022, when mortgage rates increased from pandemic-era lows. Sales of previously occupied US homes were essentially flat last year, stuck at a 30-year low. Yun expects home sales this year will likely end up lower than in 2025. The average 30-year fixed-rate mortgage was 7.33 percent in October, according to the Federal Home Loan Mortgage Corporation, more commonly known as Freddie Mac, up from 6.86 percent in September and 6.25 percent one year ago. The rate, however, averaged 7.18 percent last week, down from 7.24 percent in the previous week. Rates on home loans are influenced by inflation, Federal Reserve policy and bond-market investors’ expectations for the economy, among other factors. They generally follow the trajectory of the 10-year Treasury yield, which lenders use as a guide to pricing home loans. Until the past few weeks, mortgage rates had been on the rise since late February, when the US war with Iran began, pushing up the price of oil and driving inflation higher. The run-up in rates also reflected heightened bond market volatility, which led to rising yields on US Treasuries.

events.title: What to know about the Logan Circle shooting in Washington, DC
events.summary: Can Trump find a way to work with Democrats? Trump has showcased the capital city as an example of his tough-on-crime approach. Police say a gunman is dead after he allegedly shot five people, killing one, in a busy thoroughfare in the centre of Washington, DC, on Thursday morning. Mass shootings are not uncommon in the United States, but this one drew a swift and massive response from local police as well as federal security forces. Law and order in the capital city has been at the centre of a national debate about the administration of US President Donald Trump. About 8am local time (13:00 GMT), during a busy rush hour commute, a gunman entered a gym in Logan Circle, a trendy neighbourhood near foreign embassies and fashionable restaurants, about 1.6km (one mile) north of the White House. list 1 of 3 DC residents debate safety gains a year into Trump’s Guard deployment list 2 of 3 Two security breaches near White House prompt brief lockdown list 3 of 3 White House announces funds for law enforcement programme in several cities “Within seconds, there was a man who fell to the ground, and a pool of blood came out,” said James Spellman, who witnessed the attack and said there were about 50 people in the gym. “One gym member rushed to help him. He was instantly dead. He had been shot in the neck.” Spellman said he and other gym members ran out of the gym and he heard more gunfire in the area of 15th Street. He said he heard about two shots fired in the gym and about five or six fired outside. Law enforcement arrived within minutes, cordoning off the area and working to apprehend the suspect. They included personnel from the Metropolitan Police Department, the city’s law enforcement agency, as well as heavily armed officers from federal agencies including the Federal Bureau of Investigation (FBI) and the Secret Service. Authorities sent out alerts to people in the area warning them to shelter inside because of an “active shooter” situation. Schools near the scene were placed on lockdown. “Go inside the nearest building, stay away from windows, and remain indoors until further notice,” police instructed the public. Washington, DC’s interim police chief, Jeffery Carroll, said the suspect was a white male wearing a grey shirt. The suspect, police said, opened fire inside the gym, then exited the building and entered another adjacent building, where he barricaded himself inside a room on the seventh floor. Officers then began trying to negotiate with the suspect, with specialised negotiators talking to him over the phone, as snipers kept watch from nearby rooftops. At one point, he shot at police through the barricaded door. About an hour after they began speaking to him, police say they heard gunfire over the phone, and they decided to breach the room where the suspect had been holed up. They found him with a self-inflicted gunshot wound, and he was pronounced dead at the scene. What do we know about the suspect and the victims? Washington, DC Council member Brooke Pinto said the suspect, identified as a physician named Matt Lambert, initially shot a person in the gym with whom he was involved in a court case over a dispute over the condominium where he lived. Police Chief Carroll, speaking to reporters shortly after the suspect was found dead, said the shooting appeared to have stemmed from a “conflict between him and the homeowners association of the building”. Some unconfirmed reports cited a social media account as possibly belonging to the suspect, which appeared to frequently feature posts about bad living conditions in a condominium in the area where the attack occurred. Little has been released about the victims of the shooting. Authorities said one person had died, and another was in critical condition in the hospital. What are the larger political implications of this mass shooting? An assault in the same Logan Circle area back in August 2025 was cited by President Trump as a reason for deploying troops to the capital, launching a national push that saw controversial deployments to several Democratic-controlled cities. A former Department of Government Efficiency official said he was assaulted in the early hours in the same area by a group of teenagers attempting to carjack him and a woman he was with. Trump declared a crime emergency and said his administration was taking control of the federal district’s local police force. Although Washington, DC, has a mayor and city council, it is not treated on equal footing with other states in the country, and Congress as well as the president have some authority over things like its budget and law enforcement activities. Trump deployed thousands of National Guard troops to the capital, who continue more than a year later to patrol the city in groups, including in the Logan Circle area.

events.title: THC drink companies rush to sell inventory as Illinois ban takes effect
events.summary: Many hemp companies are shipping their remaining inventory to Wisconsin, Minnesota and Tennessee, which have different regulations At midnight this morning in Illinois , hemp-derived THC drinks transformed from grocery store commodities into illegal narcotics, and manufacturers have been rushing to sell their inventory or ship it out of state. Republicans tacked a last-minute provision on to last year’s spending bill that ended the government shutdown, banning all hemp-derived THC products, including the THC-infused alcohol alternatives sold at liquor stores and grocery stores . Under the new law, no container can have more than 0.4mg THC total. In June, Illinois passed a state-level law intended to align with the federal ban, initially set to go into effect this month. While Congress delayed the federal ban until December, Illinois did not change its state-level effective date. There has been some confusion around the Illinois ban because of a lawsuit filed last week by the Illinois Healthy Alternatives Association, a hemp lobbying trade group that includes approximately 250 Illinois businesses. Some headlines suggested the lawsuit effectively paused the Illinois hemp ban until 19 November, but that pause only applies to businesses that sued . The timing of the ban is unfortunate for Playdate, a non-alcoholic wine company that launched its first product, a THC-infused, NA rosé, less than two months ago. With less than two weeks to go before the ban, Playdate cofounders Sammy Dorf and Brian Ward were still unsure how to handle their remaining inventory. It’s possible the federal government will ultimately leave hemp-derived THC regulation to the states, mirroring their approach to medical and recreational cannabis. Many hemp companies are strategically shipping their remaining inventory to Minnesota and Tennessee, which already have their own hemp regulations. After selling off Playdate wine at a steep discount, Dorf and Ward said they have less than a truckload left, which they’ll ship to states where they can still sell it. If the hemp ban remains in place, Ward and Dorf intend to shift their focus to plain NA wine, minus the THC. Joe Chura, CEO and founder of Go Brewing in Naperville, Illinois , got into the business the other way around. Chura’s initial goal was to create the world’s first gluten-free, NA beer. He launched Easy Man, a THC-infused option, just last year, hoping to provide an alternative buzz without the health consequences of heavy drinking. “Probably a month ago, we made our last batch,” Chura said. “We were planning another one that we ended up cancelling, because we didn’t want to get stuck with it.” The last of the Easy Man left sold out on Friday, Chura added: “Had I known the demand would have been as great at the end, I probably would have made [the cancelled batch.] But it was cutting it close.” Perfectly Dosed, a Chicago-based company that sells THC emulsions to beverage companies, didn’t have the option to dispense their remaining inventory in a fire sale, as they sell it to other companies in bulk. They had a metric ton of emulsion leftover, containing more than 100m milligrams of THC, according to cofounder and CEO Alexander Choi. “We’re hopeful that more reasonable regulations will pass, and so we’d like our stuff closer to home than further,” Choi said. They shipped their metric ton of emulsion to Wisconsin. Companies outside Illinois have another month to off-load their product. Joe Gerrity, CEO of Crescent Canna, has been selling beverages off to individual consumers by the pallet. He has some sense of who’s buying. “When someone’s buying thousands of dollars worth of product, you want to do some due diligence,” Gerrity said, adding that several former NBA players bought pallets. One of the most difficult things about planning for the ban is the uncertainty around how it’s going to be implemented and enforced. “It was hard for us to tell when distributors were going to stop selling our products, when retailers were going to ask them to be off the shelves,” Gerrity said. While many in the industry don’t expect the federal government to strictly enforce the ban, alcohol distributors will probably still refuse THC beverages if there’s any possibility they could lose their license, Gerrity explained. Gerrity is also working to figure out how to destroy inventory if necessary. “You can’t just click a button and destroy thousands of pallets,” he said. Choi, meanwhile, has been reformulating his emulsions to be chemically stable in case they need to be diluted to comply with federal regulations. Despite the volatility of the industry, Chura said that he’s still hopeful that the bans will be reversed, and is even thinking about a THC beer compliant with federal regulations – that is, one that only contains 0.4mg of THC. It’s still unclear whether such a product would be legal.

events.summary: Nvidia's board announced Thursday that Jensen Huang had resigned as CEO. Tomohiro Ohsumi/Getty Images Nvidia founder Jensen Huang is out. After another report about an affair, Nvidia's board announced Thursday that Huang had resigned. This is what smart people in business and tech are saying about Huang's departure. Nvidia is without its founder for the first time in more than 30 years. On Thursday, Nvidia's board announced CEO Jensen Huang's abrupt resignation , ending the tenure of a leader who had overseen the chipmaker's rise to become one of the world's most valuable companies. Huang's ouster came after days of reports about his personal life. First, The New York Times reported that the Nvidia leader had a close relationship with someone US officials suspect to be a Chinese intelligence asset. On Sunday, Huang acknowledged having an affair, and Nvidia's board launched an investigation into whether Huang had been targeted by a foreign intelligence operation. The Times had reported that the Nvidia founder had grown close to Alice Huang , who US officials believed had been recruited to gather information for the Chinese government. Then on Wednesday, the Times reported that Huang had another affair with Kimberly Powell , an Nvidia executive who reported to him. By Thursday morning, one of the world's richest men and a face of the AI boom was out of a job. Clem Delangue, CEO of Hugging Face Hugging Face CEO Clement Delangue Bloomberg/Getty Images Hugging Face CEO Clem Delangue said, "This whole thing sucks." "I wish none of it had happened. It's a really sad day!" Delangue wrote on social media. Delangue, whose company Nvidia agreed to acquire for roughly $12.9 billion, said that he'll continue to fight for open-source AI. "I want to make one thing clear: we'll keep fighting for open-source AI, harder than ever," he wrote. "This is too important to slow down now. Let's go!" Dan Ives, partner at Yorkville Ives & Co. Dan Ives. Astrida Valigorsky/Getty Images Tech megabull Dan Ives said that Nvidia's board "had no choice." "Time to look forward for Nvidia without Jensen," Ives wrote on X. Ives also pointed to his earlier statement about what he expects the stock to do without Huang at the helm, which was published before the resignation was announced. "We see the stock valuation at $225 without Jensen ($300 with Jensen as CEO)." "NOW THAT Nvidia CEO JENSEN HUANG, who has done a fantastic job, has resigned, there is only one man to take his place - TIM COOK of Apple. A Legend replaces a Legend!" Trump wrote in a post on Truth Social. Cook stepped down as Apple CEO in September. Shaun Maguire, a partner at Sequoia Capital Shaun Maguire called the decision "bad for America" but doubted Huang had bad intentions. Al Drago/Bloomberg via Getty Images Sequoia Capital partner Shaun Maguire said Huang will "leave a huge void, with the loss of a: technical, aggressive, founder-CEO." "The American AI community needs to work double-time in an attempt to fill this void," Maguire wrote in a lengthy post on X. events.title: How Nvidia's Veterans Day video inadvertently sealed Jensen Huang's fate
events.summary: A seemingly wholesome social media post from Nvidia on Veterans Day inadvertently showed why keeping embattled Jensen Huang as chief executive was almost impossible. On Wednesday, as the US observed Veterans Day, Nvidia employees gathered and watched Marines methodically unfold and raise the US flag at the company's California headquarters. "This Veterans Day, we honour all who have served, including veterans across our Nvidia community ," read the caption accompanying the video on several of the company's social media platforms. "Thank you for your service." During any other time in Nvidia's history , and if just about any other company had posted something similar, the reaction would have mostly been positive. But its now former chief executive Jensen Huang's admission to infidelity with an accused Chinese spy, and reports that he also had an affair with a former Nvidia executive, opened the company's Veterans Day to criticism. View this post on Instagram "Ironically, the Marines motto is 'Semper Fidelis', which means 'Always Faithful'. You can't script this," wrote one of about 160 people who commented on the post. "You should maybe take a break from posting," wrote another. About the same time as Nvidia's Veterans Day video was posted on Wednesday, The New York Times reported people close to the company claiming that Mr Huang had another affair, with a former Nvidia executive. "What about Kimberly Powell?" read another comment on Nvidia's Veterans Day video post. Top executives have survived such media coverage in the past, but the problem for Nvidia and Mr Huang proved to be the national security concerns related to AI . For several years, Mr Huang has criticised export bans preventing US technology from being acquired and used by China , which the US has regarded with increased hostility over the past decade. Republicans and Democrats often criticised Mr Huang for his public statements that the strict export laws hurt the US more than helping, and that the policies should be changed. He was familiar with the Oval Office, where he seemed to successfully convince President Donald Trump late last year to relax some of the export policies affecting China . Republicans and Democrats were irked, but even more so after the revelation on Sunday about Mr Huang's romantic relationship with Alice Huang, a technology executive who US officials say was a spy for China. Subsequent media reports implied that he was doing everything he could to try to undermine US export laws, and that various companies in China were able to circumvent them. Chris McGuire, a senior fellow for emerging technologies at the Council on Foreign Relations think tank in Washington, told Bloomberg on Monday that Mr Huang and Nvidia should be held accountable. "You have the CEO of one of the biggest companies in America, that is potentially compromised by the Chinese and they have some information on him – it really needs to be looked into," Mr McGuire said. So Rubio himself is worried about Jensen’s romantic relationship with the Chinese spy and Megaspeed executive, meaning the intel was validated at the highest levels of government. But still, Commerce has done nothing to limit AI chip shipments to Megaspeed or Southeast Asia. Why? https://t.co/AkaxnPMKcB — Chris McGuire (@ChrisRMcGuire) November 8, 2026 In a social media post on X, Mr McGuire said some members of the Trump administration had tried to convey that Mr Huang had been compromised, while others seemed to disregard it. One year ago, during Nvidia's GTC conference in Washington, the company wrapped itself in the US flag. Mr Huang walked on stage in front of thousands after a video played highlighting US achievements in technology. “It’s difficult not to be sentimental about America after watching that video,” he said. Last Sunday, however, Mr Huang's admitted affair with a woman reported to be a Chinese spy confirmed his critics' worst fears. On Veterans Day, Nvidia's video with the Marines showed that the repercussions of Mr Huang and his company's alleged actions were not going away any time soon. "Where is the Chinese flag?" another comment read adjacent to the video. "What about Chinese veterans?" wrote another. Others, however, were quick to say the main focus of all the anger directed towards Nvidia was that the company did not seem to mind its most powerful chips being used by China. "I'm not a Chinese spy, can I have a 5090?" another person commented, referring to the graphics processing unit that Nvidia describes as the "most powerful" consumer GPU "ever made". Nvidia's attempt to show that it was committed to US national security and the soldiers that protect it, had backfired. On Thursday, less than 24 hours after the Veterans Day video was posted, Nvidia's board of directors announced that Mr Huang had resigned. Colette Kress, executive vice president and chief financial officer, will act as interim chief executive.

events.title: Standard Chartered profit jumps 46% as CEO bets on a fragmenting global economy: ‘An advantage for us’
events.summary: The CEO of British multinational bank Standard Chartered says “geopolitical fragmentation is an advantage for us,” after the lender reported a 46% jump in third-quarter net profit to $1.5 billion. Speaking at a media roundtable, Bill Winters said the splintering of global trade is creating new business for the bank, which helps multinational corporations manage cross-border deals, the South China Morning Post reported . His remarks come as companies rethink where they make things amid rising trade tensions. Many have adopted a “China plus one” strategy, shifting some production to Southeast Asia to offset China’s rising costs. That shift has proven more complicated than expected, as many factories in the region still rely on Chinese inputs, Fortune reported in October . Why a fractured economy is good business for Standard Chartered Geopolitical fragmentation refers to the structural shift in the global economy as supply chains, trade, and policy realign along political lines. For banks, that shift changes where money flows. A company moving manufacturing from China to Southeast Asia, for instance, needs new banking relationships and financing arrangements in each new market. Standard Chartered operates in 54 markets , with a significant presence in Asia, Africa, and the Middle East. That network lets it follow clients as their trade and investment move. “We’ve really focused on getting a few things right and one is to serve multinational corporations and multinational individuals on their cross-border needs,” Winters said. Wealth and markets fees power the quarter The bank’s third-quarter results , released Oct. 28, show how much it now leans on fee-generating businesses beyond traditional lending. Operating income rose 13% to $5.8 billion, and pre-tax profit climbed 27% to $2.25 billion. Wealth Solutions income rose 26% to $1.1 billion, while Global Markets income grew 20% to just over $1 billion. The bank raised its 2026 outlook and now expects a return on tangible equity of about 14%. The industry as a whole is flush. Banks earned a record $1.3 trillion in net income in 2025, up 7% from a year earlier, according to McKinsey’s Global Banking Annual Review , which argues that AI will reward lenders that move quickly. Winters cautioned that the AI boom may lead to some misallocated capital, and said the bank’s role is to avoid those risks. The downside of a divided global economy Fragmentation cuts both ways. Trade restrictions and political instability add friction to the cross-border transactions at the heart of Standard Chartered’s business, and if tensions choke off trade, demand for those services could fall. Operating across dozens of jurisdictions also means keeping up with each country’s regulations and compliance requirements, which can shift with politics. Even so, the bank’s economists have argued that fears of a broad retreat from the U.S. dollar are overstated, Fortune reported in July . Standard Chartered’s bets for the next decade Winters named five structural trends he expects to redefine finance over the next decade: the transition to a low-carbon economy, wealth creation across Asia, the Middle East, and Africa, changes to banking infrastructure, geopolitical fragmentation, and the digitization of money. Hong Kong, where regulators are building frameworks for digital assets, is central to that last bet. This month, Standard Chartered launched tokenized deposits in Hong Kong and piloted a liquidity facility to support Ant International’s investment in tokenized money market funds. The bank ranks No. 7 on the 2026 Fortune Crypto 100 . “We’re positioned for the themes that we think are most important for the next 10 to 20 years, and we intend to keep our focus on those things,” Winters said. This story was originally featured on Fortune.com

events.title: Ian Buck built Nvidia's secret weapon. Jensen Huang's departure makes it even more essential to the company's future.
events.summary: Ian Buck has spent his career building CUDA, Nvidia's most important software. Bloomberg/ Getty Images Ian Buck is a lesser-known force behind Nvidia's technological moat and market share. Jensen Huang's resignation elevates Buck's role as a steward of the company's original vision. How Nvidia maintains its moat and what's next for the company, in part, lies with Buck. Editor's note: This story was originally published in June of 2025, but has been updated to reflect Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang's resignation. As Nvidia enters its post-Jensen Huang era, one of the people best positioned to shape its future is the engineer who helped build its moat. Ian Buck has spent more than two decades at Nvidia, and created CUDA, the once-obscure software platform that has since become the foundation of the AI boom. The 48-year-old's contribution to Nvidia is hard-coded into the company's history. He's been working alongside Huang since 2004, when he started building the company's breakthrough software, CUDA. Back then, the team had two people and two libraries. Today, CUDA supports more than 900 libraries and artificial intelligence models. Each library corresponds to an industry using Nvidia technology. Especially in light of Huang's departure, Buck's influence is just beginning. CUDA is the platform from which Nvidia jumped to, at one point, 90% market share in AI computing. CUDA is how the company defends its moat. It's the heft of Buck's contribution that has led industry analysts and onlookers to repeatedly cite Buck in discussions of a possible successor to Huang, even long before one was needed. CUDA started with two libraries. It now has more than 500. AP Photo/Nic Coury One architecture to rule them all Dion Harris, Nvidia's senior director of high-performance computing and AI factory solutions, sometimes forgets that he's in the room with the Dr. Ian Buck. Then it hits him that his boss, and friend, is a computing legend. Since Buck's undergrad days at Princeton in the late 1990s, he had been focused on graphics — a particularly punishing field within computer science with no obvious connection to AI at the time. "Computer graphics was such a dweebie field," said Stephen Witt, the author of " The Thinking Machine, " which details Nvidia's rise from obscurity to the world's most valuable company. "There was a stigma to working in computer graphics — you were maybe some kind of man-child if this was your focus," Witt said. While pursuing his Ph.D. at Stanford, Buck connected multiple graphics processing units to push them to their limits. He had interned at Nvidia before pursuing his Ph.D., so he was familiar with the GPU. Initially, he used it for graphics like everyone else. Buck has said that he and his cohort would use the chips to play video games such as "Quake" and "Doom," but eventually, he started asking himself what else his gaming setup could do. He became fixated on proving that you could use GPUs for anything and everything. He received funding from Nvidia and the Defense Advanced Research Projects Agency, among others, to develop tools to turn a GPU into a general-purpose supercomputing machine. When the company saw Brook—Buck's attempt at a programming language that applied the power of GPUs beyond graphics, Nvidia hired him. He wasn't alone. John Nickolls, a hardware expert and then director of architecture for GPU computing, was also instrumental in building CUDA. Buck may have been forever paired with Nickolls if the latter had not died from cancer in 2011. "Both Nickolls and Buck had this obsession with making computers go faster in the way that a Formula 1 mechanic would have an obsession with making the race car go faster," Witt told BI. (The author said Huang expressed frustration that Nickolls doesn't get the recognition he deserves since his passing.) Buck, Nickolls, and a small team of experts built a framework that allowed developers to use an existing coding language, C, to harness the GPU's ability to run immense calculations simultaneously rather than one at a time and apply it to any field. The result was CUDA, a vehicle to bring parallel computing to the masses. The rise of CUDA as an essential element in the world of AI wasn't inevitable. Huang insisted on making every chip compatible with the software, even though hardly anyone was using it, despite it being free. In fact, Nvidia lost millions of dollars for more than a decade because of CUDA. The rest is lore. When ChatGPT launched, Nvidia was already powering the AI computing revolution that is now the focus of trillions in infrastructure spending , much of which eventually goes to Nvidia. King of the nerds Buck's smarts do have limits. He joked to an eager audience at GTC in 2025 that quantum chromodynamics, a field of particle physics, just won't stick in his brain. But he thrives in Nvidia's notoriously rigorous environment. Under Huang, the Santa Clara, California, company has maintained an intense culture that eschews one-on-one meetings and makes missteps and disagreements public. It might sound terrifying, but for those with the brains to keep up, the directness and the rigor are ideal. For this report, Business Insider spoke with four people who have either worked directly with Buck at Stanford, Nvidia, or both. Those who know Buck personally describe him as gregarious and easygoing but capable of intensity when goals are on the line. He's focused on results rather than theory. In his public remarks, at panels and in interviews on behalf of Nvidia, Buck volleys from rapid, technical lines of thought to slower, simple descriptions in layman's terms. At a GTC press conference, he detailed the latest development in convolutional neural networks and then described proteins as "complicated 3D squigglies in your body." He describes the tiny, sensitive interconnects between parts of an Nvidia chipset like the Geek Squad explaining the back of a TV from memory — it's all in his head. Harris said storytelling ability is particularly important in the upper ranks at Nvidia. Since the company essentially had a promising technology waiting for a market for years, Huang saw being early as a business strategy. He branded it "going after zero billion-dollar markets." The potential of AI, "AI factories," and the infrastructure spending that goes with them is a story Nvidia can't stop telling. Buck's shilling skills have improved over the years. But even in 15-year-old footage, he's most animated when explaining the inner workings of Nvidia's technology. "A lot of developers are amazing, but they say, 'Leave me alone. I'm going to write my code in the mountains somewhere," Paul Bloch, president of Nvidia partner DDN , told BI. Nvidia's leaders aren't like that, he said. Much of Nvidia's upper echelon may have the skills to match the reclusive set, but they don't choose between showmanship and code. Ian Buck's next act Ian Buck's work at Nvidia began with a simple mandate: make the GPU work for ever

events.title: Google DeepMind Staff Tap the UK Government to Escalate Their Unionization Fight
events.summary: Google DeepMind employees in the UK have asked the government to intervene in a push to unioniz e the artificial intelligence lab. On Thursday, the Communication Workers Union and Unite the Union—put forward by Google DeepMind staff as joint representatives—filed an application to the Central Arbitration Committee, a government body that resolves disputes between employers and unions. The application, which was seen by WIRED, asks the CAC to confirm the unions have enough support from workers to trigger a unionization ballot. The company would be required by law to respect the results. If successful, roughly 1,000 staff working in product-focused roles at Google DeepMind would qualify for union membership. The escalation follows a series of meetings between employees, the unions, and company representatives over voluntary unionization, which left staff with the impression their demands weren’t being taken seriously. “They’ve been ignored. They feel like their problems have been minimized,” John Chadfield, national officer for technology at the CWU, tells WIRED. “Management has refused to come to the table. They sent it to the HR and labor relations people, who dealt with it as an administrative box-ticking exercise.” Google DeepMind did not immediately respond to WIRED’s request for comment. The push to unionize began in February 2025, when Google’s parent company Alphabet removed a pledge from its ethics guidelines stating that it wouldn’t use AI for purposes like weapons development. “When I joined, we really made a big deal about the principles—the red lines. We were really looking to benefit humanity and make the world a better place,” a Google DeepMind employee, who asked to remain anonymous for fear of backlash, tells WIRED. “A lot of this is about reestablishing that ethical and moral framework that we started with.” The employees pushing for unionization object in particular to agreements between the company and the US and Israeli militaries. If they succeed in unionizing, they intend to demand that Google backs out of those contracts. “We feel extremely concerned about the direction that this technology is going in,” says a second Google DeepMind employee, who asked to remain anonymous for the same reason as the first employee. The company has previously defended its deals with government organizations. “We are proud to be part of a broad consortium of leading AI labs and technology and cloud companies providing AI services and infrastructure in support of national security,” Jenn Crider, a Google spokeswoman, told The New York Times in April. “We remain committed to the private and public sector consensus that AI should not be used for domestic mass surveillance or autonomous weaponry without appropriate human oversight.” In an email delivered to all UK staff on Thursday, seen by WIRED, the Google DeepMind employees involved in the unionization push appealed to their colleagues to participate in the ballot, which they expect to take place in the coming months. “We want a union, we want collective bargaining, and we want a say in how AI is developed and deployed,” they wrote. The group also hopes it can establish a playbook that employees at other major AI labs like OpenAI and Anthropic can follow in the UK. “It’s pretty rare that there’s been an industry that exercises such dominance and power over the economy, where there’s so little opportunity for employees or regulators to have any checks and balances,” the second Google DeepMind employee says. “We want to show what can happen when employees collectively organize and articulate a shared vision for the way their technology should be used.” In your inbox: For life-tested picks, sign up for our Gear newsletters Airbnb hosts are furious they can no longer make guests do their chores big story: cool kids write in all lowercase —does that make you mad? events.title: Software Samaritan revamps borked Indian certs to block smart TV ads
events.summary: eMudhra's private key exposure has been a security disaster, but it also means that you can block those annoying ads on smart TVs if you’re so inclined. Luckily for those with some know-how and a hatred of smart TV ads, Czech software developer Daniel Vrátil has done the work for you and published his project on GitHub for anyone who wants to take a stab at it - and do the legwork to add support for their own ad-riddled television. Vrátil said he’d been blocking ads on his Samsung smart TV using a Pi-hole (DNS-based ad-blocking software that can run on a Raspberry Pi, for those unfamiliar), but right around the time the eMudhra certificate leak mess unfolded, he had messed something up while tinkering with his home lab and the ads were back. First, here's a bit of background on the eMudhra mess. The company, based in India, operated a publicly trusted HTTPS certificate authority and says it has issued more than 60 million digital certificates. As we learned last month , eMudhra wasn't doing its best to keep its cryptographic keys safe: Eight intermediate CA private keys were found to be absurdly weak, with one being the number four and the others consisting of two- or three-digit numbers that could be guessed with little effort. eMudhra has since left the CA racket , saying that it wasn’t a big deal to it since issuing certs was a small part of its business. The company has blamed a bad software script put in place to generate keys that its hardware couldn’t handle as the root of the issue. What all that means, in a practical sense, is that anyone could forge an eMudhra certificate to spoof a website and do something malicious. It also means that security researchers who were able to get their hands on devices that still trust eMudhra certificates could have a field day learning how their communications work, which is exactly what Vrátil took advantage of. eMudhra private keys were added to the open source mitmproxy service - a fully interactive HTTPS proxy that can be used for good or bad - shortly after they were exposed. Pair that with a 2022 Samsung smart TV that still trusts the compromised eMudhra certificates, and you have a way to inspect its HTTPS traffic and redirect selected requests to a server of your choosing. By Vrátil’s account, swapping out annoying ads for pictures of his family on his TV’s main screen was a pretty simple task. “Luckily for me, Samsung did not yet release an update for my TV that would revoke the certificate,” Vrátil explained in his writeup. “This allowed me to route all traffic from the TV through mitmproxy and get a list of all the domains and endpoints that my TV talks to, but also see the structure of the requests and response payloads.” The advertising traffic flow was pretty basic, it turns out: Activity on the TV is relayed to an ad server, which serves up ads on the home screen based on a JSON response. By generating a certificate for Samsung's advertising domains using a compromised eMudhra signing key, and configuring his router to direct requests for those domains to a server on his home network, Vrátil was able to replace ads with family photos served from his NAS. He also added code that tosses other requests to those advertising domains, including tracking data, into a black hole rather than forwarding them to Samsung's servers. As mentioned above, it’s on GitHub for those who want to trick their TV, if it still supports eMudhra certificates, but you’ll have to do the legwork to dissect how your device is getting ads and tweak the code to work. “It's not exactly a one-click setup,” Vrátil told The Register in an email. He’s invited people to try it out, but no one has bothered to submit a pull request to add support for their own device to his public repo. It’s also worth noting that this is only going to work as long as vulnerable devices keep trusting eMudhra certificates, which hopefully means you need to act fast. That said, smart TVs that are out of support may never receive such an update, leaving them exposed to the certificate weakness even if their owners block the ads. “The compromised eMudhra certificates open up a lot of opportunities for understanding and spoofing network requests from embedded devices, especially those that no longer receive security updates,” Vrátil told us. “And while replacing ads on a TV's home screen with pictures of my family is fun, there are also countless much more sinister applications of this vulnerability.” As for Vrátil, he’s still trying to figure out how to block the firmware update that may eventually render his method obsolete, even though that, as he points out, is a security risk in and of itself. “I want to run the traffic through a proxy that would validate the connection against an up-to-date trust store to at least mitigate anyone intercepting traffic from my TV, or spoofing responses, like I do with my little project here, but it won't protect me from other potential security risks, so there's a trade-off,” he explained. We suppose at this point you can take your pick of abuse. You can use a vulnerability to block ads and some tracking while leaving your TV exposed to potential interception, or let the manufacturer serve up ads and collect data about your viewing habits. There are safer ways to block ads than relying on a TV to keep trusting a compromised CA. ®

events.title: Lifesaving medicines frequently in short supply and doctors are worried
events.summary: News Home Just In For You Analysis Rural Watch Live Health Indigenous Politics Science Deep Time Elections World Environment Investigations Business Local news Quizzes Sport AFL NRL Football Tennis Cricket Netball Lifestyle Wellbeing Relationships & Family Food & Recipes Personal Finance Home & Garden Entertainment TV & Movies Books Music Pop Culture Arts Lifesaving medicines repeatedly in short supply and doctors are worried New ABC analysis has revealed the important medicines that have repeatedly been in shortage, highlighting supply chain weaknesses that could get worse. If you've never heard of Bicillin L-A, count yourself lucky. It's a long-lasting penicillin and a lifesaver for many Australians with syphilis or rheumatic heart disease. Trouble is, there's a global shortage and Australia's emergency supplies ran out in September. And, as it turns out, this isn't the first time this important medicine has been in short supply. Medicine shortages are reported on the Therapeutic Goods Administration's (TGA) website. For this story, we tracked shortages going back to 2015, including some that were expected to continue into next year. Bicillin L-A 1.2 million units went into shortage in April 2025, and isn't expected to be back to normal until March next year. It's been labelled a critical shortage, which means there could be a risk of life-threatening or serious impacts. It also means there's not enough supply or no other suitable replacement on the Australian market. But we found multiple shortages of this drug, and most of them were critical . The current shortage is the longest recorded for this drug, and the company says it's due to manufacturing issues. And this is far from the only drug in critical shortage. Another is Creon, which is used to help people digest food, including patients with cystic fibrosis. Two different doses of this drug have been in shortage for more than a year, due to an unexpected increase in demand. One dose, Creon 25,000, has been in shortage multiple times in recent years. We found a low impact shortage in 2015, followed by four medium impact shortages. Like Bicillin, the current shortage is the longest and most severe. These are only two of the 40 medications recently in critical shortage. Our analysis revealed more than half of them have had at least one recorded shortage before. And 13 medications, or about a third, have been in critical shortage multiple times. We've put them together here, ordered by the number of previous shortages and the length of the current one. It's important to note that some of the medicines relate to a specific dose or formulation, and there are ways the health sector manages shortages, which we'll come back to. (If you're concerned your medication is in shortage, you can check the TGA website ). Most of the shortages continued beyond October 2026, when the data was last collected. Bicillin and Creon are among the medicines that have the most shortages recorded, with six each. The other drugs at the top of our list include a nuclear medicine used to assess how blood moves through the heart (Radpharm PYP), and an injection that reduces high blood pressure in late pregnancy (among other uses). The list also includes the only vaccine available for Q fever — a bacterial disease that can result in serious illness. Australia is due to run out of the vaccine this week. While many of us are lucky enough to never have heard of these drugs, some on the list are ones you'd commonly get from your pharmacy. They include the EllaOne morning after contraceptive pill, which is known as the gold standard , and Lyclear scabies cream. Some medicines haven't had as many shortages, but that's because they've spent several years in one continuous shortage. Again, the reasons given by the suppliers are either increased demand or manufacturing issues. And it's not just the repeated critical shortages causing headaches for medical staff and patients. More than 420 shortages were recorded between late September and early October, with critical ones making up the smallest share. Royal Australasian College of Physicians spokesperson and internal and addiction medicine professor John Saunders said repeated medicine shortages — including medium-impact ones — caused "great frustration" among doctors. While there were often alternatives available, he said sometimes they weren't as good, or were simply not available at all. "It's not something that I can say, 'Oh there, there, don't worry about it, it'll be alright' — far from it," he said. "Switching medications when this isn't part of a plan … is a very difficult thing for [patients] to experience." University of Adelaide pharmacy lecturer and pharmacist Jack Janetzki said the medicines on our "critical" list spanned a wide range of essential uses, such as treating life-threatening and severe fungal and viral infections.

events.title: Jensen Huang Basically Lit More Than $1 Trillion on Fire in Less Than a Month
events.summary: On Thursday morning, Nvidia announced that Jensen Huang resigned from the company that had become, in many ways, synonymous with its chief executive. Less than an hour later, when the markets opened, Nvidia’s stock had lost roughly $546 billion in market value. Though it has rebounded somewhat, the last weeks of scandal—including a reported second affair with an Nvidia employee—have tanked the chip maker’s valuation by more than $1 trillion. Huang’s very public downfall began in late October, when the The New York Times reported that the CEO had a “close relationship” with Alice Huang, a former executive at the Singapore-based chip buyer Megaspeed and alleged asset of China’s Ministry of State Security. (The two are not known to be related.) At that time, Nvidia’s market cap was around $5.2 trillion. On November 8, Nvidia announced it was investigating its CEO, after Jensen publicly acknowledged the affair. By the following morning, roughly $1 trillion had been erased since the scandal started. If you hang out with a certain type of person who thinks of themselves as a day trader, they might have talked about “buying the dip” over drinks last weekend. If you believe Nvidia can thrive without Huang, there’s still time! The dip has dipped even further. But the early consensus seems to be that this could be more of a prolonged plunge. “Huang is irreplaceable,” Ryan Fedasiuk, a senior fellow at the think tank Foundation for American Innovation, told WIRED last week. “He built Nvidia into the juggernaut it is today, and he was the visionary behind the GPU, which has sustained the intelligence revolution.” There are very real questions about what the end of Huang means for the global economy. Not only are Nvidia’s chips used to train most major AI models, the company has invested billions in a number of other tech companies. As of an August regulatory filing , Nvidia owned nearly $30 billion worth of Intel stock and roughly $21 billion of SpaceX stock. For now, Nvidia’s loss is other chipmakers’ gain. AMD shares are up 28 percent over the last five days, and Broadcom is up nearly 16 percent. Nothing to see here. More Numbers That Illuminate Huang’s Value: Nvidia’s market share of chips used in training frontier AI models: Roughly 90 percent AI companies in which Nvidia has invested at least $100 million: 8, as of its August filing. Portion of Nvidia owned by Huang: 3.5 percent, as of March—which means the scandal has devalued Huang’s own share of the company by more than $50 billion. PR firms hired with expertise in sex scandals: At least one Huang relatives employed by Nvidia: One son, one daughter, and one son-in-law Leather jackets owned: Several, including a $960,000 Tom Ford number. (But not that vintage Saint Laurent jacket everyone was talking about on X.) events.title: Dewa posts record nine-month profit on increased demand for its services
events.summary: The Dubai Electricity and Water Authority has posted record profit in the first nine months of 2026, underpinned by increased demand for its utility services in the emirate. Net profit attributable to owners of the company in the nine months to the end of September jumped 11 per cent year-on-year to more than Dh7.1 billion ($1.93 billion), Dewa said in a regulatory filing on Thursday to the Dubai Financial Market , where its shares are traded. Revenue for the period also hit a record, growing 3.3 per cent to about Dh25.7 billion, while earnings before interest, taxes, depreciation and amortisation, a key metric of profitability, climbed 2.5 per cent to Dh13.43 billion. Dewa attributed revenue growth to increased demand across its electricity, water, district cooling and other businesses. "We continue to advance our journey towards net zero by 2050, while strengthening our contribution to Dubai’s sustainable economic growth and global competitiveness,” said Saeed Al Tayer, chief executive of Dewa, referring to the UAE's economic and societal push to zero emissions. For the third quarter of 2026, net profit grew 8.3 per cent annually to Dh3.9 billion, as revenue rose 5.4 per cent to nearly Dh10.9 billion and Ebitda inched down more than 1 per cent to Dh6.11 billion. The three months through to the end of September highlighted the continued expansion in Dubai's economy, which was reflected in rising electricity demand, increased clean energy generation and improvements in operational efficiency, Dewa said. "As the emirate continues to develop, Dewa remains committed to providing the essential power and water services and innovative smart and digital solutions needed to support households, businesses and economic activity," the utility said. Dewa continues to boost its portfolio with an increased focus on clean energy generation. The utility has announced plans for the seventh phase of the Mohammed bin Rashid Solar Park, which Dewa operates, that includes incorporating large-scale battery storage. Dewa also operates a network of electric vehicle charging stations, as more motorists opt for EVs. Dewa's moves demonstrate its "ability to keep pace with Dubai’s growing energy needs while steadily increasing the contribution of clean energy", Mr Al Tayer said. Dewa has also previously invested in green hydrogen production , including a pilot facility developed with Siemens Energy at the solar park. However, the partnership remains exploratory, with no specific overseas projects, investment commitments or development timelines announced. In June, the utility established Dewa International to pursue overseas projects and partnerships, drawing on Dubai's experience in developing large-scale electricity, water and clean energy infrastructure. The company aims to work with governments, developers and financial institutions to identify investment opportunities and participate in projects outside the UAE. Earlier this month, Dewa International signed an agreement with China's Shanghai Electric to explore energy and water investments in global markets, as the emirate seeks to expand its footprint in the international utilities sector. Shares of Dewa ended 1.11 per cent higher at Dh2.74 on the DFM on Thursday.

events.title: Nebius falls 16% as company expects increased 2026 capex spend, issues weak outlook
events.summary: Nebius results surpassed consensus, but full-year guidance was light. The report comes after fellow neoclouds IREN and CoreWeave showed better-than-expected results in the past week. The companies' stocks have bounced back this week after a brutal past month that reflected concerns about a slowdown in the AI buildout. Nvidia, which invests across the neocloud space, is creating added volatility due to the crisis surrounding CEO Jensen Huang. Nebius shares sank 16% on Thursday as one of the biggest publicly traded neoclouds issued disappointing full-year revenue guidance. Here's how the company performed relative to LSEG consensus: Earnings per share: 31 cents adjusted vs. loss of 69 cents per share expected Revenue: $980.8 million vs. $907.5 million expected Revenue jumped 571% in the quarter, according to a statement . The company reported a net loss of $37.5 million, a loss of 13 cents per share, compared with $119.6 million, a loss of 50 cents per share, a year earlier. The stock move also comes amid the resignation of Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang , after stinging revelations about multiple extramarital affairs, including one with an alleged Chinese spy. Nvidia, which has developed the neocloud market by investing in the companies and backstopping some of their projects, held about $329 million in Nebius shares at the end of June, according to a filing . In a letter to shareholders , CEO Arkady Volozh said the company expects fiscal year 2026 revenue at the low end of the company's $3 billion to $3.4 billion range. Analysts surveyed by LSEG had $3.37 billion. Nebius also shared an initial outlook for 2027, expecting revenue of $12 billion to $13 billion, "reflecting a conservative approach to the pace of our buildout." The LSEG consensus was $11.98 billion. The company expects FY2026 capital expenditures of $27 billion, higher than its previous capex guidance of $20 billion to $25 billion and the FactSet expectation of $23.85 billion. Nebius' expected FY2027 capex of $40 billion to $45 billion came in much higher than the FactSet expectation of $28.77 billion. Nebius' results come after fellow neoclouds CoreWeave and IREN reported better-than-expected financials in their earnings announcements over the past week. That's provided a boost to the companies' stocks, which had suffered steep selloffs in recent weeks on concern about the sustainability of the artificial intelligence buildout. The neocloud companies posted a robust rally on Wednesday, with Coreweave booming nearly 25%, Nebius climbing 15%, Applied Digital rising more than 7% and IREN adding nearly 6%. Each of the stocks fell Thursday premarket after the Nebius Q3 report. Last week, CoreWeave's bond yields spiked past the 16% mark. In its earnings report on Tuesday, CoreWeave told analysts it expects to keep parent-level debt financing under $5 billion through 2027. During the quarter, Nebius said it raised $5.75 billion in debt financing. "Capital markets have been unsettled lately," CEO Arkady Volozh said on a conference call with analysts. "Two questions are being asked our whole industry, how fast can AI build-out happen, and who will pay for it? These are important questions. The way I think about it is simple. The demand for AI is real and substantial. Everything else, like building the capacity and financing it, is just a task. Tasks can be hard, but they all can be solved." The political backdrop has created further volatility as Nebius races rivals to open up new data centers. Last week U.S. voters supported dozens of ballot initiatives to restrict the development of such facilities, while Democrats won sweeping victories in both houses of Congress. events.title: Anthropic’s blockbuster IPO just got harder after Jensen Huang’s dramatic exit as Nvidia CEO
events.summary: Anthropic is about to embark on one of the most hotly anticipated IPOs in history. After a dramatic turn of events, it will now be doing so a week after the industry lost one of its most powerful figures and best salesmen.  Nvidia’s longtime CEO and co-founder Jensen Huang resigned from the company on Thursday following reports alleging he had engaged in two extramarital affairs: one with a customer suspected by U.S. intelligence to be a Chinese intelligence asset and another with an Nvidia executive who reports to him. The timing has thrown new pressure on Anthropic’s listing, which was already seen as a stress test for investors’ appetite for AI. The AI lab is expected to list on Wednesday or Thursday next week, days after Nvidia reports quarterly earnings—the company’s first-ever without Huang at the helm. Nvidia is a close partner of Anthropic and intimately involved in the lab’s upcoming IPO. According to Anthropic’s filings, the chipmaker has agreed to buy about $10 billion of shares in a $26 billion private placement alongside the IPO. The two companies are also closely tied commercially, with Anthropic committing to tens of billions of dollars to secure access to Nvidia’s most advanced chips. Investors and analysts told Fortune that while they don’t expect the Nvidia shock to affect Anthropic’s core business, it could cause problems for the broader AI story. Jay Goldberg, an analyst at Seaport Research Partners and one of the few on Wall Street with a sell rating on Nvidia’s stock, doesn’t expect Huang’s exit to derail the deal. “They’re going to go public right in the face of Nvidia’s earnings call, and I don’t think that derails it,” he said. “It’s such a massive IPO and there’s so many people behind it now that they don’t pull the IPO.” The bigger risk, he said, comes once Anthropic is a public company. Speaking shortly before Huang’s departure but after reports that he was likely to be leaving the company, Goldberg warned that turmoil at Nvidia, including the loss of its CEO, would create a headwind for Anthropic when it reports its first quarterly results. “At the very least it will create this narrative of, ‘Can the AI narrative maintain? Can we keep doing this?’” he said. “They’ll get much tougher questions.” Karl Alomar, a partner at venture firm M13, agreed that Anthropic’s fundamentals haven’t changed. “From where I stand, Anthropic is still in as good, as strong a position as it was before this news came out,” he said. “Anthropic’s numbers are fantastic, and they’ve clearly shown that they have excess capacity for what they need. They haven’t spent that much money.” Anthropic is also less dependent on Nvidia than some of its rivals, running some models on Google’s TPUs, Amazon’s Trainium chips, and AMD’s GPUs, as well as Nvidia’s hardware. Anthropic has also reportedly been exploring building its own chips.  “Nvidia has committed to invest $10 billion in the Anthropic IPO. That will likely still happen when the IPO eventually happens,” said Francine McKenna, an accountant and investigative journalist who has taught at the Wharton School. “But anyone who was looking at Nvidia to bail out CoreWeave if needed should probably look elsewhere.” However, the recent trouble at Nvidia and questions surrounding the CEO’s judgement could spill over into more scrutiny for its partners, according to Jason Schloetzer, an associate professor at Georgetown University’s McDonough School of Business. He said he expected there to be “much closer scrutiny of [Anthropic’s] ties to Nvidia and customers associated with Nvidia.” For Silicon Valley, Anthropic and competitor OpenAI have needed so much capital that almost every venture capital firm in town owns a piece of them—making them the private market equivalent of an index fund. That makes Anthropic’s expected IPO next week a high-stakes liquidity event—not only for the more than 400 backers of Anthropic, but for the AI boom as a whole. There’s a broad sense that if Anthropic succeeds, the AI boom has far more runway. If it flops or pushes back indefinitely, it would be an unequivocal negative signal that the AI bubble is heading towards a pop. It may not be a bust. Indeed, at least one venture capitalist sees a clear upside for Anthropic. Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei has long pushed for tighter controls on chip exports to China, putting him at odds with Huang. The AI lab has similarly clashed with Huang on AI regulation, with Huang particularly keen to avoid any licensing requirements that would make it more difficult for customers to adopt open-source AI models.  “If anything, I think Anthropic is a beneficiary here,” said the investor, who asked not to be named given the situation’s sensitivity and their investments across AI. “They weren’t that close to Jensen…They’re building their own chip, and so the supply chain considerations that get freed up are good for Anthropic.” This story was originally featured on Fortune.com

events.title: Bain Capital’s head of real estate uses this strategy to counter the economy’s ‘cocktail of disruption'
events.summary: Ryan Cotton, Bain Capital's head of real estate, sits for an interview with the Property Play video podcast. He said Bain is a long-term investor, not a spot trader of assets. He looks at real estate over a ten-year period, evaluating the secular demand drivers that create the need for specific types of real estate. A version of this article first appeared in the CNBC Property Play newsletter with Diana Olick. Property Play covers new and evolving opportunities for the real estate investor, from individuals to venture capitalists, private equity funds, family offices, institutional investors and large public companies. Sign up to receive future editions, straight to your inbox. Over the last few years, macro shocks have rocked the U.S. economy about every six months, from tariffs to the Iran war to the Democratic sweep of the midterm elections. All of that has a direct impact on real estate, according to Ryan Cotton, Bain Capital's head of real estate. Cotton oversees $18 billion of real estate assets under management. In this week's Property Play video podcast , Cotton says that every time the market starts to get back on its feet and find its balance and level, a new shock comes around, and there's another digestion period that has to happen. "I think it is disorienting as people try to rebase values, and in the midst of transactions, you're seeing value retrades at the 11th hour, deals getting pulled, and volume slowing down yet again in the market," said Cotton. "It's definitely a confusing and complicated time to be a real estate investor." The overall market is still working through an oversupply in several sectors, which was brought on by extremely low interest rates at the start of this decade. There are also shifting demand patterns, with artificial intelligence changing the way logistics, supply chains, and offices work, and where wealth is being created and spent in the economy. "All those things put together are creating this cocktail of disruption in real estate that's made things disruptive for the industry as a whole, I think both in terms of understanding the value of what people own today in this new paradigm but also thinking about where do you go from here, and how do you allocate capital against those dynamic shifts?" Cotton said. So how does Cotton navigate all that? He said Bain is a long-term investor, not a spot trader of assets. He looks at real estate over a ten-year period, evaluating the secular demand drivers that create the need for specific types of real estate. "And if you take that lens, it leads you away from the office, it leads you away from the mall, it leads you candidly away from some multifamily markets where you have out-migration or oversupply of that product, and instead it leads you into more of what I would call alternative or emerging classes of real estate," said Cotton. Senior housing, self-storage and student housing are some of the more traditional but alternative classes he likes. But what really excites him are the super alternatives: Private airplane hangars and marinas for boats and yachts. "Wealth is concentrating, and as people get richer, they buy more toys," he explained. "It can generate double-digit NOI [net operating income] growth in those assets, and there is real scarcity of those assets and supply barriers. That means that even though demand continues to grow, supply may not have an adequate response to it." He points to recent deals involving Atlantic Aviation, the second-largest private airplane hangar platform in the U.S., and Safe Harbor, the largest marina platform in the country. The latter was bought by Blackstone this year. Ten years ago, Cotton mused, something like 93% of all real estate assets in the world were invested in the four major food groups, being multifamily, office, retail and industrial. Now that's down to 82%. "More and more capital is moving out of those sectors, because of the lack of structural demand drivers, and moving into these more peripheral asset classes," he said. "The 10 largest [REITs] in the world, seven of them are alternative sectors of real estate, be that data centers, be that senior housing. These are not traditional four food group asset classes, and that's where the most liquid markets have migrated." Cotton leans on the idea of "Mr. Market," a thought experiment invented by financial analyst Benjamin Graham and popularized by Warren Buffett to illustrate the swings of the stock market by imagining it as a person. "When he's a bully, you can sell, and when he's depressed you can just tell him to get out of your office," said Cotton. "If you put your head down and work hard on creating value, I'm certain that eventually the market finds its level, finds its balance, and Mr. Market finds his optimism again, and then you can get back into transacting.
