events.title: Jensen Huang built an AI kingdom. Now he’s gone, will Nvidia’s ramparts be breached?
events.summary: CEO’s affair and resignation has brought company’s murky corporate contracts and supply chains into sharp focus Can the AI economy survive without its “central bank”? What does Jensen Huang’s fall mean for the world’s second-most valuable company, and what might a tremor in its fortunes mean for the world? Nvidia’s sky-high valuation is based on the fact that it designs and sells the advanced AI chips, called graphics processing units (GPUs), that underpin the AI economy. Without these, AI models such as ChatGPT and Claude could not be trained and would not run. This has made the chipmaker arguably the most important player in AI and, at times, the most valuable company in the world. Huang’s departure sent shares in Nvidia plunging 13% in early trading. Nvidia is not the only company that designs these chips. Most leading tech companies, including Microsoft , Meta and Google, are trying to make their own lines of AI chips. Some of these, such as Google’s tensor processing units, appear to be at least as good as Nvidia’s, and even better for certain purposes. What makes Nvidia irreplaceable – and far more integral to the AI economy – is its web of relationships, most of these led by Huang himself . One aspect of this is Nvidia’s complex web of ties with the companies actually building AI infrastructure, a mess of circular finance that implicates US tech giants and many of the world’s governments. In recent years, Huang has been the kingmaker when it comes to AI. In 2025, he met numerous world leaders – including Mohammed bin Salman, Keir Starmer and Emmanuel Macron – persuading them of the urgency of developing “sovereign AI” with his product. His presence served as a guarantee of those nations’ AI plans. These meetings were followed by deals in which Nvidia announced it had arrangements to supply those governments with precious, hard-to-get chips. None of these agreements were particularly transparent. While Nvidia appears to have promised 260,000 advanced chips to South Korea, for example, it was never immediately apparent when those chips would be delivered, who would pay for them, and on what terms. Meanwhile, Nvidia financed a web of companies called “neoclouds” to buy its chips and put them in datacentres, there to be rented to the world’s biggest AI companies. These neoclouds have done wonders for Nvidia, propping up demand and keeping the risk associated with building datacentres and finding customers for them off its balance sheets. Neoclouds are not the only thing financed by Nvidia. It has become known as the “central bank of AI” because it is enmeshed in almost every layer of the AI economy. Nvidia has invested in a spate of AI startups that could become future customers. It has offered massive sums of cash to companies such as OpenAI , to be used to buy its chips. This investment runs to hundreds of billions of dollars of Nvidia’s money, circling again and again through a limited set of accounts. Then there is Nvidia’s relationship with a Taiwanese company called TSMC, or the Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Company. TSMC makes the world’s AI chips, churning them out across several fabrication plants on the north-west of the island. As far as geopolitics goes, TSMC is arguably more important than Nvidia or any other chip designer. Other companies can design AI chips, but TSMC manufactures the overwhelming majority of them and has no real competitor. This is because manufacturing AI chips is one of the most expensive and challenging industrial processes to date. Each chip is etched with nanometre lines by lasers working in the extreme ultraviolet spectrum, which cost billions of dollars and two decades of research to develop. While TSMC has refined its process to make these chips for more than two decades, it still has only a 60% yield rate for its most advanced chips, which means that 40% of them have defects. It’s a staggeringly high rate for one of the world’s most expensive technologies. Nvidia has worked closely with TSMC to help it develop its processes and products. Lore has it that Huang wrote the chief executive of TSMC a letter introducing himself in 1997. These are high-trust relationships built over decades. Will it all be the same without Huang? This is almost impossible to answer because Nvidia’s relationships are so opaque. Investigators following the supply chain of its chips run up against secretive corporate contracts and tangled export records. There is known to be a years-long queue of customers waiting to obtain its chips, but questions regarding who is in that queue, in what order, and how many chips have been shipped remain open. This murkiness was brought into sharp focus by Megaspeed, a small Singaporean company that was getting access to lots of GPUs, even as other companies struggled. One of Megaspeed’s executives, Alice Huang, was later revealed to be having an affair with Nvidia’s chief executive, and to be an alleged Chinese spy.

events.title: Scout Motors has 212,000 vehicle reservations as $2 billion South Carolina plant nears completion
events.summary: Scout Motors has roughly 212,000 reservations for its Terra pickup and Traveler SUV, CEO Scott Keogh told CNBC. Construction of Scout's more than $2 billion South Carolina Production Center is in its final phase. Keogh said roughly 87% of reservations are for extended-range models and about 75% are for the Traveler SUV. BLYTHEWOOD, S.C. — Electric vehicle startup Scout Motors has notched roughly 212,000 reservations for its upcoming EVs as the company nears completion of its new $2 billion plant in South Carolina, CEO Scott Keogh told CNBC. The reservations are for the Volkswagen -backed company's Terra pickup truck and Traveler SUV, which are expected to start full production next year before deliveries begin to customers in 2028. Reservations do not necessarily translate to sales, as the U.S. automotive industry has learned during the past decade, especially with highly anticipated all-electric trucks such as the Ford F-150 Lightning, Tesla Cybertruck and others that garnered strong interest that didn't lead to meaningful numbers of purchases. Keogh said he expects Scout could roughly double those reservations by the time customer production begins, but he said the more important thing is to convert early interest into actual sales as production nears. "It's been a consistent drumbeat," Keogh said during an interview at Scout's plant site outside Columbia, South Carolina. "I think we could easily be up over 400,000 with reservations without doing too much effort. The big thing for us is how much of the initial production can we 100% presell." Keogh said achieving an order book of 12-to-18 months "would be great" and something he thinks the company can do before production. Scout on Thursday said construction is "in its final phase." Scout's vehicles will be offered as all-electric versions as well as electric hybrid variants, known as extended-range electric vehicles , or EREVs, that include an engine as a backup generator for the electric motors and batteries. Scout, a former American vehicle brand from 1961 to 1980, was expected to exclusively offer EVs in a bid for the German automaker to expand its presence in the U.S. However, slower-than-expected adoption of EVs and higher costs led the company to decide to offer EREVs as well. Keogh said the EREVs and SUV are dominating reservations thus far, with roughly 87% choosing EREV models and 75% being SUVs. The CEO also said the company is drawing interest from its target markets, which include owners of off-road vehicles such as the Ford Bronco and Jeep Wrangler as well as full-size pickup trucks and U.S. EV leader Tesla Given the interest signaled by reservations, Keogh said the company is expected to launch with the EREVs first, followed by the EVs. He also said the company plans to launch with mid-level models first, a deviation from many companies that begin with their highest-priced models. Both the Traveler and Terra are expected to start under $60,000. The EREV models are expected to feature more than 500 miles of range, according to the company, compared with 300 miles of range for the all-electric models. "The No.1 thing for me is I want to go get the best volume as soon as possible," Keogh said. "In my mind, it's how quick can you get to 100,000 units? It's at 100,000 units where you can start to punch through." His comments come months after Rivian Automotive received criticism online for launching its R2 SUV with its highest-priced models first, despite that being a common practice across the automotive industry. Keogh said Scout's South Carolina plant is about 85% complete, but supporting infrastructure and a $300 million supplier park continue to be installed. Reservations for Scout's vehicles initially opened in October 2024, when it revealed the Traveler and Terra , which feature sleek, yet rugged, exterior appearances that pay some homage to the brand's historic models.

events.title: Analysis: Nvidia’s leadership crisis tests the chipmaker’s role as the ‘central bank of AI’
events.summary: Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang resigned Thursday follow revelations that he had extramarital affairs. Nvidia has made substantial financial commitments to AI infrastructure companies, including cloud-service purchases and project guarantees. The Federal Reserve and other financial institutions are examining how leverage and interconnected financing could amplify an AI downturn. Financial experts distinguish potential losses for technology investors from the more serious risk of losses spreading through banks and credit markets. Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang 's shock resignation is raising a worrying question: Could trouble at the chipmaker spread through the tightly connected financial network Nvidia has built to support the artificial intelligence boom? Follow CNBC's live coverage of Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang's resignation Serious problems with Nvidia could do far-reaching economic and financial damage. The company has made hundreds of billions of dollars in financial commitments to other firms to help the industry grow, earning it the nickname the "central bank of AI." The Federal Reserve and other financial institutions are closely watching the AI buildout to monitor for the possibility that an unexpected event could destabilize the global financial system. Even back in July Fed officials were discussing the possibility of a "broad-based repricing of assets" in the event of problems in the AI sector. A rerun of the 2007-2008 financial crisis isn't likely, according to analysts and current and former financial officials. Nvidia isn't "too big to fail in a bank sense at all," said Sheila Bair, a former government regulator who ran the Federal Deposit Insurance Corp. Unlike a troubled bank, Nvidia isn't vulnerable to a sudden loss of confidence and would still produce a product customers want to buy even if something went wrong. And its massive equity gives it a cushion. But regulators need to watch carefully for exposure by the banks and the wider financial system to Nvidia and other firms like it, Bair said. "Nvidia going down would be a pretty seismic event," she said. Nvidia live updates: Jensen Huang agrees to testify before Congress following resignation Who is Colette Kress? Nvidia's finance chief steps in as interim CEO after Huang exit PRO: Buy Nvidia with 'both hands' because the valuation is at 'stupid' levels, says analyst Meeks Read what interim CEO Kress and board chair Harvey Jones wrote to Nvidia employees Jensen Huang's exit from Nvidia raises critical questions about the future of AI Analysis: Nvidia's leadership crisis tests the chipmaker's role as the 'central bank of AI' Investors still have high hopes for Nvidia, which reports earnings on Tuesday. Analysts expect its revenue to more than double in the current fiscal year, and then to roughly double again over the following two years, according to LSEG data. But Huang's exit from the company Thursday following a pair of extramarital affairs, including one with a woman The New York Times reported was suspected of spying for China, makes the company's fate extraordinarily hard to predict. Huang had led the company since co-founding it in 1993. Nvidia didn't respond to a request for comment. The company named CFO Colette Kress as interim CEO. Nvidia's stock fell 33% from its Oct. 6 peak through Thursday morning. Still, people who closely track the financial flows underlying AI say that even sharper losses by Nvidia likely wouldn't trigger the kind of systemic problems that regulators guard against. And yet the risks flowing from AI are keeping some finance officials up at night. They are watching for the possibility that many of the factors that have helped the AI boom could reverse simultaneously. If the value of Nvidia's GPU chips fell, for instance, it could prompt investors to ask whether companies that borrowed money to buy them would be able to pay off their debts. In that case, the financial assistance big tech firms have extended to others in the industry could suddenly become drags on their growth. Tech companies would have credit problems at the same time that their equity is falling. Problems among giant tech firms wouldn't stay contained to tech investors' portfolios, but could cause problems across the economy. "I think that's a real concern because both the economy and financial markets are standing on the same leg, which means a drawdown could have reinforcing effects between the two," said Jason Wu, an assistant director at the International Monetary Fund who oversees the Global Markets Analysis unit. Wu was the lead author of a chapter of the IMF's Global Financial Stability report published in October that warned about the potential for growing leverage among AI firms and investors to trigger broader problems. The so-called hyperscalers — the biggest tech firms — have grown from just 1% of bond issuance in the $15 trillion investment-grade debt market to 10% in just two years.

events.title: Nvidia staff wait 6 days for an all-hands after Jensen Huang’s exit. PR experts warn employees need answers sooner
events.summary: On Thursday, Nvidia announced CEO Jensen Huang’s resignation , effective immediately, following his admission to having an extramarital affair with an alleged Chinese spy. The New York Times has also reported that he had an affair with another Nvidia executive, Kimberly Powell, the company’s vice president of health care. Neither Nvidia nor Powell has publicly addressed that report. CFO Colette Kress was named interim CEO , and one of her first moves was addressing employees. But the company won’t hold an all-hands meeting until Nov. 18, six days after Thursday’s announcement, and several communications experts told Fortune that’s too long to leave a shaken workforce waiting. Kress has been with Nvidia since 2013, having previously held senior finance roles at Cisco and Microsoft . She ranked No. 49 on the 2026 Fortune Most Powerful Women list . She takes over a company whose market value topped $5 trillion at its peak. Nvidia, No. 16 on the 2026 Fortune 500, was the first company on the list to pass $4 trillion . It has since dropped below that mark after news of Huang’s affairs and his resignation. Nvidia could also be drawn into multiple Justice Department investigations, including an antitrust probe aimed at the chipmaker itself and two separate inquiries into Megaspeed and Supermicro that center on Alice Huang, the alleged Chinese spy, Semafor reported , citing two administration officials. Semafor reported no sign the DOJ currently intends to pursue criminal charges against Nvidia or Huang. Fortune has reported on why Nvidia can’t shake China smuggling allegations . Some employees have voiced their shock publicly. “Jensen Huang rescued me from probably living in debt the rest of my life … I’ve never spoken to him, and only passed by him in HQ once,” one X user who identifies themself as an Nvidia employee wrote in a post on Thursday. “His personal life is frankly none of my business. But as a leader, I have yet to meet a better one.” “Ousting him is financial suicide, and I can only assume there is a hidden ulterior motive because I can’t fathom any other reason for destroying the company’s value,” the Nvidia employee continued. Prominent business leaders, including billionaires Bill Ackman and Elon Musk, have also defended Huang online. “@JensenHuang is human. And he is an incredible human. Even incredible humans make mistakes,” Ackman posted on X on Sunday. “Onward.” Musk responded “I agree” to a post from Sequoia partner Shaun Maguire arguing “Jensen is one of the greatest entrepreneurs of this generation … he did something incredibly dumb … it was bad for America … but my guess is there was no bad intention … [and] two mistakes don’t make a right, and I believe Jensen is irreplaceable for America’s AI leadership.” Nvidia didn’t immediately respond to Fortune ‘s request for comment. PR experts question the six-day wait The timing comes from a message sent to Nvidia employees that has since circulated publicly: “You will hear more from leadership in the coming days about our future together, and we will host a meeting on November 18 at 9 am PT.” “We play a vital role in building the technology that is powering the AI revolution, and we have important work ahead of us,” the message continued. “So let’s move forward together, with the same determination and commitment that have always defined this company.” The meeting also lands the day after Nvidia reports third-quarter results on Nov. 17 , meaning Wall Street will hear from the company’s new leadership before employees get a company-wide forum. Annie Scranton, founder and CEO of Pace Public Relations, told Fortune that while Kress gets points for how quickly the message went out and its overall tone, the timing of the all-hands meeting isn’t great. “The problem lies with her giving a specific day that is nearly a week away for the all-hands,” Scranton said. “She should have just stopped after the line referencing that employees will hear more from leadership in the coming days. “‘Coming days’ to me does not mean six days away,” she continued. Scranton said that, “Understanding that they have a ton to work out,” Kress should have pushed to do the meeting on Monday, working through the weekend to figure out messaging and next steps. “Even if she didn’t have every single aspect 100% sorted out at that moment, it’s too long to wait,” she added. “It gives employees too much time to stew, talk, get upset, and have morale and their stock plummet even more than it already has.” Amy Cuthbertson, founder of ACA PR , also would’ve favored an earlier, live briefing in which staff could have heard from Kress and raised their concerns sooner, she told Fortune . “Managers also need to be given clear guidance so they can support their teams and be in a position to answer their questions consistently,” Cuthbertson said. What Kress should tell employees On what to expect from Kress, Cuthbertson said the interim CEO should avoid speculating about the investigation or promising answers she’s not in a position to give. “That said, she can still explain what is known and what remains to be determined,” Cuthbertson said. “She can also explain to staff how they will be kept updated.” To be sure, Johan Konst, founder of tech PR agency EUSA PR , said Kress “struck the right tone” by thanking employees and acknowledging the difficulty of the situation, adding he thinks six days for a company-wide meeting is “reasonable.” But “it’s too long for employees to wait to ask their first question,” he said. “I would invite questions today and answer the most pressing ones tomorrow.” This story was originally featured on Fortune.com

events.title: Jensen Huang's exit from Nvidia raises critical questions about the future of AI
events.summary: Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang has been a singular figure in the development of the AI industry, which suddenly has to survive without him. Huang founded Nvidia in 1993 and built it into the company that powered the AI boom, doing so with no second-in-command. "How companies handle a crisis determines their future," former Cisco CEO John Chambers, now a startup investor, told CNBC's "Fast Money." Michael Dell described Jensen Huang as a "visionary of the AI age." Deutsche Telekom CEO Tim Höttges said a photo with the Nvidia CEO produced more media coverage for his company than its iPhone launch. During the keynote of his annual Dreamforce conference, Salesforce's Marc Benioff said, "Jensen, we're all following you, bro," as the two paced through the audience. Follow CNBC's live coverage of Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang's resignation His fame extended way beyond tech. In May, Huang joined President Donald Trump on Air Force One for a trip to China to meet with President Xi Jinping . Three months later, Huang gathered six of the biggest names at the Nasdaq to announce on CNBC a proposed $500 billion artificial intelligence buildout plan, cementing his central role at the intersection of Wall Street and Silicon Valley. As Nvidia became the first company to rip past a $5 trillion market cap, bending the laws of physics with its advanced graphics processing units and pushing the AI boom to seemingly endless bounds, the now 63-year-old Huang, clad in a black leather jacket, traversed the globe as the face of the brand powering the next industrial revolution. Over the past week it all came crashing down. Following two reported extramarital affairs — one with an alleged Chinese spy and another with an employee — Huang is leaving the company he co-founded 33 years ago in crisis, and thrusting the AI market into chaos. The board is now left to pick a successor for a company that's been run by a singular figure with no second-in-command. Chief Financial Officer Colette Kress has been named interim CEO. Harvey Jones has been appointed chairman. Nvidia has not responded to multiple requests for comment. "How companies handle a crisis determines their future," former Cisco CEO John Chambers, now a startup investor, told CNBC's " Fast Money " on Wednesday. "How they handle this will determine if they're a great company and a great leadership team beyond one person." It had been a tumultuous stretch for Nvidia, even before the Huang saga led the board to launch an investigation of the CEO's behavior and the potential national security implications. The stock is on pace for its sixth straight weekly drop, which would be the longest losing streak since 2012. That includes a 9% slump last week after the midterm elections resulted in sweeping Democratic victories in both chambers of Congress, and the passage of dozens of ballot measures that could slow the buildout of new data centers. Nvidia is scheduled to report quarterly results on Tuesday, and expectations remain high, with analysts projecting 92% year-over-year revenue growth to $109.2 billion, according to LSEG. That's up 18-fold from the same quarter in 2022, just before OpenAI launched ChatGPT and kicked off the generative AI era. Nvidia live updates: Jensen Huang agrees to testify before Congress following resignation Who is Colette Kress? Nvidia's finance chief steps in as interim CEO after Huang exit PRO: Buy Nvidia with 'both hands' because the valuation is at 'stupid' levels, says analyst Meeks Read what interim CEO Kress and board chair Harvey Jones wrote to Nvidia employees Analysis: Nvidia's leadership crisis tests the chipmaker's role as the 'central bank of AI' It's a historic level of growth for any business, and particularly notable for a company that spent most of its first few decades as a niche technology provider for video games. Huang founded Nvidia to make chips for computer graphics, both for video games and rendering. In the early 2000s, he and other executives saw an opportunity to put GPUs to work for computationally intense projects. That technology eventually turned Nvidia into the most important player in AI and a key American asset for national defense. In the process, Huang became the ultimate decider, choosing how, when and where GPUs get allocated. The biggest buyers were the hyperscalers — Amazon, Google , Meta and Microsoft — which needed the chips to build their own AI services and make them available to cloud customers. OpenAI , meanwhile, was snapping up GPUs for its powerful models and consumer apps. To expand his customer base, Huang designated compute capacity to a number of so-called neoclouds like CoreWeave and Nebius , putting equity into the companies and helping them build big businesses around renting out GPUs. Oracle gobbled up billions of dollars worth of GPUs, going heavily into debt in the process.

events.title: Hugging Face CEO vows to keep fighting for open source AI after Jensen Huang’s exit
events.summary: Hugging Face CEO Clément Delangue briefly commented on Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang’s departure on Thursday, calling it a “really sad day.” Nvidia had announced its plan to acquire the platform for open source AI models in September for $12.9 billion, making it the second-largest acquisition in the company’s history, just behind that of chipmaker Groq’s assets for $20 billion in December 2025. “This whole thing sucks, and I wish none of it had happened. It’s a really sad day! But I want to make one thing clear: we’ll keep fighting for open-source AI, harder than ever. This is too important to slow down now. Let’s go!,” Delangue wrote on X. This whole thing sucks, and I wish none of it had happened. It’s a really sad day! But I want to make one thing clear: we’ll keep fighting for open-source AI, harder than ever. This is too important to slow down now. Let’s go! — clem 🤗 (@ClementDelangue) November 12, 2026 The post is interesting as it implies that Huang’s departure is potentially worrying to open source advocates, and he’s attempting to offer reassurance. As Nvidia’s CEO, Huang was known as a strong advocate for open source AI and open-weight models, which is why there could be concerns about how a company that’s no longer under his leadership will now approach this space. After Nvidia announced its plans to acquire Hugging Face, the U.S. Department of Justice began making inquiries about how the deal would impact competition in the AI market, Reuters reported in October . While Nvidia pledged that the platform would preserve open support, it would also allow the company to control a major distribution channel for AI models. The Hugging Face deal is still scheduled to close in the first half of 2027. Requests for further comment on the deal status and whether Hugging Face has spoken yet with Nvidia’s interim CEO Colette Kress were not returned. Huang’s advocacy for open source and open-weight AI has long extended beyond Hugging Face. In July, the CEO published an AI policy letter as his first-ever post on the social network X . The letter, which was signed by 25 companies, including Microsoft, Meta, Hugging Face, IBM, Palantir, and others, urged the U.S. government not to over-restrict open-weight AI models. It said models that “anyone can download, inspect, modify, and run on their own infrastructure” are an important part of the AI ecosystem because they make AI “more accessible, adaptable, and widely available.” Huang also wrote that open-weight models expand access to the AI economy, strengthen competition, and give customers greater control, as they know they won’t become locked into a single provider. “Open models strengthen safety and cybersecurity, accelerate innovation and diffusion, and enable sovereignty,” his post on X stated. For my first post, I’m sharing a letter @NVIDIA signed on why open models matter. AI will transform every industry, power every company, and be built by every country. Open models strengthen safety and cybersecurity, accelerate innovation and diffusion, and enable sovereignty.… pic.twitter.com/t02bi51N4C — Jensen Huang (@JensenHuang) July 24, 2026 In August, Nvidia also announced a $6 billion deal with the coding startup Poolside to help build out an open AI ecosystem in the U.S. to help the country compete against Chinese companies like DeepSeek and Kimi K3, The Wall Street Journal reported at the time. Last month, Nvidia expanded its Nemotron family of open-weight models with a large 120-billion-parameter model for agents used by the enterprise as well as with two new lightweight Bolt models that run on PCs. events.title: Betting markets see a longtime Nvidia insider as the favorite to replace Jensen Huang, interim CEO Colette Kress is second
events.summary: Jensen Huang is out, and prediction market bettors are already putting money on who will take his place atop Nvidia . Trading in contracts on his successor picked up earlier this week on Kalshi and Polymarket, generating hundreds of thousands of dollars in trading volume. On Thursday, Nvidia announced Huang’s resignation and named finance chief Colette Kress interim CEO, adding that the board is searching for a permanent successor and will consider internal and external candidates. Kress, however, is not the favorite to take the top job. Instead, Nvidia VP and general manager of its high-performance computing division, Ian Buck, who has been at Nvidia since 2004, leads the field on Kalshi with 37% odds. Kress follows at 19%, ahead of Rene Haas, CEO of Arm Holdings, at 9%. Arm is a British chip designer that licenses its technology to Nvidia. Trading volume in the market has already surpassed $1.5 million. Polymarket’s market shows a similar lineup, with the same leading contenders drawing comparable odds and trading volume nearing $630,000. Madison Huang, Jensen Huang’s daughter and Nvidia’s senior director of product marketing, trails the leading contenders, with less than a 1% chance of succeeding him on Kalshi and roughly 2% on Polymarket. Prediction markets have been capitalizing on the turmoil at Nvidia since the company announced an investigation into Huang, who told its board he had an intimate relationship with a business executive reportedly identified by U.S. intelligence officials as a Chinese spy. The scrutiny intensified Wednesday, when reports surfaced alleging that Huang also had an extramarital affair with an Nvidia employee. Bettors are wagering on more than Nvidia’s next leader. One Polymarket contract generated more than $22.5 million in trading volume on when Huang would announce his departure. Another active Kalshi contract asks when Huang will testify before Congress and has drawn nearly $170,000 in trading volume. Traders put the odds of testimony before next July at 93%, compared with roughly 91% before January and 86% before December. The turmoil has also put Nvidia’s stock price in focus, with shares down roughly 5% Thursday morning at about $165. Traders on Kalshi are also betting on those price swings through perpetual futures contracts, taking positions on whether the price will rise or fall without owning shares. Those contracts recorded $111 million in trading volume over the past 24 hours. This story was originally featured on Fortune.com

events.title: Some under-25s should get fewer benefits, Milburn review to say
events.summary: Alan Milburn will publish his review next week Some young people could see reductions to the benefits they are entitled to under a radical overhaul of the welfare system to be recommended by a government-commissioned review. As reported in the Times, , external Alan Milburn's year-long report, to be published on Tuesday, is expected to recommend moving under-25s off the main sickness and disability benefits. Milburn, a former Labour health secretary, has been tasked by the government with helping reduce the one in eight 16 to 24 year-olds in the UK who are not in education, employment or training - otherwise known as "Neet". He said on Wednesday night that his plans would not be "pain-free" and would affect both existing and new claimants. His report is expected to say that under-25s should no longer be able to claim the health element of UK-wide universal credit - or personal independence payment (Pip), the main disability benefit in England and Wales. Disabled people in Scotland can claim the devolved Adult Disability Payment. Instead, under Milburn's plan, under-25s would receive an allowance on the same basic rate as universal credit. Some could be eligible for a new "additional cost allowance" to cover day-to-day costs related to their conditions. Some claimants would receive less under the plans - although the exact amounts will not be clear until early next year, when the government publishes legislation to implement the changes. People can claim Pip to help them with the additional cost of being disabled or living with long-term physical or mental health conditions. It is available to those both in and out of work. In his interim report, , external Milburn said survey data found that 19% of young people claiming disability or health benefits were in work. Milburn, a Labour MP from 1992 to 2010, is also expected to recommend an investment of billions into more employment support for young people, including work placements, job subsidies and one-to-one personal advisers. Those with more severe disabilities and unable to work would get a new benefit paid at a higher rate. Milburn told the Times: "Candidly, it could mean that some people will get less financial support at the beginning of their benefit claim than under the current system. "But actually, for young people, there's a different debate that we've got to resolve, which is whether the priority is their longer-term life chances or just their immediate shorter-term finances. "I think what the current system does [is] it prioritises the latter over the former. I believe that's the wrong choice and it needs to be the other way around." Just under one million young people in the UK are Neets , data from the Office for National Statistics (ONS) from April to June suggests. This was a rise of 3% on the same period last year. Milburn's recommendations are likely to be backed by Prime Minister Andy Burnham but could prove controversial among Labour MPs, who opposed welfare changes last year under his predecessor Sir Keir Starmer. Dame Meg Hillier, who helped spearhead a backbench rebellion against Starmer's reforms, suggested she and her colleagues were broadly supportive this time around. "What happened last year was a cut was being proposed and none of us could explain to people what would happen to them," the Labour MP told the BBC. "Milburn has done some very good work on this so I'm giving him a fair wind," she added. But Bell Ribeiro-Addy, one of the Labour backbenchers who revolted last year, said she was "not sure" she could vote to cut the benefit entitlement of existing claimants. Tom Ashforth, a 19-year-old student at Sheffield Hallam University, receives both components of Pip at the higher rate. He said the financial support helps him manage additional expenses linked to his visual impairment, including prescriptions, mobility aids and accessible learning resources. "If I were to lose it, I would struggle to afford essential things," he said. Student Tom said he relies on the money he gets from Pip to support him through his time at university He said he believes decisions over disability benefits should be made on a case-by-case basis, rather than according to age. "You cannot assume that everyone under the age of 25 is in the same position," he said. In his Times interview, Milburn acknowledged that changing the rules for existing claimants would be "difficult politically" but stressed it was necessary. James Taylor, from disability equality charity Scope, said Pip was a "lifeline" and restricting access to it "won't make young disabled people's extra costs disappear". Harriet Edwards, from the charity Sense, said changes were "long overdue", but that without additional details, families were "deeply anxious". A government spokesperson said: "We will always ensure there is a safety net for the most vulnerable and those who are unable to work.

events.title: Home sales hit 16-year low in October amid record-high mortgage rates
events.summary: Sales of built units fell to 3.75m in October, down by 8.8% from last year, with mortgage rates at nearly three-year high US existing home sales hit a 16-year low in October as buyers were driven away by record-high mortgage rates and rising inflation, according to new data released on Wednesday. Sales of already built units dropped to 3.75m in October, down by 8.8% from last year, the National Association of Realtors (NAR) reported. The median existing-home sales price increased slightly to $416,700. Declines in sales were seen in the midwest, south and west, though sales in the north-east held steady. Mortgage rates had been steadily declining in 2024 and 2025, with the 30-year rate falling below 6% for the first time in February 2026. But increasing inflation and higher interest rates amid the Iran war have pushed rates back up to a nearly three-year high. The 30-year mortgage rate, which is the most commonly used rate in home loans, is now hovering at about 7.18%, not far from its 2023 high of 7.79%. During the pandemic, average mortgage rates were just above 3%. “Home buying is difficult when mortgage rates have climbed to their highest levels since 2000, aside from a single month in 2023,” Lawrence Yun, chief economist at the NAR. “As a result, home sales fell to their lowest level since August 2010.” Pending home sales, or the number of contracts that have been signed before closing, reached its lowest levels in the NAR’s history in September, the same month that the 30-year mortgage rate topped 7% for the first time in nearly two years. Mortgage rates have been directly affected by interest rate changes by the US Federal Reserve, which in September hiked interest rates for the first time since 2023. Rates currently sit at a range of 3.75% to 4%. The central bank is poised to raise rates again next month to combat heightened inflation, which went up more than expected in October. Get the most important news as it breaks Affordability and cost-of-living concerns played an outsized role in the midterm elections that gave Democrats control of Congress next year. According to the latest census data, growth in median rent across the US outpaced inflation. The home-ownership rate in the US has stagnated since 2021, according to the same data. “I don’t think this is a new normal for home sales,” said Danielle Hale, chief economist at Realtor.com . “Instead, it reflects a perfect storm of an abrupt shift in the financial environment and large uncertainties in the pre-election period for both policy and the economy just as the housing market usually slows for the season.”

events.title: Measures restricting clean tech exports slowing down energy transition
events.summary: Major economies representing 58% of the world’s GDP have adopted at least one measure to restrict the import of clean energy technologies, many targeting Chinese goods, according to data published by the Oxford Climate Policy Monitor . In contrast, a large number of small economies outside China, accounting for about 8% of world GDP, are liberalising imports of EVs, batteries, along with wind and solar equipment, creating a de facto free trade area for clean tech. Analysis by the Blavatnik School of Government at the University of Oxford found that restrictions are making the transition slower and more expensive, but they may also be needed to balance effective climate policy with industrial development and economic security . “Openness and protection can be combined, rather than traded off wholesale,” it said. Large economies could pursue more selective trade restrictions instead of trying to build entirely self-sufficient industries, while smaller countries could specialise in particular stages of manufacturing. “Our findings show that many countries have begun to implement this strategy,” said Claas Mertens, the brief’s co-author. — Chloé Farand

events.title: Disney's 'Star Wars' is coming to Cosm domes ahead of 50th anniversary as part of multiyear film deal
events.summary: Cosm has partnered with Disney on a multiyear, multifilm deal that will kick off with "Star Wars: A New Hope" early next year. This is Cosm's third studio deal — it already has partnerships with Universal and Warner Bros. — and sixth theatrical release. Cosm is working directly with studios Lucasfilm and Industrial Light and Magic as well as creative studio MakeMake to create the visuals and the sound mixing for a unique presentation of the film. On Thursday, the immersive entertainment technology company announced a new studio partnership with The Walt Disney Co. that will bring the original "Star Wars" to its domes early next year as part of a multiyear, multifilm collaboration. The financial terms of the deal were not disclosed. Cosm's massive concave screens will drop film fans into a galaxy far, far away starting in March, just ahead of the Academy Award-winning film's 50th anniversary in May. "We are thrilled to add the Disney partnership," Alexis Scalice, head of Cosm Studios, told CNBC. "We do look for those opportunities of these like anniversary and commemorative moments. We look for those opportunities to celebrate with the fans, but also find this mutually beneficial partnership between both parties." This will be Cosm's sixth theatrical collaboration with Hollywood, having already partnered with Warner Bros. to bring "The Matrix," "Willy Wonka & the Chocolate Factory," "Harry Potter and the Sorcerer's Stone" and "It" to its locations. The company is set to launch immersive screenings of Universal's "Shrek" in December. Each Cosm dome has stadium-style seating, with booths and tables set on each level. The dome's width fills much of the viewers' periphery, giving the sensation that they are part of the onscreen environment. In this case, "Star Wars" will be displayed in a large rectangle in the center of the dome while the background is transformed into the iconic planets of Tatooine and Yavin IV that are featured in the film as well as the infamous Death Star. Audiences will also see elements that will make it appear like they're traveling at lightspeed and getting trapped in an intergalactic trash compactor. Cosm is working directly with studios Lucasfilm and Industrial Light and Magic as well as creative studio MakeMake to create the visuals and the sound mixing for the unique presentation of the film. "We look for those moments where sound, music ... listening to Darth Vader's breath for the first time ... you feel those moments differently in an 87-foot diameter dome and 12k resolution with the sound system we have," Scalice said. "And it's one of the things that with experiential cinema and our technology that we were so excited and honestly privileged that we can take these defining moments for fans and work closely with our partners that doesn't really change the authenticity of it, it just enhances it in a different manner." The premium experience will also be paired with a themed menu. Cosm has done this with other titles, such as "Harry Potter and the Sorcerer's Stone," serving guests throughout the screening with house-made shepherd's pie, pretzel wands with cheese dip and a box of Bertie Bott's Every Flavour Beans. Cosm is trying to establish itself as a destination for fandom — both for sports and for film. It has a wide variety of live event offerings, which it telecasts using proprietary cameras mounted in arenas that broadcast back to the dome, as well as its expanding library of movies. "What I love is that we really are kind of building these Cosm communities built on fandom," Scalice said. "It's the No. 1 foundation for our business." And Star Wars is a powerful fandom. The franchise remains one of the top-ranking pieces of intellectual property across film, television and retail annually, and Disney is gearing up for a massive celebration of its semicentennial including merchandise launches, theatrical re-releases, its biannual Star Wars Celebration convention and collaborations with other brands. Correction: This story has been updated to correct the spelling of Alexis Scalice's name.

events.title: Africa to press for more adaptation finance at COP31
events.summary: African countries want the COP31 climate talks, now underway in Türkiye, to set out how the world will deliver on last year’s pledge to triple adaptation finance designed to help cope with the growing impact of extreme weather events. A large share of the money has previously come from aid budgets, which have fallen to their lowest level since 2014 , and most wealthier countries have pledged little-to-no new climate finance from this year . The African Group of Negotiators says addressing this issue is vital to a successful outcome in Antalya as support for the continent’s vulnerabilities has been “dwindling,” according to its chairperson. But even a tripling in financing will not close the gap: In 2024, the amount available for developing economies reached around $30 billion — that pales against the $305 billion the UN estimates they need annually to 2035. Plans have been announced at COP31 to scale up successful adaptation projects and attract larger investments. But these cannot be “entirely dependent on voluntary contributions,” Kenya’s climate envoy told Semafor. — Chloé Farand

events.title: IRS announces 2027 401(k) contribution limits, raises savings cap: What it means for your money
events.summary: The IRS has announced higher 401(k) contribution limits for 2027. Starting in 2027, employees can defer $25,500 into workplace plans, up from $24,500 in 2026. The individual retirement account contribution limit will be $7,500 in 2027, unchanged from 2026. The IRS has announced new retirement account contribution limits for 2027. In its release on Thursday, the agency increased the 401(k) employee deferral limit to $25,500 next year, up from $24,500 in 2026. The change applies to 401(k)s, 403(b)s and most 457 plans, along with the federal Thrift Savings Plan. The IRS also unveiled 2027 catch-up contribution limits for savers age 50 and older, new individual retirement account savings limits and higher income thresholds for Roth IRA contributions. Starting in 2027, the 401(k) catch-up contribution limit will rise to $8,500 for savers 50 and older, up from $8,000 in 2026. But investors aged 60 to 63 can instead save an extra $11,750, based on changes enacted via Secure 2.0 . That figure is up $500 from 2026. Both amounts are in addition to the $25,500 deferral limit for 2027. Market sell-off hits hard: Advisors say 'stay the course with an eye on buying' IRS announces new federal income tax brackets for 2027 These states are offering extra ACA premium subsidies in 2027 CNBC's Financial Advisor 100: Best financial advisors, top firms for 2026 ranked CNBC Elite Advisors: Top ultra-high net worth wealth management firms for 2026 The 2027 IRA contribution limit is $7,500, unchanged from 2026, the IRS announced. IRA catch-up contributions for investors age 50 and older will be $1,100, the same as 2026. The announcement comes one week after the agency released dozens of other inflation adjustments for 2027, including federal income tax brackets , higher capital gains brackets , estate and gift tax exemptions and provisions impacting families, among others. Get your 401(k) employer match first In 2025, only 14% of participants maxed out their 401(k)s , according to Vanguard's 2026 How America Saves report, which was based on data from more than 1,300 qualified plans and nearly 5 million participants. The average combined savings rate, including employer deposits, was an estimated 12.1%, according to the same report. "Before worrying about contribution limits, make sure you're capturing your full employer match," said Sean Michael Pearson, a certified financial planner with Ameriprise Financial Services in Conshohocken, Pennsylvania. During the second quarter of 2026, about 19% of employees weren't deferring enough to 401(k)s to receive their company's full matching contribution, according to a Fidelity analysis of 27,300 corporate plans and nearly 26 million participants. Vanguard suggests saving 12% to 15% of your pay per year, including employer contributions, depending on your income. But only one-quarter of 401(k) participants deferred more than 10% of earnings in 2025, according to Vanguard's report. If you plan to max out your 401(k) for 2027, you should change your savings rate in December so it's active by your first January paycheck, experts say. The update could take one or two pay periods to go into effect. Boost your 401(k) savings rate every year The "most important habit" is consistently increasing your 401(k) savings rate over time, according to Pearson. For example, if you bump 401(k) contributions by 1% every year, "you may barely notice the difference in your paycheck, but the long-term impact can be substantial," he said. In 2025, about 27% of 401(k) plans automatically increased employee deferrals over time, known as "auto-escalation," according to the Plan Sponsor Council of America's yearly survey of 401(k)s . The nonprofit trade organization's survey included 753 plans. The vast majority of plans with auto-escalation, 69%, boosted deferrals by 1% per year, the Plan Sponsor Council of America found.

events.title: ‘Her hands are as cold as ice’: Gaza families struggle to keep warm
events.summary: Will Israel’s election change life in Gaza? Flooded tents and high prices leave Gaza families struggling to keep children warm as winter approaches. Gaza City, Gaza Strip – At night, as temperatures drop inside their makeshift shelter in Gaza City, Amira Saad struggles to keep her four-month-old baby, Mohammed, warm. The baby mostly only has thin summer clothes. Unable to afford winter clothing, 27-year-old Amira has borrowed a warm garment from a neighbour, but remains worried about the cold during the night. list 1 of 3 ‘Horrific crime’: Gaza doctor killed as Israel expands war on healthcare list 2 of 3 ‘Greater Israel’: Christian Zionism’s role in US policy list 3 of 3 Israeli strike on Gaza’s Nasser Hospital kills surgeon, five others She lives with 18 family members, including nine children, under a tarp offering little protection from the elements. Finding enough warm clothes and blankets for everyone has become increasingly difficult. The family was displaced from Gaza City’s Shujayea neighbourhood earlier in Israel’s genocidal war on Gaza, and now lives in a makeshift camp west of the city. Recent heavy rain has flooded their shelter, soaking mattresses, pillows, and blankets. “We were flooded while we were sleeping. The water came inside and soaked our blankets, mattresses and pillows. Everything was wet,” Amira says. The children mostly have old, torn summer clothes. Amira’s mother-in-law, 60-year-old Basima Saad, is also worried about her own 23-year-old daughter, who has a disability, and needs warm clothes and medication. “Her hands become as cold as ice. I keep her beside me in bed to warm her, just as I would a small child,” Basima says. “I dress her before I dress myself. I have to make sure she is warm first.” With no regular income, the family relies on community kitchens for food. Spare money for winter clothes and blankets simply is not available. “My husband does not have a job. Two days ago, he went out to work breaking up rubble, but he broke his hand. The situation is very bad, and the cold is extremely severe,” Amira says. Families struggle to keep children warm The danger to the Palestinians living in these conditions, and particularly the very young, is not hypothetical. On Thursday, a nine-month-old baby, Kinan Ahmed Raqiq, died of hypothermia. His father told AFP that he woke up in his tent to find that his son’s skin had turned blue. Tragedies like that make Amal al-Maydana, a 46-year-old other of seven, fearful. She’s raising her children alone – her husband Hamza was killed by an Israeli quadcopter in January 2025, and her eldest son Haitham was killed by a sniper in November of the same year, age 25 at the time. She is originally from Gaza City’s Zeitoun neighbourhood and has been displaced six times during the war, fleeing Israeli attacks and losing the family’s home, land, and car. Now living in a tent, Amal struggles to provide for her children. Her younger daughters, Rimas and Malak, are still wearing summer clothes despite the arrival of winter . “Everything is expensive… children’s clothes, shoes, everything,” she says. Amal tries to make do with what is available, but it is not enough to meet her daughters’ needs. Rain also seeps through the damaged tarpaulins covering the family’s tent. With no heating equipment, they rely on blankets to keep warm. “We have no means of heating ourselves; we just cover the children with blankets,” she says. Amal fears another storm will bring more rain and cold. “We just pray that God makes this winter easier for the people living in tents,” she says. Aid falls short as winter risks grow The United Nations Office for the Coordination of Humanitarian Affairs (OCHA) says 94 percent of Gaza’s population urgently needs shelter assistance. Some 65 percent of households live in tents or makeshift shelters, while 650,000 children need winter aid, including warm clothing and blankets. By September, aid agencies had secured enough winter clothing for just 9,000 households and bedding for 50,000 – far short of what was needed. OCHA said funding shortages were further hampering preparations for winter. The UN Children’s Fund (UNICEF) has warned that winter conditions put children in Gaza at increased risk of hypothermia and respiratory infections – at least 11 children died from hypothermia last winter, according to the Gaza Ministry of Health. The agency is seeking $97.5m for its 2026-2027 winter response, which aims to support 540,000 children and their families across Gaza and the occupied West Bank. Recent rains have worsened the crisis. UNICEF said on November 9 that flooding had affected more than 106,000 people, while some 950,000 displaced Palestinians were living in flood-prone areas. More than three years into Israel’s genocidal war, which has killed more than 74,600 Palestinians and wounded over 176,000, homes and livelihoods across Gaza have been devastated.

events.title: United Airlines blocks AI agents from booking flights, citing cybersecurity risks
events.summary: United Airlines said it will restrict access to AI agents seeking to book flights and manage reservations on their users’ behalf, citing a risk to cybersecurity and undermining federal regulations. The airline is the latest American corporate giant to prevent customers from using AI agents and autonomous assistants to access their systems. The move comes as airlines and banks are struggling to differentiate between real customers and AI systems operating on their behalf, such as when users share their logins with their AI assistants. Sharing passwords with apps and assistants can create security risks if those credentials get leaked or exposed. United warns that “sharing account credentials with personal, third-party, AI assistants can expose sensitive information, and actions taken by these tools may result in unintended purchases, account changes, or use of MileagePlus miles.” The airline also warns of a risk of violating federal aviation rules, such as requiring that a human completes flight check-ins to acknowledge that their bags do not contain banned substances. “As a result, United is taking steps to restrict access — directly within our digital platforms and indirectly via travel agencies and aggregators — to prohibit use by unauthorized, third-party personal AI agents or assistants,” the airline said in a statement . “This work includes updates to our booking, ticketing and distribution policies.” The airline’s move follows a warning from banks, including Bank of America, which last week urged customers not to share their passwords with their AI assistants. events.title: Jensen Huang’s downfall cut the P/E of Nvidia stock by a third. But don’t call it a bargain yet
events.summary: The steep fall in Nvidia’s stock that started with revelations about CEO Jensen Huang’s romantic relationship with an alleged Chinese spy, and accelerated following his resignation on November 12 , makes Nvidia’s shares look like a historic buy. At least that’s the conclusion from analyzing its numbers by conventional metrics. The GPU-maker’s shares peaked on October 5 at $243. At that point, Nvidia sported the world’s biggest market cap at $5.85 trillion. Wall Street analysts following the stock were almost universal even then in acclaiming Nvidia as a cheap stock. And, it appeared, for good reason: Nvidia was selling at 30 times its earnings over the previous four quarters, a modest number for an enterprise growing its bottom line at an annual clip of 100%. Today, Nvidia looks like a far greater bargain based strictly on the numbers. Since the summit in early October, it’s tumbled 34% as of mid-morning on November 12 to $161, a downdraft that slashed nearly $2 trillion from its valuation , the biggest dollar drop by far, in a condensed period, in the history of capital markets. As a result, Nvidia’s PE has dropped to 20, a figure that given its current stats, tags it as practically the ultimate value play. For example, Apple and Amazon carry a PE of 40 and 22 respectively, and are expanding at a fraction of Nvidia’s speed. Indeed, despite its immense size and sorcerous growth rate, Nvidia has so far shown no signs of falling victim to the law of large numbers. In the quarter ended October 31, its sales jumped 26% over the previous three-month span, beating the around 20% jumps of the two previous quarters. What about profitability? In the October quarter, gross margins hit a sumptuous 75%, beating its FY 2026 posting of 71.3%. Make a sober assessment of Nvidia’s overall condition, however, and the best conclusion is that the market is probably right in imposing this giant discount based on Huang’s departure. Nvidia’s wild profitability arises from its virtual monopoly in the top GPU segment. According to a top industry executive who’s an Nvidia customer, it is 18 to 24 months ahead of all-comers in the quality and performance of its top chips. The rub, says this person, is Nvidia’s dependence on Huang as both an unmatched innovator and excellent operator. “Huang was the tech visionary and he also got Nvidia to operate incredibly well,” says this person. “The question is how much depended on Jensen, and how much of what he did can another person do?” This executive stresses that Nvidia has maintained its huge margins by keeping several paces ahead of the field, and never slowing, one of the greatest feats in the annals of tech. “That continuing advantage in chips is absolutely essential to Nvidia. It’s an industry where you can’t miss a step. If you do, others will catch up fast. Intel fell behind, and it never caught up.” Plus, competitors who regularly complain about the high cost of Nvidia chips are racing to create their own, in-house competitors, a list that encompasses AMD , Google, and Amazon. It’s also revealing to parse how Nvidia’s deploying its huge free cash flow to stay in front. In the past four quarters, it’s generated $105 billion in FCF. In the past, it’s channeled a huge portion of that bounty into share buybacks. But in the 12 months ended in October, repurchases fell to just $32 billion. Nvidia’s cash Hoard of $100 billion in relatively modest, and growing slowly. So where is all the rest of that capex going? Nvidia is famously making big investments in its customers, including SpaceX, CoreWeave, OpenAI, SoftBank’s SB Energy, and Intel (for CPUs). It’s also provided multibillion-dollar credit guarantees for projects built for hyperscalers and neoclouds where it’s providing the GPUs. The practice of funding its own customers is often questioned as “circular financing.” The question is whether Huang felt obliged to follow that course to protect Nvidia’s future. The reason: Locking in future sales as rivals hatch competing products at lower price points. In other words, Huang sought to forestall the commoditization of Nvidia, the threat that’s eventually hit the profitability of all tech hardware giants. And that’s just the problem. Huge prices and margins inevitably attract cheaper new supply. The market judges that Nvidia’s margins and profit growth will look far lower in the future than in the past, and that losing the genius who could hold commoditization at bay longest was a big, big loss. A former CEO whom I spoke to took a contrarian stance by arguing that the Nvidia board made a big mistake in not making every attempt to keep Huang. “I would have liked to see more facts, and maybe the board’s got them,” says this person. “The board was not thinking about shareholders. They were thinking about their reputations and not getting sued. They should have punished Huang and made it a very visible punishment like no equity or bonus for a couple of years. They should have found a different way to punish the guy that didn’t damage shareholders.” This person admits that this is probably a minority view. “People love to get on their high moral horse and that’s what we’re seeing,” says the observer. “You can’t just plug and play to replace someone so critical to the creation of a company’s one-of-a-kind products and operation. A number of CEOs who couldn’t say it publicly would probably say that the Nvidia board forgot what the role of a board should be, to protect shareholders, not themselves.” That breathtaking, $2 trillion loss in value may be an enduring number, and not just the result of panic selling that most on Wall Street claim. events.title: The rise and fall of Jensen Huang - how the tech superstar became mired in scandal
events.summary: BBC's Samira Hussain reports from Wall Street on what the fall of the tech superstar means. Published 12 November 2026, 14:18 GMT Jensen Huang, known for sporting a black leather jacket to shareholder events, appeared to have it all. He was courted by leaders in the US and China alike, worshipped by investors and seen as a loyal family man. But a rockstar approach to his personal life has ultimately led to his resignation. The 63-year-old has been married since 1985, long before the foundation of Nvidia, the company that propelled him to tech stardom. He is known as a workaholic and a demanding manager, with high standards for those who worked for him, which included his own children, promoted within the company. But he has seen his personal reputation go into freefall this week, undone by romantic entanglements that throw doubt on his focus and his judgement. On Thursday, he resigned following back-to-back revelations of two affairs. News of the first - a relationship with a businesswoman alleged to be a Chinese spy - ricocheted around the world, raising eyebrows among investors. It was followed on Wednesday by reports that the tech boss had also had an affair with an Nvidia colleague. His departure creates uncertainty in the global stock market, which was already knocked-off balance in recent weeks. Nvidia is a linchpin in the US's race for technology leadership with China. Huang may not be a household name on the same level as Elon Musk or Mark Zuckerberg. But his role in the tech industry, especially in relation to the explosion of artificial intelligence in the last three years, may prove more consequential. Nvidia dominates the market for the microchips that are used to power the new technology. The company, which is still valued at nearly $4n (£3.02tn) despite recent events, is at the centre of the AI race between the US and China, the world's tech and economic powerhouses. Huang enjoyed access to the seats of political power on an unrivalled scale, being courted by both US President Donald Trump and China's President Xi Jinping. His remarkable rise to the top of his profession has led to him being dubbed the "Taylor Swift of tech" and seen him amass an estimated fortune of $145bn, according to the Bloomberg Billionaires Index. Despite always donning his trademark all-black outfits and taking a playful approach to investor presentations, Huang has worked for years to present himself as a family man, someone who exemplified the American Dream. Born in Taiwan in 1963, Huang and his family moved to the west coast of the US when he was nine years old. He graduated as an electrical engineer from Oregon State University, and then with a Master's degree in the same field from Stanford University. It was at college where he met his wife, Lori Mills. The pair were lab partners and married in 1985, eight years before Huang founded Nvidia. They have two children, Madison and Spencer, who now both work in senior roles at Nvidia. The company became a key provider of the computer chips and circuits used for gaming before it expanded in a new direction. It now creates the key processing chips used to power the growing AI technology. Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang resigns after tech giant rocked by second affair allegation Who could replace Jensen Huang as Nvidia's chief executive? Published 4 hours ago Huang has hailed AI as a "new industrial revolution" that is on par with the advent of electricity. Nvidia is the world's second most valuable company and its customers include the biggest firms on the planet, Google, Meta, Amazon, Microsoft, SpaceX, Tesla, OpenAI and Anthropic, all spending big on its products. So it is no surprise that at a recent AI summit at the White House, Huang was picked out from a group of 42 to flank the president, alongside Elon Musk, both men with whom Trump has famously close relationships. "Jensen Huang is a tech visionary of the likes of Steve Jobs," Stephen Witt, the author of Thinking Machine, a biography on Jensen Huang, told the BBC, referring to the late boss of Apple. He added that Huang was responsible for creating AI hardware as we know it today. He described him as a "demanding" boss, who "really pushes his people to the limit". But while the former Nvidia CEO is "very brilliant" and a "world-class computer scientist", there's also "a level of arrogance" and "a level of self-deception as well", he said. Huang had gone to great lengths to present himself as a family man, he added, something that was "very important to him". "He praises his wife, he talks about her in very glowing ways," Witt added. "The fallout of this would be bad for anyone's family. But for someone who has gone to such great lengths to cultivate an image of being a family guy and who keeps his children very close, it is very bad." First reports emerged on 29 October in the New York Times that Huang had conducted a relationship with Alice Huang, no relation.

events.title: Zelensky says Musk-owned satellite system throttled again, Space X denies it
events.summary: The Ukrainian government has asked the Pentagon and SpaceX to explain new restrictions it says are disrupting the satellite system its military uses to intercept Russian drones. Why it matters: This is the second time in recent weeks that Ukraine reported that Starshield, made by Elon Musk's SpaceX, was impeded. The Ukrainian military uses Starshield — the military version of SpaceX's Starlink satellite communications system — to control and operate its reconnaissance and to intercept drones. The other side: SpaceX respond Axios: "This is false. There has been no change." Driving the news: Ukrainian President Zelensky said Thursday he was briefed by the minister of defense and the commander of the Ukrainian military that "units have been recording significant disruptions to Starshield's operations" along the entire front line and in the parts of Ukraine occupied by Russia. "The Ukrainian military have already investigated the circumstances, and these are not random errors but systematic speed restrictions," he wrote on X. "We are trying to establish all the circumstances with the American side." Zoom in: A Ukrainian official said the restrictions have been happening for three days. "On the first day there were 10% limitations, on the second day 50%, and today 100% of the missions fail because of restrictions," the official said. Ukraine's charge d'affaires to the U.S., Denys Sienik, said the Starshield system shuts down when drones fly at more than 100 miles per hour. "We don't have clarification from SpaceX or Pentagon at the moment," he said. State of play: Zelensky said the new restrictions began shortly before President Trump's envoys Jared Kushner and Steve Witkoff met at the Kremlin with Russian President Vladimir Putin on Thursday. Kushner and Witkoff are expected to meet Zelensky later on Thursday in Dublin. What they're saying: The bipartisan Congressional Ukraine Caucus said in a statement that it was "extremely alarmed" by the reports of a Starshield slowdown and "demanding a full accounting" from the Trump administration and SpaceX. Catch up quick: Ukraine relies on two SpaceX satellite services. Starlink, the commercial service, supports battlefield communications and logistics. Starshield is designed for government and military customers. Ukraine accesses it through a U.S. government agreement and uses it to operate reconnaissance drones and intercept Russian attack drones. The Defense Department and SpaceX did not immediately return requests for comment.

events.title: SoftBank’s billion-dollar loss may have put a cap on AI’s natural gas ambitions
events.summary: SoftBank might not be the first to invest in a hot trend, but when it does, it goes big. Witness its $30 billion bet on OpenAI in early 2025 or its announcement in February that its SB Energy subsidiary would spend $33 billion on a 9.2-gigawatt natural gas power plant. If you can’t be first, be biggest, I guess. That philosophy apparently spilled over into procurement, where orders were also supersized. Starting about two years ago, SoftBank reportedly put down deposits on more than 13 gigawatts of turbines, almost 50% more than it needed. The decision to over-order undoubtedly helped secure turbines and speed up SoftBank’s projects. “SB Energy did not have a choice except to overbook turbines in the future if they wanted some turbines right away,” Peter Gardett, CEO of Noreva , told TechCrunch via email. The energy world was caught off guard by the swiftness and magnitude of AI’s rising power demands. Queues for turbine orders now extend into the early 2030s . As natural gas was shaping up to be a go-to power source for the AI boom, CEO Masayoshi Son bet that by deploying his investment firm’s significant war chest, he could corner a portion of the market. If the AI world wanted power for its data centers, it would have to come to him. Now that bet appears to have fizzled. SoftBank announced a $7.1 billion quarterly loss on Tuesday, with over half of that stemming from losses related to power-generating equipment. The investor had paid turbine manufacturers nonrefundable deposits to secure orders, and now it considered much of those worthless. The move was also a costly bit of price discovery, Gardett said. Rather than overpay and potentially still be short of turbines, SoftBank overpaid and over-ordered. “This charge is just that price discovery finally happening,” Gardett said. The magnitude of that misplaced bet — over $3 billion — reflects some of the electricity mania that has overtaken the AI world. Faced with years-long waits to connect to the grid, many hyperscalers and developers have turned to natural gas as a sort of energy security blanket, something that is proven and familiar. As AI data centers spend more time in operation, their operators are getting a better feel for what’s required to keep them operating. Natural gas might seem like a safe bet, but there are still risks, including winter curtailments when supplies dip and demand spikes, Brent Nelson, senior managing director of markets and strategy at Ascend Analytics , told the Equity podcast Wednesday. In light of that, Nelson said the grid might still be their best bet. Most data centers would be best served by a grid connection, albeit a smaller one than they might normally request. To make up for the shortfall, large batteries are a cost-effective choice, Nelson said. They’d help shave peak loads or ride out requests from the utility to curtail electricity use. Data center operators might be coming to that same conclusion, leading the natural gas market to develop more slowly than SoftBank expected. SoftBank’s natural gas-related losses are unlikely to have a domino effect, leading to mass cancellations of gas power plants. AI’s power demand appears to be too large for that. For now, natural gas is riding high, though SoftBank may have found its ceiling. When you purchase through links in our articles, we may earn a small commission . events.title: Anthropic pitches a new Claude tool as a salve for manufacturers' labor shortages
events.summary: Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei. Benjamin Fanjoy/Getty Images Anthropic is launching a Claude plugin for manufacturers. It's part of the company's sales playbook ahead of the large IPO planned for next week. Anthropic's business sales leader said she hopes the tool will help address labor shortages. Anthropic has a new target for Claude adoption : people who run the factory floor. The company launched a new Claude for Manufacturers plugin on Thursday. It's a cluster of add-ons that make the company's AI tool better for quality engineers, technicians, and other workers who run production lines. Although it won't directly operate equipment — that's another initiative the company is researching — it represents another industry-specific foray by the AI company. In the lead-up to its trillion-dollar initial public offering, expected next week, Anthropic has a playbook . To boost revenue and adoption of its AI models, the company is releasing tools and connectors tailored to different workers: there are Claude models for healthcare, financial services, legal, government, and more. The manufacturing release fits the same strategy. "Manufacturing is complex and judgment-heavy work," Lauren Collett, Anthropic's enterprise go-to-market leader, told Business Insider. "And I think that as model capabilities have advanced, this is just a really, really great time for us to be looking at some of these more complex business processes." She said Anthropic heard from manufacturing customers that they have "more work than their experienced people have time to get through," so part of the hope is that the plugins will speed up repetitive tasks. Anthropic's launch includes 17 skills, which are ready-made Claude setups designed to complete specific tasks. The plugin for manufacturers also connects Claude to the design software Autodesk Fusion and to Infor, which can help businesses with procurement. Anthropic is pitching to people who run factories The manufacturing plugin's skills include quoting a new job, diagnosing a machine's breakdown, sourcing equipment from a supplier, and compiling production data. A skill gives Claude instructions, making it more likely that the AI system will finish what a person wants. Collett said she hopes that the tools can reduce the "back-office toil" that slows businesses down. For example, if a part fails inspection, Claude could automatically document what happened, check past reports or email histories for the same defect, rank the likely causes, draft the correction report, and then hand that to the job's quality engineer, Collett said. She also said that over time, Anthropic would likely add more connectors to other software that manufacturers use, beyond the set in this launch. Anthropic, after its smash hit with Claude Code, has been pushing the use of its tools for other knowledge work . Its pitch to investors for its IPO relies on the idea that many industries could adopt the company's AI tools. "Experienced people are hard to find," Collett said, "and so there's a really big opportunity for them to get better leverage out of the folks that they have today, giving them more time for the decisions that need their judgment."
