events.title: Phota Labs uses AI to turn everyday photos into professional-looking shots
events.summary: A new iOS app called Phota Labs gives users access to a personal AI photo assistant that turns everyday snapshots into images that look like they were taken by a professional photographer, all while preserving the authenticity of the image. Rather than giving consumers yet another photo-editing tool, Phota Labs aims to use advances in AI to automate the editing process so it’s easier for anyone to get access to better photos. The a16z-backed startup was founded by Cecilia Zhang and Zach Xia, who met at Adobe while working on computational photography products, including Project Indigo, Lightroom, and Photoshop. The duo saw a gap in the editing tools on the market and believed that although editing tools can be powerful for enhancing photos, they aren’t very effective at fixing a photo that wasn’t captured well in the first place. Phota Labs changes that by focusing on fixing the shot itself while preserving the natural appearances of those in the image. “Phota is your personal photo assistant that can make great photos for any moment you want to keep before you even ask, which means that it’s a very proactive experience,” Zhang told TechCrunch in an interview. “Think of it almost like a photographer or virtual photographer who looks over your camera roll and tries to understand what’s happening and how they could have taken that photo for you on the spot for that scene.” The idea is to use AI to transform photos, whether that’s turning a wide-angle group photo into a tighter portrait or transforming a selfie into a regular shot. Users can choose from different photography styles that determine how AI transforms their images, ranging from subtle edits that preserve the original lens and composition to more dramatic transformations that introduce effects like fish-eye lenses, alternative angles, and entirely different perspectives. While some people turn to ChatGPT and other generative AI tools to enhance or edit images, these tools can often alter a person’s appearance, especially when working with blurry photos because they don’t know what that person actually looks like. “For Phota, we built our own tech,” Zhang said. ”We built this personalization technology that actually learns about people’s identity and is able to preserve them in any transformation we do to a photo.” Images edited with Phota Labs feature invisible watermarks that identify them as altered by AI when shared on social platforms. The startup is initially targeting people who take tons of photos and like to share them on social media, but don’t want to deal with the tedious process of editing photos. Over time, the founders envision a broader audience, from retirees looking to create beautiful photos for their grandchildren to parents who want to share polished family albums with friends and relatives. “We have this obsession with authenticity,” Xia said. “I think there’s so much value in connecting AI with real moments and making sure those photos are not perfect, in a sense. That’s why we spend a lot of research into understanding personal context, into building this identity model because we want to make sure the photos are authentic. They’re just better photos of the same moment, rather than saying, ‘Oh, this is an AI image’.” Xia said beta users were excited to see better versions of moments they had actually lived and saw the results as photos of real memories rather than AI-generated images. The founders discovered that users were taking more photos because they knew Phota Labs could enhance them later. “We’re turning something that’s unusable into something that people want to print,” Zhang said. “People who just love photos but never really got into editing can now experience professional quality that could never have been possible. So, I think that meant so much to us. There’s so many cherished moments for photos, and we really want them to be actually meaningful and something that you can remember.” In terms of funding, the company raised a $5.6 million seed round led by a16z last year. Phota Labs is launching as a free app to build an initial user base before exploring a freemium model. The startup also plans to launch an Android app in the future. events.title: Trump says 'only one man' can replace Jensen Huang: Tim Cook
events.summary: President Donald Trump has some ideas on who should take Jensen Huang's place at Nvidia. Kent NISHIMURA / AFP via Getty Images President Donald Trump has weighed in on Jensen Huang's resignation. Trump said former Apple CEO Tim Cook is the "only one man" to replace the Nvidia CEO. Trump has long praised Cook, once saying he was the only CEO in his first term who called him regularly on the phone. President Donald Trump has his own recommendation for Nvidia's next CEO — Tim Cook. In a Truth Social post on Thursday, Trump called Cook, Apple's former CEO, the "only one man" to replace Jensen Huang after the more-than-three-decade Nvidia boss resigned . "NOW THAT Nvidia CEO JENSEN HUANG, who has done a fantastic job, has resigned, there is only one man to take his place - TIM COOK of Apple. A Legend replaces a Legend!" Trump said in the post. Trump is a longtime fan of Cook, who stepped down as Apple's CEO earlier this year and took on the role of executive chairman of Apple's board of directors. The president has previously called Cook an "amazing manager and leader" and commended him for calling him directly on the phone . "He calls me and the others don't," Trump said during his first term. "Others go out and hire very expensive consultants, and Tim Cook calls Donald Trump directly. Pretty good." In April, after Apple announced that Cook would step down as CEO, Trump called Cook an "incredible guy" in a Truth Social post. Trump added that Cook "had an AMAZING career, almost incomparable, and will go on and continue to do great work for Apple, and whatever else he chooses to work on." Nvidia's board of directors announced Huang's exit as the AI chip giant's CEO earlier Thursday, after a tumultuous week for Huang, marked by a company investigation and revelations about two extramarital affairs . On Sunday, Huang said in a note to staff that he had been "unfaithful" to his wife of more than 40 years. "My actions hurt her and our children," Huang wrote. "There is no excuse for what I did. I am deeply sorry." This followed a New York Times report last month that said Huang had developed a close relationship with Alice Huang , a former executive at Nvidia customer Megaspeed. The report said US intelligence officials believe the woman was recruited to gather information for the Chinese government. The Nvidia founder's admission of an affair triggered an independent board investigation into the billionaire businessman. Amid that investigation, led by an elite Wall Street law firm , the Times reported that Jensen Huang also had an extramarital affair with Kimberly Powell , Nvidia's vice president of healthcare. Powell was one of Jensen Huang's direct reports. Nvidia said CFO Colette Kress will serve as interim CEO until a permanent successor is named. Read the original article on Business Insider

events.title: Fed faces tougher inflation fight as pressure builds for more rate hikes
events.summary: Data: FactSet; Chart: Courtenay Brown/Axios Inflation is no longer confined to a handful of trouble spots. Now, Federal Reserve officials are starting to question whether raising interest rates gradually will be enough to contain it. Why it matters: Fed officials had hoped that a relatively modest series of interest rate hikes would be enough to bring inflation under control — more a recalibration than a tightening campaign. But stubbornly high — and increasingly widespread — price pressures are raising the possibility of a more prolonged tightening campaign, with no clear endpoint in sight. That would leave the Fed facing a more difficult balancing act: raising rates enough to contain inflation without unnecessarily damaging the economy. What they're saying: "We have got a real inflation issue on our hands that has been developing — and we're going to have to deal with that," Chicago Fed president Austan Goolsbee, who called the inflation data "borderline disturbing," said late Tuesday . Driving the news: Treasury yields are surging after Tuesday's hot inflation report and hawkish commentary from Fed officials — including governor Christopher Waller, who raised the prospect of a supersized rate hike next month. Short-term yields have risen more sharply than longer-term yields, a sign that investors expect the Fed may need to raise rates more aggressively than previously anticipated. The yield on the two-year Treasury note is still marching higher after surging 17 basis points on Tuesday, which was the biggest one-day surge since April 2025 — when markets were reeling from the "liberation day" tariffs. The yield on the 10-year Treasury note jumped about 8 basis points, putting it back above 5%. Financial markets see a December rate hike as virtually certain, according to CME FedWatch. Expectations for next year are trending higher, with traders now pricing in two additional quarter-point hikes by June. The big picture: Measures designed to strip out unusually large price swings suggest that underlying inflation pressures are gaining pace. The Cleveland Fed's trimmed-mean Consumer Price Index —which filters out unusually large price swings to give a clearer picture of underlying inflation — rose 0.4% in October, the largest monthly increase since May. The Atlanta Fed's sticky-price CPI , which tracks prices that typically change, slowly accelerated to a 4.7% annualized pace in October, its fastest since February 2025. More than three-quarters of the consumer price basket saw prices rise at an annualized rate exceeding 2% in October, the largest share since August 2022, Charles Schwab's head of macro research Kevin Gordon posted on X . Yes, but: The Fed may have reason to proceed cautiously even against the backdrop of stubborn inflation. Rising bond yields and a sell-off in technology stocks (revived again by the exit of Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang ) are already tightening financial conditions — potentially doing some of the work of higher interest rates. Fed governor Michelle Bowman said in a speech that falling stock prices, higher borrowing costs and a stronger dollar could weigh on economic growth, particularly in sectors already struggling with high interest rates. Cleveland Fed president Beth Hammack, who dissented against the decision to hold rates steady last month, said she still supported a more gradual approach to raising rates. "It's less disruptive to the overall economy than moving in sharper, more aggressive movements," she said Thursday morning . What to watch: Some of the forces driving inflation higher this year — including tariffs and the Iran war — were expected to be temporary. But the risk that they will prove more persistent keeps resurfacing. President Trump threatened on Thursday morning to double tariffs on Mexican imports unless the nation stops a caravan of migrants from reaching the U.S. border. Trump also said the U.S. doesn't need a deal with Iran , raising fresh questions about how soon the conflict (and the disruption to global energy supplies) might end.

Nvidia's new leaders sought to reassure employees Thursday after Jensen Huang abruptly resigned from the company he cofounded more than three decades ago following reports of extramarital affairs . Interim CEO Colette Kress and newly appointed board chair Harvey Jones addressed the leadership shake-up and laid out the company's next steps, according to internal memos obtained by Business Insider. Kress said leadership would host a company meeting on November 18 about Nvidia's future, while Jones said the company's board was searching for a permanent successor and considering both internal and external candidates. Read both memos in full below: Colette Kress: Dear NVIDIANs, I believe deeply in this company and in its future. More than anything, I believe in each of you, in our customers and partners and in the vital role we play every day in the global economy. The Board, Estaff and I recognize that this has been an extraordinarily difficult period and I want you to know how grateful we are for your resilience, professionalism and continued dedication. Thank you. This company has achieved so much because of the work that all of you bring to it every single day. You are our greatest strength. You will hear more from leadership in the coming days about our future together, and we will host a company meeting on November 18 at 9am PT. We play a vital role in building the technology that is powering the AI revolution, and we have important work ahead of us. So let's move forward together, with the same determination and commitment that have always defined this company. Thank you for all you do, Colette Harvey Jones: Dear NVIDIA Employees, I am writing to share an important update. Jensen has resigned as CEO and Board Member, and the Board has asked our Chief Financial Officer Colette Kress to serve as interim CEO while it conducts a search for a permanent successor looking at both internal and external candidates. I will serve as the first-ever Chair of the Board. As CFO for over 13 years, Colette has been a key architect of NVIDIA's growth and capital strategy. She possesses a deep understanding of this business and the markets in which we operate. The Board has full confidence in Colette to deliver on our commitments to shareholders, customers, partners, and to each of you. Jensen's contributions to NVIDIA are profound. NVIDIA is one of the most consequential technology companies in the world. We pioneered accelerated computing, defined the modern GPU, and built the platform that powered artificial intelligence. The Board takes seriously our duty as stewards of this great company. The strength of this company resides in our employees, leadership team, technical strength and partner ecosystem. I am confident that under Colette's leadership, with the full support of the Board, we will continue to grow our business, and lead the industry forward. Thank you for your focus, your professionalism, and your commitment to NVIDIA. Harvey Jones Chair, NVIDIA Board of Directors Have a tip? events.title: Prominent Israeli settler denied entry into France
events.summary: Israel criticises Yossi Dagan’s entry ban, labelling it ‘unacceptable’ amid tensions over illegal settlement policies. The head of an organisation representing illegal Israeli settlements in the occupied West Bank has been denied entry into France. Israel denounced the move as “completely unacceptable” on Wednesday after prominent Israeli settler Yossi Dagan said French authorities turned him back last week when he flew into a Paris airport. Dagan, who is a member of Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu’s Likud party , was “subject to an administrative ban from the territory due to his active role in implementing the settlement policy in the West Bank” according to his office. “Settlement building is contrary to international law and undermines the two-state solution,” the French ministry said. According to the ministry, Dagan was “pulled aside and questioned” at the airport’s passport control before being informed that he was banned from entering French territory “due to his active role in implementing the settlement policy in the West Bank.” Dagan said Wednesday that he was undeterred by the ban and was proud to “build the historic homeland of the Jewish people”, while Israeli’s foreign ministry said the measures against Dagan were based on “political and ideological grounds”. “Israel will demand an explanation from the French government and consider its next steps accordingly,” it added. The incident comes amid growing tension between Israel and European countries around illegal settlements in the occupied West Bank, which have proliferated under Netanyahu’s government. France, along with 11 other countries, announced its intention to restrict trade with ⁠⁠⁠⁠illegal settlements in the Palestinian territory in September, which spurred outrage from Israeli officials. On Monday, a French parliamentary committee approved a bill banning the imports of settlement goods and services contributing to settlement construction, with further discussion scheduled for November 19. There are at least 148 illegal settlements in the occupied West Bank and 15 in occupied East Jerusalem, now home to about 750,000 Israelis, according to Israeli anti-settlement watchdog Peace Now. Earlier this year, France banned far-right Israeli ministers, Itamar Ben-Gvir and Bezalel Smotrich, who are both members of Netanyahu’s cabinet.

events.title: Jensen Huang agrees to testify before Congress
events.summary: Ex-Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang has agreed to testify before Congress, House Foreign Affairs Committee Chairman Brian Mast said on Thursday, according to reports from Bloomberg and NBC News . Huang, who stepped down as CEO following reports of an alleged affair with a woman suspected of spying for China, agreed to testify Wednesday after several senior lawmakers threatened to subpoena him. Huang has agreed to testify before Congress by Thanksgiving, which falls later this month. The development comes after House Republicans Mast, John Moolenaar, and Rick Crawford sent Huang a letter on November 4 requesting that he appear before their committees . Moolenaar chairs the House Select Committee on the Chinese Communist Party, Mast chairs the House Committee on Foreign Affairs, and Crawford chairs the House Intelligence Committee. “Jensen and I have been very at odds as some of you already know on export controls, but Nvidia is a very important company to the United States of America,” Mast said to reporters. “I don’t want to see anything hurt in Nvidia, but he has some very serious questions to answer.” The testimony will take place behind closed doors, though Mast said he expects the briefing to be recorded on video and transcribed. events.title: Trump says ‘we don’t need a deal with Iran’
events.summary: The U.S. should no longer seek a deal with Iran, President Donald Trump wrote on Truth Social. Trump directed Vice President JD Vance to instead focus his attention on corruption and crime in Democratic cities and states. "We don't need a deal with Iran. Those days have long since passed," Trump wrote in the post. The U.S. should no longer seek a deal with Iran, President Donald Trump said Thursday as he directed Vice President JD Vance to instead focus his attention on corruption and crime in Democratic cities and states. "We don't need a deal with Iran. Those days have long since passed," Trump wrote in a Truth Social post. "We've got their money, Hundreds of Billions of Dollars, and we've got their Strait!" Trump wrote, referring to the Strait of Hormuz, a key chokepoint in the ongoing U.S.-Iran war. The announcement came just over a week after Republicans suffered huge losses in the midterm election. Vance and other Republicans have pinned those losses on the Iran war, which the U.S. and Israel started in late February. In the weeks leading up to Election Day, Trump repeatedly suggested the U.S. could resume launching military strikes, which have largely subsided as a tense stalemate has taken hold in the region. The Wall Street Journal on Wednesday reported that Vance, who has led diplomatic efforts with Iran in prior months, was considering face-to-face talks with a top Iranian security official. Stock futures declined following Trump's post. The unpopular Iran war, which Trump and others in his administration said would be won in a matter of weeks, is now in its ninth month with no clear end in sight. The conflict region has driven up global energy prices, creating a ripple effect through the economy and exacerbating concerns about inflation and affordability that were paramount to voters in the midterms. Corruption emerged as another top issue that broke in Democrats' favor in the election. Trump's post Thursday morning attempts to flip the script, blaming Democratic-run areas for allowing corruption and crime to proliferate. "I have asked Vice President Vance to focus his complete and total attention on the Massive Corruption and Crime taking place in Democrat run Cities and States throughout the U.S.," Trump wrote. "The Blue States, such as Minnesota, California, Illinois, and many more, are all poorly run, corrupt disasters. Billions of Dollars is being stolen each and every month," the president wrote. "Our Budget could be quickly BALANCED with the correction of this large scale criminal activity." "CORRUPTION is in the Democrat Leadership's blood!" he added.

events.title: Five ways Jensen Huang’s ouster from Nvidia could damage the AI industry
events.summary: Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang’s confession that he had an affair (and reports of another one with a direct report ) that led the board to oust him on Thursday isn’t just your run-of-the-mill salacious billionaire CEO sex scandal. In this case, one of his lovers is suspected by the U.S. government of being a spy for China . She’s also an executive of a Singapore-based neocloud that is suspected of smuggling Nvidia chips to China. These affairs show undeniably poor judgment by Huang and, I’d argue, unchecked hubris on many levels. Such choices are not only a betrayal of his wife of 40 years, they’re also a liability for his company. Sleeping with any Nvidia partner is bad enough, but he also chose one in a tinderbox of a geopolitical situation. Even if Alice Huang’s company wasn’t suspected of helping Chinese firms evade chip restrictions (and he was somehow unaware of this), it was still exploiting a legal loophole by renting powerful AI infrastructure to Chinese companies. It’s those potential national consequences that may land him in a hellscape of ongoing public humiliation. Republican committee chairs are already summoning him to testify in closed-door sessions about the security ramifications. Will Democrats, who are set to take over key committees when the new Congress convenes in January, also haul him in to testify on the Hill? No one knows yet, but Huang has flaunted his close relationship with President Trump. Remember when Trump called him while he was onstage at the All-In Summit in September? Nvidia also donated $25 million to Trump’s ballroom, a deeply unpopular project with American voters. Several Democratic lawmakers have already vowed to investigate the money behind it. In other words, he is a billionaire close to Trump. He was — until Thursday — the face of AI and data centers (also a deeply unpopular political topic with voters), and he has publicly admitted to having an affair with an alleged Chinese spy. Even though he’s no longer CEO, that seems too juicy a target for Democrats to ignore. Beyond whatever may be coming, Huang’s influence has been lost right when he was using it to push the tech industry in a number of directions. These areas have now lost their biggest champion. Open-weight AI models as competitors to closed-source labs Huang has been the biggest, loudest advocate for open-weight AI models in the tech industry and among government policymakers. Nvidia not only offers its own open-weight models, it also offers a lot of other open source tech for agents, AI security, and more. It has even agreed to acquire the biggest site that hosts them, Hugging Face, for $12.9 billion. (That deal is supposed to close in the first half of next year, pending regulatory approval.) In July, when Anthropic and OpenAI were reportedly urging the Trump administration to ban Chinese open-weight models, Huang organized a letter of support for open-weight models generally (if not Chinese models specifically), signed by hundreds of tech companies. Open-weight models give enterprises choice in the market and reduce costs. Without Huang, the next biggest advocate for them is perhaps Microsoft’s Satya Nadella, but he’s not out there organizing the industry to speak up. Pushing the AI industry to clean up its security Both OpenAI and Anthropic revealed incident after incident this year as their AI agents hacked into others’ networks or performed other misdeeds. Huang loudly proclaimed the AI industry still didn’t need regulation and would deal with safety itself. As the industry mulled over what they should do ( auditors? a FINRA-like board? ), Huang rallied the tech industry again. Nvidia got over 100 companies to sign on to his Open Agent Safety Platform, a largely open source effort to solve the epidemic of misbehaving AI agents. Naturally, this effort hasn’t instantly solved the problem , and now the top spokesperson for self-regulation via technology solutions is out of his position of influence. Arguing AI is a tool, not a life form Huang has also been among the loudest voices insisting that AI is an engineered system that creates products, and so can be controlled like any other engineered system. This viewpoint counters the AI doomers and even the big AI labs themselves, which sometimes position their models as on the verge of consciousness (Anthropic) or as alien minds (OpenAI) . While Huang deals with the fallout of his actions, the loudest voice of this counter-narrative is, for the foreseeable future, silenced. A new Nvidia-powered AI PC industry Huang also just convinced a long list of PC makers to buy into his long-time dream of providing CPUs (the main processor chips) for them. In this age, when most Americans have not experienced AI beyond a chatbot, he orchestrated a new line of high-end AI PCs geared for running agents locally. These new PCs are due out this holiday season, and they may sell well for their intended targets: creators, developers, and others already savvy with agents.

events.title: UK car industry to press EU for two-year delay to Brexit EV tariffs
events.summary: ‘Rules of origin’ on vehicle batteries due to come into force on 1 January if deal on new delay is not reached The UK car industry is preparing to push for a two-year delay to Brexit tariffs on electric cars traded with the EU, after an initial European proposal suggested a shorter delay. Tariffs are due to kick in on 1 January for the majority of electric cars traded between the EU and UK unless the two sides can come to an agreement to delay for a second time the implementation of “rules of origin” on batteries. The Brexit deal, which was rushed through on Christmas Eve in 2020, included a clause that British and European electric cars would have to use batteries made in either the UK or the EU with local materials, or face 10% tariffs . The rules would not have existed had the UK remained in the EU. The rules were initially meant to come into force on 1 January 2024, encouraging the industry to invest in local lithium-ion battery manufacturing rather than relying on the dominant Chinese battery industry . In 2020, the prospects seemed rosy, but three years later several prominent projects on both sides of the Channel had collapsed. The EU and UK agreed to extend the deadline in December 2023 . Other battery projects have since taken their place, but many are yet to produce at the scale required to meet European demand. Instead, carmakers are mainly reliant on imports from China, Japan and South Korea. Carmakers in the UK and Europe are united in their calls for the introduction of the rules of origin to be delayed again. However, an agreement has yet to be reached, with the EU and UK also wrangling over whether Britain can be included in “Made in Europe” subsidies , and whether the UK should match EU tariffs on Chinese car imports . The topics are likely to form part of an EU-UK summit planned for next week. The European Commission has shared proposals with the automotive industry to delay the start of the tariffs, although they have not yet been shared formally with the UK government. The proposals are understood to be highly technical, but essentially equate to delaying the start of the rules of origin by a year. Some of the proposals are understood to include adjusting customs procedures and origin calculation methodologies, which could offer some temporary tariff flexibility. Get set for the working day – we'll point you to all the business news and analysis you need every morning However, some parts of the UK car industry believe more time is needed for the sector to adapt and for battery gigafactories to churn out enough units. One executive in the UK said: “The industry will be really clear – two years minimum or we have the same discussion next year. Giga-industrialisation is happening in the EU and UK but it is not producing at the required volume yet.” Another person said the negotiations would also focus on the technical details of the proposals, rather than simply aiming for a set time delay. The European Automobile Manufacturers Association, an influential lobby group in Brussels, has argued that the tariffs are a serious concern for Europe’s automotive industry . It estimated that 82% of EU electric car and van exports to the UK would face the 10% customs duty in 2027 under the rules, adding costs of €1.47bn (£1.23bn) next year alone. Mike Hawes, the chief executive of the UK lobby group SMMT, said: “The UK and EU must urgently agree pragmatic solutions to the challenges of Made in Europe and EV rules of origin, which if unresolved will cause severe damage to our deeply integrated industries. “For the latter, any agreement must remove the massive tariff liability faced on electrified vehicles traded from 1 January, be workable for manufacturers on both sides and protect ongoing battery investment. events.title: I spent decades building a life in the Netherlands. In my late 40s, I sold my house and moved to a tiny French village.
events.summary: In my late 40s, I decided to follow my heart and begin a new life in the French countryside. Hans Westbeek I moved to the Netherlands 29 years ago to start a new life with my now-husband. I got a great job, bought a home, and had a daughter there, but always dreamed of moving to France. Finally, my husband and I decided to take a risk and buy a home in the French countryside . I was raised in New Jersey, but moved to the Netherlands in October 1997 to start a new life with the man who would eventually become my husband. I was 19 and, aside from my family and education, there wasn't much tying me down to the US. I was young, free, and fearless. Reality hit hard during those first months, though: Even the rosy glow of love couldn't have prepared me for the culture shock and loneliness. I wondered how I would ever learn the language, get an education, find a job, and feel at home. Undeterred, I immediately began learning Dutch. By the following May, I was studying journalism at a local university. Over the next five years, I married my partner, had a daughter, and enrolled in a graduate program, where I earned a degree in Dutch Studies. By 2008, I had become a Dutch citizen, launched a writing career, and bought a beautiful four-bedroom home with a glorious garden and dreamy kitchen in Almere, a city in the heart of the Netherlands. Three years later, I landed a dream remote job as a magazine editor. I was settled, happy, and doing well. And then, I started thinking about leaving. I fell head over heels for a small town in the French countryside Duras won me over the first time I visited. Hans Westbeek I still remember how I felt the first time I visited Duras, a village in southwest France surrounded by vineyards, prune orchards, and sunflower fields. It was 2009, and I was staying with my husband and 9-year-old daughter at a little cottage a stone's throw from the town center. I remember laying eyes on the Château de Duras — a majestic castle that has stood in the village since the 12th century — and feeling an immediate connection that I couldn't quite explain. In the years that followed, we spent at least two weeks there every summer, and each time we drove away, it felt like I was leaving a little piece of my heart behind. My husband was just as captivated, too. Before long, we started asking ourselves the obvious question: What about actually living there? By 2022, we'd started genuinely considering a move, but it felt daunting. Could I really start all over again, now, in my late 40s? What about selling the home I had poured so much love into? And what about my daughter? At 23, she had been living independently for some time, but the thought of moving to another country was difficult to contemplate. The idea of moving felt impossible, but I kept looking at real-estate listings online anyway. Hans Westbeek Still, I continued scrolling through French property listings — and one day, I spotted a house for sale in Duras. It was a stately maison de maître, with white shutters, stone floors, and even a wine cellar. Two days later, we went on a whirlwind trip to France , hoping to put in an offer. From the moment I walked in, I felt the same sense of connection that I did when I first set foot in Duras. I was so smitten that I barely registered how much work the house needed. After our visit, my husband and I realized that making it habitable would cost at least twice the purchase price, not to mention the time and patience renovations would demand. Disillusioned, we returned to the Netherlands, only to revisit our plans year after year. We viewed other properties in France , but every time, fear crept in, and we changed our minds at the last minute. Finally, we took the plunge and put our Dutch home on the market I couldn't be happier that we decided to move. Hans Westbeek In the spring of this year, we decided to put our house on the market . We knew that if we kept coming up with excuses or waiting for the perfect moment, we might never make the move. Within seven days, it was sold. As luck (or fate) would have it, we noticed a house for sale in Duras, right next door to the place we had loved so much in 2022. It had the same classic French beauty and character, and it was in excellent condition. What really caught my attention was the kitchen: it reminded me so much of the one in our Dutch home, which I had found so difficult to leave behind. We made an offer, and in September, we waved goodbye to our Dutch life and moved to France. The transition so far hasn't been easy. Nearly three decades in the Netherlands shaped me profoundly, and I miss the ease of city life. Here in southwest France, life moves at a slower pace, which I'm still getting used to. Even though I have a basic level of French, speaking confidently and with ease is still a challenge. But still, I wake up every morning and pinch myself. And then I do it again when we drive through the vineyard-covered hillsides, wander past the château, or open a bottle of Duras wine to enjoy with a lunch I've prepared using produce from the Monday market. Moving to the Netherlands all those years ago taught me that I was stronger than I thought, and that wonderful things can happen when we step outside our comfort zone and embrace the unfamiliar. events.title: From washing dishes at Denny’s to rockstar of AI: the rise and fall of Nvidia’s Jensen Huang
events.summary: Technical expertise and an ability to engage gave the chipmaker’s co-founder, who has now resigned, the edge with customers and investors Jensen Huang resigns as Nvidia CEO after alleged affairs Jensen Huang wasn’t always in his trademark leather jacket. When the multibillionaire, now former Nvidia chief executive was a teenager in the US, his first job was waiting tables and washing dishes at a branch of Denny’s. “It teaches you humility, it teaches you hard work, it teaches you hospitality,” he said in 2023 of his time at the diner chain. Decades later, having become one of the richest people on the planet, Huang put on a Denny’s apron in tribute to his former employer at an Nvidia event in 2025. By this point Huang had become a rockstar of the artificial intelligence boom – befitting his signature item of clothing – feted around the world by investors, fellow tech executives and politicians. The company that Huang co-founded makes the computer chips that are integral to the development and operation of AI systems such as ChatGPT. Demand for Nvidia’s products has surged as hundreds of billions of dollars have been poured into a technology that, according to its many promotors, will transform the global economy. The crude analogy is that Huang and Nvidia have become the main purveyors of shovels in the AI gold rush. In technical jargon, its AI chips are known as graphics processor units (GPUs), which were originally designed to handle the graphics for video games. But it turned out that a GPU’s ability to carry out masses of technical calculations simultaneously and quickly is very handy for developing and operating AI systems, which have a voracious appetite for data crunching. Nvidia is also very good at creating networks of its chips, which produces the computing power artificial intelligence needs, and provides the CUDA software that helps the company’s GPUs perform so well for AI customers. Jen-Hsun Huang, 63, was born in Taiwan to a chemical engineer father and a schoolteacher mother. Decades later, the island would become the centre of chip manufacturing and the foundry for Nvidia’s highly advanced chips. But his life was largely lived outside Taiwan. After a spell living in Thailand, Huang moved to the US when he was 10 – he is a joint citizen of Taiwan and the US – and has said he is “always an immigrant”. Accidentally enrolled by his uncle into a juvenile reform school in Kentucky, he anglicised his name and showed educational flair. Huang went to high school in Oregon and in 1984 he graduated with a degree in electrical engineering from Oregon State University, where he met his future wife, Lori, with whom he had a son and a daughter, both now Nvidia employees. He then completed a master’s degree in the same subject at Stanford University – in the heart of Silicon Valley – in 1992. A year later he founded Nvidia with fellow engineers Chris Malachowsky and Curtis Priem, during a meeting in a booth at Denny’s. The name is a riff on the Latin term for envy, invidia , an emotion that the company wanted its rivals to feel. Huang’s technical expertise also gave him an edge with customers and investors, according to The Nvidia Way, a biography of the company and its co-founder by Tae Kim. The book quotes Tench Coxe, an Nvidia board member and early investor, who said Huang stood out. “When you meet Jensen Huang, even with dozens of other graphics companies, you realise this is a guy you want to do business with,” said Tench. “What made him great is he is an engineer and he is a computer scientist.” Nvidia started out making graphics chips for personal computers. It released what is widely regarded as the world’s first GPU, the GeForce 256, in 1999 and as the technology became more and more powerful academic researchers realised it could accelerate AI development. Nvidia GPUs were used to create AlexNet, the neural network developed by Alex Krizhevsky, the OpenAI-co-founder Ilya Sutskever and the Nobel prize winner Geoffrey Hinton at the University of Toronto in 2012 – and a key moment in the history of modern AI. Six months after the launch of ChatGPT, Nvidia’s valuation reached $1tn (£756bn) in May 2023 and kept growing, hitting $5tn on October last year – the first ever company to reach such a milestone . However, it has fallen to about $4tn this week after allegations that Huang had conducted affairs with a Chinese spy and an Nvidia executive, leading to his resignation on Thursday. Huang’s 3.6% stake in Nvidia has given him considerable wealth. His fortune is valued at $145bn, according to Bloomberg, the 13th highest in the world. The importance of Nvidia’s products to the AI revolution have made Huang rich, powerful and famous. He is often seen at tech conferences or in the presence of global leaders, including Donald Trump with whom he has developed a rapport. Meta’s Mark Zuckerberg, another mighty Silicon Valley founder, has described Huang as “Taylor Swift, but for tech”.

events.title: The biggest winner from Jensen Huang's downfall is China
events.summary: Nvidia's Jensen Huang speaking at a conference in San Francisco Alistair Barr/Business Insider Nvidia's market value drops more than $300 billion as Jensen Huang resigns. Analysts warn removing Huang weakens America's AI lead as China tries to catch up. Huang had a romantic relationship with a woman who may be a Chinese spy. How valuable is a CEO? Often, it's hard to say. Sometimes, though, a series of unusual events provides a crystal-clear answer. On Thursday morning, Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang resigned after a New York Times report alleged Huang had an affair with a subordinate. That followed revelations earlier this week that he also had a romantic relationship with a possible Chinese spy . Just the concern that Huang would be out knocked Nvidia shares down about 8% in after-hours trading on Wednesday, wiping more than $300 billion off the company's market value. The Chinese spy allegations were already known days ago. The new news today is that Jensen Huang has been ousted as CEO. So we have our answer: Huang is worth at least $300 billion. That's more than Morgan Stanley and Goldman Sachs, the world's most important investment banks. And quite right, too. Huang is "the architect of the US AI trajectory," Stacy Rasgon, a top chip analyst from Bernstein Research, wrote in a note to investors earlier this week. This is the most powerful new technology to emerge since the dawn of the internet 30 years ago. And the US is in the lead — well ahead of China in second place. Now, with Huang out, America's AI lead looks shakier. "We can't even begin to speculate as to who they might find to fill Jensen's shoes," Rasgon wrote in a note to investors Wednesday evening. He slashed Nvidia's price target to $200 from $400. On Thursday, Nvidia announced CFO Colette Kress would serve as interim CEO. Earlier in the week, Rasgon warned of the geopolitical risks if Huang was forced to step down. "The primary beneficiary of Jensen's removal as Nvidia's CEO would clearly be China; we hope cooler heads prevail," he wrote. On Wednesday night, other analysts shared similar concerns. "This would be a setback for the US, particularly as China continues aggressively investing in its own AI capabilities," Brad Gastwirth, global head of research at Circular Technology, told me. "Removing Jensen would be a tremendous mistake," he added. "Nvidia is central to America's AI leadership, and losing Jensen at this stage could create unnecessary disruption." Nvidia's board had serious questions to answer about Huang's conduct, especially his relationship with a possible Chinese spy. If they did nothing, the directors could have exposed themselves to legal risk as representatives of the company's shareholders. One of the few real powers a public company board holds is the ability to hire and fire executives, so actions often involve tough decisions like this. But the board had to weigh the enormous cost of losing the man who built Nvidia into the engine of the AI boom. On Wednesday night, that cost is at least $300 billion. "The board obviously needs to take the allegations seriously, particularly anything involving national security," Gastwirth said. "Unless the investigation uncovers something that makes his position untenable, I believe the board would be making a major strategic mistake by removing him." events.title: Trump floats Apple chairman Tim Cook as Jensen Huang’s successor
events.summary: In the wake of the industry-shaking news of Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang’s resignation on Thursday, U.S. President Donald Trump is floating the idea that former Apple CEO Tim Cook should take over the position. In a post on Truth Social, Trump wrote that “only one man” could take Huang’s place: Tim Cook of Apple. “A Legend replaces a Legend!” he wrote. Cook stepped down as Apple’s CEO on September 1, 2026, after 15 years running the company , but he’s still very much involved with Apple. While John Ternus took over as Apple’s CEO, Cook transitioned into the role of executive chairman of Apple’s board of directors, which sees him continuing to engage with global policymakers and manage international relationships, including Apple’s relations with China. Trump is not the only one to suggest Cook as a replacement for Huang. Jeffrey Sonnenfeld , Senior Associate Dean for Leadership Studies at Yale School of Management, who studies CEO leadership and corporate governance, penned an op-ed in Time on Wednesday , suggesting Cook should be among the potential candidates. He wrote that Cook has “an unparalleled track record of succeeding a bigger-than-life founder,” in reference to Cook taking over from Apple founder Steve Jobs. Whether or not Trump agrees with this opinion, or is simply blasting off an idea that hopped into his mind, is anyone’s guess. “Tim Nvidia,” however, doesn’t quite have the same ring as “Tim Apple” does . events.title: The US Army is putting money on AI drones that can find hidden threats and protect its Abrams tanks
events.summary: A US service member preparing an Anduril Ghost X for flight. U.S. Army photo by Staff Sgt. LaShic Patterson The US Army awarded a $2.5 million contract for threat-detection software to help drones protect tanks. The tech is designed to identify threats like land mines, cluster munitions, and ambush drones. The Army is adapting its armored forces for battlefields where tanks are facing greater threats. The US Army is putting money on AI-equipped drones that can help protect Abrams tanks from hidden threats like land mines and enemy ambush drones before crews roll into danger zones. Defense technology company Safe Pro Group announced this week that it has received a $2.5 million Army contract to integrate its Ground Truth threat-detection software, built on datasets from Ukraine, into Anduril Industries' Ghost-X drone, a small, uncrewed aircraft resembling a helicopter. Safe Pro said that its software can identify and map more than 150 types of explosive threats from aerial imagery. Potential threats to armor include land mines, anti-personnel mines, cluster munitions, and first-person-view drones waiting to ambush troops, the company said. The aim is to give tank crews a clearer view of hazards in their path. The new contract comes as the Army rethinks how its armored forces will operate on battlefields that are littered with traditional threats like mines but are also radically transformed by aerial drones, ground robots, and artificial intelligence. On Ukrainian battlefields , tanks and other armored vehicles have faced dense minefields, drone reconnaissance, and increasingly capable FPV drones that can strike vehicles from above or pursue them through terrain once considered relatively protected. Armored combat isn't dead, but the rules have changed with the rise of new battlefield threats. The Army is adapting its armored formations for combat environments that have made tanks far more vulnerable , environments where tanks have to approach cautiously, rather than charge forward. The Safe Pro contract focuses on finding threats before a crew encounters them. Safe Pro said the Ghost-X drones will use artificial intelligence to detect and locate threats and feed that information into military networks, specifically ATAK and Anduril's Lattice. "By adding Safe Pro's threat-detection technology onto Ghost-X, we're providing soldiers with faster, more reliable situational awareness at the tactical edge — directly supporting the Army's tank survivability and reconnaissance missions," Daniel Leighton, General Manager of Tactical Effects at Anduril Industries, said in a release. events.title: Trump sticks by Commerce Secretary Lutnick despite Nvidia inaction
events.summary: The White House is standing by Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick despite a view within the administration that Lutnick delayed action to address concerns over chip smuggling to China. Why it matters: Congress smells blood in the water following bombshell reports that U.S. national security may have been jeopardized by former Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang's relationship with a suspected Chinese spy. Lawmakers want to know what the Trump administration did or did not do in response to that intelligence — and Lutnick, the official in charge of the department at the center of export control policy, is squarely in their field of view. President Trump, however, is not distancing himself from the secretary. "Secretary Lutnick is a champion of President Trump's America First trade and tariff policies, which have secured almost 20 fair trade deals and trillions in manufacturing investments," a White House official tells Axios. "President Trump maintains complete confidence in the secretary and his ability to carry out the position as the most transformative Commerce Secretary in modern history." Catch up quick: Lutnick was sent intelligence about Jensen Huang's relationship with an alleged Chinese spy and repeatedly did not take export control action — despite pressure from the broader administration and the president himself, Axios first reported. Lutnick's role is prompting scrutiny on the Hill from members on both sides of the aisle. "Secretary Howard Lutnick and Under Secretary Jeffrey Kessler must explain why they have not closed export control loopholes and act today to ensure our advanced technology is not fueling China's military," Senate Banking Committee Chair Elizabeth Warren (D-Mass.) said in a statement. "The obvious question is why did he choose to sell advanced chips?," Sen. John Kennedy (R-La.) told Politico. "Secretary Lutnick needs to answer that in front of God and country," Kennedy added. "I mean, there will be a congressional investigation. But I don't think he ought to wait on Congress." The Commerce Department has not confirmed for the record whether or not Lutnick has seen the memo. Yes, but: " It's impossible that Howard Lutnick didn't know about this memo," one senior administration official told Axios. "Of course Commerce got the memo. It had to get the memo. That's the point of the memo. It's about chips. Commerce deals with chips," a second official said. Meanwhile, Jensen Huang resigned as Nvidia CEO following reports of a second affair with a direct report. He previously admitted to an affair and apologized, but members on both sides of the aisle are also not letting him off the hook. "NVIDIA CEO Jensen Huang's decision to resign does not absolve him, other executives, or the company as a whole of responsibility for putting our national security at risk or for any potential violations of our laws," Warren said. Republican House Foreign Affairs Chair Brian Mast (Fla.) and House Intelligence Committee Chair Rick Crawford (Ark.) told reporters on Thursday that Huang's resignation doesn't change their plans to probe him and the company, Bloomberg Government reported. "Jensen Huang himself has been a pretty bold, some might even say arrogant promoter, sort of dismissing our concerns about China having access to these most advanced chips. And I do not take that lightly ... I would be happy to support a subpoena," Republican Sen. Kevin Cramer (N.D.) said on CNBC. The bottom line: Resignations and apologies aside, Washington is ready to hold someone accountable as the FBI, Congress and Nvidia's board all investigate in tandem.

events.title: All the characters being talked about in the Jensen Huang scandal
events.summary: Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang is at the center of a scandal that has wrapped up many others. WeChat; Getty Images; Tyler Le/BI Jensen Huang resigned as Nvidia's CEO after multiple alleged sex scandals. Huang led the company for over 30 years and is a central figure of the AI revolution. Here's everyone who's been talked about in the scandal, from Huang's family to top US officials. Jensen Huang has resigned as CEO of Nvidia after becoming entangled in a scandal involving extramarital affairs, a suspected Chinese spy, and a wide array of characters. Nvidia's board of directors announced on Thursday that Huang, who led the company for over 30 years, would step down "effectively immediately." Colette Kress , the chief financial officer and executive vice president of Nvidia, will serve as interim CEO until a permanent successor is determined. "The Board is initiating a search for a permanent Chief Executive Officer and will consider internal and external candidates," Nvidia said in a press release. The board also appointed Harvey C. Jones as its first board chair. The now - former Nvidia CEO on Sunday said he had an extramarital affair in a memo sent to Nvidia employees without specifying details. Nvidia's board of directors announced the same day it was launching an investigation into whether Huang was the "target of a foreign intelligence effort." The investigation came after The New York Times previously reported US intelligence officials believed a woman who had grown close to Huang — Alice Huang, a Chinese tech executive — was recruited to gather information for Beijing. The Times published a separate piece on Wednesday that said Huang was involved in another affair, this time with Nvidia's vice president of healthcare, Kimberly Powell. He said that, given the national security concerns surrounding the matter, he supported the Nvidia board in pursuing an investigation. "I love our country and our company. I am committed to protecting NVIDIA and supporting America's national security," Huang said in a memo to Nvidia employees. Alice Huang, Chinese tech executive A photo shows NVIDIA CEO Jensen Huang with a woman confirmed by a Reuters source to be Alice Huang in Taipei, Taiwan released on June 7, 2024. She was an executive at Megaspeed International, a Singapore-based cloud computing company and Nvidia customer. The New York Times reported last month that US intelligence officials believed Alice Huang was acting as a spy for the Chinese government. It's unclear when Huang met Alice Huang, but the pair have been photographed together on several occasions. Last week, Huang told Bloomberg his dealings with Alice Huang had been business-related and "completely normal and not unusual." The Wall Street Journal reported on Wednesday that Nvidia's board of directors was preparing to oust Huang from his role following the news of his affairs. Nvidia's stock took a big hit on Wednesday, falling more than 8% in after-hours trading. Lori Huang, Jensen Huang's wife Lori Huang has been married to Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang for over 40 years. Emma McIntyre/Getty Images Lori Huang has been married to Huang for over 40 years. The pair met as lab partners in an electrical engineering class at Oregon State University. Lori Huang is the president of Jen-Hsun and Lori Huang Foundation, a charitable organization founded by the couple in 2007. Huang has praised his wife for supporting his work with Nvidia. "Lori's been with me for a long time, our whole life," Huang told CNA, a Singapore-based outlet, in May. "She's been part of Nvidia every step of the way." The Huangs have two adult children, both of whom work at Nvidia. Colette Kress, interim Nvidia CEO Colette Kress, chief financial officer of Nvidia Nvidia Nvidia's board of directors named Colette Kress, the company's chief financial officer and an executive vice president, as interim CEO after Huang's resignation. events.title: Look at the Poundland scandal and see a crisis that goes beyond Britain’s high streets | Polly Toynbee
events.summary: Look at the Poundland scandal and see a crisis that goes beyond Britain’s high streets ‘I look out for my team,’ a store manager tells me, but Poundland’s US owner doesn’t care. Labour may be too late to prevent it becoming yet another casualty of venture capital I n the Poundland I visit, a treasure trove of bargains, the staff are dejected. The shelves are emptying because the owners have withheld £50m needed for new stock and paying wages. It’s just one of 600 stores in peril, and these employees just a few of 12,000 at risk of losing their jobs – with 30,000 jobs at risk in supply chains. On Tuesday £10m was released : not enough, but preventing instant collapse. Gordon Brothers, the US owner that bought Poundland for a symbolic £1 last year, specialises in buying and “restructuring” distressed companies. Under pressure, it extended the deadline by 10 working days before putting this profitable business into administration. It profits more by closing Poundland down and breaking it up. The manager, whom I’ll call Jim for anonymity, is at work an hour and a half after his paid shift ended. “I look out for my team,” he says, though Gordon Brothers doesn’t seem to be looking out for him. He says the outsourced security staff vanished this week as their pay was stopped. “The shoplifting is very bad now. Look, the high-end stuff has gone first”: the well-known brands, not unknown cheaper makes. Despite everything, he is remarkably proud of the shop and boasts of how much cheaper brands are than in Sainsbury’s. He pats the shelf with red velvet Santa stockings and glittery bows, glad some Christmas stock is in before the closure. “But no one is telling us anything.” Will the staff get jobs if it closes? He introduces me to a man in his late 50s with an easy manner and a wide grin. “My best man, by far,” he says. “He’s been here 15 years, and never a single day off sick, not one. Will any other shop see how good he is? No, because his English is bad and they won’t know his worth to any manager. I don’t know what he’ll do. I keep putting him on the till to try to improve his English, to help him along.” Jim is proud of his eye for picking good staff and keeping them on warm terms, and is fearful for their future. This is may not be the sort of shop where you expect steadfast dedication to the company. Jim’s attitude is just another reminder of what I often find reporting on work, that most people are attached to their jobs, despite recent British Social Attitudes research reporting their frustrations. Often the greatest aggravations are about lack of control. Jim says he could increase sales if he was allowed to be the buyer. “I know our customers in this area; the centre doesn’t.” He belongs to Usdaw, the shopworkers’ union, but says there’s nothing it can do. Time and again the union has watched helplessly as these private equity and venture capital buyouts bring down viable retailers. As we talk, a customer asks indignantly why there are no packs of Boost in the cold drinks cabinet. Jim explains the situation and the man looks shocked. “No! You can’t close down! I’m always in here.” Our surroundings, our streetscape is at the mercy of distant forces. Gap-toothed high streets and boarded-up shops cause us all an ache of loss. Poundland stores teetering on the edge are “anchor stores” drawing people to high streets, but may join those great voids just weeks before Christmas. Woolworths’ 807 stores closed after being taken over, losing 27,000 jobs and lifetimes of local history. BHS, sold for £1 , is gone. Debenhams, WHSmith, Toys R Us, Maplin, TM Lewin and plenty more, adversely transformed or taken over by private equity for unkindly “restructure” that usually ends in closures. Some, bought with debts that are loaded on to their balance sheets, stagger but survive – think Asda and Morrisons . Now it’s Poundland’s turn. At Wednesday’s closed-session select committee on business and trade, MPs heard its long-serving managing director, Barry Williams, challenge the owners, trying to save the business and showing that it made a £18.1m operating profit in the year to September. But Gordon Brothers has turned down offers , notably one from Martin Property Group, owners of NCP car parks. Through complex financing, it would make more by breaking Poundland up. It has £30m debt to recover but, as it is both the owner and the creditor, it comes top of the list for repayment in administration: after paying tax, it gets paid before any staff who are owed wages. If there’s no money left, redundancy is paid by the taxpayer. Andy Burnham weighed in demanding answers , but Gordon Brothers has no legal obligation to worry about staff, let alone social or public concerns.

events.title: Whoop just launched a social network
events.summary: Whoop , the maker of screen-less fitness bands, is launching a social network on Thursday that lets its members follow friends and family and share their health data. The network, called Whoop Humans, will be rolled out in the Whoop app to members at every membership tier at no extra cost. Members can follow anyone on Whoop and choose what to share, from sleep and recovery to workouts and achievements. Followers can react and comment; members can also attach photos and commentary to their data. It’s all opt-in, CEO Will Ahmed tells us. Whoop already has a social feature, Teams, which a little more than half its customers use, according to the company. But Teams is built around groups and leaderboards, and everyone in a group sees everyone else’s information. Humans is meant to be more intimate. Members decide who follows them and who sees what, so a trainer can track a set of clients without the clients seeing one another’s data, for example. I found myself questioning how much a spouse wants to know about the other’s sleep score when Ahmed mentioned this particular scenario, so I asked him how else beta members used these newer social features. He said the company learned that people were more engaged when someone reported a low recovery score than a nearly perfect one, suggesting that the new feature may be particularly helpful for understanding when someone is struggling and might need attention. Indeed, the bigger story here is where Whoop continues to be headed, which is into medical wellness. Like its most direct rival, Oura, the company is pushing faster and more aggressively into the wellness opportunity that an aging population presents. Whoop had already added FDA-cleared ECG and atrial fibrillation detection, blood pressure insights, blood testing, and medical-record uploads. Asked if older customers are gravitating to Whoop, Ahmed said, without offering specifics, that Whoop has seen “huge growth” among people over 60 over the past 18 months. He also said his was among the first companies accepted into a Medicare program that reimburses qualifying wearables that can show they improve health outcomes, and that it now has Medicare members. He added that he expects families to be big users of Humans. (You can imagine adult children checking in on aging parents.) But the company’s efforts to be thought of as the “brand for personal health” raises questions, naturally, about privacy. Ahmed said members choose which metrics to share, can remove followers, and can switch on “stealth mode” to go dark for a few days without changing their settings. Activities marked sensitive aren’t shared by default, and Ahmed said health alerts and medical information aren’t shared at all. Members can also report any comment or photo that they deem disturbing, and the company said reported content is reviewed. As for minors, Whoop’s minimum age is 13 for all members (higher in some countries), meaning customers of that age can share their data subject to consents and privacy settings. Asked whether a parent could follow a teenager’s data, he didn’t answer directly and pointed to the privacy controls. Ahmed also said Whoop doesn’t sell member data. “Our product is not you; it’s the membership,” he said, adding that the company doesn’t license data to third parties. He was candid about dealmaking. Asked about Oura’s announcement this week that it will pay $625 million for Counsel Health , a service offering on-demand physicians, Ahmed said he expects “more consolidation” among AI-focused, clinician-focused, and wearable companies, and that Whoop is always on the prowl. Its deep relationship with members, he said, puts it “in a position to be an acquirer.” He was more guarded about the company’s own finances, declining to share revenue or say whether Whoop is profitable. He did say that the company now has about 1,200 employees, membership on its software platform has increased more than 70% a year for three years running, and that it expects to have nearly 4 million members by year-end. As for an IPO (the company raised a very big round earlier this year), he said only that Whoop “will certainly IPO in the future.” He also wouldn’t comment on Oura, which shelved its own IPO of up to $2.2 billion in September citing market uncertainty. In the meantime, Whoop is widening its reach. The company announced that its devices will be sold through Ulta stores beginning next March (around 500 locations of the beauty retailer to start, and a target to retail in more than a thousand stores eventually). Indeed, Ahmed said Whoop’s female audience has more than doubled from last year. As for competition, in addition to Google’s new Fitbit Air band, Whoop may soon have to contend with Apple, which is reportedly developing a Whoop-style band . But Ahmed mostly shrugged off those concerns, suggesting that building a product doesn’t guarantee success. Instead, he said, Whoop’s job is to stay true to the “aspiring” people it serves.

events.title: In my 20s, I relocated to NYC and moved in with a 76-year-old stranger
events.summary: I moved in with a 76-year-old stranger in New York City. Andrea Fernandez Henao I'm in my 20s and moved into a 76-year-old stranger's spare bedroom in New York City . My roommate, Carmelina, and I are very close, and she's inspired me to step outside my comfort zone. Now, I see Carmelina as the grandmother I always wished I had. When I graduated from college in New York City, I had big dreams of kicking off my career in television. Instead, I found myself moving back in with my parents in the South Florida suburbs. I'd graduated amid the historic Writers Guild of America strike that lasted over 100 days and struggled to find a full-time gig in my field. Heading back home felt like the best option for me while I got my footing financially and figured out my next move. So, I found a job in Miami and took on a two-hour commute that left me exhausted and with an extensive list of excuses for not socializing with friends. Since I was living at home, I hardly left my comfort zone. After three years in Florida, I still found myself yearning for the life I'd left behind in NYC. So, I decided to move back — no job and no plan. Aware of the harsh housing market , I needed an affordable, flexible living arrangement. And just like magic, the perfect solution arose. A quick phone call led to a new beginning for me When discussing my move with a family friend, she mentioned she'd pursued her master's in NYC a few years back. During this time, she lived with a 76-year-old Colombian woman named Carmelina who rented out her spare bedroom in Queens. I decided to reach out to Carmelina — whose WhatsApp profile picture was a bushel of pink flowers — and the call lasted about four minutes. She told me her spare room was available for just a few months, and asked only for my move-in date and if I liked arepas — because she knew a guy who made them from scratch. When I asked how much the monthly rent would be, she told me $700 — a special price for being recommended by my family friend, who she adored. When I arrived in Queens that August, it hit me that I didn't even know what my new roommate looked like. I waited on the street outside the building until a petite woman with brown sunglasses and a bouncy blowout called out my name. Not long after, I sat in Carmelina's dining room while she heated up the Colombian dish she'd cooked to celebrate my arrival. It felt like a true homecoming, to be received in the city I loved by food from my own culture. As I ate, she told me she'd been living in the same building for 35 years. She had a number of friends in the neighborhood who'd also been here for decades; a couple of them worked at a barbershop nearby where she spent most of her days. She wasn't an employee, but she swept the floors, brought them lunch, and relished their company every day. I was immediately taken by how involved she seemed to be in her community. I also learned that she often rented out her spare bedroom, and I was the third young woman to stay here. She started after learning that a woman from church was looking for a place to stay, and then continued as she discovered how much she enjoyed the company after being a widow for 10 years. I never imagined my roommate would have such a profound impact on me Carmelina and I are very close. Andrea Fernandez Henao Within only a few weeks of living together, Carmelina began teaching me valuable lessons about building confidence and fostering community . When I got an opportunity to work on a small overnight film shoot. I was anxious about saying yes, unsure I was qualified and worried about coming home late and disturbing Carmelina. After voicing my hesitations, she encouraged me to seize the opportunity because it could lead to more work. She was right, because during that gig, I met people who connected me with other opportunities. Watching Carmelina, a true social butterfly, also began to push me out of my comfort zone. Despite growing up as a very outgoing child, I slowly receded into my shell during my college years, second-guessing how every action I made would be perceived. Meanwhile, Carmelina moved with confidence, and I admired how she took care of her community, which I'd quickly become part of. She makes lunch for her friends and brings me leftovers when they order in, never lets me buy groceries, and buys me sweets, even though I tell her I'm cutting out sugar. Seeing how my roommate approaches every relationship has made me more inclined to socialize in spaces I typically wouldn't. Now, I find myself making small talk in the elevators, sharing jokes with restaurant hosts, and actively inviting in the possibility of connection. Carmelina inspired me to make new connections and maintain relationships with longtime friends. Andrea Fernandez Witnessing Carmelina maintain lifelong friendships has encouraged me to be more intentional about my own, too. When I go for walks around the city, I call my friends instead of listening to music. I've since reached out to old college friends to reconnect and had dinner with a former roommate. I've learned that connections require time and attention, and I want to know about my friends' lives, even if I'm not there to witness every moment. She's taught me that the pursuit of connection isn't something to be ashamed of. It's something we should cherish and celebrate. She's like the grandmother I always wished I had Carmelina leaves me notes to read. Andrea Fernandez Henao Every morning, Carmelina lays out fruit for me and leaves sticky notes in Spanish letting me know she's out in the neighborhood and that there's food in the fridge. When she cooks for me and tells me I'm a good girl, my eyes well up. I never met my maternal grandmother, and my paternal grandmother died before we could form a bond. When I would see my friends with their grandmothers, I always felt that void grow deeper inside me. Carmelina has since filled that void. Although I'll be leaving Carmelina's apartment soon to start my new job in Manhattan, I'll miss her dearly, and we plan to stay in touch. Read the original article on Business Insider

events.title: S&P 500, Nasdaq fall as Nvidia CEO’s exit rattles AI stocks
events.summary: Traders working on the floor of the New York Stock Exchange on Nov 10, in New York City. S&P 500 and Nasdaq fell after Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang’s exit shook AI stocks. Nvidia dropped 7.6%, and Colette Kress will serve as interim CEO. AI shares weakened further after Nebius cut its 2026 revenue outlook. CoreWeave, Intel, Marvell and Micron also fell, while some other big tech names rose. Investors awaited the Producer Price Index after hotter US inflation data. Oil rose, and traders expect a December Fed rate hike, with Middle East risks still a worry. NEW YORK - The S&P 500 and the Nasdaq Composite indexes fell on Nov 12 as Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang’s exit unnerved the AI trade and higher oil prices prompted investors to retreat to the sidelines. The AI heavyweight’s shares dropped 7.6% as investors fretted over the industry impact of Huang’s resignation from the company central to the AI boom, following reports of his involvement in a second extramarital affair. Nvidia’s chief financial officer, Colette Kress, will take over as interim CEO. “It leaves the company rudderless. He was so central to all their strategy, and it just highlights that there’s quite a void there,” said Kathleen Brooks, research director at XTB. “It does throw the AI trade into a bit more confusion. You don’t have someone who was a cheerleader for AI in the same way that Jensen Huang has.” AI stocks were also reeling after neocloud company Nebius said its 2026 revenue would come in at the low end of its previous forecast, pulling its shares down 17%. Peer CoreWeave dropped about 7%. The Philadelphia SE Semiconductor index declined 1.3%, as chipmakers Intel, Marvell Technology and Micron fell between 2.8% and 4.2%. Other data centre-related firms IREN, Applied Digital and Core Scientific fell between 3% and 5%. The declines threatened to erase the gains on Nov 11, when strong results from CoreWeave helped AI stocks regain some footing. However, shares of other Magnificent Seven firms advanced, with Amazon rising 2.3%, while Alphabet, Microsoft and Apple traded slightly higher. Nvidia’s rivals Advanced Micro Devices and Broadcom were up 4.3% and 5.5%, respectively. At 09.45am ET, the Dow Jones Industrial Average rose 35.53 points, or 0.07%, to 52,522.02, the S&P 500 lost 22.06 points, or 0.29%, to 7,597.32 and the Nasdaq Composite lost 141.55 points, or 0.56%, to 25,322.31. The S&P 500 tech sector index fell 1.3%, overshadowing gains elsewhere on the benchmark. Six of 11 major sectors were in the positive territory. Investors are also gearing up for the release of the Producer Price Index on Nov 13, which could help shape inflation expectations after data earlier this week showed consumer prices rose more than expected in October. A drop in oil prices so far in November has helped ease some concerns about price pressures, but investors remain wary of geopolitical risks in the Middle East. Brent crude futures rose 0.8% on Nov 12, after US President Donald Trump said, “we don’t need a deal with Iran.” Traders see a December rate hike by the Federal Reserve as a certainty, with about a 13% chance of an outsized 50-basis-point increase, according to the CME FedWatch tool. “Energy effects will take longer to fade. Oil prices have remained near US$100 per barrel for much of the year, extending their contribution to inflation,” said Josh Hirt, senior US economist at Vanguard. “But absent a renewed and sustained increase in prices, that contribution should remain limited.” Separately, Michael Saylor’s Strategy fell 6.6% after index operator MSCI said it will remove the stock from its global indexes. Declining issues outnumbered advancers by a 1.99-to-1 ratio on the NYSE, and by a 2.68-to-1 ratio on the Nasdaq. The S&P 500 posted 16 new 52-week highs and one new low while the Nasdaq Composite recorded 27 new highs and 101 new lows. REUTERS

events.title: Jensen Huang, an architect of the AI boom, resigns as Nvidia CEO
events.summary: Jensen Huang resigned as CEO of Nvidia after he reportedly had two affairs, including one with a purported Chinese spy. Why it matters: It's impossible to overstate how critical Huang is to Nvidia, to the AI buildout, to the stock market and economy. His departure could, per Wall Street sources, be the catalyst that endangers a ballooning AI bubble. It's also unlikely to ease congressional scrutiny of the company or Huang himself. Driving the news: Nvidia's board named longtime CFO Colette Kress interim CEO, while launching a search for a permanent replacement. Kress, who joined Nvidia in 2013, will continue serving as CFO while overseeing the company. Harvey C. Jones was appointed Nvidia's first-ever board chair. The board said it expects Nvidia's operations, customer commitments and product roadmap to continue without interruption. Zoom out: Huang's resignation follows revelations about two extramarital relationships. The New York Times reported Wednesday that Huang had a relationship with Kimberly Powell, a senior Nvidia executive who reports to him. Nvidia's board had previously launched an independent investigation into Huang's relationship with Alice Huang, a Chinese businesswoman identified by U.S. intelligence as a Chinese intelligence asset. Nvidia did not provide a reason for Huang's resignation in Thursday's announcement, which comes after reports that the board had an emergency meeting over whether to oust the CEO. By the numbers: Nvidia shares fell more than 10% after news of Huang's resignation. One of Wall Street's most prominent voices on tech, analyst Dan Ives, said Nvidia was worth 25% less without Huang. 🚨 Stunning stat: At these levels, Nvidia will have lost about $1.4 trillion in market capitalization in two weeks, since the initial Times report about linking Jensen Huang and Alice Huang. The big picture: This will likely go down as one of the biggest executive scandals in history. Nvidia is also one of the largest holdings in major index funds because of its size, meaning this move has massive implications for every American with a retirement account. The intrigue: Huang's resignation doesn't look like it'll ease congressional pressure over his behavior either. "NVIDIA CEO Jensen Huang's decision to resign does not absolve him, other executives, or the company as a whole of responsibility for putting our national security at risk or for any potential violations of our laws," Sen. Elizabeth Warren (D-Mass.) said in a statement. The bottom line: The fallout is just starting. This is breaking news.
