events.title: Jensen Huang is out at Nvidia — who is Colette Kress, his interim replacement?
events.summary: The Nvidia Board of Directors announced on Thursday morning that the company’s co-founder and CEO of 33 years, Jensen Huang, has resigned as president, CEO, and member of the board, effective immediately. This is a shocking twist for one of the most valuable companies in the world, which designs the chips that make the AI boom possible. Few people would have predicted this turn of events even just a week ago, as Huang has been so central to Nvidia throughout the company’s existence that he never even established a succession plan . But Huang has now been ousted after reports that he had affairs with both an alleged Chinese spy and one of his direct reports at Nvidia. While the company conducts a more thorough search for Huang’s successor, Nvidia CFO and Executive Vice President Colette Kress has taken over as interim CEO. But beyond her name and job title, what do we know about the person who will now lead a company worth about $3.8 trillion? According to Nvidia’s website , Kress has worked at the company since September 2013. Before that, she spent three years as an SVP and CFO of Cisco’s Business Technology Operations Finance organization. She also worked at Microsoft for 13 years, where she spent four years as CFO of the Server and Tools division. She holds a finance degree from the University of Arizona and an MBA from Southern Methodist University. The California-based 59-year-old has a very limited social media presence — on Linkedin , she has commented some well wishes on former colleagues’ posts about their retirement. But as CFO, she’s been a regular presence on Nvidia’s earnings calls, making her a familiar figure for analysts covering the company. According to Forbes’ list of America’s Richest Self-Made Women, Kress’ net worth is estimated to be about $1.2 billion. Her Forbes profile adds that she initially joined Nvidia in part because her two sons endorsed the company for its role in the video game industry, which it was best known for at the time. “Nvidias strength has always come from its people, and together with our leadership team, I am committed to building on the extraordinary foundation Jensen created over the last 33 years,” Kress said in a statement . “We will continue advancing the work that has made Nvidia a leader in accelerated computing and AI, and execute on the opportunities ahead. Our focus remains on serving our customers, partners, developers and shareholders.” Nvidia is slated to report its quarterly earnings on Tuesday, when we will likely hear more from Kress about her plans for the company’s immediate future. The airline announced restrictions covering both its own digital platforms and indirect access through travel agencies and aggregators, with changes to its booking, ticketing, and distribution policies. United says automated actions could violate aviation regulations, citing the requirement for a human acknowledgment during check-in that bags contain no banned substances. A bot cheerfully ticking the box isn't quite the passenger confirmation it has in mind. And then there is the worry that "sharing account credentials with personal, third-party, AI assistants can expose sensitive information, and actions taken by these tools may result in unintended purchases, account changes, or use of MileagePlus miles." United would also rather customers use its own app than turn third-party assistants loose on its systems. AI agents are pitched as a way to outsource life's minutiae, and it's difficult to navigate the web without tripping over a breathless influencer explaining why you need one, or dozens, or hundreds of virtual personal assistants. The thing is that operating these assistants requires care and thought. Earlier this year, British mathematician Professor Hannah Fry conducted a cautionary experiment in which she gave an AI agent a bank card, and a bit too much agency, to see what it would do. Passwords were coughed up, and some ill-considered purchases were made. Still, as Fry said of the agent, dubbed Cassandra, "don't let her incompetence fool you, because these things are getting better fast." Last month, reports emerged of major US banks blocking third-party AI agents from operating inside accounts and taking actions on behalf of the customer. This month, several UK banks were reported to have followed suit. United stated: "Corporate leaders in the banking and retail industries have taken similar actions regarding AI agents and we encourage others to consider measures that preserve the data and security of their customers and strengthen safety." The Register asked United Airlines how it planned to implement the blocking. There are a few options, including physical biometric confirmation for actions or checking for signs of automated browser driving. Amazon has also moved against unauthorized AI agents, blocking Meta's Muse (the "AI that gets it done," according to Meta's marketing) in September . events.title: Who is Kimberly Powell, the Nvidia exec alleged to have an affair with ousted CEO Jensen Huang?
events.summary: Kimberly Powell, Nvidia's VP of healthcare HLTH Kimberly Powell, Nvidia's VP of healthcare, reportedly had a extramarital relationship with ousted CEO Jensen Huang. Powell joined Nvidia in 2008 and has risen through the ranks. Huang, who has since resigned, wrote in a memo to staff earlier this week that he was "unfaithful" to his wife. Nvidia founder Jensen Huang resigned as CEO Thursday, one day after a report surfaced that he had an extramarital relationship with Kimberly Powell , the AI chipmaker's vice president of healthcare. Powell, 48, reported directly to 63-year-old Huang. A New York Times report on Wednesday that cited five company sources said that the duo was "captured on video being affectionate" at an Nvidia conference hotel in San Jose in March, and that Powell is also married. Huang's ousting came as he was under investigation at Nvidia over whether he was the target of a "foreign intelligence effort" unrelated to Powell. The Times had reported last month that US officials believed another woman he grew close with, tech executive Alice Huang , had been recruited by the Chinese government to spy on the chip giant. Huang admitted to being "unfaithful" to his wife in a note to staff on Sunday, setting off a tumultuous week for the Nvidia founder. Here's what to know about Powell. Powell steered Nvidia's healthcare efforts Powell joined Nvidia as a director in 2008 and has steadily risen through the ranks. According to her corporate profile, she was originally responsible for promoting the use of Nvidia's AI chips for medical imaging. She'd previously worked as an engineer and then in product at an electronics startup and ended up getting ahold of Nvidia to talk about their computing chips. Once the company realized its technology would have healthcare applications, it got back in touch to hire her, she said on an episode of the Lifers podcast published this August. Powell called the job a "dream come true" on the podcast. Her LinkedIn says she was promoted to senior director in 2016, and she led a business development team focused on AI. Powell's authority was growing — in 2017, she became vice president of healthcare, her profile says. Her corporate profile now says she is responsible for both the hardware and software sides of the company's healthcare business, including technology for medical imaging, life sciences, and drug discovery. "I pretty much live and breathe healthcare. So I'm talking about it all the time," Powell told Business Insider in 2025. Kimberly Powell's ties to Jensen Huang Until Thursday, Huang — one of the entire tech industry's best-known representatives — had run Nvidia since he founded the company in 1993. He and Powell had worked together for more than 18 years. In the August interview with Lifers, Powell credited Huang's healthcare ambitions. "Jensen has been passionate about the healthcare industry going back 20-plus years, and that was really fueled by seeing just researchers who had dreams and aspirations to do something very, very meaningful and impactful in the healthcare domain and us potentially having the tools to do it, to achieve that goal," she said. Nvidia's code of conduct, which begins with a letter from Huang, includes personal relationships among the activities that can create a conflict of interest. It also says, "We promptly investigate reports of misconduct." Neither Powell nor Nvidia responded to requests for comment from Business Insider. CNN reporter Meg Tirrell posted on X that she'd been planning to moderate a conference panel featuring Powell on Thursday morning, but that Powell had canceled. Have a tip? events.title: What we know as Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang resigns over affair allegations
events.summary: Watch: What we know so far about Nvidia CEO resignation One of the AI industry's most important figures has resigned amid allegations that he had extramarital affairs with two women - one a suspected Chinese spy and the other a company executive. Chip-maker Nvidia hired a major law firm earlier this week to investigate CEO Jensen Huang's reported relationship with a woman who was allegedly a Chinese intelligence asset. Now he has resigned after its stocks plummeted on Wednesday following US media reports about a second alleged affair. Huang admitted , external earlier this week to having been "unfaithful" to his wife and he apologised for hurting her and their children. Here is what we know about the affair and why it matters. Nvidia stocks plummet in US after CEO Jensen Huang quits in wake of affair with suspected Chinese spy Nvidia's board met on Wednesday evening to decide whether its CEO should remain with the company. It had 11 directors on its board, including Huang. The firm's CEO could be removed with or without cause by a majority vote of directors. But that wasn't in the end needed - the board instead announced Huang had resigned as president, CEO and board member. It thanked him for his "immeasurable contributions" to Nvidia, which it said were "profound". There was no mention of the accusations of adultery. Nvidia Chief Financial Officer Colette Kress will serve as interim CEO . It is less clear is who will replace Huang on a permanent basis. One possibility is Nvidia co-founder Chris Malachowsky. He has been at the company as long as Huang, and for years led its product engineering work. Huang's children, Spencer and Madison, and son-in-law Nico Caprez also work at Nvidia in senior roles, but they are relatively young and inexperienced. And there is also the option of Ian Buck, who runs high-performance computing at the firm. He developed the technology which allowed graphics cards to be used for other computing tasks, which enabled Nvidia to capitalise on the growth of AI. A New York Times report at the weekend revealed Jensen Huang had a close relationship with Chinese businesswoman Alice Huang, who US intelligence officials believed was a spy for Beijing. She had previously been photographed with him on several occasions. The tech giant's board of directors launched an independent external investigation on Sunday following the reports. They earlier said Huang's interactions with the woman were "not unusual or unexpected". Then on Wednesday, the New York Times reported Huang also had an extramarital relationship with an Nvidia executive, Kimberly Powell, who reported directly to him. She did not respond to the BBC's request for comment. Jensen Huang (left) and Alice Huang - also known as Huang Le - at an event Born in Taiwan in 1963, Jensen Huang was nine years old when his family moved to the west coast of the US. He graduated as an electrical engineer from Oregon State University, and then with a master's degree in the same field from Stanford University. He worked at US chip firm AMD before co-founding Nvidia. Known as "Daddy Huang" in Taiwan and once lauded as the "Taylor Swift of tech" , he has a reputation as a workaholic with incredibly high standards for his staff. He has an estimated fortune of $155bn (£115bn), according to the Bloomberg Billionaires Index. "Jensen Huang is a tech visionary of the likes of Steve Jobs," Stephen Witt, the author of Thinking Machine, a biography on the Jensen Huang, told the BBC, adding that he was responsible for creating AI hardware as we know it today. The Nvidia co-founder has a famously close relationship with US President Donald Trump. At the recent AI summit at the White House, where 42 tech executives were present, the president was flanked by Elon Musk and Huang. Watch: Who is suspected Chinese spy at centre of Nvidia affair investigation? US officials believed Alice Huang had been recruited to spy by China's top intelligence agency, the New York Times reported , external . She was a top executive at Singapore-based data centre firm Megaspeed between March and November 2023. Her company had been suspected of helping divert Nvidia chips to China, which the firm said had been investigated and debunked. However, Megaspeed is under investigation by the Singaporean government regarding previous allegations that the company was circumventing US sanctions on the export of Nvidia's high-end chips. The BBC has contacted Megaspeed for comment. It remains unclear what, if any, intelligence Alice Huang – who is also known as Huang Le – allegedly gathered and passed to Beijing. When the BBC asked Nvidia if the company was aware of intelligence concerns, the company said it was not. China has rejected the spying allegations as "entirely groundless".

events.title: I've collected Starbucks cups for 12 years. I've never seen anything like the Bearista craze.
events.summary: Yolanda Cole camped outside Starbucks to get the new Bearista cup. Courtesy of Yolanda Cole Yolanda Cole, a 45-year-old, has collected Starbucks merchandise for the past 12 years. She recently woke up at 3:30 am to get a mystery Bearista cup from her local Starbucks. She said collecting the cups is just a small thing that brings her joy. This as-told-to essay is based on a conversation with Yolanda Cole. It has been edited for length and clarity. I've been a lover of Starbucks merchandise for years. Their studded cups were the first in my collection — I've got a bunch of those dating back as far as 12 years ago — but I never needed to get to the store early to buy one. I would just walk in at my normal time for coffee, and there would be one waiting. But since Starbucks started doing their Bearista launches, times have changed. I've been collecting Bearista cups Last year, I'd heard about the cute bear cup that was being dropped for the first time. I got to my local Starbucks at 5:30 am, and they were already gone. It was a bummer. Then, in the summer, I had the best surprise. I walked into the store, completely unaware that there had been another Bearista drop, and saw they were selling soccer bear cups to celebrate FIFA. I fell in love with it and actually thought it was cuter than the original. Next up, I heard that a Strawberry Bearista cup was being released. I knew I'd have to get in line early so I wouldn't miss it like I had the original, so I arrived at the store at 4:30 am. There was a huge line for that one. But then, for the next drop — the Snoopy Bearista cup — the line was surprisingly pretty short. I really wanted the Snoopy cup because it just felt so nostalgic. For that one, I arrived at 4 a.m. I woke up in the middle of the night to go to Starbucks For the last couple of weeks, the Starbucks Facebook groups I'm in have been full of news that a mystery Bearista cup was going to be dropped next. I knew this would be a super popular one, just because of the mystery element. Yolanda Cole was fourth in line at her local Starbucks. Courtesy of Yolanda Cole On Tuesday morning, I woke up at 3:30 a.m., drove for six minutes to my closest Starbucks, and waited in line with about 20 other people for the store to open at 5 a.m. I was fourth in line. Everyone in line chit-chatted while waiting. I actually knew one of the people in line from the last drop, a little community of collectors developing. While lots of the people waiting were genuine collectors like me, who just really wanted a cup for their own personal use, there were also people in line who were only there to buy and resell, which is unfortunate. Looking at the people waiting behind me, I knew it was likely only the first 10 in line would get a cup, so I told those at the end of the line that, just in case they didn't get one, they could quickly go to another Starbucks that was typically quieter. I'm so happy with my new Bearista cup Once the store opened, I got my cup. I'd planned to open it at home, but in the end, one of the other customers and I opened our mystery boxes at the same time. Yolanda Cole got a mystery Bearista cup at Starbucks. Courtesy of Yolanda Cole Mine was adorable — a white bear that turns blue when you pour liquid into it. I was so happy. For the rest of the day, I was just happy and telling everyone how happy I was. When I wrote about the morning on Threads, so many people commented, and we all enjoyed the back-and-forth about what we had managed to get. View on Threads I think that is why people love these little cups so much — happiness. We're all just looking for that little bit of joy because life is hard and people are struggling. We've got to do the little things that make us smile. And for me, these little bear cups do just that. Read the original article on Business Insider

events.title: 'Get out' of Nvidia stock, Michael Burry says
events.summary: Michael Burry, the investor of "The Big Short" fame. Bloomberg/Getty Images Nvidia's CEO Jensen Huang resigned on Thursday after fresh claims of marital infidelity. Michael Burry of "The Big Short" said Nvidia will falter without him and bulls should "get out." Burry warned Huang's departure could slow Nvidia's growth and shrink its profit margins. Michael Burry says Jensen Huang 's exit will deal a heavy blow to Nvidia, and investors should sell their shares before the company hits the skids. Huang resigned as the AI chipmaker's CEO on Thursday morning following fresh reports about two alleged extramarital affairs. After it emerged on Wednesday that Nvidia's board was considering ousting Huang, Burry — who has been publicly betting against Nvidia for many months — laid out in a Substack post why he expected Nvidia to suffer without Huang in charge. Huang has "orchestrated" Nvidia's efforts to expand the AI ecosystem, Burry wrote. He pointed to its huge investments in AI stocks, and its use of special vehicles and hidden debt to finance customers' purchases of its chips, creating "tremendous leverage in the system." He also claimed that Huang pushed customers to buy chips they didn't need yet by threatening to reduce their allocations in the future. Without Huang at Nvidia's helm, the "cash may cease to flow, " and investments could dry up or be written off, Burry wrote. Customers will be free to "slow down deals, push back, renegotiate terms, or simply walk to a competitor without fear of offending" the chip chief , he continued. "Nvidia's business will not disappear, but its growth may slow and, critically, its margins may fall," Burry added. "The terms of trade and the architecture of financing were the secret sauce that supercharged an already dominant technology," he wrote, adding that it will "take time for this Byzantine web to untangle and unwind." "Nvidia bulls will have another fluffy big chance to get out," Burry added. "Get out." Nvidia stock plunged at the start of trading on Thursday and has seen a near-35% drop from its $ 243-per-share peak in early October. Burry, who shot to fame after his prescient bet against the mid-2000s housing bubble was featured in the book and movie "The Big Short," pivoted from running a hedge fund to writing about his personal investments last year. He's one of several commentators who soured on Nvidia in recent days. Bernstein Research's Stacy Rasgon downgraded the stock to "Market Perform" and halved his price target to $200 in a research note before Huang's resignation. In a Bloomberg TV interview, he warned of more bad press and regulatory scrutiny , questioned whether Nvidia could find a CEO as visionary as Huang, and flagged the risk of an employee exodus. Oppenheimer's Rick Schafer downgraded Nvidia to "Perform" and removed his price target in a Wednesday research note. He wrote that Huang plays a crucial role as the " face of AI ," his leadership has been "critical to Nvidia's success," and the company has " massive shoes to fill and no obvious successor." He added that Huang's exit could spark a "brain drain" and result in a "lingering share overhang." Nvidia's directors have appointed the company's finance chief, Colette Kress, as interim CEO while they search for a permanent replacement for Huang. Read the original article on Business Insider

events.title: Norwest pushes deeper into AI with new $4B fund
events.summary: Norwest , a firm backed solely by Wells Fargo, has raised a $4 billion fund as it sets out to invest more in AI. This is the eighteenth fund for the 65-year-old multi-stage investment firm, and its largest to date. The fund will be invested across various sectors and multiple countries, notably the United States, India, and Israel. But the big story here is AI, and Norwest’s plans to expand its investment in this area. Norwest said Thursday it aims to capitalize on AI startups developing products and services across core industries such as consumer, healthcare, and technology. The investment firm, which has backed Plaid, Spotify, Uber, and Vuori, said it will continue to expand its investments in physical AI, voice AI, agentic cybersecurity, and aerospace. If that sounds like a broad approach, it is intended to be, Jeff Crowe, a senior managing partner at Norwest, told TechCrunch. “We’re taking a broad approach to AI because its impact is broad,” Crowe added, as AI is not limited by industry, geography, or application. “Just as digital transformation did, AI transformation has the potential to touch most layers of enterprise, consumer, and healthcare solutions: networking, enterprise IT and applications. Adapting to an agentic environment means applying AI broadly across products and services that solve problems.” Crowe added that the firm is particularly excited about early-stage companies building AI-native application and infrastructure, physical AI, domain-specific models, and cybersecurity solutions. Some of the firm’s recent investments reflect this strategy. events.title: Who is Nvidia's interim CEO Colette Kress - and who could take over permanently?
events.summary: Arm's boss Rene Haas (L), Nvidia's Colette Kress (C) and Chris Malachowsky (R) have been named as possible successors Published 12 November 2026, 10:37 GMT Nvidia is now facing a scenario few would have considered until very recently - a future without Jensen Huang. The influential co-founder of the AI chip-making giant resigned on Thursday over reports of extramarital affairs, one of which was with a woman suspected of being a Chinese spy. Chief financial officer Colette Kress is in charge, for now, as the tech giant faces one of its biggest challenges - finding the right person to permanently lead the business that Huang helped create more than three decades ago and turned into one of the world's most valuable companies. We take a look at which candidates have emerged as potential successors. Colette Kress is chief financial officer at Nvidia Colette Kress has been an industry veteran for more than 30 years, having previously held high positions at tech firms like Cisco and Microsoft. Kress, who also serves as Nvidia's executive vice-president, has seen the firm's transformation from making chips for video games in the early 1990s to becoming an AI semiconductor powerhouse. She has "fronted every earnings call" alongside Huang and is a "familiar and trusted voice for the market at a time when it badly needs one," said Josh Gilbert, an analyst at investment firm eToro. But doing the job permanently could be a different story, said Gilbert, as the firm, known for its edge in technology, could want an engineer in the chair. Chris Malachowsky is one of Nvidia's three co-founders Another option is Chris Malachowsky, who founded Nvidia alongside Huang and Curtis Priem, and is the only executive that shares the same level of seniority. Malachowsky has played a key part in developing the company's computing technology. Ian Buck, who oversees Nvidia's high-performance computing business, has also emerged as a potential candidate if the company is keen to put an engineer in the top job. Buck was among the early pioneers who helped popularise the use of graphic processors beyond gaming applications. "He could protect Nvidia's technological edge, but his ability to manage the wider commercial relationships and geopolitical challenges would face scrutiny," said Charu Chanana, investment strategist at investment bank Saxo. Today, Nvidia's leading processors are widely regarded as the gold standard for AI development. Huang's children also work at Nvidia in executive positions but are relatively young and inexperienced. Nvidia is likely to favour an internal appointment initially but could look externally for a more permanent replacement, said Jun Bei Liu, founder and lead portfolio manager at Ten Cap. Several names of tech entrepreneurs outside of Nvidia have been floated by experts. Liu said Apple's former chief executive, Tim Cook, could be a possible choice as someone familiar with managing global supply chains, though she questioned whether he would be willing to leave the iPhone maker, where he is the chair. Apple's Tim Cook (R) with Jensen Huang (L) and his wife Lori Huang at the White House Liu and Chanana also suggested Rene Haas, chief executive of Arm Holdings, the UK chipmaking giant. Nvidia's processors are made with the help of chipmakers around the world, including Taiwan's TSMC and South Korea's SK Hynix and Samsung. Rene Haas is the boss of Arm Holdings Haas is familiar with leading a publicly-listed company and would bring semiconductor experience, though Nvidia's business model is considerably different from Arm's, said Chanana. "The challenge is finding someone who can combine Jensen's technical understanding, strategic vision and relationships across the global technology industry," Liu said. Ten Cap's Liu had believed it was just a matter of time before Huang would step down as Nvidia's chief executive. "The issue is no longer simply about personal conduct," she said. "It is about corporate governance, national security concerns and maintaining confidence in the leadership of one of the world's most strategically important companies." Several major investment firms have downgraded their forecasts for the chip giant - a rare shift given investors' longstanding optimism about the company. An early indication came as markets opened in New York shortly after Huang's resignation was announced. Nvidia shares opened down more than 13%, wiping more than half a trillion dollars off the firm's share market value. Jensen Huang's departure leaves a void in the influential AI giant Stacy Rasgon, senior analyst in US semiconductors at Bernstein Research, wrote in a note to investors that "our gut tells us we probably haven't fully probed the depths of what might be found here". Rasgon halved Bernstein's share price target for Nvidia and said: "We've had enough and prefer to watch from the sidelines.

events.title: Cyberattack on Fireworks AI allowed hackers to access Notion customers’ chat transcripts
events.summary: A cyberattack at Fireworks AI has exposed some of its customers’ data, the company has confirmed. Fireworks AI, a platform that developers use to access and use open AI models, said an attacker breached its cloud provider to gain access to a Fireworks development system, which allowed access to some of its customers’ data. The company said in its latest security advisory that the cybercriminals took Fireworks’ customers’ billing information and some datasets. Fireworks touts tens of thousands of customers worldwide using its platform, including legal tech company Harvey and AI company Cursor. At least one confirmed affected customer is online document editor and notetaker Notion, which said in a disclosure that the breach affected around 1% of its own customers. Notion said that Fireworks alerted the company to a security incident and later confirmed that the hackers had stolen some Notion customer data. On November 3, Notion said it disconnected its systems from Fireworks, deleted the data stored in its systems, and stopped all connectivity between the two. Notion confirmed this week that the hackers took chat transcripts of its Notion AI customers who used the “Insights” feature. The company said that the transcripts include “any input to or output from the model that was written to the chat,” but added that much of the data was unattributable and could not be determined from which customer it was obtained. The breach at Fireworks AI shows how tech companies are reliant on other tech providers for their own offerings, and how cyberattacks can, as a result, spill over into other customers. Fireworks said that it believes the hackers are financially motivated and that their goals are focused on selling tokens from breaching access to large language models, or LLMs. These schemes rely on selling to unauthorized third parties, who can burn through AI model usage without using their own resources. This is the second breach affecting Fireworks in as many months, following a security incident in October . When you purchase through links in our articles, we may earn a small commission . events.title: Nvidia CEO’s ouster leaves AI world reeling
events.summary: The News Jensen Huang was ousted as Nvidia’s CEO Thursday, a stunning fall for one of the world’s most powerful figures. His downfall sparked fears of what his departure means for one of America’s chip champions and the unwind of the AI money machine he assembled. Nvidia’s CFO, Colette Kress, will serve as interim CEO while the board conducts a search for Huang’s replacement. Huang will also leave the board, which he chaired, and will be replaced by Harvey Jones, a board member since Nvidia’s founding in 1993 who ran chip design company Synopsys in the 1980s and 1990s. Semafor had earlier reported that Kress was in the lead to run the company on a temporary basis. The company said it will look at both internal and external permanent successors to Huang, whose departure leaves the giant chipmaker without a tested leader. Huang had nearly single-handedly turned Nvidia from a niche maker of graphics chips for video games into the centerpiece of the world’s AI boom, and the company has never had another leader. It has no succession plan and few apparent internal successors. One external candidate under consideration is Apple hardware chief Johny Srouji, who was among the executives considered for Intel CEO in 2019, Semafor reported Wednesday. Other names that have been floated are AMD’s Lisa Su, Huang’s first cousin once removed, as well as an offbeat suggestion by US President Trump on Thursday to tap former Apple CEO Tim Cook for the job. Huang’s ouster came four days after he admitted to an affair with a suspected Chinese spy and followed a New York Times report that he had another affair with a subordinate. He is now wrapped up in a series of investigations by the board, Congressional leaders, and by the Department of Justice , Semafor reported on Thursday. The ongoing saga has also shaved hundreds of billions of dollars off of what was once the world’s most valuable companies — one crucial to the US remaining at the forefront of AI development around the world. Shares fell as much as 7% Thursday, adding to Nvidia’s losses since the first reports of Huang’s relationship with the suspected Beijing spy, who ran a Singaporean company that was a major buyer of Nvidia’s advanced chips. Shares of neoclouds Nebius and CoreWeave, which rely on Nvidia to help AI startups rent space in their data centers, fell as much as 19% and 9%, respectively. Shares in Alphabet, whose TPU chips compete with Nvidia’s GPUs, rose slightly. Key-man risk Huang’s ouster raises questions around Nvidia’s ability to remain the de-facto central bank of the AI boom — and the fate of billions of dollars of chip financing from a slew of Wall Street firms that are tangled up with the company. Nvidia has provided tens of billions of dollars in financing to its customers, invested more than $50 billion in AI startups, and guaranteed huge data-center leases for firms including OpenAI. Much of that spending rested on Huang’s singular credibility and power in the tech world, as well as his close ties to US President Donald Trump. His successor will likely have far less leeway from the chipmaker’s board, which is facing its own mountain of litigation, government investigations, and public scrutiny. Still, Huang will remain one of Nvidia’s largest shareholders, with a 3.6% stake in the company worth about $160 billion at today’s price. While he doesn’t have the same sort of control afforded to other former tech founders through super-voting stock, such as Alphabet’s Larry Page and Sergey Brin, he’ll maintain a meaningful seat at the table. It’s unclear what his exit package looks like and whether the board will claw back any additional share-based compensation from previous years. Washington fallout Rep. Brian Mast, R-Fla., chair of the House Foreign Affairs Committee who’s been pushing for stricter export control laws, said Thursday that Huang agreed to come in for a closed-door briefing before lawmakers break again for Thanksgiving on Nov. 20. Other Congress members have sent letters asking Huang to come and testify in Washington. Meanwhile, Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick is under increasing pressure from members of Congress over how his office allowed Nvidia to to sell its advanced chips to what reports allege to be a front for banned Chinese buyers. The Trump administration is made more vulnerable by Huang’s close relationship with Trump and its deference to the Nvidia CEO on chip policy matters. “This incident raises significant concerns about the federal government’s ability to effectively enforce our export controls and protect our national security,” Sens. Chris Coons, D-Del., and Elizabeth Warren, D-Mass., wrote in a letter to Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick, Secretary of State Marco Rubio, and White House chief of staff Stephen Miller on Thursday, asking them to preserve documents related to Nvidia. Reports suggest government officials “were aware of concerns about Nvidia, its relationship with Megaspeed, and the suspected Chinese intelligence operation, yet did not move to block the continued flow of advanced AI chips,” the senators said. So far, Trump is standing by Lutnick. The president “maintains complete confidence in the secretary and his ability to carry out the position,” a White House official told Semafor. Winners and losers Jensen’s exit could scramble the AI chip market, elevate rivals that have been relegated to operating in Nvidia’s shadow, and ensure more chips stay in the US rather than in China, which could explain hyperscalers’ share rises Thursday. While long chip design cycles mean it could take years for a competitor to eat into Nvidia’s lead, a few companies stand out as beneficiaries. AMD, whose stock is surging, competes most directly with Nvidia on data-center products. Broadcom and other custom silicon makers could gain as tech giants look to design more of their own chips, rather than relying on Nvidia’s. Google may also get more momentum on its TPUs, which it began selling directly to outside customers this year. And Qualcomm offers a competing line of chips for robots. China’s chipmakers are also poised to benefit: Any tightening of US chip export controls could push more resources toward building out China’s domestic chip sector, a long-term priority of Beijing’s. And China hawks in Washington are newly empowered to push for more restrictions on American chipmakers’ overseas dealings.

events.title: Nvidia without Huang is like Apple without Jobs: A cash spigot without real innovation
events.summary: Some Silicon Valley executives are quietly celebrating Jensen Huang’s ouster from Nvidia and the national furor over chip exports to China. The good news for American companies is that tech exports that were going to China are now expected to be redirected to US firms, one person told me. That could accelerate the growth of the big AI labs and other Silicon Valley companies, and hobble Chinese rivals. In the short term, they’re probably right. There’s strong evidence that export controls have successfully slowed China’s technological progress. The problem is that the US can’t win the technological race with China in the long term by slowing its rival down. The bigger and more difficult part of that victory is speeding up American innovation. And that’s where Huang’s ouster is a counter-force to the gains made on China policy. Huang is one of Silicon Valley’s great innovators. In the short term, his ouster won’t be terrible for Nvidia. Nvidia may actually become a more profitable company now, because any new CEO will optimize for profitability, as Apple did under Tim Cook. Innovators burn a lot of money thinking about the long term. And Nvidia will never be as innovative as it was under Huang. Huang was Nvidia’s one-man, long-term moat. That’s especially true now, in an era when AI allows pretty much any company to design a chip just like Nvidia’s, as OpenAI did in a matter of months. A less innovative Nvidia is not just a problem for Nvidia. It’s a problem for the entire technology ecosystem. Big, powerful incumbents tend to be barriers to innovation. Cook’s Apple built the iPhone and then sat on that invention by defending its turf — a great business strategy but one that let the entire mobile ecosystem stagnate. The key risk to the US tech industry isn’t that Chinese spies will steal its cutting-edge technology. It’s that Silicon Valley is at risk of seeing the magic formula that brought that technology into being in the first place weakened.

events.title: Global AI stocks sink as Nvidia CEO’s exit deepens sector sell-off
events.summary: Jensen Huang’s exit plunges the US$4 trillion (S$5.14 trillion) company into uncertainty and threatens to disrupt an AI ecosystem. Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang resigned after a scandal, and CFO Colette Kress will serve as interim CEO while the company searches for a permanent leader. Global AI stocks fell as Nvidia shares slid 10.3% pre-market, with the firm losing about US$300 billion since its Nov 8 investigation and facing funding and regulatory worries. Rivals like AMD and Broadcom rose on hopes of market share gains, while other chip and neocloud stocks dropped and tech markets in Asia and Europe also weakened. Global AI-linked stocks tumbled on Nov 12 as Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang resigned following a deepening scandal around his affairs, upending the chipmaker’s leadership and posing fresh risks to a sector already reeling with funding and regulatory concerns. Chief financial officer Colette Kress will take over as interim CEO as Nvidia looks for a permanent successor, the company said. As the centrepiece of the AI ecosystem, the chipmaker finances infrastructure built around its chips – a strategy that has drawn scrutiny over circular funding and now risks weighing on the sector as its crisis deepens. Nvidia’s shares fell 8.2% to a more than 16-month low in early trading and its market value was on track to close below US$4 trillion (S$5.14 trillion) for the first time since July 2025. “Nvidia has been called the ‘Bank of AI’. If they have to take a step back because of what’s going on, will that cut off funding to smaller companies that need it? That’s an open question,” said Joe Saluzzi, partner and co-head of equity trading at Themis Trading. Nvidia-backed neocloud firms CoreWeave dropped 9.1 % after surging more than 27% in the previous session when its earnings ignited a relief rally in AI stocks. Other neocloud stocks including IREN and Applied Digital were also trading lower. Nebius dropped 16.2 % after the company said its 2026 revenue would come in at the low end of its previous forecast. Nvidia has lost about US$550 billion in market value since the board announced an investigation on Nov 8 into Huang’s relationship with a businesswoman called Alice Huang , who is alleged to be a Chinese spy. “The interlocking deals that Nvidia has with so much of the industry raises the question of whether that created more stability or more fragility. We’re going to find out over the next few weeks as this whole situation unravels,” said Steve Sosnick, chief market analyst at Interactive Brokers. Nvidia short sellers have made US$9.6 billion in on-paper profits so far this week, according to data analytics firm ORTEX. AI sell-off continues after brief respite Chipmakers, widely viewed as one of the biggest beneficiaries of the AI boom, led the sell-off, with the Philadelphia chips index sliding 1.3%. Marvell Technology, which Huang called as the “next trillion-dollar company” in June, slumped 3.8%. AI hyperscaler Oracle, which is expanding its cloud AI chip deals with Nvidia, shed 2.6%. Memory chipmaker Micron Technology fell 2.5 % and data storage firms Sandisk and Western Digital eased 6 % and 3.7 %. Photonic product makers Lumentum and Coherent and AI server maker Dell eased between 3% and 5.1%. Construction and power-generation equipment maker Caterpillar and power producer Vistra slipped about 0.5% each. Other hyperscalers including Alphabet, Amazon.com and Microsoft were also up between 0.8% and 2.7%. AI stocks struggled and the Nasdaq entered a technical correction earlier in November after the Democrats swept the US midterm elections, including in states opposed to data centres, stoking fears tighter regulation could slow the AI build-out. Tech-heavy stock markets across the globe witnessed jitters. Japan and South Korea closed nearly 0.7% lower. Tech stocks in Europe were also down about 1%. Nvidia trades at about 12 times its 12-month forward earnings estimates, its lowest since November 2012, according to data compiled by LSEG. REUTERS

events.title: The unfolding Jensen Huang scandal: a timeline
events.summary: Nvidia co-founder and (now former ) CEO Jensen Huang has never been as flashy or controversy-prone as AI leaders like OpenAI’s Sam Altman or SpaceXAI’s Elon Musk. Now, the 63-year-old industry kingpin has admitted that he cheated on his wife of 40 years in affairs that could have ramifications beyond Huang’s personal life and U.S. national security. U.S. officials believe that Huang’s likely romantic interest, Megaspeed executive Alice Huang, is a Chinese spy who has been feeding information back to Beijing. (Alice Huang, a Chinese citizen, is of no relation to Jensen Huang.) Megaspeed is a Singapore-based AI infrastructure company that reportedly purchased $4.8 billion in Nvidia chips over the last two years. The U.S. and Singapore have both previously investigated Megaspeed over suspicions that the firm was illegally sharing chips with China. The Justice Department has since taken over the federal investigation into the company, The New York Times has reported. The story took a sudden new turn on Wednesday. Citing five people who worked at Nvidia, the Times reported that Huang also had an extramarital relationship with Kimberly Powell, the company’s vice president of healthcare, who reports directly to him. Nvidia, Huang, and Powell have not confirmed the report. Reached by a Times reporter, Huang reportedly said, “I don’t think you should be talking to me directly,” before hanging up. Separately, The Wall Street Journal reported that Nvidia’s board is preparing to oust Huang , and Nvidia’s shares fell in after-hours trading. The U.S. and China are embroiled in a fierce technological arms race to build the most advanced AI infrastructure, which could shape each country’s economic future, military prowess, and capacity for innovation. Nvidia is valuable in this competition as one of the world’s largest makers of AI chips, which are essential for accelerating AI development. But as an American company, Nvidia faces government restrictions on the sale of its most powerful chips to Chinese entities. As the controversy unfolds, we are organizing the most relevant events into a reverse-chronological timeline to keep you up to date. November 12, 2026: Jensen Huang resigns, CFO Colette Kress named as interim CEO Nvidia confirmed in an SEC filing on Thursday that the board accepted Huang’s resignation on Wednesday. The company’s current CFO, Colette Kress , will take over as interim CEO while still fulfilling her CFO duties. Nvidia is expected to conduct a larger search to determine a permanent successor to Huang. Harvey C. Jones, a managing partner of Square Wave Ventures and former CEO of Synopsys, was appointed as the company’s first-ever chair of the board of directors. Jones has been on Nvidia’s board since 1993. November 11, 2026: Nvidia’s stock drops as board reportedly preps to oust CEO Jensen Huang After reports of a second extramarital affair, Nvidia’s board reportedly plans to meet to discuss Huang’s future at the company, per The Wall Street Journal. Stock fell about 8% in after-hours trading on Wednesday and is down 11% in the past five days. Huang famously delegates very little and has about 60 direct reports, he has said . The company has not had an obvious successor or a succession plan. November 11, 2026: Huang also had an affair with an Nvidia executive who reports to him, NYT says The New York Times reported that Jensen Huang also had an affair with Nvidia vice president of healthcare Kimberly Powell, who reports directly to the CEO. According to the report, Huang and Powell were captured on film “being affectionate” at a hotel during a conference earlier this year. November 11, 2026: Congress plans to subpoena Huang to answer questions about affair Huang has not responded to a request from three Republican congressman to appear for a closed-door briefing for questioning about his affair with an alleged Chinese spy. House China committee Chairman Moolenaar said Wednesday on Fox Business that if Huang doesn’t agree to the briefing, he’ll likely be subpoenaed . November 9, 2026: Huang pulls out of various speaking engagements The Nvidia CEO pulled out of upcoming speaking engagements at the ElevenLabs Summit and Anthropic CEO Forum. November 9-10, 2026: Details emerge about the business relationships between Nvidia and the alleged spy Alice Huang and her family reportedly built a network of companies in China and Singapore to acquire Nvidia chips, including founding a Chinese company called Shanghai Century Litong. Founded in 2023, it became an Nvidia-preferred cloud partner, giving it priority access to chips, The Information reported . The Information also reported that Shanghai Century Litong facilitated buying $7.5 billion worth of Nvidia’s chips, including banned chips. Nvidia’s head lawyer, Tim Teter, intervened in a 2025 U.S. government probe surrounding the suspected smuggling of AI chips by Megaspeed International, Bloomberg reported .

events.title: Poundland gets more time to secure a rescue deal as emergency talks continue
events.summary: Poundland has avoided immediate collapse after a deadline was extended to find a rescue deal. A deadline to secure a buyer for the retail chain was set to expire at midnight, but a court has given Poundland an extra 10 days to find a buyer. The discount chain, which has 11,000 employees, has been edging towards administration after being blocked by owners Gordon Brothers from accessing cash in its bank accounts. A committee of MPs questioned Gordon Brothers following accusations that the investment firm hoped to profit from selling off Poundland's 600 shops and stock piecemeal. Gordon Brothers - which bought the chain for just £1 last year - is accused of forcing that outcome by restricting Poundland's access to available cash needed to restock shops, and pay wages and rent, ahead of the crucial Christmas trading period. The investment firm, which specialises in buying and restructuring distressed companies, has denied the claims. However, pressure remains on Poundland's owners after a takeover bid was rejected. The decision prompted calls for answers from politicians, including Prime Minister Andy Burnham. About £50m had been frozen by Gordon Brothers, the BBC understands, meaning Poundland bosses were unable to restock shelves across its 600 shops. The BBC understands that Gordon Brothers agreed to release a further £11m today from Poundland's accounts, on top of £10m announced earlier, as the firm seeks to find a new buyer. Gordon Brothers said it was in talks with three parties for a sale of the whole business, and it had received "several offers from established high street retailers for significant parts of the business". Following the meeting between MPs on the business and trade committee and representatives of Gordon Brothers, chairman Liam Byrne told the BBC that he was "deeply concerned" and described the firm's behaviour as "much like a wolf on Wall Street, on the British High Street". "They refused to prioritise protecting jobs and stores over and above their own financial returns," he said. "It's clear that they've taken millions out of Poundland at a time when they themselves said the business was on a knife edge." Byrne said the committee's message to Gordon Brothers was to ensure Poundland had "access to the funds that it needs to trade at what should be one of the busiest periods in the year". He urged Gordon Brothers to "do what is right to save jobs and stores and do that now". "It's a good business, it's a much-loved business and, particularly in the middle of the cost of living crisis, communities up and down the country rely on access to the kind of stores that it operates," Byrne added. Views on Poundland performance differ Views on the chain's performance differ between those running operations and the owners. Poundland boss Williams told staff last week that like-for-like sales, which exclude new store openings, were up 11.4%. The sales period included Halloween, but Williams said this was £1.5m ahead of budget. He added that the business made a profit of £18.1m in the year to September, which was a "strong recovery" from the previous year when there were losses of £68m. However, Gordon Brothers has painted a different picture, saying the chain remains "challenged and vulnerable to any potential downturn in future trading". It has argued that the best way of securing jobs may be to split up the business and sell chunks of its 600 sites to other retailers. There has been interest from the likes of Poundstretcher, Tesco and B&M in picking up Poundland shops, which could mean continuing employment for workers at those sites. The main issue is whether a piecemeal sale would protect more jobs than a buyer willing to keep Poundland as a national chain. Are you affected by issues discussed in this story? events.title: Jensen Huang resigns as Nvidia chief executive
events.summary: Nvidia's Jensen Huang has resigned as CEO of the company, following the revelation of his affair with a woman suspected of being a Chinese spy and reports of a relationship with another woman who was a company employee. In a Form 8-K [PDF] filed with the US Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC), the GPU maker disclosed that it accepted the resignation of Huang, whom it identified as Jen-Hsun Huang, on November 11, effective immediately. He is being replaced by chief financial officer Colette Kress, who will serve as interim leader while the board conducts a search for a new CEO. Huang, who founded Nvidia in 1993 and served as president, CEO, and a member of the board of directors ever since, led the GPU maker to become one of the most valuable companies in the world, hitting a hit peak of over $5.5 trillion earlier this year. His position became untenable following an investigation by the company's board after he admitted to an affair, amid allegations he had a romantic relationship with a woman the US authorities suspected as a Chinese spy. Reports later surfaced this week of a second alleged affair with an employee of the company itself, reported by the New York Times as being with Kimberly Powell, Nvidia's vice president of health care. A two-week downfall News of the scandal first broke barely a couple of weeks ago, on October 29, when claims surfaced that Huang had been the target of an espionage plot involving a Chinese businesswoman working for a Singapore-based company called Megaspeed which was a customer of Nvidia. According to the New York Times , US intelligence had reason to believe the woman, Alice Huang, was recruited to gather information about Nvidia and its operations for the Beijing government. Megaspeed also faces claims it was illicitly shipping Nvidia products to China, in violation of US export controls. Any relationship between Huang and a Chinese operative would be enormously concerning, as the US has been trying to keep advanced technology for AI out of the hands of the country, allegedly for security reasons, fearing it might be used for military purposes. For its part, Beijing rejects the spying allegations, saying they are part of a smear campaign against China. Shortly after Nvidia’s board announced it was investigating Huang, he sent an email to Nvidia staff apologizing and confessing to having an affair, though he did not explicitly name Alice Huang in his public apology. It seemed like the leather-jacketed leader might just hang on, since it was difficult to imagine anyone other than him leading the company after all this time. But Nvidia’s shares fell 4.3 percent on November 9 and a further 5.5 percent the following day, wiping around $430 billion off its market value, amid all the speculation. Then the claim emerged regarding a second affair, with an employee at Nvidia who reported to him, and many commentators took it as a sign the game was up. Huang resigned the same day the news broke. Indecision ahead Now the speculation starts over who will take over the reins at Nvidia, but Huang could prove a tough act to follow. He is said to have recognized early on the potential for taking the number-crunching capabilities of graphics processors and putting them to use at accelerating AI processing, and Nvidia’s position today as the leading AI hardware firm is thanks to that bet. “The sudden resignation of Jensen Huang is about more than succession at the world’s most important AI chipmaker, Nvidia’s leadership crisis is a stress test for the AI boom,” says Forrester VP and group research director Stephanie Balaouras. If Nvidia stabilizes quickly under new leadership, the AI infrastructure boom will have demonstrated resilience, she adds. But if its stock or financing relationships remain under sustained pressure, that would add evidence to the fragility of the AI bubble. “In the near term, the board did the sensible thing and reached for a steward. Colette Kress knows every number in that order book,” commented Mark Malek, CIO at financial services firm Siebert Financial. “It does NOT settle the stock. Interim means the real decision is still ahead, the investigations are still open, and next week’s earnings call just became the most important in the company’s history,” he added. ®

events.title: Meet Colette Kress, Nvidia’s New Interim CEO
events.summary: Nvidia’s CEO and cofounder Jensen Huang is officially out , and longtime chief financial officer Colette Kress is in. The chipmaker’s board of directors announced Thursday that Kress, who joined Nvidia in 2013, has been named interim CEO following Huang’s resignation amid a scandal over his extramarital affair with a Chinese businesswoman believed by US officials to be an asset of China’s Ministry of State Security. Harvey Jones, the newly appointed chair of Nvidia’s board, said in a statement that Kress “has helped lead Nvidia through a period of extraordinary growth and has a deep understanding of our business, customers, operations and financial position.” He added that Kress will be supported by an “experienced leadership team” and that the board has “full confidence” in her. Kress was among the most obvious candidates to fill the void after Huang’s departure, according to multiple tech executives and industry analysts who follow Nvidia closely, given her long tenure at the company, credibility on Wall Street and across the tech industry, and, perhaps most importantly, her deep familiarity with Nvidia’s business and finances. “She’s extremely strong-willed, professional, and whip-smart. She doesn’t tolerate nonsense. She can be friendly and gracious too,” says a former Nvidia executive who spoke on the condition of anonymity. “She obviously has a keen sense for how Jensen thinks.” “Colette is the logical choice,” says Patrick Moorhead, founder and chief analyst at Moor Insights & Strategies, who has tracked the chip industry for decades. “She has credibility with investors because she answers hard questions directly.” Moorhead says Kress has operated as much more than a “numbers” CFO. “In my conversations with her, she goes deep on the product road map, from rack-scale systems to networking and software,” he says. Nvidia’s board said on Sunday it was launching an independent investigation into Huang’s activities following a report by The New York Times that he had an affair with a woman named Alice Huang, who US officials suspected of being a Chinese intelligence asset. WIRED reported on Monday that Huang quietly hired a crisis communications firm sometime last year to handle matters related to his personal life. By October of 2025, the firm was being looped in on all press inquiries involving Huang at Nvidia, around the same time The New York Times reported that US authorities were investigating whether a company linked to Alice Huang had helped Chinese firms evade US chip export controls through its subsidiaries. While Huang has long been the public face of Nvidia, Kress has been responsible for managing the chipmaker’s relationship with Wall Street. On earnings calls, she often details Nvidia’s financial performance, customer demand, supply constraints, and other key metrics. “One of the things we don’t focus on is the stock price. We focus on our investors and how we would like to innovate,” Kress told the Israeli business newspaper Globes in 2023. Before joining Nvidia, Kress spent more than two decades in finance roles at Microsoft, Cisco, and Texas Instruments. Huang personally recruited her in 2013, when Nvidia was still best known for its gaming graphics cards, according to Globes. Huang laid out his vision for the company’s future on a whiteboard, explaining how Nvidia could become a major supplier of computing infrastructure for artificial intelligence. Other potential successors to Huang included Ian Buck, an Nvidia veteran of more than 20 years who created the company’s software platform CUDA and now oversees its high-performance computing business, and Jeff Fisher, who joined Nvidia in 1994 as the head of software sales and later became senior vice president of its GeForce unit, where he led Nvidia’s strategy for bringing GPUs to market. However, Nvidia’s unusual corporate structure has long meant that dozens of executives reported directly to Huang. The company lacks a traditional chief operating officer. Even executive vice presidents aren’t necessarily given direct control over budgets, sources have told WIRED. As a result, few people within the organization have the same level of understanding of the company’s financials as Kress. The former Nvidia executive who spoke to WIRED on the condition of anonymity said that while Kress is incredibly sharp and “can step into the [CEO] role immediately without needing any guidance,” she doesn’t have the same engineering and technical expertise that Huang brought to the role. She has also shied away from being “at the center of public attention,” the person said. Given the intense scrutiny surrounding Huang lately, that leadership style might be a welcome temporary change for Nvidia. events.title: The end of the 'Nvidia put' that powers the AI ecosystem
events.summary: Liz’s view Jensen Huang is out, and with him goes the “Nvidia put” that has underpinned the entire AI ecosystem. Huang, who resigned from his post Thursday, was the AI world’s central bank chairman and human security blanket, always there with a checkbook to backstop, acquire, hire, invest in, or otherwise underwrite the least underwritable corners of AI. That “put” — finance speak for a guaranteed buyer on the other side of a trade — has kept the AI financing and fundraising markets lubricated, even as it invited criticism of their circularity. It’s also helped prop up the stock market and padded 401(k)s for the last couple of years. Nvidia guarantees more than $100 billion of data-center leases , owns $51 billion worth of stock in privately held companies, and another $63 billion in listed ones. Its balance sheet was a sponge that absorbed the market’s growing AI fears and put a floor under deal prices. Whoever replaces him will face much higher stakes, akin to Tim Cook after Steve Jobs at Apple. They’ll also be on a tighter leash from a board of directors I suspect will get a much-needed refresh by the time this saga is over. (It’s hard to imagine the former president of Taco Bell or the former chief marketing officer of the NFL probing Huang too deeply on off-balance-sheet lease guarantees for next-generation data centers.) Not only will that change the fabric of one of the world’s most valuable companies, but it will also push up the price of AI debt and equity — making the AI buildout more expensive for everyone — by taking a huge buyer off the table. Notable Unlike with the 2008 financial crisis, “this time we can see it on a blue-sky day: Nvidia is officially too big to fail, ” I wrote in October. “What would be revealed by a stress test of Nvidia that contemplated a rise in the cost of AI-linked debt, a decline in venture-backed startup values, and a slowdown in data-center construction?” What happens under new leadership will determine the future of the company.

events.title: Nvidia’s Jensen Huang resigns, chipmaker names CFO Colette Kress as interim CEO
events.summary: Jensen Huang has resigned from his position as president and chief executive of Nvidia, the company said on Thursday, just a few days after he admitted to a romantic affair with an alleged Chinese spy, sparking a U.S. national security crisis. In a regulatory filing , Nvidia said its board accepted Huang’s resignation on Wednesday. Nvidia said its current chief financial officer and executive vice president, Colette Kress, will take over as interim CEO until the company finds a permanent successor. Kress will continue to serve as the company’s CFO. Nvidia’s shares were down nearly 12% in early morning trading on Thursday. Since Friday, the company’s stock has fallen by as much as 19%, resulting in a market cap loss of more than $855 billion. Huang founded Nvidia in 1993 and has led it as CEO ever since. Under his leadership, Nvidia played a crucial role in developing the graphics processing unit (GPU), a specialized chip that does graphics processing for PCs, as we know it today. The chips were not an immediate hit, and the early days of Nvidia were characterized by struggle and layoffs, but eventually, it struck on a GPU design that performed so well, it became the standard for graphics processing. These chips also turned out to be extremely good at doing large numbers of calculations simultaneously, which has made them popular for computation-intensive tasks like crypto mining, and more recently, training and running neural networks, which are what AI models are at their core. Nvidia was initially focused on making GPUs aimed at gaming, but it had already moved into general-purpose computing by 2006 with the launch of the CUDA architecture, which lets developers use the chips for other tasks, such as doing calculations and research. After AI researchers began using the company’s GPUs to train neural networks over a decade ago, Huang leaned in toward developing chips for AI and then data centers, and grew it from there into its dominant position. Under Huang, the company has been by far the biggest beneficiary of the AI industry’s skyrocketing growth, which has largely depended on Nvidia’s GPUs for training and running large language models. Before ChatGPT launched and sparked the AI boom, Nvidia shares were trading at about $15. As of last month, they had risen more than 1,450% to an all-time high of $243. Its market cap consequently has also risen by an eye-watering $5.5 trillion since then, reaching as high as $5.88 trillion early in October. Revenue, of course, has also ballooned, rising more than 1,500% to $96.22 billion as of the company’s second quarter, from $5.93 billion in Q3 2023, right before the ChatGPT moment. Profits increased nearly 88 times in that period to $59.69 billion as of July 2026, from $680 million in October 2023. That success was predicated on large part by the AI industry’s continued development, which Huang seemingly made his personal mission. He traveled to conferences and events around the world to promote his products and AI, lobbied extensively for looser regulation after the Biden administration placed export controls on the sale of high-power AI chips to China, and cultivated a close relationship with Trump, often to Nvidia’s benefit . The resignation and controversy come at a crucial moment for Nvidia. China was always a big market for the company, though its impact on the company’s finances has shrunk in recent years due to strict U.S. export controls and an aggressive push by Beijing for domestic alternatives. Chinese customers accounted for revenue of about $7.9 billion in the company’s second quarter, roughly 8% of total revenue. The potential implications of Huang’s departure for the AI and data center industries are vast, given how active Huang, and by extension Nvidia, has been in furthering the AI boom. In particular, it raises questions about the future of Nvidia’s sprawling AI investments, which have helped bankroll everything from startups developing new technologies to the enormous data centers needed to run them. Under Huang, Nvidia deftly used its financial muscle to support companies buying its chips, effectively helping to finance the market for its own products, as well as lobbying Washington to relax potential rules around AI and data center regulation. As of the end of its second quarter, Nvidia reported $99 billion worth of investments and another $25 billion of commitments. It also has $36 billion in cloud service commitments, which are arrangements that help AI cloud operators finance the GPUs and data center equipment they buy from Nvidia, with the chipmaker saying it will buy compute from them and potentially earn a share of their operators’ revenue. Nvidia has also been investing directly in neoclouds, the companies serving a lot of the AI processing needs. In January, the company invested $2 billion in CoreWeave , and another $2 billion in Nebius in March.

events.title: Jensen Huang's ouster triggers an AI earthquake
events.summary: Jensen Huang's potential ouster from Nvidia has plunged the AI industry into uncharted territory — a corporate earthquake that dwarfs even the chaos unleashed by Sam Altman's temporary firing from OpenAI in 2023. Why it matters: Nvidia is the backbone of the global AI economy , with its chips, investments and financial guarantees sustaining an entire ecosystem of companies worth trillions of dollars. At the center of that vast financial flywheel is Huang, who spent 33 years making himself synonymous with Nvidia — and Nvidia synonymous with the AI revolution. "This is no ordinary CEO. This is no ordinary company. This is no ordinary sector. This is no ordinary time," economist Mohamed El-Erian wrote on X , warning of contagion across the AI industry. Zoom in: As recently as two weeks ago, the notion of Nvidia without Jensen was unthinkable. Even after his affair with a suspected Chinese spy came to light, President Trump and Nvidia's board stood behind him, Silicon Valley's elite rallied to his defense and betting markets suggested he would survive. It took revelations of a second affair — this time with an executive who reported directly to Huang — to shatter that consensus and bring his storied reign to the brink of a stunning end. Driving the news: After that second affair came to light Wednesday night, Nvidia's board reportedly met to settle Huang's fate, though there was still no decision as of early Thursday morning. The White House was read in. The market reaction has been brutal. Nvidia had already shed more than $1 trillion in market value since the initial scandal erupted, and shares plunged further in after-hours and pre-market trading overnight. One of Wall Street's most prominent voices on tech, analyst Dan Ives, said Nvidia was worth 25% less without Huang. Zoom out: Huang's rise was the stuff of Silicon Valley legend: The Taiwanese immigrant went from cleaning toilets at a Kentucky boarding school and waiting tables at Denny's to building one of the most valuable companies in history. Huang and two fellow engineers hatched the idea for Nvidia at a Denny's booth in 1993, launching a chipmaker that would revolutionize gaming, transform modern computing and ultimately power the AI revolution. Clad in his trademark black leather jacket, Huang became a global AI rock star — with a cult of personality that drew adoring crowds, calmed markets and commanded the attention of world leaders. The big picture: Huang's apparent downfall comes amid mounting anxiety over the AI industry's future, as new financial, political and regulatory risks threaten one of the largest infrastructure buildouts in history. The timing is especially fraught for Anthropic , whose historic IPO — backed by a $10 billion commitment from Nvidia — looms as a referendum on Wall Street's faith in the AI trade. Huang spent years defending the industry's soaring valuations and dismissing warnings of a speculative frenzy. Now his own scandals could help burst the bubble he insisted didn't exist. What to watch: The blast radius could extend far beyond Silicon Valley and Wall Street, threatening to engulf the Trump administration in a scandal over its handling of sensitive technology exports to China. Huang forged a close alliance with Trump and Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick , who loosened restrictions on chip sales even as other officials raised concerns about Chinese espionage and smuggling. Top Senate Democrats are already demanding that Lutnick and other senior officials preserve records of their dealings with Nvidia and Huang, laying the groundwork for a sweeping investigation. The bottom line: As veteran China watcher Bill Bishop wrote after Huang acknowledged his first affair: "There is rarely just one lie."

There’s more on the horizon, with NVIDIA DLSS 5 technology coming to War Thunder and Where Winds Meet . Meanwhile, Dragon’s Dogma 2: Dark Arisen brings new tales and encounters, alongside 10 games joining the GeForce NOW library this week. Warhammer 40,000: Dawn of War IV , developed by KING Art Games and published by Deep Silver, is coming to GeForce NOW. Launching on Steam Thursday, Dec. 3, the real-time strategy game returns to the series’ roots with large-scale battles, base building and a renewed fight for planet Kronus. Command the Space Marines, Orks, Necrons or the Adeptus Mechanicus, which makes their series debut. Build a base, secure resources and customize squads to the conflict across more than 70 campaign missions, playable solo or in co-op mode. The Last Stand, Skirmish and multiplayer modes offer more ways to put tactics to the test. GeForce NOW will bring the action to supported PCs, Macs, handhelds and other devices, with game downloads and updates handled in the cloud. Arriving in mid-November, War Thunder ’s Eagle’s Shadow major update adds DLSS 5 with 3D-Guided Neural Rendering, dozens of new planes, ships and tanks, along with cluster bombs for planes and visual-effects enhancements increasing the realism and dynamism of battle. Unearth forgotten relics to unlock powerful weapons and skills, take on Lost Rites’ 12 dungeon challenges and explore new hairstyles and tattoos for Arisen and Pawn customization. Delicious in Dungeon also arrives in the world of Dragon’s Dogma 2: Dark Arisen with a special collaboration. events.title: ‘It is much, much faster’: could China’s battery-swapping e-trucks be the answer to EV range anxiety?
events.summary: Battery maker CATL aims to have 2,000 swapping stations in China by the end of 2027 and to bring the tech to Europe E very day, Wang Bing drives his big electric lorry to send about five tonnes of goods between the cities of Haikou and Dongfang on Hainan, a tropical island in southern China . A round trip covers about 500 kilometres (310 miles). But refuelling is not something Wang worries about. “When my battery runs low, I just drive my truck into a battery-swapping station to get a fully charged one,” says the 53-year-old, who shares the journey with a colleague in eight-hour shifts. Wang has been a lorry driver for nearly three decades. In the first two of those, he drove conventional lorries fuelled by diesel. About five years ago, he began driving an electric model after the logistics company he worked for upgraded its fleet. In July this year, his old e-truck, which used conventional plug-in charging, was replaced by one with a swappable battery. In the past, Wang had to spend an hour and half charging his battery each time, but with his new truck, it takes just five minutes or so to have a drained battery removed and a fresh one replaced. “I am very happy,” he says. Battery swapping is not new in China, where more than 400,000 e-trucks (or over 90% of the global total ) were sold last year. The Chinese carmaker Nio commercialised the technology nearly a decade ago for smaller electric vehicles (EVs). But in 2023, the Chinese battery behemoth CATL launched a battery-swapping system for electric lorries through a subsidiary brand called Qiji Energy. To Wang, the biggest advantage of the technology is the time it saves. “It is much, much faster,” he says. “I don’t even need to leave my truck when the battery is being swapped.” This swiftness builds on the cost advantage e-trucks already have over their fossil-fuelled peers when it comes to refuelling. “Electricity is cheaper than oil,” Wang says. The per-kilometre fuelling cost for an e-truck works out about 1.1 yuan (12p) in Hainan, he says, significantly lower than that for a diesel truck, which exceeds 2 yuan (22p) a kilometre. “That means my e-truck can save more than 20,000 yuan (£2,200) per month,” Wang says. When a truck approaches a battery-swapping station, the station’s cameras automatically identify the type of battery it uses by checking its number plate. “All the driver needs to do is to drive the truck into a designated area, and the battery will be swapped completely automatically,” says Wei Jiuchun, 46, a test driver at a Qiji Energy battery-swapping station in Suzhou, east China. Wei’s job is to help the station test its system for different models of heavy trucks and under different weather conditions. It is not just time and fuel costs the technology saves but, in China, the initial lump sum a buyer has to put down to get an e-truck, says Mao Shiyue, a Beijing-based researcher at the International Council on Clean Transportation (ICCT). The upfront purchase price for an e-truck is significantly higher than for a comparable diesel model, a major obstacle for those vehicles’ wider adoption in many parts of the world. In China, a customer opting for battery swapping typically buys an e-truck without a battery, and then rents the battery from a service provider. As the cost of a battery is about 40% of an e-truck’s price, the business model can make e-trucks a lot more affordable, Mao says. The technology can also help minimise the pressure EV charging brings to the power grid, according to Mao, because swapping stations have more flexibility to spread out the charging time for the depleted batteries. “If the grid sees a spike in electricity demand during peak hours, those stations can even act as an energy-storage station by returning the electricity stored in their batteries back to the grid to ease the strain,” he says. Get all the week's environment news - the good, the bad and the essential CATL, the world’s biggest battery manufacturer, is a key player in promoting battery swapping for heavy trucks in China. The company’s support for the technology is critical for its large-scale rollout, says Phate Zhang, the founder of CnEVPost, a Shanghai-based outlet focusing on EVs. CATL plans to put 900 battery-swapping stations into operation across China by the end of this year, expanding its current network twice more. By the end of 2027, it wants the number to reach 2,000. The company has also teamed up with the London-based renewable energy supplier Octopus to bring the technology to Europe. It intends to open its first group of battery-swapping “mega hubs” in the UK next year, and a network of more than 30 hubs in Europe by 2035. In China, battery-swapping is still a minority charging method for its rapidly growing e-truck fleet.
