events.title: A new AI model wants to read between the lines
events.summary: The Scoop New York-based AI startup millionways on Thursday launched its new AI model that claims to offer insight into human intent and motivations. The company also told Semafor it has raised $6 million in US funding, with investors including football stars Jason Kelce and DK Metcalf. The Thorsten-4 model was born out of a research project in Germany in which dozens of psychologists interviewed more than 7,000 people about their personal lives and aspirations. That data — which the psychologists labeled by hand to capture what people’s words revealed about their motives and thinking — was used to train the model. Millionways cofounders Martin Cordsmeier and Max Weidemann argue that understanding is missing from regular AI models, which are trained on internet text. They see the model as particularly useful in sales and executive hiring, where a search firm could prompt it to evaluate an interview transcript to gauge how a candidate will behave under pressure. “We can add a level of human understanding that the language models cannot get to by themselves,” Weidemann said, adding that the model should be “a decision-making support tool rather than the ultimate decision-maker.” J.D.’s view Enterprises are increasingly injecting task- and industry-specific models into their tech stacks, rather than defaulting to the frontier models for every task. Just this week, leading voice AI company ElevenLabs, for example, announced a healthcare-focused version of its new transcription model. This gives CIOs more choice and customization, but it also adds the burden of testing whether specialized models actually beat fast-improving frontier ones. Cordsmeier and Weidemann ran our conversation for this story through Thorsten-4, which deduced that I was most focused on relationship-building and being conscientious: “You move between logic and intuition, and tough questions energized you.” (I’ll take the compliment!) I ran a transcript of the same call through Anthropic’s new Claude Fable 5.2 model and asked for a psychology analysis: Claude also gave a solid assessment, though it was less sure of itself, focusing more on the job I was doing than on me as a person. It (correctly) noted that my “unstated goal was source cultivation.”

In our latest Short-Term Energy Outlook , we expect a 23,000 barrels per day (b/d) (6%) increase in 2026, followed by a 60,000 b/d (13%) rise in 2027. At a forecast 505,000 b/d in 2027, output would be the most since 2014. If realized, these annual production increases will be the largest since the 1980s, when Alaskan crude production peaked at 2.0 million b/d. The recent growth is attributable to two projects on Alaska's North Slope: The Nuna project, owned by ConocoPhillips, started production in December 2024 and is expected to produce 20,000 b/d at its peak. So far this year, it has produced an average of 10,000 b/d, partially offsetting existing production declines. The Pikka Phase 1 project, jointly owned by Santos and Repsol, began production in May 2026 with initial average monthly production of 2,000 b/d and reaching 38,000 b/d as of September 2026, according to data from the Alaska Oil & Gas Conservation Commission . We expect peak production of 80,000 b/d by winter 2026–27, nearly 20% of total Alaskan production in 2025. Notably, our STEO production data indicate that third-quarter 2026 production grew 4% as Pikka Phase 1 came online, marking the first third-quarter production increase in more than 40 years. events.title: Alibaba-Megaspeed financing link traced via S’pore, Malaysia units amid Nvidia chip scrutiny
events.summary: Speedmatrix, one of Megaspeed’s Malaysia subsidiaries, has an office in the Eco Botanic township in Johor. Alibaba-owned Singapore firm Apex had a financial arrangement with Megaspeed’s Malaysia unit, Speedmatrix, which pledged its computer equipment and other assets to Apex. Megaspeed, a major Nvidia chip buyer, is under US and Singapore scrutiny over possible chip diversion to China and suspected breaches of export laws. It has hired a US law firm to review compliance. Megaspeed’s overseas network spans five markets, with subsidiaries in Malaysia, Thailand, Indonesia, Australia and the US. SINGAPORE – A Singapore company owned by Chinese tech giant Alibaba had a financial arrangement with the Malaysian subsidiary of Megaspeed International, a major Nvidia chip buyer under scrutiny over the possible diversion of advanced artificial intelligence chips to China . Corporate records obtained by The Straits Times show that Speedmatrix, Megaspeed’s Malaysian subsidiary, pledged specified IT and network equipment, intellectual property and related rights to Apex Enterprise Solutions (Singapore) under an agreement dated June 18, 2024. The arrangement gave Apex security over the assets should Speedmatrix fail to meet certain contractual obligations. Malaysian corporate records show that the arrangement remained active as at Nov 11, 2026. The financial connection was highlighted in a May report by US short-seller Culper Research, which alleged that Alibaba may have channelled billions of dollars through Apex to finance Megaspeed’s purchases of Nvidia chips. The research firm, which had taken a position that would benefit from the fall of Nvidia’s share price, suggested that Alibaba had provided the funds to Apex, which may have passed a substantial portion to Megaspeed for distribution to its overseas subsidiaries. Apex was incorporated in Singapore in July 2023 and it is registered at Lazada One in Bras Basah Road, which is leased by Alibaba and its South-east Asian online shopping unit, Lazada Group. Accounting and Corporate Regulatory Authority records show that Apex’s immediate holding company is Cloud Intelligence (Cayman) Holding. Its ultimate holding company is Alibaba Group Holding, which is incorporated in the Cayman Islands and has contractual rights to Alibaba China’s profits. Apex, in its audited financial statement for the financial year ended March 31, 2025, described its business activity as “providing procurement activities”. Its corporate records also showed that Yuan Qian served as a director from August 2023 to August 2025. The name matches the Chinese name of Selina Yuan, a former Alibaba executive who has headed Alibaba Cloud’s international business in Singapore, but ST has not independently confirmed that she is the director named in Apex’s records. Apex’s current directors are Gong Zhengyuan, Zhu Bofu and Madelyn Kwang Yeit Lam, a Singaporean who also serves as the company secretary. Kwang has also been listed as a director and secretary of Alibaba Cloud (Singapore) since 2016. She did not respond to ST’s queries. Apex’s auditor is PwC. When contacted, a spokesperson said: “This relates to a client matter, we are therefore unable to comment.” The Financial Times reported in November that Alibaba was one of Megaspeed’s major customers for its South-east Asian cloud service operation. Alibaba and Megaspeed did not respond to ST’s queries on the nature of their commercial relationships and whether the relationships have remained intact with investigations into Megaspeed. Megaspeed owns seven subsidiaries across five overseas markets, according to its financial statements for 2024, which are its latest publicly available records. Three are in Malaysia: Speedmatrix, Megaspeed International Sdn Bhd and MSFusion. All three are private limited companies. Speedmatrix and Megaspeed International Sdn Bhd were described as cloud-hosting service providers. MSFusion was classified as dormant at end-2024, but it entered a RM263.2 million (S$82.8 million) agreement to buy a site in Johor for a proposed data centre, according to the seller’s bourse filing in August 2025. Megaspeed also owned 99.99% of Megaspeed (Thailand) and 99% of PT Megaspeed International Indonesia, both cloud-hosting businesses. The other two Megaspeed’s wholly owned subsidiaries are in Australia and the US. Megaspeed’s latest shipment recorded on corporate intelligence platform Sayari was to Speedmatrix – an Nvidia baseboard for high-performance graphics processing units, which arrived on Nov 18, 2025. The top receivers of Megaspeed’s shipments were Speedmatrix and PT Megaspeed International Indonesia, according to Sayari. Megaspeed has attracted international attention because of its massive purchases of Nvidia’s advanced AI chips, some of which are subject to US export restrictions intended to limit China’s access to powerful computing technology.

events.title: Jensen Huang Resigns as Nvidia CEO
events.summary: Jensen Huang stepped down as the chief executive of Nvidia on Thursday, four days after the company announced its internal investigation into an affair he had with Alice Huang, also known as Huang Le, an alleged asset of China’s Ministry of State Security. “Jensen Huang has resigned as President, Chief Executive Officer, and a member of the Board, effective immediately,” the Nvidia board said in a statement. Nvidia’s chief financial officer, Colette Kress, will serve as interim CEO. The board said it “will consider internal and external candidates” for a permanent replacement. The board’s investigation was announced on November 8, slightly less than two weeks after The New York Times reported that the chief executive had been the target of a Chinese intelligence operation facilitated through his relationship with Alice Huang, who has no known relation to Jensen. The pair have been spotted in public together at least twice, in June 2024 and May 2025 . On November 11, The New York Times reported that Jensen Huang also allegedly had a relationship with a direct report at Nvidia. The alleged relationship with a subordinate, along with Huang’s business dealings with Megaspeed, a Singapore-based AI company where Alice Huang previously held a senior position, likely played a greater role in the board’s decision to oust Huang than the Chinese espionage allegations, a source familiar with the matter tells WIRED. US intelligence officials reportedly briefed President Donald Trump on Huang’s relationship with Alice last year, but the president did not act on it. On November 6, The New York Times and Financial Times reported that Alice was a spy for China’s Ministry of State Security and that she had been recruited to collect information on the Nvidia executive. (The Chinese government has rejected all claims that Alice was a spy for the country. ) Huang sent a companywide email on Sunday acknowledging his affair, apologizing to his family and Nvidia employees, and pledging cooperation with the internal investigation. The executive has been married to his wife, Lori Huang, since 1985 , and both of the couple’s two children work at the company. On Monday, WIRED exclusively reported that last year Huang began working with a crisis PR firm to manage his personal communications. In October 2025, those PR consultants started to be looped in on all press inquiries involving Huang, whether those inquiries were personal or professional in nature. The timing lines up with a New York Times report that month that the US Commerce Department was investigating whether Alice Huang’s Megaspeed was helping Chinese companies get around American export controls with the help of a vast web of subsidiaries. The investigation was reportedly halted and transferred to the Justice Department after Nvidia general counsel Tim Teter inquired about it. Huang has been a vocal critic of these export controls, which he argues unnecessarily constrain the market for American chips, create discrete Chinese and American tech ecosystems, and spur China to build competitive chips of its own. Huang has worked to develop a relationship with Trump in order to advocate for policies that are advantageous for Nvidia, including the idea of opening its markets to China. Huang cofounded Nvidia in 1993 with friends Chris Malachowsky and Curtis Priem. The trio reportedly brainstormed their vision for the company in a Denny’s diner and aspired to bring realistic 3D graphics to personal computers. For the first few decades of its existence, Nvidia was primarily known in the gaming community for creating chips powerful enough to render high-quality in-game graphics. In 2012, after a new kind of neural network known as AlexNet won a high-profile prize in computer vision, Nvidia pivoted from high-speed computer graphics to building chips that would support artificial intelligence. Huang has repeatedly said that the introduction of AlexNet, which was developed by AI engineers Alex Krizhevsky, Ilya Sutskever, and Geoffrey Hinton, was a “Big Bang”–like event for computing. Because its new GPUs proved highly effective at powering AI models that require massive amounts of processing power, the value of Nvidia shares soared in 2023 and 2024, in lockstep with the broader AI boom that began sweeping through the world economy. In the summer of 2025, Nvidia became the first company in history to cross $4 trillion in value. As of September 2026, the company controlled about 90 percent of the GPU market. Much of Nvidia’s epic rise over the few decades has been attributed not just to its cutting-edge chips and its software “moat,” CUDA, that keeps developers locked into those chips, but also to the fast-thinking, controlling, charismatic, and often bombastic leadership style of Huang himself. Now, that critical part of the company’s success is out.

events.title: Jensen Huang resigns as Nvidia CEO after affair with suspected Chinese spy
events.summary: Embattled Nvidia co-founder and chief executive Jensen Huang resigned on Thursday, marking a stunning fall from grace for the leader of a vital US computing giant that has long helped fuel the artificial intelligence boom. Mr Huang’s departure came days after he admitted to having an affair with a woman suspected of being a Chinese spy. In a statement, Nvidia's board of directors thanks Mr Jensen for his "profound" contributions to the company. "The board and the company thank Jensen for his immeasurable contributions to the company and the industry," the statement read. Colette Kress, current executive vice president and chief financial officer, will serve as interim chief executive, Nvidia announced. Nvidia stock was down more than 10 per cent in pre-market trading. Harvey Jones, chairman of Nvidia's board of directors, said Ms Kress had helped lead the company through a “period of extraordinary growth and has a deep understanding of our business, customers, operations and financial position”. “She is supported by an experienced leadership team that has been instrumental in executing Nvidia's strategy and advancing its technology road map. Political fallout US President Donald Trump, a long-time ally of Mr Huang, posted about the AI tycoon's departure on Truth Social, Mr Trump's social media platform. "Now that Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang, who has done a fantastic job, has resigned, there is only one man to take his place, Tim Cook of Apple," President Trump wrote in part. "A legend replaces a legend," he added. It was Mr Huang's many meetings with Mr Trump, however, that often fueled controversy. It was no secret that Nvidia's former chief executive would lobby President Trump to try and relax US chip export policies impacting China, which caused an uproar with both Democrats and Republicans. Jensen Huang’s decision to resign from NVIDIA does not absolve him, other executives, or the company as a whole of responsibility for putting our national security at risk or for any potential violations of our laws. They still owe Congress answers. — Elizabeth Warren (@SenWarren) November 12, 2026 Democratic US Senator Elizabeth Warren didn't mince words on Thursday shortly after Mr Huang resigned, and alleged that US President Donald Trump and his appointees at the US Department of Commerce were enablers for some of the controversies that engulfed Nvidia. " Secretary Howard Lutnick and Under Secretary Jeffrey Kessler must explain why they have not closed export control loopholes and act today to ensure our advanced technology is not fueling China’s military," she said, referring to reports of Nvidia's dealings with China. Alice Huang affair Though not without controversy since he co-founded Nvidia in 1993, Mr Huang sparked a crisis early this month when he admitted to having an affair with a technology executive going by the name of Alice Huang. US officials and investigators said they believe Ms Huang to be a spy working on behalf of China, a top US rival in the tech and AI field. To maintain its edge in the AI race, the US implemented various export policies designed to keep some of the most powerful US-made semiconductors and computers away from potentially adversarial countries. But Mr Huang and Nvidia were vocal in recent years in opposing such export policies, with the company’s chief executive saying the restrictions hampered US influence and prevented American technology from becoming a global standard. Proponents of the export policies, however, said the rules bolstered the US lead and made it difficult for countries such as China to catch up, particularly in the need for computing power to train large language models. Some of those supporters of the export policies accused Nvidia and Mr Huang of simply wanting to boost revenue at all costs, even if it was to the detriment of US national security. As the overall mood towards AI, big tech executives and unregulated technology began to sour among US voters, politicians stepped up the scrutiny of Nvidia. Infidelity By the time Mr Huang admitted to the affair, several media reports had accused his company of turning a blind eye to various products entering China. Mr Huang’s admission of infidelity expedited and amplified calls for further inquiries. Shortly after Mr Huang’s mea culpa, Nvidia’s board of directors announced an independent investigation to address reports of whether he had been the target of a foreign spy operation, and what, if anything had been compromised. Company representatives initially insisted Mr Huang would remain chief executive but pressure grew. Mr Huang founded Nvidia, along with Chris Malachowsky and Curtis Priem, in 1993, as the personal computer sector was booming. A major part of that was gaming but many computers at the time were not designed for the gamers and Nvidia saw an opening in the market. The company designed special graphics cards and video boards that, while popular, did not make Nvidia a household name. As a result, its name was mispronounced by many for a lengthy period of time. Profits steadily grew, however, and the company methodically expanded. As progress in AI started to hit its stride, Nvidia soon found its custom graphics processing units and boards in unprecedented demand. Stuff of legend Nvidia could hardly build its products fast enough to keep up with demand, yet it knew how to manufacture them to perfection. Revenue and profits skyrocketed, and Mr Huang’s presence became almost impossible to ignore, even among those who had zero interest in AI. events.title: Trump orders Vance to focus on "corruption" in Democrat-run areas, not Iran
events.summary: President Trump directed Vice President JD Vance on Thursday to turn his "complete and total attention" toward alleged corruption in Democrat-run cities and states, contending that "[w]e don't need a deal with Iran." The big picture: After Vance concluded that the Iran war drove Republicans' stunning midterm walloping, Trump is reorienting his No. 2's focus — and directing him to go after Democrats the president labeled as "CORRUPT AND EVIL." Oil prices surged, and stocks sank after Trump's post reinjected a note of uncertainty into a market that was acting like the Iran war was all but over. Driving the news: "We don't need a deal with Iran. Those days have long since passed," Trump wrote on Truth Social. Also on Truth Social Thursday, he threatened new tariffs on Mexico and criticized GOP senators for failing to pass the Save America ACT — adding that failure to do so was "devastating" for Republicans during the midterms. He said that he had asked Vance to "focus his complete and total attention" on so-called "Corruption and Crime" in Democrat-run cities and states, naming Minnesota, California and Illinois. Vance has chaired Trump's Task Force to Eliminate Fraud since the president created it via executive order earlier this year. Throughout the first half of his administration and federal crackdown on U.S. cities, Trump has repeatedly framed blue areas as hotbeds of crime and corruption, even when the stats haven't necessarily backed up those arguments. Catch up quick: Vance was recently heavily involved in a push to reach a new ceasefire with Iran and resume nuclear negotiations, Axios' Barak Ravid reported. Vance was a skeptical voice in Trump's inner circle about the war, Ravid reported, and led U.S. negotiating delegations after it began. Vance's office and the White House did not immediately respond to Axios' request for comment. Between the lines: Vance offered a surprisingly candid assessment of the midterm shellacking, writing in an X post last week that "[t]he reason we lost is the war." He continued: "If you'd like to argue it was worth it, that losing the Senate for the next 6 years was worth it, then do so. Argue it was a worthwhile cost to pay. Agree or disagree, that's at least honest." "But everyone knows why we lost." What we're watching: Secretary of State Marco Rubio met with his G7 counterparts in Paris on Tuesday, where he said Trump had considered resuming the war or cutting a deal but instead settled on strangling the Iranian regime, Axios previously reported . Rubio has signaled skepticism of a diplomatic breakthrough — and Trump's post indicates that door is closed, for now. Go deeper: Trump: New Iran attacks "quite unlikely"

events.title: NVIDIA Announces CEO Transition
events.summary: Colette Kress, Executive Vice President and Chief Financial Officer, Appointed Interim CEO Harvey C. Jones Appointed First-Ever Chair of the Board NVIDIA (NASDAQ: NVDA) Board of Directors announced today that Jensen Huang has resigned as President, Chief Executive Officer, and a member of the Board, effective immediately. Colette Kress, current Executive Vice President and Chief Financial Officer of NVIDIA, has agreed to serve as Interim Chief Executive Officer. Kress will continue to serve as Executive Vice President and Chief Financial Officer while serving as Interim Chief Executive Officer until a permanent successor has been named. The Board is initiating a search for a permanent Chief Executive Officer and will consider internal and external candidates. Kress has served as Executive Vice President and Chief Financial Officer of NVIDIA since joining the company in September 2013. During her tenure, she has led the company’s finance organization and has played a key role in NVIDIA’s growth and evolution. Prior to joining NVIDIA, Kress spent nearly 25 years in finance roles at leading technology companies, including Cisco and Microsoft. The Board of Directors appointed Harvey C. Jones as its first-ever Chair of the Board. Mr. Jones has been an entrepreneur, technology executive, and active venture investor for over 30 years, including serving as Chief Executive Officer and Executive Chairman of Synopsys. “Colette has helped lead NVIDIA through a period of extraordinary growth and has a deep understanding of our business, customers, operations and financial position,” said Harvey Jones, Chair of the NVIDIA Board of Directors. “She is supported by an experienced leadership team that has been instrumental in executing NVIDIA’s strategy and advancing its technology roadmap. The Board has full confidence in Colette and the leadership team, and we expect the company’s operations, customer commitments and product roadmap to continue without interruption.” “NVIDIA’s strength has always come from its people, and together with our leadership team, I am committed to building on the extraordinary foundation Jensen created over the last 33 years,” said Colette Kress, Interim CEO and CFO, NVIDIA. “We will continue advancing the work that has made NVIDIA a leader in accelerated computing and AI, and execute on the opportunities ahead. Our focus remains on serving our customers, partners, developers and shareholders.” Jensen’s contributions to NVIDIA are profound. NVIDIA is one of the most consequential technology companies in the world. The Board and the company thank Jensen for his immeasurable contributions to the company and the industry. NVIDIA will report its third-quarter fiscal 2027 financial results on Tuesday, November 17, at approximately 1:20 p.m. PT, as previously scheduled, followed by its earnings call at 2 p.m. PT. events.title: Poundland owner secures two extra weeks to ensure retail chain’s survival
events.summary: US investment firm Gordon Brothers is ‘taking due care’ to consider if one of three bidders has enough funds Poundland’s owner has said it is “taking due care” to consider if one of three bidders had enough funds to ensure its survival after the troubled budget retail chain secured two more weeks to find a deal. The management of Poundland , which employs approximately 12,000 people and operates 600 stores in the UK and Ireland, won approval from the high court for an extension of legal protection from creditors on Thursday morning. Poundland’s board said it had sought the extra time “with a view to identifying the best available prospects for shareholders, creditors and our people”. It added: “Our stores remain open as usual during this period and we thank our colleagues, suppliers and customers for their incredible and continued support.” The retail chain’s owner, the US investment firm Gordon Brothers, has been under pressure to accept a bid for the company that would save retail jobs and protect thousands of suppliers since Poundland filed a notice of intention to appoint administrators two weeks ago. A spokesperson for Gordon Brothers said on Thursday: “We support the board’s decision to extend the legal moratorium over the company by a further 10 working days. This brings additional stability amid an ongoing sale process in the backdrop of increasing cost pressures and a difficult inflationary economic environment. “With this decision, we are today able to confirm to Poundland employees that funds will be released to allow payroll to be made in full this month, while additional funds continue to be released to support Poundland’s ongoing trading. “We are in discussions with three parties for a sale of the whole business, and we have also received several offers from established high street retailers for significant parts of the business. “While our preference remains a sale of the whole company, we are taking due care to ensure that any successful offer can provide the funds required to acquire the business and see it through to sustainable cash generation. We, the board, and all involved are working to secure a credible plan that delivers certainty, preserves value and protects as many jobs as possible.” Gordon Brothers confirmed it had provided £85m of financing, understood to be via an asset-backed loan that Poundland has only partially used over the past year. That financing is in addition to a £30m shareholder loan largely taken on by Gordon Brothers when it bought the business for a nominal £1 last year. Gordon Brothers fought back after MPs on Wednesday accused the Poundland owner of extracting millions of pounds from the retailer when it was on a “knife-edge”. Documents provided to MPs showed the finance firm had taken close to £20m in interest payments and various fees, including those relating to store closures since acquiring Poundland. Gordon Brothers said it had provided finance for Poundland “when no one else was willing to finance the company – and has contributed substantial efforts to support a turnaround. “Had we not, the company would have collapsed into insolvency in August 2025. Our efforts have continuously focused on the company’s value and its people, not prioritising one over the other.”

events.title: Extreme weather risk is scaring big corporations away from poorer countries – that hurts the companies, too
events.summary: When multinational companies decide where to build a factory, open a mine or establish a regional office, they have to consider whether the investment will still be profitable years into the future. Making that decision increasingly means thinking about risks, like whether surrounding roads will flood, worker safety will be compromised by extreme heat in the summer, and clean water will be available. As climate change increases the frequency and intensity of extreme weather events around the world, these effects can be especially severe in poorer countries that lack the resources to prepare for disasters or recover quickly after they hit. I study how political and environmental risks affect international business . In my new book, “ Multinational Corporations and Climate Change: Risks, Responsibilities, and Resilience ,” I explore how disaster risk is affecting the ways global companies see these climate-vulnerable markets, and how those views are leading some foreign investors to avoid these developing nations altogether. Low- and middle-income countries aren’t the only ones that suffer when multinational corporations pass them by. The companies themselves also stand to lose out on business opportunities in emerging markets if they pull away. How climate risk affects foreign investment Evidence from several studies suggests that multinationals are systematically avoiding investing in the most climate-vulnerable countries. These include my own analysis of 159 countries. Although these studies focus on different samples, they identify the same trend: Countries characterized by greater climate vulnerability received less foreign investment . The results are not trivial. My book identifies a 12% reduction in foreign direct investment for each 1-point rise in climate vulnerability on a 100-point scale, while holding other relevant factors constant. This vulnerability data measures countries’ exposure to climate hazards as well as their capacity to adapt. Companies rarely say why they’re avoiding a particular location, but their climate-related concerns occasionally become visible. For example, Google halted plans to build a US$200 million data center in Chile after an environmental court revoked its construction permit over the likely effects on water supplies and the environment. Similarly, a $1 billion data center proposed in Kenya by Microsoft and the Abu Dhabi-based artificial intelligence company G42 was delayed and ultimately suspended amid concerns about water stress in the area. Companies have reason to be cautious about climate risks. One analysis of 71 large publicly traded companies found that firms reporting major flood losses experienced a 5% average decline in shareholder value over the following year, after accounting for broader market movements. In Vietnam, typhoons and floods caused an estimated $475 million in damage to energy and transportation infrastructure in 2022. Unreliable infrastructure cost companies there about $280 million . An aerial view shows scores of vehicles submerged at a flooded Honda factory in Thailand in November 2011. Paula Bronstein /Getty Images Severe flooding in Thailand in 2011 forced several companies, including Toyota, Nissan and Honda, to temporarily suspend production as factories flooded, shutting down production of parts or vehicles made there. Costs like those shape where companies choose to invest next. While climate risk does not stop all investment in climate-vulnerable markets, it does make projects in these nations relatively more expensive, less attractive and more difficult to finance than less risky locations. Who loses from investor avoidance? For developing countries, less foreign investment means fewer jobs are created . These countries also have fewer opportunities to benefit from exposure to the new technologies that multinationals bring when they invest abroad. Those results highlight another way climate change is deepening global inequality. It reduces the economic activity that could support future development, while simultaneously damaging physical infrastructure and threatening human health and well-being. Developing countries are especially vulnerable to the effects of rising global temperatures, whether for their dependence on agricultural markets, geography or relatively fragile infrastructure . A report from the Climate Impact Lab at the University of Chicago projects that 90% of heat-related deaths in the coming decades will take place in low- and middle-income countries. Similarly, a 2022 study found that around 90% of people exposed to flooding live in developing nations. Yet poor countries have contributed only a tiny fraction of the emissions that are causing climate change, even as they face the brunt of the damage. For example, African countries are responsible for less than 4% of greenhouse gas emissions globally. But they stand to experience the greatest negative effects of climate change. Lost opportunities for multinational companies When a company avoids investing in climate-vulnerable countries, that may reduce its exposure to floods, droughts or extreme heat, but the decision also carries potential costs for the company. Many of these countries have growing consumer markets, energy resources or critical minerals that multinationals need. Companies that dismiss them as too risky may lose out on promising opportunities. For example, the Democratic Republic of Congo supplies most of the world’s cobalt , while Indonesia has become the dominant producer of nickel . These countries are highly vulnerable to climate change , which is likely scaring some companies away . Yet companies with a greater tolerance for risk have established strong positions in those countries’ mineral industries . Thus, more cautious firms may reduce their risk exposure, but they are also surrendering access to important resources and growing markets. Reducing investor avoidance There are ways to help companies overcome their climate-risk avoidance so more investment can pour into these countries: Foreign aid from wealthy countries can help developing countries shore up their roads, ports, electrical grids and water systems before extreme storms or droughts occur. My 2025 study found that climate-vulnerable countries that received more aid for climate adaptation also received more foreign direct investment than those receiving less aid. The result suggests the funding may reassure companies that climate risks are being addressed. International development banks can share some of the risks by providing climate risk insurance to multinationals. This would offer a safety net to absorb some of the losses if a covered disruption prevents a project from operating as intended. The World Bank already offers similar coverage against political risk incidents, which has given companies confidence to invest in countries such as Kenya , Mozambique and Nigeria . events.title: While California’s wealth tax failed, states are taking other steps to collect more revenue from the rich
events.summary: State efforts to tax the rich did relatively well in the 2026 midterm elections, following a series of state legislative moves in that direction in recent years. That might come as a surprise because a majority of voters rejected California’s Proposition 40 . The much-publicized ballot initiative would have imposed a one-time 5% tax on the net worth of the state’s roughly 200 billionaires. Google co-founder Sergey Brin and several other billionaires spent nearly $400 million trying to persuade voters to reject it. Emmanuel Saez, a University of California, Berkeley economist who studies inequality and helped design Proposition 40, lamented the loss, saying: “ Today oligarchy has won .” As a law professor who recently wrote a book about wealth inequality , I have been monitoring the results of these efforts aimed at taxing the rich. Despite Proposition 40’s failure, I think it’s important to observe that many Americans expressed support during the midterms for hiking income taxes on the rich, and to a lesser extent, taxes on the second – or third or fourth – homes the very wealthy possess. Taxing the rich at the ballot box Taxing income is proving a more successful strategy than taxing wealth. Major changes to income taxes were up for a vote in five states during the midterms. Three of those ballot initiatives were proposals that sought to boost income tax rates on the rich or maintain those rates. All three prevailed. In Washington state , for example, voters backed a measure that will preserve its new 9.9% income tax on household income above $1 million. This “millionaire’s tax,” signed into law earlier in 2026, is the state’s first personal income tax. Meanwhile, Colorado voters rejected Proposition 136 , which would have capped the state’s income tax rate at 4.4%. They also approved Amendment 87 , a new graduated income tax that raises rates on households and businesses with incomes over $500,000. And even though California’s voters rejected Proposition 40, they did approve Proposition 3 . That measure makes permanent the income tax rates enacted in 2012 for the state’s highest earners, which were set to expire in 2031. The surcharges, adjusted annually for inflation, start at 10.3% for incomes of $360,000 and go up to a 12.3% surcharge for taxpayers earning over $721,000. And in August 2026, Missouri voters overwhelmingly rejected a measure that would have required the state’s lawmakers to eliminate its income tax. This would have meant losing $8.5 billion in revenue annually. The change would have let rich income taxpayers off the hook and replaced lost revenue through an increased sales tax that would have hit low-income taxpayers hardest. The two losses were in North Carolina and Iowa . Neither state voted directly on a tax to be levied on the rich. But both approved constitutional amendments that will make it harder for the state legislatures to enact these kinds of taxes in the future. North Carolina’s governor, Josh Stein, called the amendment in his state a “ millionaire protection cap .” People visit the Billionaire Tax Now booth at the 2026 California Democratic Party State Convention in San Francisco, on Feb. 21, 2026, months before a ballot initiative that would have introduced such a measure failed to garner enough support. AP Photo/Jeff Chiu State legislatures raising income tax rates on high earners Ahead of the midterms, new taxes on the rich introduced via state legislatures , rather than ballot initiatives, also emerged. In Maine, legislators voted in April 2026 for a tax surcharge of 1% on income over $1 million. The following month, Hawaiian lawmakers created a new 13% income bracket for single taxpayers earning above $500,000 or couples filing jointly who make over $1 million. This change is paired with a reduction in rates for lower-income brackets. And one month after that, Rhode Island enacted a surcharge for millionaires’ income to be phased in over the next three years, reaching a maximum 3% rate. In 2009, New York became one of the first states to pass one of these high-earner income taxes . Washington, D.C., Massachusetts and Maryland also enacted these “millionaire taxes” in 2022, 2023 and 2025, respectively. Taxing additional homes Another way that state and local governments are boosting the tax revenue they get from wealthy constituents is by levying special taxes on pricey homes that aren’t the owners’ primary residences . These initiatives have succeeded both in state legislatures and voting booths. Montana lawmakers, in April 2025, approved a new tiered property tax system , which took effect on Jan. 1, 2026. It raised property tax rates on vacation homes and short-term rentals to 1.9%, while primary residences and qualifying long-term rentals pay lower, tiered homestead rates . New York City rolled out its “ pied-à-terre tax ” in July. The new tax imposes an annual surcharge of 0.8% to 1.3% on single-family homes valued at $5 million or more, and 4% to 6.5% on condos and co-ops valued at $1 million or more. The surcharge only applies to homes that are not a primary residence . Rhode Island has a similar property tax that took effect at the same time as New York City’s. It’s an annual surcharge of $2.50 for every $500 of assessed value above $1 million that applies to non-primary residences. And on Nov. 3, voters in Boulder, Colorado, approved a residential vacancy tax on homes that sit empty more than half the year. The surcharge, which goes into effect in 2028, will be roughly $4,000 a year for each vacant property. It applies across the board, but homes that aren’t primary residences are the clear target. However, just west of Boulder in Crested Butte, Colorado, a second-home tax failed. So did an effort to levy a similar surcharge in San Diego, California. New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani speaks about the fiscal year 2027 budget in New York City on May 12, 2026. Timothy A. Clary/AFP via Getty Images Why income taxes are attractive to voters and lawmakers There is a good reason why taxing the income of rich people is easier to pull off than taxing their wealth: Income taxes are much easier to calculate . Income taxes can be based on annual income tax filings, whether state or federal. It requires no extra work to value someone’s net worth. There are no such filings for wealth, except after death, if a large estate is left behind . Wealth taxes also require the annual valuation of businesses, farmland, artwork, intellectual property and other assets – many of which are hard to estimate. The downside of taxing income instead of wealth is that it limits how much revenue can be raised from the people most able to pay taxes. Most wealthy people convert little of their wealth into income. One common exception occurs when they sell some of their stock . Property taxes, like income taxes, are an exception to this rule. AWS New Horizon Digicert Netscout Resources Intelligence Webinars & Events Newsletters New unit sports more qubits and is planned to be part of future fault-tolerant rig AMD: Where we're going we don't need (as much) DRAM 1 day ago AMD's Epyc X-chips are back after a three-year hiatus 2 days ago A closer look at Verano, AMD's first step toward a Zen-based superchip to rival Nvidia's Vera Rubin 2 days ago EU's €212M border IT project lands IBM and Atos in legal water 2 days ago Anthropic's super bug-finding Mythos model is going into Cisco and IBM products 2 days ago IBM has unveiled the Nighthawk r3, an upcoming next-gen quantum processor that will feature 520 qubits, as another step towards a planned fault-tolerant quantum system it hopes to launch in 2029. Big Blue's current Nighthawk r2 was only made available in September and features 120 quantum bits (qubits) capable of handling circuits using 7,500 operations. Its successor, IBM claims, will have more than four times as many qubits and execute 10,000 quantum operations to tackle larger, more complex problems while maintaining the same speed and accuracy. Nighthawk r3 is slated to arrive in 2027, when Big Blue plans to link two of the quantum processors into a single system with more than 1,000 qubits. IBM said applications increasingly require circuits executing thousands of quantum operations on approximately 100 qubits or more, speeding up collection of the millions or billions of samples needed to perform complex computations. Speed determines whether such demanding workloads can be completed in practical timeframes and at a reasonable cost. The new quantum processor will feature 10 chip-to-chip interconnects, called l-couplers, designed for linking together processors that it will use to enable a single 1,040-qubit system. This tech was tested using Nighthawk r1 processors . IBM previously outlined its goal of reaching reliable error correcting territory in 2029 with a quantum processor codenamed Starling. Now it intends for this to be the world’s first fault-tolerant quantum computer , capable of running quantum circuits comprising 100 million quantum operations on 200 logical qubits. This is an ambitious goal, considering fault-tolerant quantum technology always seems to be at least a decade away, despite numerous breakthroughs and technology introductions. However, some in the technology industry believe the odds on a working system are shortening , given the increased activity around making encryption ready with support for quantum-resistant algorithms. Then again, a professor at the University of Auckland New Zealand famously claimed last year that quantum computers hadn't so far managed to factor any number greater than 21 without cheating. IBM presented a framework for Starling in a 2025 paper outlining hardware to implement the improbably named bivariate bicycle quantum low-density parity check (qLDPC) error correction codes. These significantly reduce the number of physical qubits needed to store and process quantum information, compared to existing surface codes. Using the architecture in the paper, Big Blue intends to assemble Starling from modules that each contain a quantum memory and logical processing unit (LPU), allowing logic operations on the memory. The modules will have universal adapters letting them connect using l-couplers. IBM is also preparing the way ahead by combining its quantum processors with classical high-performance compute (HPC) systems to research better quantum error correction. Last week, Oak Ridge National Laboratory (ORNL) in the US announced such a system , combining an IBM Quantum System Two with Nighthawk r2 quantum processors and Umbra, powered by AMD 5th Gen Epyc CPUs and Instinct MI355X GPU accelerators. IBM also has a partnership with Japan's RIKEN scientific research institute under which an IBM Quantum System Two has been integrated with the Fugaku Arm-based supercomputer, once the most powerful system in the world.

events.title: Faisal Islam: Why the UK economy is surprisingly resilient
events.summary: Published 12 November 2026, 13:26 GMT The UK economy grew at its fastest rate for more than two years in the three months to September. "Top gear" and "strikingly strong" were among the descriptions of the 0.7% growth offered by the economists who track every minor murmur of Britain's economy. It is an upgrade on "solid" and "resilient", and in turn a world away from "hardest hit by the Iran War". Against the backdrop of the world's biggest disruption to energy flows, rising market borrowing costs - and the cruel summers since the pandemic - it is impressive growth. It should reset some of the swirl of self-reinforcing negativity. The UK's economic growth has averaged less than 0.1% in the four Q3s [ie July to September] since the pandemic. The average prediction just months ago for this July to September was just 0.1%. Even the UK's official forecaster the Office for Budget Responsibility (OBR) effectively pencilled in 0.3% at the Budget just 3 weeks ago. This figure has not been exceeded outside the pandemic since 2017. It puts the UK on course to be the second fastest growing economy after the US across the major G7 countries which also includes Canada, Japan, Germany, Italy and France. It is tempting to think about what the economy would have done if the Iran War hadn't happened. If interest rates had been cut instead of their recent rise. While the latest figure kills the doom, it is clearly not a boom either. Spending on AI and tech have driven the surprise upside over the year. While the AI data centre boom may at any point turn to bust, these figures suggest that spending across the economy on investing in these technologies is helping to boost growth. Consumers have been resilient, at least till the autumn, perhaps helped by better economic vibes. While there has been an understandable focus on high UK borrowing costs, another measure of the international standing of the UK economy, sterling's value, reached post Brexit referendum highs last week. Productivity and investment is also looking stronger, especially after recent revisions. Some of the most encouraging figures are in private sector business investment. I spoke to the chancellor at Nexeon in Oxfordshire, which is searching for a UK factory to manufacture its cutting edge electric vehicle battery - and British - technology. My colleagues visited British watchmakers in Maidenhead carving out a niche to take on the Swiss. However, this may well not last for the final three months of the year. Consumer confidence has already fallen as petrol and domestic energy prices start to rise again. There is a significant challenge with everyday cost-of-living pressures in the coming months. Construction and private house building remain depressed. The Iran conflict remains the big unknown and whether post the US midterm elections there could be a durable end to the conflict in the Gulf. Some oil and gas production there is starting to normalise. It could bring down petrol prices, energy bills, government borrowing costs, and mortgage costs too. Expect to see Downing Street investing heavily in "settlement of the conflict", which the chancellor told me is the "best economic policy". events.title: Washington risks misinterpreting Iran's 'peacemaker', according to analyst
events.summary: Washington is at risk of mistaking Mohsen Rezaei’s new prominence for a willingness to make concessions, Iran analyst Alex Vatanka argues. The former Revolutionary Guards commander, now secretary of Iran’s Supreme National Security Council, has received a letter from US Vice President JD Vance and is reportedly seen by American intelligence as the figure best placed to deliver a deal across Tehran’s factious institutions. But Rezaei’s comeback owes little to public legitimacy — he lost four presidential bids and his economic ideas were widely mocked — and much to a leadership vacuum left by the war and a network of IRGC loyalists built over decades, Vatanka writes for the Saudi-owned magazine Al Majalla. Rezaei has already shown the limits of his flexibility. He welcomed the letter’s tone, then insisted Washington accept Iran’s conditions first. Yesterday he went further, telling Al Mayadeen that not “ a single speck ” of enriched uranium would leave the country because Iran needs it to build nuclear-powered submarines — a rejection of the core US demand. His appointment was itself a product of hardline frustration: Rezaei was elevated by people close to Supreme Leader Mojtaba Khamenei who were unhappy with parliament speaker Mohammad Bagher Ghalibaf’s handling of the talks, a Crisis Group analyst told Radio Free Europe . — Ed Clowes

events.title: Nine Korean startups vie for a spot in Disrupt 2027’s Startup Battlefield 200 competition
events.summary: TechCrunch’s yearly Startup Battlefield 200 competition sees hundreds of companies from across the world trying every year to get a chance to pitch in front of VCs and the international tech community at the TechCrunch Disrupt conference. This week, nine early-stage South Korean startups pitched at DETO 2026 , a technology conference in Seoul, to earn a spot in next year’s Startup Battlefield 200. The startups work across the deep tech sector, including healthcare, fintech, energy, semiconductors, and AI. All nine startups are looking to enter the U.S. market as part of the broader international expansion plans. Voinosis, which develops AI to detect changes in brain health through voice analysis, won the competition. The other eight startups are listed below in alphabetical order. Voinosis is developing an AI tool that analyzes speech patterns such as pitch, pauses, rhythm, and response times to detect changes linked to brain health. Each voice check takes less than five minutes. The company says its technology has been tested in Greek, Japanese, and English, and its product doesn’t require separate training for each language. In a clinical study involving 146 participants, the startup claims its tech achieved 88% accuracy in screening for potential cognitive issues. Voinosis targets hospitals, senior living facilities, insurers, and individual consumers. It also plans to link voice checks with cognitive training, assessments, and treatment provided by healthcare professionals. The startup was founded by Grace Shin, who spent more than 25 years as an otologic surgeon. The startup is currently raising a Series A round and has already secured a South Korean pharmaceutical company as a strategic investor. Awesome Lab , based in Seoul, makes ThermoFlux, a heating system that uses water electrolysis and ionization to generate heat. The system can manage heat production for buildings, water supply, and industrial processes. The company says its technology can reduce energy consumption and carbon emissions. For its international expansion, Awesome Lab is taking a different approach in each market. In the U.S., it plans to supply core OEM modules and work with boiler, water heater, and HVAC companies on product development. Crosshub helps travelers and international visitors verify their identities and set up payment methods abroad. Its platform, IDBlock, combines identity verification and payment services using self-sovereign identity (SSI) and zero-knowledge proof. The company says its platform helps users prove their identity across borders without sharing unnecessary personal information. Crosshub is also integrating this technology with payment systems to improve access to financial services for travelers. DeepFusion AI has developed a 4D radar-based imaging system with additional sensors for autonomous mobility, robotaxi, maritime surveillance, and defense applications. The system combines RF sensors with radar and lidar to detect objects, movement, or distance without a direct line of sight. All sensors are supposedly packed into a single, customizable unit. EFLOW develops special motors that can produce more torque, or rotational force, while taking up less space for use in robots, drones, satellites, and other mobility applications. The startup also develops actuators that control how robotic joints move. Otiton Medical makes two medical devices: One specializes in measuring body temperature, while another can capture ear canal images and analyze the eardrum. The company says its AI was trained on about 55,000 images of eardrums, and the device has received medical certification in South Korea. Riibotics says it can deploy robots into warehouses within a day. Riibotics wants to reduce deployment costs for warehouses by streamlining setup, which includes infrastructure setup, warehouse mapping, system integration through custom middleware, task programming, and safety checks. Ternell , a semiconductor startup based in Ulsan, is developing a new type of memory to help AI chips use less power. Unlike conventional two-state memory, Ternell’s T-SRAM system adds a third state for more efficient data storage. Founded in 2019 by KyungRok Kim, a former Samsung Electronics engineer, Ternell reports that tests with 28-nanometer chips showed a 33% to 102% increase in memory capacity per area, and a 55% to 71% reduction in energy needed to access data, compared with conventional SRAM. Testbank is a Korean edtech startup developing Solve, an app that converts printed study materials, such as workbooks and test-prep books, into interactive digital versions. The startup uses AI to identify question and answer spaces in publishers’ PDF files while preserving the original layout. Solve lets you write answers directly on the page and be graded automatically. When you purchase through links in our articles, we may earn a small commission . events.title: UAE billionaires optimistic about foreign investment despite eight months of war
events.summary: UAE officials and billionaires had a unified message to foreign investors today: After eight months of conflict, the country has emerged as an even more attractive destination for global capital. They can be forgiven for talking up their own book, but foreign investors seem bullish too. At the Bloomberg Invest Dubai conference on Thursday, Blackstone executives said the firm had deployed more capital in the region over the past year than ever before, and opened a DIFC office for its growing private wealth business. Meanwhile, PIMCO highlighted opportunities to finance infrastructure projects. UAE Investment Minister Mohamed Hassan Alsuwaidi said the country plans to draw more foreign capital into energy, industry, infrastructure, AI, and logistics. He also pointed to shortages of offices and warehouses as opportunities. Real estate has gone through multiple boom-and-bust cycles over the past two decades, but when viewed over the long term, the trend line has clearly been up. Mohamed Alabbar, founder of Emaar Properties — which built the world’s tallest skyscraper — was characteristically upbeat. The developer recently unveiled a $3.3 billion business district at Dubai Creek Harbour, with 300,000 square meters of commercial space. And while the war has taken a toll on its hotel business, Emaar’s hospitality unit was able to boost profits last quarter by cutting costs. Alabbar acknowledged rising construction costs, but dismissed concerns that the property market was set for a sharp decline. Though the eight-month Iran conflict was a test, “I would say that if there was a bubble, it would have burst.” — Mohammed Sergie

events.title: Fallout from Nvidia CEO’s likely ouster could slow Gulf AI buildout
events.summary: The fallout from Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang’s likely ouster will reach the Gulf, where ambitious AI buildouts depend on advanced US chips. Fear over China’s access to American technology through intermediaries has forced local AI champions like PIF-owned HUMAIN and Abu Dhabi-backed G42 to fight hard for chip access. Huang’s affair with a woman US intelligence officials allege is a Chinese spy will no doubt sharpen that scrutiny. Lawmakers are already pushing for new curbs on chip diversion, a move that could threaten the speed of development here. A friend-of-the-Gulf in Washington is also under pressure as Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick, who greenlit the supply of tens of thousands of advanced GPUs to Saudi Arabia and the UAE, faces allegations that he stalled action against the Singapore firm tied up in the Huang scandal; Commerce denies the account. Still, the region’s relationship with the world’s largest chipmaker has long been one of customer and vendor: Great fortunes are tied to Nvidia, but the loss of the company’s leader shouldn’t undermine its ability to produce silicon. The question for the Gulf is, as it’s always been, about access. Dubai real estate tycoon Hussain Sajwani — who is building data centers around the world and expects his early investments in Anthropic, OpenAI, and SpaceX will yield a “few billion dollars of profit” — said at the Bloomberg Invest conference in Dubai that “Nvidia is the most important company today in the world. It is by far. It has a genius CEO … I think if he’s forced to depart, it will be a big loss for the whole. This guy has done a great job.” — Kelsey Warner

events.title: Saudi oil production rebounds to near prewar levels
events.summary: Saudi oil production rebounded in October, driving up overall output by OPEC members to near prewar levels for the first time and helping keep down crude prices even as Iranian attacks in the Strait of Hormuz have picked up. OPEC production rose by 1.97 million barrels a day, the majority of which was accounted for by higher Saudi output, according to the latest data from the cartel. Aramco CEO Amin Nasser said last week that the company aimed to “maximize production” in the fourth quarter, with the expectation that demand will be bolstered by efforts to replenish global oil inventories drained during the initial months of the Iran war. US military escorts, ship-to-ship transfers, and pipelines to ports away from the Strait of Hormuz have all helped restore output, although Saudi Arabia has stepped up shipments through its eastern ports as Houthi militias in Yemen threaten the Bab el-Mandeb strait. Iraq and UAE output also hit fresh highs for the year. Boosting oil flows is essential for Gulf states as they look to restore public finances bruised by the war and higher spending on new trade routes and defense. In contrast, Iranian production was almost half of prewar levels, according to OPEC. — Matthew Martin

events.title: AI helped UK defy expectations – but will economy’s resilience fizzle out?
events.summary: Despite John Healey’s defiance, the economy faces threats from a tech slowdown and energy bills this winter AI helps UK economy grow at fastest pace for more than two years The forecasters were clear when John Healey became chancellor in July: Britain’s resilience to the war in the Middle East would not last. The global economic headwinds were too strong, inflation was beginning to rise and growth would slow to a trickle. Four months into the job, the economy is continuing to defy expectations after growing by 0.7% in the third quarter – the fastest expansion in two and a half years. It puts the UK on course to be the second-fastest growing G7 economy this year. On his first day in Downing Street the memo from the Treasury showed the most optimistic City analyst expected 0.3% quarterly growth. Most had pencilled in a figure close to zero. Some were warning that the UK could edge towards a recession. Despite the gloomy outlook households have continued to spend and business investment has powered ahead, driven by the rollout of AI. Underneath the bonnet, growth is being spearheaded by IT and professional services – together contributing about half of the rise in activity. As the central sectors in the AI boom, that is hardly surprising – with analysts at ING suggesting the strength in IT was “very clearly a datacentre story” thanks to the UK’s status as a leading destination in Europe for investment. Overall, Deutsche Bank estimates that AI-related spending has added about 0.3% to 0.4% to GDP growth this year. It is clear to see why Healey is keen to build on the groundwork laid by his immediate predecessor, Rachel Reeves, to harness AI amid government efforts to court global business investment. Meanwhile, household consumption is up by 1.6% so far this year – helped by spending over the warm summer months even as consumers faced a living standards squeeze because the Iran war fuelled a surge in petrol and diesel prices. However, the fear is that the UK’s initial resilience to the global economic storm emanating from the Middle East will soon fizzle out. Both of Britain’s recent growth engines face a tougher period ahead. After the US midterm elections and revelations at the chipmaker Nvidia , the outlook for the AI investment boom is less certain. Financial markets have been rocked in recent weeks amid fears that a bubble in AI stocks could be about to burst . A slowdown in technology investment could hit the UK. Still, the hope is that swelling demand for AI will not evaporate overnight. Get set for the working day – we'll point you to all the business news and analysis you need every morning For households, however, a tough winter lies ahead. Energy bills are poised to increase by about a quarter in January, with the average annual household gas and electricity bill expected to climb to more than £2,000. Analysts say it is hard to see how consumer spending would not come under greater pressure in the new year. In the latest data there were some early warning signs: retail sales and consumer discretionary spending fell in September. Real wage growth is cooling and the headline inflation rate is on track to reach a fresh peak of close to 5% next year. With growth proving resilient, the Bank of England will feel emboldened to raise interest rates to combat imported inflation. City investors expect at least two more quarter-point increases to 4.5% before the end of next year. That will hit the brakes on the economy and add to the cost of living squeeze. At last month’s budget Healey struck a defiant tone by arguing that the UK could continue to defy forecasters expectations. That task, however, is becoming increasingly tough.

events.title: Hackers exploiting ScreenConnect plugin flaw to spread malware across hundreds of PCs
events.summary: Hackers have used a dodgy third-party ScreenConnect extension to push malware onto at least 288 machines across 48 organizations, prompting ConnectWise to disable a handful of plugins in hundreds of customer environments. Security outfit Huntress first raised the alarm in a Reddit post on Wednesday, warning of an active campaign targeting cloud-hosted ScreenConnect instances. At the time, its security operations center was tracking six compromised managed service providers (MSPs) and more than 286 affected endpoints, with the numbers still climbing. ConnectWise acquired popular remote supporttool ScreenConnect in February, 2015. Huntress spotted the attacks at around 1747 UTC, when someone began using ScreenConnect's remote command feature to install rogue clients on machines managed by multiple IT service providers. All 288 endpoints were hit within 90 minutes, with roughly a third compromised in the first ten minutes. Huntress suspects more MSPs may have been compromised, as the attackers appeared to be numbering their victims sequentially, with the numbers suggesting earlier attacks that it hadn't detected. The attackers deployed a 16-file malware toolkit dubbed SCKit, which installs a separate ScreenConnect client to maintain remote access even if the legitimate connection is shut down. It also contains code designed to spread the infection to IT technicians and potentially other customers under their control. Huntress has since traced the activity to a possible authentication weakness in RMM+, a third-party extension that lets other management tools issue commands through ScreenConnect without technicians using its console. Versions 1.0.31 and 1.0.32 of the extension contain a flaw that means installations without a configured access key will accept a blank one. Because RMM+ operates independently of ScreenConnect's normal user accounts and authentication controls, an attacker could potentially execute commands without defeating MFA. Huntress said the findings matched what its investigators saw during the attacks, with commands reaching machines across several ScreenConnect installations despite no corresponding login activity. The researchers also confirmed that the attacks affected ScreenConnect versions 26.6.6.9747 and 26.7.6.9783, meaning administrators running the latest releases weren't necessarily safe. ConnectWise has acknowledged that third-party extensions may have been involved but has stopped short of confirming how the attackers initially gained access. In a security advisory , the company said it was investigating unauthorized access to certain partner environments and had identified approximately 400 installations containing at least one extension from the RMM+ family. It has disabled five extensions, including RMM+, RMM Plus, and Labtech Plus, wherever it can do so remotely, and urged customers running their own ScreenConnect servers to follow suit. ConnectWise stressed that the 400 environments were identified because they had the extensions installed, not because they were necessarily compromised. The company said: "At this time, we have found no evidence of a compromise of ConnectWise infrastructure or a vulnerability in ScreenConnect itself." There's another nasty trick buried in SCKit. According to Huntress, the malware is designed to turn an infected computer into a trap for the technician sent to investigate it. If the technician connects through ScreenConnect, the toolkit attempts to transfer malware back to their workstation, steal authentication cookies, and use their access to infect other machines. That could give attackers a route from one compromised customer into others managed by the same IT provider. However, Huntress says it has yet to see that part of the attack succeed. "We have not observed that method to spread work successfully. The console-takeover attempt failed in every recovered host log we have checked so far," the researchers wrote. Huntress also suspects that some of the malware's C# code was generated using an LLM, pointing to unusually detailed comments explaining what the code is supposed to do. Apparently, even malware authors appreciate a little help with their homework. Both Huntress and ConnectWise are urging administrators not to investigate suspected infections by remotely connecting through ScreenConnect, since doing so could put the technician's own machine at risk. Administrators are being advised to use other security tools to investigate affected machines, look for rogue ScreenConnect clients, and check what commands have been run. Any malware left behind will also need to be removed before the machines are brought back online. Huntress warned on Reddit that some machines were becoming reinfected within minutes of being taken out of isolation because the malware had not been properly removed. Simply disabling the vulnerable extensions won't necessarily undo the damage, either. As ConnectWise warns, "Disabling extensions and resetting credentials alone may not remove unauthorized software, persistence mechanisms, or access already established on endpoints." And with the attackers already able to install their own remote access software, kicking them out could prove considerably harder than closing the door they came through. ®

events.title: Metro Bank up for sale, with billionaire investor in line for £420m windfall
events.summary: Metro Bank is putting itself up for sale three years after its near-collapse, in a move that could hand a £420m windfall to its Colombian billionaire investor, Jaime Gilinski Bacal. Metro Bank made the rare decision to publicly announce it was open to bids on Thursday, paving the way for a wider pool of suitors. The announcement pushed the share price up by 7% by mid-morning, valuing the bank at about £1.3bn. If successful, the sale would allow Gilinski Bacal a chance to sell out of the bank he helped save from near-failure in late 2023. The 68-year-old banking tycoon, who took a seat on Metro’s board after securing a 53% stake three years ago, has already seen a sixfold increase in the value of his shares, which he bought for just 30p each as part of a wider rescue deal. That means that at Thursday’s 190p share price, his British Virgin Island-based vehicle Spaldy Investments, could cash out with a £427m windfall. It would mark the latest turnaround success for the billionaire, who made his fortune snapping up assets of struggling lenders on the cheap, before overhauling their operations and selling them on for a big profit. Gilinski Bacal is one of the wealthiest people in Latin America, worth about $16.9bn (£12.7bn), according to Forbes. Metro Bank has been focused on a turnaround plan – which has involved lending more heavily to businesses and people with more erratic incomes – since it was forced into the £925m rescue deal in 2023. Metro was the first high street bank to open in the UK in more than 100 years when it was launched by another billionaire, the US businessman Vernon Hill, in 2010. It attracted a wave of customers, and offered dog-friendly branches with seven-day openings. However, it struggled after a major accounting blunder in 2019 that prompted investors to dump their shares and fearful customers to pull their cash. It led to the resignation of top executives, as well as the then chair, Hill, who was well-known for having his yorkshire terrier Sir Duffy (and later Sir Duffy II) in tow. Metro’s shares took another dive in 2023. That year, it emerged that the bank would need more cash from investors, having failed to convince regulators that it could be trusted to assess its own risks. Get set for the working day – we'll point you to all the business news and analysis you need every morning The lender finally secured a rescue, which was brokered in part by UK regulators at the Bank of England, in 2023. It has since embarked on the turnaround plan, which has increased its profits but came at a cost for staff and customers. Metro’s chief executive, Daniel Frumkin, slashed more than 1,000 jobs in spring 2024 and decided to close branches on Sundays. The bank said on Thursday that a sale was just one of the options on the table and that it would still be able to go it alone if no suitable bidder came through. Metro’s board “unanimously believes that evaluating potential interest in the company” through a potential sale “will maximise the value creation opportunities available to shareholders and deliver benefits for all stakeholders”, the bank said.

events.title: Emaar’s mall footfall down 10 per cent due to Iran war, says Alabbar
events.summary: Footfall and retail sales at Emaar’s malls have fallen by about 10 per cent and hotel occupancy has dropped sharply as the Iran war weighs on tourism and consumer spending in Dubai, Emaar founder Mohamed Alabbar said on Thursday. “In our mall business, we are 10 per cent less in traffic. We were growing 10 per cent per year for the last five years,” Mr Alabbar told the Bloomberg Invest event in Dubai. He did not specify which malls were affected or over what period. He also said retail was down about 10 per cent after growing by a similar percentage annually in recent years. The hospitality business was affected too, with occupancy levels falling to about 65 per cent from 80 per cent, he added. The war, which started in late February with attacks by the US and Israel on Iran, has affected sectors in the UAE including property, tourism and aviation. The countries have yet to reach an agreement to end the war, now in its ninth month. However, US President Donald Trump has hinted that he is not planning to resume the bombing campaign as he faces calls to wind down the conflict after his party's defeat in last week's midterm elections. Mr Alabbar said the company was not slowing down its development activity, with construction continuing and projects being delivered ahead of time. “Development contractors are moving on time … material coming in … cost increasing about 5 per cent, which is OK,” he said. However, the company is “holding back” on tendering a big tower until the regional situation cools down. He did not provide further details on the new project. In June, Emaar Properties announced an “extraordinary” Dh200 billion ($55 billion) megaproject in Dubai , set to house nearly 150,000 people. The master plan, spread across more than 4.5 million square metres, is to feature residential towers, villas and mansions, Grade-A commercial offices, shops, luxury hospitality and other amenities. “It will all depend on what happens between Donald Trump and the Iranian leadership. That's really the key to everything, and [if] that happens in one month, I think the market will take 12 months, and then [it] will be in good shape,” Mr Alabbar said. He is also betting big on India, which he said “will be a major [market] for us” in the next five years as part of the company's global expansion plans. Emaar already has a presence in the country with projects in Gurugram, Mohali and other cities. The company will continue to grow in the Middle East, including the UAE, Egypt and Syria. Mr Alabbar’s developer Eagle Hills is working on two major projects in Syria, including a residential and tourism development, as part of a framework agreement the company signed with the Syrian government in October. Data centres and Anthropic investment Damac Properties founder and chairman Hussain Sajwani also spoke during the Bloomberg Invest event, outlining global expansion plans of the company. Damac is looking to expand in the UK and Australia with new data centre projects, after announcing $20 billion of investment in US data centres last year. The company is present in 14 countries and “we are in serious negotiations in the UK for a big parcel of land. We are in serious negotiation in Australia for a big parcel of land”, Mr Sajwani said. The company hopes to reach 10 gigawatts of capacity by the end of next year. “Our focus is on large data centres, which are 100MW and above. We go into where the large populations are, so the US, the EU and Asia.” The company also has investments in AI firm Anthropic and is making a lot of money from them, he said. “What I have made in 30 years [since starting his business], I made in Anthropic in less than two years. At [an] $18 billion valuation, it is going public at $1.4 trillion.” Last week, Anthropic reported revenue of nearly $17 billion in the period ending September 30, as investors brace for its potentially record-breaking IPO . The maker of Claude , a family of large language models and an AI chatbot, reported $33.24 billion in revenue for the nine months ending on September 30. “Between only three companies, OpenAI, SpaceX and Anthropic, we're making [a] few billion dollars a month.” Mr Sajwani also spoke about Nvidia and its chief executive Jensen Huang, who is embroiled in controversy over alleged extramarital affairs. “If he is forced to depart, it will be [a] big loss for the world, not for America, for the world. This guy has done a great job.”
