events.title: Nvidia board prepares to oust CEO, name interim chief
events.summary: The Scoop Some members of Nvidia’s board favor appointing Chief Financial Officer Colette Kress as interim CEO at the beleaguered chipmaker if CEO and founder Jensen Huang is ousted, according to people familiar with the matter. The board met on Wednesday evening, though it has not yet announced its decision. Nvidia’s board has debated whether, as part of its potential replacement of Huang, to introduce a chief operating officer to serve alongside the interim chief executive, some of the people said. Semafor earlier confirmed that Nvidia’s board is preparing to oust Huang as soon as Wednesday, after media reports detailed that he had a second extramarital affair. The Nvidia board briefed the White House on its planned meeting, according to a senior administration official. Nvidia has tapped an outside search firm to find the company’s next CEO, Bloomberg reported. One person being considered for the top job is Apple hardware chief Johny Srouji, who was among the executives considered for Intel CEO in 2019, according to another person familiar with the matter. Whirlwind Saga Nvidia’s stock fell more than 8% in after-hours trading, hitting a 52-week low. Spokespeople for the company didn’t immediately provide a comment. Huang’s firing would cap a whirlwind saga that’s seen the global frontman for the AI boom admit to an affair with a suspected Chinese spy. The $4 trillion company’s long-tenured board announced a Wachtell Lipton-led probe into whether Huang may have divulged corporate secrets or endangered US national security. In addition to providing many of the most advanced chips for hyperscalers, Nvidia has entered into billions of dollars worth of financing deals underwriting the AI buildout. Democrats Move In Sens. Chris Coons, D-Del., and Elizabeth Warren, D-Mass., sent a letter to members of President Donald Trump’s Cabinet on Wednesday asking them to preserve documents related to Nvidia’s chip exports to China or entities that could divert such chips to the country. They also asked Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick, Secretary of State Marco Rubio, and White House chief of staff Stephen Miller to preserve documents and communications concerning Huang and the suspected Chinese operative he had an affair with, as well as the correspondence between Huang and Trump. “This incident raises significant concerns about the federal government’s ability to effectively enforce our export controls and protect our national security,” the senators wrote in the letter . “Reports suggest that officials within the government — including at the White House, State Department, and Commerce Department — were aware of concerns about NVIDIA, its relationship with Megaspeed, and the suspected Chinese intelligence operation, yet did not move to block the continued flow of advanced AI chips.”

events.title: The latest FreeBSD report is here, and the AI debate is ongoing
events.summary: The FreeBSD project's status team has published FreeBSD's third status report of 2026, showing plenty of ambitious work underway and a community still undecided on how to treat code from AI coding assistants. The FreeBSD Status Report Third Quarter 2026 is a substantial document, with 51 entries from five teams covering 16 projects, plus six other sections with more detailed reports. There are updates on the progress of the Sylve project, which is an attempt to bring a smooth polished GUI for managing FreeBSD virtualization hosts – something akin to Proxmox for FreeBSD. We mentioned this when we looked at the new Daemonarchy project last month. Another covers the new AppJail effort – a containerized app distribution system for FreeBSD, including for GUI apps, which aims for something broadly comparable to Snap, Flatpak and AppImage on Linux. In other words, interesting and quite radical stuff is happening in the FreeBSD space. What this particular LLM-skeptical vulture was most interested to see, though, was an update on the internal discussion about how to handle code generated by AI coding assistants in the project. We first reported on this vexed subject back in September 2025 and no final answer has yet been published. NetBSD banned AI-generated code in 2024 and although the bot-boosters say this will doom it to irrelevance, as we reported last month, the project is thriving . Also back in October, we looked at OpenBSD 8.0 , whose launch materials are full of mockery for AI users. Under the FreeBSD Core Team section , there is a subsection headed "FreeBSD Developer AI survey." The survey was created by Baptiste Daroussin, and received 140 responses. Although the percentages show that there is some resistance to AI, there are hints here as to why it’s taking so long. Some project committers are against it, yet many more are proponents. Since there are only seven bullet points, we thought we would quote them in full: Policy: 88 percent want the Project to adopt a policy, either a formal, written policy (49 percent ) or light guidance and best practices (39 percent ). Six percent said that AI should be explicitly discouraged, and three percent that the existing contribution rules are sufficient. AI-assisted code: 35 percent said it must be disclosed, 25 percent that it must be reviewed more strictly than human code, 22 percent that it should be treated like any other contribution, and 16 percent that it should be rejected outright. Safeguards: mandatory human review (78 percent ) and mandatory disclosure (69 percent ) were requested most often, followed by provenance or licensing documentation (47 percent ) and mandatory testing (39 percent ). Disclosure: 84 percent want AI use disclosed, either always (48 percent ) or when its involvement is significant (36 percent ). 79 percent want AI-assisted commits marked in the commit log, and 56 percent prefer a tag that names the tool. Concerns: the main concerns about quality are correctness and subtle bugs (39 percent , licensing and provenance (26 percent ), and maintainability (21 percent ). 75 percent are somewhat or very concerned about copyright and licensing. Principles: accountability, meaning that a human remains responsible (91 percent ), and transparency (78 percent ) were selected most often, and preserving code quality was the top-ranked goal for a policy. Other uses: 65 percent would allow AI-generated documentation with human review. 54 percent would allow AI tools on Project infrastructure, most of them with restrictions, and 29 percent would not. Only six percent for explicit discouragement, 16 percent for outright rejection, and 35 percent against LLM-generated documentation. This plus the usual sort of calls for responsible use and disclosure, concerns about copyright issues, and so on. The Reg is strongly reminded of the Debian developer poll we reported on in August . This had no fewer than four slightly different AI-refusal options out of eight, and despite the Condorcet voting method it uses, the result was giving permission to use bots . With such relatively weak opposition, we suspect that FreeBSD will go the same way as Debian: tell developers to be careful, but allow bot usage, resulting in LLM-extruded code being committed into the project. ®

events.title: UAE has come out of the war 'exceptionally well', investment minister says
events.summary: The UAE has come out of the war “exceptionally well” and the continued economic momentum despite uncertainty is driving the government to open new sectors for foreign investment, a senior official has said. “I think we have to show investors the positive side of this, which is there is opportunity in every crisis, and [we are looking into] how do we present those opportunities to investors, how do we open up sectors that previously weren't open to investors, especially around infrastructure projects,” Mohamed Alsuwaidi, Minister of Investment, told Bloomberg Invest on Thursday. The UAE is investing heavily in infrastructure with new pipelines and ports to bypass the Strait of Hormuz. It is also looking to expand port capacity on its eastern coast, including at Fujairah, projects that are expected to cost billions of dollars. The scale of the financing needs was underlined by First Abu Dhabi Bank's plan to raise as much as Dh15 billion ($4 billion) in the country’s largest rights issue, which will help support the country’s infrastructure expansion and diversification beyond oil. “I don't see a slowdown in what we're doing. We see more opportunities for investors, bigger projects coming to life,” Mr Alsuwaidi said. “AI is booming, logistics is booming, air freight is becoming a bigger business. Multiple sectors are opening up, and we need to help our investors see that and follow those trends.” The UAE continues to grow despite the impact of the Iran war. The country was attacked with hundreds of missiles and drones after the conflict broke out in late February, with damage to civilian infrastructure and energy sites. The UAE's real gross domestic product grew 0.4 per cent annually to Dh961.9 billion in the first half of the year, driven by non-oil business activity, despite the war's impact . Foreign direct investment into the UAE rose by about 6 per cent last year to a record $48.24 billion, the ninth highest total in the world, according to UN Conference on Trade and Development data. The Emirates was also the top recipient of FDI in the Middle East, ahead of Saudi Arabia, which ranked 13th, Unctad said in its World Investment Conference 2026 report released in July. There is no dearth of capital or talent in the country and the government is moving towards new capital models to fund the massive infrastructure needs, Mr Alsuwaidi said. “I don't see a challenge in the UAE on the funding front. I see opportunity to attract third-party capital in ways we haven't in the past,” he said. “More and more projects around energy, around industries, around infrastructure in general, are being open to the public through either public-private participation, but also through partnerships with governments or local governments, but also privatisation of certain government assets.” There's also a high demand in the housing market because people are interested in coming to the UAE, and “we can't keep up with the demand, so we keep building”. Some parts of the property market, particularly offices and warehouses, were facing shortages, he added.

events.title: Fertiglobe boosts UAE exports to 95% of production but logistics costs hit profit
events.summary: Fertiglobe, the world’s largest seaborne exporter of urea and ammonia, said it has restored UAE exports to 95 per cent of production in the third quarter, despite continuing disruption at the Strait of Hormuz . That is up from 56 per cent in the second quarter, it said in a statement on Thursday to the Abu Dhabi Securities Exchange, where its shares trade. Reaching that figure involved extensive efforts by Fertiglobe's production and supply-chain teams as well as working with majority shareholders XRG and Adnoc, and even the government, Ahmed El Hoshy, chief executive of Fertiglobe, told The National , without disclosing the specifics on how it was achieved. The company, however, said UAE exports were supported by active inventory, logistics management and a “focused commercial approach”. The effective closure of Hormuz, through which about one third of global seaborne fertiliser passed before the Iran war began on February 28, has significantly affected the supply chain. While Fertiglobe has been transporting the stocks it had stored during the peak of the war, “we still have inventory left over, so I'd even like to export more than we've produced”, Mr El Hoshy said. However, higher freight and logistical costs have affected earnings. Net profit attributable to the owners of the company for the third quarter dropped by 90 per cent to $22.7 million. Revenue for the period, however, rose by 19 per cent to $904.5 million, driven by higher ammonia prices and sales volumes. Along with the higher logistics costs, “sometimes the logistics to get product out also made it a little bit challenging to know the timing of exports”, Mr El Hoshy said. The company also carried out a turnaround at its EBIC plant in Egypt, and during that process had to use inventories to continue selling products. “When you use inventory to sell in Q3 instead of actual production, you end up getting charged with the fixed cost for the product … [and] you end up paying a larger amount,” he said. And while ammonia prices were higher, the lower cost of urea also brought down margins, he added. Urea, the most commonly used chemical for fertiliser, recorded a significant price increase to about $720 a tonne in mid-April from about $465 a tonne on the eve of the war, according to Trading Economics. Prices have now cooled to about $430 a tonne. Fertiglobe is the largest producer of nitrogen fertilisers in the region, with a production capacity about of 6.6 million tonnes of urea and ammonia through subsidiaries in the UAE, Egypt and Algeria. Last year, it also established Fertiglobe Australia to operate assets it acquired from Chinese-based company Wengfu. Gas price impact While Fertiglobe uses long-term contracts for gas that are not linked to European gas prices, the benchmark acts as a bellwether for the industry, Mr El Hoshy said. High European gas prices have caused about 35 per cent of European ammonia capacity to remain offline, he said. Dutch front-month futures, which tracks European gas prices, was at about €90 ($100) per megawatt-hour on Thursday, more than double annually. “There's 19 million tonnes of ammonia capacity that sits in Europe today,” Mr El Hoshy said. “Their cash cost today to produce ammonia is $1,000 a tonne, and the price that is in Europe today is $750 a tonne. So there's some mismatch. Either their cost needs to come down, or the price of ammonia needs to go up to justify them restarting their plant.” Given the current situation and how low the inventories are, “we continue to be relatively constructive on the outlook for the market for ammonia and urea because the Europeans are now operating at a rate where they're not able to make money unless the price of ammonia goes up”, he said. Robots cleaning up Fertiglobe, which has implemented its initial $55 million cost optimisation target, has launched FIT3, a new programme aimed at achieving a further $30 million of annual non-gas cost savings by the end of 2028. “Together with maintenance capex normalising from 2027, this will strengthen our competitiveness and cash generation through the cycle,” the company said. The turnaround programme in Egypt and the UAE is expected to deliver strong results, Mr El Hoshy said. At the EBIC plant, production has increased by more than 20 per cent on a run rate basis. Outside of regular maintenance, the programme in Egypt used artificial intelligence to go through data from every single interruption the plant has had since it started in 2009 and it came up with a list of things needed to be done. “We discovered things and took care of it. We also used robotics for the first time to clean areas in the plant that humans couldn't get to, never been touched in 17 years, and that has allowed us to remove dust and debris,” Mr El Hoshy said. “Since we started up in September for our plant in Egypt, we have achieved rates not achieved ever in these plants, so record daily production.” Outlook The company is preparing for different scenarios and aiming to see how it can reduce costs when faced with issues such as higher temporary logistics costs. “What we've done internally is looked at … how we procure things, how we do things logistically, how we load product, where it's basically across all functional groups, [we are looking for] ways that we can reduce costs using simplified processes,” he said. Looking ahead, if the war continues, “I still think that we're in a very tough position having the Strait of Hormuz compromised for exports of sulphur, which is a which is a very important input for fertiliser, urea, ammonia and natural gas”, Mr El Hoshy added. The products must get to global markets because it's in a “very vulnerable position”. Any impact will be felt mainly in low to medium-income countries in terms of not being able to secure the adequate fertilisers they need to increase the crop yields to feed their populations, he said.

events.title: Burberry returns to profit as sales soar, from £85 socks to £9,000 coats
events.summary: CEO says ‘democratic approach’ has helped brand outperform tough market, with big rises in China and US Burberry has returned to profit as its back-to-basics strategy drove strong sales of the British brand’s coats, jackets and handbags over the summer. Joshua Schulman, the chief executive, said the luxury brand had outperformed a “challenging luxury market” to achieve sales growth of 6%, helped by strong online and wholesale sales particularly in China and the US. “Our strategy is working,” he said. Burberry said it made a pre-tax profit of £19m in the six months to 26 September after a loss of £48m a year before, as sales rose to £1.1bn. Sales rose 15% in China and 14% in the Americas but fell 1% in the Europe and Middle East region, partly due to the Iran war. Schulman said Burberry’s focus on a “pyramid of pricing” ranging from more “affordable” scarves, starting from £195, and cotton-cashmere socks from £85, to its top-tier bags and coats, which can cost more than £9,000 for a leather version, had helped it achieve growth despite a tough market. Wealthy shoppers around the world are travelling less and being more cautious about spending, hitting luxury brand sales globally. Sales of lightweight jackets and “tropical” gaberdine raincoats as well as its Cotswold range of leather bags and accessories featuring the brand’s famous check had proved popular. Schulman said: “Luxury customers around the world are experiencing some fatigue with exorbitant pricing and in this context our strategy of having great value for money is resonating strongly with Chinese customers.” “Burberry has always had a somewhat more democratic approach than some of our European peers and has a universal appeal,” he added. Schulman said the brand had spent the last two years of its Burberry Forward strategy returning to its historical position at the “sweet spot in the luxury market”. He said investment in locally relevant marketing, such as special product for China’s Valentine’s Day celebrations this spring and for the upcoming lunar new year, were also helping drive sales. “It is no secret global tourism is down but the local customer has been spending in their respective regions,” Schulman said. “This is a trend we have been seeing all year long.” While people were spending less as tourists which was hitting sales in discount outlets, Schulman said local spending was holding up in the brand’s flagship city centre stores including in London. He said that while “nobody has a crystal ball” about whether customers would begin spending more freely, history suggested “this is a very cyclical business”.

events.title: Bracing for Nvidia's impact
events.summary: Data: FactSet; Chart: Matt Phillips/Axios Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang's apparent from grace is a shock to a company at the core of the U.S. markets and the AI ecosystem that he did much to create. Why it matters: CEO scandals happen at companies. Their stocks fall. But there is no other company quite like Nvidia. Its size, financial resources and strategic position in the AI boom have made both the chipmaker and Huang, personally, pillars of the industry that has come to drive both the stock market and the economy. Catch up quick: Following revelations this week that Huang had admitted to an extramarital affair with a woman believed by the U.S. government to be a Chinese intelligence asset, the New York Times reported Wednesday evening that Huang also had a romantic relationship with an Nvidia executive who reports to him. The Wall Street Journal and other outlets are reporting that the company's board of directors was preparing to oust Huang. Nvidia shares plunged in the after-hours trading session. Context: The uncertainty surrounding Huang's position comes as the AI trade is going through one of the crises of investor confidence that have periodically hammered AI shares in recent years. The concern this time centers on the ability of the AI build-out to continue, as rising interest rates and a saturated market curtail the sale of bonds to pay for data centers. Chip makers like Nvidia have been particularly hard hit by this recent AI slump. Its shares were down roughly 30% from their recent high through Wednesday's close, vaporizing nearly $1.59 trillion in shareholder wealth. There have been market drawdowns around AI before, says Eric Sheridan, a research analyst at Goldman Sachs, in a big new report on the investment cycle. "The stakes are undoubtedly higher now as we're further along in the cycle and the dollars being spent have grown considerably, which may be adding to investor skittishness." Stunning stat: Since the end of last week, the company lost over $600 billion in market value through Wednesday's after market session. Zoom out: Those losses will touch a lot of portfolios. With a market capitalization of roughly $4.18 trillion — through Wednesday's close — Nvidia is the world's second-largest publicly traded company, behind Apple, giving it significant sway in market capitalization-weighted indexes, such as the S&P 500 and the Nasdaq 100. Yes, but: If anything, a focus on Nvidia's massive size obscures how important the company is. It dominates the market for the graphics processing units, or GPUs, that are the costliest input into AI data centers — about 75% of a data center's total cost, per Goldman. It also finances and backstops significant chunks of AI computing power. That means Nvidia is bankrolling a small army of AI firms: AI coding companies, data center operators, neoclouds. For example: Nvidia has put more than $2 billion into CoreWeave, the troubled neocloud that's seen its borrowing costs soar in recent weeks. It has equity stakes in Anthropic and OpenAI. Follow the money: Such was Nvidia's — and Huang's — stature in the tech world that in recent years, the mere mention of a company by the Nvidia CEO could create big market winners and losers . In June, for example, positive comments from Huang about Marvell Technology sent the company's stock soaring nearly 33% in a single day. State of play: Now, it's Nvidia shares that might need words of encouragement. On Wednesday the stock received a downgrade to "market perform" from "outperform" from Bernstein Research. "We admit to struggling mightily with this call, and can sympathize with the case to buy the dip," Bernstein's analysts wrote. "But our gut tells us that we probably haven't yet fully probed the depths of what might be found here; we've had enough, and prefer to watch from the sidelines." Morgan Stanley also removed the company from its list of "top picks" earlier in the day, after the stock had declined more than 25% since it was named top pick last month. What's next: Whatever comes next for Nvidia, the company is likely to be in an extended period of strategic paralysis. "Decisions about acquisitions or investments or product roadmaps, those are the kinds of things that will now have to be paused, if — again — if this happens, all these things are going to have to pause," Gil Luria, an analyst covering Nvidia for the brokerage firm D.A. Davidson, tells Axios. "So it just slows the company down when it can't make the most important, biggest decisions." The big picture: Huang has presided over one of the most remarkable explosions of wealth creation in market history. From the closing price on its first day of trading, Nvidia's total compound return with dividend reinvestment is 462,906%, according to FactSet. He has been at the helm of the company since he co-founded it in 1993. The bottom line: But depending on how the situation plays out, shareholders may be about to find out what an Nvidia without its charismatic leader looks like.

events.title: UK appoints climate security envoy as Thunberg criticizes COP31 leaders
events.summary: The United Kingdom has appointed a special envoy to address climate change security threats ANTALYA, Turkey -- The United Kingdom on Thursday announced the appointment of a special envoy to tackle security threats from climate change while small island leaders called for urgent action, describing planet heating as a life-or-death issue for their people at the climate talks in the Turkish resort town of Antalya. Alix Sebastien Pillay, the vice president of Seychelles, a 115-island archipelago in the Indian Ocean, said his country's very survival is at stake. “It is time to move past the talking,” Pillay said. “For Seychelles, climate action is not simply an environmental priority.” Pillay was speaking on the second day of the leaders' summit at the U.N. climate talks, where government leaders addressed the state of a warming world and what they plan to do about it. While the entire globe is threatened by souped-up storms, hotter heat waves, worsening droughts and floods, island nations are among the hardest hit by climate change as they also have to deal with rising seas swallowing up their land. Pillay said Seychelles is experiencing millions of dollars of damage as a result of storms and floods, despite contributing little to increased global warming. He said a U.N. fund created for compensating for climate-related loss and damage needs to be urgently strengthened. “Climate recovery must not come at the expense of our development or push vulnerable nations further into unsustainable debt.” Speaking at the talks, Dalton Tagelagi, prime minister of the small Pacific Island of Niue, said the El Niño conditions which have driven up global temperatures are a warning of what might happen if planet heating is not controlled. “Sea temperatures in the central Pacific are more than three degrees above normal. It is a warning of what is coming if we do not cut emissions now," Tagelagi said. The comment came as a report said the world has failed to slow global warming trends in the past five years because plans weren’t realized and efforts that would have helped were canceled out. “Aggregated climate action has now essentially stalled for five consecutive years with positive and negative actions canceling each other out,” the independent Climate Action Tracker said in its report. The first five years after the 2015 Paris Agreement, the world did so much that it trimmed an entire degree Celsius (1.8 degrees Fahrenheit) from warming projections, but nothing has changed since, the report said. Climate change is caused mainly by the release of greenhouse gases, which happens when fuels like gas, oil and coal are burned. Confronting climate change means finding ways to drastically cut the amount of emissions put into the atmosphere each year. Countries establish plans to reduce emissions, called nationally determined contributions. The speed of reductions and ways to achieve them are different by country. Because collective efforts of countries haven't significantly reduced global emissions, the world is now “headed toward an irrecoverable overshoot of 1.5 degrees Celsius” (2.7 degrees Fahrenheit) above pre-industrial temperatures, which is the warming threshold the world adopted during the Paris Agreement, according to the report. The report said if the nations of the world fulfill all their climate promises — which is a big if — the globe will end the century 2.6 degrees Celsius (4.7 degrees Fahrenheit) warmer than preindustrial times. On Thursday, British Prime Minister Andy Burnham announced the appointment of a special representative to deal with security risks from the climate crisis, one of the first such appointments anywhere in the world. “Climate is a national security issue,” Burnham said at the summit. “The climate crisis is not a distant threat. It is upon us all now devastating lives and livelihoods everywhere." He said Britain would place climate resilience high on the agenda when it assumes the G20 presidency next year. Climate activists said, however, that Burnham’s policies do not fully align with the sense of urgency he expressed in his speech. “Burnham needs to start bridging the widening chasm between words and deeds on climate action,” said Ami McCarthy of Greenpeace UK in a statement. “The future we feared has become the present we are living. Climate change knows no borders. No nation can face it alone. Solidarity must mean real action,” said Pakistani Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif.

There might be a culprit… Microsoft has admitted that a change has caused linked server queries to fail to close connections. Linked servers via OLE DB providers have been around for years and are a useful way of, for example, using additional data sources in queries. Once a provider is added, SQL Server can open a connection to grab data, and close it again when the query is complete. Or, at least, that's the theory. The problem is that after the October 13 (KB5126646) update, connections created by SQL Server linked server queries might remain open. According to Microsoft, "As additional queries are performed, connections to external databases can accumulate instead of closing as expected. "This can slow or degrade server performance after prolonged run time." You think? Administrators will likely have already noted a suspicious number of open connections to external databases on affected systems. Microsoft said the issue affects SQL Server linked server queries that use OLE DB providers to connect to external databases. It gave PostgreSQL and Oracle as examples of connections known to be affected. And the fix? "If idle connections can be identified, it is possible to manually close them to temporarily relieve server load. "It is also possible to temporarily restore system stability by restarting the SQL service." The Windows behemoth went on to state the obvious: "However, these steps can also interrupt active queries or transactions, and the problem can resurface again after sufficient operation time." Bouncing a SQL Server to deal with connection leakage is less than ideal, although it would at least be a good failover test and, let's face it, having to restart Microsoft services regularly is something many administrators will be all too familiar with. There is a mitigation available, although only through Microsoft support for business. Otherwise, an out-of-band update should be along within the next few days to deal with the problem. According to Microsoft, the technical glitch affects every version of Windows except Windows 11 26H2, stretching back to Windows 10 1809 and LTSC 2019, and Windows Server from 2025 back to 2012. events.title: European tech buyers add digital sovereignty to cyber shopping list
events.summary: European tech buyers are increasingly choosing cybersecurity vendors from their own continent in a bid to reduce their reliance on American technology. Digital sovereignty isn't only prompting enterprise customers to question their clouds of choice, it is also reshaping other parts of the industry too, and the shift is marked. According to sales figures compiled by Context, distributor sales in EMEA of cybersecurity products from EU-headquartered vendors jumped 35 percent in the two years to calendar Q3 2026. Total cybersecurity sales grew up 10 percent over the same period, and sales by US-run companies went up just 8 percent. That growth is from a relatively small base, though EU vendors gained nearly three percentage points to reach 15 percent of tracked sales by value. There is still a long way to go as US-headquartered vendors accounted for 62 percent. The trend coincides with a loss of trust in the Trump administration among customers outside of America, after it cosied up to autocratic rulers while criticizing and punishing allies with tariffs and more. Context stopped short of assigning blame. It said organizations are reviewing their reliance on third-party tech in light of EU compliance regimes: the NIS2 Directive and Digital Operational Resilience Act (DORA). NIS2, transposed into national law in October 2024 , requires organizations in the bloc to raise their common level of security in the face of digital threats and risks to critical infrastructure. DORA, introduced in January last year, is designed to strengthen cyber security in the financial sector. "Digital sovereignty is becoming a buying decision. As customers and resellers get clearer about what it means in practice, they're asking who holds the encryption keys, who can access sensitive logs and where that data is stored," said Context veep of research Joe Turner. "We're seeing a measurable shift in the EMEA channel. EU vendors gained nearly three points of sales share in two years. An organization can keep its existing identity platform and still choose a European supplier to manage its security logs. That's the kind of decision that gives European vendors an opening." The stats indicate that EU-HQd vendors comprised 92 percent of tracked sales in security awareness training, 82 percent in vulnerability management, and 52 percent for SIEM and log management. US-headquartered companies held into 74 percent of identity and access management sales and 54 percent of cloud security sales. The Reg has asked Context for UK-specific figures to see whether British customers are also voting with their wallets for European alternatives. That certainly isn’t the case for tech purchases in the British public sector, despite Prime Minister Andy Burnham’s professed desire to buy British. Data released yesterday by the Institute for Public Policy Research showed just £1 in every £6 spent by government with the biggest technology suppliers goes to Brit businesses. Still, Burnham only came to power in July so there is time yet for him to put his money where his mouth is. Sovereign AI is another area of concern for enterprise customers. Analyst Omdia said last month that despite the marketing adjective meaning "local assets," almost a third AI providers disclose no proof of sovereignty, and some "expect enterprise to pay for audits to verify their claims." Omdia also found that 80 percent of contracts say network resilience is "out of providers control or responsibility," and "US-headquartered AI providers offer better service transparency and contract terms than a majority of local sovereign AI providers, with providers in India a notable exception." Sovereign services in Omdia's classification include data residency, operational autonomy, jurisdictional sovereignty, and technological autonomy. "Local hosting is not sovereignty. Serious providers must demonstrate their credibility through transparent operations, fair contracts and proof of competence. That includes the network, because data in transit must be sovereign too," said Camille Mendler, research director for telco B2B at Omdia. Someone should tell Microsoft and Anthropic . ®

events.title: UK economy grows at fastest rate for more than two years
events.summary: Computer programming and consultancy services in particular contributed to overall growth (generic photo) Published 12 November 2026, 07:05 GMT ﻿The UK economy grew at its fastest rate for more than two years in the three months to September. Between July and September, the economy expanded by 0.7%, accelerating from the previous three months, official figures , external show. The robust growth suggests a far more resilient economy than expected over the summer, despite the impact of higher energy prices from the Iran war. Strong growth in the services sector - the largest part of the economy, which includes non-physical goods such as consultancy services and computer programming as well as hotels and restaurants - helped boost the numbers. Within services, computer programming registered its fastest growth for the past three years, helped by cloud computing and AI-linked spending. The boost from computer programming and consultancy services has been the biggest driver of growth so far this year. Grant Fitzner, chief economist at the Office for National Statistics, said it was "possible growth could have been even stronger" if there hadn't been a war in the Middle East. But he says households may still not feel better off, and that prices might soon start to rise more quickly than wages. However, Prime Minister Andy Burnham said the figures were "welcome news". "Despite a year where events around the world have pushed up costs here at home, our economy is growing, bringing hope for the future," he said. Chancellor John Healey told the BBC the figures showed a "remarkable resilience" in the face of global conflicts, and hopes they "bring back confidence in Britain". Asked about how government decisions could be the reason for growth when AI investment has been a main driver, Healey said ministers can always "help or hinder" business confidence and investments. Although investors have recently been concerned about slower artificial intelligence development in the US and the long term viability of AI firms' business models, businesses have continued to invest in the technologies. Sarah Coles, from investment platform AJ Bell, said that since the start of the year, "it's the less visible back-office work that has delivered, with administrative and supportive services seeing strong growth" noting that these are the areas benefitting from the increasing use of AI. The latest figures put the UK on course to be the second fastest growing economy across the major G7 countries which also includes Canada, Japan, Germany, Italy and France. However, Jake Finney, senior economist at consultancy PwC, cautioned that growth was likely to slow over the coming months "unless energy markets stabilise". A sharp rise in energy bills is forecast for January, which is likely to hit consumer spending and confidence, he said. High energy costs have been stoked by the ongoing conflict in the Middle East and Russia's invasion of Ukraine. US and Israeli attacks led to Iran blocking the Strait of Hormuz - a vital shipping route for the world's oil and gas. Meanwhile, Russia and Ukraine have been attacking each other's oil refineries, leading to a squeeze on global refining capacity, hitting diesel and petrol prices. What's happening to the UK economy and how does it affect you? "We've seen more resilience than we had forecast for and expected. We are still projecting growth this year," he says. The business exports about 80% of its watches. "We've seen a surprising amount of resilience, particularly from our US customers," he adds, although some UK customers are now taking longer to buy watches. events.title: Billions lost and markets roiled by one man’s indiscretion. Isn’t it now clear that these tech bros are too powerful? | Aditya Chakrabortty
events.summary: Billions lost and markets roiled by one man’s indiscretion. Isn’t it now clear that these tech bros are too powerful? Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang’s affair must be the costliest fling in human history – and a preview of what awaits when the tech bubble bursts O ne thing we all know about the tech billionaires is they are super-smart. We know this largely because they never stop telling us. The “ cognitive elite ”, to use their favoured phrase, are entitled to shape our future without our say-so. When Elon Musk goes hiring, he wants “super-high-IQ small-government revolutionaries”. Long before they got private jets, what fuelled these boys was faith in their own brainpower. As a teenager, Jensen Huang wooed his future wife, Lori, thus: “If you do homework with me every Sunday, I promise you you’ll get straight As.” Lord Byron: I believe it’s your move. Which raises the question: if you’re that clever, why act so dumb? At last week’s midterms, it was Musk who backed Team Trump to the tune of $446m. With unhedged bets like that, why wouldn’t you want him gambling with your livelihood? This week, it is 63-year-old Huang and his affair with a much younger woman, who the US government strongly suspects is a Chinese spy. That scandal wiped more than $400bn off the value of his company in just two days, making it the costliest fling in human history. But who knows? Perhaps she loved the centibillionaire for his mind. Forget Sam Altman and Dario Amodei: no one is more central to the future of technology than Huang. He runs Nvidia, which makes the chips powering AI. Previous generations of chips have been compared to kitchen knives: however sharp, they only chop one vegetable at a time. But the graphics-processing units made by Huang’s business are more like food blenders – they can blitz an entire veg patch. That’s what makes Nvidia the foundational infrastructure company of AI and one of the most valuable businesses in the world. And it uses its power: in some of the biggest funny-money deals over the past year in AI, Nvidia has been the money printer . It also stumped up at least $20m for Donald Trump’s new ballroom . Smart! Not only is Huang one of Trump’s favourite businessmen, he’s warmly welcomed by leaders around the world – including Andy Burnham, who last month in London sank a whisky with him . Even as he falls from grace, Huang’s supporters have brought out the superlatives : “torchbearer”, “irreplaceable”, “incredible human”. Huang is boss of the most strategically important business in the fastest-growing, biggest-spending industry in the world’s No 1 capitalist economy. He is part of a tiny coterie of people, who may well feel they sit above the norms and laws that govern the rest of us. That’s certainly the way he has been treated so far by Trump, who was personally warned aboard Air Force One that Huang’s love interest is believed to be a spy for Beijing. Not only is China an ever-greater threat to US AI dominance, it has been banned by Washington from getting Nvidia’s top-of-the-range chips. And the US president takes no discernible action. Some people are in a huge tizz about the spy part of this story, notably the Tory MP Tom Tugendhat, who, after Vladimir Putin invaded Ukraine , demanded that every Russian in Britain be rounded up and expelled. The force is not strong in that one. Personally, I can’t get too excited about the threat to the Trumpian model of AI. Neither, it seems, can Washington: it’s been more than a year since Nvidia was revealed to be selling some of its best stuff to a “ dilapidated storefront ” outside Kuala Lumpur, which sounded awfully like a pit stop on the way to China. Again, no action. The message ordinary Americans can take from this is that a company so vital to America’s AI-military complex is too big to subject to ordinary laws. In the everyday world, a CEO who gets into both a sex scandal and a national-security imbroglio wouldn’t stay CEO for more than a minute. At Nvidia, the board has moved with incredible sloth. It declared on Sunday that it “has no reason to believe that either national security or Nvidia secrets were compromised” – before any independent investigation. It finally met on Wednesday evening after further revelations of a separate extramarital affair with an Nvidia executive. Huang’s fate now reportedly hangs in the balance, but the company board, it may surprise you to know, includes several of his longstanding business associates . You’ll also be gobsmacked to learn that several members of his family are serving in senior positions at Nvidia. One of the protections for Huang, like Musk and Zuckerberg and Altman, is that there appears to be no succession plan in place should any of those men fall under a self-driving automobile. A suggestion doing the rounds is that the father may now be replaced by one of his children. The Vatican has a more codified succession process for the pope, even if it includes white smoke and Ralph Fiennes .

AWS New Horizon Digicert Netscout Resources Intelligence Webinars & Events Newsletters UK staff get their say while a separate union-busting dispute heads towards its conclusion White House nixes NASA unions amid budget uncertainty September 1, 2025 BT won't budge over pay hike for manager grade employees June 9, 2025 More layoffs at Microsoft as axe falls in Washington June 3, 2025 Apple settles unfair labor charges brought by fired engineering manager April 10, 2025 Amazon accused of using algorithms to push warehouse workers to breaking point March 18, 2025 More than 1,600 Rockstar Games employees in the UK will begin voting on union recognition on Thursday, with the ballot kicking off just a week before the long-awaited launch of Grand Theft Auto VI. The ballot, which opens on November 12 and runs until November 26, will determine whether Rockstar formally recognizes the Rockstar Game Workers Union, part of the Independent Workers Union of Great Britain (IWGB). Nearly all UK employees below director level are eligible to vote. If successful, the union would become the largest recognized union in the UK games industry, giving workers a collective voice. The proposed recognition agreement follows four months of negotiations between Rockstar management and employees. It would allow workers to negotiate over pay, overtime, pensions, bonuses, leave and other employment conditions, while securing consultation rights over HR policies and AI. The vote comes at a particularly busy time for Rockstar, with GTA VI finally due to arrive on November 19, more than 13 years after its predecessor. The game is expected to be one of the biggest entertainment launches in history, although the people responsible for making it have rather more immediate concerns than sales records. "I am incredibly proud of the work we've put into making this game. I'm also proud of the union we've built here. For me, those two things are connected," said Nestor Uriate, an animation programmer and Rockstar Game Workers Union representative. "We care deeply about the games we make, and we want to make sure we can continue doing that work in an environment where we're respected, have a meaningful say over our conditions and can feel secure about our futures." The vote follows a year of bad blood between Rockstar and the IWGB. The union accused the GTA developer of union busting after it fired 31 members in October 2025, claiming they had been singled out for taking part in a private Discord group. Rockstar denied the allegations, insisting the workers were dismissed for gross misconduct rather than their union activities. The dispute subsequently reached an employment tribunal, where Rockstar unsuccessfully attempted to have blacklisting allegations struck from the case . Closing submissions are expected on November 17 and 18, meaning the legal proceedings will reach their final stages just as GTA VI prepares to hit shelves. Despite the ongoing dispute, Rockstar's head of publishing, Jennifer Kolbe, recently indicated that management would respect the outcome of the recognition vote, telling Bloomberg : "We go where the team goes. So if they want a union, they will have a union." The union campaign has also attracted support from elsewhere in the games industry, including SAG-AFTRA and the Communications Workers of America (CWA), which represents workers at Blizzard. Alex Marshall, president of the IWGB, said the vote was an opportunity for Rockstar employees to take greater control over their working conditions. "What happens at Rockstar matters beyond the studio. Workers across the games industry are watching, and this ballot is an opportunity to show what can be achieved when people come together, organize and build the collective power to shape their own working lives." For Rockstar, November was already shaping up to be a big month. By the time GTA VI has been in players' hands for a week, the company should also know whether its UK workforce has voted to secure a formal seat at the negotiating table.

events.title: Datacentres are deeply unpopular. Has Sweden made one we can all love?
events.summary: It is built of wood, resembles an Ikea and its power is totally renewable. Plus, it was built with the local community in mind. Is this facility in Falun the best datacentre in the world? ‘I t was pretty cool, when they were building it. It looked like a very large Ikea,” says John Wernvik, of EcoDataCenter. He is giving me a tour of their facility in Falun, Sweden , which could lay claim to being the world’s greenest datacentre – although to many, that is a contradiction in terms. One difference is immediately visible: this datacentre is made out of wood. Huge panels of cross-laminated timber arrived at the site pre-cut, and were assembled by crane according to instructions, like flatpack furniture. Aesthetically, this section of the datacentre is more like an Ikea before the fit-out, a cavernous, echoey, immaculately clean hangar. The wood is not EcoDataCenter’s only claim to sustainability; it is more than just cosmetic, says Wernvik, the company’s chief external relations and sustainability officer. “Compared with a traditional datacentre built with steel and concrete, we lower the embodied carbon of the full structure by three times.” With a complex the size of a football pitch, that is a lot of wood, but, says Wernvik, “the amount of timber one of our datacentres uses takes the Swedish forest about 10 to 15 minutes to grow back”. Datacentres have become a dirty word and a political issue in much of the world – especially the US, where opposition to them was said to be a factor in the recent midterm elections – but here in Sweden, not so much. There is a familiar litany of reasons why datacentres are bad: they are being built without the consent or knowledge of local people; they consume vast amounts of land, electricity and water, with knock-on effects for communities and the environment; they provide no jobs and enrich rapacious tech companies. What’s remarkable is how little any of those arguments apply in Sweden, especially here in Falun, a former copper-mining town a few hours north of Stockholm. If your abiding image of a datacentre is something like xAI’s Colossus facility in Tennessee , built at lightning speed with little public notice, partly powered by banks of unpermitted, methane gas-burning temporary generators, releasing huge amounts of CO 2 and harmful pollutants into the atmosphere and the community, then EcoDataCenter is practically the polar opposite. “I’m biased, but we believe that we build datacentres in a somewhat different way,” says Wernvik. For starters, the company’s electricity supply is 100% renewable: 75% from hydroelectric power and 25% from wind. Sweden’s power mix as a whole is virtually carbon-free – just 1% of it comes from fossil fuels (in the EU as a whole, the figure is 29% , in the US it is 55%). In rural areas like Falun, there is sometimes too much electricity being generated by nearby hydroelectric, solar and wind, so power-hungry datacentres are actually helpful in balancing the grid. Conditions for datacentres are pretty good in Sweden as a whole. The cold northern climate means less cooling is required; the energy is not only green, it is cheap and reliable; there is plenty of water and space; and the country is relatively politically stable and well-regulated – as Wernvik puts it, “it’s very hard to develop something in Sweden where there’s not a consensus”. Energy is still a concern at EcoDataCenter, considering this place has a capacity of 80MW (the equivalent of about 60,000 homes). There are two key measures of datacentre performance. One is carbon usage effectiveness (CUE): the carbon emissions for each kWh of energy consumed. The average for US datacentres is 414gCO2/kWh, the European Union’s is 263gCO2/kWh, EcoDataCenter’s is 1.17gCO2/kWh. Another key measure is power usage effectiveness (PUE); how efficiently the datacentre uses the power going into it. The EU average is 1.36 (where a score of 1 would be 100% efficiency), EcoDataCenter’s is 1.15. The company is bringing down both its CUE and PUE year by year, according to EcoDataCenter’s sustainability report . The primary use for energy is powering the graphics processing units – the expensive chips that do the computing, mostly made by the US company Nvidia. (Wernvik reminds me that although 70% of their computing power goes towards AI, almost everything online is run through datacentres somewhere, from banking transactions to streaming TV.) The supply must be constant – even a small drop in current for a few milliseconds could be consequential – so there are numerous backup generators on site, but even these are fuelled by hydrotreated vegetable oil (HVO), a biofuel made from waste vegetable oil and animal fat, so also fossil fuel-free. The other main energy use is cooling; removing the vast amounts of heat the chips generate. This is where controversies have arisen in the US over extracting from the local water supply, but it is less of an issue here, says Wernvik.

events.title: New business-class seats, Air India plans among key takeaways from SIA’s first-half results briefing
events.summary: Higher jet fuel prices meant that SIA’s net profit for the first half was 43.9% lower despite a strong second quarter, but it was cushioned by a lower share of losses from its stake in Air India. SIA may adjust its new business-class seats after mixed feedback. The airline will review the design to “further enhance” customer travel, while the $2 billion cabin overhaul stays on track. SIA posted $5.6 billion in revenue and $209.7 million net profit for Q2. First-half net profit still fell 43.9% to $134 million, hit by higher jet fuel costs from the Middle East conflict. Air India is chasing profit under new leadership and new growth plans. SIA also said its AI push is widening, with use cases up 67% and work with OpenAI and Meta’s Muse. SINGAPORE – A week after receiving mixed feedback on its newly unveiled business-class seats , Singapore Airlines chief executive Goh Choon Phong said the airline would explore the possibility of making adjustments where it deemed fit. Without elaborating on the extent of any possible changes, Goh said at SIA’s results briefing on Nov 12 that the group acknowledges the feedback it had received and would review it so that it could “further enhance” the travel experience for its customers. SIA also elaborated on the growth strategy for loss-making Air India, in which it holds a 25.1% stake , noting that the airline is aiming to achieve profitability under new leadership and with growth opportunities emerging in the market. The company posted $5.6 billion in revenue , 14.3% higher year on year, for the second quarter ended Sept 30. Net profit also quadrupled to $209.7 million. Despite the strong quarter, the airline’s net profit for the first half of its financial year still fell 43.9% to $134 million, as rising jet fuel prices driven by the Middle East conflict took a toll on its performance. Jet fuel prices were lower in the first quarter than the second quarter, said group chief financial officer JoAnn Tan. The surge, however, still led to a 90.3% increase in fuel costs before hedging for the first half of the financial year. Here are the key takeaways from SIA’s results briefing for the first half of its 2027 financial year: Possible changes to the business-class seat SIA’s long-haul business-class seats, revealed on Nov 7 alongside refreshed products across all its other cabin classes, has sparked substantial debate. Central to the discussion were the seat’s shape and grey palette, which drew comparisons to a dental chair, and the bright yellow stripe across the backrest, which critics said strayed too far from the colours traditionally associated with the airline. The business-class cabin was designed by BMW Group’s Designworks, one of three design studios hired by SIA to design its fleetwide overhaul for $2 billion in total. Due to launch in the second half of 2027, the seats will be introduced progressively on 41 Airbus A350-900 long-haul and ultra-long-range aircraft as they are retrofitted, as well as on SIA’s upcoming Boeing 777-9 planes. Deliveries of the Boeing aircraft have already been delayed by five years, and the model is still awaiting certification. SIA has defended the seat’s design following the public outcry and now says it will consider adjustments in response to feedback. A petition on Change.org is calling for the airline to remove the yellow accents. Asked by The Straits Times whether engaging a single agency for the entire redesign could have produced a more unified look and reduced costs, Goh said the airline’s decision was based on the different requirements of each cabin class. “What we’ve done is to choose the most appropriate agency for the needs of that specific business class,” he said. An SIA spokesperson added that the airline has historically hired multiple agencies for its cabin overhauls. This includes the 2017 refresh for its Airbus A380 aircraft, where one design studio was involved in its Suites design and another for the business-class and premium economy seats. Design studios must comply with both US Federal Aviation Administration and European Union Aviation Safety Agency regulations before they are invited to bid. The spokesperson added that the $2 billion investment was not a huge sum when compared with SIA’s financials. Air India pursuing new growth opportunities A lower share of losses from Air India helped support SIA’s earnings for the second quarter. SIA, which owns a 25.1% stake in Air India, recorded a $361.7 million share of the carrier’s losses, down from $429.5 million a year earlier. Tan said this was mainly due to a reversal of provisions that SIA had made in previous years, and not because Air India had performed better. In its next stage of growth, Air India will pursue opportunities within and outside of India, Goh said, adding that the airline has already taken steps to improve revenue generation and cost management under a new CEO.

events.title: Arada and Alya target $1.63bn property pipeline across UAE and Saudi Arabia
events.summary: UAE developer Arada has teamed up with Alya Developments to explore co-investment opportunities in premium property in the Emirates and Saudi Arabia, following the former's entry into the kingdom. Arada's newly established investment management platform, Arada Capital, and Alya signed a preliminary agreement to explore premium developments in the Emirates and Saudi Arabia under a potential Dh6 billion ($1.63 billion) pipeline, they said in a joint statement on Thursday. The companies will initially pursue two projects in the UAE, with Abu Dhabi's Yas Island and Downtown Dubai earmarked as potential areas, they said in a joint statement on Thursday. It did not provide plans for Saudi Arabia. Arada Capital, the investment management platform of Arada Group, was announced in July and is aiming for $5 billion in assets under management within four years. Arada Group is jointly owned by Saudi businessman Prince Khaled bin Alwaleed’s KBW Investments and Sharjah-based Basma Group. Alya is backed by Canada's Brookfield , which manages about $1 trillion in assets, and Abu Dhabi-based Lunate , a global investment firm with more than $125 billion in assets. The move follows last month's launch of Arada's Dh14 billion residential project in Riyadh, as the developer expands into the kingdom. Arada's group chief executive has separately outlined plans to build 100,000 homes across Saudi Arabia over the next three to five years. Arada also has operations in Australia, Syria and the UK. “This partnership represents an important milestone in Arada Capital's ambition as a fund manager … we see significant potential to bring forward premium residential projects distinguished by their quality, thoughtful design and disciplined delivery,” said Moustafa Fahour, chief executive and managing director of Arada Capital. “Our shared ambition is to create homes of enduring quality and value, for the people who live in them and those who invest in them,” added Otto Dreyer, chief executive of Alya. Property developers are continuing to launch projects in the UAE despite concerns about the slowing of the market as the Iran war continues. This week, Dubai’s Nakheel unveiled the new Palm Springs master development next to Palm Jebel Ali, while Abu Dhabi’s Aldar Properties last month said it plans to launch a major development of villas and townhouses in Dubai by the end of this year as part of the company’s expansion across the UAE. In September, Arada and Aldar teamed up to build new housing projects on Yas Island and at Seih Sdeirah in Abu Dhabi, representing a combined value of about Dh15 billion. Arada also unveiled plans for a $7 billion “UAE-style” development in Damascus. Saudi Arabia, meanwhile, has boosted its real estate sector as it continues its economic diversification strategy. In January, the kingdom began implementing an updated property ownership law for non-Saudis, allowing foreign individuals and companies to acquire real estate subject to regulatory and geographical restrictions. The authorities expect the changes to attract international developers, stimulate investment and support economic diversification. “The UAE and Saudi Arabia continue to present compelling long-term opportunities and our focus is on bringing together the right partners, capital and expertise to deliver sustainable value for investors and communities alike,” Mr Fahour said. Second Australia approval secured Separately on Thursday, Arada said it has received approval for its Dh1.6 billion Wattle Green residential community in Castle Hill, New South Wales, Australia. The 14,000-square-metre project is planned to feature 445 residences across three buildings. The approval is Arada's second major planning consent in Australia within a little over a month, after securing a similar decision for the 33-storey London Place residential project in Campsie, south-west of Sydney, early last month. “We are pushing ahead with our pipeline of projects at a time when we know delivery in this market demands real conviction,” Arada group chief executive Ahmed Alkhoshaibi said.

events.title: Long John Silver’s White Sands outlet to shutter on Nov 18
events.summary: The upcoming closure of the Long John Silver’s White Sands outlet marks the latest of several in 2026 for the fast-food chain known for battered seafood. Long John Silver’s White Sands outlet in Pasir Ris will close on Nov 18, with its last day of trading on Nov 17. The chain has not given a reason. The closure adds to several Long John Silver’s shut-downs in 2026, including Woodlands and Jurong Point. Its Singapore outlets have fallen from 17 in July 2025 to 10 now. Some diners were upset about losing another halal option, while others said there are still other food choices nearby. The outlets are run by Zensho Food Singapore, a unit of Japan’s Zensho Holdings Group. SINGAPORE – Fast-food chain Long John Silver’s will be closing its restaurant at White Sands shopping mall in Pasir Ris on Nov 18. According to a notice pasted outside the outlet, its last day of operations is Nov 17. A homemaker, who wanted to be known only as Afifah, said she often takes her children to the White Sands outlet for meals after school. “I’m sad that there will be one fewer halal meal option after this place closes. My children like the food here,” said the 40-year-old, who was having lunch there . Another diner, human resources executive Benjamin Lee, who works in the area, said he sometimes patronises the White Sands outlet during his lunch hour. “I don’t feel much about the outlet closing as there are always other lunch options around,” said the 38-year-old. “But it seems like a lot of food and beverage outlets have been closing in 2026, so that’s a pity.” The impending outlet closure marks the latest of several in 2026 for the fast-food chain known for its golden battered seafood. Its Woodlands outlet was permanently shuttered on Oct 31. Long John Silver’s Singapore website now lists 10 outlets, including White Sands. This is down from the 17 outlets reported by the media in July 2025. Its Jurong Point outlet shut on Oct 19, and checks show that at least four other locations closed earlier in 2026. Based on social media posts as well as media reports, those affected outlets were in Suntec City, Admiralty, Commonwealth and Tampines. Long John Silver’s traces its roots in Singapore back to the 1980s, as part of the wave of US fast-food chains that entered the local market. Today, its outlets here are all managed by Zensho Food Singapore, a subsidiary of Japanese conglomerate Zensho Holdings Group, which is listed on the Tokyo Stock Exchange. The parent group manages a global portfolio of popular F&B brands, including Japan’s leading beef bowl restaurant chain Sukiya and Ichikokudo Hokkaido Ramen, which both have a presence in Singapore . The Straits Times has contacted Zensho Food Singapore for more information. Rosalind Ang is a business journalist who has been with The Straits Times since 2021. She covers e-commerce and stories on retail businesses.

events.title: From Emmett Till to Robert Johnson, the Delta powered Scott Colom's historic Senate bid
events.summary: Scott Colom 's path to a historic U.S. Senate upset ran through the Mississippi Delta — where Emmett Till was abducted, Fannie Lou Hamer fought for the ballot and the blues became an American art form. Why it matters: Nearly 150 years after Reconstruction, Mississippi sent a Black American to the U.S. Senate for the first time since 1881. The votes pushing Colom toward that milestone came from communities where Black residents spent generations fighting for the ballot. Driving the news: The Associated Press projected the race for Colom on Wednesday, handing Democrats a historic upset over Republican Sen. Cindy Hyde-Smith. By the numbers: An Axios analysis of AP county returns found Colom ahead in 16 of the 18 counties in the Mississippi Delta National Heritage Area . Colom collected roughly 100,000 votes to Hyde-Smith's 62,000 — a 38,000-vote advantage. In 2020, Democrat Mike Espy carried 15 of those counties by about 25,000 votes, according to Mississippi's certified county returns . Colom's share of the two-party vote climbed from about 56% to 62%. Statewide, Colom led Hyde-Smith by about 4,700 votes out of more than 962,000 counted when the AP called the race Wednesday — a margin of roughly half a percentage point. What they're saying: "Mississippi voters made history because they refused to be intimidated, discouraged, or counted out," NAACP president Derrick Johnson said in a statement. Johnson said Mississippi voters showed up despite efforts to remove voters from the rolls . Zoom in: Colom's electoral map traces some of the most painful and defining chapters of Black American history. Coahoma County: Home to Clarksdale and the famed crossroads associated with the legend that bluesman Robert Johnson sold his soul to the devil. Colom led with about 4,700 votes to 1,300. Leflore and Tallahatchie counties: Emmett Till was abducted near Money in Leflore County in 1955. His body was recovered from the Tallahatchie River in Tallahatchie County, where an all-white jury acquitted his killers. Colom led by about 4,200 votes in Leflore and 1,300 in Tallahatchie, according to AP returns . Sunflower County: Fannie Lou Hamer, who lived in Ruleville, challenged Mississippi's racist voting restrictions. As late as the spring of 1965, only 155 Black residents had registered to vote in the county, according to the Mississippi Department of Archives and History . Colom led with about 5,300 votes to 1,700. Washington County: Robert F. Kennedy visited Greenville during his 1967 tour of Delta poverty . 29.4% of Washington County is still in poverty per the Census Bureau's 2020–2024 estimate . Colom led with about 8,700 votes to 2,400. Zoom out: Colom didn't suddenly turn the Delta blue. Espy won most of it in 2020. But Colom widened the Democratic margin. In DeSoto County, which falls within the heritage area but outside the Delta's historic heartland, Colom led by about 3,300 votes. Hyde-Smith won there by roughly 12,100 in 2020. Colom also swept the Golden Triangle counties of Lowndes, Oktibbeha and Clay, his home region in northeastern Mississippi. He won all three by double-digit margins and improved on Espy's 2020 performance. Between the lines: The historical symbolism stretches beyond the Delta. Colom led with about 12,100 votes to 9,700 in Forrest County, named for Confederate Gen. Nathan Bedford Forrest, the Ku Klux Klan's first grand wizard. Hyde-Smith faced criticism during her 2018 race against Espy after saying she would sit in the front row if invited to a public hanging . She later apologized to those offended. The bottom line: The region where Black Mississippians fought some of America's fiercest battles for voting rights helped elect the state's first Black U.S. senator in 145 years — and raised a new question. Can political representation finally bring economic change to the Delta?

events.title: Saudi Arabia sets October 2027 date for next iteration of flagship FII investment summit
events.summary: Saudi Arabia's annual international investment and economic conference, the Future Investment Initiative, has been postponed to 2027 after it was stopped this year because of attacks on the kingdom by the Houthi rebels in Yemen The 10th iteration of the flagship investment conference will take place from October 25 to 28 next year in Riyadh, the Future Investment Initiative (FII) Institute confirmed. It was set to be held in October, but Houthi strikes on Riyadh's King Khalid International Airport disrupted air travel and raised security concerns among international executives and investors. The rescheduled summit, held under the patronage of King Salman, will take place under the theme The Power of Legacy, marking a decade of global investment dialogue and partnerships, the institute said on Thursday. “We are deeply grateful for the continued support of the kingdom’s leadership,” said Princess Maha Al Saud, chief executive of the FII Institute. “The decision to move this landmark edition to October 2027 reflects our commitment to ensuring the highest level of international participation, visibility and impact.” Launched in 2017, FII has become a key platform for Saudi Arabia to attract international investment and advance its economic diversification agenda under Vision 2030. The annual gathering has attracted senior policymakers, global investors and business leaders, with previous events focusing on investment opportunities and economic growth . At last year's summit, the kingdom called for greater private sector investment in its major development projects, while its sovereign wealth fund has since outlined plans to increase its domestic investment allocation . The postponement also affected a major gathering for the kingdom's technology sector, which continues to pursue large-scale artificial intelligence investments . Ahead of FII10, the institute will host its FII Priority Miami summit from March 31 to April 2, 2027, followed by an Asia summit, with dates and location yet to be announced.

events.title: UK drone maker founded by Ukrainians hits £4.5bn value after raising £500m
events.summary: Britain’s national wealth fund invests £113m in UForce, whose equipment has been used heavily in war with Russia A London-based naval drone maker founded by Ukrainians has reached a £4.5bn valuation after it raised more than £500m from investors including the UK government. UForce, which makes military drones for land, air and sea, received £113m from the UK’s national wealth fund. The investment makes UForce one of the UK’s fastest-growing unicorns – or startups with a valuation of more than $1bn. Its drones have been used extensively in the war in Ukraine . The UK defence secretary, Wes Streeting, met the UForce chief executive, Oleg Rogynskyy, on Thursday onboard the British aircraft carrier HMS Prince of Wales during a defence conference in Oslo, Norway. The UK’s Ministry of Defence noted UForce’s maritime capabilities in particular, amid concerns over the increasing threat from Russia in the north Atlantic and North Sea. Russian naval vessels and its “shadow fleet” have been accused of sabotage and spying operations on cables and pipelines , while the UK is planning a fleet of sea-borne drones in the northern seas to track Russia’s nuclear submarine fleet . Streeting on Thursday piloted a UForce MV7 uncrewed vessel located more than 1,500 miles away in the Atlantic Ocean near Portugal. Rogynskyy grew up in Dnipro, an industrial city in eastern Ukraine, before founding People.ai, a Silicon Valley tech unicorn focused on data on sales and operations performance for businesses. Rogynskyy said UForce wanted to “make aggression unaffordable”. The investment would allow UForce to scale up production for Ukraine as well as for its allies, he added. “The war in Ukraine has shown that in an increasingly volatile world, effective defence requires systems that can keep improving as threats change,” he said. “Governments and the technology ecosystem need to come together to develop cost-effective, interoperable, and autonomous platforms that are ready to fight now, and can evolve to meet future needs.” The other lead investor was Valor Equity Partners, a private equity investor founded by Antonio Gracias, a former director of Tesla who is also on the board of Elon Musk’s rocket launch company, SpaceX. One of Valor’s partners is Christopher Cavoli, a retired US general who was Nato’s supreme allied commander for Europe until last year. Cavoli will join UForce’s board. The Ministry of Defence said UForce would invest in a British supply chain as part of the deal, with hulls, engines, electronics and fit-out sourced in the UK. The MoD said more than 70% of the content of each UK-built boat would come from British suppliers. Get set for the working day – we'll point you to all the business news and analysis you need every morning Streeting said: “Ukraine is rewriting the rules of warfare. In just a few years the UK has gone from training Ukraine to being trained by Ukraine, as they prove that who can innovate fastest is a key measure of modern military power. “Bringing battle-tested expertise to the UK will create high-skilled jobs, spur innovation and strengthen our war-fighting readiness, enhancing our ability to deter our adversaries.” The former Conservative UK defence secretary Ben Wallace is also on UForce’s board.
