events.title: Democrats debate taking a page from Trump's economic playbook
events.summary: President Trump is turning the federal government into an investor in dozens of private companies, and some Democrats are considering following his lead as their party emerges emboldened from the midterm elections. Why it matters: Democrats are gaining new power to scrutinize Trump's corporate investments, even as his approach gains traction within their own party. They're looking at investments and aid for clean energy and other priorities, like support for energy infrastructure. State of play: The Trump administration's investments in energy, critical minerals and other industries are already drawing calls for congressional investigations . "The Trump administration has widened the aperture for industrial policy," Jennifer Granholm, who served as President Biden's Energy Secretary, said at a gathering of energy and climate experts Axios attended in Berkeley, Calif., last month. "You're not going to have state ownership of enterprises," Granholm told Axios in an interview afterward. "But maybe you do take a little bit of an ownership slice" for national security or global competitiveness reasons, she said. Sen. Chris Van Hollen (D-Md.) has also expressed openness to federal ownership stakes, while raising concerns about the Trump administration's lack of transparency and accountability, he told Semafor . Rep. Sean Casten (D-Ill.) has argued that the U.S. needs to consider a more aggressive industrial policy to compete with countries like China, while warning against direct government ownership. "We are long overdue for having a conversation about, 'should the United States even have an industrial policy?'" Casten said at a recent University of Chicago event . "For a long time, we viewed industrial policy as something that socialists do." Casten said he would support the U.S. ensuring domestic manufacturing of certain parts of supply chains, like electronic control systems that operate energy infrastructure, and even pursuing "smart tariff policy" to have competitive markets. The big picture: The Biden administration spent billions subsidizing clean energy and semiconductor manufacturing. Trump has taken government intervention a step further by acquiring ownership stakes in companies ranging from Intel to critical mineral producers. It's been a striking reversal for a president who has repeatedly criticized Democrats for government overreach. How it works: The Trump administration has announced more than $30 billion in investments across nearly 50 deals involving government ownership and related financial arrangements, according to a Council on Foreign Relations tracker . The investments span semiconductors, critical minerals and energy — strategically important industries where high costs and long development timelines can make private financing difficult. Flashback: Washington has taken ownership stakes in private companies before, including during the 2008 financial crisis. But those investments were intended as temporary measures to rescue struggling businesses, unlike Trump's national security-focused investments. What they're saying: "Equity from the U.S. government can act as patient capital that helps derisk an investment with a long time horizon or technological risk that would otherwise not attract sufficient private investment," said Jonathan Hillman, a Council on Foreign Relations fellow behind the tracker. Hillman said the deals announced since January 2025 have also mobilized $28.5 billion in private capital. Yes, but: Some politicians and energy leaders warn that direct government ownership could open the door to political favoritism and market distortions. "Government is not a venture capital fund. It's not a private equity fund. It's not well suited to pick winners and losers in the marketplace," said Tim Pawlenty, former Republican governor of Minnesota who now leads the Solar Energy Industries Association, at the same University of Chicago event. "If it starts to go down the slippery slope of 'it's just the flavor of the day company because we like it' or they're well connected or whatever, then you got problems." Threat level: "Buying stakes in public companies is so, so, so dangerous," Casten said. "I have no idea how a future president unwinds our stake in Intel without totally tanking Intel stock," he added, referring to the administration's roughly 10% stake in the semiconductor giant. To avoid such concerns, Hillman suggests creating a federal chief investment officer to oversee investments and eventual sales. The other side: The White House defended the investments as a way to rebuild American manufacturing and secure critical supply chains, emphasizing that companies participate voluntarily, spokesman Matthew Middleton said. What we're watching: Democrats could spend the next two years scrutinizing Trump's investments — while debating whether a future Democratic administration should make similar deals of its own.

events.title: Democrats unite against Big Health Care
events.summary: Newly elected Democrats from ruby red states are leading a charge to take on corporate health care and some business practices that they say drive up health care costs. Why it matters: Democrats may not be anywhere close to agreement on Medicare for All, but they're relatively united around confronting Big Health Care after campaigning hard on the populist theme. Driving the news: While expanding Medicare, reversing GOP Medicaid cuts and reviving enhanced Obamacare subsidies are getting most of the attention, there's a subtle shift in rhetoric and policy positions toward blaming big health companies for the affordability crisis. It reflects the reality that a substantial expansion of the federal government's role in health care isn't in the cards while President Trump is in office, but populist themes could unite the rank-and-file and even draw in some Republicans. Even candidates who didn't constantly rail about drugmakers or insurers have adopted policy ideas that, until recently, were confined to left-leaning think tanks. Case in point: Incoming Texas Sen. James Talarico ran on breaking up big health care companies and "stop[ping] hospitals and insurance companies from overcharging patients." (He also supports allowing Americans under 65 to join Medicare.) South Carolina Sen.-elect Annie Andrews ran on limiting insurer profits per enrollee, expanding the number of drugs subject to Medicare drug price negotiations and banning private equity-owned hospitals. Incoming Kansas Sen. Adam Hamilton supports expanding Medicare drug price negotiations and extending the negotiated prices to private health plans, as well as addressing Medicare Advantage overpayments from the federal government. Other targets include medical debt, pharmacy benefit manager practices and caps on out-of-pocket drug costs. Many of these ideas already have buy-in from more-senior progressives. Sen. Elizabeth Warren (D-Mass.) has sponsored the Break Up Big Medicine Act, which is co-sponsored by Republican Sen. Josh Hawley of Missouri, which would prohibit common ownership of health plans and providers. Incoming Michigan Sen. Abdul El-Sayed, an avid Medicare for All supporter, ran on support of the Warren-Hawley bill, as well as expanding Medicare drug price negotiations. The House's health care working group , made up of both progressives and moderates, pitched capping "excessive" hospital prices and enacting site-neutral payments. The big picture: Voters have made clear that they want lower health care costs. So while a broad overhaul of the health system may not immediately be on the table, Democrats are looking for ways to deliver. Powerful health industry groups are poised to push back, arguing that the populist policies would threaten patient care and access in some communities. But the ideas under discussion could gain favor with some Republicans. What they're saying: When asked at an Axios event on Tuesday whether Congress should address ownership ties between insurers, PBMs and pharmacies, Rep. Morgan Griffith — the top Republican on the House Energy and Commerce's Health Subcommittee — said, "I've only heard the case for breaking them up." "There's just something in your gut that bothers you when your pharmacy, your PBM and your insurance company are all owned by the same people," he added. What we're watching: Forcing drugmakers to lower prescription drug prices could be a particularly compelling target, given Trump's demonstrated interest in the topic. He has previously called on Congress to codify the "most-favored-nation" deals he made with pharmaceutical manufacturers that require the companies, in some cases, to offer Americans prices on a par with what's paid abroad. The Senate Finance Committee's top Democrat, Ron Wyden of Oregon, told reporters this week that he's open to a deal codifying those agreements in exchange for an expansion of the number of drugs Medicare can negotiate on, according to InsideHealthPolicy . The bottom line: It was only four years ago that Democrats struggled to find enough votes for the modest drug price negotiations that exist today, marking the first successful legislative attempt to directly lower health care costs in any sector by either party. Now, they're more willing to push for change and confront big industry players.

events.title: Scoop: AOC shakes up team again as 2028 decision looms
events.summary: New York Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez is shaking up her team for the second time in the past few months as she prepares to make the biggest decision of her political life. Why it matters: The overhaul comes as the democratic socialist leader is debating whether to run for president in 2028 — or Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer's seat, which is up the same year. Zoom in: Ocasio-Cortez has parted ways with her longtime digital fundraising firm, Middle Seat, according to three people familiar with the decision. At the same time, sources said, she's brought on Aisle 518 Strategies — the company led by Democratic strategist Tim Tagaris, who oversaw Bernie Sanders' record-breaking online fundraising strategy in his two presidential campaigns. Middle Seat has been key to Ocasio-Cortez's operation. Over the past two years, she has paid the firm more than $6 million — about a quarter of her operation's disbursements during that period. AOC is close with Sanders, and if she decides to run for president, progressives say, she would be able to quickly staff up with his former advisers. But Ocasio-Cortez's latest move doesn't necessarily signal that she's leaning toward a presidential run or a Senate bid. Tagaris' firm has helped power the small-dollar fundraising operation for California Gov. Gavin Newsom, who's widely expected to run for the White House. It also has worked with other Democrats who are potential contenders for president — Arizona Sen. Mark Kelly, Georgia Sen. Jon Ossoff and former Vice President Kamala Harris, according to the company's website . Middle Seat, the firm AOC is leaving, has Sanders roots as well: It was founded by alumni of the Vermont senator's 2016 campaign. Flashback: Ocasio-Cortez's reorganizing follows several changes she made to her staff this year, as Axios previously reported . They included parting ways with her longtime campaign manager and creative director, as well as bringing aboard a few former aides. The Washington Sun reported this week that AOC had hired Freeland Ellis, a Sanders alum, as a communications aide. What they're saying: A spokesperson for Ocasio-Cortez declined to comment. Tagaris declined to comment, and Middle Seat partner Kenneth Pennington did not respond to a request for comment.

events.title: How the midterms swing each party's economic feelings
events.summary: Note: Figures compare average daily sentiment readings over the seven days before each election with the five days after. Election Day is excluded; Data: Morning Consult; Chart: Emily Peck/Axios There was an unusually sharp partisan mood shift in the wake of the midterms, according to sentiment data from Morning Consult that was shared exclusively with Axios. Why it matters: While big partisan swings in consumer sentiment are typical after a presidential election, they have been much smaller in midterm races. The latest numbers show just how tightly Americans' views on the economy are now intertwined with politics. By the numbers: Democratic consumer sentiment rose 6.5 points in the five days after the election compared with the week before, while Republicans' mood fell 6.4 points. How it works: Morning Consult's index considers survey responses from approximately 5,000 U.S. adults. They're asked five questions, including on people's personal finances and financial outlook, as well as their views on overall business conditions. Zoom in: The biggest shifts in sentiment were in respondents' feelings about the future. Republicans' outlook across all five metrics fell after the election. Their confidence in business conditions over the next five years plummeted 12 percentage points. Democrats, meanwhile, had a jump of 9 percentage points in confidence about business conditions (although they remain negative about it) and an even bigger increase — 12 percentage points — in optimism that their own finances would improve over the next year. Of note: Both sides were more negative about their own finances compared with a year ago. Zoom out: Overall sentiment, which includes Independents, barely moved — ticking up less than one point, per Morning Consult. The opposing partisan shifts appear to have canceled each other out. Reality check: It's early days, and sentiment could shift quickly. Between the lines: Consumer sentiment was once a telling measure of how people would actually spend their money: Good vibes meant more spending. Lately, it's looked more like a political measure. "Sentiment matters because it's vibes," says Eli Yokley, a U.S. politics analyst at Morning Consult.

events.title: Alex Karp Said He’s a ‘Progressive.’ OK! Here’s Some Other Stuff He’s Said Recently
events.summary: When Palantir chief executive Alex Karp sat down with Politico this week, he reportedly used the word “progressive” eight times to describe both his political philosophy and his company . “I’ve been a Democrat my whole life,” Karp told Politico, which noted that he called the Democratic Party “ totally irresponsible ” in the distant time of October 2025. “I know more about being a progressive than almost anybody on the planet, and I absolutely believe Palantir—all of our products are essentially progressive.” This isn’t the first time Karp has called himself a progressive. In 2018, The New York Times reported that Karp described himself as such. In the same article, he claimed to have voted for Hillary Clinton. Karp has also donated money to Democratic candidates. In 2023, for instance, he donated $360,000 to a joint fundraising committee for Joe Biden and Kamala Harris. The next year, he donated $1 million to MAGA, Inc. Palantir has a share of supporters from the Democratic party. However, it’s not necessarily clear how the products of Palantir—a company that built the technology that underpins much of the Trump administration's brutal arrest and deportation campaign, sold tools to the US military that can use generative AI to help plan and execute drone strikes, and partnered with the Israeli military to assist in its devastating war on the Gaza strip, among other things—could reasonably be seen as progressive. It’s instructive, then, to look at what else Karp has said in recent weeks, and how it lines up with his idea of what’s “progressive.” In his most recent quarterly letter to Palantir shareholders, Karp actually doubled down on his basic premise. In it, he argued that Palantir employees are “the pioneers of a genuine and viable antiwar movement.” “We are all, in no uncertain terms, living through what John Lewis Gaddis, the professor of naval and military history at Yale, presciently described decades ago as the long peace ,” Karp wrote, despite the fact that the US and Iran are currently engaged in direct warfare. During Palantir’s corresponding earnings call on November 2, Karp was asked to clarify the statements in his letter. “Our products are built to avoid war, meaning the adversary knows that they will have such pain inflicted upon them that in fact it's not worth going to war,” Karp said. He did not, however, address the relevant possibility that the US is the party that initiates war. “I grew up as a lefty,” Karp continued. “I don't actually like war. I want to avoid war. I don't support wars.” But he said, “Sometimes they are necessary, and when they are necessary, America and its allies need the very, very, very best tools.” Karp went on to say that Palantir has both a “moral imperative” and a “mission reason” for having the “somewhat crazy aspiration” of dominating its market. That mission, Karp said, is supporting the war fighter. Conveniently, it’s also very profitable. “We are delighted that we can support the war fighter even more because we're making so much money,” Karp said. Karp’s recent comments in Politico could also be seen through the lens of convenience. Democrats will have a majority in both chambers of Congress next year, and since about half of Palantir’s revenue comes from government work, it’s pragmatic to sow goodwill. Palantir has seen continued success, after all, across Democratic and Republican administrations. However, Karp doesn’t care about cultivating favor with everybody. events.title: Murders plunge 15% in America's biggest cities
events.summary: Data: Major Cities Chiefs Association (MCCA) ; Note: Tulsa Police changed crime-reporting systems, which may affect year-over-year comparisons.; Chart: Russell Contreras/Axios Homicides fell 15.2% across major U.S. police jurisdictions through the first nine months of 2026, extending a retreat from pandemic-era violence that began under President Biden and continues under President Trump . The big picture: A new Major Cities Chiefs Association report found declines in all four major violent-crime categories among 66 reporting U.S. large law enforcement agencies from January through September, compared with the same period last year. Homicides dropped 15.2%. Robberies fell 9.1%. Rapes declined 3.5%. Aggravated assaults decreased 3.4%. State of play: Combined, the four categories fell 4.9% — or 13,822 fewer reported offenses. Fifty-one of the 66 agencies reported overall declines. Homicides dropped in 49 jurisdictions, increased in 15 and remained unchanged in two. Zoom in: Some of the nation's largest cities recorded striking homicide declines. Memphis: Homicides plunged 36.5%, from 156 to 99. San Antonio was down 36.5%, Indianapolis down 33.6%, Philadelphia down 21.2%, Aurora, Colorado down 65.2% and Newark, New Jersey down 59.1%. The other side: New York City was a major outlier and reported more violent crime in all four categories, including 24.5% more homicides and 14.2% more robberies. Its combined violent crime total was up 5.1%. San Diego reported 45.2% more homicides and Las Vegas recorded a 23.4% jump. Washington, D.C., saw homicides fall 29.9%, but robberies surged 41.1%, pushing its combined violent-crime total up 9.7%. The caveat: The figures remain preliminary. Houston reported no data because of a records-system transition, and Tulsa recently transitioned to a new crime reporting system, the report notes.

events.title: Orbit Global Menu: A working global menu addon for GNOME
events.summary: A new extension brings a working global menu bar to the GNOME desktop, even for some apps that don’t have menu bars at all. Orbit Global Menu is a new GNOME extension that gives the GNOME desktop a feature it was intentionally designed without, and one that some users miss very badly – this vulture being one of them. It adds a working global menu bar to the GNOME top panel. We suspect this is something that will cause strongly contrasting opinions among many GNOME users: some will by puzzled why anyone would bother, while others may think "at last!" and rush to try it. There have been other attempts to do this before, and the Reg FOSS desk has tried several of them, but we never found one that worked with the majority of applications. Our fondness for this UI feature was visible in the two-part series we wrote in September on how to customize Xfce and then in part two how to get the global menu working with more apps. The problem is getting worse over time, as in recent versions (since GNOME 40 and Gtk4), the GNOME human-interface guidelines encourage smartphone-style hamburger menus, replacing the traditional horizontal menu bar. It is tricky to add global menu bar support to apps that lack a menu bar, but Orbit's developer "Unmade" found a rather labor-intensive solution. The menu bar applet contains maps of keyboard controls for 292 different apps, so it can show a menu all on its own and then send those apps simulated keystrokes to operate it. It's not the programs' full menu trees, just a subset of them, but it works. It's also not the most elegant solution, but it is a solution and it works. We tried it on Ubuntu 26.10 and every app in the full install worked to at least some extent. If you are willing and able to build and install a small additional connector, it lets the global-menu applet talk to lots more applications. The GNOME shell is unusual among open source desktop environments, to an extent that we have criticized before. GNOME Shell was designed with a distinctive look and feel of its own, unlike almost all other desktops. It has a minimalist, stripped-down layout that doesn't look or work quite like anything else, and it's intentionally not very customizable. To change how GNOME works means writing new Javascript code, then packaging it as an extension that users can install from the GNOME Extensions website. This requires both a browser extension and a "native host messaging" connector to be installed into the underlying OS – or a purpose-written app. By default, the desktop comes with neither. The end result is that GNOME lends a visual identity to the Linux desktop, one that is clear and distinct from either Windows or macOS. (Back in 2013, this vulture argued that when Microsoft threatened to sue multiple Linux vendors over infringing Windows UI patents, some 20 years ago, this UI fragmentation was just what the company wanted .) GNOME 2 was the Linux world's default desktop. GNOME Shell was controversial in its early days, and lost pole position, but it has since won it back. Today, GNOME is the default desktop on all the major distros: Ubuntu, Fedora and Red Hat Enterprise Linux and the RHELatives, as well as Debian and SUSE, all default to GNOME. GNOME does away with a lot of features that are significant functional parts of other graphical desktops. For instance, it has no desktop icons, no system tray or defined place for status indicators, and neither GNOME nor GNOME-compliant applications have menu bars, either inside windows (Microsoft style) or in the top panel (Apple macOS style). This is disorienting and confusing for those used to controlling software mainly using their menus – but now, that's mainly older hands. This design suits those who grew up on smartphones and tablets, or who feel more comfortable with their stripped-back keyboardless UI than a full desktop WIMP, which can be overwhelming to newbies and non-techies. If you've followed the evolution of graphical desktops for some 40 years, as this gray-plumed vulture has, some trends are very apparent that aren't so clear if you came in once evolution was underway. Apple introduced the first global menu bar in the Lisa, and improved on that in the Macintosh. DR GEM copied it very early on , but Apple sued and DR changed the PC version of GEM to be less Mac-like. Microsoft's Windows came along after this, and moved menu bars inside windows instead. When Apple acquired NeXT in 1996 , it moved NeXTstep's patent-avoidant vertical menus back to a global bar at the top, along with the clock and some status indicators. There they remain, 30 years later. In 2007, it launched the iPhone, containing a very cut-down OS based on OS X, replacing the Finder with a cut-down version of the Dashboard layer from OS X 10.4 . The panel remained, shorn of its menus, which were too fiddly for a small screen. As The Register mentioned in 2017 , in its preliminary releases, Android started out as a keypad-driven Java phone that looked and worked very much like BlackBerry. When the iPhone appeared, Google changed course . The new Android UI resembled iOS, complete with that top panel, still without menus. GNOME 3.0 was not far behind: in 2009 the team promised a revamp of the user experience, and in 2011, launched GNOME 3.0. It too has the fixed top panel — now huge on a laptop or desktop landscape screen – and mostly empty. Now that top panel regains its original 1983 function. We're rather impressed by the Orbit global menu. It does the job, and it even works with apps that don't have menu bars. It's not perfect: for instance, over-long menus have to scroll, and may fail to do so if new submenus appear. The GitHub repository has extensive instructions, including how to build and install the optional connector module that lets more apps export their real menus to the extension. It also tells you how to instruct some apps, notably Firefox, that there is a global menu for it to use. We are saddened to note that, as is so often the case, Wayland gets in the way here. It works rather well with some other extensions, too. With a menu bar, GNOME's strangely centered clock seems out of place, but several extensions, such as F rippery Move Clock , shove it over to the right where we still feel it belongs. If you prefer a lighter-colored panel and dock, it also plays nicely with Blur my Shell . ®

events.title: FCA proposes greater pension investment flexibility to support long-term value for savers
events.summary: Workplace pension providers could have greater flexibility to invest for the long term under proposals from the FCA, helping them deliver better outcomes for savers while ensuring savers' interests remain protected. The FCA is consulting on excluding certain performance-linked fees from the charge cap for default funds in workplace pensions it regulates.Performance-linked fees are common in private markets, including private equity, venture capital and private credit. The proposed change would give providers greater flexibility to access a broader range of investments where this could help improve long-term returns and value for savers.The FCA is clear that greater flexibility is not a licence to charge more. Providers should carefully weigh potential returns, risks and costs when making investment decisions, and any higher charges should be justified by the additional value delivered to savers.Alongside the proposed flexibility, the FCA is proposing safeguards covering transparency, fair allocation of fees between savers and scrutiny of how private assets are valued. Providers and Independent Governance Committees would need access to the information necessary to assess whether performance-linked fees offer value for money.Therese Chambers, executive director of enforcement and market integrity at the FCA, said: 'People's pension savings should work hard for them. We want providers to have greater choice over how they invest for the long term where this can deliver better outcomes for savers.'But greater flexibility is not a licence to charge more. Any higher charges must be justified by additional value, with firms carefully weighing returns, risks and costs when deciding what is in savers' best interests.'The proposals would bring FCA rules more closely into line with the regime for trust-based pension schemes, where certain performance-linked fees have been excluded from the charge cap since 2023.Greater alignment would support competition and choice and reduce unnecessary complexity for providers operating across both parts of the market.The proposals would give providers an option, not an obligation, to use the exemption. Providers should do so only where it is in savers' interests, and they can meet the relevant protections.The FCA is seeking responses by 14 January 2027 and currently expects to make final rules in summer 2027 following consideration of feedback.Notes to editorsThe consultation is open until Thursday 14 January 2027. Read CP26/40: Exempting performance fees from the workplace pensions charge cap.This work is a priority under the FCA's Pensions Regulatory Priorities (PDF) and forms part of the wider pensions reform.In 2023, the Government changed the rules so certain performance fees sit outside the limit on charges, with protections for members. The proposals build on changes made for trust-based schemes in 2023, while reflecting developments in private markets and strengthening protections in areas such as how investments are valued.The FCA enables a fair and thriving financial services market for the good of consumers and the economy. Find out more about the FCA .

events.title: More Than Numbers: Portraits of U.S. Citizens Detained by Immigration Agents
events.summary: The Department of Homeland Security says it’s not detaining Americans.  In written statements, it has said that “allegations that ICE is arresting and deporting U.S. citizens is FALSE.” It has said that “when individuals are briefly questioned under ‘reasonable suspicion’ and are found to be U.S. citizens, they are immediately released.” And it has said that “U.S. citizen agitators are only held while they actively remain a safety threat to our officers and the public.” But ProPublica has identified more than 500 citizens detained since President Donald Trump returned to office. They are not just numbers.  Among them is an elderly car wash owner whom agents repeatedly knocked to the ground as they detained several of his workers. A 6-year-old whose mother says still has nightmares after agents pointed guns at him and his siblings. A high school senior who was detained after she tried to stop officers from questioning her autistic younger brother. A dad who was held for several days and missed his daughter’s third birthday.  Over the past year, several of these people shared the lingering effects of what happened to them with ProPublica. Ana Michelle Ramirez Sanan In their own neighborhood Photographed at their home in a Boston suburb “We have so much trauma just from the 30 minutes we were held.” Ana Michelle Ramirez Sanan In September 2025, Ana Michelle Ramirez Sanan learned that ICE agents had intercepted members of her family as they drove one of her uncles to a court hearing. Ramirez Sanan, then 17, said she rushed to the scene and discovered agents had broken the car windows and pulled her two uncles, her mother and her younger brother out. Video of the incident showed agents kicking and slamming Ramirez Sanan’s mother to the ground and then twisting her arms to handcuff her. Ramirez Sanan said she saw other agents questioning her brother against a fence, threatening to arrest him if he couldn’t prove he had legal status. Both she and her brother are citizens. “Him being a 13-year-old with autism, he doesn’t understand these things like we do. He didn’t know what ‘a legal status’ is. He’s not able to tell them: ‘Yes, I have a legal status. I’m born here,’” Ramirez Sanan said. She said that when she rushed toward her mom and brother, begging agents to let them go, they detained her. “It was really scary thinking that they might have taken us and deported us to Guatemala, where we don’t have anything.” DHS said that its agents intercepted the car in order to detain the uncle who was going to court that day, and that they “used the appropriate force necessary.” He was facing charges of sexual assault on a child and remains in ICE custody. He has pleaded not guilty.  As for Ramirez Sanan, her mother and her brother, they were released the day of the incident. Her mother, who has lived in the United States for 20 years and has a green card, was treated at a hospital for a concussion, bruising and nerve damage in one of her arms.  DHS denies that they were ever detained. “We have so much trauma just from the 30 minutes we were held,” said Ramirez Sanan, who struggled with anxiety and depression after the incident. “I lost my whole senior year fighting this. My brother isn’t the same either.” Andrea Velez On her way to work Photographed in Los Angeles In June 2025, Andrea Velez was dropped off at work at a shoe company in downtown Los Angeles and inadvertently walked into an immigration raid on street vendors. She said one of the masked agents rushed toward her, grabbed her and slammed her to the pavement. Velez said she attempted to shield herself with her work bag.  “Throughout the whole time, I kept saying I was a U.S. citizen,” Velez recalled, saying that agents called her an “alleged U.S. citizen” even after they checked her ID. “They kept saying how many ‘bodies they got’ that day.” Velez said that she was detained for two days, and that she was denied an opportunity to call family or a lawyer for most of that time. The government charged Velez with assault. DHS said she “made physical contact” with agents and tried to impede them. A judge ultimately dismissed the case.  After her arrest, Velez said she was so afraid of being detained again that she worked remotely and avoided going outside. Quentin Williams At the end of his school day as a teaching assistant Photographed in Inver Grove Heights, Minnesota In January, not long after immigration agents in Minneapolis had shot and killed an American woman named Renee Good, Quentin Williams, a teaching assistant at nearby Roosevelt High School, was guiding students toward buses when more agents arrived outside his building. Williams said that agents began confronting students and staff. At some point during the commotion, he said, the agents threw him to the ground and choked him so hard he couldn’t breathe. “They didn’t even know what they were doing — just kind of being reckless [with] assault rifles out and pepper-spraying staff after they took me down,” Williams recalled.  Agents drove Williams to the Bishop Henry Whipple Federal Building, where they detained him for several hours. Later, then-Attorney General Pam Bondi published his photo on her social media accounts, describing him as a “Minnesota rioter.” Federal authorities issued a warrant for his arrest for assaulting officers. The charges against him were eventually dismissed, and he’s filed a claim against the government for damages over his arrest.  Williams said he’s still haunted by the idea that he came close to meeting the same fates as Good and George Floyd, who was killed by a Minneapolis police officer in 2020. “I didn’t leave the house for at least up to a week,” he said. “I felt lucky to be alive.” Anabel Romero, John Carter, Juana Rodriguez and their children Attending a horse race In October 2025, some 200 federal agents and local police officers in armored vehicles, a helicopter and on horseback conducted a raid on a racetrack in Wilder, Idaho, and detained hundreds of people, including dozens of children . Among them ProPublica identified at least 30 U.S. citizens. Photographed at a park in Meridian, Idaho Anabel Romero had left her kids eating in the car while she went to look at the horses. They were on opposite sides of the track when the raid began.  Romero said the agents wore camouflage and had their guns drawn. She had no idea who they were. So she ran and tried to hide. “They didn’t identify themselves,” Romero said. “I didn’t know who they were.”  She said unidentified officers tackled her, zip-tied her and threatened to “fucking blow your head off.” On the other side of the track, Romero’s 14-year-old daughter, SueHey Tello, said officers surrounded their car, pointing guns at her brother, 6, and sister, 8. events.title: Some Democrats push to keep House’s China committee
events.summary: As House Democrats debate the future of the select committee on China, some in their party are arguing for keeping it around. “If you want to be able to look at the comprehensive issues facing the US-China relationship, there is not a single committee that covers all of it. It’s spread all over. So this puts it in one single committee,” said Rep. Greg Stanton, D-Ariz., who hails from a more centrist wing of the party and sits on the select panel now. Some progressive groups led by Just Foreign Policy are mobilizing to defend it, too, after Semafor reported some lawmakers were lobbying to kill it . A letter from the groups shared with Semafor praises the “different approach” from Rep. Ro Khanna, D-Calif., its current top Democrat. “We believe Democratic leadership now has an important opportunity to build on this progress and demonstrate a more responsible and constructive approach to US-China relations,” it states. There’s a bipartisan push to save the committee as members consult House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries on its future. He told reporters Wednesday the discussions with committee leaders and the caucus on the future of the China select panel and a proposed AI select committee were “ongoing.” Rep. Greg Meeks, D-N.Y., the top Foreign Affairs Committee Democrat, who favors folding the select panel under his committee, has been pushing to make it a “special” committee under House Foreign Affairs, a person familiar with the talks said. That would mean it would resemble a Foreign Affairs subcommittee that off-committee members could still join. Republicans made a similar move last Congress, putting a committee on the “Weaponization of the Federal Government” under the Judiciary Committee rather than standing up a separate panel. “We will follow the lead of the incoming speaker on how he wants to handle the China select committee, but the Foreign Affairs Committee is well poised to conduct oversight of this administration’s China policy,” a spokesperson for Meeks said.

events.title: Some Democrats want to pump the brakes on Hegseth impeachment
events.summary: Some top Democrats want to pump the brakes on impeaching Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth next year after this week’s attempt came up short. “We have a very difficult set of decisions to make and I don’t think we should hastily make them,” said Rep. Adam Smith, D-Wash., the top Armed Services Democrat. He worries the party could get stuck in internecine conflict after a sizable number of Democratic absences on the impeachment procedural vote caused hand-wringing this week, which could take attention away from cost-of-living issues that powered their midterm gains. “Strategically and tactically, what’s going to best advance our agenda? And I worry that what you saw yesterday is a preview of one of our biggest challenges,” Smith added. With plenty in the caucus pushing for a Hegseth impeachment, though, another lawmaker could force a vote next Congress — whether Democratic leaders want it or not. House Minority Whip Katherine Clark told Democrats in a closed-door meeting Wednesday morning that the party had disappointed the American people by not having all of the members there for the impeachment vote, and that it was their job to show up for the people who sent them there, according to people familiar with her comments. Still, Democrats, including Clark, note that they likely couldn’t have won the vote, given the lack of GOP defections beyond Rep. Thomas Massie, R-Ky., who introduced the resolution. Nearly a dozen Democrats missed the vote Tuesday referring the impeachment articles to the Judiciary Committee, with Democratic lawmakers blaming traffic and scheduling conflicts , among other issues. Looking ahead to the next Congress, top Democrats plan to conduct investigations into Hegseth on their own terms, rather than letting their hand be forced early. “I think we should do oversight and investigations under our own timetable, not Tom Massie’s,” said Rep. Jim Himes, D-Conn., the top Intelligence Committee Democrat. “And I’d really like to see affordability stay at the center of the agenda.” Still, others wanted to keep impeachment in mind. “Everything’s on the table there. I don’t think there’s a single Democrat or a lot of Republicans that think that Hegseth is qualified for the job and has done the job well,” said Rep. Greg Meeks, D-N.Y., the top Foreign Affairs Committee Democrat.

events.title: Nvidia fallout could hamper US-China trade talks
events.summary: The fallout from Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang’s affair with a suspected Chinese spy may complicate US-China trade talks at next week’s APEC summit, where President Donald Trump is slated to meet with Chinese leader Xi Jinping. That’s because the ordeal has heightened bipartisan scrutiny of the administration’s handling of export controls on AI chips, just months before Democrats assume control of Congress. “Up until this point in time, Trump and the Republican Party had full control over what to do with export controls,” Bloomberg analyst Michael Deng, a former Commerce Department official, told Semafor. “The issue going into APEC is the Chinese side is going to know that Trump may not necessarily be able to hold any commitments he makes.” China, which agreed this week to extend the current truce until January, is already seeking to exploit the GOP’s midterm losses. Deng predicted subsequent extensions “will get progressively harder to negotiate,” noting that lawmakers are already debating including multiple export-control proposals in defense legislation. “We already didn’t expect much from many of the previous meetings,” Deng said. “You could probably expect even less coming into this, because now the US side can’t even make true commitments to preserve the status quo.” US Trade Representative Jamieson Greer said in September that negotiators had taken export controls “off the table” as a “national security issue.” Some doubted that Democrats would focus their new power on US-China trade over juicier priorities, like investigating the Trump family. “It’s probably too early to tell” given “there’s going to be a lot of things on the Democrats’ priority list,” Caleb Max, CEO of the National Artificial Intelligence Association, said. “Do people go vote against Republicans because they didn’t like the [Nvidia] H200 [chips] getting sold to Shenzhen? Probably not.” — Eleanor Mueller

events.title: Democrats mire themselves in Schumer debate after landslide win
events.summary: The News Some Democrats say they won’t vote for Chuck Schumer to be Democrat leader. Others are declining to endorse him publicly as Sen. Chris Van Hollen, D-Md., weighs a challenge and dials up colleagues. But a confident Schumer is acting like he’s staying put. And many of his colleagues are itching to skip the Democratic infighting altogether and reach the moment when Schumer is reelected Democratic leader on Dec. 1. “Schumer has been an unpopular figure among people who don’t understand the role of the Senate party leader. And I think it probably helped them on the trail,” Sen. Sheldon Whitehouse, D-R.I., told Semafor. “It’s not the first time that a Senate leader has helped elected members who have opposed his leadership.” He said he was confident when all is said and done, Schumer will emerge as the victor. Schumer is, too. The New York senator has asserted repeatedly he’ll be the majority leader again next year. And in a sign of that confidence, he’s already plotting out a unified Democratic agenda with House Democratic Leader Hakeem Jeffries. He spent his Wednesday doing things that only a returning leader would: meeting with incoming newly-elected senators like Rep. Chris Pappas, D-N.H., and Sen.-elect Adam Hamilton, D-Kan., to discuss their priorities and what committees they’d like to serve on. Schumer is not acting like a guy who is short of the votes. Hamilton has called for new party leadership and told Semafor that Schumer didn’t ask him to reconsider that demand during their sitdown on Wednesday: “No, he didn’t at all, actually.” “We talked about being overwhelmed when you’re first getting into this and talked about stories, things that matter, committees,” Hamilton said. Path to victory Schumer recruited a number of strong Democratic candidates, including former Sen. Sherrod Brown of Ohio, former Gov. Roy Cooper of North Carolina, and former Rep. Mary Peltola of Alaska (who is ahead of Sen. Dan Sullivan, R-Alaska, in a race that has yet to be called). Still, there’s no question that the core of the Democratic Caucus is changing and Schumer has to adapt to it. Whitehouse is from the class of 2006, the year of Schumer’s first big Senate triumph, when he flipped the chamber as party campaign chair. He then achieved a stunning 60-seat majority two years later. Those Democrats were the bulwark of Schumer’s political power as he became leader in 2017, and his support remains strong within the caucus even as his reputation has eroded outside the Capitol. And despite Schumer’s relentless fundraising on candidates’ behalf and candidate recruitment, the class of 2026 has its own ideas. The Schumer-aligned Senate Majority PAC and its affiliates spent $67 million in Michigan, $65 million in Maine, and $14 million in Kansas, only to see those senators say they do not support him. “We have a lot of new voices coming into the Senate and folks who have been on the ground hearing directly from their constituents about how frustrated they are. So we just have to make sure that leadership recognizes the urgency of this moment,” said Sen.-elect Peggy Flanagan, D-Minn. “We’ll see who decides to step in,” she added, calling Van Hollen “fantastic.” Schumer also has moves to make to reshape his caucus. He may elevate progressive Sen. Elizabeth Warren, D-Mass., to a more prominent leadership position as Sen. Amy Klobuchar, D-Minn., prepares to be sworn in as governor of her state. Sen. Adam Schiff, D-Calif., a vocal critic of President Donald Trump who was elected to the Senate in 2024, is also making calls about a position in leadership. So far, no one besides Sen. Kirsten Gillibrand, D-N.Y., is raising their hand to be chair of the Democratic Senatorial Campaign Committee — a position appointed by the party leader. Gillibrand just enjoyed a wildly successful 2026 cycle. And most importantly, Schumer will have to decide whether he will run for another six-year term as senator in 2028. Votes in hand Even as a number of Democrats like Sens. Raphael Warnock, D-Ga., and Mark Warner, D-Va., decline to publicly back Schumer, Democrats believe Schumer’s private commitments range far beyond his public ones. The long windup to the Dec. 1 leadership election, which is conducted by secret ballot, offers little upside for members with national ambitions to endorse Schumer early. But even so, a number of Democrats are still publicly backing him. Brown, who was first ushered into the Senate in 2006, says he’ll support Schumer after Schumer-aligned groups spent an eye-watering $150 million in Ohio. Sen. Angus King of Maine, an independent who caucuses with Democrats, said on CNN that expects the caucus to unite around Schumer. Sen. Tammy Baldwin, D-Wis., said she’ll back Schumer, as did Sen. Richard Blumenthal, D-Conn. “When the manager takes you to the World Series, you give him another contract,” added Sen. Ruben Gallego, D-Ariz. And Schumer is already plotting out next year’s schedule. Senate and House Democrats are planning fast legislative action on potentially bipartisan bills by picking up the four or more Republican Senate votes they need to pass legislation. If Republicans block those bills, Jeffries and Schumer would move more quickly to party-line budget reconciliation legislation that can reach Trump’s desk. If Schumer were somehow dislodged as leader, the new Democratic majority would be way behind the eight-ball. Room for Disagreement As Gallego and Gillibrand lauded Schumer this week, Sen. Bernie Sanders, I-Vt., announced he can’t support him, while Sen. Elissa Slotkin, D-Mich., said she’s a no until she gets a “concrete plan” from a Democratic leadership candidate. Sanders called for a “vigorous debate about the direction of the Democratic Party” to show voters the party is changing. And Van Hollen criticized Schumer and Gillibrand’s electoral approach, accusing them of siding “with the crypto industry and AIPAC” in their candidate endorsements. Burgess’s view After their biggest victory since post-Watergate, Democrats are spending weeks picking apart Schumer and, to a lesser extent, Jeffries. That’s not exactly the thank-you one might expect after winning the largest Senate majority since 2010. Not to mention that Schumer is still being second-guessed for not spending more in Florida and Louisiana, on Senate races that ended up closer than expected. Talk about a thankless job. The infighting could extend for weeks if Van Hollen runs against him. Schumer would be the heavy favorite, but it would be an unwanted distraction for Democrats ahead of 2027. But for now, Schumer is the only one who wants the job. As Senate GOP Leader John Thune found out this week, your critics lose steam pretty quick if they can’t put up an opposition candidate.

events.title: Asian shares slip as Nvidia's troubles weigh on AI stocks, despite a rally on Wall St
events.summary: European benchmarks are mostly higher after Asian benchmarks finished lower, as concerns over leadership at chipmaker Nvidia weigh on artificial intelligence-related stocks TOKYO -- World shares were mixed on Thursday as concerns over leadership at chipmaker Nvidia weighed on artificial intelligence -related stocks. In after-hours trading, Nvidia’s shares fell 8.6% after reports said Nvidia’s board was meeting late Wednesday to discuss the situation surrounding its CEO, Jensen Huang, whose affair with a Chinese woman has raised national security concerns in the U.S. Nvidia 's shares climbed 2.9% on Wednesday. Its shares have fallen after the company said it was investigating Huang, who has admitted to a relationship with a businesswoman who reportedly fed intelligence and advanced chips to China. The future for the S & P 500 slipped 0.4%, while that for the Dow Jones Industrial Average was nearly unchanged. In early European trading, France's CAC 40 added 0.7% and the German DAX rose 1.0% to 26,939.92. Britain's FTSE 100 jumped 0.3% to 10,868.98. In Asian trading, Japan's benchmark Nikkei 225 shed 0.7% to 60,819.36. In South Korea, the Kospi gave up early gains to slip 0.6% to 5,342.73. Taiwan's Taiex lost 2.6%. Australia's S & P/ASX 200 declined nearly 0.1% to 9,146.80. Hong Kong's Hang Seng lost 1.3% to 24,008.55, while the Shanghai Composite fell 0.7% to 3,655.83. Apart from Nvidia's situation, investors are worried about a potential slowdown in the overall AI industry given longstanding questions about whether it will prove profitable enough to make massive investments in the technology worthwhile. This week, we welcome you to a London hotel where you could check out its admin credentials for a booking website just by walking past the front desk. Our story comes courtesy of Neycho Tepavicharov, co-founder of Flashcloud, a Delaware-based web hosting company. He was staying at a hotel in London when he noticed a shocking breach of basic security protocols by management, who were a little too hospitable with their credentials. As he was passing through the lobby, Tepavicharov noticed that the door behind the front desk was open and, inside that back room, there was a whiteboard. On the whiteboard, written in plain English, were the hotel’s Booking.com administrative username and password. Anyone near the desk could clearly see the login information, and if they didn’t have time to write it down, they could have snapped a picture for later use. As Tepavicharov explains, there’s plenty of mischief you could perform with these credentials. “With that login, someone could change or cancel reservations, see guests’ names and contact details, or message guests pretending to be the hotel,” he said. “Fake 'please confirm your payment' messages sent from compromised hotel accounts are a well-known scam.” An attacker could potentially exploit that access to disrupt hotel operations or target guests with convincing scams. Whether the exposed credentials alone would have been enough to access the account would depend on its security settings. Tepavicharov decided to play the role of good samaritan and warn the hotel’s manager that the business was endangering itself by showing everyone its password. Have a story about someone leaving a gaping hole in their network? Share it with us at pwned@sitpub.com . Anonymity is available upon request. “I asked to speak with the manager and showed him what I’d seen. He was mortified and very grateful,” Tepavicharov said. “Nobody on staff had thought of it as a risk. It was just the easiest way for the whole team to share one login.” After Tepavicharov talked to the manager, not only did the hotel change its ways, but it also moved its website to his hosting service, Flashcloud. Tepavicharov notes that there are plenty of takeaways from this incident. Most important: give each user dedicated credentials with their own separate login, and use multi-factor authentication. “The lesson is an old one, but it keeps happening,” he said. “Shared logins end up written somewhere convenient. Give each staff member their own login, turn on two-factor authentication, and keep passwords in a password manager, not on the wall.” ® Jensen Huang's self-sabotage sends Nvidia into a midlife crisis The competition is circling like vultures Palantir’s Karp takes a sharp left turn, says he and the company’s products are actually ‘progressive’ Trump donor says he privately questioned deportation tactics. events.title: Singapore life insurers pay out more than $15 billion in first nine months of 2026
events.summary: A further $1.7 billion was paid out under individual life policies for critical illness, death and total permanent disability. Singapore life insurers paid out more than "$15 billion" in the first nine months of 2026. Maturity benefits made up 74%, while health, critical illness, death and disability claims also rose. New business premiums increased 15% to "$5.5 billion". Investment-linked policies led growth, reaching 46% of total sales, as buyers sought savings, investment and protection. LIA Singapore said it is working with the Monetary Authority of Singapore to improve ILP disclosures. It also plans regular reviews of critical illness rules to keep cover "meaningful, affordable and accessible". SINGAPORE – Life insurers in Singapore paid out more than $15 billion in insurance claims and maturity benefits in the first nine months of 2026. Policy maturities accounted for the bulk of payouts, followed by claims for healthcare and other forms of insurance protection. Maturity benefits comprised about 74% of total payouts, or $11.2 billion, while claims under individual health policies amounted to some $2.2 billion, according to figures released by the Life Insurance Association (LIA) Singapore on Nov 12. A further $1.7 billion was paid out under individual life policies for critical illness, death and total permanent disability. Critical illness claims alone amounted to $756 million. Of the $2.2 billion in health insurance claims, $2.1 billion came from Integrated Shield Plans (IPs) and their riders, with IP riders accounting for 24.1%. The remaining $115.2 million was paid under other medical plans and riders. Claims under IPs and their riders rose 6.7% quarter on quarter, from $695.1 million in the second quarter to $742 million in the third quarter . Investment-linked policies gain share Separately, the industry recorded a 15% year-on-year increase in total weighted new business premiums in the first nine months of 2026 to $5.5 billion, a rise that LIA attributed to strong economic momentum. In the third quarter alone, weighted new business premiums rose 4.2% year on year to $1.8 billion. Investment-linked policies (ILPs) accounted for an increasingly large share of new business. New business weighted premiums from ILPs rose 22.6% year on year to $2.5 billion in the first nine months. ILPs made up 46% of the industry’s total, up from 43% in the same period the prior year and 37 % in 2024. Their share reached 49.7% in the third quarter , compared with 42.7% in the first quarter and 44.9% in the second quarter . LIA Singapore president Wong Sze Keed said the growing share of ILPs suggests that consumers are placing a greater emphasis on savings and investment priorities, alongside meeting their protection needs. “For some, access to professionally managed funds and financial advice may be part of the appeal,” she said. The industry is working closely with the Monetary Authority of Singapore to strengthen disclosures through product highlight sheets and help customers better understand the overall costs and benefits of ILPs, she added. Participating policies also recorded growth, with weighted new business premiums rising 5.7% year on year to $1.2 billion. These plans provide insurance protection, while policyholders may receive non-guaranteed bonuses or dividends depending on the performance of the insurer’s participating fund. They accounted for 23% of total weighted new business premiums, down from 25% in 2025 . As of September, about three million people in Singapore were covered by IPs. Including other medical plans and riders, around 3.4 million people were covered by individual health insurance. Wong said the industry will continue reviewing how insurance responds to evolving healthcare needs and developments in medical care, including through regular reviews of the critical illness framework and how definitions take into account the seriousness of an illness and developments in its treatment. “This is balanced against the implications for coverage and premiums, with the aim of keeping protection meaningful, affordable and accessible over the long term,” she said. events.title: Nvidia’s Asian supply chain prepares for life after Jensen Huang
events.summary: Jensen Huang has built strong networks in both Taiwan and South Korea, with companies such as TSMC, SK Hynix and Samsung. Nvidia’s board is meeting on Nov 11 to decide Jensen Huang’s future after reports of two extramarital affairs. Asian suppliers are preparing for possible leadership change. Huang built strong ties with TSMC, Foxconn, Wistron and South Korean partners. He drove major AI deals, including a planned US$500 billion (S$642.35 billion) effort with SK Group. Analysts warn his exit could slow aggressive AI investment and weaken Nvidia’s roadmap. Some investors say near-term chip shipments and customer plans should stay stable. TAIPEI/SEOUL – US chip giant Nvidia’s partners and suppliers across Asia, from memory chip powerhouse South Korea to advanced chipmaking hub Taiwan, are redrawing plans in case Chief Executive Jensen Huang is ousted over reports of two extramarital affairs . Nvidia’s board is meeting late on Nov 11 to decide on Huang’s future, a source familiar with the matter told Reuters, in a sharp shift of tactics from Nov 8 , when the board expressed confidence in Huang and his leadership team. “We will support whatever capacity Nvidia needs, but the new CEO may not be as aggressive as Jensen,” said an executive at a Taiwan supplier who feared his company’s expansion could slow if a successor was not as quick to tie up manufacturing capacity. The executive sought anonymity because the subject is a sensitive one. Huang has never anointed a successor, but analysts and investors see two candidates as particularly likely , at least for the short term: Nvidia’s uber-engineer Ian Buck and Chief Financial Officer Colette Kress. Any setback for Huang could deprive the AI industry of one of its most vocal champions. His long-term strategy and direction have turned the chip giant’s swelling cash pile into a war chest to fund companies ranging from AI cloud-computing providers and suppliers to the biggest labs. “Without him at the helm, we will likely see a slowdown in new, aggressive ecosystem-level investments and lucrative bilateral AI infrastructure deals from NVIDIA side,” said Neil Shah, vice-president of research at Counterpoint Research. Built strong supplier network during frequent visits The longtime Nvidia leader has built a strong supplier network in Taiwan during frequent visits to strengthen ties with key manufacturing partners such as TSMC, Foxconn and Wistron. In May, he said Nvidia planned to invest about US$150 billion ( S$192.74 billion ) a year in Taiwan . “He can take technologies his engineers believe are possible and turn them into products the whole company commits resources to, takes risks on, and has to deliver,” said Ming-Chi Kuo, an analyst at TF International Securities. “That’s why the supply chain gets such strong order visibility and is willing to keep up with aggressive spec upgrades. “It also forces competitors to follow, which drives technology upgrades and supply chain investment across the entire AI industry.” TSMC, SK Hynix and Samsung did not immediately respond to requests for comments. In China, AI companies are seeking to secure overseas access to Nvidia chips, concerned that the scandal could spur Washington to tighten curbs on remote access to advanced processors, Reuters reported on Nov 12 . Companies in South Korea, home to key suppliers of the high-bandwidth memory used in Nvidia’s AI chips, were assessing what a leadership change could mean for their expanding ties with the US firm. Nvidia and SK Group, parent of memory chipmaker SK Hynix, are pursuing an AI initiative encompassing large-scale data centres and next-generation chips valued at about US$500 billion. Ties extend beyond chips into robotics In forging and deepening Nvidia’s ties with South Korean business leaders, Huang has extended partnerships beyond semiconductors into robotics and AI factories . He personally sketched a roadmap for collaboration on a whiteboard when Lee Hae-jin, founder of South Korean internet firm Naver, visited the US, the latter said. “We’ve built strong ties with Huang over the years,” said an official at a South Korean chip company with business ties to Nvidia, citing Huang’s accessibility whenever business matters needed to be discussed. “Our biggest question is whether a potential successor would maintain the same favourable relationship with us.” Lian Jye Su, chief analyst at Omdia, said Huang’s exit may shift Nvidia’s long-term direction and any slowdown in its execution or loss of clarity over its product roadmap could give rivals more room to catch up. Still, some investors and analysts expect limited immediate impact from any change of leadership. “The chips Nvidia will ship over the next year or two are already designed and in production, and its customers’ 2027 spending plans don’t depend on who runs the company,” said Armina Rosenberg, portfolio manager and co-founder of Minotaur Capital, which holds Nvidia shares. events.title: Temasek to invest $342m in Godrej Industries’ financial services arm
events.summary: Godrej Capital operates in over 100 cities and has assets under management of S$4.8 billion. Temasek will invest 25 billion rupees (S$342 million) in Godrej Capital, valuing the business at up to 280 billion rupees. Godrej Industries chairman Pirossha Godrej aid the group is aiming for Godrej Capital to reach 1 trillion rupees in assets under management by 2031. The deal adds to strong interest in India’s financial services sector. Godrej Capital, founded in 2020, works in over 100 cities and plans a listing within five years. NEW DELHI – India’s Godrej Industries said on Nov 12 that Singapore’s Temasek Holdings will invest 25 billion rupees (S$342 million) in Godrej Capital through its affiliate, valuing the financial services business at up to 280 billion rupees. Godrej Industries will retain about 80% ownership following the deal. Temasek’s investment in Godrej Capital marks another bet on India’s financial services sector. Temasek also holds a stake in ICICI Bank, India’s second-largest private-sector bank by market capitalisation. The deal adds to a series of large transactions in India’s financial services sector in 2026, including Fairfax Financial Holdings picking up a 60.7% stake in IDBI Bank and Bank of America entering a joint venture to buy 49.9% stake in Jio Credit, the lending arm of Jio Financial Services. “Financial services represents a major long-term growth area of focus for our Group, and our ambition is to build Godrej Capital into a 1 trillion-rupee AUM franchise by 2031,” said Pirojsha Godrej, chairman of Godrej Industries Group. Founded in 2020, Godrej Capital operates in over 100 cities and had assets under management of 350 billion rupees as of Oct 31, 2026. The company, through its subsidiaries, serves businesses and individuals across India with home loans, loans against property, working capital loans, construction finance and personal loans, among others. The investment comes after Godrej Industries said it plans to list the financial services arm in the next five years. REUTERS

events.title: AI helps UK economy grow at fastest pace for more than two years
events.summary: GDP ‘grew robustly’ by 0.7% in third quarter and by 0.2% month on month in September despite high oil prices AI helped the UK defy expectations – but will Britain’s resilience fizzle out? The UK economy grew by 0.7% in the third quarter, its fastest expansion in two and a half years, as the rollout of AI services increased activity. The Office for National Statistics reported that the economy “grew robustly” in the July to September quarter, almost entirely due to strong and widespread growth in the services sector, led by the IT sector. The quarterly growth rate matched economists’ expectations, and was the fastest recorded since the first three months of 2024, when GDP also rose by 0.7%. In a boost to the chancellor, John Healey, the ONS also said the economy grew by 0.2% in September, though the ONS revised down the growth rate in August from 0.1% to zero. September’s data beat forecasts of zero growth in the month. The UK’s information and communication sector grew by 2.1% in the quarter, mainly driven by increases in computer programming, consultancy and related activities. This industry has been the largest driver of GDP growth across 2026, the ONS reported, adding that the businesses related to AI and cloud computing have been reporting the largest increases in turnover. Sarah Coles, the head of personal finance at the investment platform AJ Bell, said AI continued to do “a significant portion of the heavy lifting” in the last quarter. “Since the start of the year, it’s the less visible back-office work that has delivered, with administrative and supportive services seeing strong growth. These areas are benefiting from the increasing adoption of AI,” Coles said. Healey said the UK was showing “standout resilience”. The chancellor added that the economy was growing at the fastest rate in almost 10 years, excluding the time of the Covid-19 pandemic – when lockdown restrictions distorted economic growth. “GDP is up 1.8% so far this year, and pushing at an annualised pace of just above 2.5% – marking the best first three quarters since the pandemic rebound. Strip out the pandemic years and you have to go back to 2017 to find the economy running this hot,” Sanjay Raja, the chief UK economist at Deutsche Bank, said. “Compared to its G7 peers, the UK has relinquished its title as the fastest-growing economy this year to the US, but only just,” Raja added. The services sector proved to be the most important engine of growth over the third quarter of 2026, rising by 0.9%. There was also a positive contribution from the production sector, which grew by 0.1%. It was a sharp drop in construction that dragged down economic growth, even though it only accounts for about 6% of economic activity. Construction work on new projects has fallen more than 7% from mid-2025 while private housebuilding has fallen 30% from its 2022 high. Suren Thiru, the chief economist at the accountancy body ICAEW, said the figures confirmed a “strikingly strong” third quarter as the UK remained resilient to the economic fallout from US-Iran hostilities”. He said it was becoming clear that investments in artificial intelligence were driving the expansion of services sector activity. “The third quarter showcased the continued resilience of households and firms. Businesses ramped up investment amid an AI boom, while stronger consumer spending suggests households continued to draw on savings to support consumption despite rising inflation,” he added. James Smith, an economist at ING, said much of the rise in investment and growth could be traced back to IT and professional services – sectors that have grown rapidly this year despite shedding staff. “IT is very clearly a datacentre story,” he said. “The UK is one of the leading destinations for investment in Europe. And while output here actually fell through August and September, we expect this to remain an area of outperformance in 2027.” Get set for the working day – we'll point you to all the business news and analysis you need every morning The Office for Budget Responsibility said at the time of the budget at the end of October that it expected the economy to expand by 1.2% this year, which already looks out of date as growth continues to exceed expectations. Policymakers at the Bank of England voted last week to raise interest rates by a quarter of a percentage point to 4% to cool inflationary pressures in the economy. Inflation has risen this year mostly in response to higher motor fuel prices, which in the UK have pushed the cost of petrol above £1.70 a litre and diesel towards an average of £2 a litre . The ONS said wholesale electricity prices were about double the level of a year ago. “Automotive fuel prices also remained elevated following increases in recent months, reflecting continued pressures in global energy markets,” it added. Analysts said the strength of the economy could persuade the Bank of England to raise rates when policymakers meet again in December.

events.title: Argentina threatens UK oil firm CEO with jail over Falklands drilling
events.summary: Exclusive: Legal notice comes as Buenos Aires ramps up rhetoric over UK territory and seeks to halt Sea Lion project The Argentinian government threatened a British businessman involved in an offshore Falkland Islands oil project with jail, the Guardian can reveal. Sam Moody, the chief executive of Rockhopper Exploration, and his company’s chief financial officer received the correspondence this autumn as Buenos Aires began ramping up its rhetoric over the British overseas territory. “As recently as 1 September 2026, Argentina wrote to me and Rockhopper’s chief financial officer personally threatening us with criminal prosecution, imprisonment and fines under its domestic legislation,” Moody said. The disclosure was made in a witness statement submitted by the UK to the international tribunal for the law of the sea (Itlos) before two days of hearings that were held this week. The sealed document was made available for viewing after an application by the Guardian. Argentina is seeking an order from Itlos for the urgent suspension of drilling at the Sea Lion offshore oil project north of the Falklands, which is being led by Rockhopper, a British firm, and Navitas, an Israeli company. Buenos Aires has passed domestic legislation criminalising the project and in Moody’s statement to the tribunal, the oil executive also said he believed there was a risk in him engaging with the hearing in Hamburg. “I also want the tribunal to be aware that I, in common with others, [am] taking some personal risk by preparing the statement as I have repeatedly been under threat of criminal prosecution and a custodial sentence in Argentina,” he wrote. Moody’s submission listed a series of other actions taken by Buenos Aires that he said had made it increasingly difficult to finance Sea Lion. They included Argentina banning Navitas from operating in the country for 20 years. It is also claimed that Argentinian officials wrote to Standard Chartered bank, which has a branch in Port Stanley, the capital on the Falklands, urging it to “refrain from participating in oil and gas development in the Falkland Islands to avoid falling within the terms of certain Argentine domestic legislation”. In a further submission to the tribunal, it emerged that Navitas and Rockhopper had not named their partners in court documents for fear that they would be subject to Argentinian retribution. “The names of the contractors engaged by Navitas UK have been witheld to preserve their confidentiality in light of the ongoing scrutiny by Argentine authorities and their ongoing efforts to frustrate the project, including through purported actions directed at contractors and partners involved in the project,” according to a submission made by Ian Ramsay, chief executive of Navitas Petroleum Development and Production. The US firm Halliburton recently issued a statement in which it said it would not conduct any work on the Sea Lion project after discussions with Argentina. Last month, the Guardian revealed that the UK government had written to Interpol seeking reassurance that the international law enforcement agency would not act on any Argentinian “red notices” requesting the arrest of those deemed criminal by Buenos Aires for their involvement in the Falklands economy. Argentina’s application for suspension of the Sea Lion project is based on the claim that Britain’s agreement to drilling is illegal as the sovereignty of the Falkland Islands is a matter of dispute between the UK and Argentina. In 1976, a UN resolution called for the two countries to settle their rival sovereignty claims and to refrain from acting unilaterally to modify the situation in the Falklands. Argentina seeks a temporary suspension of the project before further arbitration, claiming that the oil drilling is “aggravating” the sovereignty dispute. In response, the UK claimed this week that the tribunal did not have jurisdiction in the dispute and that the UN resolution cited was not legally binding. Ellie Reeves, the attorney general for England and Wales, further told the tribunal that the oil project’s suspension would be terminal to its hopes of success with “devastating consequences” for the people on the islands. The Sea Lion project is expected to double the island’s GDP, providing an £8bn uplift in revenues of the Falkland government over the oilfield’s active lifetime. In a further submission to Itlos, Jack Ford, a member and the current chair of the Falkland Islands’ legislative assembly, told the tribunal that the impact of the collapse of the Sea Lion project would “not just be economic but also social, and felt across the whole of the Falkland Islands”. In September, Argentina’s president, Javier Milei, told the UN’s general assembly that reclaiming the sovereignty of the Falklands, known as the Malvinas in Argentina, was a national cause and that Buenos Aires was taking “matters into our own hands” through peaceful means. Argentina invaded the Falklands in 1982.

Not Chaos. AWS New Horizon Digicert Netscout Resources Intelligence Webinars & Events Newsletters SPONSORED POST: Knowing where your data lives is only part of the challenge. Who controls it, who can access it and how quickly you can recover when things go wrong matter just as much. Keeping sensitive data within national borders might satisfy a residency requirement. But does it mean your organization is genuinely in control? Not necessarily. Data could be stored locally while remaining subject to another jurisdiction's laws, dependent on overseas service providers or exposed to disruption beyond your control. For enterprise IT teams, that distinction is becoming harder to ignore. Geopolitical tensions, evolving regulations and the growing use of AI are forcing organizations to reconsider what data sovereignty means in practice. Yet translating those concerns into a workable strategy is another matter. And simply throwing more money at the problem won't necessarily solve it. In The Register's on-demand webinar, Data Sovereignty By Design, moderator Tim Phillips speaks with Patrick Smith, Field CTO for EMEA at Everpure, formerly Pure Storage, about moving beyond compliance checklists and taking a more strategic approach to data control. Drawing on findings from Everpure's research, Smith explores a curious disconnect: organizations are increasing their investment in sovereignty initiatives, yet many still lack a coordinated strategy. Some of the risks attracting the most attention aren't necessarily those receiving the greatest investment. The discussion examines why sovereignty shouldn't be treated as an IT-only responsibility. Decisions about which data needs protection, which services must remain operational and what level of risk is acceptable require input from business leaders, security, procurement and legal teams. There's also the question of priorities. Not every workload needs the same sovereign controls, and attempting to protect everything equally can make an already complicated challenge considerably harder. Smith explains the concept of the "minimum viable company," identifying the critical services, applications and data an organization needs to keep operating through disruption. He also considers why visibility into data access, supplier dependencies and potential exit strategies should influence technology decisions from the outset. For IT leaders trying to turn sovereignty from an abstract boardroom concern into something actionable, the conversation offers useful questions to take back to their organizations. Because knowing where your data sits is one thing. Knowing whether you can maintain control when circumstances change is quite another.
