events.title: Your AI agent is only as good as your endpoint data
events.summary: Every so often a flaw comes along that shows how fast the ground can shift under IT and security teams. PHP2Shell, a pair of critical flaws in PHP, was one of them. Details leaked before the planned disclosure, frontier AI helped researchers find the flaws, and PHP shipped fixes the next day. For many teams, though, the patch was the easy part. So what does it take to respond at that speed, and where should teams begin? What does governed autonomous IT look like in practice? Picture a loop. Software finds where a risk lives and ranks what matters most. It proposes a fix, then, inside limits people define, carries it out and checks that it worked. Routine, low-risk actions can run on their own. Higher-impact ones wait for a person to approve. A few are never handed over at all. Each step leaves a record that someone can review and reverse. What challenges do IT and security teams face today? Three problems keep coming up. The first is visibility. PHP2Shell reportedly sat undetected for more than a decade. For these two flaws, the fix was a version upgrade. The hard part was finding every copy of PHP, including copies bundled inside other software or extracted by hand onto Windows machines that never registered as installed applications. Then teams had to work out which copies the internet could reach and check for signs of earlier attack. An inventory built from a periodic snapshot can't answer those questions on the day they matter. The second is tool-hopping. Answering "where does this run, and can the internet reach it?" often means pivoting across an asset inventory, a vulnerability scanner and an external attack surface tool, each with its own view. Every hop adds delay. Every console is another chance to disagree with the last. The third is pace. Several security firms reported exploitation attempts before PHP released its fixes, and Cloudflare reported early attacks hours ahead of the patch. Frontier AI models helped find PHP2Shell, and in April Anthropic said its Claude Mythos Preview model had found thousands of previously unknown flaws across every major operating system and browser. With models like these in the picture, the old rhythm of disclose, patch and verify assumes a gap that keeps shrinking. Put an AI agent on top of stale, fragmented data and these problems don't go away. They scale. Why does real-time endpoint data make autonomy trustworthy? Endpoints are where work happens and where many attacks end up, so they are the ground truth for any decision about the estate. Four qualities make that data a sound foundation for autonomous action: Accuracy: Live data from the endpoints themselves, not a snapshot that was true last week. Speed: A short path from question to action, with no hopping between tools to reconcile answers. Control: Approvals and an audit trail, plus the ability to roll back, so any automated action can be reviewed and reversed. Shared truth: IT operations, security and the system of record working from one view, rather than arguing over whose data is right. Matt Psencik, a threat research engineer at Tanium, put the visibility problem bluntly when PHP2Shell broke: "The installations that worry me most are the ones a security team doesn't know it owns." How does AI fit in? AI sits on both sides of this. It helped researchers find the PHP2Shell flaws, and attackers can use it to build exploits too. For defenders, AI works best as the operator and the interface: it takes a plain-language question, works out what to ask of the data, and proposes or carries out the next step. But it is only as good as the data it is grounded in. A fluent answer built on outdated information is still wrong, just more confidently so. Keeping people in the loop where stakes are high is what makes automation safe to expand. What are the practical first steps? Teams don't need to hand over the keys all at once. Start here: Find every copy: Don't stop at the installed-applications list. PHP2Shell showed that software bundled inside other products can slip past it. Compare your CMDB against what is really on your network and record exact versions. Draw the lines: Rank systems by what the internet can reach, then decide which response actions run automatically, which need approval and which are never delegated. Write it down before an agent needs it. Pilot one low-risk workflow: Pick something contained, build approval into it, and read the audit trail before widening the scope. Teams can also shorten the pilot with a partner. World Wide Technology (WWT), a Tanium partner, works with many large organizations on technology rollouts and hosts a Tanium lab in its Advanced Technology Center, where customers can test an approach hands-on before moving it into production. That second problem, the hopping, is the one Tanium Atlas was built to close. Instead of moving between consoles, an operator asks a plain-language question, gets an answer from live endpoint data, and acts on it inside limits the team sets, with every action recorded. events.title: Ireland faces pressure to stop sending Russia ingredient vital to its war on Ukraine
events.summary: A cargo ship is set to leave Ireland for Russia with alumina, a white powder that experts say is likely used to make weapons AUGHINISH, Ireland -- The Karin, a 400-foot-long (120-meter-long) cargo ship, sat moored this week on Ireland’s boggy River Shannon estuary. Soon it set sail for Russia laden with a white powder that can be forged into weapons vital to Moscow’s war on Ukraine. Alumina, the key ingredient in aluminum, goes into everything from toothpaste and lipstick to missiles and drones. A Russian-owned plant in southern Ireland is Europe’s biggest alumina refinery and regularly sends shiploads of the substance directly to St. Petersburg and other Russian ports. Almost five years into Moscow’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine , alumina has escaped European sanctions intended to hobble Russia’s economy. That leaves the refinery in Aughinish free to send its product to Russia, where some ends up in weapons, experts say. “The material is clearly ending up in military supplies,” said Irish lawmaker Ivana Bacik, who leads the opposition Labour Party. “It would be unthinkable for Ireland to be contributing, even in that indirect way, to Putin’s war machine.” Ireland is facing calls to stop the shipments as dozens of European leaders gather in Dublin this week to discuss support for Ukraine. A summit of the 47-nation European Political Community on Thursday is being followed by a meeting of European Union leaders. Irish government minister Niall Collins told The Associated Press that “there’s absolutely no evidence” the material is ending up in military supply chains, though the government has declined to make public the findings of its investigation into the alumina shipments. Aughinish Alumina said in a statement its product “has no connection to the Russian military supply chain” and that it hired an independent company to provide monthly audits to Irish authorities for “enhanced traceability.” Alumina is a chemical compound refined from bauxite, a red ore mined primarily in Guinea, Australia and China. The chalky white substance can be smelted into aluminum, which is then forged with other, rarer elements to make strong, heat-resistant and flexible alloys used in missiles and aircraft; aluminum is also used in the manufacture of rocket fuel and explosives. The Aughinish plant in County Limerick was built in the 1970s and bought in 2007 by Rusal, a Russian aluminum producer. The company was founded, and is still part-owned, by Oleg Deripaska , a sanctioned oligarch with ties to Russian President Vladimir Putin. Rusal makes virtually all of Russia's aluminum, according to the U.S. and Australian governments. While many cargo ships leave Aughinish bound for Europe and beyond, a steady stream of them heads straight to the port of St. Petersburg, according to data from MarineTraffic analyzed by AP. The activist group Alumina 22, which is lobbying to sanction the trade in alumina to Russia, estimated that between March and October some 491,307 metric tons of alumina from Ireland was shipped to Russia. These shipments have grown in importance. Since Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022, two alumina factories — one in Australia, the other in Ukraine — stopped exporting to Russia, crimping its supplies by about 40%, according to a 2026 report by the Economic Security Council of Ukraine, or ESCU. Roughly 17% of Rusal's alumina supply now comes from Ireland, according to ESCU. An investigation by the Organized Crime and Corruption Reporting Project and the Irish Times published earlier this year found that alumina from Aughinish is smelted in Russia into aluminum, with some of it sold to a metals trading company that supplies Russian defense contractors. “Virtually everything that comes from Rusal is with a high probability ending up in the hands of Russian military enterprises,” said Olena Yurchenko, director of analytics, research and investigations at the ESCU. Standing next to Irish Prime Minister Micheál Martin in Dublin in June , Ukraine’s President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said “Unfortunately, there are companies in Europe that are owned or effectively controlled by Russia and its sanctioned oligarchs. They keep supplying the aggressor with essential materials, even now.” Baby buried alive for 24 hours released from the hospital; father charged House tables Hegseth impeachment, effectively killing it in current Congress Wisconsin state trooper detained by ICE Martin acknowledged that “we do not want to be in a position where material emanating from a plant in Ireland goes to support the Russian war machine.” Ireland has not found evidence that is happening — but also no proof it isn’t, said Enterprise Minister Peter Burke, who is in charge of the country's sanctions enforcement. He said in July it had been impossible to prove Rusal’s assertion that alumina from Ireland is only used to make aluminum for export from Russia.

events.title: Taiwan’s Foxconn bullish on outlook but warns about supply chain tightness
events.summary: Foxconn has also been building factories in Mexico and Texas to make AI servers for Nvidia. Foxconn reported net profit of NT$77.5 billion (S$3.02 billion) for July to September, up 34% on year and above forecasts, helped by strong AI demand. Chairman Young Liu said the company is confident about 2027 and expects “high double digit growth” in AI rack shipments, with strong revenue growth also seen in 2026. Foxconn warned that chips, memory and key parts are tight, and said demand may keep exceeding supply even as new capacity comes online. TAIPEI – Taiwan’s Foxconn, the world’s largest contract electronics maker, said on Nov 12 it was confident about its business in 2027 given strong AI demand as it reported forecast-beating quarterly profit, but it warned about supply chain tightness. Net profit for the July to September period for Nvidia’s biggest server maker and Apple’s top iPhone assembler was NT$77.5 billion ( S$3.02 billion ), up 34% on year and beating an LSEG consensus estimate of NT$69.6 billion. In an earnings release, Foxconn stuck to its previous forecast of “strong” growth for revenue in 2026 and said it saw strong AI demand throughout 2026 and into 2027 . The company, which does not give numeric forecasts, said it predicted “high double digit growth” in 2027 for AI rack shipments. “We remain very confident about our operations next year and expect continued growth,” chairman Young Liu told an earnings conference, although warning there were also “several external variables worth continued attention”. Looking at the AI and consumer electronics supply chains, chips, memory and some key components are currently tight, which is a challenge facing the industry as a whole, Liu said. “Although supply bottlenecks should gradually ease as new capacity comes online, overall demand is expected to still exceed supply next year, and the tight supply-demand situation may persist for some time,” he said. Foxconn, formally called Hon Hai Precision Industry, in October reported a 47% year-on-year jump in third-quarter revenue. Most of the iPhones Foxconn makes for Apple are assembled in China, but it now produces the bulk of those sold in the United States in India. The company is also building factories in Mexico and Texas to make AI servers for Nvidia. Foxconn has been looking to expand its footprint in electric vehicles as well. The company’s shares have risen 4% so far in 2026 , underperforming a 49% gain on the broader Taiwan index. Foxconn shares closed 0.8% lower on Nov 12 ahead of the earnings release. The main index ended down 2.6%. REUTERS

events.title: Adnoc L&S expects $4 billion full-year profit as tanker rates surge
events.summary: Adnoc Logistics and Services raised its full-year profit forecast for the fourth time this year after third-quarter earnings more than quadrupled, as disruption from the Iran war drove up tanker charter rates. Net profit attributable to the equity holders of the company jumped 310 per cent to $842.7 million in the three months to the end of September, from $205.4 million a year earlier, the Abu Dhabi-listed company said on Thursday. Revenue rose 160 per cent to $3.29 billion, while operating profit nearly quadrupled to $898.7 million. The shipping arm of Abu Dhabi National Oil Company now expects annual net profit of about $4 billion, growth in the low-360 per cent range, up from its previous forecast of growth in the high-110 per cent range. “Resilience has defined our performance this year,” said chief executive Capt Abdulkareem Al Masabi. Daily rates for very large crude carriers (VLCCs) on the Gulf-to-Asia route reached about $1.4 million in early October, according to data compiled by Bloomberg. That compares with about $30,000 to $45,000 before the war began in February, as fewer shipowners are willing to send vessels through the Strait of Hormuz. Shipping was the main driver of growth. Revenue rose 244 per cent to $5.09 billion in the first nine months, from $1.48 billion a year earlier. Tankers brought in $4.15 billion, up 249 per cent, on higher charter rates and a larger VLCC fleet. Gas carrier revenue surged nearly five-fold to $619 million, helped by new liquefied natural gas contracts and three second-hand very large gas carriers deployed with Adnoc. Dry bulk and container revenue rose 93 per cent to $318 million. Much of the growth came from moving the parent company's own oil and gas. Sales to other Adnoc group companies reached $2.26 billion in the third quarter, about 69 per cent of revenue, up from $620 million a year earlier, according to the company's bourse filing. Nine-month attributable profit rose 219 per cent to $1.96 billion, while revenue climbed 88 per cent to $6.96 billion. The board approved a third-quarter interim dividend of $85.3 million for shareholders on record as of November 23. The company has maintained its policy of raising annual dividends per share by at least 5 per cent to 2030. 'Challenging' as it enters 2027 Adnoc L&S chief financial officer Hugh Baker, in a conference call after the results were released, said the company had a "very high degree of confidence" in its newest guidance uptick. However, he acknowledged the difficulty of projecting its performance entering 2027, given the uncertainty surrounding the situation in the Middle East. "I have to say that I don't think we can really sustain any of the previous projections into next year. We are starting 2027 and with a very challenging guidance outlook, the ability to guide for 2027 is challenging because, obviously, there is uncertainty about the events," he said. Adnoc L&S is "sort of normalising our response to the current extreme market circumstances", Mr Baker said, adding that the carry-over effects of higher shipping rates won't result in a "dramatic decrease in earnings in the first quarter". Fleet expansion Adnoc L&S is using the windfall to expand. It has committed $7 billion in capital expenditure to 2030 and took delivery of 14 vessels in the third quarter, including six VLCCs, with another 10 due before the end of the year. After the quarter ended, some of its owned and chartered vessels were struck by projectiles while crossing the Strait of Hormuz, the company said. It added that the vessels were insured and the financial impact was still being assessed. On Tuesday, Adnoc L&S said one of its vessels was damaged in an attack in UAE territorial waters in the Gulf, without identifying the ship or the extent of the damage.

events.summary: Blackstone , the world’s largest alternative investment manager, has expanded its footprint in the UAE with the launch of a wealth management office in Dubai International Financial Centre. The new outpost in Dubai’s onshore financial centre will serve as the regional hub for the nearly $1.4-trillion investor , which looks to court the wealthy, as well as institutions and family offices, to boost growth of its wealth management business in the Gulf and beyond, it said on Thursday. “The UAE has built an extraordinary position as a global finance and investment hub and is becoming an increasingly important centre for wealth management,” said Jon Gray, Blackstone's president and chief operating officer. The company has been present in the UAE since 2010 and Mr Gray said the new Dubai office builds on that long-standing commitment, allowing the company to “deepen our partnerships and broaden access to alternatives” for investors. The DIFC office adds to the Blackstone’s presence in the Abu Dhabi’s financial centre ADGM and expands its reach across the oil-rich Gulf region as well as the broader Middle East. Blackstone’s private wealth business aims to build on its partnerships with leading banking institutions in the region and has already established more than 40 distributor relationships across the region. Blackstone is the latest among global investors and money managers to set up a base in the UAE or expand presence in the Arab world’s second-largest economy as they look to capitalise on rapidly growing wealth management market in the region. Both DIFC and ADGM have attracted a steady stream of global financial institutions, and trillion-dollar dollar asset managers over past few quarters despite the geopolitical headwinds. Blackstone has already committed more capital to the Gulf region in the past 12 months than at any point in its history and it plans to invest more despite the continuing US-Iran conflict, its chief executive Steve Schwarzman told The National last month. Despite the months-long war , the investment appeal of the Gulf remains intact and the company aims to substantially grow the percentage of its assets under management in the Gulf by the turn of this decade, he said at the time. Blackstone has already upgraded its Abu Dhabi office licence to boost deal origination in the region. It also plans to open an office in Kuwait and expects to further expand its presence across the region over the coming year, the company said on Thursday.

events.title: Megaspeed has hired a US law firm to review export control compliance, says Singaporean director
events.summary: Megaspeed said the US law firm would conduct a comprehensive inventory of its graphics processing units. Megaspeed has hired a US law firm to review its export control compliance and check its graphics processing units, said Singaporean director Tan Yong Pong. The company said it has cooperated with the US Commerce Department’s Bureau of Industry and Security and will work fully with other US authorities. The move comes as Megaspeed faces scrutiny over Nvidia chip purchases, possible chip diversion, and ongoing investigations in Singapore and the US. SINGAPORE – Megaspeed International, the Singapore buyer of Nvidia’s advanced artificial intelligence chips that has come under global scrutiny, has engaged a US law firm to review its compliance with American export control laws. In a Nov 12 statement issued by its Singaporean director Tan Yong Pong, also known as James Tan, the company said the law firm would conduct a comprehensive inventory of its graphics processing units and independently verify its export control compliance practices. Tan signed off as Megaspeed’s chairman and chief executive. Previous attempts by The Straits Times to contact him were unsuccessful. Tan said Megaspeed had also cooperated with inspections by the US Department of Commerce’s Bureau of Industry and Security, which oversees American export controls. The company added that it was prepared to cooperate fully with other relevant US government authorities. “Megaspeed takes its compliance obligations under US export control laws extremely seriously,” Tan said. He added that compliance was a fundamental priority for the company, which was committed to working constructively and transparently with the US government. The statement comes amid scrutiny of Megaspeed’s purchases of advanced Nvidia chips, some of which are subject to US export restrictions aimed at limiting China’s access to cutting-edge computing technology. The Financial Times reported in November that the US authorities had considered placing Megaspeed on a trade blacklist over concerns about possible chip diversion, but a decision had been delayed. Singapore’s Ministry of Home Affairs said on Oct 31 that investigations into Megaspeed remained ongoing. Megaspeed said it welcomed appropriate government scrutiny and was committed to demonstrating through concrete actions that it operated responsibly and in accordance with applicable US laws. Megaspeed was previously known as 7Road International, a Chinese gaming company with ties to state-backed investors. Huang Le, or Alice Huang – who was reported to have had an affair with Nvidia chief Jensen Huang – joined the company as a director and managing director in March 2023, around the same time it was renamed. She left Megaspeed on Nov 10, 2023, the same day Tan and another individual, Kang Kai, were appointed directors. Kang left the board of the Singapore-registered company on Dec 28, 2023, but his name still appears in the corporate filings of Megaspeed’s overseas subsidiaries. Cheong Poh Kwan is assistant business editor at The Straits Times.

events.title: Rethinking Memory For AI Inference
events.summary: Key Takeaways: Moving compute closer to memory can reduce data movement, power consumption, and latency. Different AI workloads require different approaches to memory architecture, interconnects, and processing. Software support, standardization, and thermal management remain major barriers to wider adoption. The shift from AI training in data centers to AI inferencing at the edge will require a fundamental rethinking of where and how data is processed and stored, how it is prioritized, and what needs to be traded off in terms of power and performance to stay within a limited power budget. At the center of these efforts is a recognition that the explosion of data — especially in physical AI where data is being live-streamed from sensors — requires much of that data to be processed as close to memory as possible. This has been a topic of discussion since the inception of the Internet of Things, but it really began gaining traction with AI due to the flood of data and concerns about the amount of power required to move and process it. In battery-electric vehicles and drones, for example, the less energy spent on processing data, the greater the range per charge and the more energy that can be allocated to critical and not-so-critical functions. The challenge is understanding what data needs to be kept, what can be discarded, and what needs to be acted upon. Those are very different priorities. Making those choices requires advanced processing, and the quickest path to results using the least amount of energy is to minimize the distance data needs to travel between processing and memory. “The realities of these LLMs getting into physical devices are causing everyone to rethink how they architect their memory,” said Frank Ferro, group director for product management at Cadence . “Even with conventional memory — without even talking about processing in memory — how do I partition these models to maximize the performance both of the overall processor and memory subsystem?” Solving those issues will require several new approaches, such as processing near memory (PNM) and processing in memory (PIM), as well as improvements across multiple technologies and approaches. Compilers and operating systems will need to catch up, and standards will need to be established. “AI in the data center and all these large language models have been the focus of everyone’s attention for the last couple of years, and now these models have been trained and pushed out into the field, into the edge of the network and physical AI,” Ferro said. “The reality is you have limited compute power and limited memory.” AI inferencing at the edge presents different challenges than training AI models in AI data centers. “Training almost always involves highly variable memory access patterns, and mostly involves the use of interpreted code — for example, Python to PyTorch — which necessitates the complexities of coherence across layers of memory,” said Steve Roddy, chief marketing officer at Quadric . “Once inference begins, the use model changes dramatically. Whether you are looking at big LLMs running in a data center, or models running locally, such as smaller LLMs or VLAs (vision-language-action) in cars, the model is known before you run it. That means the data access patterns are known ahead of time. This is where ahead-of-time compilation can start to take great advantage of the various at-memory, processing-in-memory, or in-memory-compute (IMC) options. The system knows exactly where, when, and how the compute is going to occur. There is no need for one element of a compute solution to guess if something manipulated the data while it was in another memory subsystem, because the entire system orchestration was planned out hours, days, or weeks before, when the AI inference model was compiled.” Certain stages of the AI inference pipeline benefit from near-memory solutions more than others. “Pushing the compute into the DRAM or near the DRAM has interesting implications,” said Sharad Chole, chief scientist and co-founder of Expedera . “You’re moving your communication pattern — my activation goes to memory, rather than my memory goes to activation — and that changes how much communication you need to do. These sort of solutions are okay for low-batch decode. For example, if you have batch one and you are trying to do decode and you are not reading all the weights, as soon as we move to large-batch decode, which is cost-optimized, or prefill, which is large-batch execution, the activation communication becomes the challenging part. These are the two ways to think about it. In the end, you have to break your execution into parts that are either storage-sensitive, in terms of how much data you need to store, or bandwidth-sensitive, or batching-sensitive.” Either way, bringing compute closer to data can reduce the time and the energy spent moving it, and processing in the same memory package (custom HBM), or on the same memory die (LPDDR6-PIM), provides two fundamental advantages. “One of them is performance,” said Kos Gitchev, product marketing director at Cadence. “If we’re looking at a CPU or a core sitting inside the SoC, and every time you need to do an operation you’ve got to go out to memory, there’s a transaction that says, ‘Okay, get me some data from the memory that’s going to hit a cache somewhere in the SoC.’ That will eventually go to memory. It will come back to the cache and eventually come back to the processor. This operation really takes some time.” So while chip architects can get compute running quickly on an SoC, the SoC has to wait for data to arrive. “Processing in memory to a large degree addresses this,” said Gitchev. “Now you can say, ‘I have this chunk of memory data in the memory, go do something with it, and I’m just going to go read the results. I’m going to skip this whole step of reading it, compute again, and putting it back. I’m just going to do a read, and that’s all I need.'” .heartland-swipe-cue{display:none}.heartland-desktop{width:100%;max-width:100%;overflow-x:auto;-webkit-overflow-scrolling:touch;clear:both}.heartland-desktop th,.heartland-desktop td{white-space:normal!important;word-break:normal!important;overflow-wrap:normal!important;-webkit-hyphens:none!important;hyphens:none!important}@media (max-width:800px) and (orientation:portrait){.heartland-swipe-cue{display:block;background:#EEF2FF;border:1px solid #17365D;font-weight:bold;font-size:14px;text-align:center;padding:6px 8px;margin:0 0 6px 0}.heartland-desktop table{width:900px!important;min-width:900px!important}} Swipe left to view all columns → Term Domain What it means Where the math happens Data form Examples CIM (compute-in-memory) / IMC (in-memory computing) Hardware The memory array its

events.title: Beyond Bandwidth: AI Inference Is Reshaping The Memory Wall
events.summary: AI infrastructure has spent the past several years in a race for compute. More accelerators, larger heterogeneous clusters, and higher peak performance have enabled increasingly capable models. As AI moves into large-scale deployment, infrastructure must support more users, larger models, longer context windows, and more complex applications. Performance still matters, but so do latency, power, utilization, predictability, and cost per inference. The challenge extends beyond bandwidth. AI systems must balance memory capacity, bandwidth, latency, power, data movement, utilization, and cost. Improving one dimension can create pressure elsewhere. The key-value (KV) cache illustrates this trade-off. KV cache reduces repeated computation during generative AI inference, but requires the system to retain and repeatedly access growing amounts of data. As context lengths and concurrent requests increase, the trade-off becomes more significant. The result is not simply another memory bottleneck. It is a coordination problem across compute, memory, interconnect, and software. Adding capacity or bandwidth helps only if the system can place, move, and retrieve data without allowing latency, congestion, power, or complexity to erase the benefit. The memory wall is getting wider The memory wall predates AI. Processor performance historically has improved faster than the ability of memory systems to supply processors with data. AI magnifies that problem. Increasing arithmetic throughput delivers limited benefit if accelerators spend more time waiting for data. But bandwidth is only part of the constraint. AI systems also need sufficient capacity for models, intermediate data, application context, and inference state. Latency affects responsiveness. Power constrains how much data can be moved economically. Packaging and physical connectivity limit how much high-performance memory can be placed near compute. These requirements frequently conflict. High-bandwidth memory close to an accelerator can deliver tremendous bandwidth, but its capacity, power, and cost are constrained. Larger-capacity memory may be more economical but may not provide the same bandwidth or latency. Moving data among tiers can expand effective capacity, but consumes bandwidth, power, and time. The memory wall is therefore becoming a multidimensional system constraint. Fig. 1: AI scaling turns the memory wall into a system-level trade-off among bandwidth, capacity, latency, power, cost, and utilization. A system may have substantial aggregate memory, but not all of that capacity is equally useful. Data in a lower tier may technically be available, yet still be too distant, congested, or costly to move within the application’s service-level objective (SLO). The practical limit is not installed capacity alone. It is usable capacity within the workload’s latency, bandwidth, and power envelope . Inference changes the economics Training large models requires enormous compute resources and memory bandwidth, but it is fundamentally a process of building or updating a model. Inference is dynamic and ongoing. Every prompt, generated token, agent action, and application interaction consumes infrastructure resources. Inference also is not one workload. A conversational assistant may emphasize latency. An enterprise AI assistant may process substantial proprietary context while supporting many users. AI agents may retain information across multiple steps. Consumer services may prioritize throughput and cost per token. Batch inference may emphasize utilization. Each creates a different balance among bandwidth, capacity, latency, power, and cost. The architecture must follow the workload. KV cache exposes the trade-off During transformer inference, attention mechanisms generate key and value representations for tokens in a sequence. Retaining those representations allows subsequent decoding steps to reuse prior states rather than recomputing them for earlier tokens. That improves inference efficiency, but reduces repeated computation while increasing pressure on memory capacity and data movement. Longer context windows increase the KV-cache footprint of each sequence. Higher concurrency multiplies that requirement across simultaneous requests. An optimization intended to reduce compute demand therefore creates more data that must be retained and accessed. Fig. 2: Reducing repeated computation improves efficiency, but longer contexts and greater concurrency increase the data that must be retained, moved, and managed. KV state also has a lifecycle. It is created during prefill, repeatedly accessed during decode, and may be retained for reuse. Depending on the serving architecture, it may be moved, replicated, compressed, or evicted. Each phase places different demands on bandwidth, capacity, latency, and control. KV cache is therefore a data-lifecycle problem, not only a memory allocation. Moving KV state to a lower-cost tier is beneficial only when the higher-tier capacity it frees, or the recomputation it avoids, outweighs transfer latency, bandwidth consumption, energy, and the risk of missing an SLO. In other words, every movement of data must earn its cost . The workload determines the architecture A latency-sensitive assistant may benefit from keeping frequently accessed data close to the accelerator. A long-context enterprise application may emphasize capacity. AI agents may require longer-lived state and more frequent reuse. Large-scale consumer inference may prioritize throughput, utilization, and cost per token. Frequently accessed data may justify residing near compute. Other data may tolerate additional latency for greater capacity or lower cost, or move among tiers as access patterns change. The objective is not to eliminate the memory hierarchy. It is to coordinate that hierarchy efficiently. There is no single memory metric Bandwidth remains critical, but optimizing exclusively for bandwidth ignores other constraints. Capacity determines how much model and inference state can remain accessible. Latency affects response time. Power determines whether increasing data movement is sustainable. Utilization indicates whether expensive compute resources are working or waiting for data. High aggregate throughput can hide unacceptable time to first token, inter-token latency, or tail latency during congestion. A more meaningful measure may be tokens per watt or dollar while meeting latency targets. Headline bandwidth alone does not solve the memory wall. The relevant question is: Which combination of compute, memory, interconnect, and software delivers predictable performance within the available power and cost envelope? Adding memory is not enough High-bandwidth memory can supply data quickly near accelerators. Larger-capacity tiers can complement it where capacity matters more than maximum bandwidth. events.title: The Semiconductor Singularity: When AI Starts Accelerating The Silicon That Accelerates AI
events.summary: AI is entering the inner loop of semiconductor engineering by reducing the effort required to develop software, operate software tools and carry out engineering analysis. Ray Kurzweil described the broader pattern as the Law of Accelerating Returns: accumulated technical capability helps create the next computing paradigm. In my recent white paper, The semiconductor singularity: Accelerating IC innovation with AI , I applied that idea to semiconductor engineering. Better computing improves the tools used to design and manufacture semiconductors, and those tools help create the next generation of computing. Figure 1 places that loop in the longer history of computing. The technologies change, but each generation contributes tools, knowledge and capacity that help create its successor. Fig. 1: Successive computing paradigms have built the technical capacity used to create the next generation. Lowering the effort required for the next experiment Progress in semiconductor engineering never follows a smooth exponential curve. It advances when a bottleneck is overcome sufficiently for engineers to try something that previously cost too much money, time, computation or organizational effort. I saw this firsthand with machine learning in computational lithography. Early demonstrations were exciting, but production adoption required developers who understood both ML and semiconductor applications, representative data, model management, IP controls and customer confidence. Production adoption followed only after the model, data, deployment environment and customer requirements matured together. Generative AI relieves many of the user-complexity bottlenecks characteristic of EDA flows. When I created my original SPIE machine-learning course for lithography, the prototype work took roughly 200 to 300 hours, including some help generating training data. In a later experiment, I used generative AI to recreate and expand a surprising amount of that prototype functionality in roughly 30 hours. These were notebook-level prototypes, not production computational-lithography tools, but the change in exploratory effort was striking. The practical effect is more engineering exploration within the same schedule. Experienced silicon engineers can examine more alternatives and produce more usable results while spending less time on software and workflow mechanics. Extending the reach of engineering expertise Agentic AI extends this effect from delivering predictions or analyses to carrying out sequences of engineering work. The LLM interprets intent, assembles the workflow, retrieves relevant context and coordinates specialized tools. Engineering authority remains in the EDA tools, models, qualified data and deterministic analysis. Semiconductor workflows have traditionally depended on experienced engineers who know which analysis to run, which data matters, when a result is credible and when something requires closer examination. That expertise takes years to develop and cannot expand as quickly as computational capacity or engineering demand. Agentic systems can increase the reach of that expertise. In computational lithography, an agent might collect recent SEM data, configure model calibration, invoke the appropriate analysis, inspect convergence and runtime, and return exceptions to the engineer for judgment. More computation, data and tool activity can operate under the direction of each expert. Siemens Fuse EDA AI implements this architecture by connecting AI models to EDA tools, engineering knowledge, specialized languages and data formats. Manufacturing connects models to physical evidence Computational lithography shows how this works. A fab collects wafer and metrology data, calibrates models, uses those models to drive correction, measures the resulting silicon and feeds what it learns into the next calibration and process change. The model improves through repeated comparison with physical evidence. Different parts of that loop require different computational methods. Physics-based simulation predicts physical behavior. Qualified models, rule decks and deterministic verification establish engineering and signoff authority. Specialized machine learning supports prediction, classification and optimization. Generative AI improves access to knowledge and tools. Agents coordinate workflows. Accelerated computing expands the analyses that fit within practical schedules. The result of these workflows is usually the conversion of physical understanding and manufacturing observations into evidence-backed engineering interventions. Simulation directs exploration, metrology records what happened, models reconcile prediction with observation, and engineering action changes the design or process. As EDA tools, manufacturing systems and digital twins become accessible to agents, this loop can operate across more of the workflow. Agents can explore design-technology tradeoffs, run simulation and computational-metrology flows, evaluate alternatives and organize evidence for the next engineering decision. Trust is engineering infrastructure As engineering cycles accelerate, the value of trust increases. AI can generate hypotheses, assemble workflows and explore alternatives quickly. Semiconductor development advances through evidence that engineers can responsibly act on: verified designs, qualified models, measured silicon and data whose origin and applicability are understood. Agentic EDA needs engineering context, secure data access, traceable actions, deterministic authority and human control over consequential decisions. These properties belong inside the workflow and provide a foundation of trust. A Calibre nmOPC model earns trust through calibration against physical metrology data and continued comparison with what appears on the wafer. The model, calibration data, process conditions and physical evidence together establish where the model can be relied upon. As conditions change, the model is recalibrated and the evidence base grows. AI-enhanced metrology tools such as Canopus can strengthen that foundation by increasing the quantity and quality of SEM data available for calibration. Calibre, together with foundry-qualified rule decks and verification flows, establishes that a design complies with the physical requirements of manufacturing. Agents can orchestrate more work and explore more possibilities, while trusted engineering tools determine which results are allowed to move forward. With access to more tools within a well-designed trusted software foundation, engineering analysis may encounter bottlenecks in the larger organization or ecosystem. The time required to establish data access, protect IP or authorize a production change can become the limiting factor on acceleration. Reducing the time required to establish access, protection and authority becomes the next engineering problem. events.title: EGA’s nine-month profit and revenue fall as Iran war disrupts aluminium sales
events.summary: Emirates Global Aluminium has reported a 9 per cent decline in its nine-month adjusted net profit, driven by impairments for lost production after an Iranian attack on its Al Taweelah plant as well as disruption of exports. Adjusted net profit for the nine months to the end of September stood at $744 million, compared to $817 million in the same period in 2025, EGA, one of the UAE ’s largest non-oil industrial conglomerates, said in a statement on Thursday. Net profit during the period stood at $547 million, after recognising a net impact of $197 million linked to the war-related incident in March, which led to an an emergency shutdown of all of EGA’s Al Taweelah plants at Khalifa Industrial Zone Abu Dhabi (Kizad). The company’s revenue fell 16 per cent annually to $5.28 billion during the nine-month period. “In the first nine months of 2026, EGA has been tested like never before,” said Abdulnasser bin Kalban, chief executive of EGA. “During this challenging period of recovery, we have continued our focus on delivering long-term growth. While challenges remain ahead of us, across EGA we share determination and full confidence that EGA will come back stronger than ever.” The shutdown after the March incident resulted in a $53 million impact on adjusted Ebitda. However, operations at Jebel Ali and EGA’s international recycling plants remained uninterrupted throughout the period. Despite the setback, EGA said it lifted its adjusted earnings before interest, tax, depreciation and amortisation margin to 30 per cent in the January to September period, from 28 per cent a year earlier, helped by higher aluminium prices and disciplined cost management. Sales volumes The shutdown at Al Taweelah also weighed on aluminium sales volumes. Total sales fell 36 per cent to 1.33 million tonnes during the nine months, reflecting lower metal availability from Al Taweelah and constraints on outbound logistics from the UAE during the period, EGA said. The company then established alternative export routes through corridors to ports outside the Strait of Hormuz , supporting continued customer shipments. In September, EGA signed an agreement with Gulftainer to expand aluminium exports through the UAE's eastern coast ports. The arrangement will enable EGA to ship up to 250,000 tonnes in the first year, rising to 300,000 tonnes in the second year. The company has also diversified inbound supply routes and secured a renewed bauxite agreement with Guinea's Compagnie des Bauxites de Guinee for up to 4.9 million tonnes annually until 2044. EGA said on Thursday it is continuing to restore its Al Taweelah smelter , with 766 of the 1,262 reduction cells that need restarting now operational. This represents 61 per cent of the total, with the company aiming for a full restart in the first quarter of 2027. Production is increasing as more cells come back online. The disruption also affected the company’s alumina refinery , which produced 899,000 tonnes in the first nine months of 2026, down from 1.75 million tonnes a year earlier. After its restart in July, the refinery had reached about 70 per cent capacity in September. EGA estimates that fully restoring Al Taweelah production will require capital expenditure of about $400 million. This will be financed from the company's balance sheet and operating cash flow, EGA's chief financial officer Pal Kildemo told The National in August. The company's balance sheet remains robust, with $1.93 billion in cash and term deposits and a further $1 billion available through an undrawn revolving credit facility. Meanwhile, EGA is continuing its global expansion, having completed the acquisition of an 80 per cent stake in Italian aluminium recycler Eco Green in September. The deal takes its global recycling capacity to more than 400,000 tonnes annually, with another 200,000 tonnes under development. Although the aluminium market remains undersupplied, EGA expects it to move towards a more balanced position in 2027, Mr Kildemo said on Thursday.

events.title: Designing Edge AI SoCs At Near-Threshold: Why Foundation IP Can Help You Break Down The Power Wall
events.summary: Lowering operating voltage is a key to SoC power optimization. In advanced FinFET processes at ~0.4–0.5V, it can also start to become a design risk. As edge AI pushes inference closer to endpoints, edge-AI SoCs must deliver real-time performance within tight energy and thermal limits. Traditional voltage scaling is no longer sufficient. SoC designs are shifting towards much more extensive use of near-threshold operation to achieve step-function improvements in performance per watt. But this shift fundamentally changes how chips behave: delays increase non-linearly, variability grows significantly, and underpinning predictable operation becomes a critical enabler to minimizing power. Design success in this operating regime depends heavily on the underlying quality, modeling accuracy, and integration of Foundation IP with EDA flows and silicon validation. Embedded memories, logic libraries, and I/Os must be selected carefully and any targeted optimization carried out and fully validated at an early stage—not treated as a possible downstream option. What changes at near-threshold Every SoC designer understands that lowering supply voltage reduces energy—but at near threshold voltages, it changes transistor behavior and challenges traditional design assumptions. Fig. 1: Energy efficiency improves at lower voltage, but delay and variability increase sharply near threshold. As shown in Figure 1, reducing voltage lowers energy per operation, but comes with significant trade-offs: delay grows rapidly, variability increases, and noise margins shrink. In this regime: Timing paths become highly sensitive to small voltage variations IR drop and local voltage droop become first-order effects Guard-banding becomes less effective Nominal-voltage models no longer predict behavior accurately Voltage scaling is no longer an isolated optimization—it introduces tightly coupled challenges across the entire design stack. Foundation IP: The differentiating layer Meeting power targets at ultra-low voltage is not sufficient; designs must achieve this predictably and without introducing additional silicon risk. This can be where Foundation IP moves from an incidental enabler to a significant part of the design success. The quality of logic libraries, memory compilers, and I/Os can directly determine the robustness of design closure and silicon outcomes. A unified, silicon-proven Foundation IP platform—tightly coupled with EDA flows, built with the most accurate modelling and characterization methodologies and meticulously validated on silicon —provides the accuracy and consistency needed to enable PPA winning designs at ultra-low voltages, with reliable behavior from early design through signoff. Embedded memories: Where the voltage floor lives Memory is a dominant contributor to area and power—and often determines the system’s minimum operating voltage (Vmin) if not architecturally decoupled. This is addressed through flexible architectures: Single-rail memories with silicon-validated assist features support operation down to ~600 mV Vmin, enabling direct V² energy reduction without architectural disruption Dual-rail memories decouple logic and memory voltages, allowing deeper scaling of compute blocks. As shown in Figure 2, this approach has been validated at ISSCC 2025 with a 38 Mb/mm² dual-rail SRAM at 380/540 mV in 3nm FinFET Ultra-low-power register files support localized data storage in compute-intensive regions Fig. 2: Dual-rail memory architecture decouples logic and memory VDD, validated at ISSCC 2025 with a 38 Mb/mm² SRAM at 380/540 mV in 3nm FinFET. Different AI subsystems require different memory strategies: MAC tiles benefit from small, distributed SRAM blocks; activation units from ULP RFs with wide data-paths; and shared system buffers from high-bandwidth AXI interfaces. Logic libraries: Accuracy where it matters most Logic libraries must be engineered specifically with low-voltage operation in mind: Advanced characterization, such as moment-based LVF timing and noise models across wide bands of PVT coverage Delay and slew models that capture near-threshold non-linear sensitivities Enhanced verification checks—including MIS effects, pulse-width integrity, skew interactions, and mixed-device behavior—to address reduced noise margins Targeted silicon validation, including extended timing and functional sweeps, to ensure model accuracy This modeling accuracy is essential to avoid unexpected surprises during low voltage signoff or timing failures on silicon. I/O: Don’t let the periphery block the core In many designs, I/O domains define system-level Vmin. If I/O cannot operate reliably at reduced voltages, it blocks near-threshold logic benefits regardless of how well the core is optimized. The portfolio spans control interfaces (GPIO, I3C/I2C, SWI3S), high-speed data links (LVDS, RGMII), clock and reference inputs, storage interfaces (SD/eMMC), test I/O, and 2.5D/3D integration I/O for chiplet-based systems—each validated for consistent operation across varying supply levels. Co-optimization: Standard IP alone sometimes isn’t quite enough Achieving predictable, optimized operation at ~0.4–0.5V requires tight alignment across Foundation IP, EDA tools, modeling, and silicon validation. Fig. 3: A closed-loop methodology aligns Foundation IP, tools, and silicon feedback to ensure optimized low-voltage design. As shown in Figure 3, optimal low-voltage design depends on an iterative, closed-loop enablement process: Early exploration of PPA trade-offs, along with specific voltage targeting Selection of right IP architectures, technology options and configurations, maybe with specific cell tuning Flow and signoff refinement targeted for low-voltage conditions Feedback from silicon validation to continually improve accuracy and raise confidence Synopsys Application Engineers bridge the gap between IP/EDA R&D experts and SoC designers during the customer design engagement, ensuring that the features are fully exploited and technologies are optimally deployed. The co-optimization of tools and IP keeps device physics, modeling assumptions, and silicon outcomes tightly coupled—transforming near-threshold design into a low risk, production-ready solution. Proof point: ~20% power reduction, zero schedule impact A power-sensitive AI networking SoC targeting high volumes in an advanced technology node, using near-threshold design, needed expert enablement. Supporting extremely low operating voltages for a design executed under a very compressed schedule. The Foundation IP solution included specially tuned low-voltage logic cells, custom level shifters and a custom dual-rail memory compiler, with specifically targeted PVT corner set all specifically selected to achieve the optimum design trade-offs for the best power efficiency through near-threshold signoff. The results: ~20% reduction in power consumption Full achievement of performance and area targets No schedule impact R

events.title: IP Integration Challenges Evolve
events.summary: Key Takeaways: Integration challenges go beyond making sure a block is properly connected. Semantic issues cause the most problems, and many are due to incomplete or bad specifications. Complexity, including increasing software content, makes keeping track of everything included in a design more challenging. Many designs are pushing power and thermal boundaries, and this requires a new layer of information that must be specified and tracked. IP integration is not the most glamorous task in semiconductor design, but it often is one of the most troublesome. At the intersection of block-level verification and system-level interactions, bugs are often very difficult to find. The creation of the Virtual Socket Interface Alliance (VSIA) in 1996 was, for many, the first time the notion of designing a system by integrating third-party IP blocks became a reality. Its charter was to unify and standardize the way IP was constructed, verified, delivered, and supported. The alliance dissolved in 2008, considering its work to either be complete, or transferring parts of it to other organizations that were more focused on specific pieces of the problem. Eighteen years later, the problem continues to evolve. The idea was that each company should focus on developing the part of the design that was novel and unique, adding their expertise, and allowing the rest to be developed by domain experts. “Ten years ago, a design may have had tens of IP blocks,” says Pedro Pires, SOS product manager at Keysight EDA . “Today, a company may have thousands of IPs, dozens of different versions of the same IP, and you want to make sense of all of this. In addition, they are much more configurable than they were in the past. With the increasing quantity and different types of data now required for each block, it is becoming very difficult to manage in an ad hoc way. “ This puts a lot of stress on verification. “The nastiest failures are almost never inside a single block,” says Ashish Darbari, founder and CEO of Axiomise . “They show up between blocks — message-dependent deadlock, credits that slowly leak away, a reorder buffer that gets corrupted, an ordering rule broken across a bridge. Each block passes its own verification, yet the system hangs because two teams read the same protocol rule slightly differently.” Over time, the number of cross-IP issues has increased. “From an SoC point of view, it could be a lot of different issues, including address mapping, interrupts, coherency, QoS, security,” says Madhumita Sanyal, senior director for technical product management for HPC IP portfolio at Synopsys . “Then there are physical implementation scenarios like DVFS, dynamic voltage scaling for lower power. Plus, there is software and operating system interaction. If you consider a die-to-die IP, there’s interoperability. There is known-good-die package, signal integrity, power integrity, power delivery network, thermal coupling, telemetry, and so forth.” While design size has steadily increased, that alone is not an indicator of complexity. “I may be designing a giant CPU with 32 cores, but that is just 32 copies of the same thing,” says Dean Drako, CEO of IC Manage. “It may have a giant cache on it. That is just one cell repeated 100 million times. The complexity is not always proportional to the size of the chip. They are complicated, but the complexity has not linearly grown with the size of the chips. The human brain can’t deal with it.” What matters is how many assumptions a block makes about the world around it, and that number climbs much faster than size. “A UART needs a clock, a reset, and a register interface, and that’s about it,” says Axiomise’s Darbari. “A coherent cache, a CHI home node or a NoC carries hundreds of assumptions. There are ordering rules, credit contracts, limits on outstanding transactions, reset and power sequencing, address-map expectations and security attributes. On top of that come configuration parameters whose effects the datasheet often doesn’t fully explain.” Increasing pressures Many areas add to the integration pressures, such as badly written or incomplete specifications for the IP blocks. At the system level, there is increasing software complexity, power and thermal issues – especially when associated with chiplets, increasing analog content, and added complexity with licensing, geopolitical restrictions, and export controls. Each of these will be touched on briefly. Bad or incomplete specifications: Specifications are notoriously difficult to make unambiguous or complete. “The information is oftentimes not complete enough to give you an accurate picture of how it’s going to behave under all circumstances,” says Keysight’s Pires. “Knowing the conditions in which the system is going to operate will probably help you, depending on the quality of the documentation of your IPs. It might be that the IPs have information that is relevant for that particular set of circumstances, and in that sense, knowing the circumstances where the system is going to operate will help you, but it might not.” The problem is often discovered when a bug escapes. “The architect, the designer, the software team, the DV lead and the formal team all look at the same failure and see something different,” says Darbari. “Nobody can agree on what the system was supposed to do, because nobody ever wrote that down in a form everyone shared. Those differences of opinion were there from day one. They just surface two years later, often in post-silicon debug, when they are most expensive to fix.” Software complexity: While some software is fully encapsulated and hidden from any external interfaces, much is not. “Even something as simple as a PHY has a significant software content,” says Synopsys’ Sanyal. “There is the boot firmware that will establish all the clocks, resets, and memory. Then the PHY has calibration firmware, which will do the initial calibration and adaptation, and it’s updated continuously. That driver needs to tie in to the operating system interrupt and the DMA framework, and the BIOS and hypervisor or coherency or IOMMU dependencies for PCI controller and stuff like that. These all extend the dependency to interrupt between topologies and operating system services and power management framework.” These issues are problematic enough that the UCIe standard attempted to address it. “UCIe 3.0 standardizes how firmware gets downloaded early in initialization,” says Darbari. “The trouble is that the hardware is often only correct under some software assumption. events.title: The Memory Challenge Of Physical AI
events.summary: Most AI hardware conversations start with compute, which is understandable since accelerators are visible, easy to compare, and often tied to headline performance metrics. Physical AI broadens that conversation by placing greater emphasis on how compute, memory, and data movement work together under real-world operating constraints. For intelligent systems that must see, interpret, decide, and act in the physical world in real time, it’s critical that the right data reaches the right engine at the right time. As a result, data movement has become an increasingly important consideration when architecting physical AI systems. A physical AI device may simultaneously handle sensor streams, model weights, activations, temporary buffers, control loops, and safety functions. If memory access becomes unpredictable, compute engines can stall. Power consumption rises when data is moved too often, and poorly planned buffering can cause latency accumulation that is hard to recover from later. As physical AI workloads become more complex, architects must now consider how predictably the complete system performs when multiple real-world workloads are active simultaneously. Avoid unnecessary data movement Physical AI systems rely on a memory hierarchy that coordinates on-chip memory with larger-capacity external memory. LPDDR or GDDR may hold model weights, sensor data, activations, and other working data, while on-chip SRAM and cache keep the portions currently needed by the NPU, CPU, DSP, ISP, or other processing engines close to compute. As workloads move through the processing pipeline, required data is transferred from external memory into on-chip memory, where it can be accessed and reused with lower latency and energy. The more effectively the architecture reuses that local data, the fewer times it must retrieve the same information from external memory. However, because SRAM and cache consume silicon area, their capacity is limited. Data that does not fit on-chip, or is used less frequently, remains in LPDDR or GDDR until it is needed. This coordination is important because every unnecessary transfer across the memory hierarchy consumes energy, adds latency, and uses external-memory bandwidth. Physical AI systems are also constrained by device size, package complexity, power delivery, and thermal headroom. The goal is therefore not to eliminate external memory access, but to keep the right data close to compute for as long as it is useful and avoid moving it more often than necessary. A well-planned dataflow coordinates compute engines, on-chip SRAM and cache, external LPDDR or GDDR, buffering, and interconnect around the workload. This helps keep compute resources productive while using external-memory capacity and bandwidth efficiently. Real-world applications clarify the tradeoffs Humanoid robots, drones, autonomous vehicles, smart cameras, inspection robots, industrial robots, and autonomous mobile robots may all run local intelligence, yet each stresses memory and interfaces differently. Their architectures must determine which data should remain close to compute for immediate access and which should reside in higher-capacity external memory. Humanoids may combine cameras, depth sensing, audio, inertial data, balance control, object recognition, path planning, and actuator feedback within a limited power and thermal envelope. If perception data arrives late, control decisions may be delayed. In addition, sustained performance drops and power rises if model weights and intermediate data are reloaded too often. In this kind of system, memory efficiency affects how smoothly the robot can perceive, decide, and move, all of which are key to successful real-time operation. A drone or autonomous mobile robot has a different set of constraints. It may need visual navigation, obstacle avoidance, stabilization, object tracking, wireless communication, and video processing, all while staying within a limited power and thermal budget. Unnecessary external memory accesses reduce operating time, add heat, or introduce latency into the control loop. For these physical AI systems, bandwidth per watt is as important as raw bandwidth. Autonomous vehicles and advanced driver assistance systems (ADAS) present an even greater challenge. With cameras, radar, lidar, ultrasonic sensors, vehicle telemetry, map data, and control functions, competition for memory access is fierce. Some data streams need continuous throughput, while others need fusion across sensor domains. Retaining relevant data long enough to support planning and decision-making is also an important consideration. In this environment, memory behavior affects both throughput and response predictability. Memory choices must follow the workload When building a memory architecture, architects should begin with the behavior of the physical AI workload itself. The objective is not simply to select the fastest external memory technology or provision the greatest possible bandwidth. It is to right-size the complete memory hierarchy, including local storage, external memory capacity, bandwidth, power, buffering, and integration, around the device’s data streams, reuse patterns, latency requirements, and operating constraints. LPDDR and GDDR address different architectural priorities. LPDDR is often a strong fit when bandwidth per watt and memory capacity are needed to sustain local inference performance. When continuous image or sensor-stream bandwidth is the primary requirement, GDDR may be a viable option because its high bandwidth can meet those performance needs with fewer DRAM devices. Available solutions give architects considerable flexibility in making this tradeoff. For example, Cadence offers LPDDR6/LPDDR5X PHY and Controller IP supporting data rates up to 14.4Gbps, as well as GDDR7 PHY IP supporting data rates up to 36Gbps for high-bandwidth applications. These options allow the external memory interface to be aligned with the workload rather than treated as a one-size-fits-all design choice. A humanoid robot may prioritize power-efficient access to model weights, perception data, and control information. A smart camera or autonomous-vehicle perception processor may place greater pressure on sustained vision-stream bandwidth. In each case, the architecture should keep frequently reused and latency-sensitive data close to compute while selecting an external memory interface sized for the remaining capacity and bandwidth requirements. This helps avoid both memory bottlenecks and unnecessary over-provisioning. events.title: Introduction To FP8 Formats: Part 1
events.summary: The industry is moving from high-precision formats (FP32, FP16, BF16) to lower-precision data types for Machine Learning (ML) inference and training. In cloud and data center environments, lower-precision data types deliver higher throughput by packing more compute per cycle from the same platform. On edge and mobile devices, smaller formats reduce model size, memory footprint and bandwidth, which directly affects power consumption and latency. Arm, Intel, and NVIDIA published an OCP 8-bit Floating Point Specification (OFP8). It is an interchange format that allows software systems to share the models easily. FP8 is not a future concept, it is being deployed today. It is already supported by NVIDIA’s Hopper H100 GPU, with software deployment appearing in major ML frameworks. Arm added the FP8 support to the Arm v9 ISA and is exploring the best way to integrate the FP8 across all the ML platforms. This blog post explains the FP8 data formats, the new Floating-point Mode Register (FPMR), and the instruction set that makes FP8 practical on Arm CPUs. FP8 data format Unlike IEEE FP64, FP32, and FP16, FP8 is not a single format, it is a family. The whitepaper FP8 Formats for Deep Learning proposes an FP8 format consisting of two encodings: E4M3 and E5M2. Why a family of formats? With only 8 bits available, FP8 makes a trade-off between precision and dynamic range. A single encoding cannot fit all tensors equally well. Activations and weights usually have a smaller and more stable value distribution after training or calibration. They can therefore benefit from more mantissa bits, which help represent nearby values more precisely. Gradients can change much more during forward and backward passes. They can therefore benefit from more exponent bits and a larger dynamic range, which helps avoid overflow or underflow. The two encodings enable software to choose the right format for each tensor role. Use E4M3 when precision is more important and use E5M2 when dynamic range is more important. This is the key idea from FP8, and Arm reflects the same idea in the FPMR register. With FPMR, each source operand can independently select which FP8 format it uses. Supported data types E4M3 E5M2 Exponent bits 4 5 Mantissa bits 3 2 Bias 7 15 Max normal value 448 57344 Special values NaN only Inf and NaN E4M3 uses 1 sign bit, 4 exponent bits, and 3 mantissa bits, with a bias of 7. E4M3 uses most bit patterns for normal finite numbers instead of saving many of them for special values. This helps E4M3 extend dynamic range, which is more useful for deep learning workloads. E5M2 uses 1 sign bit, 5 exponent bits, and 2 mantissa bits, with a bias of 15. E5M2 follows IEEE 754 conventions for the exponent field and special values, including infinities and NaNs. Because of this, it can be viewed as IEEE FP16 with fewer mantissa bits, like how bfloat16 and TF32 can be viewed as IEEE FP32 with fewer bits. This makes conversion between E5M2 and IEEE FP16 straightforward, while still providing a wider dynamic range than E4M3 FPMR: The Floating-Point Mode Register When hardware executes an FP8 instruction, it must know the format of each source operand, the format of the destination result, and the scale factors to apply. Because FP8 modes can change per tensor, software may need to update the format and scaling settings frequently inside performance-critical code. For this reason, Arm introduced a dedicated control register – FPMR. FPMR is separate from FPCR. Hardware can recognize and rename FPMR writes more efficiently, making per-tensor FP8 mode changes closer to a normal register write rather than a pipeline-serializing control update. FPMR contains the following fields: Field Bits Description F8S1 [2:0] Format of 1st FP8 source. 0b000 = E5M2, 0b001 = E4M3. F8S2 [5:3] Format of 2nd FP8 source. Same encoding as F8S1. F8D [8:6] Destination result Format for instructions that convert other floating-point formats to FP8. Same encoding as F8S1. OSM [14] Overflow Saturation for FP8 multiplication instructions. OSC [15] Overflow Saturation for FP8 convert instructions. LSCALE [22:16] Unsigned Log2 down-scaling factor. Result × 2^(−LSCALE). NSCALE [31:24] Unsigned Log2 up-scaling factor for widening FP8 sources. LSCALE2 [37:32] Second down-scaling value for dual-source convert instructions. FP8 instruction set on Arm The 2023 and 2024 architecture extensions add FP8 instructions across Advanced SIMD, SVE and SME. The following table summarizes the architectural features and the instructions they provide. Architectural features Supported category Instructions Description FEAT_FP8 Advanced SIMD/SVE/SME FCVTN, FCVT, F1CVT, F2CVT, BF1CVT, BF2CVT, FSCALE FP8 convert instructions; a floating-point scale instruction. FEAT_FP8FMA Advanced SIMD/SVE FMLALB, FMLALT, FMLALLBB, FMLALLBT, FMLALLTB, FMLALLTT FP8 widening multiply-accumulate. FEAT_FP8DOT4 Advanced SIMD/SVE FDOT (.S) FP8 → FP32 4-way dot product. FEAT_FP8DOT2 Advanced SIMD/SVE FDOT (.H) FP8 → FP16 2-way dot product. FEAT_SSVE_FP8FMA SME FMLALB, FMLALT, FMLALLBB, FMLALLTT FP8 widening multiply-accumulate in Streaming SVE mode. FEAT_SSVE_FP8DOT4 SME FDOT (.S) FP8 → FP32 4-way dot product and accumulate in Streaming SVE mode. FEAT_SSVE_FP8DOT2 SME FDOT (.H) FP8 → FP16 2-way dot product and accumulate in Streaming SVE mode. FEAT_SME_F8F32 SME FMOPA, FDOT, FVDOTB, FVDOTT, FMLALL FP8 outer product and accumulate into FP32 ZA tile; FP8 dot product and accumulate into FP32 ZA array; FP8 widening multiply-accumulate into FP32 ZA array; FEAT_SME_F8F16 SME FMOPA, FDOT, FVDOT, FMLAL FP8 outer product and accumulate into FP16 ZA tile; FP8 dot product and accumulate into FP16 ZA array; FP8 widening multiply-accumulate into FP16 ZA array. FEAT_F8F32MM Advanced SIMD/SVE FMMLA FP8 matrix multiply-accumulate to FP32 FEAT_F8F16MM Advanced SIMD/SVE FMMLA FP8 matrix multiply-accumulate to FP16 All FP8 compute instructions read the source format from FPMR (F8S1/F8S2) and apply scaling via LSCALE/NSCALE. These widening instructions always use FP8 data as the input format. Accumulation uses a wider type, such as FP16 or FP32. This keeps the bandwidth advantage of FP8 inputs while preserving numerical stability during accumulation. Further reading For more detailed information about FP8, see the Arm Architecture Reference Manual for A-profile architecture and the FP8 Formats for Deep Learning paper . Part 2 will explore FP8 instructions, from conversion and scaling to dot products, matrix multiplication, and outer products in Advanced SIMD, SVE, and SME. The post Introduction To FP8 Formats: Part 1 appeared first on Semiconductor Engineering .

events.title: Alphabet raises almost US$4 billion from Hong Kong, Singapore bond sales
events.summary: The strong order books give Google parent Alphabet flexibility to increase its planned financing. Alphabet raised almost US$4 billion through inaugural Hong Kong and Singapore dollar bonds, showing strong demand for a high-rated tech borrower in local Asian markets. Orders were strong, with demand above HK$32.5 billion and S$4 billion. Pricing tightened from initial guidance, according to a person familiar with the matter. The funds will support general corporate purposes, including debt repayment, as Alphabet and other hyperscalers borrow heavily to finance AI projects amid rising investor caution. HONG KONG – Alphabet raised almost US$4 billion (S$5 billion) in equivalent funds in Asia through inaugural Hong Kong- and Singapore-dollar bond sales, testing investor appetite at a time of increasing volatility for companies focused on artificial intelligence. The Google parent sold a three-part Hong Kong dollar bond, consisting of two-year, five-year and 10-year tranches, for a total of HK$16 billion (S$2.6 billion), and a four-part Singapore dollar bond, consisting of two-year, five-year, 10-year and 30-year tranches, for S$2.28 billion, according to a person familiar with the matter. The Hong Kong dollar-denominated bonds tightened by 25 to 30 basis points from initial thoughts, while the Singapore dollar notes priced at 20 to 25 basis points tighter than initially indicated, said the person, who asked not to be identified discussing non-public information. Orders for the Hong Kong dollar tranches exceeded HK$32.5 billion by the time final guidance was released, while demand for the Singapore dollar tranches topped S$4 billion at that stage, according to the person. “Asia’s local currency market is less crowded compared to the dollar market,” said Gary Ng, senior economist at Natixis. “Deals such as Alphabet’s offer local investors a rare combination of highly rated global technology company and debt in their own currencies, which should attract strong demand,” he said. Proceeds from the offering will be used for general corporate purposes, which may include the repayment of outstanding debt. The deal comes at a challenging moment for technology industry borrowers. Investors have become more cautious toward AI-linked assets after a broad market selloff last week fuelled by concerns that a Democrat sweep in the US midterm elections could lead to greater scrutiny of data centre development and AI infrastructure spending. The sector has also been shaken by market turmoil sparked by Nvidia , the leading maker of AI chips, which has been working with an outside firm to identify potential replacements for chief executive Jensen Huang. Alphabet’s fund-raising effort is part of a broader push by global hyperscalers to tap new debt markets as they seek financing for AI-related projects. The company sold its first Australian dollar bonds in August and has also issued notes in Swiss francs, British pounds, Canadian dollars and Japanese yen in 2026. Alphabet and other firms, including Microsoft, Amazon.com and Meta Platforms, have been borrowing at a record pace while simultaneously committing tens of billions of dollars to build out AI capabilities. Earlier in November, Alphabet raised €6 billion (S$8.5 billion) through a multi-tranche euro bond sale, its second offering in the currency in 2026. The company paid materially higher borrowing costs than in its inaugural euro deal in May as concerns over the pace of AI spending rose. BLOOMBERG
