events.title: RISC-V For AI: Breakthrough Or Bad Idea?
events.summary: Key Takeaways: RISC-V’s role in AI is contested. Its customization offers flexibility, but splitting inference workloads between CPUs and accelerators can introduce costly data movement and compiler complexity. Control may be RISC-V’s best option. Custom instructions can help orchestrate accelerators, reduce load/store latency, and handle limited mathematical tasks without taking on heavyweight inference. Correct instructions don’t guarantee a working chip. Custom AI systems also need observability and system-level verification to expose performance bottlenecks, cache-coherency problems, and interconnect deadlocks. Experts At The Table: Demand for parallelism and power efficiency is shifting chip design from general computing to AI, increasing the need for flexible, modular, and open hardware. This trend is bringing RISC-V into AI acceleration. Customizable hardware can implement AI computations directly instead of relying on fixed CPU designs. Semiconductor Engineering sat down to discuss these issues with Steve Roddy, chief marketing officer at Quadric ; Francisca Tan, director of product management and product engineering for Tessent at Siemens EDA ; Ewald Liess, senior vice president of sales and business development at SignatureIP ; and Dave Kelf, CEO of Breker. What follows are excerpts of that conversation. L-R: Quadric’s Roddy; Siemens EDA’s Tan; SignatureIP’s Liess; Breker’s Kelf. SE: With AI models evolving rapidly, architects use RISC-V to design highly specialized extensions. From an IP provider standpoint, how would you balance delivering a standardized, reusable IP core with the extreme customization that customers are demanding for AI workloads? Leiss : We don’t think that we need to configure because we provide NoC and PCI Express and CXL CHI AMBA interfaces. Based on this, we don’t need to customize. Instead, it’s the NoC that will be configured. Because we have a pre-verified NoC, we can do that with our tools. We can configure customized RISC-Vs. Of course, the customers may modify the RISC-V core with new instructions, but they will stick to the interfaces like the AMBA bus, or CXL, PCI Express interfaces, because this enables them to access the external components that they need, like memory or going off-chip. And this is where we come in. So the RISC-V guys should feel free to do whatever they want. Tan : Custom verification and validation also become important, as does observability. For test and embedded analytics, engineers doing debug or silicon bring-up can monitor, introspect, and inspect internal signals, or calculate whether performance is being met. In my view, it’s also about hardware observability, as the industry moves into various challenges and complexity in the chip. Roddy : We’ll take the contrarian view in this particular area. We think that starting with RISC-V to do an AI accelerator is a flat-out bad idea, because you instantly create a problem. You now have a partition between some things running on a programmable processor with good ALU capacity, and some external accelerator where you’ve now had to partition the system. The minute you partition, the minute you create a problem, you need fancy compilers to go fix it and figure out how to move data from the accelerator or accelerators across a nice NoC over to a programmable core, and back and forth. That’s a problem that scales badly. The bigger the accelerator, the worse it gets. And so now you’re compounding the problem. If you have something that’s, say, 100 TOPS and you have to have, say, 16 RISC-V processors slave to a whole bunch of accelerator blocks, sure, you need great interconnect, and you need great verification, and all those things that go with it because you’re trying to solve the underlying fundamental problem, which is starting with a CPU. And CPUs are great for chasing pointers. That’s what CPUs do. CPUs have wonderful logic to handle the fact that you’ve got 40 threads running, and on the very next clock tick, you have no idea what you’ll be running. That’s not what you’re doing when you’re doing AI inference. You know for millions of cycles in advance what’s happening. You don’t need most of the CPU hardware. DSPs are a little closer to what you need, but DSPs are vector machines — vector-by-scalar or vector-by-vector. And most of what is challenging in AI is matrix-by-matrix. So we built a matrix-native machine. The only other one I know of that’s close to that is in the data center, and that’s the big giant TPUs from Google. Literally, everybody else has a partitioned problem, and then they struggle and spend billions of dollars trying to handle that partitioning problem and figure out how to make up for the fact that they started from, we think, a bad place. Kelf : I agree with Steve’s point, because what we’re seeing is large AI accelerators — which might be different architectures, SIMD, SIMT — are pretty common. These kinds of things basically are controlled, or have been controlled, by a complex state machine of some sort, and then there’ll be some kind of host processor driving several of these different things and telling the state machine what to do, and then driving the accelerator. What we’ve seen in four instances now, both big and small companies, is that the state machines are hopeless. So they’re taking a RISC-V processor, and they’re using that as the control function on top of these accelerators for a number of reasons. One is that they can, in fact, build in a bunch of mathematical engines — exactly what Steve was mentioning — vector type, using either the RISC-V vector instructions or those. And then they add in their own, as well, or some of the new matrix multiplication instructions. They’re also putting in their own instructions for very efficient load/store to reduce the latency that you see between partitions. So they’re trying to figure out how they can adjust these RISC-V processes to reduce that latency and to reduce that partitioning problem. We have a number of examples where some are successful, some are less so. They’re still working on this problem, but RISC-V is nice because they can add whatever custom instructions they want, still use a regular compiler, and create a mechanism to drive a very efficient load/store that they can’t with other processors. Then, of course, there are people like Arm and others who have built instructions into some of their processors, but they’re not variable. RISC-V is ideal for this, and pretty unique in its ability to create these powerful custom instructions. events.title: Foundation IP For The AI Era: Why Execution Shapes SoC Cost ─ eBook
events.summary: Manufacturing, Packaging & Materials Technical Papers Home '; AI/ML/DL Architectures Automotive/ Aerospace Communication/Data Movement Design & Verification Lithography Manufacturing Materials Memory Optoelectronics / Photonics Packaging Power & Performance Quantum Security Test, Measurement, Analytics tech papers Transistors Z-End Applications Videos & Research Videos Industry Research Newsletters & Store Newsletters Store MENU Home Special Reports Systems & Design Low Power-High Performance Manufacturing, Packaging & Materials Test, Measurement & Analytics Auto, Security and AI Knowledge Center Videos Startup Corner Business & Startups Jobs Technical Papers Events Webinars Industry Research Newsletters Store Special Reports How an integrated foundation IP strategy can reduce execution risk, enable faster tape-out, and lower TCO. As AI workloads push power, performance, voltage, and process variation to new limits, the economics of advanced-node SoCs are changing. In addition to the cost of the IP itself, hidden costs often arrive later in the design cycle: integration delays, schedule slips, re-spins, and missed market windows. As design complexity rises, predictable execution is becoming a critical factor in total cost of ownership (TCO) alongside power, performance, and area (PPA). Sourcing Foundation IP piece by piece can add another layer of complexity. Logic libraries, embedded memories, I/Os, and OTP NVM IP from multiple suppliers bring different deliverables, roadmaps, support models, and integration requirements. An integrated Foundation IP platform can reduce these seams by bringing the core building blocks together as one silicon-proven, verified stack, with sign-off-ready characterization and IP + EDA co-optimization to improve PPA and accelerate implementation. This tighter alignment helps design teams move toward tape-out with greater predictability. The impact extends beyond integration. Across HPC and Edge AI designs, improvements in PPA can translate into meaningful economic value through smaller die area, lower operating power, and increased performance, while avoiding a re-spin or major tape-out delay can protect even more value. The Synopsys eBook “ Foundation IP for the AI Era ” explores these tradeoffs through 3nm data center and Edge AI SoC examples, combining silicon-proven Synopsys Foundation IP PPA benchmarks with modeled cost estimates based on public market data to illustrate how execution decisions can affect TCO. Download the eBook to see how an integrated Foundation IP strategy can help reduce execution risk, enable faster tape-out, and lower TCO for HPC and Edge AI SoCs. events.title: Water industry bonus ban to be tightened as Ofwat warns of ‘damage to public trust’
events.summary: Regulator to hasten review over concerns that firms are ‘undermining’ rules to make large payments to bosses The water company bonus ban is set to be tightened after the regulator accused the industry of a risk of “damaging public trust” with large payments to bosses that appeared to get around the rules. Anglian Water was singled out for particular criticism over “retention payments” worth up to £800,000 for its chief executive, Mark Thurston, despite the bonus ban. Anglian will face increased monitoring of its governance arrangements because of the controversial payments. Angela Eagle, the environment secretary, said she wanted to “close loopholes” so that “failure doesn’t pay”. Nine water companies in England and Wales – including Thames Water and Yorkshire Water – were banned from paying bonuses for the 2025-26 financial year, the regulator Ofwat said on Thursday. Seven of the bans related to environmental pollution. The Labour government introduced the bonus ban last year amid public outrage over sewage leaking into Britain’s rivers and seas. Yet water company bosses’ pay has risen in the past two years despite the ban, according to Guardian analysis. Campaigners and opposition politicians have argued that companies are circumventing the ban through a variety of payments which are not “performance-related” – but which effectively replace the banned bonuses. Ofwat on Thursday said it would accelerate a review into the rules, over concerns that companies were deliberately “undermining” the ban. It is understood that ministers will also consider whether payments from water companies’ parent companies could be included in the ban. The regulator said: “The growing use of fixed so-called ‘retention payments’ and substantial increases in base pay without sufficient explanation or supporting evidence risks damaging public trust and creating a perception that companies are circumventing the rule.” Anglian’s payments to Thurston “could give the impression the company had prioritised offering executive directors a cash award in a way that would not technically breach the rule and would in practice replace the loss of PRP [performance-related pay] prohibited by it”, Ofwat said. As well as Anglian, Ofwat highlighted potential retention payments of £1m for Thames Water’s chief financial officer, £1.5m for Northumbrian Water chief executive, Heidi Mottram, and £1.7m for Louise Beardmore, the chief executive of United Utilities. Andy Burnham is under pressure to clamp down on the water industry. He has said he wants to exert “more public control” over the water industry , although he is yet to give details. He is yet to make a decision on whether to move Thames into temporary government ownership after years of financial struggles and mismanagement, months after suggesting he might do so. Thames Water paid its chief executive, Chris Weston, a previously deferred bonus of £99,000 during the year , despite the ban. Ofwat said that Thames Water’s future owners would have to pay for the bonus, rather than the money coming from customer bills. Thames was also criticised for raising executives’ base pay. Get set for the working day – we'll point you to all the business news and analysis you need every morning The other companies banned from paying bonuses were Severn Trent Water, Southern Water, South West Water, Wessex Water and Dŵr Cymru (Welsh Water). Ofwat said they would have paid out another £6.5m to executives during the year had the ban not been in place. Eagle said: “People are sick of seeing water bosses profit while rivers are polluted and customers are repeatedly let down. A wide-ranging review launching today will ensure that failure doesn’t pay, whatever name the payment goes by. “The bonus ban was the first step. Where there are loopholes, I want them closed.” South East Water was not subject to the ban, but Ofwat said the company’s shareholders would have to pay for future bonuses after huge supply failures left tens of thousands of households without water during the financial year . Helen Campbell, the interim executive director for delivery at Ofwat, said: “It is disappointing that so many companies continue to trigger the rule through serious performance failures which has seen £10m in payments blocked in the past two years. “Public trust in the water sector remains low, and executive bonuses which do not reflect performance, use of retention payments and poorly explained increases in base pay contribute to that low trust. That is why we are accelerating our review to ensure the rule better delivers the outcomes customers rightly expect.” Ofwat also criticised the paucity of information on pay reported by South Staffs Water.

events.title: Data centre industry butts up against community challenges
events.summary: News Home Just In For You Analysis Rural Watch Live Health Indigenous Politics Science Deep Time Elections World Environment Investigations Business Local news Quizzes Sport AFL NRL Football Tennis Cricket Netball Lifestyle Wellbeing Relationships & Family Food & Recipes Personal Finance Home & Garden Entertainment TV & Movies Books Music Pop Culture Arts Data centre industry faces community challenges amid cancelled projects Data centre companies are reportedly grappling with how to get community engagement "right". ( ABC News: James Wakelin ) The industry body for data centre proponents says its members are battling community hesitancy and policy uncertainty. It comes amid calls by minor parties for SA to halt approvals for new centres. The state government is preparing legislation to regulate the industry. The peak body representing data centres in Australia say its members are still grappling with "getting community consultation right" after several AI companies have either dumped or paused their plans for building centres across the country. South Australia has today seen the first sign of data centre development in retreat , with Quantum DC announcing it will pause plans to build a 1200-megawatt AI data centre in Tungkillo, in the Adelaide Hills, following deep frustration, anger and protests from the surrounding community. In New South Wales, another AI data centre proposed for Sydney's south, on the Cooks River, was scrapped over the weekend, the latest in a series of proposed NSW data centres to be dumped following community opposition. Peak body Data Centres Australia does not represent Quantum DC. Speaking broadly, its CEO Belinda Dennett said the challenge with community engagement was choosing the right time. "Communities want early engagement, but they also want detailed answers, so there is a bit of a trade-off. "Often, early engagement means you don't have all those answers around design plans, around energy source, around how much water that may use." She said there was great potential and interest to build data centres in South Australia, but operators and investors wanted policy certainty. "That's the challenge for all the states at the moment, the challenge of not having federal rules in place … we don't have that policy certainty," she said. "The quicker we have certainty, the more viable I think Australia's going to be." Tungkillo's rolling hills won't have a data centre, for now. ( Supplied: Magdalene Lippett ) All sides of politics welcome pause On Thursday, political parties including the Liberals, One Nation and the Greens welcomed the pause on the Tungkillo development, while the SA government criticised the developer for its consultation process. The Greens went a step further, calling for a data centre moratorium. SA's minister for artificial intelligence (AI), Chris Picton, said the Tungkillo announcement highlighted why the state government was keen to get legislation through the parliament to enable proper regulatory control. "[It's] going to be critical to making sure that we can think through all these issues with data centres to make sure that can be managed in an appropriate way, whether that be issues about energy, or water, or land use," Mr Picton said. Opposition leader Ashton Hurn said it didn't make sense for a data centre at Tungkillo to be built on "prime agricultural land", but there was also a need to make sure the community understood why data centres are needed. "We believe that a vehicle to do that is including them in the royal commission," Ms Hurn said. When details of the state's Royal Commission into Artificial Intelligence were released in early October , its terms of reference did not include data centres. Mr Picton said it wasn't remiss of the government not to include them: "They are completely separate things. "Data centres have issues, but they're infrastructure issues … They're issues about energy use, water use and where the land is." Community protests against the Tungkillo data centre seem to have had an effect. ( ABC News: James Wakelin ) The Greens, One Nation and the Liberal Party united in the upper house on Wednesday to establish a parliamentary inquiry into data centres, which was not supported by Labor. One Nation SA leader Cory Bernardi said the party would like to see a pause on data centres until the inquiry is finished. "But we're also recognising that data centres per se are not bad," he said. "We have a data centre here in the metropolitan area of Adelaide that hasn't caused any fuss at all. "But what we want is a community licence for it." events.title: Nvidia without succession plan as CEO Jensen Huang resigns
events.summary: News Home Just In For You Analysis Rural Watch Live Health Indigenous Politics Science Deep Time Elections World Environment Investigations Business Local news Quizzes Sport AFL NRL Football Tennis Cricket Netball Lifestyle Wellbeing Relationships & Family Food & Recipes Personal Finance Home & Garden Entertainment TV & Movies Books Music Pop Culture Arts Jensen Huang's departure from Nvidia could leave a leadership vacuum at the leading AI chip company. ( AP: Go Nakamura/Pool ) When reports of an espionage plot against Nvidia's Jensen Huang first emerged, the company stood by its chief executive. Nvidia spokesperson John Rizzo released a statement saying Mr Huang was committed to keep leading the firm "without interruption". Before its probe into Mr Huang's romantic relationship with a suspected Chinese spy was even underway, Nvidia said it had "no reason to believe" either US national security or company secrets had been compromised. Just days later, Mr Huang has resigned effective immediately. How Nvidia came to investigate Jensen Huang's affair The chief executive of the world's most valuable company and a close ally of Donald Trump admitted to an affair with a woman suspected of being a Chinese spy. Here's what we know. The New York Times reported he had a second extra-marital affair with Nvidia executive Kimberly Powell, the company's vice-president of health care, who also reported to him. This week, shares in the multi-trillion-dollar tech giant tumbled, while Nvidia and Mr Huang have faced a ‌proposed class action accusing them ‌of ⁠defrauding ‌shareholders . But what is perhaps most extraordinary is that Nvidia has had no obvious successor to Mr Huang, who had run the company since it was created 33 years ago. Holding the position of co-founder, president and chief executive, Mr Huang had created an unusually flat corporate structure, with about 60 executives reporting directly to him. He once said he did not believe in succession planning, according to The Wall Street Journal, despite his family being woven into the company's fabric. Jensen Huang's daughter, Madison (left), is a senior marketing director at Nvidia and Spencer (right), his son, is a product line manager in robotics. ( Thu Hoang Ly/The Mercury News/Getty Images ) Mr Huang was the only Nvidia insider on the company's board, which operates without a permanent chair. Instead, a lead director is chosen annually by a majority of board members. "Jensen is not replaceable … there is no other person on the management team bench that can step in seamlessly as CEO," tech analyst Dan Ives had told Reuters. After his resignation was announced, shares of Nvidia, one of the largest companies in the world, plunged 13 per cent in early Wall Street trading overnight on Thursday, dragging the broader stock market lower. Jensen Huang admitted to being unfaithful to his wife after reports emerged he had developed a relationship with Alice Huang (no relation), a data centre executive at the centre of the alleged spy plot. ( Reuters: CTI ) Mr Huang's departure could leave the world-leading chip maker and global AI trade in an even more precarious position, according to investment analyst Jun Bei Liu. "He's the face of Nvidia and Nvidia has been front and centre of the AI build-out," she said. "If we look at how many new cloud data centre businesses have been sponsored in this circular financing world, it's pretty much all by Nvidia. "There's just a lot of uncertainty to come … not just for Nvidia, it's for the whole AI, the circular financing, the AI build-out, all the ⁠businesses that they co-invest and sponsor." Mr Huang spent decades building Nvidia into a leading developer of graphics processing units, the hardware that AI companies such as OpenAI and Anthropic rely on to operate. One of the world's most valuable companies, Nvidia hit a market capitalisation of $US5.7 trillion ($8.3 trillion) at its peak in early October. Jensen Huang is one of the world's most influential figures in the tech and AI industry. ( Reuters: Kim Soo-hyeon ) In America's pursuit to win the AI race against China, Mr Huang emerged as a close ally of US President Donald Trump and was one of the few people known to have a direct line to him. He has been to the White House at least five times since Mr Trump returned to office and just months ago he accompanied him on a trip to Beijing. Mr Huang's star power also extends to other tech billionaires such as Larry Ellison and Elon Musk, who famously begged him for more Nvidia chips. (Already, the SpaceX founder has suggested he would hire him). NYT tech reporter Ryan Mac told the ABC's Afternoon Briefing that Mr Huang was a person "that sets the tone when it comes to AI regulation or lack thereof". "He is an agenda-setter, someone that has a close relationship with Donald Trump and influences policy not just in the US but globally.

events.summary: News Home Just In For You Analysis Rural Watch Live Health Indigenous Politics Science Deep Time Elections World Environment Investigations Business Local news Quizzes Sport AFL NRL Football Tennis Cricket Netball Lifestyle Wellbeing Relationships & Family Food & Recipes Personal Finance Home & Garden Entertainment TV & Movies Books Music Pop Culture Arts Qld coalmine employs 275 workers to reopen after being in receivership Dump trucks on the haul road at the mine. ( ABC Tropical North: Liam O'Connell ) A Queensland company has reopened the New Burton Coal Mine in the Bowen Basin. Premier David Crisafulli officially reopened the mine today. Mine owner Argo Resources Queensland says the state's coal royalties did not deter it from investing. A Queensland mining company has employed 275 workers and reopened a Bowen Basin coalmine that went into receivership in 2025. Argo Resources Queensland purchased the New Burton Mine near Moranbah, about 120 kilometres south-west of Mackay, from Bowen Coking Coal in June. It is the fourth mine Argo has a controlling interest in after acquiring a 70 per cent stake in Bowen Basin mines Broadlea, Carborough Downs and Ironbark in March for an undisclosed sum. Premier David Crisafulli reopened the mine today, saying coal mining had a "bullish future". "People need to know that the future of mining in Queensland is secure," Mr Crisafulli said. "But also, the future of coal mining in Queensland, and I'm talking about both thermal and met [metallurgical] coal, there's a future for both." David Crisafulli visits the mine for its reopening. ( ABC Tropical North: Liam O'Connell ) He said the Queensland government had not contributed to the mine with financial incentives or delayed royalty payments. Argo CEO Richard Livingstone-Blevins said royalties were not a deterrent to acquiring coalmines. "At the end of the day, we invested in the state based on the current royalty regime that's in place," he said. The mine entrance near Moranbah in the Bowen Basin. ( ABC Tropical North: Liam O'Connell ) Mr Livingstone-Blevins declined to comment on why the previous mine owners were not profitable. "We've got great infrastructure, we've got great people, we've got coal on the ground at economic strip ratios, and we've got a lot of ground that we can open up, moving forward," he said. "We all run vastly different businesses with vastly different cost profiles and different assets that have different operating costs." Mr Livingstone-Blevins said Argo planned to mine 10 million tonnes of saleable coal by 2028. "We have two prep plant hubs, we've got two rail loops, we're serviced by our own haul road, we've got our own camp, we've got four mines along the strike, and we've got over 4 billion tonnes of resource in the ground, which we seek to develop as we push forward," he said. events.title: Gas bills to rise as Middle East turmoil persists
events.summary: Island Energy said customers can contact its customer team for support Published 12 November 2026, 06:15 GMT Gas customers in Jersey will see their bills increase by about 5% from 1 December after Island Energy announced a rise in tariffs for households and businesses. The company said its mains gas, mini bulk tank and cylinder tariffs would increase by 1p per kilowatt hour (kWh) for all domestic and commercial customers from 1 December 2026. It said the increase reflected higher wholesale gas and liquefied petroleum gas costs amid disruption to exports and shipping routes in the Middle East after the conflict with Iran. Chief executive Graeme Millar said: "We recognise that any price increase is unwelcome, particularly during winter." Listen to the latest news for Jersey Securing fuel at lower prices in advance had limited the impact of wholesale cost increases on customers, Millar said. However, the energy boss added: "It cannot fully protect customers from sustained increases in the cost of fuel and bringing it to Jersey." Island Energy said customers concerned about paying their gas bills could contact its customer team to discuss what support might be available. events.title: AWS distills its cloud into a local emulator that runs on your PC
events.summary: Security All Security Cyber-crime Patches Research CSO Off-Prem All Off-Prem Edge and IoT Channel PaaS and IaaS SaaS On-Prem All On-Prem Systems Storage Networks HPC Personal Tech Cx0 Public Sector Software All Software AI and ML Applications Databases DevOps OS Platforms Virtualization Offbeat All Offbeat Columnists Supercomputing BOFH Legal Site News About Us Special Features All Special Features Supercomputing Month 2026 Nvidia GTC Berlin 2026 Cybersecurity Month 2026 VMware Explore 2026 Cloud Infrastructure Month 2026 HPE: AI Explainers Agentic AI The Future of the Datacenter AWS:Reinvent Nvidia GTC Computex 2026 AI Infrastructure Month 2026 The State of Storage 2026 RSA Conference Vendor Voice All Vendor Voice Modernizing Financial Services with FIS and AWS Barco Infinidat Everpure Rubrik Make it real with Capgemini and AWS Money Movement Hub ZTE Nutanix: Scale Kubernetes. Not Chaos. AWS New Horizon Digicert Netscout Resources Intelligence Webinars & Events Newsletters Hyperscale meets micro-computing by offering APIs to test your apps Attackers backdoor trusted AWS integrations to steal secrets 2 days ago Home Office cloud services contract may net AWS £1B 6 days ago AWS installs an AI accelerator every 14 seconds and eyes $1 trillion annual revenue 13 days ago Startup wants to make AI agents safe for DevOps duty 13 days ago Amazon tells tokenmaxxing devs to slow their AI roll 15 days ago AWS has released an emulator that kind-of-almost lets you use its cloud on a PC. As explained in the GitHub repository for the prosaically named “AWS Emulator,” the tool “is a local program that serves an AWS API endpoint.” The emulator doesn’t replicate the whole AWS cloud, instead offering its APIs. “You use it to test your software without calling AWS, on your own machine, on a development server, or in continuous integration (CI),” the repo explains. Because those tests never touch the AWS cloud, the tool is free to use. AWS wrote the emulator in Rust, a choice that senior specialist solutions architect Daniel Abib wrote helps to ensure the tool “stays light on CPU and memory on a laptop.” The emulator tool doesn’t replicate the entire AWS cloud. Abib said it supports the APIs of AWS services that have an API model in the AWS API models repository on GitHub . The Register found over 1,300 items on that page. While the tool lets developers test APIs, it doesn’t replicate anywhere near all the features of the Amazonian cloud. “It doesn’t evaluate IAM [Identity and Access Management] policies the way AWS does, and each emulator acts as a single account, with no cross-account or cross-Region behavior,” Abib wrote, adding “How closely it matches AWS varies by service and feature.” AWS publishes “fidelity scores” that detail how closely the emulator works on different AWS services. Amazon tries to achieve full fidelity, so the emulator produces the same results as AWS for valid API calls, and the same errors for invalid ones. Coding agents can also drive the Emulator, an option The Register mentions because AWS advises the easiest way to check if a project will work with the tool is to use the aws-emulator skill for AI coding agents. “With the skill, your agent finds the AWS operations and resources that your project depends on. It checks them against the fidelity tests and fidelity scores for the emulator. It then tells you which parts of your project you can rely on the emulator for, and which ones might behave differently from AWS,” according to AWS documentation. AWS has made the emulator available as an RPM or Debian package. Mac and PC users will need to run Docker and an image of the Emulator. “You install the emulator, start it, and point your tools at the local endpoint,” Abib instructed. “When AWS Emulator starts, it generates its own credentials, a config file, and a certificate, and writes them to ~/.aws/emulator/9297/ . You set environment variables so the AWS SDK talks to your laptop instead of AWS, and your application code stays unchanged.” “From there, your existing tests, CLI scripts, and coding agents keep working the way they already do. A unit test that creates an Amazon DynamoDB table, writes an item, and reads it back is the same test, and it runs on your machine without a deployment.” The cloud colossus’s intent appears, as ever, to encourage more use of its cloud – in this case by satisfying developers their code will run well when deployed there, and making it easy for them to test for that. ® Jensen Huang's self-sabotage sends Nvidia into a midlife crisis The competition is circling like vultures Palantir’s Karp takes a sharp left turn, says he and the company’s products are actually ‘progressive’ Trump donor says he privately questioned deportation tactics.

events.title: Hunt is on for heir to strange block of land
events.summary: News Home Just In For You Analysis Rural Watch Live Health Indigenous Politics Science Deep Time Elections World Environment Investigations Business Local news Quizzes Sport AFL NRL Football Tennis Cricket Netball Lifestyle Wellbeing Relationships & Family Food & Recipes Personal Finance Home & Garden Entertainment TV & Movies Books Music Pop Culture Arts Qld government hunts for heir to strange block of land needed for Logan-Gold Coast Faster Rail project Des Crump is a historian and bottle collector who has researched August Thorsborne. ( ABC News : Phoebe Hosier ) The Queensland Department of Transport and Main Roads is looking for the owner of a 10sqm block of land. The department intends to resume the land as part of upgrades to Holmview Station in Beenleigh. Objections to the land being acquired must be lodged by November 17. Local sleuths and state bureaucrats are trying to find the true heir to a strange block of land in Logan, south of Brisbane, with only five days left. The Department of Transport and Main Roads is looking for anyone who believes they have an interest in the August Thorsborne estate. That tiny block of land, 16 metres long and 60 centimetres wide, is needed to facilitate upgrades to the Holmview station precinct, which is part of Logan and Gold Coast Faster Rail. A published Notice of Intention to Resume states: "To: The beneficiaries, heirs or any party establishing an interest in the estate of August Thorsborne (deceased) Take notice that on 13 October 2026, the Chief Executive, Department of Transport and Main Roads (TMR) pursuant to the provisions of the Acquisition of Land Act 1967, the Transport Infrastructure Act 1994 and the Transport Planning and Coordination Act 1994 issued a notice that intends to take an area of 10 square metres … in the locality of Beenleigh, for a purpose incidental to transport (railway) namely road… Any written objections to the intended take are required by 17 November 2026." Des Crump is a historian and bottle collector; the reason the latter is important will become clear shortly. He spoke to Steve Austin about his research into Mr Thorsborne on 612 ABC Brisbane Mornings. "It's [a] funny little shape, [a] funny little bit of land, but it's surprising that there's no descendants because he [August Thorsborne] had quite a few children," he said. "It doesn't seem to be specifically connected to where he ran his soft drink business, and he had a brewery, and all those other things that wouldn't fit on that sort of block of land." Despite the lack of heirs apparent, the family name is still prominent in the areas around Holmview station, with a road and a park named after the family. Mr Crump, who has roles at The University of Queensland and the State Archives, has some of the bottles from the soft drink company in his collection. "(The Thorsborne family) came out from Sweden, ended up in Beenleigh in the 1870s, had interests in the hotel area, mostly known for his soft drink factory," he said. "It was a Beenleigh Soda with this gauntlet trademark." He said the bottles in his collection were rare because the early ones had marbles in them and children would break them to get to them. Mr Thorsborne was also a member of the Beenleigh Shire Council in 1888. Mr Crump said Mr Thorsborne had 11 children, two died in childhood, and the family had the soft drink factory through to the 1930s. "So, you think there must still be family there," he said. A Department of Transport and Main Roads spokesperson said it had released an updated design for the Holmview station precinct as part of Logan and Gold Coast Faster Rail. "The updated design of the Logan and Gold Coast Faster Rail (LGC) project includes upgrades to local roads and a new road connection from Spanns Road to Thorsborne Street," the spokesperson said. "Anyone who believes they may have an interest in the August Thorsborne estate or the land is encouraged to contact TMR." events.title: Jensen Huang faces second affair claim as Nvidia board considers his future
events.summary: BREAKING: Jensen Huang resigns as Nvidia chief executive Nvidia chief executive Jensen Huang is facing new allegations of a second affair, this time with a senior executive at the chipmaker, as the company's board meets to decide whether he should keep his job. The New York Times has reported that Mr Huang had a relationship with Kimberly Powell, Nvidia's vice president of health care and one of his about 60 direct reports, quoting five people who have worked at the company. Ms Powell has been with Nvidia for more than 18 years. Nvidia has declined to comment on the allegation and has not said whether its board inquiry, launched on Sunday into Mr Huang's relationship with Alice Huang and led by law firm Wachtell, Lipton, Rosen & Katz, will be widened to cover it. The company's code of conduct addresses conflicts arising from personal relationships and requires reported misconduct to be investigated. The allegation came days after Mr Huang admitted he had been “unfaithful” to his wife , following reports of a relationship with Alice Huang, a businesswoman whom US investigators accuse of spying for China. Nvidia's board opened an inquiry into whether he had been targeted by a foreign intelligence operation, while expressing confidence in his leadership. China has called the allegations “entirely groundless”. The Wall Street Journal reported late on Wednesday that the board was preparing to oust Mr Huang. Directors have also hired an outside firm to identify possible replacements, according to reports. Under Nvidia's bylaws, a majority of its 11 directors, all of whom, except Mr Huang, are independent, can remove the chief executive “with or without cause”. Nvidia shares, which closed 2.9 per cent higher at $173.73 on Wednesday, fell more than 8 per cent in after-hours trading . The fallout extends well beyond the boardroom. Nvidia's chips underpin the global AI build-out, from US technology giants to sovereign projects in the Gulf, and the scandal has emboldened lawmakers seeking tighter controls on where those chips can be sold. Analyst Dan Ives of Yorkville Ives has estimated the company's value at $300 a share with Mr Huang as chief executive and $225 without him. Mr Huang, 63, co-founded Nvidia in 1993 and has no obvious successor. Analysts have suggested chief financial officer Colette Kress as a possible interim leader. Pressure is also building in Washington as House Republicans are pushing for Mr Huang to testify and have raised the possibility of a subpoena. Legislators from both parties are calling for tighter curbs on chip exports to China. US President Donald Trump has called Mr Huang “an honourable guy”. Mr Huang remains listed as the keynote speaker at Nvidia's GTC event in Washington from December 1 to 3.

events.title: Rupiah’s drop to record low spurs Bank Indonesia intervention
events.summary: The rupiah weakened as much as 0.3% to 18,204 per US dollar on Nov 12, falling past the previous record low of 18,190 seen in early June. Bank Indonesia is intervening in currency and bond markets after the rupiah hit a record low of 18,241 per US dollar, its worst level in 2026. The fall was driven by a stronger US dollar, Fed rate fears, weak investor sentiment and MSCI reclassification risks, which may trigger heavy passive outflows. Political uncertainty, including Vice-President Gibran Rakabuming Raka’s resignation, has added to fragile markets, while regulators try to improve transparency and avoid a downgrade. JAKARTA – The Indonesian rupiah fell to an all-time low, adding pressure on authorities to contain a recent sell-off that also hit the nation’s stocks and bonds. The central bank said it is intervening in the offshore non-deliverable forwards, domestic non-deliverable forwards and spot markets, as well as via government bond purchases in the secondary market to stabilise the rupiah, Asia’s worst-performing currency in 2026. “Bank Indonesia remains present in the market to maintain the stability of the rupiah exchange rate, ensuring it aligns with its fundamental value,” the central bank’s executive director of Monetary and Securities Management Erwin Hutapea said in a statement on Nov 12. The rupiah weakened as much as 0.5% to 18,241 per US dollar on Nov 12, falling past the previous record low of 18,190 seen in early June. The 10-year bond yield climbed four basis points to 7.66%. The rupiah has come under renewed pressure as the dollar strengthened overnight on expectations that the Federal Reserve would resume raising interest rates in December. Investor sentiment remains fragile after MSCI in October unveiled a proposal to reclassify Indonesia as a standalone market, compounding a host of concerns already weighing on Indonesian assets, including political uncertainty. “The rupiah continues to face relatively poor investor sentiment due to the confluence of unfavourable news headlines and the shift in the outlook for the US inflation and Fed policy,” said Homin Lee, senior macro strategist at Lombard Odier in Singapore. “MSCI reclassification risk and Bank Indonesia’s relatively slow tightening cycle are also deterring value-seeking investors for the rupiah,” he added. The rupiah has weakened more than 8% against the US dollar in 2026. Bank Indonesia has said it remains vigilant about market developments and is monitoring capital outflows following the MSCI announcement. Local regulators have stepped up efforts to improve the equity market’s transparency and surveillance to avert MSCI’s double-downgrade threat, with the decision to be announced by the end of June. They fined companies and individuals involved in stock manipulations, excluded tightly held shares from the benchmark index and enhanced shareholders’ affiliation information. Goldman Sachs Group estimated about US$5.6 billion (S$7.2 billion) of passive outflows in the event the country’s stocks are removed from MSCI’s indexes. The rupiah was also weighed down by a stronger dollar, which climbed to an 18-month high on Nov 11 as traders began pricing in a small chance of a half-point Federal Reserve rate hike in December following hawkish comments from officials and hotter-than-expected inflation data. Meanwhile, renewed concerns over political uncertainty are also hurting markets after Vice-President Gibran Rakabuming Raka’s resignation. Gibran, the son of former President Joko Widodo, had faced growing calls from politicians for his impeachment over questions about his educational credentials. “The optics around the resignation are negative, the politics remain messy and investor sentiment is still fragile,” though there should be little fundamental spillover from this, said Galvin Chia, an emerging Asia strategist at Societe Generale. events.title: Japan top currency diplomat says yen’s recent fall ‘too rapid’
events.summary: Japan and the US carried out a joint intervention earlier in 2026 to stem the yen’s depreciation. Japan’s top currency diplomat Atsushi Mimura said the yen’s fall is “too rapid” and warned it is “too early” to forget the summer US-Japan intervention. The dollar stayed near 159 yen after stronger US inflation data raised expectations of a Federal Reserve rate rise, while Japan’s policy rate remains much lower. The weak yen is hurting Japan by lifting import costs, and earlier market intervention has not stopped the decline, amid worries over fiscal spending and the economy. TOKYO – Japan’s top currency diplomat Atsushi Mimura said on Nov 12 the yen’s fall in recent days has been “too rapid”, in an apparent warning after the Japanese currency slipped toward 160 against the US dollar. Mimura, Vice-Finance Minister for international affairs, also said it is “too early” to forget what happened this summer, referring to a joint Japan-US intervention in the foreign exchange market to stem the yen’s depreciation. The dollar was trading around the mid-159 yen line after the comments, still sharply higher than 158.87-158.89 yen as at 5pm local time on Nov 11. The dollar got a boost overnight from growing expectations that the US Federal Reserve will raise its key interest rate, supported by stronger-than-expected US consumer inflation data , according to dealers. “I get the impression that the movements we’ve seen over the past few days are too rapid,” Mimura told reporters. Financial markets expect the BOJ to proceed with another interest rate increase as early as its next meeting in December, as inflation remains entrenched. While the BOJ has signalled that further hikes may be in the offing should the risk of inflation overshooting its 2% target grow, its current policy rate of 1.25% is still lower than those in the US and Europe. The still-wide interest rate differential is one of the key factors keeping the yen weak against the dollar. A combination of high energy prices amid heightened Middle East tensions and a weak yen, which inflates import costs, has dealt a blow to resource-scarce Japan. Japan stepped into the market to prop up the yen earlier in 2026 . But it has failed to reverse the currency’s declining trend, partly reflecting market worries about the country’s fiscal health as Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi pushes for more fiscal spending. The yen had fallen to levels unseen in about four decades, beyond 163 per dollar, before Japan carried out a series of interventions this summer, including jointly with the US on July 31. KYODO NEWS

events.title: AI won't transform your business unless you transform it first
events.summary: Organisations need to overhaul their processes to truly reap the benefits of artificial intelligence , according to experts. Bolting the technology to existing systems will not bring about the drastic changes that AI providers are touting. “It's a huge change and that's why the dynamic is not going to be as fast as people imagine,” said Denis Torii, vice president analyst at Gartner. “It's not an IT story for sure. It's not [the case of] only the business stakeholders who are pushing us to adopt more AI ,” he said. "It's actually an organisational story, where the organisation needs to adapt to it." AI is only working as an accessory today. “Right now [organisations] are doing the same stuff but with AI in the middle, and that probably is not going to bring that transformation that people are expecting,” he told The National on the sidelines of the recent Oracle AI World event in Las Vegas. Currently, organisations are using AI across the enterprise with a range of tools – from chatbots and software coding agents to agentic systems capable of acting autonomously across workflows, a McKinsey report in August found. However, enterprise-level financial impact remains limited. Only 37 per cent of respondents reported an AI contribution to their organisations' earnings before interest and tax (Ebit), unchanged from a year earlier, McKinsey's Global Survey on the State of AI found. To benefit from AI requires a shift in leadership mindset, according to Gabby Fredkin, head of analytics and insights at Adapt, a specialist IT research advisory. A fundamental change is needed to go from “we're just going to layer technology on, to we're actually going to think about the ethos of our organisation, what we do, the type of roles that we have”, he said. “So, it's a complicated process.” The organisations that generally succeed with AI tend to have a leadership that has a good conceptual understanding about it and encourages people to innovate, he added. The experience of a small group of high performers highlights the technology’s successful use, the McKinsey report said. “High performers pursue growth and/or innovation alongside efficiency; they fundamentally redesign workflows that are enabled by AI rather than insert AI into existing ones; and they back their deployments with the leadership commitment and operational rigor needed to achieve real gains," the report found. Mr Fredkin said companies must look into their operating models to see how they can go beyond traditional processes and capture new revenue streams. “If you're a bank and you've got data because you've got investments in different infrastructure, do you want to get into infrastructure as an investment? Do you want to start a real estate investment trust? How are you thinking about what you have and what you do, and what are the parallels outside of that?", he said. Such a shift would be harder for some organisations than others, he added. Cost factor AI-related operating costs are beginning to constrain its use for about one in five organisations, the McKinsey report said, even as most respondents expect their companies to increase AI investments in the year ahead. Companies are taking a cautious approach as they prepare their data and processes for AI integration, said analyst John Reed, co-founder of US-based tech platform diginomica. “If companies know that it's not going to be that expensive to use these technologies, I think they are going to find significant benefits,” he said. AI could prove particularly valuable in complex, mission-critical tasks that humans struggle to perform in real time, Mr Reed added. “For example, it's very difficult for a human to assess global supply chain impacts in real time … these [AI] systems actually are able to, if you provide them with the right data.” However, adoption will take time, as many companies grapple with fragmented data and legacy systems, he added. The trillion-dollar ROI challenge Investment in AI is soaring. Worldwide spending is forecast to total $2.7 trillion this year, up 49.5 per cent annually, Gartner said in a report in September. AI infrastructure, particularly data centres and specialised servers, remains the biggest spending driver, with Gartner describing the buildout as the “largest infrastructure project humanity has ever undertaken”. Goldman Sachs Research separately estimates $1 trillion in global AI-related investment this year, including $581 billion in the US. It expects AI capital expenditure to rise from 0.9 per cent of global GDP in 2026 to 1.4 per cent by 2028. But the spending boom is raising questions about the revenue needed to justify it. The AI industry needs to earn $6 trillion in annual revenue by 2031 to justify the capital being deployed, a report by consultancy Bain in September found. “Return on investment is still one of the biggest issues [with AI],” said Mr Torii. “People are putting all this faith in AI, [with the assumption that] there's a lot of potential. “When you look at the broad picture, it's still lacking evidence that return on investment is there,” he said, adding, however, that vendors need to invest heavily upfront. “They need to help customers somehow to get to that journey. So there's a lot of friction and inertia that needs to be overcome.” He compared AI's trajectory to the early days of cloud computing, when heavy infrastructure investment preceded widespread adoption. The question, Mr Torii said, is how long it will take for AI to bridge the gap. Measuring returns is another challenge, Mr Fredkin said. “They [organisations] feel a productivity uplift. They feel better employee engagement. Putting an actual figure behind that is incredibly complex,” he said. “From the perspective of the CFO [chief financial officer], the calculations for how they look at ROI [return on investment] have changed significantly. It's not a line item any more; it's a meter.” He cited an emerging term “double T Ebitda”, which refers to earnings before interest, tax, tokens, depreciation, and amortisation. Unlike blockchain and metaverse technologies, AI is already gaining traction across businesses and is likely to see wider adoption, Mr Reed said. Looking ahead, he is slightly pessimistic about its broader implications. “I think we're in some significant trouble because we put a lot of eggs in the basket of a technology that, while it's good for business, I'm not convinced [about] the ultimate impact in terms of surveillance and disinformation and deep fakes and the inability to trust content and the displacement of humans from jobs,” he said. “But one of the things about technology is that it can be decentralised and changed and appropriated too. And there's a lot of very thoughtful people that are using some of these tools for really cool, worthwhile projects as well,” he added.

AWS New Horizon Digicert Netscout Resources Intelligence Webinars & Events Newsletters Couldn’t get the hardware it needed to generate certs, so tried to code a workaround Software Samaritan revamps borked Indian certs to block smart TV ads 1 hour ago Disgraced Indian cert issuer leaves the cert issuing business 21 days ago Certification authority eMudhra defends its laughably weak private keys 21 days ago Indian certification authority eMudhra’s private keys compromised – one of them was the number ‘4’ 22 days ago Turns out Brits would quite like their private messages to stay private August 30, 2026 Former certification authority eMudhra has claimed a buggy Python script is the main reason it issued laughably insecure digital certificates. The company posted its account of the matter on Bugzilla where a user with the handle “Naveen Kumar ML” wrote “During a single key‑generation ceremony on 30 April 2025, sixteen subordinate (issuing) CA key pairs in eMudhra’s ‘B’ and ‘C’ series were generated correctly on a hardware security module and then processed through an approved wrap/unwrap round‑trip using a custom python key‑handling script.” eMudhra aimed to create eight ECDSA P-384 private keys which should have been 48 bytes long. But the script contained what Kumar described as “a bug/defect in the import code [which] resulted in a read‑back from the unwrapped object that truncated the private value, so the certified public keys correspond to private scalars below the expected range and are recoverable from public information.” The truncation is the key problem here, because it appears that eMudhra ignored 47 of the 48 bytes, producing its infamously insecure single-byte keys such as the number four. Whatever the nature of the bug, Kumar asserts it was “a custom script run only on an isolated ceremony host and was not a function of the emCA software.” eMudhra needed that script because “global supply chain constraints” meant it couldn’t acquire the hardware security modules (HSMs), devices that generate and store cryptographic keys, that it wanted to use when creating a set of certificates for use in the USA. It therefore used HSMs made by a company called Utimaco to generate keys and planned to transfer the keys it produced to a different set of HSMs from a company called Crypto4A. Kumar explained that eMudhra decided on that move, which is unusual, because changes to policy about provenance of certificates meant it had to generate new certs by the end of May. The plan went sour when the company didn’t notice the errors in its script and didn’t test the keys it created. The rest is history: a Mozilla team member noticed that the company’s keys were woefully weak and pointed out that attackers could therefore issue fraudulent certificates that allowed them to impersonate servers, observe traffic, or even modify data in transit. Browser-makers quickly tweaked their software so it would not recognize certs from eMudhra. The Indian business then quit the SSL/TLS certification business, which it said was never a major source of revenue but had suddenly become a severe source of embarrassment. Kumar’s new post lists three steps eMudhra will take to wind up its certification business, one of which will see the company “Put in place improvements motivated by findings of [an] independent review to strengthen our general PKI operations.” Jensen Huang's self-sabotage sends Nvidia into a midlife crisis The competition is circling like vultures Palantir’s Karp takes a sharp left turn, says he and the company’s products are actually ‘progressive’ Trump donor says he privately questioned deportation tactics.

events.title: Commercial rock lobster fisheries closed due to antibiotic trade risk
events.summary: News Home Just In For You Analysis Rural Watch Live Health Indigenous Politics Science Deep Time Elections World Environment Investigations Business Local news Quizzes Sport AFL NRL Football Tennis Cricket Netball Lifestyle Wellbeing Relationships & Family Food & Recipes Personal Finance Home & Garden Entertainment TV & Movies Books Music Pop Culture Arts Antibiotic trade risk forces three month closure of commercial rock lobster fisheries in parts of Tasmania Topic: Fishing and Aquaculture Industry The fisheries in parts of Tasmania's south-east will be closed to mitigate trade risks. ( ABC News: Bec Pridham ) Tasmania's environment department has announced the closure of commercial rock lobster and commercial dive fisheries in parts of the state's south-east. The move is designed to reduce international trade risks linked to the use of the antibiotic oxytetracycline (OTC) in salmon farms in the area. The salmon industry is seeking an emergency permit to use the antibiotic florfenicol in salmon pens in the state's south-east, which could trigger further closures. Commercial rock lobster and dive fisheries in parts of Tasmania's south-east will stay closed for three months to "mitigate trade risks" linked to antibiotic use by the salmon industry. The Department of Natural Resources and Environment (NRE) has issued two notices declaring certain commercial areas closed from November 15 this year to February 14 next year. The commercial taking of rock lobster and the setting of rock lobster pots will not be allowed within parts of the Southern Channel "Therapeutic Management Area" (TMA). The new closures are linked to salmon company Tassal's recent use of the antibiotic oxytetracycline. ( ABC News: Bec Pridham ) Commercial divers will not be allowed to take short-spined sea urchins, long-spined sea urchins and periwinkles in the Northern Channel TMA. The notice for commercial divers says the closure is "part of the arrangements to mitigate trade risks associated with aquaculture therapeutant use." Tassal is one of three major salmon producers with pens in Tasmanian waterways. ( Bob Brown Foundation ) NRE last month released its Wild Fisheries Market Access Plan ahead of the planned use of antibiotics to treat a bacterial disease that caused mass deaths in salmon farms over the past two summers. Under the plan, wild fisheries near salmon pens treated with antibiotics get temporarily closed. This is done to avoid the risk of antibiotic detections in wild seafood that could trigger export bans by countries with zero tolerance. The industry has struggled with mass deaths of fish during recent summers. ( Supplied: Bob Brown Foundation ) Closures linked to use of oxytetracycline by Tassal The new closures are linked to salmon company Tassal's recent use of the antibiotic oxytetracycline (OTC) at its salmon farms at Great Taylors Bay and Meads Creek in the lower D'Entrecasteaux Channel. A map showing the areas of the rock lobster fishery that will be closed from Sunday. ( ABC News: Hamed Akrami ) Tassal has been administering OTC by injection, rather than orally through medicated food. The industry has lost large amounts of fish stocks to disease recently. ( Huon ) When it first started using the antibiotic last month, the Department of Health said it posed no risk to the public. "Public Health has confirmed swimming and recreational fishing remain completely safe," the Tassal spokesperson said. "We recognise the consequences for any affected commercial rock lobster fishers and are working with the wild fisheries sector on appropriate support, with monitoring underway to support reopening as soon as possible." The industry has been adminstering the antibiotic via injection. ( ABC News: Maren Preuss ) Salmon Tasmania, which represents the state's three main salmon companies, has separately applied for an emergency permit to use the antibiotic florfenicol to treat the bacterial disease. The Australian Pesticides and Veterinary Medicines Authority (APVMA) is currently seeking public submissions about the application, with a decision likely this month. The salmon industry received an emergency permit to use florfenicol late last year, but it was revoked in March this year after florfenicol was detected in wild seafood more than 10 kilometres away. In a statement, an NRE spokesperson said it was a "precautionary closure, in line with the Aquaculture Therapeutant Wild Fisheries Market Access Management Plan, designed to protect market access for Tasmania's wild fisheries and was not related to any food safety concern". Salmon in a fish farm enclosure. ( Supplied: Tassal ) 'Stand up' to salmon industry, Greens say Tasmanian Greens leader Rosalie Woodruff called on the state government to "grow a spine, look after our wild catch sector, and stand up to the salmon industry".

events.title: Wheelock Place renamed Landmark Orchard after $1.1 billion acquisition by Hongkong Land
events.summary: The 21-storey building, which has been in Orchard Road for more than 30 years, houses offices and shops and is directly linked to Orchard MRT station. Hongkong Land renamed Wheelock Place as Landmark Orchard after its Singapore fund bought the Orchard Road site for about US$1.1 billion (S$1.4 billion). The 21-storey building has offices and shops, links to Orchard MRT, and existing tenants will stay while the new owner plans improvements. The deal is the fund’s first Orchard Road purchase and expands its reach beyond the Central Business District, as it targets about $15 billion in assets under management. SINGAPORE – Wheelock Place has been renamed Landmark Orchard, the first time property group Hongkong Land has used the Landmark name outside Hong Kong. The new name took effect on Nov 12, three months after Hongkong Land’s Singapore Central Private Real Estate Fund bought the Orchard Road property, the developer announced that day. The fund agreed in July to pay about $1.1 billion to an entity owned by Hong Kong-listed Wharf Real Estate Investment Company. It was the fund’s first acquisition since its launch in February . The 21-storey building, which has been in Orchard Road for more than 30 years, houses offices and shops and is directly linked to Orchard MRT station. Existing office and retail tenants will continue to operate under the new name. Hongkong Land said it plans to improve the property, but did not provide further details. In Hong Kong, Landmark is at the centre of the group’s Central portfolio, which is undergoing a revamp under a more than US$1 billion (S$1.3 billion) programme. Foo Pei Teng, chief executive of the Singapore fund, said the group would bring its long-term approach to investing in its properties to Landmark Orchard. The purchase extends the fund’s reach into Orchard Road from its initial portfolio in the Central Business District. That portfolio comprised Asia Square Tower 1, Marina Bay Financial Centre Towers 1 and 2, One Raffles Quay and One Raffles Link. The fund is targeting about $15 billion in assets under management. Hongkong Land manages the fund and is its largest unit holder. Correction note: In an earlier version of the story, we said Wheelock Place was acquired for $1.4 billion. It should be $1.1 billion. Kang Wan Chern is deputy business editor at The Straits Times.

He says he is not expecting Australia's economy to experience a recession. Mr Matos says governments should be thinking about how they compete for global capital. The head of ANZ says he sees a "dangerous situation" with global markets. Nuno Matos, ANZ's chief executive, says the competition for capital is intense globally, driven by the AI and data centre build-out, which is feeding an expenditure super-cycle. He says the combination of that race for capital, the prevailing level of government expenditure, higher and stubborn inflation and rising interest rates are a serious problem. Technology and artificial intelligence have enthralled investors, and Australia's super funds have dived in with their ears pinned back. But now comes the reckoning. "Globally, undoubtedly, the combination of those four factors, and Australia is not different in that regard," he said today. "They are contributing to a competition for capital. We never saw this amount of spending in our lives, in our lifetimes. "We have a very curious situation in the world where we have equity markets at record highs, basically because of the tech wave and basically because of the AI wave, but at the same time you have record highs of interest rates. Mr Matos was giving evidence at a parliamentary inquiry in Canberra. The chief executives of Australia's big four banks will appear before the inquiry. Global shock could hit Australia's economy Mr Matos said he did not think Australia was heading for recession. He said he was expecting Australia's economy to slow down noticeably in the near future, but he did not think it would contract. Nuno Matos says he is not expecting Australia's economy to suffer a homegrown recession. ( ABC News: Luke Stephenson ) Last week, Reserve Bank governor Michele Bullock said something similar. She said the RBA was not forecasting a recession for Australia. However, Mr Matos said it was possible that Australia could be hit by a negative global shock, linked to the AI build-out and intense global competition for capital, which would cause serious economic problems in Australia. Is the Firmus fiasco a crack in the AI boom? events.title: Asian stocks fragile, Nvidia plummets as board to decide CEO’s fate
events.summary: Asian stocks were mixed as Nvidia fell more than 8% after reports its board may decide on CEO Jensen Huang’s future amid affair allegations. Wall Street rose on Nov 11, with the S&P 500 up 1.3%, as renewed optimism around AI lifted US shares, helped by CoreWeave and Anthropic news. The dollar stayed near a high, and traders priced in an 87.3% chance of a 25-basis-point Fed rate hike in December; bitcoin and ether also fell. SINGAPORE – Global stocks wobbled at the start of Asian trade on Nov 12 , while Nvidia shares plunged in after-hours trading on news that its board may oust long-time chief executive Jensen Huang. Nvidia’s board is meeting late on Nov 11 to decide whether to oust Huang , a source familiar with the matter said, as the world’s dominant supplier of AI processors grapples with the fallout of allegations that he had an affair with a suspected spy for China. The New York Times has also reported that Huang had an affair with a company executive who reported to him. “It looks bad from every single angle,” said Jake Dollarhide, CEO at Longbow Asset Management in Tulsa, Oklahoma. “I believe the board won’t oust him until they have an all-star, a known entity in the tech sector, to replace him,” he said. “At the end of the day, let’s not forget that the Nvidia chip is the centrepiece of the AI story.” Regional indexes fared better after a choppy start. South Korea’s Kospi rose 0.2%, Taiwanese shares gained 0.5%, Japan’s Nikkei 225 climbed 0.5% and MSCI’s broadest index of Asia-Pacific shares outside Japan was 0.1% lower, weighed down by shares in Hong Kong. Stocks on Wall Street made gains on Nov 11 , with the S&P 500 rising 1.3% and coming close to retracing all the losses since last week’s US midterm elections. “Renewed optimism around AI drove US equities higher overnight, with positive developments around CoreWeave and Anthropic adding to enthusiasm around the sector and helping the S&P 500 and NASDAQ rally,” Westpac analysts wrote in a note. The dollar index, which measures the greenback’s strength against a basket of six currencies, was steady in Asian trade at 102.87, its highest level since April 9, 2025 in the aftermath of Trump’s Liberation Day tariff announcement. The currency rose 0.6% on Nov 11 as traders repriced the odds the Federal Reserve will lift interest rates in December . Fed funds futures are pricing an 87.3% chance of a 25-basis-point hike at the US central bank’s next two-day meeting on Dec 9, compared to a 12.7% chance of a larger 50-basis-points hike, according to the CME Group’s FedWatch tool. In cryptocurrencies, bitcoin slipped 0.9% to US$73,617.58 (S$94,600), while ether was 0.9% lower at US$2,049.44. REUTERS

events.title: 'If they're winning, we're winning': Suppliers on David Jones closures
events.summary: News Home Just In For You Analysis Rural Watch Live Health Indigenous Politics Science Deep Time Elections World Environment Investigations Business Local news Quizzes Sport AFL NRL Football Tennis Cricket Netball Lifestyle Wellbeing Relationships & Family Food & Recipes Personal Finance Home & Garden Entertainment TV & Movies Books Music Pop Culture Arts David Jones suppliers saddened but understanding of plans to close half the store network David Jones has announced plans to close half its stores. ( ABC News: Fletcher Yeung ) David Jones's receivers are set to close 19 of its 38 stores. Suppliers say they are sad but supportive of the decision. The affected stores are expected to continue trading through the peak seasonal period. While news of David Jones's plans to close half of its stores may sadden some customers, some suppliers say a streamlined operation could boost sales by attracting more shoppers into fewer, higher-performing stores. The 188-year-old department store went into administration last week. On Wednesday, its receivers announced plans to close 19 of its 38 stores. Owner of Spice brand Lord and Lion, Eresha De Zoysa, whose products have been stocked across the David Jones network for five years, said she was concerned the closures would wipe out a significant amount of her business. "The way that we were able to access people in communities that we ordinarily would not be able to access was by David Jones," she said. "So even though, on the whole, those stores may not make commercial sense for Anchorage to keep or David Jones to keep … our brand did really well, and we were successful in those stores. "It's a sad day, but I think we just have to be a bit more clever in how we're going to access [those customers]." Eresha De Zoysa says she is grateful to be stocked in David Jones. ( Supplied ) Documents seen by the ABC show an uncertain future for suppliers that have been asked to continue supplying the store despite unpaid debts. Ms De Zoysa, a former corporate lawyer who has worked in administration and previously advised David Jones, said she had no doubt a restructured David Jones would succeed and thrive. "I do hope that the suppliers find a way to renegotiate an outcome with David Jones to continue supplying into the future because it is actually those brands that make David Jones worthwhile," she said. David Jones 'could not continue operating' McGrath Nicol has been appointed administrator for David Jones, but separately FTI Consulting has been appointed as receiver for the company's biggest lender, Hilco. An email sent to suppliers from David Jones chief executive Erica Berchtold, seen by the ABC, said the store portfolio was "no longer the right shape for the business" and the change was about "creating a network that is financially sustainable for the future." It said the last day of trade for the 19 stores marked for closure was anticipated for later in the year, with the stores expected to continue trading through the peak seasonal period. David Jones will close 19 of its 38 locations. ( ABC News: Daniel Irvine ) "The business could not continue operating as it was. We had a plan to reset the business, and we still have a plan to reset the business," the email said. Carlos Martins, owner of men's fashion brand Coast Clothing, said the store closures were the "right way forward". "Fewer stores will be better for me in the long term," he said. "Loyal customers will likely shift to online shopping, which will bring greater exposure to my brand, compared to instore where we didn't have a presence." Slow Down Studios owner Jacob Leung. ( ABC News: Fletcher Yeung ) Jacob Leung, owner of handwoven blankets business Slowdown Studio, which is not stocked in the closing stores, said although the news was sad, it was good for suppliers. "It's going to have a massive impact on all of those employees, as well as the communities of the stores that are closing down," he said. "We only want the best for David Jones because if they're winning, that means we're winning. "At the end of the day though, it's clear that the business model that David Jones currently operates in is not working, and that's why we are all in this situation." David Jones in Claremont in Perth's Western Suburbs is one of the stores continuing to trade. ( ABC News: Zahra Anwary ) Mahala Joyce, co-founder and director of distribution business Over The Fence, has organised pop-ups in David Jones flagship stores for international brands, including Bellroy and Topologie. Like other suppliers, he said he had negotiated 14-day settlement terms that came with a 5.75 per cent discount. Yet across three purchase orders over six months, he said none was paid on time, while the discount was still applied. Relevant documents have been seen by the ABC. "Essentially the way that their system is set up is it's set up that those discounts are applied at the start, prior to any payment date," he said.

events.title: HSBC explores bolstering Singapore to balance China reliance: Sources
events.summary: HSBC’s review highlights how some of the world’s largest financial groups are moving to insulate their Asian assets from mounting geopolitical risks. HSBC is exploring ways to make its Singapore business more independent to reduce reliance on China and Hong Kong. The project is called “Project Sirena”. The bank plans to combine its main Singapore banking units first. It may later move other regional operations there, creating a second Asian base alongside Hong Kong. HSBC says there are no firm decisions yet and no plan to change its Hong Kong-led structure. The move could upset regulators and Beijing, while Singapore gains as a stable wealth hub. HSBC Holdings has been exploring ways to ease its reliance on China, including Hong Kong, and give more independence to its Singapore operations as the bank seeks to diversify risk across its Asia business, according to people familiar with the matter. The London-based lender, which generated about 40% of its pre-tax profit in the first half from Hong Kong, has internally discussed several options to give its Singapore arm greater autonomy, the people said, asking not to be identified discussing a private matter. The initiative is being carried out under the name Project Sirena . HSBC’s review highlights how some of the world’s largest financial groups are moving to insulate their Asian assets from mounting geopolitical risks. Singapore, bolstered by relative political stability and its standing as a premier wealth and banking hub, has emerged as a top beneficiary as firms look beyond Greater China for operational flexibility. It comes even as chief executive officer Georges Elhedery has repeatedly voiced confidence in Hong Kong’s prospects, predicting the city would overtake Switzerland to become the world’s largest cross-border wealth hub by the end of the decade, even before it happened late in 2025. In a first step, HSBC plans to combine its major banking services in Singapore under one entity over the next few years. A possible next move would be to bring in the other regional operations under the Singapore subsidiary, with the ultimate goal of establishing a second regional base alongside Hong Kong, according to the people. In a statement, Surendra Rosha, co-CEO of Asia and the Middle East, confirmed the bank will combine its separate units in Singapore as part of a simplification drive, though he said it had no further plans after that. “All of our Asia-Pacific banking entities remain under the ownership and management of the Hongkong and Shanghai Banking Corporation subsidiary head office in Hong Kong, and there is no plan to make any changes to this,” Rosha said in a statement via e-mail. The deliberations remain fluid, with no firm decisions on the path forward, the people said. Like other multinationals, HSBC is also wary of appearing to hedge its bets, given its significant exposure in Greater China and concerns about provoking regulators, the sources added. HSBC shares fell as much as 0.8% in early Hong Kong trading. Making its Singapore operations more independent would be a major step for the 161-year-old lender, which was founded in Hong Kong and moved its headquarters to London in 1993. At the same time, the bank is becoming more reliant on the Chinese territory after announcing in 2025 a US$14 billion (S$18 billion) takeover of partly owned Hang Seng Bank, while it has also exited businesses in Europe and the Americas. Any signs of hedging Hong Kong, where HSBC serves as one of three currency-issuing lenders, would face stiff local pushback. It would also risk alienating Beijing, where the bank maintains expansive China operations. HSBC’s assessment is not without precedent. In 2019, smaller rival Standard Chartered consolidated its operations into a locally incorporated subsidiary, creating dual hubs in Singapore and Hong Kong to simplify its network and trim costs. HSBC has recently faced intense scrutiny on other fronts from the Hong Kong authorities over its allocation of artificial intelligence talent to Singapore as both Asian financial hubs battle for dominance. The lender operates a hybrid structure in jurisdictions such as Singapore. In May 2016, HSBC locally incorporated its retail banking and wealth management business in Singapore under HSBC Bank (Singapore) while also operating a branch under Hong Kong. It runs locally incorporated subsidiaries in countries such as Malaysia and Indonesia, though both remain under its Hong Kong-based business. A subsidiary is more freestanding than a branch, with its own governance, capital needs and deeper local regulatory oversight. Such a structure also faces different treatment in the event of financial difficulties. The lender has, over the past couple of years, radically overhauled its business following the appointment of CEO Elhedery in September 2024.
