events.title: Who could replace Jensen Huang? A highly unscientific list of possible successors
events.summary: It’s almost inconceivable that Nvidia would fire its rock star CEO. Yet here we are, on the precipice of this happening. Over at Kalshi, Jensen Huang’s odds of surviving the week are sitting at a lowly 30% . Even though he built one of the world’s most valuable — and, many would argue, dangerously powerful — companies, the tides have completely turned against him. He has confessed to an extramarital affair, but as of Wednesday afternoon it isn’t even clear who he meant: Alice Huang, the Chinese executive suspected by U.S. intelligence of spying for her country, or Kimberly Powell, an Nvidia executive who reports to him and who, five sources told The New York Times in an explosive new report, was also a paramour. Even if Huang is pushed out as CEO, the board members he has made very rich are unlikely to cut him loose entirely. Barring another shoe dropping, they could keep him on as chairman, a role Nvidia doesn’t currently have. But someone still has to run the company, and there’s no apparent succession plan, which leaves us, like everyone else, to speculate while we wait to see what happens next. While Huang’s 60 direct reports undoubtedly get a closer look, consider this our own parlor game, featuring some obvious and less obvious candidates: Lisa Su . The AMD CEO runs Nvidia’s most credible rival and is a distant cousin of Huang. The Information floated her name this week, but why would she leave her job for his? Her company stands to benefit from every day that Nvidia spends distracted by an investigation, congressional briefings, and all the mini dramas that are sure to follow. Her best move might be to send a nice note and keep her current corner office. Eric Schmidt. He was the pick of Jeffrey Sonnenfeld, senior associate dean for leadership studies at the Yale School of Management, who we talked with earlier this week. Schmidt could “parachute in tomorrow and do a very good job,” Sonnenfeld said, and perhaps he could. He ran Google from 2001 to 2011, chaired the National Security Commission on AI from 2018 to 2021, and now runs the rocket company Relativity Space. Chips, software, government, rockets — it’s an impressive range. Then again, Schmidt would bring a lot of baggage when it comes to his own extramarital dalliances . It’s hard to see him clearing the board for that reason. Lip-Bu Tan . Intel’s CEO knows chips, and right now he might welcome a very soft landing. Last month, Intel reported third-quarter revenue up 21% to $16.5 billion, then warned its fourth-quarter results would fall short of Wall Street’s forecasts. The AI boom has caused a memory-chip shortage, pushing up PC prices and cutting PC sales. That’s hurt Intel (PC chips are a big part of its business), and its stock plunged 20% in after-hours trading on the warning, having already slid more than 30% since September. A move to a company that’s eating everyone’s lunch would be a pretty amazing escape hatch. Bret Taylor. The former Salesforce co-CEO and OpenAI board chair now runs the AI startup Sierra, and his résumé includes a lot of the biggest brands in Silicon Valley. He co-created Google Maps, served as Facebook’s CTO, and chaired Twitter’s board through its sale to Elon Musk. He then took over as OpenAI’s board chair after the “Blip,” Sam Altman’s firing and fast return. When companies need an unflappable, likable adult in the room, they call Taylor. He probably knows nearly every customer Nvidia has, too. Ian Buck. If the board feels strongly about having a “builder” at the helm, they could do worse than the Nvidia VP who helped develop CUDA, the chip software that has become central to Nvidia’s dominance in AI. Analysts and former employees have floated him as a possible successor, and Kalshi traders give him a middling shot . He’s no household name, but the Stanford PhD seems more viable if Huang can keep that chairman title and push for a successor he can work with. Someone else down the hall. Andrew Bell, Nvidia’s senior vice president of hardware engineering, arrived 25 years ago as a fresh Cornell grad and has been on an upward trajectory at the company ever since. Like Buck and dozens of other executives who are presumably being scrutinized, he reports directly to Huang. Nvidia CFO Colette Kress is the insider most often named, but analysts say she isn’t necessarily a natural successor as an innovator and visionary, and Bell has the chip pedigree. The wild card? Lori Huang . Nobody has floated her, but hear us out: Jensen met his wife as lab partners at Oregon State, so she has been working with him since before Nvidia existed. After graduating, she worked at Silicon Graphics as a microchip engineer (making more money than her husband, he has said), then scaled back to raise the couple’s family, and she now co-leads the family trusts. If the board wants continuity, they could do worse than a humbler Huang who is also a brainiac. There’s a reason they say that behind every great man is a great woman (and vice versa).

( Supplied: Riley Hudd ) More than 100 passengers were stranded after fallen powerlines forced their train to stop on Queensland's Fraser Coast. The passengers were stranded at Gundiah without air conditioning or food for about six hours. Train services north of Gympie have been affected while repair work is underway. No food or air conditioning and "pretty full" toilets is how more than 100 passengers spent the night when their train lost power, leaving them stranded. Fallen power lines forced the northbound Bundaberg Tilt Train to stop about midnight at Gundiah, about three hours north of Brisbane. Passengers were stranded on the train for about six hours before being transferred to buses. Riley Hudd, who was travelling from the Gold Coast to Hervey Bay, said his journey took about 19 hours. Riley Hudd had a slow journey from the Gold Coast to Hervey Bay. ( ABC Wide Bay: James Taylor ) He said it was a shock when the train stopped. "It came to a screeching halt and pretty much slammed on the brakes. Everyone was looking at the sparks," Mr Hudd said. He said the stranded passengers were only provided water. "There was a bit of complaining and a bit of worry." A storm downed powerlines at Gundiah. ( Supplied: Riley Hudd ) Mr Hudd said there was limited information about what was happening. "The team [on the train] handled it in a good way, but I think the response [from Queensland Rail] could have been better," he said. "Queensland Rail was probably just as much in the dark as we were, so they gave us what [information] they could when they could, but it was just a waiting game. Energy crews working to repair the damage. ( ABC Wide Bay: James Taylor ) Replacement buses, some cancellations Queensland Rail head of regional Scott Cornish said long-distance travel and freight trains on the North Coast line were affected by downed powerlines at Gundiah, and repair works were underway. "Queensland Rail crews have worked continuously overnight and will remain onsite repairing damage to more than 500 metres of overhead line equipment," he said. "We appreciate customers' frustration and we apologise for the inconvenience." Passengers were escorted off the train in the early hours of the morning. ( Supplied: Riley Hudd ) Queensland Rail said buses were transporting Spirit of Queensland, Bundaberg and Rockhampton Tilt Train passengers where possible. events.title: CDL shares fall 6.7% after developer warns of significantly weaker second half
events.summary: CDL shares were trading at around $6.50 at 10am on Nov 12, down almost 8.6%. At the start of 2026, they were trading for as much as $10. CDL shares fell as much as 8% after it warned second-half 2026 results will be much weaker, hit by inflation, high rates and delayed deal completions. The company expects foreign exchange losses and possible impairment losses after revaluing its property portfolio, adding pressure on earnings. CDL still saw stronger Singapore sales, plans more launches in 2027, and aims to sell $6 billion of assets and cut net borrowings by about $3 billion by 2029. SINGAPORE – Shares of City Developments Limited (CDL) slipped 6.7% when the market closed on Nov 12, after the property developer warned that its second-half performance for 2026 would be significantly weaker than a year earlier. CDL shares closed at $6.64 on Nov 12, down 6.7%. At the start of the year, they were trading for as much as $10. In an operating update released after the market closed on Nov 11, CDL said persistent inflation and elevated interest rates had pushed back some deals it had expected to complete by the end of 2026. The year-on-year decline is likely to look more stark as the company booked a $473.1 million gain in the second half of 2025 from the sale of its stake in South Beach Consortium. The slowdown comes after the developer in September revealed a new strategy targeting $6 billion in asset disposals by 2029. CDL said foreign exchange losses are likely to also weigh on earnings. It noted specifically that the Korean won’s appreciation against the Singdollar since July has led to significant foreign exchange losses for its South Korean subsidiary on a Singdollar-denominated loan owed to it by another group entity. The developer added that it is revaluing its property portfolio, a process that could lead to impairment losses. It said its Singapore property sales picked up in the third quarter, although demand came mainly from existing projects due to the absence of new launches. CDL and its joint venture partners sold 124 units worth $322.6 million, up from 88 units worth $313.2 million a year earlier. In the first nine months of 2026, CDL and its partners sold 476 units worth $1.2 billion. Sales were largely driven by Newport Residences, a 246-unit freehold project in Anson Road that is now 83% sold. In October, CDL launched the 570-unit Lucerne Grand in Lakeside. It sold 61% of the units over the launch weekend at an average price of $2,480 per sq ft. The project was 73% sold as at the Nov 11 update. The developer plans to launch two executive condominium projects – Wynwood Grand in Woodlands and Solano Grand in Senja – in the first quarter of 2027. CDL, which is aiming to cut net borrowings by about $3 billion and bring net gearing down to 55% by 2029, noted that net gearing stood at 75% as at Sept 30, after accounting for the fair value of its investment properties. The group attributed that level mainly to spending on two government land sale sites in Tanjong Rhu Road and Peck Hay Road, which were secured in the first half of 2026.

events.title: Outgoing Trump foe Massie forces new Epstein files showdown
events.summary: Outgoing Rep. Thomas Massie (R-Ky.) secured the 218 signatures needed to force another House showdown over the Jeffrey Epstein files Wednesday, just one day after fellow Republicans blocked his attempt to impeach Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth. Why it matters: Congress overwhelmingly voted last year to force the release of the Epstein files, but survivors and lawmakers say the Trump administration has still withheld records. The new bill would give them the power to sue the DOJ and help state prosecutors pursue investigations. Driving the news: Massie announced Wednesday afternoon that his discharge petition for the Epstein Files Transparency Act II had reached the required 218 signatures. Rep. John Garamendi (D-Calif.) provided the final signature Wednesday, according to the House clerk's records . Just four Republicans signed the petition: Massie, Nancy Mace of South Carolina, Ralph Norman of South Carolina and Brian Fitzpatrick of Pennsylvania. The other 214 signatures came from Democrats. What he's saying: "I'm working closely with @RepJayapal, @RepTeresaLF and @RepRoKhanna to get this to the floor for a vote soon," Massie wrote on X . The White House and Speaker Mike Johnson's offices have not yet provided comment. The intrigue: President Trump helped drive Massie out of Congress by backing a primary challenger, but the Kentucky Republican is using his final weeks in office to challenge the administration on some of its most politically sensitive topics. This latest effort could force Republicans to revisit a scandal that dogged the Trump administration for more than a year, even after Congress overwhelmingly voted to require the release of Epstein's files. This time, Massie wants to give Epstein survivors, state prosecutors and lawmakers the power to sue the Justice Department over records they believe it has unlawfully withheld. Catch up quick: Massie and Rep. Ro Khanna (D-Calif.) led the original push to force the release of the Epstein files. Their first bill passed the House 427-1 in November 2025 after they secured enough signatures to bypass Speaker Mike Johnson. Trump ultimately signed it into law. The law required DOJ to release its Epstein-related investigative records by Dec. 19, 2025, with limited exceptions to protect victims, ongoing investigations and other sensitive information. The department missed that deadline but announced in January that it had released nearly 3.5 million pages. The controversy: Epstein survivors and lawmakers have accused DOJ of withholding too much information while simultaneously exposing victims through inadequate redactions. A report released Tuesday by the Republican-led House Oversight Committee faulted the Trump administration's handling of the disclosures, including failures to protect victims and excessive redactions concealing alleged co-conspirators. The committee also said its investigation found no evidence implicating Trump in Epstein's crimes. What's next: Massie's petition is expected to become eligible for a floor vote by early December, with more than enough legislative days remaining under the House's current schedule. But passage is not guaranteed, and Senate Republican leaders could still decline to consider the measure before the new Congress takes office in January.

events.title: How India is marketing its skilled workforce to Australian businesses
events.summary: News Home Just In For You Analysis Rural Watch Live Health Indigenous Politics Science Deep Time Elections World Environment Investigations Business Local news Quizzes Sport AFL NRL Football Tennis Cricket Netball Lifestyle Wellbeing Relationships & Family Food & Recipes Personal Finance Home & Garden Entertainment TV & Movies Books Music Pop Culture Arts Qantas the latest in list of companies to outsource jobs to India Qantas is cutting 850 local jobs with some roles to be outsourced to Accenture workers in India. ( ABC News: ABC News: Adriane Reardon ) Qantas's announcement to shift 850 local jobs to India is the latest in a wave of white-collar jobs moving offshore. Some of Australia's biggest companies are outsourcing jobs to India. India has marketed its large, mostly English-speaking workforce to businesses for decades, but the nature of the jobs has changed. From clothing to credit cards, some of Australia's largest companies are shifting hundreds of jobs overseas, and the trend is not slowing down. NAB, Westpac, Telstra, Bank of Queensland, Coles, Officeworks and Qantas are among companies that have announced plans to cut Australian jobs and move roles to Asia in recent years — most under so-called global capacity centres (GCCs). Qantas announces cuts to 850 corporate jobs Qantas announces it will slash 850 roles in the coming years, with the first changes expected to be in place by mid-2027. GCCs are subsidiaries of foreign companies that allow them to maintain full control of their business rather than contracting a third party. Bunnings announced plans for a GCC in India in 2020, but has not yet announced job cuts. Kmart opened one in 2018. The companies said roles needed to move to cope with rising costs and the rapid adoption of artificial intelligence (AI). The Finance Sector Union has called the cuts "callous" and "ruthless" in the face of soaring corporate profits. From call centres to corporate hubs India is home to about 50 per cent of the world's GCCs, the latest evolution of offshoring, which began with contracting out call centre work decades ago. Global Capacity Centres take up a huge footprint in the city of Bengaluru in India's south. ( Reuters: Vivek Prakash ) In 2024, Australia's high commissioner to India, Philip Green, estimated Australian companies directly employed about 30,000 people in Indian GCCs. "In very simple terms, a GCC is setting up another office for a company. Instead of hiring contractors, you're hiring employees," said Lalit Ahuja, the chief executive of ANSR, which helps companies establish GCCs in India. Mr Ahuja said tighter immigration restrictions were accelerating the trend. Rather than waiting for skilled workers to migrate to Australia, he said, companies were moving operations to where the talent was. The shift could eventually extend to senior executives. "It's quite conceivable that one day for a large Australian company, they may have some key leaders sitting in Bangalore or Hyderabad," Mr Ahuja said. Arya Roy Bardhan, a junior fellow at the Observer Research Foundation in Kolkata, said that while India did offer skilled workers, it was the cost savings that attracted foreign companies. "If you're comparing India with Australia, the average wage is one third of what you have to pay in Australia," he said. "The only incentive for opening a GCC in India is cost savings. It's lower tax rates and major savings in wages." Dr Kanupriya, an assistant professor in the Department of Economics and Trade Policy at the Indian Institute of Foreign Trade, said it was a combination of both. "It's a cost-saving measure, and it taps into the diverse talent pool that India has to offer." A big part of that is the sheer number of potential employees available. India has marketed its large, mostly English-speaking workforce to foreign businesses since the 1990s, offering cheap wages and tax breaks to offshore companies. India has a huge number of tech graduates to offer Australian companies amid a domestic skills shortage. ( Reuters: Rishika Sadam ) By the early 2000s, more technical jobs shifted to the country as India prioritised tech and engineering graduates. With the world's largest youth population and about 830,000 engineering and technology graduates annually, according to India's Ministry of Education, creating jobs is a major priority. "Post-COVID, people realise this workforce has the skill and technical expertise needed to work with new products and even innovate," Mr Bardhan said. Time zones also did not matter when the work was not customer service. "Now you want us for tasks which can be done overnight, we don't have to operate at the same hours," he said. Before COVID, Mr Ahuja said his pitch to foreign companies was "anyone, any work, anytime, anywhere". With remote work normalised, companies became more comfortable running operations across borders. "You can run the company from India and have stores in Australia," Mr Ahuja said.

events.title: Personal data stolen after National Parks booking service hacked in three states
events.summary: News Home Just In For You Analysis Rural Watch Live Health Indigenous Politics Science Deep Time Elections World Environment Investigations Business Local news Quizzes Sport AFL NRL Football Tennis Cricket Netball Lifestyle Wellbeing Relationships & Family Food & Recipes Personal Finance Home & Garden Entertainment TV & Movies Books Music Pop Culture Arts Personal user data breached after Qld, Victoria and SA's National Park booking systems hacked Park users are being warned to keep an eye out for Queensland Parks and Wildlife staff impersonators. ( ABC News: Peter Quattrocelli ) The National Parks booking system for Queensland, Victoria and South Australia has been hacked. Queensland's environment department says it does not believe financial information has been compromised. Park users should be wary of phishing attempts. Hackers have stolen personal user information from Queensland, Victoria and South Australia's National Parks booking systems. The Queensland Department of Environment, Tourism, Science, and Innovation told 612 ABC Brisbane that the third-party provider Bookeasy had been hacked. Bookeasy processes camping and vehicle access permits for the National Parks Booking System, storing personal emails, addresses, and phone numbers. The spokesperson said "at this stage" they did not believe customers' financial information was accessed, as payments are processed through a separate system. The department spokesperson said park users should remain wary of phishing attempts by hackers impersonating national park staff. "If you receive an unexpected email, text message or phone call claiming to be from the department and asking you to confirm or provide personal information, do not respond, click on any links, or provide any personal information," the spokesperson said. "We take the privacy and security of your information extremely seriously and will provide further information to affected customers as soon as we know more." The spokesperson said any suspicious activity should be reported directly to the Queensland Parks and Wildlife Service at QPWS@detsi.qld.gov.au. A Parks Victoria spokesperson said they were aware of "suspicious Whatsapp messages" being sent to their customers. The spokesperson said they had temporarily suspended all new campsite bookings while investigations continued. "We are working urgently with Bookeasy to understand the issue and proactively communicating with our customers who may be impacted," the spokesperson said. "Existing bookings have not been cancelled and remain valid. "While we investigate, we are also temporarily unable to make changes or modifications to existing bookings." In an email, National Parks and Wildlife Service South Australia told users to remain vigilant. "Bookeasy recently detected unauthorised activity within its platform and has engaged cyber security experts to investigate," the email said. "As part of this investigation, it has been identified that some customer information, including names, contact details, and booking information, may have been accessed. "At this stage, there is no evidence that credit card details were accessed." events.title: Scott Colom ousts Cindy Hyde-Smith in historic Mississippi Senate flip
events.summary: Democrat Scott Colom defeated Republican Sen. Cindy Hyde-Smith in a stunning Mississippi upset , becoming the first Democrat elected to the state's Senate delegation since 1982, AP projects. Why it matters: Colom's victory marks another extraordinary breakthrough for Democrats in the Deep South, extending the historic blue wave that handed the party control of both chambers of Congress. Colom also becomes Mississippi's first Black senator since Reconstruction. Hiram Rhodes Revels became the nation's first Black senator in 1870. Mississippi's last Black senator, Blanche K. Bruce, served until 1881. Catch up quick: Colom's victory expands Democrats' 55–44 advantage over Republicans in the Senate. Worries of a recount — which requires a court order, as Mississippi has no recount law — seemed moot as Hyde-Smith posted a video message to X shortly after AP called the race, appearing to concede to Colom. "While this is not the outcome we worked for or hoped for, I respect the decision of Mississippi voters. I want to congratulate Scott Cologne and wish him well as he takes on the tremendous responsibility of representing our great state," she said. Hyde-Smith also addressed another worry from Mississippi voters following a significant purge of the state's voter rolls, saying that her campaign "has worked tirelessly to ensure every legally cast vote was counted and that the people of Mississippi received a fair and transparent election." "I am proud of what we have accomplished together, but I want to make one thing very clear: an election may come to an end, but our commitment to Mississippi never will," she said. The big picture: Colom's victory followed a late surge of Democratic spending and organizing in a state Trump carried by 23 points in 2024. Hyde-Smith faced warning signs in the campaign's closing months, when Colom raised twice as much as the GOP senator despite her overall cash advantage. She was also outspent on TV advertising , with a flood of ads from left-leaning PACs and super PACs pushing support for Colom and attacking the senator for her vote not to release files related to the convicted human trafficker Jeffrey Epstein. Hyde-Smith's campaign also faced criticism over an interview she gave to WLOX-TV in Biloxi, Mississippi, where she fumbled an answer about the price of beef, saying that Mississippians had "so many other proteins to choose from." Colom's campaign capitalized on her blunder, creating a viral campaign ad urging voters to "choose another senator." The GOP made a late push to help Hyde-Smith, including President Trump speaking at a rally for her in Alcorn County, where he won by 68% in 2024. But it wasn't enough. Hyde-Smith's term will end after eight years. She was appointed to the Senate in 2018 by then-Mississippi Gov. Phil Bryant, and ran for a full term in 2020, where she bested her Democratic challenger Mike Espy by 10 points. Zoom in: Colom, a 43-year-old district attorney from Columbus, campaigned on lowering the cost of living, raising wages and protecting rural hospitals. His campaign also drew in heavy Democratic hitters to stump for him, including former President Bill Clinton, former Vice President Kamala Harris and Georgia Sen. Raphael Warnock. The bottom line: Colom's win adds Mississippi to a growing list of Republican strongholds where Democrats broke through in the midterms, including Texas and South Carolina. It also reinforces the role of Black voters in the Democratic comeback, after the party rebuilt support among a crucial voting bloc that showed signs of shifting toward Trump in 2024. Editor's note: This is a breaking news story and will be updated. This story has been corrected to show that Hyde-Smith's interview was conducted in Biloxi (not Jackson, Mississippi).

events.title: MSCI says Indonesia’s Barito Pacific will be removed from its indexes
events.summary: The latest setback comes a month after MSCI warned Indonesian stocks could be removed from its indexes next year and the market relegated to “standalone” status. MSCI will remove Barito Pacific from its indexes and move Bumi Resources Minerals to small cap, forcing index funds to sell after Nov 30. The move adds pressure on Indonesia, whose market is down over 40% in 2026 and faces a possible downgrade to “standalone” status. Authorities have tightened rules and MSCI is seeking feedback until April 30, 2027, but investors have already pulled out US$5.4 billion this year. SINGAPORE/BENGALURU / JAKARTA – Global index provider MSCI will remove one Indonesian company from its indexes, it said on Nov 11 , dealing a blow to the country’s efforts to avoid a downgrade and retain its emerging-market status. The latest setback comes a month after MSCI warned Indonesian stocks could be removed from its indexes in 2027 and the market relegated to “standalone” status, a much harsher fate than the one the index provider first threatened in January. The deletions will force funds that track its indexes to sell the shares, and take effect after the close of trading on Nov 30. Barito Pacific will be removed from MSCI’s global standard index, while Bumi Resources Minerals will be moved from that index to the small-cap index. Neither firm immediately responded to requests for comment. Once the removal takes effect, MSCI’s Indonesia index will be left with seven companies after the index provider culled six firms in May and two more in August. At the start of 2026, the Indonesia index had 18 firms. Barito Pacific, a company with interests in petrochemicals, energy and infrastructure, is controlled by business magnate and billionaire Prajogo Pangestu. In May, MSCI removed from its Indonesia index three firms in which Prajogo has controlling stakes: Chandra Asri Pacific, Barito Renewables Energy and Petrindo Jaya Kreasi. Indonesia’s benchmark stock index was up 1.3% at 0340 GMT (11.40am Singapore time), while the rupiah slid 0.6% to hit a new all-time low of 18,248 a US dollar. The currency was affected by US monetary policy expectations, concerns about MSCI’s decision on Indonesian stocks, domestic economic issues and higher year-end demand for foreign exchange, Bank Indonesia said in a statement on Nov 12. The threat of a downgrade has cast a shadow over Indonesian markets, with the benchmark index down over 40% in 2026, making it the world’s worst-performing major stock market. In October, MSCI cited Indonesia’s failure to improve ownership transparency and curb coordinated trading, turning what had been a downgrade risk to “frontier” market status into a full-blown crisis of investor confidence. The Indonesian authorities have spent much of 2026 trying to address MSCI’s concerns, tightening disclosure requirements and laying out plans to raise minimum free floats. In October, the regulator announced sanctions linked to alleged manipulation. Earlier this week, the stock exchange removed the 5 trillion rupiah (S$352 million) market cap threshold for screening companies that breach high shareholding concentration rules. MSCI is seeking feedback on the reclassification proposal until April 30, 2027, and will announce its decision on or before June 30, 2027 , although analysts worry that many active investors may exit Indonesia before that . Foreign investors have already pulled out US$5.4 billion (S$6.9 billion) from Indonesian equities in 2026. Goldman Sachs has estimated MSCI’s removal of the country’s stocks from its indexes could spur US$5.6 billion of passive outflows. Indonesia has been an MSCI emerging market since 1989, and a downgrade would be a huge reversal for a market that until recently was a favourite of foreign investors. More than US$1.8 trillion in assets are benchmarked to MSCI’s emerging-market indexes , according to the index provider’s website . REUTERS

events.summary: Nvidia’s board is reportedly preparing to oust chief executive Jensen Huang, who admitted to having an affair with an alleged Chinese spy. Nvidia shares fell 9% after reports raised doubts about CEO Jensen Huang’s future, with investors worried about leadership and governance. The New York Times said Huang had a relationship with a direct report, and the Wall Street Journal said the board may be preparing to oust him. Nvidia faces pressure before its Nov 17 results, as analysts say any removal could hurt client trust and force a more traditional structure. Nvidia stock sank in extended trading on Nov 11 as investors grappled with the possibility of the company without chief executiveJensen Huang at the helm. The stock began to fall in post-market trading following a New York Times report that the CEO had a relationship with a direct report. Losses extended after Wall Street Journal reported Nvidia’s board is preparing to oust Huang, who over the weekend had admitted to having a separate affair with an alleged Chinese spy. “It is going to be a very challenging situation,” said Michael O’Rourke, chief market strategist at Jonestrading. “Jensen had forecast 70% sales growth this year (2026). With the vendor financing and the aggressive tactics, his successor will spend the next year putting out fires and cleaning up messes.” He added: “If these allegations are confirmed by the independent investigation, one has to expect the board to remove him. That is the standard for corporate governance today. Even worse this is a pattern.” Other AI-linked stocks followed shares of Nvidia lower in post-market trading. Nvidia shares have been under pressure amid growing concern around the strength and longevity of the artificial intelligence trade. The chipmaker is scheduled to report quarterly results on Nov 17. It “will be interesting how it handles next week’s earnings call. Their CFO (chief financial officer) can handle the numbers but markets will want more on changes to the governance”, said Dec Mullarkey of SLC Management. “It’s hard to imagine him stepping down but also hard to imagine how he could stay on. I think the board will ultimately be forced to push him out and establish a more traditional organisational structure. The gap in judgment may be hard to repair with critical clients.” BLOOMBERG

events.title: Nvidia’s Jensen Huang resigns, CFO Colette Kress named interim CEO
events.summary: Nvidia Chief Executive Jensen Huang has resigned, the company announced Thursday, an ouster that follows his admission of having an extramarital affair with a woman U.S. intelligence officials deemed to be a Chinese spy. The decision by the chipmaking giant deals a swift end to Huang’s 33-year reign as CEO and upends America’s race in artificial intelligence. In his place, the board has tapped Chief Financial Officer Colette Kress as interim CEO. A steadfast presence, Kress will be a familiar face and voice to Wall Street as Nvidia navigates an abrupt CEO transition. Nvidia’s board has started a search for a permanent successor to Huang, and will consider internal and external candidates. The board has also appointed its first chair, Harvey Jones. Jones, a managing partner with Square Wave Ventures, joined the board in 1993 when the company was founded. As a veteran who has overseen Nvidia since its earliest days, Jones will serve as a conduit for the institutional memory that departs with Huang. In addition to Huang’s entanglement with a suspected Chinese intelligence asset, the New York Times on Wednesday reported that Huang, 63, had an extramarital relationship with Kimberly Powell, the company’s vice president of health care. Powell could not immediately be reached for comment. “Colette has helped lead NVIDIA through a period of extraordinary growth and has a deep understanding of our business, customers, operations and financial position,” Jones said Thursday in a written statement. “She is supported by an experienced leadership team that has been instrumental in executing NVIDIA’s strategy and advancing its technology roadmap.” In a statement, Kress said, “NVIDIA’s strength has always come from its people, and together with our leadership team, I am committed to building on the extraordinary foundation Jensen created over the last 33 years.” Shares of Nvidia initially fell more than 6% on Thursday. Huang holds a 3.6% stake in the company, valued at about $150 billion. On Sunday, Huang acknowledged being unfaithful to his wife, and Nvidia announced an investigation into the reports that he had been targeted by a foreign intelligence effort. At the time, the board said it had “no reason to believe that either national security or NVIDIA secrets were compromised,” but that its inquiry would examine “all available information.” Huang co-founded Nvidia in 1993 and has been integral to the company’s success, particularly its magnificent run in recent years. Growth accelerated in the first half of its fiscal 2027, with revenue of $96 billion, up 85% year over year. Kress previously said the company expected 70% revenue growth in fiscal 2028. Huang has reigned supreme over the company . Since its founding, he has created a unique, flat structure in which he has sat at the center of most decisions, with about 60 direct reports. Before Jones’ appointment, Nvidia’s board operated without a chair, and the company has not set out a clear succession plan. It also does not have a chief operating officer. Huang has been known to text and call small clients himself. Nvidia’s succession challenge will not be whether its engineers can keep building chips without Huang, analysts say. It is whether anyone, or any leadership team, can inherit his authority to decide what gets built, secure the industry’s commitment to it, and keep customers confident in the next bet. Bret Greenstein, chief AI officer at tech consulting firm West Monroe, said that Huang’s resignation represents an Nvidia reset that presents an opportunity to the broader market. Nvidia’s momentum will be disrupted, Greenstein wrote in a note. “At the same time, Anthropic recently demonstrated that it could move its inference workloads from Nvidia’s CUDA software stack to AMD in just three days, suggesting that Nvidia’s software moat may no longer be as strong as it once was,” he wrote. “This could turn what has effectively been a monopoly into a horse race again, as competitors rush to meet growing demand.” With Huang’s ouster, the biggest questions are who will succeed him in the long run and what plan the company will put in place to fill the power vacuum. “Rarely has a board faced this much pressure. This is the board’s moment to shine or fade,” Michael Useem, a professor of management at the Wharton School of the University of Pennsylvania, told Fortune . “If the board had been doing its job, it would already have a slate of possible successors.” Jeffrey Sonnenfeld, senior associate dean for leadership studies and Lester Crown Professor in Management Practice at Yale University’s School of Management, told Fortune that the Huang saga can be compared to what happened at McDonald’s with former CEO Steve Easterbrook, who was ousted in November 2019. The McDonald’s board investigated Easterbrook for a consensual relationship with an employee that involved the exchange of videos and romantic text messages, and then found that other undisclosed, improper relationships had occurred. Easterbrook was later charged by the Securities and Exchange Commission with making false and misleading statements to investors about the circumstances that led to his termination. Easterbrook didn’t admit or deny the findings, but agreed to be barred from serving as an officer or director of any public company for a period of five years, and he paid a $400,000 civil penalty. Huang’s ouster creates a massive hole for the AI industry. Huang has been central to the industry’s rapid growth. His success in creating world-leading graphics processing units, the chips that power AI by handling model training and regular user queries, has been instrumental in ushering in the AI boom and in the U.S.’s leading position. Few executives in Silicon Valley and beyond exert the level of power and influence over one company and industry. Huang’s institutional knowledge and deep industry connections have been among the reasons tech analysts and other experts said it would be impossible to replace him. Another reason has been President Trump, who has become a close friend of Huang and has stood by the executive since Sunday’s revelations, saying Huang is an “amazing guy” and “honorable man.” This story was originally featured on Fortune.com

events.title: Oil rises on mixed signals over Iran war outlook
events.summary: The Iran war, which started on Feb 28, has caused gas prices to rise worldwide. Oil climbed on Nov 11, as traders weighed mixed signals on the prospects for a conclusion to the Iran war. While US President Donald Trump has said further strikes on Iran would not be necessary , regional flare-ups have persisted and peace talks have shown little progress. Iran will not remove “a single atom” of enriched nuclear material from the country, Secretary of the Supreme National Security Council Mohsen Rezaee said in an interview with Al Mayadeen. West Texas Intermediate futures rose above US$86 a barrel after sliding about 5% in the previous two days, while Brent closed near US$93. “We’ve shifted from a market that needed things to get worse to move higher, to one where things simply not getting better could be enough to push prices up,” said Rebecca Babin, senior energy trader at CIBC Private Wealth Group. The US benchmark is up roughly 50% this year, but the market has reversed sharply in November, with Brent tumbling from a six-month high on hopes the conflict will ease and as Persian Gulf energy exports rise. Saudi Arabia’s crude output climbed 26% in October to the highest since the war began despite attacks on ships, as a recovery in regional flows pushes prices lower. Saudi Arabia told OPEC that its output rose to 10.56 million barrels a day in October, according to a monthly report seen by Bloomberg from the organisation’s secretariat. The bigger flows from the Saudis and other exporters around the Persian Gulf are showing up in physical markets at a time when consumption remains constrained. “We have seen a sharp re-pricing of the oil market over the past two weeks” as election results in the US and Israel “reduced the likelihood of renewed escalation in the conflict,” said Jens Naervig Pedersen, a strategist at Danske Bank AS. Still, “Iran seems hesitant to meet US demands on its nuclear programme, which may test the durability of the recent decline in oil prices.” Meanwhile, the American Petroleum Institute reported US crude inventories rose by nine million barrels last week. Stockpiles of distillates such as diesel, which had fallen below 100 million barrels for the first time since 2003, climbed by 1.5 million barrels, API said. Official data is due on Nov 12. Separately, the Energy Information Administration raised its 2027 forecasts for retail gasoline prices to an average US$3.73 a gallon and diesel to US$5.03, citing tight global fuel supplies. The agency left its US crude production estimate unchanged at 14.3 million barrels a day in its Short-Term Energy Outlook. A tanker carrying Russian diesel that had briefly signalled a US destination made a U-turn off New York, adding uncertainty over deliveries to the North American market. Last month, Russian President Vladimir Putin agreed to supply fuel to the US and global markets in a deal with Trump, though the arrangement drew criticism from Democrats. BLOOMBERG

events.title: China’s marriage rate drops to lowest level in almost two decades
events.summary: China’s marriage rate fell to its lowest level in almost two decades , adding to worries about the country’s demographic crisis. Data this week showed 4.65 million couples tied the knot from January through September, while 2.08 million couples got divorced. Beijing has in recent years rolled out a series of measures aimed at increasing marriage rates and childbearing. But while some regions have seen results from such policies, fertility rates for the country as a whole continue to plummet, with women on average having fewer children than even during the era of the one-child policy . The demographic shift will have huge fiscal consequences for decades to come, with one prominent China academic urging Beijing to “formulate forward-looking plans for immigration .” — Jeronimo Gonzalez

events.title: Superhuman AI bots will not steal this man's job
events.summary: News Home Just In For You Analysis Rural Watch Live Health Indigenous Politics Science Deep Time Elections World Environment Investigations Business Local news Quizzes Sport AFL NRL Football Tennis Cricket Netball Lifestyle Wellbeing Relationships & Family Food & Recipes Personal Finance Home & Garden Entertainment TV & Movies Books Music Pop Culture Arts Until superhuman swimming bots are invented, these jobs will be safe from AI Luke Gnocco is the founder of Poseidon Adventure, which operates out of Townsville and Brisbane. ( ABC News: Isabella Garrido ) Until superhuman swimming robots take his job, Luke Gnocco remains pretty relaxed about artificial intelligence (AI). "Electronics and water usually don't work," he points out. Luke Gnocco says most of his staff come from marine science backgrounds and are passionate about the reef. ( ABC News: Isabella Garrido ) Mr Gnocco's marine tourism business in north Queensland takes people on snorkelling tours on the Great Barrier Reef, jet ski tours and guided walks around Magnetic Island. He said hands-on, manual and interpersonal interactions were core aspects of the job. "With a reef tour guide, there's literally no part in the process that could be replaced by AI. Luke Gnocco says it is unlikely AI will affect hands-on jobs in the tourism industry. ( Supplied: Poseidon Adventure ) "Especially being Australia, a lot of our tourism and a lot of our products are the country, they are the reef, they are the water, and I don't think it's ever going to go backwards." While he is confident the tourism industry will weather any AI boom, recent research by public policy consultancy firm SGS Economics and Planning found about 30 per cent of work tasks across regional Queensland could be exposed to AI automation. Principal and partner Alison Holloway said regional locations were more resilient to change from AI. SA gives green light for gas to help power future data centres Victorian Labor's multi-million-dollar social media ad spend revealed Topic: State and Territory Elections Regulator warns of 'interruptions' to business as AI models evolve Data centre industry butts up against community challenges Alison Holloway says AI will affect some locations differently than others. ( Supplied: Alison Holloway ) "A lot of the knowledge jobs and professional services jobs are located in the city centres … and they're the jobs that are most exposed to AI automation," Ms Holloway said. The report found almost 40 per cent of work tasks in Brisbane were at risk of AI automation, followed by the Gold Coast on 37.1 per cent. The Sunshine Coast sits at 36.4 per cent, followed by Cairns at 36, followed by Townsville and Rockhampton at 35.6, and Mackay at 34.9. Despite the Gold Coast's status as a major tourism hub, Ms Holloway said there was a mix of occupations in the region, including many administrative tasks within tourism that were not in-person. The Gold Coast is just behind Brisbane in the number of jobs at risk of AI automation. ( ABC News: Emily Dobson ) SGS Economics and Planning drew upon research by Jobs and Skills Australia and data from the Australian Bureau of Statistics to determine the risk of exposure in different locations. Ms Holloway said roles susceptible to automation were concentrated in the professional hearts of cities, such as finance, professional services and office-based jobs. She said those less exposed to AI disruption required in-person engagement or a physical presence. SGS Economics and Planning says AI is set to disrupt how work gets done at a pace and scale few industries have faced before. ( AP: Michael Dwyer/File ) "If you think about the care economy, nursing and aged care, they're all things where a physical person is engaged in that job," she said. Christoph Breidbach, an associate professor of Business Information Systems at the University of Queensland, said many regional occupations were inherently different because they required local knowledge, human relationships or engaging with unpredictable natural environments. Dr Breidbach said farming, for example, required responding to changing weather or soil conditions and livestock behaviour. Christoph Breidbach says this time around, jobs in cities are more likely to be affected by AI than those in regional areas. ( Supplied ) "What AI does is that it could assist with planning or with scheduling or with decision support, but you simply can't replace the physical execution of these tasks, unless you have very advanced robotics," he said. While previous waves of technological change disproportionately affected regional economies, Dr Breidbach said the AI wave was different for industries like agriculture and manufacturing. "It's not so much the physical labour that is now being automated or even augmented, but you can see change to cognitive tasks. So, your writing, your analysing of information, preparing of reports, and those are tasks that you would associate with white-collar jobs.

events.title: Clashes erupt in Barcelona after thousands join Spain general strike
events.summary: Watch: Protesters and police clash in Barcelona Clashes have broken out between groups of masked men and police in Barcelona after tens of thousands of people took part in Spain's first general strike for 14 years, called by the country's main unions over housing and the high cost of living. Some 120,000 people joined a demonstration in the capital Madrid and more than 50,000 turned out in Barcelona, where footage showed masked men setting fire to rubbish bins and smashing shop windows as police fired tear gas. Transport and other public services across Spain faced serious disruption. Spaniards are due to vote in parliamentary elections on 29 November. The head of the big UGT labour union, Pepe Álvarez, said the strike was a success with "massive" participation, while Unai Sordo of the CC OO union said turnout was "very significant." There was a heavy police presence in the centre of Barcelona on Wednesday evening, with officers wearing helmets and riot shields. Some of the disturbances took place in the Passeig de Gràcia, close to the iconic Plaça de Catalunya in the centre of the city. Small fires burned in the middle of the streets as bins were set alight. Local media reported that a group of people fired fireworks towards police and looted shops including the Lego store. Protesters were also seen trying to enter the Apple Store. The BBC spoke to a woman who attended the protests in Barcelona who said it was mostly very peaceful and "joyful". She said she was there to protest about the housing costs and that "there were a lot of children and old people there." She was in the area of Las Ramblas in the evening and saw fires in the streets. "The fires were everywhere, it was very intense," she said. Earlier in the day there was major disruption around Madrid and Barcelona, with traffic halted on several main roads. The interior ministry said dozens of people were arrested for a variety of incidents and Spanish reports said estate agencies had seen attacks on their offices. Police said they had made dozens of arrests "We've completely brought the city to a standstill," a protester in Madrid told Reuters news agency, adding there was widespread support for the general strike. "Everyone's out there, despite the rainy weather; everyone's out on the streets." Another protester, 37-year-old teacher Olga Domingo, said she was protesting because "the housing situation is outrageous. The current cost of living compared to wages is completely unsustainable". The strike was triggered by widespread protests over affordable housing and rising living costs, after the eviction of 87-year-old Maricarmen Abascal from a flat in Madrid where she had lived for seven decades. She died in hospital weeks later. Rental prices in the capital have risen in recent years. The monthly cost of a 50 sq m apartment in Madrid was an average of €1,170 ($1,300; £1,000) in October, according to property portal Idealista, while Spain's average gross monthly salary is about €2,460. That amounts to nearly half the average gross salary, well above the 30% level of affordability often recommended by housing experts and public institutions. Watch: Protesters gather across Spain for first general strike in 14 years Socialist Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez called snap elections last month after parliament failed to approve his plan for housing reform. Not since 2012, under the conservative government of Mariano Rajoy, has Spain held general strikes. And while previous strikes have been problematic for the government in power, this one is different. Sánchez and his ministers have even encouraged workers to down tools and demand affordable housing. "Your eight-hour day. Your pension. Your public healthcare… These were collective conquests," he wrote on social media, praising those who took part in previous strikes. Tyres were set on fire in the city of Gijon in northern Spain The conservative People's Party (PP), by contrast, has accused the government of attempting to weaponise the strike for electoral gain. PP leader Alberto Núñez Feijóo called the general strike "nonsense", calling the unions "mafia" and "trash". Feijoo's party is leading in the polls and party spokesman Miguel Tellado accused the government of exploiting the strike to warn voters against allowing a right-wing government to be formed, which looks the most likely outcome of the 29 November election. Sánchez told Spanish TV this week: "What is nonsense is to question the rights of workers to strike." Among those taking part in the general strike was Gonzalo Álvarez, 27, who was visiting different picket lines in central Madrid. Although he works in sales, he has been volunteering for a housing union that tries to protect tenants and makes them aware of their rights. The eviction of Maricarmen Abascal at the end of September "was the little fire" that sparked this protest, he told the BBC.

events.title: Developer says gigantic WA data centre will not use fracked gas
events.summary: News Home Just In For You Analysis Rural Watch Live Health Indigenous Politics Science Deep Time Elections World Environment Investigations Business Local news Quizzes Sport AFL NRL Football Tennis Cricket Netball Lifestyle Wellbeing Relationships & Family Food & Recipes Personal Finance Home & Garden Entertainment TV & Movies Books Music Pop Culture Arts Gingerah says it will not use fracked gas to power proposed WA data centre Gingerah Energy's proposed data centre project includes a local micro-grid powered by a 5,200-megawatt solar farm and 250 wind turbines. ( Supplied: Jop van Hattum ) The company behind a proposed data centre has sought to ease fears it will power the facility with fracked gas. Gingerah Energy says the centre will be mostly powered by renewables, with gas sourced from "the domestic gas market" as backup supply. The company intends to refer its project to the WA Environmental Protection Authority for review within weeks. The company proposing to build a massive data centre in northern Western Australia has sought to ease concerns the facility will be powered by gas sourced through fracking. Gingerah Energy referred its plan to build a 1,000-megawatt data centre and renewable energy hub to the Commonwealth's environmental agency last month. The site proposed is on Karajarri country, near Broome, about 2,000 kilometres north of Perth. Jop van Hattum says Project Meridien will be mostly renewables-powered. ( Supplied: Energy Club WA ) Chief executive Jop van Hattum said Project Meridien, which Gingerah hopes to be delivered by 2030, would initially be powered by solar, batteries, gas, and later also by wind. He said renewables would initially provide more than 85 per cent of the facility's total energy demand, with that figure rising as it expanded towards its full one-gigawatt capacity. The gas used would most likely come from Karratha, Mr van Hattum said. "We target for that renewable energy capacity to increase to 94 per cent," he said. Environmentalists have suggested Gingerah might source the gas it needs for the centre through fracking in the Kimberley. While there is no ban on fracking in the region's Canning basin, no projects have received the required approvals to proceed. Critics of fracking, or hydraulic fracturing, say it is harmful due to risks involving water contamination and long-term climate impacts. Mr van Hattum said the project's gas would be sourced from "the domestic gas market". "As energy storage systems and technology improve and costs reduce, our preference would obviously be to be free of the gas and use those technologies to make the project fully carbon-free if we can," he added. Environs Kimberley director Martin Pritchard called for greater clarity on where the gas would come from. "Could it come from another company that is planning to do fracking in the Kimberley? Could it come from a new conventional well that Buru Energy is working on at the moment? Could it come from Theia Energy, and are they going to want to start fracking to supply gas to this AI data centre?" Meridien is proposed to be developed on the KTLA-held Frazier Downs pastoral lease, about 100 kilometres south of Broome in WA's west Kimberley. ( Supplied: Jop van Hattum ) Gingerah is a joint venture between Karajarri Traditional Lands Association (KTLA), Dutch geodata company Fugro and Australian geoscience firm Longreach Capital Investment, which owns Theia Energy — a company that previously applied to drill and frack exploration wells in the Kimberley. Grattan Institute energy expert Alison Reeve estimated the Meridien data centre would need about eight terajoules of gas a day in its initial 240-megawatt phase and about 32 terajoules at full capacity. "All of WA consumes about 1,100 terajoules a day," she said. Ms Reeve said the project was not large enough to lead to more gas exploration or fracking in the Kimberley because the state already had enough gas to cover it. Traditional owner confident no fracked gas will be used KTLA director Justin King Senior said the gas needed for Meridien would "absolutely not" come from fracking. KTLA director Justin King signed the Gingerah Energy Indigenous Land Use Agreement in 2024. ( Supplied: Jop van Hattum ) "I say with conviction and reassure the people, our members, and the public [fracking] would never be part of the project make-up of energy," he said. Among KTLA members, Mr King said "a small minority" were opposed to the project for several reasons, including the increase in negative sentiment towards data centres online. "Social media plays a big part in giving out information," he said. The Raging Grannies protest data centres and power hikes in North Carolina, US. ( ABC News: Bec Symons ) This month's US midterm elections put data centres in the spotlight , with voters overwhelmingly rejecting their development. Ms Reeve said this resistance was also prevalent in Australia.

events.title: What it takes to bring an AI research assistant to thousands of medical experts
events.summary: From custom infrastructure to hosted agents What we learned rebuilding Novo’s clinical trials data agent on Microsoft Foundry: a simpler operating model, a stronger session isolation, and a direct path from tracing to evaluation and optimization. Clinical research rarely ends with the questions defined in a trial protocol. Medical experts also explore the data from new angles: testing a hypothesis, comparing patient populations, visualizing a trend, or identifying a promising direction for further research. As part of a forward-deployed engineering engagement, a joint Microsoft and Novo Nordisk development team built an agent that helps medical experts perform this kind of secondary analysis of clinical trial data. We described the original project in a Microsoft customer story . More recently, we reimplemented the solution as a hosted agent in Microsoft Foundry . The move gave us a simpler operating model, stronger session isolation, and a direct path into Foundry’s tracing, evaluation, experimentation, optimization, and governance capabilities. It also taught us practical lessons about infrastructure planning, observability, and preserving the learning loop that already made the agent better over time. Here’s what changed, what we measured, and what we would recommend to teams making a similar move. An agent for questions that don’t have a fixed workflow Secondary analysis of clinical data is a great task for an agent because the execution path depends heavily on the question. The agent interprets the request, inspects the available data, writes and executes analysis code, examines the result, and often revises its approach before returning a summary and visualization. This isn’t just attaching a chat interface to a single API. The agent needs a reasoning loop, access to domain-specific skills, and tools for working with data. In our implementation, code execution is the central tool. The agent can generate analysis code and visualizations inside a controlled environment while the surrounding application manages the conversation and presents the result to the user. Our first production architecture ran the agent in Azure Container Apps . We used PostgreSQL for conversation storage and Azure Container Apps dynamic sessions for sandboxed code execution. That architecture gave us explicit control over every component, and it proved the value of the use case. It also meant that our team owned much of the platform around the agent: container scaling, session lifecycle, conversation persistence, execution isolation, networking, telemetry, and the integration among them. Foundry hosted agents offered a simpler division of responsibility. Moving the runtime boundary into Foundry A hosted agent is our code, packaged as a container, running on infrastructure managed by Foundry Agent Service . We retain control of the orchestration logic, models, tools, and runtime behavior. Foundry manages the endpoint, agent identity, session compute, state persistence, scaling, and lifecycle around it. At runtime, each session gets its own VM-isolated sandbox. Foundry provisions compute on demand, keeps it active while the session is in use, and de-provisions it after the configured idle period. Session files can persist and be restored when the session resumes. Scaling follows active sessions rather than a replica count that we have to predict and configure. For Novo’s workload, that model aligned well with the unit of work we were building for: one expert conducting one analysis session. It also changed the architecture in four important ways: Scaling became session-native. We no longer needed to connect application-level session creation to a separately scaled pool of execution environments. The platform owns that lifecycle. Isolation became the default unit of execution. Each session runs in a VM-isolated sandbox rather than sharing a process or general-purpose application container with other sessions. That matters when the workload includes model-generated code operating on sensitive clinical data. Network isolation became part of the service architecture. Foundry Agent Service supports private networking, including virtual network integration and private access to dependent Azure resources. This lets us design controls for both ingress and egress around the agent environment. Those controls are especially important for data that must remain inside an approved network boundary. The agent joined a broader development lifecycle. Traces, evaluations, experiments, monitoring, and optimization can now be connected through the same platform. Microsoft Agent 365 integration also provides a path to enterprise inventory, identity, access control, and lifecycle governance. Using Foundry hosted agents didn’tt remove our responsibility for security or quality. We still had to define access controls, minimize and protect telemetry, test the agent for our use case, and review every system it can call. What changed is that several controls we previously assembled ourselves are now platform capabilities we can configure and operate consistently. Here are the top lessons we learned during this project—and some practical advice for your own hosted agents projects in Foundry: Lesson 1: Treat infrastructure choices as product decisions Private networking should be an early architecture decision, not a production hardening task left until the end. Hosted agents consume network capacity according to sessions. The Foundry account, its projects, hosted agents, concurrent sessions, and agent revisions all contribute to IP usage. Because the assigned subnet is an immutable reference at the account level, an undersized range can turn a capacity adjustment into a broader infrastructure migration. Our advice is to estimate peak concurrent sessions across the account, include headroom for deployments and growth, and involve the network team before creating the Foundry resource. The current networking guidance recommends a /24 subnet for production hosted agent deployments and documents /27 as the supported minimum for smaller deployments. We used Azure Verified Modules as the foundation for repeatable environments. That gave us a strong starting point, but infrastructure as code doesn’t remove the need to inspect generated dependencies. Throughput for resources like Azure Cosmos DB should reflect expected concurrency and data access patterns. Where a setting requires an operational adjustment, capture it in the deployment process or operator runbook rather than leaving it as unwritten production knowledge. Subnet sizing, database throughput, private endpoints, DNS, and concurrency aren’t separate infrastructure details. Together, they shape the scale ceiling and reliability of the product. Lesson 2: Make traces easy to navigate Foundry tracing uses OpenTelemetry and stores telemetry in Azure Monitor Application Insights.

events.title: Local media startup City Cast reshuffles leadership
events.summary: The locally-focused media startup City Cast has named Andi McDaniel, the company’s chief creative officer, its new CEO, replacing David Plotz. City Cast launched in 2021 as a local podcast and newsletter venture aimed at serving cities where local news was shifting from old newspapers and radio to screens. The company has since expanded to 13 cities, including Austin, Las Vegas, and Philadelphia, among others. “This next chapter for us is about expanding audiences. It’s about adapting to AI, and it’s about making the business successful,” McDaniel, a veteran public radio executive and co-founder of City Cast , told Semafor. City Cast has gained greater visibility in recent months, primarily for its expansion in its hometown. As Semafor first noted last year, in response to what the company saw as an opportunity created by the turbulence at The Washington Post, City Cast scaled up its newsroom and business in Washington. City Cast is backed by Graham Holdings, which owned the Post before selling to Jeff Bezos. City Cast DC now has 20 people on staff, and said it has found some success attracting a younger audience to its content, tripling the size of people it reaches regularly from roughly 100,000 at the beginning of the year to around 300,000. Not every bet has paid off. The company shuttered two arms, in Boise and Houston. In a telephone interview, Plotz said Houston was too large and sprawling an area to cover with the company’s resources — most cities operate with a staff of just 5 or 6 employees — while he said the company didn’t understand Boise enough when City Cast launched there. The company learned that their podcasts were not a replacement for radio, and that the City Cast model seemed to resonate best within mid-sized cities with concentrated downtowns that orient residents’ perspectives. Plotz said that revenue was up 40% this year, but the company was still not profitable. In the six years since the company’s launch, the company’s founder told Semafor he’d grown to better understand habits in the local media landscape. He noted that many people under the age of 60 largely got their information from social media, neighborhood listservs, local newsletters, and Reddit. “People do not want local news,” Plotz said. “They want to know about things to do in their city. They want to know what’s going on in their city. But if you ask them about local news, they do not express an interest. “Local news as a concept does not really have a lot of valence. It’s more like learning about my city.” He also noted that national media narratives and big political fights were not as animating to local audiences, who seek out information to be connected to their local communities. “The need that people are finding met in local media has almost nothing to do with the highly partisan, cortisol-driven conversations that drive national media and national news media,” he said.

events.title: Scoop: Lutnick stalled curbing Nvidia chip sales to China — again — after Oval Office showdown
events.summary: President Trump on Thursday authorized a crack down on companies suspected of diverting Nvidia's advanced AI chips to China for the third time this year — even consulting Elon Musk before giving the go-ahead. One administration official has repeatedly stood in the way: Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick. Why it matters: This standoff illustrates a breakdown in efforts to keep American technology out of China's hands as the world wonders why the Trump administration has not taken action against the company at the center of suspected chip smuggling — and an espionage scandal. This report was assembled from interviews with six high-level sources who were briefed on or, in some cases, heard the discussions. Inside the room: On Thursday, as the spy scandal rocked the administration, Lutnick met in the Situation Room with Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent, Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth, U.S. Trade Representative Jamieson Greer and National Security Adviser and Secretary of State Marco Rubio. During the meeting, Bessent confronted Lutnick about why his department has resisted implementing the export controls, particularly on Megaspeed, the company at the center of the spy scandal. The group sided with Bessent. Lutnick appeared to agree, but then muttered under his breath, "I need to check with the president." Friction point: Lutnick's seemingly innocuous comment raised concerns, the sources said, because officials have repeatedly believed the Commerce Department would impose the export controls, only to have nothing happen. "He's stalling it out," said one official, describing how Lutnick had previously met privately with the president to change his mind about the export limit. "This is an ongoing concern with Howard and this issue," said another. This time, one person in the room called his bluff by saying: "Great. Why don't we do it today?" Around 5pm, the group headed to the Oval Office. Trump called tech advisor Elon Musk and agreed to move forward. Musk supported Rubio, Bessent, Greer and Hegseth's case to impose the controls while Lutnick warned it "will start a trade war with China." "Everyone argued back that China is already doing to us what Lutnick warned would happen," a source said. Behind the scenes: With Lutnick the lone holdout, Trump made his decision: "Let's get it done." But once everyone was outside of the Oval Office, Lutnick proposed a new delay tactic. "I'll develop some options and come back," he said. "Everyone was like: 'No, no, the decision's been made. Go fucking execute,'" one source said. "Well, it still hasn't happened." The other side: Commerce Department spokesperson Kristen Eichamer denied that Bessent confronted Lutnick and would not immediately comment on the other allegations. Flashback: On at least three separate occasions — in May, August, and Nov. 5 — Trump approved taking action against suspected diversions of Nvidia chips to China. But Lutnick and Commerce Undersecretary Jeffrey Kessler resisted pressure from Bessent and others to move forward. In May, a highly classified memo warning about Jensen Huang's relationship with Alice Huang, a Megaspeed employee suspected by U.S. intelligence of being a Chinese agent, was shared with the president and other officials. In a subsequent meeting, Bessent, Director of National Intelligence Jay Clayton, Hegseth and White House officials pressed Lutnick and Kessler to act, the source said, "and they were refusing." Catch up quick: The Trump administration last year announced it would loosen export controls on Nvidia H200 chip sales to China — something Nvidia has lobbied hard for. Trump has taken a more lax approach to export controls on China, agreeing to allow sales of Nvidia's H200 chips, which are older but still powerful, in exchange for a 25% tariff. Long before the affair with Alice Huang, Jensen Huang has pushed for tapping into the Chinese market. The CEO at the center of an AI boom Trump is dead set on winning has largely been successful at convincing Trump and Lutnick that selling less powerful chips to China is good for national security because it prevents China from developing its own alternatives and keeps the adversary dependent on the U.S. The bottom line: While Lutnick oversees the department squarely at the center of export control policy, Trump is the ultimate decider.

events.title: Scoop: U.S. asks Russia to propose new security agreement with Europe
events.summary: The U.S. has asked Russia to submit a new proposal for a future security agreement with Europe that includes Russian steps to ease tension with the continent, two sources with knowledge of the matter said. Why it matters: For years, Russia has sought a European security deal that limits NATO expansion and scales back its military presence in Eastern Europe. The U.S. has rejected those demands in the past, but now appears open to them in some form as part of a broader agreement to end the war in Ukraine. But many European governments are deeply suspicious of the administration's approach. State of play: President Trump's envoys Jared Kushner and Steve Witkoff will meet with Russian President Vladimir Putin in Moscow on Thursday to reiterate the request. They also want Putin to allow European representatives to join the next round of Russia-Ukraine peace talks, a U.S. official said. From Moscow, Kushner and Witkoff are expected to travel to Dublin to meet with Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky on Thursday night. Catch up quick: The talks on Tuesday and Wednesday were the first time Ukrainian and Russian officials met with U.S. mediators present since February, when they were suspended due to the war in Iran. In recent weeks, Witkoff and Kushner met with both Putin and Zelensky, creating a bit of momentum. Putin agreed to resume peace talks and release U.S. citizen Stephen Hubbard, who was detained by Russia in 2022 . Together with First Lady Melania Trump and her team, Witkoff and Kushner also brokered a humanitarian ceasefire in the city of Oleshky. Driving the news: The talks in Abu Dhabi started on Tuesday with Witkoff, Kushner and commander of the U.S. European Command Gen. Alexus Grynkewich mediating between the Russians and the Ukrainians. The parties agreed to a prisoner exchange deal that Kushner and Ukrainian negotiator David Arakhamia said could be the biggest since the war began. U.S. and Ukrainian officials said the exact number of prisoners to be released will be decided during meetings with Putin and Zelensky on Thursday. Before and after the talks, the U.S. and Ukrainian negotiating teams briefed a delegation of senior diplomats from Germany, the UK, France, Italy, the EU and NATO. Behind the scenes: The meetings between the Russians and the Ukrainians on Tuesday were tense and at times emotional, with both sides airing grievances after nine months of not talking directly, according to a source in the room. Kushner and Witkoff tried to lower the temperature, telling Russian and Ukrainian negotiators that the goal is to end this round of talks with options for the leaders on both sides. Eventually, after each party made its case, the discussion became more constructive, the source said. "We had pretty tough discussions," Kushner said at a press conference after the talks concluded on Wednesday. "The Russians came with strict directives. It was very hard to soften it, but it ended productively," Arakhamia said. Zoom in: The U.S. proposal to secure a deal on a new Europe-Russia security architecture as part of an agreement to end the war in Ukraine was a key focus of the Abu Dhabi talks. Russian negotiators said Putin launched the invasion of Ukraine because then-President Biden did not reply to his 2021 letter laying out his security concerns, two sources with knowledge of the talks said. According to one of the sources, Kushner and Witkoff told the Russians that the world has changed a lot since 2021. They proposed that Russia draft a new proposal that includes its security concerns and demands, but also lays out what "symmetrical steps" it's willing to take to de-escalate and reassure Europe that it will not attack in the future. Kushner and Witkoff also told the Russians that in order to seriously discuss security issues in Europe, they need to agree to allow European representatives to participate in future peace talks. "We told the Russians, they have their desires and fears, but they have to provide different de-escalation and different proposals as well, if they want Europe to be able to receive those proposals in a good way," Kushner said at the press conference. The other side: So far, Russia has been unwilling to allow Europeans to be part of peace talks with Ukraine. "As for the leadership of a number of European countries, they are essentially engaged in a collective deception of the Ukrainian people and contributing to the mass deaths of civilians," Putin adviser Vladimir Medinsky, who headed the Russian delegation, said at a press conference after the talks. "Therefore, I don't understand what can be discussed with them." Still, Medinsky said that Russia wants to reach a broader security deal with Europe as part of an agreement to end the war. "In Ukraine, an abscess has simply burst. The entire body needs to be treated — a Band-Aid won't do the trick," he said. What to watch: The Trump administration wants to negotiate a new Europe-Russia security architecture and a Russia-Ukraine peace deal simultaneously. But the implementation of a security arrangement would only happen after a deal to end the war is reached, according to a source familiar with the White House's thinking. The president of the European Commission, Ursula von der Leyen, said before the talks in Abu Dhabi that Europe will discuss a new security architecture only after the war in Ukraine ends. But two sources with knowledge said European officials who were in Abu Dhabi this week agreed to engage on both tracks simultaneously, while stressing that final decisions on European security architecture would be made only after the war in Ukraine ends. The U.S. hopes giving European representatives a seat at the peace talks will make their governments more willing to discuss and agree on a broader security agreement before the war ends. "Zelensky won't agree to a deal until he knows what happens next regarding security guarantees and Putin wants to know this, too. This is why the security issue is so important," the source said. The source added that the U.S. made it clear to European countries that it would not agree to a security deal with Russia unless Europe and Ukraine are on board. The U.S. also wouldn't give Russia a veto over Europe's security considerations, the source said. The bottom line: Security will be a key issue at a summit of European leaders in Dublin later this week. European diplomats said the idea of a Russia-Europe security arrangement still faces a lot of resistance and unanswered questions.
