events.title: At COP31, Turkey pushes zero-waste plan to curb climate change
events.summary: As world leaders arrive at United Nations climate talks in the Turkish resort town of Antalya, calling for urgent climate action, co-host Turkey also wants to halve the amount of global waste in the next decade ANTALYA, Turkey -- As world leaders gathered for United Nations climate talks in the Turkish resort town of Antalya on Wednesday, host Turkey urged countries to commit to a zero-waste initiative aimed at reducing emissions and helping get global efforts to curb climate change back on track. Turkish President Recep Tayyip Erdogan touted his country's progress on recycling, saying its rate had risen from about 13% in 2017, when the zero waste movement began, to about 40% by the end of 2025. "Some 90 million tons of waste have been brought back into our economy,” Erdogan told the leaders' summit. “We’ll not stop here and we will continue working and making every effort until we achieve the goal of zero waste." Turkey has outlined 10 priorities for this year’s climate talks, known as COP31 , with a pledge to accelerate electrification and the zero-waste initiatives emerging as major talking points during the opening days of the conference. Turkish first lady Emine Erdogan, who attended Wednesday's talks, has been a driving force behind the zero-waste initiative, which aims to reduce methane emissions, cut food waste and promote a circular economy in which materials are reused and recycled. “Recovered materials can be cheaper when reliable supplies, efficient processing and nearby demand outweigh the costs of collection, sorting and transport,” said Samed Agirbas, president of the nonprofit Zero Waste Foundation and a COP31 high-level climate champion. If implemented, energy experts say the initiatives could slow global warming and reduce the environmental footprint of renewable energy technologies, like solar panels and batteries. But there is still a risk these climate ambitions may fall flat. Conference agreements are often nonbinding and past hosts have been criticized for failing to follow through on promises. Turkey also faces scrutiny over its own climate record. “The Zero Waste target is a good target. It definitely needs to be supported with concrete measures and further action,” said Berk Butan, who heads the waste campaign for Greenpeace Turkey. “But fundamentally, we also need to recognize its shortcomings.” As the second biggest cause of climate change after carbon dioxide, the reduction of methane emissions could significantly slow global warming, according to the U.N. During the first three days of the climate talks, leaders repeatedly called for urgent climate action. The U.N. recently had to readjust a decades-old goal of limiting the rise of global temperatures because the world was blowing past previous thresholds. While Turkey wants countries to commit to reducing methane emissions, it has not signed the Global Methane Pledge. Launched at the 2021 climate talks in Glasgow, the initiative aims to reduce methane emissions by at least 30% from 2020 levels by 2030. Turkey is also the world’s fifth-biggest emitter of methane from solid waste, according to nonprofit emissions tracker Climate TRACE. “Methane emissions from waste disposal are an important challenge,” said Agirbas, with the Zero Waste Foundation. Ke Wang, an energy expert at the WRI's Polsky Center for the Global Energy Transition, said that this is “a vital strategy for cutting greenhouse gas emissions." But recycling food waste is difficult because it decomposes quickly, making separation and processing expensive. Collecting and transporting wet, smelly food waste also requires specialized logistics and infrastructure that many countries lack. “Waste and food loss account for almost 10% of total emissions, so we need to integrate these actions,” Adalberto Maluf, a top official in Brazil’s environment ministry, told The Associated Press. The recycling of already-mined materials is key to reducing the reliance on mining, according to experts, which will only become more important as the world relies more on critical mineral-dependent renewable technologies. The International Energy Agency estimates that scaling up recycling could lower the need for new mining by between 25% and 40% by 2050. Most countries don’t recycle critical materials because it’s cheaper to mine them. events.title: Apple's touchscreen MacBook Pro does not like to be taken apart
events.summary: Apple's first touchscreen MacBook got a mixed reception from iFixit's teardown specialists, who praised its easily replaced lid but found fans and USB-C ports buried beneath the logic board. The MacBook Pro with PROLED XDR display was unveiled at the end of October. It features a tandem OLED screen that stacks two layers of organic light-emitting pixels, eliminating the need for a backlight, and adds touch capability to the MacBook line for the first time. Although the vendor was patted on the back in recent years for improving the repairability of its famously locked-down products, this machine shows Apple still has some way to go. The good? The entire lid comes off relatively easily. Its three-screw hinges closely resemble those on the M6 14-inch MacBook Pro, while streamlined display cable brackets simplify removal. Apple's Repair Assistant tool also handled a full system board swap well. Despite concerns about Touch ID fingerprint authentication, everything went relatively smoothly when iFixit paired a touchscreen from one machine with a logic board from another. On the first boot, Repair Assistant recognized the battery, display, and Touch ID sensor, and touch control needed no separate calibration. The bad? Replacing the panel alone is not possible. When iFixit tried to separate it from the lid, the glass delaminated, cracking the OLED and touch-sensitive layers beneath. That could make for a costlier repair than bargained for. Under the bottom cover, the PROLED has a similar internal layout to the last few models of MacBook Pros, with the fans, board, speakers, and trackpad all in the same places. That means the same annoyances persist. The MagSafe power connector can be removed via two screws and a bracket, yet the USB-C ports can't be extracted the same way because the logic board is in the way. The headphone jack and the fans also require removing the system board first, and the HDMI port and SDXC card reader are soldered to the board itself, as is the storage and memory. Another gripe is that this MacBook's battery pack is hard to remove, though at least it is removable, unlike in many thin-and-light laptops. The tested Pro weighs 1.38 kg or about 3 pounds. For these reasons, the MacBook Pro with PROLED XDR display earns a 5 out of 10 repairability score from iFixit , but this is actually a one point increase over the score it gave the M5 MacBook Pro. The Apple logo has its own lighting. Older MacBooks with illuminated logos borrowed light from the LCD backlight shining through an apple-shaped window in the lid. This model uses a strip of LEDs along one edge of the logo, passing through a diffuser for an even glow. Because it sits behind the display panel, it would be nearly impossible to repair if it failed, especially if the panel is destroyed during removal. Under a microscope, the PROLED XDR display looks very different from earlier MacBooks: the blue subpixel is significantly larger than the green and red ones. The reason, we're told, is that blue OLED materials wear out faster, so a larger subpixel can emit the same amount of light while putting less strain on the material. ®

events.title: China’s Nvidia Honeypot Isn’t Surprising. Jensen Huang Fell for It Anyway
events.summary: There’s a specific mantra drilled into government workers, military officers, and intelligence personnel during counterintelligence briefings: “If she’s a 10 and you’re a 5, she’s a spy!” Or, as the US Army’s Counterintelligence Command posted on Valentine’s Day: “It doesn’t take a mathematician to figure out ‘10 + 5 = honeytrap.’” The very beautiful woman who is suddenly interested in your very ordinary existence probably has ulterior motives , is the message. Jensen Huang surely doesn’t live a typical life—he’s a centibillionaire, the swashbuckling CEO of Nvidia, one of the hottest and most geopolitically consequential companies of the 21st century. Surely he’s aware of the possibility that he’d cross paths with intelligence assets. In fact, it’s hard to think of many companies in the world that would be a higher priority target for foreign intelligence agencies. All of that makes the stock-shaking news this week all the more surprising. How did Huang get embroiled in a spy scandal that mixes infidelity, international espionage, the Trump administration, and the economic behemoth of the multitrillion-dollar AI industry? The story kicked off just before Halloween, with a six-byline story in The New York Times reporting that Huang was the target of a Chinese spy plot. Starting somewhere between 2024 and 2025, Huang allegedly had an affair with Alice Huang (no relation), a one-time executive at a Singapore-based cloud provider known as Megaspeed. US intelligence agencies warned top US officials that they believed she was a Chinese intelligence asset. So far, Nvidia’s board, which has launched its own investigation, says it has “no reason to believe that either national security or Nvidia secrets were compromised,” but that’s far from the only concern. As one would expect, China has denied any nefarious plot centered on Jensen Huang. A Chinese foreign ministry spokesperson on Monday said , “The narrative about so-called Chinese spies is entirely based on groundless speculation—it’s nothing more than slander and smearing.” But according to reporting by The New York Times and the Financial Times , US intelligence officials also claim that Alice Huang, also known as Huang Le, was reporting to China’s Ministry of State Security intelligence agency. On Monday, Megaspeed said on LinkedIn that US authorities found “no evidence of any violations concerning the illicit transfer of chips or any illegal activities." (There’s no indication so far that Alice Huang, a one-time Chinese state journalist, is an employee or “officer” of Chinese intelligence; she’s believed to be an “asset,” an outsider who aids an intelligence agency, sometimes for pay, sometimes not.) China, though, has elevated economic espionage to a core pillar of its economic and military development, stealing the designs for everything from US fighter jets to solar panels and commercial paint recipes . “Honeypots” or “honey traps”—positioning an alluring operative to seduce or develop a relationship with a key target—are one of intelligence’s most infamous and well-established strategies. French officials have warned specifically about Chinese honeypots since at least 2011, when intelligence reports cited a pharmaceutical researcher who was seduced and then blackmailed by a Chinese spy operation. Over the past quarter of a century, as Silicon Valley emerged as a center of political and economic power, it has become a key focus of Chinese intelligence. In one plot, a Chinese national named Fang Fang spent years trying to cozy up to Bay Area politicians , including then US Representative Eric Swalwell. (While intelligence officials at the time reportedly believed Fang to be an operative, law enforcement officials never brought any charges against her). When traveling to China, US business executives have become accustomed to leaving their regular phones and computers at home and using burner devices to prevent the installation of spyware or malware (as I did, when I traveled to China for WIRED in 2019 to report on Huawei ). In 2012, when Leon Panetta was making his first trip to China as defense secretary, he and his team were advised to bathe and shower in the dark in the event his hotel room was bugged. Last year, the threat of honeypots prompted the US government to explicitly ban personnel working in China and Hong Kong from engaging in romantic or sexual relationships with Chinese citizens. More recently, US officials joined with allies to warn about China’s increasingly sophisticated “ LinkedIn espionage ”: using the business-focused social networking site to recruit and build relationships with unwitting executives. Alice Huang’s Megaspeed, for its part, is a major Pacific region player in cloud services focused on the advanced computer chips that are the heart of Nvidia’s business.

events.title: Nvidia handed downgrade on Jensen Huang and AI uncertainty
events.summary: BREAKING: Jensen Huang resigns as Nvidia chief executive Financial services company Baird has given Nvidia a rare downgrade as chief executive Jensen Huang 's alleged affair with a Chinese spy casts doubt over his tenure. Baird analyst Tristan Gerra more than halved the chip maker's target from $500 to $200. Mr Gerra delayed his forecasts for data centres in 2027, saying supply issues are “mostly behind a potential slowdown, alongside potential demand softening”. AI hyperscaler capital expenditure could also slow to 40 per cent growth or slightly less for 2027, he said. Baird downgraded Nvidia stock to neutral, while a separate analysis from Morgan Stanley removed it as a top pick. Nvidia was trying to rally after a difficult period for tech-related stocks. Shares in the chip bellwether rebounded on Wednesday as CoreWeave's better-than-expected quarterly results lifted other chip stocks. Nvidia closed 2.92 per cent higher on Wednesday at $173.73 a share, after ending 5 per cent lower in the previous session. However, shares in Nvidia are on track for a sixth consecutive losing week. The company's stock is down about 8 per cent for the year. Mr Huang admitted to an extramarital affair in a letter to employees on Sunday. “To my colleagues at Nvidia, including those I have worked alongside for decades, and to our board, partners and shareholders around the world: you deserve better from me. Leading Nvidia is the privilege of my life. My responsibility is to serve you and be worthy of your trust. I have fallen short of that responsibility. I am fully committed to Nvidia and will work to earn back your confidence,” he wrote. Nvidia's board of directors has launched an investigation into the affair, adding that Mr Huang fully supports the review and is committed to co-operating with it. “While the board has no reason to believe that either national security or Nvidia secrets were compromised, the board's inquiry will examine all available information … The board has confidence in Jensen and his leadership team and will provide further updates as appropriate,” it said. The explosive allegations come at a time when traders were already scrutinising AI tech stocks after recent earnings reports stoked fears over data centres and the financing behind them. Mr Huang's affair has also rocked Washington, with some legislators calling for investigations . The House foreign affairs committee has requested US President Donald Trump to appear for a closed-door briefing with Mr Huang on his interactions with the alleged spy. US Representatives Brian Mast, John Moolenaar and House permanent select committee on intelligence chairman Rick Crawford requested in a letter to Mr Huang that he brief their committees by November 18. “The issue of PRC infiltration and access to cutting-edge US technology is core to the investigative work of our three committees this Congress. It is vital that Congress determines the extent to which US national security has been placed at risk,” they wrote, referring to the “People's Republic of China”. Analysts are also considering Mr Huang's future as they assess the direction of Nvidia, one of the key nodes in the broader AI nexus. Morgan Stanley analyst Joseph Moore wrote that Mr Huang's leadership is “crucial to the company's direction”. On Tuesday, tech analyst Dan Ives said he estimates there is a 15 per cent chance Mr Huang is removed as chief executive. We believe if Jensen was removed as CEO, Nvidia is worth a lot less (25%-30%) as a company/stock and would change the future direction of the company and create a dramatically different competitive environment around AI GPUs globally especially for China. ~15% chance he removed… — Dan Ives (@DivesTech) November 10, 2026 “We believe if Jensen was removed as CEO, Nvidia is worth a lot less (25 per cent to 30 per cent) as a company/stock and would change the future direction of the company and create a dramatically different competitive environment around AI GPUs globally especially for China ,” Mr Ives wrote. The next test for Nvidia will be on November 16, when it is due to report its third-quarter results.

events.title: Is AIIB's complaint mechanism failing affected communities?
events.summary: The Asian Infrastructure Investment Bank has a grievance redress mechanism for people affected by projects it finances. But those seeking to file a complaint face significant hurdles. Critics say reforms are needed. For members of the Indigenous Sasak community on the Indonesian island of Lombok, the conflict over their land is not over. For them, a tourism and infrastructure project co-financed by the Asian Infrastructure Investment Bank (AIIB) is a source of frustration, as they believe it has led to the expropriation of their land and destruction of their livelihoods. In late September, they officially filed a complaint with the bank . It remains unclear whether this complaint will lead to an independent investigation. The AIIB, which finances major infrastructure projects across Asia, has a mechanism in place to deal with such complaints. Individuals who suffer adverse effects from the bank-financed projects may, under certain conditions, file a complaint with the institution. However, access to this process — known as the Project Complaints Mechanism (PPM) — remains controversial. According to a report by The Diplomat , a magazine that covers political and economic developments in Asia, none of the 45 complaints listed on the AIIB's website had been deemed admissible as of mid-September. The bank acknowledged that "no cases have passed the PPM's eligibility assessment," but it stressed that this is "only part of the story." South Asia projects boost China's presence in India's sphere The AIIB emphasized that not every issue needs to be resolved through this mechanism. The PPM is "only one part of AIIB's grievance redress ecosystem," the Beijing-based bank said in response to a query from DW. Those affected should first attempt to resolve concerns directly with the project team at the local level, it said. According to the bank, "twelve complaints were in fact resolved at the project level — as a direct result of AIIB's follow-up and intervention — and one was resolved through domestic courts." But critics see this as a major weakness. "The mechanism must be easily accessible," said Arntraud Hartmann, a development economist at the Johns Hopkins University School of Advanced International Studies (SAIS Europe) in Bologna, Italy. She argued that people affected by the projects, for instance, are required to document potential violations of environmental and social standards from the start. "How is the affected party supposed to know which standards might have been violated?" she questioned. The AIIB disputes this claim. "In terms of accessibility, we have made the submission form simpler and translated it into 12 languages," it said, adding that complaints can be submitted online, by phone, or by email. Urgewald, a German environmental NGO, cites another problem with AIIB-financed projects. For many of them, information on environmental impacts and resettlements is either missing or published late, it noted. For 2024, the NGO found that 11 of the 16 projects it examined lacked complete environmental and social impact assessments. In many cases, information on the potential number of displaced residents was also missing, it added. "The information published on the bank's website is often insufficient and inconsistent. Particularly important documents, such as environmental impact assessments or resettlement plans, vary widely or are missing entirely," said Nora Sausmikat, a China expert at Urgewald. The lack of information makes it difficult for those affected to respond promptly and report violations early on, she underscored, adding that the situation is particularly difficult for people without formal land titles. Christoph Steinert, a political scientist at the University of Konstanz, said the mere existence of such grievance redressal mechanisms "is not enough." Particularly vulnerable groups often know little about their rights, he said, adding that information should be available in local languages and targeted outreach directed at affected communities. Criticism of the AIIB's procedures is not new. A 2023 report by international aid organizations, including Recourse, Accountability Counsel, and Inclusive Development International, revealed that the AIIB's grievance mechanism had failed to accept a single complaint since its 2019 inception. The study highlighted that 101 of the 219 AIIB-financed projects, or 46% of the total projects at the time, were ineligible for review due to co-financing exemptions. The AIIB typically provides funding without leading projects, a standard practice in development finance. When complaints arise, it directs complainants to the lead lender. As a result, nine of the 45 complaints fell outside its jurisdiction. For Sausmikat, this is part of the problem. "The AIIB, however, decided against revising this requirement and established a mechanism that is very difficult to access," she said.

events.title: Microsoft's Patch Tuesday can't break stuff if it won't install
events.summary: Users are having difficulty installing Microsoft's latest Windows patch. Patch Tuesday contained a truckload of fixes for Microsoft products . However, for some users, installing the update, KB5132061, is proving challenging. In the hours after the patch was released, multiple complaints began to surface that the download and installation were failing, with some customers reporting a 0x800F0993 error code. Others say they received a 0x800F0989 error. Microsoft does not currently list any known issues with the update and is yet to make a statement or provide explanation for the glitch. In addition to the security fixes, this patch resolves a number of known issues from previous updates, including a problem where USB Audio 1.0 devices might fail to start and display an error code 10 in Device Manager. In the absence of a statement from Microsoft, several users have taken to sleuthing. One, with the handle of Forceflow on the ElevenForum site, suggested the bug might be related to Windows Sandbox, and said that after disabling the feature and rebooting, the patch installed successfully. However, others reported problems regardless of Windows Sandbox status, and alternative solutions included using DISM (Deployment Image Servicing and Management) to check the package or downloading the update manually. It's an important patch to install, since it addresses 726 vulnerabilities in Windows alone, and the difficulties affected users face are less than ideal. Microsoft patches have lately displayed more gremlins than usual. Out-of-band releases are depressingly regular after updates break functionality. A September Out-of-band release, for example, was hurriedly pushed out after the September 2026 Windows security update caused trouble for Remote Desktop Services. The October Patch Tuesday for Windows Server sent Exchange Servers toppling , with a registry edit workaround suggested. There was no out-of-band update - Microsoft said the problem had been resolved in the November update. At least this latest release appears to be failing before users get a chance to see what is broken this time. ® Updated to add on November 12: Microsoft has confirmed that there was indeed a problem with installing the update for some users, but the good news is that a fix is rolling out and no action is required on the part of customers (at least those connected to the internet and using Windows Update). The bad news is, alas, there appear to be a few issues with the update around printing and activation. Microsoft giveth, and Microsoft taketh away.

events.title: Vodacom rules out financial services spin-off
events.summary: African telecoms heavyweight Vodacom has ruled out spinning off its financial services unit, its CEO Shameel Joosub told Semafor, rejecting a path taken by rivals seeking to extract more value from fast-growing mobile money businesses. Joosub’s stance potentially sets up a test of two competing strategies across Africa’s telecoms sector after Airtel Money’s London listing gave it a valuation of about $7 billion, or roughly five times annual revenue. Using the same yardstick, Vodacom’s larger financial services business would command roughly $13.5 billion. “We don’t want to sell the crown jewels,” Joosub said. Yesterday the company issued an earnings report that showed revenue from the fintech business rose by almost 20% in the first half of 2026 compared to the same period a year earlier, contributing about a third to the group’s core earnings of $2.6 billion.

events.title: UAE's biggest bank FAB to raise $4.08bn to boost next phase of growth strategy
events.summary: First Abu Dhabi Bank plans to raise Dh15 billion ($4.08 billion) through a rights issue as it prepares for “the next phase” of its growth strategy across the UAE and its global portfolio. The UAE's biggest bank will be offering 1,109,467,456 new shares, with each to be offered at Dh13.52, a 30 per cent discount on its closing share price on Tuesday, a FAB statement on Wednesday said. Mubadala Investment Company, FAB’s largest shareholder, plans to subscribe for its full pro-rata entitlement, which is a reflection of its “continued confidence” in FAB’s strategy and long-term growth prospects, the bank said. “The UAE continues to advance an ambitious long-term economic agenda, underpinned by diversification, investment, innovation and a growing role in global trade and capital flows,” said Sheikh Tahnoon bin Zayed, chairman of FAB. “FAB is at the centre of this growth, enabling strategic investment across the UAE and internationally. The proposed rights issue will further strengthen FAB’s ability to support the UAE’s ambitions and capture the opportunities ahead.” The rights issue is also meant to capture “significant opportunities” in the UAE and across FAB's international network, group chief executive Hana Al Rostamani said. Aside from the Gulf, FAB also maintains a presence in the Middle East, Africa, Asia, Europe and the Americas. “The strength of our home market, combined with the reach and connectivity of our international network, gives us a strong platform for growth,” Ms Al Rostamani said. Capital markets in the UAE continue to sustain their momentum despite the fallout from the war in Iran, prompting companies to tap into equity markets for additional funds through secondary shares sales and rights issues. Other notable companies to have done so include Adnoc, Abu Dhabi Commercial Bank, artificial intelligence company G42 and Mamoura Diversified Global Holding, an investor in Dubai telecom firm du. “We will deploy capital with discipline and focus, pursuing opportunities that deepen our competitive position, expand the scale and reach of our franchise, and deliver superior, sustainable returns for our shareholders,” Ms Al Rostamani said. Last month, FAB reported a 6 per cent annual jump in third-quarter profit , as net interest income, and fee and commission income grew on the back of strong business activity. Net profit attributable to shareholders for three months to the end of September climbed to Dh5.73 billion. Nine-month profit grew 3 per cent to Dh16.4 billion.

events.title: NASA asks Earthlings to wave as Voyager 1 reaches a light-day away
events.summary: Voyager 1 will become the first human-made object to reach one light-day from Earth next week, and NASA wants us to mark the occasion by flashing our lights at the sky. The spacecraft, which suffered a communications hiccup last month, is traveling at approximately 38,000 mph (61,000 kph) and will mark the 50th anniversary of its launch next year. Before then, it has another distance record to set. "Light-day" is a bit snappier than 16,094,799,096 miles (25,902,068,356 kilometers). NASA puts the crossing at 05:16:07 EST (10:16:07 UTC) on Wednesday, November 18. For "Shine Bright for Voyager's Light-Day," participants are invited to flash the mission's three-letter designation – VGR – in Morse code after sunset on November 17, using a flashlight or NASA's website. According to the space agency, this will create "a symbolic wave of golden light encircling the planet after sunset." It is also a nice way to mark the achievement – Voyager 1 is the most distant human-made object from Earth, and its extraordinary longevity remains a testament to the skill of engineers past and present. Not that Voyager 1 will be able to detect any flashlights on Earth. Its cameras were turned off decades ago, after the famous Pale Blue Dot image was captured. NASA has invited the public to join in a spacecraft photo opportunity before. On July 19, 2013, Cassini photographed Earth and the Moon from its orbit around Saturn for "The Day the Earth Smiled," while people back home were encouraged to look up and "just smile at the sheer joy of being alive on a Pale Blue Dot." Voyager 2, the spacecraft's sibling, is not expected to reach the same milestone for another nine years. It took a different path through the solar system to swing past Uranus and Neptune. It will, however, be uncertain as to whether Voyager 2 will still be able to communicate by then – even with recent efforts to eke out the probe's dwindling power supply, margins are razor thin. ®

But analysts say byzantine regulations and intra-continental barriers have hampered development of the continent’s capital markets. events.title: MSF urges global health officials to widen Ebola vaccine access
events.summary: Global health officials have been urged to widen the use of an existing Ebola vaccine in DR Congo following reports it may provide protection against a strain it was not designed to target. The Bundibugyo strain — for which there is currently no vaccine — has killed more than 5,300 people in the country’s largest-ever outbreak. Medical charity Doctors Without Borders said restrictions on using Ervebo, developed by Merck for use against a prior Ebola strain, should be lifted so more people at risk, including young children, can be vaccinated. The charity said DR Congo requested 500,000 doses of Ervebo, but only 70,000 were released. The World Health Organization recommends limiting its use against Bundibugyo to research studies because its effects remain unproven. Doctors Without Borders said early observations of fewer infections and deaths among previously vaccinated people justified wider use. A larger release from the global stockpile requires backing from the WHO’s vaccine advisers, who meet next week. — Ruben Nyanguila

events.title: Africa calls on COP31 to boost adaptation finance
events.summary: African countries want the COP31 climate talks, now underway in Türkiye, to set out how the world will deliver on last year’s pledge to triple adaptation finance designed to help cope with the growing impact of extreme weather events. A large share of the money has previously come from aid budgets, which have fallen to their lowest level since 2014 , and most wealthier countries have pledged little-to-no new climate finance from this year . The African Group of Negotiators says addressing this issue is vital to a successful outcome in Antalya as support for the continent’s vulnerabilities has been “dwindling,” according to its chairperson. But even a tripling in financing will not close the gap: In 2024, the amount available for developing economies reached around $30 billion — that pales against the $305 billion the UN estimates they need annually to 2035. Plans have been announced at COP31 to scale up successful adaptation projects and attract larger investments. But these cannot be “entirely dependent on voluntary contributions,” Kenya’s climate envoy told Semafor. — Chloé Farand

events.title: Dubai's public parking fines overtake fees
events.summary: It’s been inching in that direction for years, and now it’s official: Dubai’s public parking monopoly earns more from fines than public parking fees. Parkin reported record third-quarter revenue , up 21% to 415 million dirhams ($113 million), driven by enforcement, expanding business with private developers, and longer-term permits. The latter may have skewed the results: Sales of discounted “seasonal cards” were up 37%, the company said, and those permits aren’t counted in public parking utilization and revenue, even though their holders occupy spaces. Parkin also expanded its portfolio to 272,500 spaces, nearly tripling the number managed for private developers over the past year. Still, for anyone parking in Dubai, it feels like enforcement is stricter, aided by the deployment of advanced cameras and AI-powered monitoring. — Mohammed Sergie

events.title: US futures climb and Nvidia shares stabilize in a brutal week for the chipmaker
events.summary: U.S. futures are rising as Nvidia’s shares look to rebound and Brent crude remains below $100 a barrel U.S. futures are rising with crude still below $100 a barrel as shares of Nvidia stabilize in a brutal week for the chipmaker. Futures for the S & P 500 gained 0.9% on Wednesday, while those for the Dow Jones Industrial Average edged up 0.2%. Nasdaq futures climbed 1.9%. Nvidia was the single heaviest weight on the S & P 500 on Tuesday, but shares are up 3.7% in early trading Wednesday. They are still down almost 10% this week. The company that is central to the artificial intelligence boom has been under pressure since the company’s board announced an investigation into its CEO, Jensen Huang, following revelations of his affair with a purported Chinese spy. President Donald Trump said the FBI is investigating the affair , which Huang has acknowledged and apologized for. Among other technology stocks, CoreWeave jumped more than 15% before the market opened after posting better-than-expected third-quarter revenue and a boost in its 2026 revenue outlook. The U.S. bond market is closed Wednesday for Veterans Day, but the stock markets remain open. The price of Brent crude, the international standard, rose 1.9% to $93.22 a barrel. U.S. benchmark crude oil gained 1.2% to $87.05 per barrel. Brent remains well below $100 a barrel, with Trump saying late Monday that the war in Iran, which sent oil prices much higher, “militarily is effectively over.” Baby buried alive for 24 hours released from the hospital; father charged House tables Hegseth impeachment, effectively killing it in current Congress Wisconsin state trooper detained by ICE Oil prices are still about $30 higher per barrel than at this time last year. New data on consumer inflation Tuesday upended markets and sent the 10-year Treasury yield charging above 5% again. On Friday, the U.S. releases its producer price index for October, which captures inflation before it reaches consumers. The September report showed the biggest increase since December 2022 and that data showed that rising fuel prices, particularly for diesel fuel, continue to push shipping and warehousing prices higher. In Europe, Germany’s DAX rose 0.7% to 26,531.66 after inflation fell to 2.8% in October from a year earlier, according to the federal statistics office on Wednesday. The CAC 40 in Paris climbed 0.3% to 8,302.23. Britain’s FTSE 100 added 0.4% to 10,797.68. Asian markets were mostly higher. China’s biggest online shopping festival, Singles Day, began Wednesday. events.title: Spain’s workers hold a general strike over housing costs ahead of a national election
events.summary: Millions of Spanish workers have shut down businesses and disrupted transport in a massive protest over housing costs BARCELONA, Spain -- Millions of Spanish workers shut down businesses and snarled transport in a massive protest Wednesday over housing costs that the government hopes to leverage ahead of a national election later this month. The walkout — under the slogan “Salaries. Housing. Prices.” — was the first general strike in Spain in 14 years. In Barcelona, the country’s second-largest city, most storefronts on a main shopping boulevard were boarded up in anticipation of violence during protests later in the day. Some retail chains were open to business while public transport was at a standstill or facing long delays. The subway opened only for the rush hour. Carlos Ferrer, a 45-year-old customer service worker who was trying to get back home to Alicante by train from Barcelona, said sometimes only “radical measures, such as a general strike” can force a change of course. “Authorities need to feel pressure from the citizens so they can do something," he said. Rain pelted the capital, Madrid, as strikers marched down main streets and blocked off Gran Vía, the city’s main thoroughfare, where big brand stores remained open although some were also boarded up. Unions have called for workers to march through the city center later Wednesday, and protests are also planned in more than 50 cities and towns. Manuel Gómez, a 19-year-old student in Madrid, welcomed the protests, which he said marked a change for the country. “In Spain, we have a serious problem, which is that when we don’t like something, we never go out to protest,” he said. About 5% of flights for Wednesday were canceled at airports across the country, according to the country’s airport operator, AENA. “The strike has exceeded the labor unions’ expectations,” said Unai Sordo, secretary general of CCOO, one of the two unions calling the strike. “It has been a success in terms of turnout.” Earlier, the two unions — CCOO and UGT — reported significant work stoppages in strategic sectors. They said the stoppages amounted to 90% in the automotive and port sectors, 85% in the meat industry, 82% in waste collection, and 75% in the energy sector. Minor incidents were reported in the first hours of the strike. Tires were set on fire at roadblocks in Barcelona, and scuffles with police were reported near the main wholesale market on Madrid’s outskirts. Police also used pepper spray against the strikers in some places. Many schools and universities reportedly closed or are working at minimal capacity. In Madrid, this added to an ongoing strike started by teachers nearly a month ago demanding better working conditions. In southwestern Spain, classes were suspended due to bad weather. “It’s extremely important to remind people that we, the workers — who are also renters or who also pay mortgages — are the ones with the power to halt production and bring the economy to a standstill,” Sandra Mora, spokesperson for the Tenants Union, told national radio, RNE. The strike brought workers, activists, politicians and ordinary Spaniards around the same interests — accessible housing. The average rent in Spain has almost doubled in the last 10 years, eating into household budgets and angering voters. The subsequent death of Maricarmen , as the woman became known, caused even more indignation and solidified her as a symbol of Spaniards who feel they pay too much in rent and can’t even dream of homeownership. Housing activists leveraged the uproar over Maricarmen's eviction to call for the general strike, and soon won the backing of the UGT and CCOO unions. The housing activists are seeking the elimination of pricey tourist apartments, a crackdown on real estate speculation and the automatic renewals of leases as a way to protect renters. Unions demand more government intervention in the housing market and a new minimum wage agreement through talks with the business owners' association. The nationwide protests over Maricarmen's eviction propelled Spain’s government to push through emergency measures to limit evictions and help tenants, but right-wing parties in the Parliament refused to ratify them , claiming they would provoke a flight of properties from the rental market. Spanish Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez then doubled down and called an early election , hoping to earn four more years in power for his left-wing coalition. The vote is set for Nov. 29. Then, in late October came a brutal high-speed train collision — Spain's second deadly rail disaster of the year — that killed 69 people.

events.title: Duolingo, Strava, and Ticketmaster Are All Caught Up in EU’s New Digital Fairness Rules
events.summary: The European Commission announced a sweeping set of updates to consumer law on Wednesday to protect European Union citizens from “harmful digital practices”—whether while online shopping, browsing social media , or doing their Duolingo lesson. Within the package, the Commission unveiled its Digital Fairness Act to address harmful practices online. Proposed rules include banning dark patterns —practices that manipulate consumers into making decisions they would not otherwise make, such as falsely claiming a product is running low. They will also ensure ticket retailers, like Ticketmaster, make tiered pricing transparent; force influencers to disclose when they are being paid to promote a product; outrule personalized advertising and pricing targeting minors or taking advantage of sensitive data; make digital subscriptions easier to cancel; and give consumers a right to interact with human customer service. The package “represents the most significant reform of EU consumer protection rules in more than 20 years” according to Michael McGrath, the EC Consumer Protection Commissioner, noting that existing consumer rules were developed before ecommerce, the attention economy, and use of personal data for marketing took off. “The digital fairness act will make sure the digital economy works for consumers and not against them,” he said at a press conference. The bill will also enable all consumers to turn off addictive design features on digital services, such as autoplay of videos and streaks—including on apps like Strava and Duolingo. Some of these patterns the EU has already restricted for children through its Kids Act , which in addition to banning under-13s from accessing social media and chatbots, targets addictive designs in those services. Some European rights groups have called for those protections to be extended to all consumers and, teasing the Digital Fairness Act in September’s State of the Union address, President Ursula von der Leyen said: “But it is not only minors who are at risk. Addictive design, for example, is harming everyone. That is why we need a wider framework.” Some of the risks are also already regulated by the EU Digital Services Act. On Friday, the European Commission said ByteDance’s TikTok had breached those rules with the “rabbit hole effect” of its “For You” feed algorithm which personalizes content recommended to users. The tech regulator had previously found TikTok’s “addictive design” broke the rules by including features such as infinite scroll, autoplay, and push notifications, in addition to the algorithm. In July, it found Meta to be in breach of the act due to similar features on Instagram and Facebook . If confirmed, both companies may now face fines of up to 6 percent of worldwide annual turnover. The new regulation is designed to fill the gaps between this, the Digital Markets Act, and August’s AI Act , says executive vice president Henna Virkkunen, “not duplicate this.” The package should simplify consumer protection rules across the bloc’s 27 members and be a “strong safety net in the digital world,” she adds. The Commission aims to accelerate cross-border cooperation through strengthened enforcement rules. These would also give the regulator direct powers to investigate large-scale impact and fine firms up to 6 percent of their worldwide annual turnover. Non-EU companies would be required to appoint a local legal representative to cooperate with authorities. Correction: 11/12/2026, 10:15 GMT. WIRED updated this article to correct that Ticketmaster does not use dynamic pricing in the EU. events.title: 2013 breach at Russian cybercrime forum resurfaces with millions of victims' credentials
events.summary: A 2013 breach of Russian-language cybercrime forum YouHack exposed its members' login details – and millions of credentials they had posted about other victims, according to newly cataloged data. Have I Been Pwned (HIBP) added the breach on Wednesday, recording 7.2 million unique email addresses. Around 107,000 belonged to forum members, whose exposed data included usernames, IP addresses, and mostly unsalted MD5 password hashes. Unsalted MD5 is a poor choice for protecting passwords. It's fast to compute, allowing attackers to test guesses at speed, and identical passwords produce identical hashes. Hardly good hygiene for a hacking forum. You might expect members of a cybercrime forum to know better than to reuse passwords or register with an email address tied to their real identity. Expectations and reality are not always on speaking terms, as AlphaBay founder Alexandre Cazes demonstrated. YouHack, a longtime cybercrime forum, moved to a different domain after the 2013 breach and remains active, giving cybercrims a place to trade stolen credentials and financial data. The data collated from that digital burglary was eventually bundled into 2024's so-called Mother of all Breaches – a 12TB, 26 billion-record mega-dump of files taken from myriad data security lapses. Millions more HIBP separately published its findings concerning another Russian data breach today. It said the 2023 breach of Russian bank Sberbank's loyalty program (SberSpasibo) contained records belonging to 48 million users. The dataset included 3.3 million unique email addresses, alongside phone numbers and dates of birth. Bank card numbers were stored as unsalted SHA-1 hashes, which could let attackers test possible numbers against the leaked hashes for a match. Reporting on the SberSpasibo breach at the time suggested the records were dated between April 2017 and February 2022, and the attack was claimed by the pro-Ukraine hacktivist outfit NLB. NLB also claimed responsibility for an attack on Sberbank's internal systems at the same time, and later took partial credit for an attack on Alfa-Bank , Russia's largest private bank. ®

events.title: The Download: preserving minds and weighing open AI risks
events.summary: This is today’s edition of The Download , our weekday newsletter that provides a daily dose of what’s going on in the world of technology. Six wild ideas for perpetuating your mind As we age, we forget most of what we’ve experienced, yet there’s still undeniable continuity: At 30, or 50, or 70, you will still be you.  To preserve that elusive continuity of self, some far-thinking technologists are exploring ways to keep the brain going, even beyond death. Their ideas range from freezing brains in liquid nitrogen to augmenting living ones and uploading our memories to the cloud. Here are six possible paths for keeping your mind going, and how feasible they might be . —Antonio Regalado This story is from the Impossible edition of our print magazine. Subscribe now to get every issue as soon as it lands. MIT Technology Review Narrated: Open models have real benefits. Do they outweigh the risks? Anthropic recently released a report arguing that a powerful new model released by the Chinese company Z.ai, poses a major cyberattack risk. Its core concern was that it is freely available for anyone to download and modify. The warning was the latest flashpoint in the debate over open frontier AI models. Critics warn that bad actors can misuse them, while supporters argue they prevent a handful of companies from controlling the technology. The debate, however, is more complicated than it seems . This is our latest story to become an MIT Technology Review Narrated podcast, which we publish each week on Spotify and Apple Podcasts . Just navigate to MIT Technology Review Narrated on either platform, and follow us to get all our new content as it’s released. events.title: A Newborn Died in a Faith-Healing Sect. The State — and One Ex-Believer — Stepped in to Save Her Twin.
events.summary: Evelyn at the grave of her twin, Ginnifer The deputy medical examiner thought the family was being evasive. Eric Tonsfeldt had been dispatched to the pistachio-green house in Oregon City on the night of March 5, 2017. Inside he found Sarah Mitchell in bed, her dead newborn in her arms. Mitchell is a member of the Followers of Christ, a sect known for refusing medical treatment. She had received no prenatal care. Three women without medical training guided her delivery that afternoon. Tonsfeldt listened as the family insisted that the baby, whom they had named Ginnifer, had seemed healthy for most of the afternoon, then suddenly stopped breathing. They couldn’t explain why the baby appeared so underweight. Their answers to many of Tonsfeldt’s questions were vague. Nobody would make eye contact with him. Later, investigators would discover that 13 minutes after Ginnifer’s birth, Followers began exchanging a series of worried texts. “Not good breathing,” one wrote in a group chat. Another requested prayers: “She’s really bad.” (One person in the chat would later advise deleting the messages.) No one had called 911 as the gaps between each breath increased. When asked why not, Ginnifer’s father later said, “Because it’s in God’s hands.” He anointed his daughter with olive oil and wept as he prayed that she would be OK. Ginnifer died in his arms at 7 p.m., four hours after she was born. Tonsfeldt gently collected the newborn and examined her in another room. She weighed 3½ pounds, roughly half that of an average full-term infant. He found no signs of injury or trauma. The living room in the house where Ginnifer was born and died. Dozens of Followers of Christ members filled the home that day, but none called 911. Clackamas County District Attorney’s Office Followers anoint the ailing with olive oil. Clackamas County District Attorney’s Office The medical examiner still felt that something was awry. To play for time, he asked if someone would make him a cup of coffee and headed to the kitchen. As Tonsfeldt waited, one of the baby’s grandfathers approached him and blurted out an unexpected question: Would it make a difference if Ginnifer had a twin? There was another baby, a girl named Evelyn. She was alive. In the dim light of a bathroom, Tonsfeldt found women huddled over a tiny newborn, who was barely making a sound. They were feeding her from an eyedropper. He told the family to get her to a hospital. After Evelyn’s grandfather made it clear they weren’t going anywhere, Tonsfeldt summoned the police, who delivered an ultimatum: Take Evelyn to the hospital or they’d do it themselves. Evelyn, at 14 days old, was still so small she could fit into dolls’ clothes. Courtesy of the Phillips family Evelyn’s family relented. A patrol car followed to make sure they got there. She was admitted to a neonatal intensive care unit in Portland with respiratory distress syndrome. With the help of a breathing machine and a feeding tube, Evelyn began to stabilize. An autopsy would later conclude the same condition, common in premature babies, had caused her sister’s death. The Mitchells were charged with murder by neglect, as well as criminal mistreatment for failing to get Evelyn medical care. That left authorities with another challenge: Who would care for Evelyn? Her family assumed any custody arrangement would be temporary and suggested Marshall and Jennifer Phillips, a couple born and raised in the Followers. But Marshall was no ordinary Follower. Once, when his young son became gravely ill, he brought him to a hospital. In the eyes of the state, that made Marshall and his wife suitable candidates to look after Evelyn. Evelyn’s family didn’t know then that Marshall’s choice to save his son had set him on a yearslong journey, one that would eventually lead him away from the only life he’d ever known. And that he would take Evelyn with him. Jennifer and Marshall Phillips For more than a century, states have wrestled with how to address the deaths of children whose parents refuse them medical care for religious reasons. As early as 1901, a father in New York who believed in the “power of God to heal the sick through prayer” was prosecuted for failing to call a doctor for his young daughter who died from pneumonia. Since then, courts have repeatedly held — in cases where Christian Scientists refused treatment or Jehovah’s Witnesses declined blood transfusions — that adults are free to reject medical care for themselves. Whether they can be compelled to provide medical care for their children is another matter, one that’s been left to states to decide. Courts have generally deferred to legislatures on this question. Video: This Secretive Religious Sect Doesn’t Believe in Medical Care Marshall Phillips was raised in the Followers of Christ, which forbids medical care. When his son fell gravely ill, he took him to the hospital. That choice set him on a yearslong journey, one that would eventually lead him away from the only life he’d ever known. Teresa Mahoney, Noelle Crombie, Beth Nakamura and Samantha Swindler/The Oregonian For decades, Oregon’s law gave latitude to faith healing and authorities did little to intervene. Between 1989 and 1999, 18 children of the Oregon City-based Followers died. (The sect numbered between 1,500 and 2,000 at its peak.) Most or all of those deaths were preventable, according to the state medical examiner at the time, who estimated that the child death rate in the sect was 26 times that of the general population. The revelation of those deaths, in The Oregonian and other news outlets, prompted state lawmakers to act. In 1999, they removed spiritual treatment as a defense for second-degree manslaughter and criminal mistreatment. In 2008, prosecutors filed their first case against Followers parents after a 15-month-old died from untreated bronchial pneumonia and a blood infection. A jury convicted the girl’s father of a single count of criminal mistreatment, a misdemeanor, and acquitted her mother. Two more children in the sect died without medical attention during this period, prompting the Legislature in 2011 to do away with the spiritual defense for any crime. Among those supporting the change: the Christian Science church, which by then had softened its stance amid a steep decline in membership. In a letter to lawmakers that year, a church official wrote: “Spiritual care should never be practiced at the expense of a child’s life.” Evelyn in her room Changes in Oregon law — and prosecutors’ willingness to pursue parents who watched their children die — spurred a slow but perceptible shift: Deaths of children in the Followers have become an anomaly. Ginnifer Mitchell’s death in 2017 came amid that yearslong decline. Since then, one child has died due to lack of medical care. events.title: CoreWeave reports positive Q3 results, but faces tough road ahead
events.summary: One solid quarter does not make a rebound. CoreWeave, the battered AI computing provider, surprised Wall Street yesterday by posting better-than-expected earnings and raising its annual forecast. But shares are still down nearly 40% so far this year, and the company is still not throwing enough cash off its business to cover its roughly $41 billion of net debt. “Narratives shifted, sentiment swung, and people scrutinized the build-out of AI,” CoreWeave CEO Michael Intrator said in a blog post that pledged to “calibrate investment” to demand, regulatory winds, and, probably most importantly, the availability of money. Intrator said the company would no longer be turning to unsecured borrowing to fund its business. — Ellen DiMauro

events.title: Anthropic IPO could lead to 'large correction' in markets, Fed official says
events.summary: Just as the proverbial ink was drying on Anthropic’s updated prospectus for the frontier lab’s expected $1.4 trillion IPO, a Federal Reserve official warned of a “large correction” in stock prices if AI returns fall short of expectations. Citing $800 billion in AI-related debt, plus off-balance-sheet liabilities and the circular financing powering the AI trade, Fed Governor Michelle Bowman said any “shock would likely slow the AI buildout” and “soften” the economy. Nowhere are expectations loftier than at Anthropic, the first frontier lab to go public. Its valuation has already come in below initial expectations. It’ll still be one of the biggest listings of all time, pegged at $90.4 billion, but any wobbles around the IPO — set to price on Nov. 18 and start trading the next day — “might mean a selloff of the AI theme around the IPO,” said Tore Opsahl, head of quantitative solutions advisory group at Nomura. — Ellen DiMauro

events.title: Prophecy, Scorn and a Rejection of This World: The Forbidding Vision of a Faith-Healing Preacher
events.summary: Walter White baptizes a Followers of Christ member in 1951. He led an Oregon City, Oregon, offshoot of the sect. Courtesy of the Phillips family It was a stark and forbidding vision for those who followed the righteous path. Scorn, the preacher told his congregation, was a person’s lot if they led an “honest, clean, pure, godly life.” The world hated “people that live like that,” he said. “They want you to be just as ungodly and filthy as they are,” he said in a rare audio recording, obtained by The Oregonian/OregonLive, of a 1958 sermon. The preacher was Walter White, who led an Oregon City offshoot of the Followers of Christ, an Idaho sect that spurns medical treatment as a show of faith. White was a grocer, originally from Picabo, Idaho, whose congregants came to view as a prophet. He rambled at times during his sermon but always returned to simple and severe messages about choosing righteousness rather than the ways of the world. A trim figure in wire-rim glasses and dark combed-back hair, he spoke in a voice that evoked the stentorian tones of an old newsreel announcer. In the scratchy recording, people cough and babies cry as he preaches. White was uneasy about being taped, according to a note by the congregant who made the recording. White didn’t want his message to fall into what he thought were undesirable hands. He viewed disbelievers with disgust. They put their trust in human experts, such as doctors, rather than in God. People like that, he told the faithful, “want to be somebody.” They want “the wisdom of the world and admiration.” Today, nearly 60 years after White’s death, his pronouncements continue to influence the faithful. For many Followers, White remained “the highest authority,” said Mark Shaw, who left the sect in 2019 and keeps in touch with some Followers. Members invoked his teachings to settle disagreements. “It was used as the trump card,” he said. “It was the discussion-ender.” White’s grave in the Followers’ cemetery outside of Oregon City Beth Nakamura/The Oregonian To understand the modern-day Oregon City congregation, it’s essential to examine White’s role. No pastor ever succeeded him, leaving the sect all the more reliant on his teachings. The Oregonian/OregonLive and ProPublica have published a series of articles in recent months about the Followers of Christ in Oregon and Idaho , focusing on the long history of parents in Followers congregations declining to seek medical care for their critically ill children and the sometimes fatal consequences . Little has been publicly known about White, likely due to the Followers’ culture of isolation and secrecy. The Oregonian/OregonLive was able to piece together details through documents we obtained, including biographical sketches, a transcript and the recording of the sermon, along with written accounts of dreams White purported to have and records of baptisms he performed. Among the documents was a list of his prophecies and even a sex guide he disseminated. White was born into the Followers, whose members migrated to Idaho from the Midwest around the turn of the 20th century. Men in White’s family preached, and he joined them in his 20s, the story goes, after he dreamed that worms would devour him if he didn’t. In the early 1930s, White joined two church elders on a journey from Idaho to Oregon City to minister to a dying man. After talking with them, the man readily discarded his medications and was relieved to see White, an avid smoker, roll a cigarette because the man didn’t want to kick the habit. For the next five years, White traveled between Idaho and Oregon to preach and by 1938, he had moved to Oregon to lead a fledgling congregation. Followers at the time were led by a constellation of preachers and elders, all men. Notes from one of their meetings in 1937 revealed that Followers believed White possessed the “gift of prophecy.” It also recorded the debates that simmered among them — whether women should be allowed to cut their hair, for instance. They talked about the value of dictionaries, which some classified as “worldly” items to be avoided, and determined that women assisting with home births should not “look under the cover” as women labored. One account written years later by a Follower suggested that White split with a prominent Idaho preacher after revelations that the man had sexual contact with a 15-year-old girl. Some of those values still shape the Followers today. Congregants tend to stay out of what they view as the worldly affairs of politics and civic life, and they generally don’t pursue education beyond high school or vocational training. The Followers remain patriarchal; men are expected to lead their households. White, second from left in the back (in suspenders), with Followers leaders in Oregon City in 1937. By 1938, he had moved to Oregon to lead a fledgling congregation. Courtesy of the Phillips family White was known among Followers as “brother Walter.” An undated black-and-white photograph shows him baptizing a child in what appears to be a baptismal pool, his arm raised in prayer. In another image dated 1951, he wears a suit jacket and tie, a mug in one hand and a cigarette in the other. As much a ruler as a spiritual leader, White enjoyed near-absolute authority. Followers believed he possessed such divine power that he knew their thoughts and secrets. They turned to him for approval on matters both consequential and mundane, from marital advice to appliance purchases. (White even weighed in on where to shop: He owned a local market and made it clear he expected to see Followers there.) White’s earthly teachings extended to a perhaps unexpected realm: Couples on the cusp of marriage received a sex guide, which continued to be distributed as recently as 2018. Complete with explicit detail and anatomical diagrams, the 15-page manual includes chapters titled “the ideal love act” and “the control of climax.” And, in a seeming exception to the prohibition on medical treatment, it goes so far as to recommend that women who feel inhibited should consider seeing a doctor “who has given the sex problems sincere study.” White preached the Oregon City sect’s singularity: His flock was spiritually superior to other Follower congregations, he contended, including ones in Idaho and Grants Pass, Oregon. By the 1950s, he had cut off ties to those groups. In 1965, White told his congregation of his prophecy that the end times were near. He recounted a dream, which he said was set against the backdrop of the Kennedy Space Center in Florida, that involved walking with Jesus Christ, according to one account. He dreamed they climbed a launchpad, and White noted he was impressed with Christ’s physical agility. Days before White shared his vision, NASA launched Gemini 3, the first U.S. mission to send multiple astronauts into space. events.title: From blood group ID to cycle racks: I asked for little ways to fix broken Britain and the public’s ideas give me hope | Martin Lewis
events.summary: There are thousands of small tips to make our country better. People know what is wrong, and it’s clear they have solutions Have you ever come across an annoying little problem and thought, “why don’t they just fix that?” If so, I want to hear from you. I’m looking for your ideas for practical, low-cost, non-controversial ways to improve the UK – whether that’s health, schools, transport, business, housing, policing, justice, tech, shopping, money – or owt else entirely. The spark for this happened just over a year ago, when I spoke at Politico’s fringe event at Labour’s conference. The key discussion was about Keir Starmer’s unpopularity. I was asked what I’d have advised the government when it took power, so I said : “Come up with 100 small things that piss people off and that you can fix, and they can see that you have fixed them.” Then I reeled off a list of small fixes for my subject area: the counterproductive way council tax debt is escalated; renaming “tax-free childcare”; and so on. Tell people their blood group at their first adult blood test. Knowing you’ve a common or rare type may make you more inclined to donate. It’s a brilliantly simple nudge that could widen the donor pool and save lives. A mandatory “AI-edited” label on property photos on estate agency sites. A “no wrong door” rule for councils and public bodies: report a problem anywhere, and they must pass it to the right place, rather than bouncing you from department to department, or from council to contractor to agency. Cycle racks on the back of buses. Cinema seating plans that clearly show aisles and walkways for disability access. A voluntary wheelie-bin sharing scheme, so neighbours with spare capacity can help stop bins overflowing. Martin Lewis is the founder of MoneySavingExpert.com and the Money and Mental Health Policy Institute charity. He has just set up the Small Ideas Initiative Continue reading...

events.title: What are cold weather payments and who can get them?
events.summary: As temperatures drop, heating costs rise, but there is some help for many households through cold weather payments. This financial help is triggered across hundreds of postcodes in England, Wales and Northern Ireland when there is a prolonged period of below-zero temperatures. In Scotland, those on low incomes and benefits may receive a separate winter heating payment, which does not depend on how cold it gets. The cold weather payment is a government benefit top-up to help with fuel bills , external . The average temperature in a local area must be recorded as, or forecast to be, 0C or below for seven days in a row. The temperature is recorded by the relevant weather station for your postcode. England and Wales: Enter your postcode here to check eligibility , external Northern Ireland: Enter your postcode here to check eligibility , external More than 1.4 million cold weather payments were made during winter 2025-26. Check the UK weather warnings in place Who can get cold weather payments and how much are they worth? To qualify, you must live in England, Wales or Northern Ireland. Payments are not age-related but you must already be receiving certain benefits, including: income-based job seekers' allowance income-related employment and support allowance universal credit - although there are certain exceptions Each cold weather payment is for a seven-day period and is worth £25. More than one payment will be made during the course of the winter if there are enough periods of cold weather. The scheme runs between 1 November and 31 March each year. Hospital stays can affect your entitlement to the payment so you should tell the Pension Service , external or Jobcentre Plus , external if you become an inpatient. You should also update the relevant service if you have a baby, or if a child under five comes to live with you. In Scotland, the winter heating payment is worth £62 , external , and is paid automatically between December and February. Heating tips to keep your home warm when budgets are squeezed Published 2 January How to keep babies warm in cold weather and other winter tips Published 2 January How to drive in snow and icy weather Published 2 January How do cold weather health alerts work? Published 22 June How do I get cold weather payments and how long does it take? You do not have to do anything in order to receive cold weather payments. The money should be paid automatically into the same bank or building society account as your benefits, within two weeks of the qualifying period of cold weather. If you do not receive a payment, you can contact the Pension Service , external or Jobcentre Plus , external . Cold weather payments do not affect other benefits. They are separate to the winter fuel payment , which is worth £100 or £300 depending on your individual circumstances. About nine million pensioners get the Winter Fuel Payment, after a government u-turn over changes to the eligibility rules. events.title: Tracking how Jensen Huang changed his stance on China
events.summary: Jensen Huang’s public rhetoric on China became more admiring, and his stance on export controls more critical, after the US restricted Nvidia’s made-for-China chip in 2025 — and as he had an affair with a suspected Chinese spy. A Semafor analysis of 42 podcast interviews with Huang since early 2022 shows how Huang’s argument around global chip policy evolved in a series of long-form, unscripted, and often friendly settings: Huang talked up China’s strengths and cast Beijing as a formidable competitor as he argued more forcefully for a careful balance between protecting US interests and making US technology the backbone of global AI development. Whether the Nvidia CEO’s position was shaped by his affair with an executive at a Singapore-based data center firm with alleged ties to Beijing is now a matter for the company’s board, which hired Wall Street law firm Wachtell Lipton to investigate, and for Congress, who plan hearings on the matter. But his stance on China and chip controls is freshly in the spotlight. Semafor identified dozens of exchanges about China across the interviews and used a pair of AI models from Anthropic and OpenAI to score each one on Huang’s stance on export restrictions and how he regarded China. Before China’s DeepSeek burst onto the global stage and Washington put new limits on Nvidia’s sales to the country in early 2025, Huang spoke on podcasts about export restrictions in a largely neutral tenor, framing them as a matter of compliance, according to our review. Mentions of China in Huang’s interviews rose roughly sixfold after those 2025 curbs, as the chip CEO argued that the restrictions hurt the US more than China. “If we leave a market altogether, there’s no question somebody else would step in ,” he told Michael Milken in May 2025. In 14 interviews since the 2025 curbs, he talked up China’s AI researchers, open-source models, and manufacturing, often as reasons the US can’t afford to cut the country off, or rejected the idea of treating it as an enemy. He invoked the “American tech stack” 34 times across eight interviews since July 2025, arguing that the world’s developers should build on US technology. In eight interviews he said that 50% of the world’s AI researchers are Chinese or in China, suggesting the country’s tech talent can’t be ignored. — J.D. Capelouto

events.title: A top lobbyist returns to the White House
events.summary: The News A conservative firebrand who helped craft the Trump administration’s campaign against Ivy League universities has returned to the White House to help chief of staff Stephen Miller build his team, a move that will test the administration’s efforts to contain the influence of lobbyists within the White House. May Mailman, who left her post as Trump policy adviser in 2026 to launch her own lobbying firm, will join the White House on a temporary basis as a special government employee, Axios first reported and Semafor confirmed. In recent months, Mailman had built a healthy stable of corporate clients with active matters before the Trump administration, including Vestis, a uniform supplier which has pushed the FTC to block a rival’s acquisition, people familiar with the matter said. The FTC is poised to block that deal , Semafor earlier reported. Other companies she’s worked for include Netflix, Meta, HPE, Comcast, and KKR, according to the people. Mailman, as well as the firms, either declined to provide a comment for this story or did not return a request for comment. Mailman served as a policy adviser early in Trump’s tenure, helping Miller go after Harvard and Columbia for what the administration called indifference to antisemitism on college campuses. She decided to return to the administration in recent days after Miller was named chief of staff, with Miller asking her to help him staff up his team and find ways to optimize relationships between government entities. Mailman ruled out a policy role when discussing her return to public service, though, in part over concerns that it would fuel a perception of impropriety, one person with knowledge of her thinking said. Still, the revolving door between the White House and lobbying work raises questions around how much Mailman stands to benefit personally from her new role and about the level of influence that corporations have held over this White House. The White House didn’t immediately respond to a request for comment. Mailman informed clients of her new role within recent days, and has instructed her firm — which she has taken a leave of absence from — to not engage with the White House while she is serving there for the next few weeks, some of the people said. Rohan’s view Americans on both sides of the aisle have grown frustrated with the level of influence big corporations have over this administration — with a CNBC survey of voters finding that corruption was the number one issue going into the midterms. That perception has only been fueled by the list of Trump-connected lobbyists who have gone in and out of the White House, perhaps the only bipartisan move left in DC. Mailman, perhaps uniquely, has shied away from the kind of publicity that some lobbyists have courted. And her efforts to create a firewall between her clients and her firm, as she returns to government service, stand in contrast to other administration power brokers, who openly tout their relationships with administration officials.

events.title: Apple tells its Support Community to STFU
events.summary: Apple has abruptly stopped accepting new posts on its Support Community, putting the forum into read-only mode ahead of permanent closure on November 20, 2026. Users seeking help with their gizmos from other Apple customers were greeted with the message : "The Apple Support Community will permanently close on November 20, 2026. Starting today, the site will no longer accept new posts and is available in a read-only state. "We want to thank the community members who have contributed their time and expertise to help others with their Apple products." Need help? Head to the official Apple Support site. Want to see if your fellow Apple users have an answer to what ails your device? This is no longer the forum for you. Some reports date the site's origins to 1998, when Apple was busy killing off the Newton platform and launching Mac OS 8.5. Technology has come a long way since then, and recent AI developments have made user-to-user forums like Apple's Support Community less popular. Other places to seek advice remain, and useful answers were never guaranteed. As one user put it on X : "rip to every thread that ended with 'same problem here' and zero solutions." Still, it's an abrupt end to almost three decades of accumulated advice, troubleshooting, and unanswered questions. Apple hasn't said whether that archive will remain accessible after the closure. The Register asked Apple for the reasoning behind the termination. The company has yet to respond. ®

events.title: UK’s Cheval Collection launches Dubai project in expansion push
events.summary: Cheval Collection , the UK-based luxury hospitality firm, has launched a development in Dubai, with plans to expand in the UAE and the region as property demand increases. The project in Dubai South will have 98 serviced hotel apartments ranging from studios to three-bedroom units, and 95 one-, two-, and three-bedroom branded residences. It is scheduled to open in 2030. Cheval South Bay is the fourth development for the company in Dubai and its sixth in the Middle East. It has two more under-construction properties being built in Saudi Arabia. Sales for Cheval South Bay are expected to start next year. Prices and the total value of the project have yet to be disclosed. “Announcing this project today shows what our confidence is like in Dubai, our confidence in the UAE, and our confidence in the wider GCC [Gulf Co-operation Council],” Nick Pilbeam, Cheval Collection’s chief commercial officer, told The National. “Cheval already operates two properties in Dubai, Cheval Maison The Palm, Cheval Maison Expo City Dubai … in the last six months, in the current situation, they've [performed] well. They've outperformed the market, certainly in occupancy because of this long-stay angle.” Cheval Maison The Palm and Cheval Maison Expo City, opened in 2023 and 2025, offer serviced apartments. The company also launched a branded residence development in Dubai Island in April. Cheval's latest announcement comes as property developers continue to launch projects in the UAE despite concerns about the slowing of the market as the Iran war continues. This week, Dubai’s Nakheel unveiled a 3.8 million-square-metre residential development next to Palm Jebel Ali, with a mix of villas, townhouses and apartments. It will also have education, health care, sport and leisure facilities across 15 neighbourhoods in southern Dubai, with two schools, a hospital and six mosques. In September, Aldar, Abu Dhabi’s biggest listed developer, and Sharjah-based Arada revealed plans to build new housing projects on Yas Island and at Seih Sdeirah in Abu Dhabi, representing a combined value of about Dh15 billion ($4 billion). Cheval is also exploring opportunities to start a new project in Abu Dhabi as the emirate’s property market has been performing strongly this year, with real estate transactions surging. A total of 38,483 transactions worth Dh171.26 billion were registered in Abu Dhabi in the first nine months of 2026, marking a 76.1 per cent increase in value and a 32.8 per cent rise in volume on an annual basis. “There's a lot going on in the Abu Dhabi real estate market,” Mr Pilbeam said. “I can't talk anything concrete just yet, but it is certainly a city and an area that we're looking at and interested in.” The privately owned company is also looking to expand in other parts of the Middle East and North Africa region, with a new property launch being planned “in a few weeks time” expected to take its portfolio to about 1,000 units. “We're clearly on a growth journey. However, we're still very selective about the projects that we go in for. We want to be in prime locations, in tier-one locations, tier-one destinations. We are negotiating multiple projects,” he added.
