events.title: Fireworks AI gets burned twice as customer data exposure widens
events.summary: Fireworks AI has disclosed another cyberattack in October and a wider customer data exposure involving billing records, datasets, and incomplete model weights. The company, which lets customers train and run AI models, said a third-party cloud provider hosting its research and development machines was compromised on October 23. Attackers used that access the following day to reach Fireworks development systems and run an unauthorized workload. Fireworks suspects links to financially motivated criminals involved in LLMJacking – selling unauthorized access to AI models through illicit gateways. Fireworks grouped the affected data into three categories: Resource metadata: Resource identifiers, display names, descriptions, creation times, and more Billing information: Billing and shipping addresses, invoice and payment histories, account balances, and credit usages. Payment card numbers are not saved and therefore unaffected Model weights and datasets: For certain customers, a subset of incomplete model weights and datasets were accessed, Fireworks said Lin Qiao, Fireworks co-founder and CEO, said the apparent motive was not stealing model weights in response to concerns raised by Cantina Security CEO Hari Mulackal. "From what we see attackers are not after weights," said Qiao. "Most downloads were partial and stopped." Render founder and CEO Anurag Goel shared a notification from Notion warning that some chats with its AI assistant may have been exposed through the Fireworks incident. "Following an investigation by the Notion security team, we have determined that your workspace, Render, was among the <1 percent of Notion workspaces that may have been affected by the Fireworks security incident," the email sent to Goel stated. "Some unattributable chat sessions with Notion AI may have been exposed in this incident." Notion said the exposed transcripts lacked separate information linking them to particular users or workspaces. As Reddit users pointed out , however, the conversations themselves could contain identifying details. "Beyond what's in the chat transcript itself, there's no information tying the chat back to your workspace, users, or company," the email added. "No other data from within your workspace is affected." Bloomberg reports that Fireworks is also working with customers including Cursor and Harvey to assess the impact. Fireworks' update confirmed that it worked with Palo Alto Networks' Unit 42 team to remediate the attack, which included rotating credentials, isolating affected systems from the network, and tightening up data storage access and monitoring systems. The update did not state how many customers were affected by either of the two attacks in October. Fireworks first disclosed an incident on October 9 after detecting unauthorized use of internal credentials on October 6. Attackers accessed environment variables in evaluation jobs, including API keys and tokens belonging to some customers. At the time, Fireworks said it had found no evidence of access to models, datasets, training data, inference traffic, or personal information. Monday's update substantially broadens the disclosed impact. ®

events.title: Paid recruits tied to banned group behind 3-day crude bomb attacks in Bangladesh, police say
events.summary: Unidentified individuals have exploded crude bombs and torched vehicles in Bangladesh's capital and other areas over the past three days DHAKA, Bangladesh -- Dozens of crude bombs have exploded and passenger vehicles have been set on fire in Bangladesh’s capital and elsewhere over the past three days, leaving one person dead and others injured, authorities and media reports said Tuesday. The violence coincided with reports that the ousted former prime minister, Sheikh Hasina, plans to return from exile next month, though any connection remained unclear. Mohammad Akhtar Hossain, a police spokesman, said at least 33 people were arrested Monday in Dhaka and more arrests were made elsewhere. He said a banned group was behind the attacks but did not identify it. As many as 15 crude bombs exploded in the central district of Manikganj, near Dhaka, early Tuesday, and a driver was killed when a parked bus was set on fire, the country's leading newspapers reported. In Dhaka, crude bombs exploded over the three days, including at the Dhaka University campus and at the premises of a court on Tuesday, with two people injured. Several vehicles were also torched. Hossain said seven crude bombs were recovered during search operations, and two motorcycles used in the attacks were also seized in Dhaka. He said security has been increased across the city. The ruling Bangladesh Nationalist Party accused Hasina’s followers of the violence, saying they want to destabilize the country. Hossain, without naming any suspected perpetrators, said: “We have found that those involved in these activities are linked to an organization whose activities have been banned, or to its affiliated groups. In many cases, we have also found that some individuals were paid to carry out these acts." Hasina has been in India since Aug. 5, 2024, when she fled the country as a student-led mass uprising ended her 15-year rule. Baby buried alive for 24 hours released from the hospital; father charged House tables Hegseth impeachment, effectively killing it in current Congress Wisconsin state trooper detained by ICE A special tribunal sentenced her to death in 2025 for ordering a deadly crackdown on protesters. On Monday, Hasina requested a new passport to facilitate her return from exile. The government has been seeking her extradition from India and has dismissed suggestions she needed new identification documents to return home. Hasina says she wants to return to Bangladesh in December voluntarily, despite being sentenced to death. In a letter seen by The Associated Press that was emailed to Bangladesh’s diplomatic mission in New Delhi, Hasina’s counsel urged the top diplomat to take necessary action to provide her a passport and national identity card. The government of Prime Minister Tarique Rahman said Hasina’s email seeking the passport was a mockery. It said Hasina would be required to submit her application in person, and that an emailed request is not enough. events.title: Another contract extension for Fujitsu on the Post Office's Horizon
events.summary: The UK Post Office is extending its contract with Fujitsu to give it time to move services to a new supplier, after a scandal that has long marred the relationship between the two. The current contract runs until March 2027, and the publicly owned company has announced a short, time-limited contract extension to cover the transition. Accenture will take over running the Horizon system, which was at the center of a string of miscarriages of justice, from September 2027, after winning a £410 million contract in May this year. Meanwhile, the Post Office is developing a replacement for the aging system to serve its network of 11,500 branches. The Post Office began rolling out the legacy Horizon IT system for accounting in 1999, along with two subsequent upgrades. The electronic point-of-sale (EPOS) and back-end finance system was first implemented by ICL, a UK tech firm majority-owned by Fujitsu in the 1990s and which it fully acquired in 1998 . From 1999 until 2015, around 736 subpostmasters were wrongfully prosecuted and convicted over Horizon errors, devastating lives in the process. The Post Office, Accenture, and Fujitsu have agreed that Fujitsu will hand over the operation of Horizon to Accenture between 1 June and 1 September 2027, with the final date set to be confirmed in March 2027. Accenture is set to "walk in and take over" the current Horizon system by assuming day-to-day operations from Fujitsu, as well as developing the back-end of the new system to replace Horizon. Post Office CEO Neil Brocklehurst said: "Ending our contract with Fujitsu is a critical milestone in Post Office's transformation, and today's agreement secures the transition away from Fujitsu and over to Accenture safely and responsibly to achieve our target of summer 2027. "In addition to ending our contract with Fujitsu, we are also working at pace with our leading technology suppliers, Accenture, OneView Commerce, and Escher, to build a modern, resilient platform able to make everyday life easier for customers and postmasters for years to come." Fujitsu has also been awarded a contract extension to run the UK Government's Emergency Alerts platform until October 2029. The contract is worth £9.6 million ($12.8 million). The company committed to not bid for new public sector contracts while the inquiry into the Horizon scandal continues. ®

events.title: US solar learns to live without China
events.summary: The News Washington wants to make it harder for US solar firms to rely on China. A panel factory in Texas shows how that’s already happening — but why weaning them off entirely could be harder than it looks. The industry is bracing for one of its biggest shocks in years: In December, new Commerce Department rules will require panel manufacturers to pay a fixed minimum price and a tariff of up to 15% for cells and certain other specialized components they import from abroad. The rules, under a provision called Section 232, are designed to finally quash a cat-and-mouse game US trade officials have been playing with China for years, in which Chinese solar makers shift between factories in various Asian or African locales to stay one step ahead of American tariffs. One of the companies navigating this change is the Texas-based panel manufacturer T1 Energy, which has roots linked to China but is now racing toward greater independence. Because the new rules will drive up panel prices, some solar installers are panicking; at least 1 gigawatt worth of large-scale solar projects has been cancelled in recent months because of 232-related price adjustments, according to solar research firm Anza. But T1 CEO Daniel Barcelo can’t wait. The rules “will really level the playing field” against Chinese rivals, he told me. “Building something in America still takes longer and costs more than building it in most countries.” Tim’s view US President Donald Trump may not be a big fan of solar, but it’s the country’s fastest-growing source of power generation. Standing up an independent domestic solar supply chain is critical to the country’s energy security and AI ambitions, and to lowering power prices, especially as Beijing moves to restrict the export of some key solar technologies . But, although it may be wise to raise trade barriers that push more China-affiliated solar components out of the US market, China’s role in global solar supply chains is so pervasive that instantly severing all ties could kill many US solar manufacturing efforts in the crib. Future growth for this industry depends on a more nuanced trade policy that gives US companies the space to benefit from China’s world-leading solar expertise while the next phase of home-grown plants gets built. At this point, the US imports almost no solar cells or other core components from China, and imports of panels from anywhere recently hit a seven-year low now that more US module assembly factories are cropping up. But even T1, like many of its peers, still needs China for some vital aspects of its operations. And when I visited the company’s factory, it was clear that achieving a full divorce between the American and Chinese solar industries could be more complex than many in Washington appreciate. T1 operates a sprawling, cutting-edge solar module factory on the outskirts of Dallas, and is a few months away from finishing a second factory to manufacture its own cells based on technology that was first developed for the Chinese firms it’s looking to supplant. Last month, the company was granted special permission from Commerce to continue importing cells from Asian suppliers without being penalized for stockpiling ahead of the 232 deadline. It is also awaiting a verdict on a second Commerce waiver that would allow it to dodge the 232 tariffs altogether while it completes its onshoring investments. The company was born from the clean tech trade wars that have engulfed the US, Europe, and China in recent years. In the early 2020s Barcelo, whose background is in global oil and gas finance, was working to set up an EV battery factory in Norway. But that company, Freyr, got pushed by intense competition from Chinese rivals — and simultaneously pulled westward by inducements in Biden’s Inflation Reduction Act. The company’s first plan was to build a $2.5 billion battery factory in Georgia. But that was scrapped after Barcelo spotted a better deal in solar, where there were only a few domestic manufacturers at a moment when demand was exploding and Chinese firms, who could see a US crackdown coming, were looking to pull up stakes. He pivoted, and agreed in December 2024 to a $621 million deal to buy the Dallas factory, along with supply contracts and other assets, from Changzhou-based Trina Solar, one of the world’s biggest producers, which had just completed building it. A wave of similar US takeovers swept the industry around that time, including some in which Chinese firms retained a minority stake. Indeed, more than 40% of the 66 GW of operational US module manufacturing capacity today originated as facilities owned by Chinese manufacturers or joint ventures involving Chinese firms, according to Wood Mackenzie analyst Elissa Pierce. Trina continues to own approximately 11% of T1’s public shares, according to SEC filings. T1’s relationships with Trina and other Chinese firms have also remained essential: A Trina executive briefly came over to serve as the new venture’s chief strategy officer. The factory’s anchor customer became Trina itself, which committed to buy 1 GW of panels per year, one-fifth of the factory’s capacity; on the day I visited, robotic arms were gingerly packaging panels into Trina-branded boxes. The first thing I saw on the factory floor was a stack of specialized glass from a company in Zhejiang. Other Asian countries are essential, too: T1 imports cells and other components from a range of suppliers in Southeast Asia and elsewhere. T1 inherited Trina’s polysilicon supply contract from a Michigan company called Hemlock, which is minority owned by a Japanese chemical firm. In July, it paid $135 million to a Singaporean solar firm for intellectual property behind the cell and module technology that Trina and others use. Russell Gold, a veteran Wall Street Journal energy journalist who is now T1’s spokesperson, said that although the company now feels “pretty comfortable running this factory by ourselves,” it still works closely with outside contractors, including some from China, to maintain equipment and train its workers on what is essentially a Chinese factory floor plopped in East Texas. Chinese solar manufacturing equipment, Gold said, is still “the best in the world.” Inside a gleaming warehouse the width of a few Manhattan avenues, a succession of machine arms, conveyor belts, and ovens press cells onto dinner-table-sized panels, more than 17,000 every day. Several hundred humans are needed to keep things moving and ensure quality control. A few autonomous robots roll around moving heavy stuff while playing Darth Vader’s Imperial March to signal their approach. The staff reflects the diversity of the strong immigrant communities in Dallas: I met workers, at least half of whom seemed to be women, from Equatorial Guinea, Mexico, Peru, and Venezuela. events.title: NYC’s $325B pension giant can’t hide from AI, but it wants to
events.summary: New York City’s $325 billion pension system has started turning down private-market AI deals it considers strong on the merits, because it already owns too much AI. “It’s hard to diversify such a big portfolio under any circumstances because you’ve really got to be in every asset class, and we are in every major economy on Earth. But now so much of that, sector by sector, market by market, is AI,” NYC Comptroller Mark Levine said on this week’s episode of Semafor’s . That level of “over-concentration” is “a risk that we’re leery of.” It’s getting harder to find places to hide: AI-heavy companies account for almost half of S&P 500 market value, 40% of US high-yield bonds sold this year, and one in every six dollars of blue-chip corporate debt. Everything else, from private credit to real estate to Asian stocks, is increasingly a dressed-up bet on data centers. On the flip side, owning so much of the AI buildout also gives the city’s chief financial officer some leverage over the tech CEOs running the companies, and he isn’t happy with them. He called CEOs’ appearance at Trump’s state dinner for China in September “a national embarrassment,” saying they’d “kissed the ring” of a president who is himself “a massive threat to pulling off the AGI transition safely.” One option: formal AI standards for the companies the fund owns, similar to its existing climate and labor rules: “We have a lot of fights to wage as shareholders.” — Liz Hoffman and Rohan Goswami

events.title: Price pressures persisted in October
events.summary: Data: Bureau of Labor Statistics ; Chart: Courtenay Brown/Axios Inflation remained hot in October, according to data from the Labor Department released on Tuesday. Why it matters: The Consumer Price Index shows that even as gasoline prices steadied, inflation pressures elsewhere remained stubborn. By the numbers: CPI rose 0.4% last month, slowing from the 0.6% increase in September. Gasoline prices gained 1% in October, a sharp slowdown from the 9.1% surge in September, the Labor Department said. Core CPI, which excludes volatile food and energy prices, advanced 0.3% for the third straight month, with higher prices for recreation, medical care, car insurance and airline fares contributing to the increase. Of note: The Labor Department did not publish year-over-year inflation rates for October. Last year's government shutdown left a gap in the data that prevents direct comparisons with October 2025. But if one assumes the October 2025 readings were halfway between September and November, year-over-year inflation comes to 4% — or 2.8% excluding food and energy. That compares with September's annual inflation rate of 3.7%, or 2.6% excluding food and energy. The big picture: The inflation report was already shaping up to be a crucial piece of the Federal Reserve's interest rate decision next month. But the stakes grew just hours before its release when Fed governor Christopher Waller raised the prospect of a larger-than-usual rate hike if inflation remains stubbornly elevated. In a speech , Fed governor Christopher Waller said a half-point rate hike should be considered next month if core inflation rose by at least 0.3% in October — exactly what Tuesday's report showed. The yield on the two-year Treasury note, which is particularly sensitive to expectations for Fed interest rate policy, jumped 0.13% on Tuesday following Waller's comments and the CPI report. What to watch: The report also offers a fresh measure of the inflation problem that helped shape last week's midterm elections. Nearly nine in 10 voters said the cost of living was a "crucial" or "major" factor in their vote in last week's midterms, according to national exit polling data . Democrats won on promises to lower prices for groceries and other essentials. Now they face the more difficult task of delivering on their promises, with limited power to reverse years of price increases. The bottom line: Inflation remains stubbornly hot, strengthening the case for another Fed rate hike and prolonging the cost-of-living pressures that have frustrated American households. events.title: Stanford's century-long AI study admits it's already out of date
events.summary: Twelve years into Stanford's 100-year study of artificial intelligence, the project's third report raises more questions than it answers. The 2026 AI100 Study Panel report acknowledges its limitations in its twelfth takeaway: "This report will be out of date by the time you read it." But it's nonetheless a worthwhile exercise for those who haven't been paying close attention to the development of machine learning over the past few years and for policymakers who may benefit from a review of AI's metastatic growth. "The last five years constitute a watershed moment in the history of AI," said Professor Sheila McIlraith, chair of the AI100 Standing Committee, in a statement. " This report examines what led to the extraordinary capabilities of today's AI systems, and how they are reshaping society. As we look ahead, we anticipate continued increase in AI capabilities alongside transformative advances in science and medicine. "Rapid change will challenge governments and industry to support and safeguard our people, our institutions, and our critical infrastructure. Both the benefits and the risks of AI technologies require the same clear-eyed scrutiny." Established in 2014, the One Hundred Year Study on Artificial Intelligence (AI100) is overseen by a Standing Committee of AI experts and administered by Stanford's Institute for Human-Centered Artificial Intelligence (HAI). It's charged with producing reports every five years, the first of which debuted in 2016. The 2026 report's other key points highlight the transformation brought about by increasingly capable machine learning software. It identifies scaling as the engine of AI's advance, but also points to the growing cost and difficulty of obtaining training data as constraints on further progress. The report likens AI's disruptive potential to that of the World Wide Web – without dwelling on the irony that the web itself is among the things being disrupted. It points to creative industries, computer programming, and mathematics as fields once deemed beyond the reach of automation that are now being upended. Science, the report says, is being transformed by AI as it accelerates research timelines and opens up novel challenges. At the same time, the report cautions that "we will need to understand how AI-mediated information environments reshape collective cognition and moral behavior." The recent retraction of some 1,400 scholarly papers for failure to meet academic standards highlights the urgency of that message. Then there's the AI investment boom and "fears of a financial bubble, " which won't be assuaged by recent NASDAQ volatility and revelations about Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang's relationship with an alleged intelligence operative for China. Concerns about the concentration of frontier AI development, the pressure AI puts on cybersecurity, and the active use of AI for military applications are also noted in the report. So too are worries about what AI-generated media does to trust. Item nine on the report's takeaway list is perhaps the most noteworthy: "AI is reshaping the lives of billions of people, yet the public has had little say in how it is developed and deployed." The recent US midterms suggest voters are finding ways to make themselves heard about AI datacenters, even if that falls short of shaping broader AI policy. Item ten posits that longstanding academic concerns about AI bias, ethics, and safety are beginning to converge with what until recently seemed like worries inspired by speculative fiction, such as AI agents hacking into companies without human oversight. And item 11 frames the entire report by calling out the lack of a coherent regulatory response to AI: "AI governance is fragmented and increasingly framed in terms of national security, with little international consensus among states on its direction." Those takeaways introduce the AI100 Study Panel's examination of 12 standing questions about what AI makes possible and how humans are handling it. Easy answers are in short supply. But as the report's disclosure section makes clear, even the people taking the century-long view are using the technology to assess itself. "Reflecting the progress in AI over the period this report covers, AI tools were used extensively in its production," the report explains. "The report was written by humans, and its authors used AI primarily to transcribe and summarize meetings, support dictation, and check drafts for typos, consistency, duplication, tone, and structure. In some cases, AI suggested rewording of human-written text. AI was also used to compare this report with previous AI100 reports, identifying where expectations and reality have diverged or converged over five years. After completion, AI tools checked for inadvertent plagiarism and signs of AI-generated content." ®

events.title: Wall Street mixed in early trading ahead of a new peek at inflation
events.summary: Premarket trading on Wall Street was mixed but relatively calm and oil prices fell again, one day after stocks rallied to recover most of their big losses from last week Early trading on Wall Street was mixed and oil prices fell again, one day after stocks rallied to recover most of the big losses from last week. Futures for the S & P 500 rose 0.1% before the opening bell, while futures for the Dow Jones Industrial Average gained 0.3%. Nasdaq futures dipped 0.3%. Oil prices continue to decline, with Brent crude falling below $91 per barrel, the lowest level in three months. The declines came after President Donald Trump said that the war in Iran “militarily is effectively over,” a week after American voters, angered by skyrocketing costs, handed both chambers of Congress to Democrats in midterm elections. Brent crude, the international standard, fell 2.2%, or $2.02, to $90.55 a barrel. U.S. benchmark crude oil slid 1.8%, or $1.65, to $84.94 per barrel. Nvidia shares were off less than 1% before the bell. Shares fell 4.3% on Monday after the AI chip company said it’s investigating after its CEO, Jensen Huang, acknowledged an intimate relationship with a business executive who, according to The New York Times , U.S. intelligence determined was gathering information for China. Nvidia’s board said it has “no reason to believe” that either national security or Nvidia secrets were compromised but its inquiry would examine all available information. China has rejected the allegations. Artificial intelligence giant Anthropic filed papers with regulators Tuesday seeking a $1.3 trillion valuation ahead of its IPO, expected later this month. Anthropic’s quarterly revenue swelled to $17 billion but it still posted a net loss for the latest three months, the artificial intelligence giant said in an updated IPO filing. Last week, the San Francisco company behind the Claude chatbot said its quarterly revenue swelled to $17 billion though it still posted a loss for the last three-month period. Anthropic said it has committed to spend $895.4 billion on AI computing and infrastructure like data centers, including $70 billion that’s due to be spent in the next 12 months. Global demand for AI chips remains robust with AI chipmaker Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Co. reporting after the market closed that its October revenue was nearly six-fold that of a year earlier. In Asian trading, Taiwan’s Taiex jumped 2.5%. Baby buried alive for 24 hours released from the hospital; father charged House tables Hegseth impeachment, effectively killing it in current Congress Wisconsin state trooper detained by ICE Japan’s benchmark Nikkei 225 closed 2.9% higher at 60,459.58. SoftBank Group reported a $7 billion loss for the three months through September as worries about investments in artificial intelligence hurt the Japanese technology company’s bottom line. Computer chip equipment maker Tokyo Electron surged 6.1% and testing equipment maker Advantest gained 4.6%. South Korea’s Kospi climbed 4.4% to 5,239.13. Samsung Electronics gained 4.7% and SK Hynix climbed 6.7%. In Hong Kong, the Hang Seng rose 0.6% to 24,584.81, while the Shanghai Composite index edged 0.1% higher to 3,663.72. China’s exports in October climbed 35.2% from a year earlier, while imports grew 41.6%, according to customs data released on Tuesday. That has put the country on track for another record for the year since the trade surplus for 2026 has already surpassed $1 trillion. At midday in Europe, Germany’s DAX rose 1.2%, as did the CAC 40 in Paris. Britain’s FTSE 100 was up 0.5%. Investors are waiting for the U.S. consumer price index report for October , which comes out later Tuesday. Data is expected to show inflation rose 3.9%, up from 3.7% in September, which many analysts expect will force the Federal Reserve to raise its benchmark interest rate in the coming months. events.title: More renewables and Hormuz disruption drive emissions fall
events.summary: Global fossil fuel emissions are projected to fall by 0.4% in 2026, driven by the rapid expansion of solar and wind power and the energy supply shock caused by the Iran war, according to research by the Global Carbon Project. But the decline is not yet fast enough to be durable , an accompanying study published in the journal Nature found. Emissions from oil are expected to decrease by 1.9% , which is likely a short-term response to the closure of the Strait of Hormuz. “A reduction driven partly by geopolitical shocks is not a sustainable climate solution,” said Pierre Friedlingstein, an Exeter University professor who led the GCP study and was a co-author of the Nature paper. Total carbon emissions are set to rise around 1% this year, as emissions from deforestation and land-use change are projected to increase for the first time in a decade. At the current rate, the world will deplete its remaining carbon budget aimed at keeping global temperature rises to 1.5℃ in fewer than four years. — Chloé Farand

events.title: ADNOC Gas lifts profit outlook after beating earnings forecast
events.summary: ADNOC Gas has raised its outlook for full-year profits by at least 14% after third-quarter earnings smashed expectations — and views a looming glut of LNG on the global market as an opportunity rather than a risk, CEO Fatema Al Nuaimi told Semafor. Although overall Gulf LNG exports are recovering — in October they reached the highest level since the start of the US-Iran war — ADNOC Gas’ exports remain slightly below what they were when the conflict began. Still, the company was able to ride soaring LNG prices to third-quarter net income of $1.3 billion, double its forecast. ADNOC Gas is weighing whether to invest in new infrastructure to bypass the Strait of Hormuz, including a potential new export terminal at Fujairah, Al Nuaimi said. While global LNG supplies are currently tighter than they’ve been in years, some analysts expect to see an oversupply by the early 2030s as a raft of new terminals come online. “I don’t call it a glut, I call it market creation,” Al Nuaimi said of the possibility of a major price dip in the next few years. “That’s where you can attract more consumers to be hooked into the LNG value chain.”

events.title: US Senate backs permitting bill aimed at accelerating energy construction
events.summary: The US Senate advanced major permitting reforms aimed at speeding up the construction of energy infrastructure, seen by green-power advocates as much-needed progress to accelerate the country’s energy transition. Democrats’ decisive victory in last week’s midterms — where several candidates ran on an “all-of-the-above” approach to electricity generation — have added impetus to permitting reform. But Democrats and environmental groups remain divided over the long-awaited bill, which would overhaul major environmental laws to streamline the permitting process for building power projects, AI data centers, and distribution grids. Both fossil fuel and clean energy companies have backed the bill, which would help connect more renewables to the grid, although President Donald Trump said he would not approve permits for new wind projects . Modelling by the Rhodium Group found the reform would reduce electricity bills and economy-wide emissions . But the effects are difficult to quantify and won’t be immediate, some analysts warn: “The bill’s greatest affordability benefits will start accruing to the president who follows Donald Trump ,” Heatmap wrote. — Chloé Farand

Hegseth's news conference was less than 30 minutes long, including the questions he fielded from generally friendly outlets. The conference clearly pleased Trump, who gave Hegseth "an 'A' PLUS, PLUS, PLUS" in a Truth Social post. Driving the news: "They impeached President Trump over a perfect phone call. They impeached him again in his final week in office," Hegseth said, referencing Trump's first impeachment over a phone call where he pressed Ukraine to investigate Joe Biden and his second over the Jan. 6 attack. "Both times he came back stronger, and the American people sent him back to the White House. Now they're trying a third time. This time against a member of his Cabinet," he continued. "They will fail again, and if standing with President Trump puts me in that company, I'll take that company every day of the week." Catch up quick: Massie, who Hegseth labeled a "disgruntled congressman," introduced his articles of impeachment against the defense secretary Monday over his handling of the war in Iran and other alleged misconduct. Republicans who were defeated in last week's stunning midterm shakeup have little left to lose and could get on board with impeaching Hegseth, Axios previously reported. Post-election attendance could also be an issue. What he's saying: Hegseth mounted a defense of scrutinized U.S. military operations in Iran, Venezuela and the Caribbean. "We sank the boats carrying poison into our communities. We put a narco dictator in handcuffs. These are not high crimes. This is the job, and it's the job well done," he said. Massie condemned the boat strikes on alleged drug smugglers in the Caribbean and Eastern Pacific in his resolution , alleging Hegseth "arrogated to himself and the Executive Branch the roles of judge, jury, and executioner." The operation has killed well over 200 people. Massie's resolution included eight charges, including the accusation that he violated the 1973 War Powers Resolution in connection with the war in Iran and that he retaliated against Sen. Mark Kelly (D-Ariz.) for his constitutionally protected speech. What we're watching: Hegseth's impeachment would be monumental. The House has only impeached two Cabinet secretaries in U.S. history. events.title: US national debt keeps rising after years of tax cuts – and this will make policymaking all the more difficult
events.summary: A series of tax cuts since President George W. Bush's 2001 legislation have helped push the national debt to US$32 trillion. AP Photo/Ron Edmonds Democrats, set to take over Congress with robust majorities, will face at least one expensive obstacle to their policy agenda: a national debt that now equals the size of the U.S. economy. Clocking in at US$32 trillion, this debt-to-GDP ratio of 100% would likely raise alarms for other countries. But it attracted relatively little attention in an election season dominated by concerns over the economy and the cost of living . Debt has grown to these levels because over the past 25 years, the federal government has been spending more than it collects in taxes . Even as the U.S. economy grew, lawmakers have cut taxes repeatedly, sometimes with bipartisan support, instead of paying down debt. The series of tax cuts since 2001 has added over $10 trillion to the debt, according to an analysis of Congressional Budget Office data by the Center for American Progress. In fact, without these series of cuts, the debt-to-GDP ratio would be decreasing, the study found. The debate over taxation often falls along partisan lines, with arguments focusing on which income groups are affected or the potential impact on economic growth. But as a public policy scholar , I believe that important context is often overlooked. Under conditions of strong gross domestic product growth and low debt, tax cuts may have a relatively benign fiscal impact . But today, because debt as a share of GDP is so much higher, and interest rates are steeper , the cost of adding new debt is much greater than 15 or 20 years ago, whether through additional spending or through tax cuts. I believe Democrats will have to wrestle with this math as they try to advance a policy agenda focused on affordability that minimizes the risk of further borrowing. It’s all relative Proponents of fiscal austerity argue that lower spending should accompany tax cuts so that debt doesn’t rise. U.S. federal spending, however, has remained relatively flat – outside of emergencies like the 2009 recovery package and COVID-19 stimulus funds – even as GDP has risen. At the same time, each round of tax cuts over the past quarter century has actually gotten smaller over time if they’re assessed as a share of GDP, as a study by the Tax Foundation , a nonpartisan think tank, noted. President Ronald Reagan’s 1981 tax cuts were the most expensive in history, reducing annual federal revenue on average by 2.9% of GDP, according to the Tax Foundation’s analysis . The next two biggest cuts occurred in 1945 and 1948, when the government rolled back the wartime hikes that helped pay for World War II. President Barack Obama’s 2012 legislation, extending most of the temporary tax cuts passed under President George W. Bush, comes in fourth at 1.8% of GDP, while cuts passed under President Lyndon Johnson in 1964 rank fifth. Coming in sixth place at 1.2% of GDP: President Donald Trump’s sweeping policy and tax legislation in 2025, which made permanent most of his 2017 tax cuts. Costly extensions While the Trump cuts amounted to a relatively small share of GDP, they had a much larger effect on the national debt due in part to the higher cost of borrowing. The original 2017 legislation was projected to increase public debt from 91.2% to 97.1% of GDP by 2027, with an overall 10-year cost of $1.5 trillion . That was based on the assumption the cuts would expire after 2025. But just like the earlier round of Bush tax cuts, Congress was loathe to let those provisions lapse. In 2025, the narrow Republican majority pushed through Trump’s legislation that extended or made permanent the 2017 cuts. The Congressional Budget Office, the independent government scorekeeper of legislation, estimated that the 2025 bill would add another $3.4 trillion over 10 years. And it projected that increasing deficits would push debt to 116% of GDP by the end of 2034 . Why deficits and economic growth matter so much A basic calculation explains when debt stays stable, and when it does not. If a government runs a “primary” budget surplus – that is, excluding interest payments – and economic growth is higher than the interest rate on government bonds, debt remains stable . The problem for the U.S. is that budget deficits have been growing faster than the economy, while interest payments on government debt are rising as well. This math explains why the trajectory of economic growth is so important in understanding the impact of tax cuts. When taxes were cut after World War II, the economy was booming, the U.S. carried little debt, and reducing taxes didn’t further add to it. By contrast, government spending ballooned under Reagan, thanks in large part to defense outlays. Combined with lower tax revenue due to tax cuts , the national debt tripled during Reagan’s time in office. In 2000, the economy was surging again. That was the last time the U.S. took in more tax revenue than it spent and began paying down the debt. President George W. Bush cited this surplus to justify his first round of major tax cuts in 2001, which also drew support from some Democrats. It remains to be seen how much leverage the results of the midterms will grant Democratic lawmakers in the next two years as they try to enact legislation under Trump. But I believe lawmakers of all stripes will have to confront the hard choices that the U.S. national debt imposes on policy directions going ahead, thanks to a long series of decisions made over the past quarter century. events.title: When a Walmart closes, what happens to nearby stores?
events.summary: Nearby stores might not actually win out with extra shoppers if a Walmart shutters. Mark Ralston/AFP via Getty Images Shoppers often greet the closure of a Walmart with dismay , while competitors find cause to celebrate. Among critics of the big-box behemoth, a long-held assumption is that once a Walmart disappears, shoppers seeking groceries, household goods, meals and services will flow to businesses down the road. But what if the economic downside of a closure is bigger? We are marketing scholars who have studied dozens of Walmart closures in the United States. We found that nearby stores saw a slump in both monthly shopper traffic and sales revenue by roughly a quarter in contrast to comparable stores near Walmart locations that remained open. Our sample covered 39 Walmart stores that closed across 20 states from 2019 to 2026. This finding suggests a large retailer can play two roles at once. Walmart competes with neighboring businesses for shopper visits and spending. But it can also act as an anchor, giving people a reason to travel to a shopping area in the first place. When that anchor disappears, the loss of shared shopper traffic can outweigh the benefit of having one less competitor. The benefits of an anchor Our finding underscores that retailers don’t operate as isolated dots on a map. Shoppers often decide where to go before deciding which stores they’ll visit once they get there. A trip to Walmart can generate a stop at a nearby restaurant, pharmacy, salon, specialty retailer or service business. Economists call this kind of benefit an agglomeration effect : Businesses can gain from being near other businesses because the location itself attracts shoppers. Shopping center owners have long recognized this logic by using prominent stores to anchor a mix of tenants. Other researchers have found that Walmart’s entry into a shopping area causes sales in nearby existing stores to drop . But these shops can adjust their product assortment, prices and promotions to mitigate this effect, follow-up studies suggest . What has not been studied until now is what happens when a Walmart store – or any other anchor store – closes. A Walmart closure creates a tug-of-war between two forces, we argue. Competitive relief helps nearby businesses because a formidable rival is gone. But agglomeration loss hurts them because fewer shoppers have a reason to visit the area. This means a store can capture a larger share of local consumer demand after Walmart leaves and still end up worse off if the total pool of shoppers arriving in the area shrinks enough. Developers often place an anchor store in a bigger retail center to attract more foot traffic overall, which in turn goes to other stores. David Cooper/Toronto Star via Getty Images What happened after a Walmart closed We combined closure dates with monthly store-level shopper traffic and spending data. For each closed Walmart, we identified nearby non-Walmart businesses and compared their post-closure performance with that of businesses near Walmarts that stayed open. We discovered not just a sizable decline in both shopper traffic and sales revenue after closure but a worsening trend in both over time. Specifically, following a Walmart’s closure, nearby stores experienced a roughly 5% drop in the following month and 6% in the month thereafter. The decline keeps getting worse, reaching about 17% in the ninth month and 20% a year after the anchor store closes. That parallel movement in traffic and sales matters. If nearby stores were simply selling less to the same number of shoppers, we would expect spending per visit to fall. Instead, what was also happening is that fewer shoppers visited nearby businesses after the anchor disappeared. In short, competitive relief didn’t overcome the loss of traffic that would have been generated by trips to the anchor store. But not all nearby businesses were affected equally. Stores that competed more directly with Walmart had better post-closure sales than noncompeting stores. That is what we would expect if competitive relief is real: Grocery stores and other close substitutes are better positioned to capture some of the displaced consumer demand. Well-known brand stores also fared relatively better than unbranded businesses. A recognizable brand can give shoppers an independent reason to visit, reducing reliance on traffic generated by the nearby anchor. And stores surrounded by more outlets with its own brands also had more favorable post-closure sales. Another important factor is digital reach. Not surprisingly, the more a business engages with customers online, the less it depends on people physically traveling to a cluster of stores. We found that stores with a higher share of revenue from online orders saw a less severe drop in sales after a Walmart closed. These patterns suggest that managers have options and can act: Opening another location or expanding online sales can protect a retailer from an anchor closure. Why a store closing can become a neighborhood shock A large retailer decides whether to keep a store open based primarily on what makes sense for its own portfolio. But the surrounding businesses face a different calculation. A location that looks weak from the anchor retailer’s perspective can still drive valuable traffic to neighboring stores. That creates what economists call an externality – a positive or negative effect of an economic activity that impacts other parties even though market prices don’t reflect it. In this case, some of the economic value produced by an anchor sits outside the anchor’s own sales and profits. For neighboring businesses, the lesson is not to assume that a powerful competitor’s departure will create a windfall. Rather, managers need to know how many customers arrive because of the broader shopping destination, not merely how much their store’s products overlap with the anchor’s. Meanwhile, commercial property owners should treat losing an anchor as more than risking an empty storefront. It can also hurt the rest of their portfolio by reducing consumer demand. Replacing the tenant quickly matters, but so does finding a replacement that can generate trips to the area. Finally, local governments and economic development organizations need to understand that a major retail closure may affect businesses with no contractual relationship to the closed store. So their responses should extend beyond the vacant property itself – whether it’s speeding redevelopment, coordinating with local businesses and property owners to improve shoppers’ access, or helping create a new destination that restores shopper traffic. events.title: The path ahead for the permitting bill
events.summary: The Senate's bipartisan permitting bill advanced in a lopsided vote on Monday, but key hurdles lie ahead. Why it matters: The legislation could have far-reaching consequences for how energy projects get built across the U.S. A few takeaways from Monday's vote: The big margin was politically lopsided. The 73-25 split to advance the bill "was as good or a little bit better" than what co-author Sen. Shelley Moore Capito (R-W.Va.) was expecting, she told reporters in the Capitol. The GOP split was 51-1 in favor, with only Sen. Mike Rounds (S.D.) voting no. 21 Democrats and Maine independent Sen. Angus King voted yes, while 23 Dems and independent Sen. Bernie Sanders were against advancing the bill toward full debate. It was tentative. Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer (D-N.Y.) said in a statement afterward that he has "outstanding concerns" with the bill that he'll "fight to address" through amendments. He's not alone in only a tentative yes vote. For instance, Sen. Catherine Cortez Masto (D-Nev.) is against final passage unless changes to the National Historic Preservation Act are jettisoned, citing tribal concerns. Sen. Lisa Murkowski (R-Alaska) is in a similar place. Climate hawk vs. climate hawk. The most outspoken Senate Democrats on climate change split on the vote. Sen. Brian Schatz (D-Hawaii) joined coauthors Sheldon Whitehouse (D-R.I.) and Martin Heinrich (D-N.M.) in backing the measure. But Sens. Jeff Merkley (D-Ore.) and Ed Markey (D-Mass.), along with Sanders, all voted no. Watch the clock. Whitehouse pledged a "very healthy" amendment process. But the Senate is now up against the lame duck calendar, and the House would still need to act on whatever emerges. Plus, any changes would need to thread a political needle of maintaining Democratic support without losing too many Republicans. Climate's cachet has fallen. Heinrich and Whitehouse, at a pre-vote press conference, emphasized affordability, data center accountability and jobs before touting power sector emissions curbs from the bill. But Whitehouse also sought to reassure climate and environmental organizations. "This bill is the floor, not the ceiling, of our climate and environmental aspirations, and we look forward to working to accomplish big things with our big Democratic majorities," he said in the Capitol. President Trump is a wild card. His comments shortly before Monday's vote that he would not approve wind turbines, while reiterating his full support for the bill, rocketed around the Capitol. And the White House reaffirmed that the president "stands 100%" behind the bill. The bill's success depends on Trump officials "getting wind turbines up and spinning to get affordable energy on the grid," and progress is needed before final passage, Whitehouse said in a statement. What we're watching: Proposed amendments as they roll in, but also the politics in the closely divided House. House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries (D-N.Y.) criticized the bill last week and called for more engagement with his caucus. Asked Monday whether the Senate co-authors' revisions addressed his concerns, Jeffries told reporters that it's still under review. Sign up here for Axios' Future of Energy newsletter.

events.title: Gulf sovereign wealth funds are among those hit by the AI sell-off
events.summary: Sovereign wealth funds, including some of those in the Gulf, are among the big losers from the AI sell-off, with their listed portfolios slumping $30.5 billion since the end of June. Globally, sovereign wealth funds and public pension investors hold about $335.5 billion of exposure to AI companies, according to consultancy GlobalSWF. Gulf funds have been a big part of that, both domestically and around the world, backing AI firms in private funding rounds and as they list on public markets. Among those with some of the highest disclosed exposures is Abu Dhabi’s Mubadala, which may have seen its portfolio shrink by $17.5 billion, mostly due to a more than 50% slump in chipmaker GlobalFoundries stock. Saudi Arabia’s PIF is estimated to have seen its AI exposure fall in value by $5.64 billion, mostly attributed to its SpaceX holding. Despite the stock market slump, it is unlikely to change how sovereign funds bet on AI. “We would not expect strategic investors to retreat wholesale from AI,” said Daniel Brett, head of research at GlobalSWF. “Lower valuations could create opportunities for long-term funds to increase exposure selectively, although this does not imply an imminent rebound.” — Matthew Martin

events.title: Agentic commerce is slow to catch on
events.summary: Silicon Valley’s bet that billions of agents will be out ordering food, booking travel, and filling up their humans’ shopping carts is running into an (admittedly early) reality check. Airbnb CEO Brian Chesky said Friday that the site was seeing “very, very low numbers” of bookings by Meta’s Muse and Instinct AI agents, while DoorDash has received “maybe several hundred orders in total” from personal AI assistants, CEO Tony Xu said. “The adoption of these horizontal personal agents may be much slower than is anticipated,” Booking Holdings CEO Glenn Fogel said. Either adoption is slow, or much of Silicon Valley is dead wrong in its assumptions about regular people’s behavior (it wouldn’t be the first time ). That could validate decisions by big retailers like Amazon to block agents , whose robot eyeballs can’t be monetized the same way humans’ can. — Jake Angelo

events.title: The Download: Pelosi’s successor targets AI and data centers face power woes
events.summary: This is today’s edition of The Download , our weekday newsletter that provides a daily dose of what’s going on in the world of technology. Nancy Pelosi’s replacement is ready to regulate AI —Grace Huckins As a California state senator, Scott Wiener authored legislation aimed at curbing the risks of advanced AI. Now, after winning a tight congressional race for Nancy Pelosi’s open San Francisco seat, he could play a key role in setting federal AI policy. I spoke with Wiener only a few hours after he had been declared the victor. But he was already thinking about AI risk: during our 20-minute conversation, he used the phrase “recursive self-improvement” half a dozen times.  “We need to slow this down,” he told me. “Because it’s moving very quickly, and we could sleepwalk into a disaster.” Still, he describes himself as only “cautiously optimistic” about Congress’s ability to rein in AI. Here’s what he plans to do about it . The backlash about data centers might really just be about electricity  —James O’Donnell As voters went to the polls across the US last week, I was in Ashburn, Virginia, part of what’s known as Data Center Alley—the world’s largest data center hub. It’s also where the backlash sweeping the country arguably first began to take shape. Big Tech has framed the data center uproar as a culture war over progress. But a few days in Ashburn convinced me the real fault line may be electricity: drawing it from the grid or generating it onsite provokes different forms of blowback. The industry can improve its image, but it can’t escape the consequences of its enormous appetite for electricity. Find out why .  This story is from The Algorithm, our weekly AI newsletter. events.title: Wall Street bonuses set to grow after banner year for IPOs and AI
events.summary: A word of caution for Wall Streeters planning how to spend their year-end bonuses: This may be as good as it gets for a while. Bonuses at big banks and investment houses are set to grow again thanks to a blockbuster year of historic IPOs, AI financings, and zippy markets, according to pay consultancy Johnson Associates, whose annual bonus report is required reading across the financial industry. But the AI trade is now starting to sour, interest rates are rising, and last week’s Democratic gains may darken the backdrop for 2027. Even this year’s bumper crop will be shared unevenly, tilted more heavily toward the best performers rather than spread “peanut-butter-like” across and within divisions, Alan Johnson told Semafor. “Firms now value the best people more than they ever have, and value the average person less,” he said. “Nobody is going to wring their hands if an average performer is complaining — ‘don’t let the door hit you on the way out.’” Financial executives are keen to avoid the trap of 2021, when their efforts to gift-wrap the fruits of a banner year as special, one-time bonuses got baked into expectations anyway, with predictable howling in 2022 . — Liz Hoffman

events.title: Wall Street is unbothered by Nvidia's Jensen Huang scandal
events.summary: Wall Street giants have hundreds of billions of dollars riding on Jensen Huang, but sound remarkably unfazed by the trouble the company is in. Goldman Sachs CEO David Solomon said on CNBC that the key-man concerns around Huang are overblown. “I don’t think the ecosystem is centered around one individual,” Solomon said. “I think no matter how this plays out, Nvidia will continue to be a great and important American company.” Goldman is part of the Wall Street consortium that has committed to raising $500 billion to help Nvidia finance the AI buildout, an alliance that will allow the company’s ambitions to outrun even its own healthy balance sheet. The other five finance heavyweights in the group — BlackRock, Brookfield, Blackstone, KKR, and Apollo — either didn’t provide a comment when asked about Nvidia’s troubles, or pointed to Solomon’s remarks. Meanwhile, the tech-heavy Nasdaq closed up nearly 3% Monday and shares of hyperscalers and neoclouds like CoreWeave soared, perhaps on the theory that the scandal could bring tougher export controls on chips, leaving more supply for US buyers. — Ellen DiMauro

events.title: Evolving metal extraction processes
events.summary: The metals industry has experienced transformational moments before: the Bessemer process, flash smelting, electric arc furnaces, and modern continuous casting all changed what was possible. Yet, for more than a century, most extraction processes rely on techniques and pathways that would be familiar to metallurgists from generations ago. Processes have become larger and control systems smarter, but the fundamental science behind separating metals from ores has changed less than many realize. Today’s materials challenges are different from those of the 20th century, but why are critical metals still produced using largely the same scientific foundations? EvoMaterials, a technology platform developed by Outokumpu—the global leader in sustainable stainless steel and the producer of ferrochrome with 67% lower carbon footprint than the industry average—is exploring that question by rethinking how metals can be extracted: “We decided to go beyond the current constraints and look fundamentally at what’s the best way to do this with the benefit of the scientific engineering knowledge and hindsight that we have today,” says Caspar Stinn, technical director for extractive metallurgy at Outokumpu. “We’re looking at how we can reimagine metals production.” A supply chain problem disguised as a materials problem As economies expand and the world becomes increasingly electrified, data and scientific models point to rising demand for many minerals, driven by technologies ranging from data centers to aerospace, water treatment, energy systems, and defence. According to Antoine Allanore, professor of metallurgy at the Massachusetts Institute of Technology (MIT) this coincides with many Western economies having reduced their domestic processing capacity for the very metals those industries depend on. Metallurgy is now strategically important, shaped not only by cost and availability but also by carbon footprint, geographic origin and supply-chain resilience. That reality is particularly relevant for chromium and other specialty metals used in high-temperature and extreme environments. Chromium-based materials play a critical role in aerospace systems, power generation, corrosion-resistant infrastructure and defense technologies, where materials must perform under demanding conditions. Beyond optimization For decades, metallurgical innovation largely focused on improving yields, energy efficiency and process control. EvoMaterials is based on the idea that some metallurgical processes may benefit from entirely different chemical pathways. The platform originates from research into sulfidation-based processing technologies, initially pursued to reduce carbon emissions associated with ferrochrome production. Laboratory work revealed broader potential. Lab-scale trials demonstrated that these alternative process chemistries could potentially do more than lower emissions. They could recover valuable metals from lower grade resources and industrial side streams while fundamentally altering how separation processes are performed. The opportunity is to rethink how mineral resources are used and how much value can be extracted from them, bringing in greater resource efficiency and stronger industrial competitiveness. Understanding traditional smelting vs. new proprietary technology Source : Outokumpu Development of the technology began in the United States in 2021 for chromite from Outokumpu’s Kemi mine in Finland, the only chrome mine in the European Union and one of the few such operations across the Western world. Since then, Outokumpu has evolved the technology through extensive research and development, combining new process chemistries with proprietary metallurgical expertise, supported in part by a non-exclusive patent license agreement from MIT. “The technology is a new application for separating metallic elements from materials,” explains Allanore. Historically, that separation has been achieved using carbon- and energy-intensive approaches. The new method creates a different chemical environment that enables more efficient extraction with fewer losses and fewer unwanted by-products, recovering critical materials from resources considered waste. Innovation happens at the boundaries EvoMaterials sits at the intersection of several scientific disciplines, a combination that strongly resonates with Stinn, who completed his PhD in Materials Science and Engineering at MIT, where his research focused on low-carbon metals processing and recycling technologies. Modern materials innovation draws on a growing mix of chemistry, materials science, physics, computational modeling, and engineering. With advanced simulation tools and AI helping researchers identify promising directions, scientific discovery still depends on experimentation and testing in the lab—on getting your hands dirty and doing the hard work. “Science today is much more interdisciplinary than it was, and the collaboration across disciplines reveals new scientific opportunities,” says Stinn. Engineering can translate those opportunities into more efficient and cost-competitive metals production. Building a technology platform A technically significant aspect of EvoMaterials is that it’s not a single process, but a technology platform. Allanore compares EvoMaterials to platform technologies in other industries, where a single scientific breakthrough can enable multiple downstream applications. Once a new extraction pathway has been mastered for one material system, the same scientific principles may be adapted to entirely different metals and mineral resources. The initial application becomes only the starting point. “The future and the potential impact might be much broader than the original and current developments that are happening,” Allanore explains. That possibility is increasingly important as industries seek secure supplies of nickel, chromium, molybdenum, and other strategic materials needed for advanced manufacturing. The future of materials companies The broader implication extends beyond metallurgy. Companies that develop proprietary process technologies may create value through production but also through intellectual property and scientific expertise. Based on Outokumpu’s technology leadership, that transition could create entirely new categories of value, enabling the production of high-value critical materials from ores and resource streams that previously appeared uneconomical or inaccessible. The result would be a fundamental shift in how metals are manufactured, where sustainability, resource efficiency, supply security, and economic value become outcomes of the same technological architecture rather than separate objectives. The next step for EvoMaterials is pilot-scale validation, with a pilot plant in New Hampshire to begin operations in the first half of 2027. The facility will scale the proprietary technology from laboratory to one-ton production, providing a step toward industrial-scale deployment targete

events.title: COP should put itself out of business
events.summary: Tim’s view In the decade since the Paris Agreement, the annual round of UN climate summits has seemed like a parallel universe, increasingly out of touch with geopolitics and the real economy. Between the idealism-bordering-on-naivete, and the impenetrable thicket of acronyms, jargon, and obscure treaty provisions, “sometimes I come into negotiation rooms and the contrast with the real world cannot be any bigger,” Ali Mohamed, Kenya’s special climate envoy, told me here. There are still many people here at COP31 in Antalya, Türkiye, this week who would love to see the oil and gas industry shuttered tomorrow, energy access and prices be damned. Fossil fuel companies’ record-breaking profits this year are proof that, like it or not, the world still needs a lot of this stuff. While the Iran war certainly did drive some countries to accelerate their adoption of renewables, the global reprioritization of energy security means “there is no doubt we’re backsliding” on the goal adopted at COP28, in Dubai, to transition away from fossil fuels, Mohamed said. And needless to say, nothing that happens at COP has any real legally binding force on any country. So what’s it all for? I’ve asked myself this question a lot in the past 48 hours, while navigating Antalya’s maddeningly overwhelmed transit system (although I will say the COP venue itself, if you can manage to get inside, is the nicest one we’ve had in years). One answer is that pragmatism was never the point. Idealism is a feature of UN summits, not a bug, Eurasia Group analyst María José Valverde said: “COP goals aren’t designed to be achieved. It’s about where we want to take humanity.” Another answer is that, while it may not get headlines, “there’s still all kinds of shit happening behind the scenes,” as one diplomat put it to me this morning, from deals on clean cooking stoves in Africa to negotiations among European countries to remove bureaucratic barriers between their rail networks that force more commercial traffic onto dirtier highways. And while it may not be happening at activists’ preferred pace, clean energy adoption already driving a tangible transition away from fossil fuels. That’s in spite of a surge in overall energy demand that has made it harder to displace any one source. In the absence of all renewables that have been built since 2010, the International Energy Agency reported last week , global fossil fuel demand in 2025 would have been 8% higher, “an amount equivalent to India’s total energy consumption.” The big goal for this particular COP is to drive this trend forward by getting countries to agree on a target to raise the share of total global energy demand served by electricity from 23% today to 35% by 2035. That’s basically another version of the fossil fuel transition goal, viewed through the opposite end of the kaleidoscope, which could be more palatable to the oil-producing countries that are usually the spoilers here. Whatever is negotiated here will, again, be nonbinding. And it’s impossible to say precisely what role COP, per se, has had in the pace of the clean energy rollout up to now. But to the extent that these meetings mainly serve to send long-term political signals that buttress — if not dictate — the economic signals companies use to make energy investment decisions, the best outcome for COP is to put itself out of business, as clean energy projects increasingly beat fossil fuels on merits unrelated to environmental ideology. “In the real world, things are happening and not waiting for the negotiations,” Mohamed said. “The transition is going to happen whether you want it to or not.” Notable In December, new US Commerce Department rules will make it costlier to import Chinese manufacturing components for solar panels, as part of an effort to make it harder for US solar firms to rely on China.

events.summary: China’s trade surplus passed $1 trillion for the first 10 months of the year, as the country’s exports grew at record speed despite several countries putting up trade barriers. Flatlining consumption at home has pushed Chinese manufacturers to find customers abroad, fueling anger in foreign markets over their domestic industries being hollowed out. Soaring fuel prices caused by the Iran war have also helped drive demand: China’s EV and plug-in hybrid exports for October surged 145% year-on-year. AI-related exports have also jumped. Beijing, meanwhile, is unlikely to accede to US and European calls to bolster its domestic demand, with one asset manager telling the South China Morning Post he did not think the country’s “macro policy stance will change significantly .” — Jeronimo Gonzalez

events.title: ExxonMobil eyes Venezuela return after two decades
events.summary: ExxonMobil signalled it would resume operations in Venezuela almost two decades after leaving the country, a boost for Washington’s campaign to increase oil and gas output in its de facto protectorate. While crude production has risen moderately since the US ousted Venezuela’s president in January, it remains far below its 1990s peak, held back by outdated infrastructure and a lack of experienced workers: Exxon’s boss called the country “ uninvestable ” just a few months ago. Oil majors fear that Venezuela — which has the world’s largest stated reserves — is still too politically unstable to commit billions of dollars to its economy, though the recent return of opposition leader María Corina Machado and her push for elections may help assuage those concerns . — Jeronimo Gonzalez

events.title: Honda reports robust results on the back of healthy motorcycle sales
events.summary: Honda has reported a 66% rise in net profit for the first half of its fiscal year, driven by strong motorcycle sales TOKYO -- Honda’s net profit rose 66% in the first half of its fiscal year, the Japanese automaker reported Tuesday, driven by strong motorcycle sales. Tokyo-based Honda Motor Co. reported a profit of 516.76 billion yen ($3.3 billion) for the six months through September, up from 311.83 billion yen a year earlier. First half sales rose 13% to 12 trillion yen from 10.6 trillion yen. The robust results came despite costs in its electric vehicle program, where it dropped some models. Honda said EV-related losses erased 484.8 billion yen from its operating profits. But officials stressed that Honda expects battery EVs might eventually become more popular and it will remain flexible enough to switch to EV production in the future. Honda raised its full-year operating profit forecast to 780 billion yen from 650 billion yen. Honda attributed the more optimistic forecast to favorable exchange rates and efforts to reduce the impact of U.S. tariffs, including shifting production to the United States. The maker of the Super Cub motorcycle and Accord sedan also announced major production investments in North America and Brazil. Honda plans to build a new auto production plant in Ohio, increasing production capacity in North America to 1.91 million vehicles by 2029 from 1.67 million. The company expects U.S. demand to grow, especially for its hybrid models. It sold 11.9 million motorcycles during the six months, up from nearly 10.8 million the previous year. However, Honda sold 1.57 million automobiles globally in the first half of the year, down from 1.68 million. events.summary: The FBI is investigating the CEO of Nvidia’s affair with an alleged Chinese spy, US President Donald Trump said, widening the fallout from the scandal engulfing the world’s biggest chipmaker. Nvidia shares fell following Jensen Huang’s admission of infidelity with an executive tied to Chinese intelligence, while lawmakers in a soon-to-be Democrat-controlled Congress have pledged investigations into the episode , and the US Commerce Department has reportedly begun readying a new set of semiconductor export controls . Pressure is mounting on Huang, but he appears unlikely to lose his job, at least for now: Trump has publicly backed the executive, and Nvidia is highly dependent on him , with no clear successor in view and a board that is relatively low on heft. — Prashant Rao

events.title: Grand Theft Auto VI is almost here. What to know about the characters, music and billions at stake
events.summary: Grand Theft Auto VI is set to release on Nov. 19, marking a return to the neon-lit streets of Vice City LOS ANGELES -- LOS ANGELES (AP) — Grand Theft Auto has never been much for following the rules. Nearly three decades after a video game built around stealing cars, outrunning police and embracing criminal mayhem first arrived, the franchise has survived controversy, transformed open-world gaming and become one of the biggest sellers in entertainment. Now, after a 13-year wait since its last main installment, Grand Theft Auto VI is preparing for another big score. The latest chapter arrives Nov. 19 with a return to the neon-soaked streets of Vice City with two protagonists. For longtime fans, GTA VI is a highly anticipated return. For everyone else, here’s what to know about the blockbuster video game, its characters and the enormous business riding on its release: The franchise began in 1997 as a relatively simple, top-down game that allowed players to roam fictional cities, steal vehicles, evade police and commit crimes. The release of Grand Theft Auto III in 2001 helped redefine open-world gaming. It gave players greater freedom to explore a sprawling three-dimensional city, pursue missions and interact with their surroundings. Later installments expanded that freedom with larger environments, cinematic storytelling, social satire and detailed worlds. The influence reached far beyond games about stealing cars. Ubisoft’s Assassin’s Creed series brought open-world exploration to historical settings, while Bethesda’s The Elder Scrolls games expanded their own longstanding tradition of open-ended fantasy role-playing. Nintendo’s The Legend of Zelda: Breath of the Wild later emphasized experimentation and discovery, allowing players to use the environment itself to solve problems. For Grand Theft Auto: San Andreas and Grand Theft Auto V, Rockstar Games recruited real-life gang members to help bring authenticity to background characters and dialogue. Former writer and audio director Lazlow Jones has said some performers challenged scripted lines, prompting developers to let them use language drawn from their own experiences. That attention to detail helped create the sense of a living world that became a hallmark of the franchise, even as the series drew criticism for its depictions of violence, crime and women. But controversy did not stop the franchise’s commercial rise. According to publisher Take-Two Interactive, the franchise has sold more than 470 million units worldwide. Grand Theft Auto V, released in 2013, accounts for more than 230 million of those units and reached $1 billion in retail sales in just three days. Its online multiplayer component, Grand Theft Auto Online, has helped keep players engaged through years of updates, new activities and in-game purchases. This time, the action returns to Vice City, Rockstar’s fictional version of Miami, and expands across the surrounding state of Leonida, a Florida-inspired setting filled with beaches, highways, nightlife and criminal enterprises. At the center are Lucia Caminos and Jason Duval, a couple trying to improve their circumstances through a life of crime. Lucia has recently been released from prison while Jason, a former soldier who became involved with drug runners in the Leonida Keys, is looking for a different path. Their plans become more complicated when a seemingly straightforward criminal job goes wrong, drawing them into a conspiracy that stretches across Leonida. Baby buried alive for 24 hours released from the hospital; father charged House tables Hegseth impeachment, effectively killing it in current Congress Wisconsin state trooper detained by ICE The trailers suggest a story mixing romance, robberies, betrayals and the series’ familiar satirical take on American culture. Rockstar has revealed several supporting characters, including bank robber Raul Bautista, aspiring music executive Dre’Quan Priest and nightclub owner Boobie Ike. Rockstar has kept much of the voice cast under wraps, including the performers behind Lucia and Jason. One familiar actor has confirmed his involvement: Stephen Root , known for his work in “Office Space,” “King of the Hill” and “Barry.” He told The Associated Press in September that he appears in the game, adding that fans had already recognized his distinctive voice in promotional footage. Root has been identified in reports as the voice of Brian Heder, an aging drug runner operating out of the Leonida Keys. Rockstar has introduced the character but has not publicly confirmed Root’s casting in that specific role. Beyond the return to Vice City, one of the biggest changes is the focus on two protagonists whose relationship drives the story. Grand Theft Auto V featured three playable main characters. The new installment centers on Lucia and Jason as partners navigating the criminal underworld together.
