events.title: Jensen Huang has lost the debate on China chip sales
events.summary: Andy’s view Nobody outside the Oval Office has been more influential on US policy toward chip sales to China — and, by extension, the superpower race for AI supremacy — than Jensen Huang. The Nvidia CEO had Donald Trump’s ear. And he used his privileged access to make the case that keeping China hooked on Nvidia hardware and software was critical to maintaining the US technological lead. Cutting off sales to America’s chief strategic rival, he cautioned, only encouraged Beijing to speed up development of its own AI technologies that would, over time, become the global default. Whatever the merits of that argument, the events of the past 48 hours have almost certainly doomed his central contention. Huang’s admission of an affair with a woman who, according to US intelligence, is a Chinese spy plays directly into the hands of hawks in Washington pressing to clamp down on tech transfers to China. This camp has insisted all along that Huang’s advocacy was not only self-serving — a thin justification for his pursuit of profits — but, on its face, absurd. Under Chinese leader Xi Jinping, China is going all out for tech self-sufficiency precisely to escape the kind of dependencies that Huang envisages. Indeed, Xi has been cool on Huang’s marketing pitch. Although Trump greenlit sales of Nvidia’s H200 chips to China (taking a cut of revenues for the US government), Beijing is strictly limiting imports. Huang’s defenders insist he’s been arguing in good faith. Ben Thompson, the author of the influential Stratechery newsletter, argues that “it is entirely rational — and defensible — for Nvidia to want to sell chips to China.” By doing what he thinks is right, Thompson contends, Huang and Nvidia have “achieved unimaginable success.” It also needs pointing out that Huang stands by his patriotism. In a letter to staff, he insisted, “I love our country and our company.” But having allegedly been compromised in a Chinese “honeytrap,” one of the central figures in US technology and co-founder of one of the world’s most valuable companies, will be hard pressed to convince US congressional investigators he’s always put US national interests first. They’ll want to know whether Alice Huang extracted any Nvidia secrets in the course of their affair. Did she have access to his unguarded laptop? Or his cellphone? Did she garner any insights into White House strategy during their assignations? Of special interest to lawmakers looking at potential conflicts of interest: The Nvidia CEO’s relationship with the Singapore company Megaspeed, where Alice Huang was an executive and that was under investigation by the US Commerce Department over suspicions it formed part of a clandestine supply chain shipping Nvidia chips to China and Southeast Asia data centers. The issue is whether the romance influenced his business decisions. (The New York Times reported on Monday that the Commerce Department’s inquiry was suspended following outreach from an Nvidia executive. The department denied wrongdoing, and Nvidia said the company regularly consults with officials.) This drama will run and run. For the new Democrat-controlled Congress, the scandal offers multiple lines of attack against Trump. I’ve been predicting a backlash to the president’s China policies, widely criticized by politicians in both parties as weak and feckless — particularly his relaxed approach to tech transfers, but also on Taiwan, human rights, and military readiness in the Asia Pacific. The onslaught has now been brought forward. Chris Coons, the incoming chair of the Senate Committee on Foreign Relations, signaled the start of hostilities in a post on X. “The more I learn about the insane relationship between the Trump Administration, Chinese spies, and AI billionaires,” he wrote “the more I’m convinced there is nothing this administration does that isn’t corrupt .” Whether Huang will keep his job or not is an open question. Those who claim that he’s irreplaceable may be underestimating the political storm that’s about to break. In any event, he’s lost the debate on chip sales to China, with significant commercial consequences for Nvidia, and even larger implications for superpower rivalry. He may well feel wronged, but as Thompson, the Stratechery analyst, put it, “he has only himself to blame.” Notable WIRED reported that in October 2025, around the same time he was first linked to Alice Huang, Jensen Huang hired consultants from the crisis communications firm Heller, which is known for managing sex scandals.

events.title: Louis Rossmann Wants More People to Care About the Right to Repair
events.summary: I love my old iPhone 14 , but I’m starting to face the facts: It’s going to die. The battery is about to go; apps take longer to load than they used to. Some of it I can fix. I can go to the Genius Bar and swap the battery. Maybe I could even do it myself; that’d buy me some time. But eventually, Apple won’t support this wildly expensive device at all, and there’s not much I can do about it. Apple did start offering self-repair services a few years ago, but it involves renting nearly 80 pounds of equipment and requires you to use official parts. When all is said and done, it doesn’t save you that much money versus just going to the Apple Store . But if I buy a screen or a camera component from a third party, there's a chance my iPhone is gonna lock me out of certain features because it doesn't recognize it. This problem goes far beyond iPhones. Manufacturers have put similar locks on all kinds of gadgets, from video game consoles to cars to smart home devices, making them hard to modify and even harder to restore after some firmware update renders a certain feature unusable. Not surprisingly, a lot of people think this isn't fair, that there should be a better way to do it. I think at this point it's safe to say it qualifies as a movement, one that unites under the banner of “right to repair.” Built around the radical idea that when you buy something you should be able to truly own it, right-to-repair advocates believe consumers have the right to maintain, fix, or modify any piece of hardware they’ve purchased. The movement has gained even more traction now that AI makes it even easier to hack the software powering consumers’ devices. To find out what’s next for the right-to-repair movement, I went straight to the source: Louis Rossmann, a YouTuber and consumer rights advocate who recently organized the Own Your Shit tour , which went around the US earlier this year to call for the death of Section 1201 of the Digital Millennium Copyright Act, which prohibits users from bypassing digital restrictions put on devices by manufacturers. Rossmann and I talked about more than just Section 1201. We also discussed the US midterm elections , putting out bounties to find product fixes, and what will happen as the right-to-repair movement collides with the rise of AI. This interview has been edited for length and clarity. BRIAN BARRETT: Louis, thank you so much for being here. You're someone who spends a lot of time not just evangelizing over “right to repair,’ but I would imagine introducing it to people who don't know what it is. How do you do that? LOUIS ROSSMANN: I try to avoid talking about it, and I try to show people. So instead of telling people, “Here’s why you should care about this issue,” which sounds like lecturing, what I’ll do is if I’m done fixing something for a customer and they say, “The Apple Store told me $2,000," and we could do it for $200, when they’re giving me the hug and saying, “Thank you for getting back all of our baby pictures” or something, I’ll say, “Here’s how close you were to this never happening.” I like to tell them, “This is the document that I used to fix your device.” When they ask me what was wrong with it, I’ll tell them, “By the way, you should know that Apple tells the company that makes this chip not to sell it to me, and if everybody in that chain listened, I would not be able to fix this, and you wouldn’t have any of your data back.” So I always try to show people and get them excited about what it is I’m doing. I have over 1,000 repair videos on YouTube where I show people how to do what I do, and there are people that say, “I was working at Walmart for seven bucks an hour, and I picked up a soldering iron and started fixing boards on eBay, and now I make triple what I did before.” There are people that fix their own things, so not just making careers for people, but maybe somebody saved themselves some money by doing a repair themself. Or when I fix something for somebody that otherwise wouldn't have been fixed or that they were told couldn’t be fixed. I always try to get people personally invested because lecturing people about it just doesn’t make it very fun. Your organization has a wall of shame, almost, of examples of things that companies have done to take away the ownership of a product. Because that’s really what it is, right? It's like you buy something, you expect to be able to own it and do what you want with it, but that's not always how it plays out. To your mind, what are some of the more egregious instances of companies not letting you know what you want? Some of my favorites are some of these thermostat companies. One of them sent out a firmware update after the company went bankrupt that required that you pay $117 a year to get some of the functionality that you had beforehand. So it’s not even necessarily when a company has a device that has a specific date when it’s gonna turn off.

events.title: Trump plans imperial final act to his presidency
events.summary: President Trump, with the clock ticking and congressional investigators closing in, plans to govern even more imperially , hell-bent on stretching executive power, targeting those on his enemies list, pardoning allies, and daring the courts and Congress to slow him down. Why it matters: Trump and his allies are exploring executive action on new tariffs and immigration restrictions, and asserting greater control over spending. On X over the weekend, Trump discussed targeting and perhaps jailing Democrats who investigate administration officials. He claimed politically motivated harassment . Trump is retooling his White House by elevating the one official who's synonymous with his all-gas-no-brakes style: Stephen Miller, who took over for Susie Wiles as White House chief of staff on Monday. Watch Miller and Russ Vought , the White House budget director, to understand how this approach will unfold. Both are architects and advocates of vastly expanding presidential power, believing there are virtually no restraints on what Trump can do as president. The Swamp can expect tougher sledding: Miller, unlike most of his predecessors, is driven more by ideology than by meetings with lobbyists or industry groups. "Stephen gives zero f*cks what K Street thinks," a Trump confidant told us. Between the lines: Midterm losses pushed Presidents Clinton and Obama to the center. Trump's instincts are the opposite: Assert maximal power. The playbook: Restore MAGA. Two years ago, MAGA — mostly its network of podcasts , YouTubers and online activists — was a powerful, united force in media and politics. Today it's a hot, divided mess. Trump's attention to his base drifted. Now Vice President Vance and Miller desperately want to rebuild and rev up MAGA. That's why ending the Iran war , curtailing aid to Israel and pushing harder on RFK Jr.'s MAHA agenda are suddenly top-tier topics. Rule by pen. Miller, Vought and White House lawyers have been drafting executive actions to govern without Congress, with Justice Department opinions ready to defend them, Reuters reported just before the election. Remember: Vought was an architect of the Heritage Foundation's Project 2025 blueprint for maximizing executive power in Trump II. Target enemies. Before, it was pure payback. Now, it's also a preemptive warning that the Trump administration will target anyone, including elected members of Congress who target them. Trump ally Roger Stone told us: "Many Democrat lawmakers are going to find themselves under indictment and fighting conviction. Watch." Purge the "deep state." The Supreme Court's ruling in a case about independent agencies, Trump v. Slaughter , widened the president's power to remove officials. "The Slaughter case gives the president tremendous powers," Trump said in an Election Day phone interview with CBS News' Robert Costa. The June ruling handed Trump the power to fire the heads of the FTC and other independent regulators ( like FERC ) for any reason or no reason. More monuments. Trump's pharaonic need to gild the White House, build a ballroom, erect a triumphal arch and slap his name on buildings is also an exercise in raw power. He told New York Magazine's Ben Terris why he's honoring himself: "Nobody will do it once I'm gone. When I leave here, nobody will." No one can stop him. The Republican resistance: Expect very little inside the new Congress. The reason: Most of Trump's Capitol Hill critics are gone. What's left is a much smaller, but more Trumpian, band of middle-aged and older white Republicans with margins too small to matter much. The Trump bet: Congressional Republicans will quickly feel Democrats are overreaching and unify in solidarity with Trump, even if it's forced or begrudging. Yes, but: One of Trump's most predictable attributes is his unpredictability. He said on election night that he'll " work together " with Democrats. What that may look like (with a heavy emphasis on "may"), based on reporting by Axios' Marc Caputo: Soften aspects of immigration enforcement, particularly regarding masked agents harassing U.S. citizens. Find common ground with MAHA's healthy food agenda, which has become the subject of vicious post-election infighting among Trump insiders. Sign legislation from the new Congress that would undo massive Medicaid cuts in his "One Big Beautiful Bill." The bottom line: Trump is still Trump. He's 80 and it shows. But he meets force with force and he'll go down swinging the more Democrats attack him. "Trump and his team are at our best when our backs are against the wall," one adviser told Caputo. "Trump comes out fighting. We're full-throated and full-throttle." Go deeper : Texas, Texas, Texas.

events.title: The AI Safety Debate Has Lost the Plot. We Asked 10 Experts What the Real Nightmares Are
events.summary: In early fall, I felt my anxiety rising from its usual baseline. Was it September’s back-to-school energy? The looming midterm elections? Nope, I realized with annoyance: It was AI—again. Only this time, instead of its purveyors warning of massive job displacement, they were foretelling mass extinction. Who needs jobs when we’re all dead? Curiosity soon replaced my knee-jerk irritation. The summer of 2026 was a clear turning point in the AI narrative. Less than four years after ChatGPT launched, OpenAI software broke out of a supposedly safe test environment and hacked into a major open-source platform, Hugging Face . These bits of software— AI agents —were assigned human attributes: They had “gone rogue,” displayed “bad behavior,” “cheated.” Soon after, former and current Anthropic researchers suggested that advanced AI might kill us all in the next decade. Is any of this real ? On the one hand, from my desk as a Silicon Valley correspondent, I often hear that workers in the AI labs are stunned by the advancements they’re seeing. On the other, the end of humanity seems extremely far-fetched. Amid the hyperbolic discourse, whose views can we trust? So WIRED set out to compile a guide to AI safety—a set of ideas that rewire our collective thinking around what safety really means and how it should work. I spoke with a panel of experts across disciplines, asking each of them: Is the world going to end? Once that was covered, I grilled them on the biggest risks they think we’re facing. Almost no one, it turned out, was Pollyannish. Nearly everyone I spoke to expressed genuine concerns about the threat of cyber and biological attacks. One expert who studies the risks of AI in nuclear operations said she’s stunned by how quickly error-prone AI systems are being adopted in defense. AI-enabled attacks in these areas could be catastrophic, if not fully apocalyptic. Is AI safe? For our ongoing series , WIRED assesses the real threats of artificial intelligence. Most members of the panel were skeptical about any pause in development: They nearly all agreed that, with big AI companies so tightly cuffed to the trains of capitalism, a pause wouldn’t last long. “Democracy” and “governance” came up often—or anti-democracy, as more than one person suggested that AI’s current trajectory is tyrannical. Lawmakers have a big role to play, but many of my sources think governments will be too slow; one prominent technologist said it’s almost absurd to view the US courts as arbiters of global AI safety. Still, the famed computer scientist Yoshua Bengio urged the public to apply pressure to politicians, adding to me, “That’s your job too.” So, what—or who—will keep us safe from AI? Looking to regain some faith in humanity, I called a theologian who often meets with the AI labs. If there’s even a slim chance that we’re losing control of the essential institutions that undergird society, he said, then we should focus on foiling that. But AI raises other questions too. What does it mean to be conscious? To create? To commune with other people? The answers are “entirely up for grabs,” he said. My anxiety’s still kicking around, but I took some comfort in knowing that corporations don’t get to call all the shots on the future. The bigger questions facing humanity are in all our hands. BIGGEST CONCERN: Nuclear catastrophe I’ve been working hard to educate the nuclear community on the risks and lack of reliability of AI systems, and I’m concerned by the willingness of many people in the sector to integrate these models into their workflows, into nuclear operations. I think this is incredibly urgent. I’m not a doomer, but to me, if these AI models make it into the operations of nuclear systems, we’ll be introducing an incredibly faulty, unreliable system that could lead to catastrophic failures. MOST OVERBLOWN RISK: Extinction As true safety engineers, we don’t engage with that because there are no numbers to back it. This is a very cold way to say it, but when we are talking about how safe is “safe enough,” we’re examining how many people might die. There’s an entire science behind it. Our claims have to be falsifiable and verifiable. You can’t just say, “Humans are going to go extinct in 10 years. Believe me. It might be a 10 percent chance; it might be a 25 percent chance.” How should people think about AI safety? Some of the comparisons that people draw between AI and nuclear are quite frustrating. Despite constantly comparing AI to nuclear, they’re denying standard risk assessment techniques as being sufficient to control AI. I wrote an entire paper on this. Part of this field of risk assessment was born out of the Manhattan Project. Scientists were very concerned, and they developed rigorous standards around systems to limit harm to human life, the environment, and even financial and national security assets.

events.title: How a MAHA leader turned and torched the White House
events.summary: Calley Means quickly rose from wellness entrepreneur to senior Trump health adviser — and now he's attacking the White House and suggesting top aides undermined the president's health agenda. Why it matters: His scorched-earth campaign — which continued Monday in comments to Axios — marks a stunning turn for a figure who was the administration's most vocal advocate of the "Make America Healthy Again" agenda. It also raises questions about what the escalating fight between Means and former White House officials will accomplish for the movement. Driving the news: Means told Axios he's going public with his allegations of corruption — especially by former White House chief of staff Susie Wiles — because of the high stakes. "It is existential to the survival [of] America that we rid DC of Susie's brand of politics," Means said in a text exchange. Means' initial comments on Friday's episode of "The Joe Rogan Experience" went viral , and he continued the campaign with an appearance on CBS' "Face the Nation" Sunday. Asked if he's worried about lawsuits after comments from a Wiles spokesperson and former White House deputy chief of staff James Blair — who Means has also accused of wrongdoing — Means pointed to his X post warning them and other parties to "immediately preserve all potentially relevant records and communications." Means has kept up a steady stream of X posts about his allegations and the way he claims the officials have responded to them. "Susie - I'm not intimidated and you will not scare me. Again, please stop sending me emotional texts. This is not personal - this is civilizational," Means posted Monday . White House spokesperson Allison Schuster said in a statement the Trump administration has won "extensive victories for the MAHA Agenda." The Department of Health and Human Services and a Wiles spokesperson didn't respond to requests for comment. The big picture: After hitching their wagon to President Trump ahead of the 2024 election, MAHA leaders have been complaining for months of a lack of progress on issues around healthy foods and pesticide use. But whether the public feud Means has initiated will have any impact on the policy agenda he's championed — or whether it's more of a personal grievance tour — remains to be seen. A former HHS official said that after Republicans' midterm wipeout, Means is "highlighting that one of the more popular aspects of Trump's domestic agenda should be something [the administration] spends more time on to prepare the party for 2028." The intrigue: The MAHA base sees incoming chief of staff Stephen Miller as an ally, even though he hasn't said much about movement priorities like cleaning up the food supply, curbing food additives or scrutinizing vaccines. Miller's wife, Katie, hosted Health Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. on her podcast and has posted photos of dishes with ingredients like raw milk, per the Washington Sun . Means told "Face the Nation" that Miller understands corporate influence over health care and that he represents a break from Wiles. "Stephen Miller has been nothing short of a champion in Making America Healthy Again. As a father of four, Miller is acutely aware of the importance of transforming our food, health, and scientific systems for the next generation of Americans," Schuster said. Zoom in: Means, who resigned from his senior adviser post late last month, grew up in Washington and interned in George W. Bush's White House and at the Heritage Foundation before going on to work as a consultant to beverage and drug industries. He told Axios in 2024 that his mother's preventable death from a chronic disease in 2021 prompted him and his sister, "functional medicine" physician and health influencer Casey Means, to advocate and work to reverse the chronic disease crisis. The siblings wrote a best-selling book called "Good Energy." Calley Means also co-founded Truemed, a company that helps people buy wellness equipment using money in health savings accounts, retaining an interest while advising Kennedy, per the New York Times . Means is widely credited with facilitating the alliance between Kennedy and President Trump in the summer of 2024 and became a special government employee in the new Trump administration. He made frequent, at times flamboyant appearances in public forums, railing against a "crisis of trust" in health care institutions and claiming at one 2025 Axios event that Kennedy "has a spiritual mandate" from voters to reform broken government institutions. Means' sister was tapped by Trump to be surgeon general, only to see the nomination withdrawn in April amid questions over whether she could win over enough Republican senators to be confirmed. Calley Means at the time blamed Senate health committee Chair Bill Cassidy (R-La.) for delay tactics. What we're watching: It's not clear what role Means will play outside the administration — or whether his turnabout has helped or hurt the MAHA cause. Key initiatives like developing a definition for ultra-processed foods remain unfinished, and the Food and Drug Administration appears to be taking a more conciliatory stance toward drug developers and other industries it regulates.

events.title: Trump diplomatic nominee shaped a pro-Russia Balkans policy
events.summary: The Scoop President Donald Trump’s nominee for US ambassador to Azerbaijan has played a leading role in his administration’s headline-grabbing alignment with a pro-Russian government in the Balkans, more than half a dozen people familiar with his involvement told Semafor. Senators had eyed a hearing as soon as Tuesday on whether to confirm Alexander Alden, currently a senior adviser to Secretary of State Marco Rubio, to the high-stakes diplomatic job . With Democrats readying to take control of the chamber next year, Republicans are under growing pressure to advance Trump’s nominees in the lame-duck session. It’s not clear why Alden didn’t make the cut this time — but whenever he does appear, he’s likely to face questions about his behind-the-scenes advocacy for Republika Srpska, a Russia-linked territory in Bosnia and Herzegovina. The territory’s Serb-controlled government gained national attention last month when two of Trump’s top advisers , James Blair and Chris LaCivita, traveled there ahead of its elections. The ruling party in Republika Srpska is helmed by Milorad Dodik, a Bosnian Serb who was under US sanctions for undermining peace in the region until Trump lifted them last year. Lawmakers in both parties have urged Trump to reimpose the sanctions as Dodik continues his calls for Republika Srpska to secede. Inside the administration, however, Alden is seen as a Dodik champion, according to the people who spoke with Semafor: “Some have referred to him as the ‘Serb in the State Department,’” one person said, adding that “a lot of the lines he was using are exactly the same things that we hear Dodik saying.” A second person described Alden as “the principal driver behind Bosnia policy as it relates to Dodik and Republika Srpska” whose “fingerprints are all over” Trump’s second-term moves. A third person expressed concern that “over the next two years, we’re going to see Dodik move for secession … as a consequence of some of the policy decisions that Mr. Alden has been involved in.” Azerbaijan, where Alden is nominated to serve, is an Eastern European ally of Serbia whose president also maintains a good relationship with Dodik. The US is also seeking to keep Russian influence at bay there, a mission that could prove complicated for Alden to execute if he’s confirmed. “If these allegations are true, it shows incredibly poor judgment,” which “would be of concern for anyone becoming a US ambassador,” said Jim O’Brien, who served as assistant secretary of state for European and Eurasian affairs during the Biden administration. Alden previously changed his name from the common Bosniak surname Mulabdic, two of the people said. He currently advises Rubio as a special government employee, which allows him to remain a senior counselor for Palantir. His first Senate-confirmed job never materialized amid allegations of workplace misconduct . “Alden is a seasoned national security official who provides valuable policy advice drawing upon his extensive experience and expertise,” a State Department spokesperson said, adding that he “enjoys the full trust and confidence of senior leadership at the Department of State.” As for his name change, the spokesperson said “Alden is first and foremost an American working to advance American foreign policy around the world.” ‘Pretty Aggressive’ The people who spoke with Semafor said an understaffed State Department had allowed Alden the opportunity to intervene on behalf of Russia’s allies in Bosnia before senators confirmed Brendan Hanrahan as assistant secretary of State for European and Eurasian affairs three months ago. Five of the people said that Alden traveled to Bosnia in June for meetings of the region’s Peace Implementation Council, where he threatened European officials in attendance to approve the US’ choice to lead the region’s Office of the High Representative. Deputy Assistant Secretary of State for Western Central Europe and Southern Europe Dan Lawton led the delegation, but “it was clear [Alden] was the guy in charge [and] he wanted to force this guy through,” a fourth person said. “So the dynamic was pretty aggressive and oppressive; he was kind of looming over everybody.” The High Representative is an international body that enforces the Dayton Peace Accords, which ended Bosnia’s gruesome civil war three decades ago. Its previous leader, Christian Schmidt, quit, citing US pressure to leave the role. Dodik had long raged against Schmidt, whom he views as an impediment to Republika Srpska’s secession from Bosnia. He told a Serbian media outlet last month that he’d asked the Trump administration to “get rid” of the high representative in exchange for repealing certain laws. Alden personally selected the US pick to replace Schmidt, Italian diplomat Antonio Zanardi Landi, according to two of the people Semafor interviewed. Five of the people told Semafor that Alden warned the US might defund the office if European officials didn’t accept Landi, whom the European officials ultimately rejected. Landi was seen as likely to “do Dodik’s bidding,” as House Democrats laid out in a September report . Transparency International’s Srdjan Blagovcanin called the fallout the most “visible” evidence of a “wider divergence between EU and US” when it comes to Bosnia. The State Department spokesperson pushed back on the characterization of Alden’s behavior the meeting, saying Lawton was “the only one who spoke at the meeting” and “any assertion that he was looming over” attendees “pointed political nonsense.” A senior State Department official, who confirmed that Alden accompanied Lawton to the meetings, called Lawton “responsible for day-to-day US foreign policy in the Western Balkans.” They described the Trump administration’s approach as “led by Rubio,” with support from Deputy Secretary of State Christopher Landau, Hanrahan, “and other senior officials and advisers.” ‘Boot-On-The-Neck-Type Feeling’ The enduring stalemate over choosing a new high representative threatens to hurt US-backed plans for a gas pipeline that could counter Balkan dependence on Russian gas. Alden’s role in weakening the office, which was created to promote regional stability after the bloody civil war in the 1990s, is a potential red flag for senators in both parties. Yet senators may also not advance his nomination out of broader concern about Republika Srpska’s influence on the Trump administration. The territory’s government has spent more than $11 million lobbying the administration since 2025, according to Justice Department filings, and even more on informal efforts, like Dodik’s visit to Mar-a-Lago last week. That’s about four times what it spent between 2022 and 2024 . “Officials involved in corrupting US policy to Bosnia and Herzegovina and obstructing this committee’s oversight of the region should be held accountable for their complicity in advancing lobbying interests at the expense of peace in Bosnia,” Senate Foreign Relations Committee ranking membe

events.title: House Republicans to pick new leaders
events.summary: House Republicans will vote on Tuesday on whether to overhaul their leadership. Rep. Jim Jordan, R-Ohio, and current Majority Leader Steve Scalise, R-La., are competing for minority leader, after Speaker Mike Johnson opted against running for minority leadership (he might not even serve his full term next Congress). House Republicans will hold their candidate forum Tuesday morning and vote on their picks in the afternoon. Some in the party are hungry for new blood. Jordan, who rose up the ranks as a pugnacious Freedom Caucus and Judiciary Committee leader, would be the one to best demonstrate the “divergence in values between the two parties,” said Rep. Brian Mast, R-Fla. Others want to stay the course. “This election was not the fault of our leadership,” said Rep. Mike Simpson, R-Idaho. Current Majority Whip Tom Emmer, R-Minn., and Rep. August Pfluger, R-Texas, are running for minority whip. There’s competitive races downballot, too. Current Conference Chair Lisa McClain, R-Mich., faces challenges from Reps. Erin Houchin, R-Ind., and Greg Steube, R-Fla. And Reps. Brian Jack, R-Ga., and Rudy Yakym, R-Ind., are running for NRCC chair. Rep. Mark Alford, R-Mo., is running unopposed for conference secretary. — Nicholas Wu

events.title: The blue wave's tough-on-crime surprise
events.summary: Democrats swept into power last week as voters also embraced tougher criminal penalties and restrictions on bail. Why it matters: Six years after the George Floyd protests, Democrats won big without promising a return to sweeping 2020-era reforms. Some even adopted border-security rhetoric associated with Republicans. Democrats gained at least 12 state legislative chambers and won governorships in Georgia, Iowa, Nevada, Ohio and Texas. By the numbers: Voters approved all six statewide ballot measures Ballotpedia tracked that proposed tougher sentences, criminal penalties or bail restrictions in 2026. Five passed Nov. 3 in Indiana, Louisiana, Tennessee and Colorado. Alabama approved the sixth in May. Four expanded when courts could deny or restrict bail. Two increased penalties, including for fentanyl offenses and child sex trafficking. The shift: Some Democratic winners embraced tougher border-security language while opposing Trump's immigration crackdown. Texas Sen.-elect James Talarico called himself a "border security Democrat ," criticized former President Biden for failing to secure the border and said there needs to be comprehensive immigration reform. Michigan Sen.-elect Abdul El-Sayed , a progressive, said days before the election : "We needed tougher border security." He also criticized Trump's use of ICE. Zoom in: Colorado voters backed Democrats, tougher penalties and limits on federal immigration enforcement. That included electing Phil Weiser (D) as governor and approving tougher fentanyl penalties and life without parole for child sex trafficking. They rejected a measure requiring police to notify federal immigration authorities in certain cases involving violent crime suspects or people with prior felony convictions whose immigration status was unlawful or uncertain. Weiser and state Democrats are now weighing changes to the fentanyl measure, arguing it falls short on promised addiction treatment. Yes, but: Virginia voters approved automatically restoring voting rights to people convicted of felonies upon release from incarceration. Zoom out: Ballotpedia's historical analysis found more punitive sentencing and bail proposals dominated from 2022 through 2026, reversing 2012–2020, when less punitive measures appeared more often. Meanwhile, the nation's violent-crime rate plunged 9.7% in 2025 , its steepest annual decline in 90 years. The murder rate fell 18.5%, according to the FBI.

events.title: Scoop: El Salvador blasts U.S. State Dept. over Haiti gang war
events.summary: State Department officials have quietly raised objections to El Salvador's gang-fighting efforts in Haiti — even as President Trump has offered his full support, according to diplomatic notes and informed sources. On Monday, El Salvador issued a formal rebuke that questioned the "credibility" of the top U.S. diplomat in Haiti. Why it matters: The controversy exposes the tension between Trump's MAGA foreign policy objectives and the professional diplomatic establishment in the State Department. "There is a class of bureaucrats who don't want to see the change in the Western Hemisphere that POTUS wants," a U.S. official told Axios. Zoom in: Haiti is a failed state racked by extreme corruption and gang violence despite years of international efforts, including the UN-backed Gang Suppression Force (GSF) that El Salvador and other nations have backed. Four Salvadoran aviation technicians supporting medical evacuations were captured Oct. 18 by gangs that refused to heed the entreaties of El Salvador's President Nayib Bukele to return the men or their bodies. Bukele responded by surging special forces units to Haiti after receiving the blessing of Trump, an ally, on Oct. 27, Axios first reported . "You have to do what you have to do," Trump told Bukele, who proceeded to launch military operations that resulted in firefights with gangs in the streets of Port-Au-Prince. Friction point: Tensions between State Department officials and El Salvador erupted after an Oct. 31 gang attack on a Salvadoran convoy of five armored personnel carriers near the U.S. embassy, which was struck by gunfire. On Nov. 3, Salvadoran attack helicopters repelled gangs attacking GSF soldiers from Chad, Bukele posted on X . The next day, U.S. Chargé d'Affaires David Howell complained in a text message to Haitian Prime Minister Alix Didier Fils-Aimé that El Salvador wasn't "coordinating" with the GSF. "They took at least three casualties. They don't have a medical plan. They nearly killed GSF troops as I understand it," according to a copy of the text message shared with Axios. Howell asked the prime minister to tell El Salvador's defense ministry to stop operations "as soon as possible ... until they coordinate. They are going to kill [GSF] troops or civilians and or get themselves killed." El Salvador later accused Howell of spreading misinformation. On Nov. 5, the U.S. embassy in San Salvador sent a formal protest in a diplomatic note to Bukele's government, saying that the U.S. "strongly opposes this lack of coordination by Salvadoran military personnel," the document shown to Axios says. The note said El Salvador's "failure to coordinate" endangered the GSF and that "Salvadoran small arms fire" struck the U.S. embassy, "nearly hitting U.S. personnel." Behind the scenes: Bukele was infuriated by the so-called "dipnote," a source said. "His attitude was, 'What the f*ck? I checked with Trump. He said do what we have to do, and some bureaucrat is fighting this?' " said a source who spoke with Bukele. State Department officials said it was unclear who authorized the diplomatic note and didn't comment about Howell's correspondence to Haiti's prime minister. On Monday, Bukele's government fired back at Howell and the State Department officials. El Salvador's diplomatic note provided a point-by-point rebuttal with 4 "clarifications:" Regarding the gunfire that hit the embassy, El Salvador's ministry of foreign affairs wrote that its troops essentially had their backs to the building and were firing away from it. "It is ruled out that the fire from the Salvadoran personnel struck the facilities of the American Embassy," El Salvador wrote. 2. During the attack on troops from Chad, El Salvador wrote, "Salvadoran personnel repelled the attack. It is ruled out that the fire of the Salvadoran elements was directed toward the position of Chad." 3. El Salvador also said that since Oct. 26, its armed forces repeatedly have coordinated "air assets" with the GSF and Haitian officials. 4. In its most caustic reply, El Salvador said it "categorically denies" Howell's claim that three of its soldiers were casualties. "The fact that false information has been disseminated on a matter of such gravity, without providing any evidence to support it, generates serious doubts about the credibility of the rest of the assertions contained in the aforementioned report, which likewise lack any type of evidence that would allow their accuracy to be verified," the note said. What they're saying: An official spokesperson for El Salvador couldn't be reached. Haiti's prime minister didn't return messages seeking comment. A State Department official insisted that "three Salvadorans were injured ... one of which was serious enough to have been medevaced outside the country for additional treatment." A source close to El Salvador's government showed Axios a picture of the smiling soldier with a leg brace on and said he was flown out of Haiti because there were no adequate medical facilities, not because the injury was serious. The State Department, echoing comments from U.S. Secretary of State Marco Rubio on Sunday, said it appreciates El Salvador's efforts, "but the Trump administration has also been clear on the need to deconflict anti-gang operations to ensure seamless implementation of President Trump's policy to support efforts to free Haiti from gangs."

events.title: How Nvidia's crisis and politics could deliver the pause AI leaders want
events.summary: A political backlash against AI and data centers — now compounded by a crisis facing the technology's most influential champion — could help force a slowdown that industry leaders have struggled to achieve voluntarily. Why it matters: Tapping the brakes on AI development — which frontier AI developers claim to want but have so far failed to do given the risk of offering an advantage to a competitor — could give society more time to prepare for economic upheaval and the risks of superintelligent systems. A wave of Democratic victories and data center moratoriums is now joined by a potentially weakened Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang, who admitted to having a relationship with an alleged Chinese spy. Huang, who has led the industry in barreling through past resistance to AI acceleration, may be less able to do so while under a microscope. While both factors could stymie data center expansion in the U.S., it's far from clear that would slow AI's advance. Between the lines: Huang has been a powerful counterweight to calls for AI restraint, dismissing fears of an AI bubble or purported catastrophic risks to humanity from the technology. An investigation — by the board, an ascendant Democratic Congress or federal authorities — could curb his ability to make the case for continued expansion, leaving an opening for those calling for more restrictions. Nvidia says Huang will remain CEO and the news won't slow the company, but the potential impact on his political influence is hard to measure. The fallout extends beyond that. Nvidia is both the dominant supplier of AI chips and an investor in companies building AI infrastructure. A crisis that raises questions about its leadership, business practices or financial relationships could ripple through the industry's expansion plans. The intrigue: Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei, OpenAI CEO Sam Altman and SpaceX CEO Elon Musk have all warned about the potentially catastrophic risks of advanced AI, with all expressing, at times, the need to slow or pace the development of advanced AI. But the competitive race has made it difficult for any one company to hit the brakes without risking falling behind rivals or China in a high-stakes race for supremacy. What they're saying: Anthony Aguirre, CEO of the Future of Life Institute, says a slowdown in data center construction would be welcome, even if it wouldn't accomplish nearly as much as more direct restrictions on frontier AI development. "I'll take whatever I can get," Aguirre told Axios in an interview. Aguirre and a number of other researchers have long seen the development of increasingly powerful AI as an existential threat. But he is skeptical that slowing data center construction alone would buy society an additional year or two, given the vast computing resources companies already possess and the growing ability of AI systems to help improve themselves. Aguirre said the bigger opportunity may be political: Resistance to data centers could help generate momentum for legislation and regulation that more directly limits the development of potentially dangerous AI systems. The big picture: Aguirre argues that the goal shouldn't simply be to delay superintelligence by a year or two, but to reconsider whether humanity should build it at all. He favors a "pause and pivot" toward AI systems designed to augment human abilities rather than replace them. Other researchers and executives favor continued development with stronger safeguards, reflecting a broader debate over how much restraint is necessary and what form it should take. Yes, but: Slowing data center construction in the U.S. doesn't necessarily mean slowing AI progress globally. Meta and other companies are exploring data center construction outside the U.S. Google announced a plan last week to invest $15 billion over two years in Malaysia. And Chinese AI developers wouldn't face the same U.S. restrictions, potentially allowing them to narrow the gap with American competitors. The other side: The threat from China isn't as straightforward as it appears. Chinese AI companies benefit in part from distillation of leading American models and technical knowledge developed in the U.S., Aguirre said. Slowing the American frontier could therefore have some effect on China's pace as well. A U.S. decision to slow frontier development could open the door to direct conversations with China about mutually pacing the technology, rather than treating superintelligence as an unavoidable arms race. The bottom line: The AI industry is hoping to overcome political resistance and keep building. Advocates of slowing frontier AI see an opportunity to turn that resistance into something bigger: a chance to reconsider not just how fast AI should advance, but how far it should go.

events.title: The new battle for Congress: Trump's veto
events.summary: Democrats will charge into January with a sweeping mandate — but as President Trump has repeatedly noted, his veto power can deliver a robust roadblock to his opponents' agenda. Why it matters: Democrats may be forced to compromise to get legislative priorities through. Trump will have to decide how frequently he'll use the power — and whether he'll strike down bills popular among Americans. State of play: Democrats have secured 54 seats in the upcoming Senate, per the AP's projections , and are leading in two tight races in Mississippi and Alaska that have yet to be called. In the House, they've won 254, per AP , with several race calls still to come. Neither majority will be large enough to cross the two-thirds threshold Democrats would need to override a presidential veto on their own. Friction point: Trump knows that — and has teased his plans to impede Democrats' progress by using the power liberally. On Tuesday night, as election results rolled in, Trump posted an image of a red MAGA-esque hat that read "VETO" in all caps. A similar hat was displayed on the Resolute Desk during a Thursday signing ceremony. Asked on Fox News how he'd work with a Democratic Congress, Trump pointed to the veto: "They're in control, but they're really not in control because they can send over, you know, 50 different great bills that they're all excited about and I send them back with a nice stamp, veto." White House spokeswoman Lauren Bis said in a statement provided to Axios that Trump is "willing to work with anyone to continue delivering victories for hardworking Americans." She added, "If Democrats choose to pursue radical left policies, they are choosing to work against the American people." Worth noting: Lawmakers secured enough support to override a Trump veto across party lines during his first term on the National Defense Authorization Act in 2021. Yes, but: While Trump could use veto threats to force lawmakers to negotiate or to halt legislation altogether, vetoing popular measures could benefit Democrats' messaging for 2028, when a potential trifecta in all three branches of government would let them enact their agenda with little interference. Responding to an image of Trump's "VETO" hat Thursday, Sen. Elizabeth Warren (D-Mass.) wrote , "If Donald Trump wants to be Mr. Veto, let's test that out. The new Democratic majority in Congress should pass bills to make life more affordable and our government less corrupt." But doing so will still require coalition-building on the Hill, says Jonathan Lewallen, an associate professor at the University of Tampa who has studied policy agenda-setting and veto threats. He highlights two key issue areas where Trump has already threatened vetoes in the first half of his administration that Democrats have pledged to tackle: defense policy and consumer protection . Yes, but: "There may come a point in the next two years where Trump is still issuing lots of veto threats and potentially even vetoing the occasional bill, and it just becomes less effective as a strategy," Lewallen says. That means the administration might instead use another tactic with legislation they disagree with: quietly letting them become law automatically after 10 days without Trump's signature. The bottom line: Reversing Trump's agenda from Capitol Hill isn't expected to be smooth sailing. But winning back control of both chambers isn't just about passing bills, with Dem-led investigations, hearings and subpoenas expected on the horizon . events.title: AI stocks bounce back — with one notable exception
events.summary: Data: FactSet; Chart: Matt Phillips/Axios The AI trade has regained momentum despite — or maybe because of — Nvidia's struggles following the weekend revelations from CEO Jensen Huang. The big picture: Monday's sudden burst of exuberance for AI was the latest wide swing for a market upended by last week's "blue tsunami" in the midterm elections and the threat they could pose to the data center boom. By the numbers: The Nasdaq 100 index of large-cap technology shares soared 3.4%, its biggest daily jump since late March and its second-best showing of the year. Zoom in: Stocks romped across the AI ecosystem — well, with one important exception. Pick-and-shovel plays such as engineering and construction companies, and makers of data center inputs like fiberoptic cables, servers and data storage devices soared. The companies that build and lease out data center computing power, known as neoclouds, also jumped. (Those companies had been at the epicenter of recent jitters about financing for the AI boom.) Hyperscalers rose, paced by Meta, which notched a gain of 5.1%. Semiconductors roared, with the SOX index posting its best gain — 6.9% — since late July. Yes, but: The glaring exception to the AI-palooza was its best-known player, Nvidia. Weekend revelations from CEO Jensen Huang — who acknowledged having an affair with a woman suspected of connections to Chinese intelligence — left investors grappling with uncertainty about the CEO's future. The intrigue: Some investors may see Nvidia's pain as potential gain for rivals. Broadcom jumped 8.8%, its best day in nearly a year. Advanced Micro Devices soared 13.3%, benefiting also from an upgrade to "Outperform" — effectively, a "buy" recommendation — from Oppenheimer analysts on Sunday. Context: Bullish commentary from Wall Street established the background music for Monday's big bounce, as analysts urged investors to buy into the market's recent soft patch. "We believe stocks are now clearly in oversold territory," Goldman Sachs analysts wrote in a note Monday. "We believe the market's reaction to the midterms is overdone," wrote Morgan Stanley tech analysts in a note entitled "Buy the Drop: AI Investment Opportunities Post the U.S. Midterms," which it published Sunday night. "We do not think AI is a continued sell here. In fact, tech drawdown is offering certain opportunities. The selloff was very sharp," JPMorgan equity strategists wrote Monday. These analysts could be right. The recent slump has been deep in certain sectors such as chips. And buying the dip has been a solid strategy in recent years, especially for retail investors . The other side: On the other hand, there may be good reasons such stocks sold off. For example, even before the news about the Nvidia CEO or the anti-data center vote at the polls, Wall Street expectations for capital expenditures from hyperscalers had been looking a bit flat. Given that a large percentage of that AI investment is spent on the semiconductors needed to make these computing centers, well, compute, that would seem to be important for tech investors. What's next: Will the stock market's rally be the start of a new phase of AI exuberance? Or is it just an example of Wall Street's proverbial dead cat bounce ?

events.title: Support for death penalty reaches 50-year low, poll finds
events.summary: Support for the death penalty in the US has dropped to a more than 50-year low following a botched execution in Tennessee. Forty-nine percent of American adults approve of the death penalty for convicted murderers, according to Gallup , the first time the figure has dropped below 50% since 1971. Support for the death penalty is sliding among all political groups but most among Democrats, only 28% of whom are currently in favor. Seventy-three percent of Republicans are in favor of it, as well as half of independents. The poll was taken after the botched killing by lethal injection of Christa Pike, which caused Tennessee to pause executions for the remainder of the year. Outgoing California Gov. events.title: The Garbage Man: Bill Gates Has Earned Billions Investing in Climate-Polluting Landfills
events.summary: Mark Harris for ProPublica. Source images: Getty Images, RMI. In November 2015, world leaders descended on Paris to negotiate a historic agreement to limit global warming. But on the summit’s opening day, attention turned to a private citizen slouched awkwardly in a chair on stage: Bill Gates. Gates, with his characteristic flop of sandy hair, grinned impishly as President Barack Obama called him a “visionary” and a “driving force” behind a pair of pledges that both saw as key to the larger agreement. First the world’s largest economies would double their spending on research into clean-energy technologies. Then investors like Gates would back the startups that emerged. The Microsoft cofounder had already enlisted two dozen other billionaires to join the effort. For Gates, who’d become increasingly consumed by this unprecedented threat to human well-being, the moment marked his arrival as a leading figure in the fight against climate change. “If we back over 50 different breakthrough approaches, we know that several of those will give us the solution that we need,” Gates said during his own speech. He would invest at least $2 billion of his own money in companies developing geothermal wells, new kinds of nuclear reactors and machines that pull carbon from the air , to name just a few. With much less fanfare, however, Gates has put more than double that amount into a very dirty, old-school industry. At the time of the Paris summit, he was already the dominant shareholder of America’s No. 2 landfill operator, Republic Services. He has since increased his stake to 38% of the company, a position worth $29 billion. Bill Gates’ Stake in Republic Services, a Landfill Operator, Now Exceeds a Fifth of His Net Worth Note: “Other” includes stakes in other publicly traded companies and accumulated dividends and investment returns. Sources: Forbes’ The World’s Billionaires, Bloomberg’s Billionaires Index, SEC filings, StockAnalysis.com Chris Alcantara/ProPublica While fossil fuels get most of the attention, scientists increasingly see landfills as a crucial climate issue. They’re responsible for as much as a fifth of the country’s emissions of methane , a highly potent greenhouse gas, studies show. Republic alone generates as much climate pollution as 3 million gasoline-burning cars each year, according to its own reports. One might imagine that a landfill operator with Gates as its largest shareholder — and with three people closely linked to Gates on its board — would lead the way in tackling those emissions. Even after seemingly softening his stance on global warming in a controversial blog post last year, Gates remains one of the world’s most prominent voices on the issue. As he did in his bestselling 2021 book “How to Avoid a Climate Disaster,” he continues to advocate for cutting emissions , and he has called on his fellow business leaders to do their part.  Gates, though, has failed to make Republic live up to his own climate principles, a ProPublica investigation has found. Federal inspectors have repeatedly found methane escaping from Republic landfills at levels above federal limits. The company has refrained from adopting the ambitious emissions-reduction goal embraced by its main competitor. Republic has even lobbied against policies that could make the wider industry cleaner, including by keeping organic waste out of landfills in the first place. “It seems very likely that Bill Gates has the power to influence Republic’s behavior to make it more climate-friendly, even if that costs the company profits,” said Ann Lipton, a legal scholar who studies corporate governance at the University of Colorado, Boulder.  As for whether he should, in her words, “put his money where his mouth is,” Lipton said, “you can leave it to the reader to make the moral judgment.” Gates’ Climate Awakening Gates didn’t respond to repeated requests to discuss his landfill investments, and ProPublica couldn’t find any public comments he’s made about them. But the bet has proven wildly lucrative. Since November 1999, when he emerged as the owner of 5% of Republic’s shares — “ It’s ‘Garbage In’ for Gates ,” the New York Post headline read — the company’s stock price has soared thirtyfold. And Gates has personally received $2.6 billion in dividends, a ProPublica analysis of securities filings shows. In those early days, Gates hadn’t yet awakened to the threat of global warming. It was a different time. Microsoft Windows ran on more than 80% of personal computers. Gates was the world’s richest person, and his bespectacled face graced the cover of Time magazine twice that year . He was simultaneously criticized for what a federal judge determined to be Microsoft’s monopolistic practices and admired for establishing what was soon to become the world’s largest charitable foundation.  A rare clue to why Gates made his foray into landfills can be found in an interview he gave to Fortune that year. To fund his plan to give away virtually his entire fortune, he said he’d given his personal money manager, Michael Larson, a simple remit: Sell Microsoft shares, buy safe, boring assets.  Republic’s then-chairman, billionaire Wayne Huizenga , had flown Larson by helicopter to his private golf course in Florida, according to the article. It’s unclear if Huizenga pitched Republic there, but it fit the remit. America would always produce trash, ensuring a steady stream of revenue. After that initial investment, Larson progressively increased Gates’ stake in Republic over the years that followed. Larson would also acquire a small chunk of Republic’s main competitor, Waste Management — which Huizenga also once led — on behalf of the Gates Foundation. It was only in 2006, when he asked two climate scientists to educate him, that Gates started to grasp the potentially “catastrophic” effects of greenhouse gases , he later wrote. But he also saw that the poorest people in the world needed more energy to improve their lot. The solution, he concluded, was something climate activists often underplay: innovation that could make clean energy cheap enough to naturally displace fossil fuels. That was the idea behind Breakthrough Energy, the initiative he launched in Paris in 2015. Microsoft co-founder Bill Gates, right, then-U.S. President Barack Obama, left, and then-French President François Hollande applaud a speech during the United Nations conference on climate change in Paris in 2015. Jim Watson/AFP via Getty Images Around the same time, methane began to emerge as a focus of climate action. The gas can trap 80 times more heat than carbon dioxide in the near term, and it’s responsible for one-third of the global warming we experience today, according to the United Nations Environment Programme. events.summary: Dubai’s Nakheel has unveiled a new master development next to Palm Jebel Ali as property developers continue to launch housing projects despite Iran war-driven uncertainty. Palm Springs, a 3.8 million-square-metre residential masterplan, will have a mix of villas, townhouses and apartments, Nakheel said on Tuesday. It will also have education, health care, sport and leisure facilities across 15 neighbourhoods in southern Dubai, with two schools, a hospital and six mosques. Property developers are continuing to launch projects in Dubai despite concerns about the slowing of the market as the Iran war continues. events.title: China's trade surplus surpasses $1 trillion for a 2nd straight year, as exports surge 35%
events.summary: China says its trade surplus exceeded $1 trillion for a 2nd straight year HONG KONG -- China’s trade surplus exceeded $1 trillion for a second straight year , according to official data released Tuesday, as pressure mounts for greater balance in trade with Beijing. Exports in October surged 35.2% from a year earlier, the customs agency said. Exports have grown rapidly this year supported by high-tech goods like semiconductors and autos. Imports rose 41.6% year-on-year. Between January and October, China logged a $1.04 trillion trade surplus, even as the trade surplus narrowed last month to $105.3 billion from $133.5bn in September as imports picked up pace. That puts China on track for surpassing last year’s record $1.2 trillion trade surplus. “We expect Chinese exports to stay strong for the rest of this year, led by electronics and autos,” said Dave Chia, an economist at Moody’s Analytics. Overcapacity in many industries, excess domestic savings and weakened domestic demand are still forcing China to ship its goods abroad as some countries move to protect their own industries, said Alicia García-Herrero, chief economist for Asia Pacific at French bank Natixis. The situation is not sustainable, she said. Businesses are feeling the pressure of ferocious competition as China’s economy has slowed , said Cinders Zhou, who sells eyewear for a manufacturer in Linhai city in eastern China’s Zhejiang province. “It comes down to product quality, or rather the increasingly the lack of it across the industry, since there’s significant homogenization,” said Zhou, whose company makes frames and lenses sold both in and outside China. “That has forced everyone to compete on price,” she said. Trade curbs by the European Union pose an important risk at a time of heightened U.S. trade barriers and tariffs , Chia said. Top Chinese officials insist Beijing is not seeking to expand the trade surplus but wants more balanced global trade. House Republicans consider issuing subpoena to Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang resigns amid alleged affair with reported spy China says its trade surplus exceeded $1 trillion for a 2nd straight year, as exports in October surged 35% China’s exports could be vulnerable to setbacks for the artificial intelligence industry, a concern that deepened with the Democratic victories in the U.S. midterm elections given the public backlash against expansion of data centers. “If the AI boom slows or turns into a correction, lower chip and electronics prices and smaller shipping volumes would hit China’s exports hard,” Chia said. Trade is among the top issues likely to be on the agenda in planned meetings between U.S. President Donald Trump and Chinese leader Xi Jinping on the sidelines of the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation leaders summit later this month in China’s technology hub Shenzhen. A two-month extension of a trade truce until January has provided some relief to exporters, though it’s unclear how long that may last. U.S. and European trade policies have added “a lot of difficulties” for Chinese businesses to expand in the markets, said Wang Xin, head of the Shenzhen Cross-Border E-Commerce Association, an industry group. Strong exports have helped offset sluggish domestic demand in China, where the economy is forecast to meet Beijing’s official target of a 4.5% to 5% annual growth this year, slightly slower than last year’s 5% expansion. events.title: House Dems size up 2028 Senate map after midterm landslide
events.summary: Current and former House Democrats, flush with victory following their landslide midterm wins , are already looking at potential opportunities to run for Senate in 2028, Axios has learned. Why it matters: Democrats' 2026 romp — with wins in Texas, South Carolina, Kansas and possibly even Mississippi — has some party members reevaluating what were once considered impossible targets. A source close to Rep. Sharice Davids (D-Kan.) — who was reelected by 21 percentage points in a district former Vice President Harris carried by four points in 2024 — did not rule out her running against Sen. Jerry Moran (R-Kan.). "All options are on the table," the source said, adding that Davids' "focus right now is on delivering actual results and overcoming the chaos from these extreme policies we're seeing." Sen. Roger Marshall (R-Kan.) was defeated by Democrat Adam Hamilton last week, marking the first time in nearly a century a Democrat has been elected to the U.S. Senate from Kansas. North Carolina: Rep. Don Davis is "taking a look at" a run against Republican Sen. Ted Budd, a source familiar with his thinking told Axios. Davis won a third term on Tuesday after defeating his GOP opponent in a district President Trump carried by 12 points in 2024. Republicans redrew the district with the express goal of ensuring Davis' loss. Former Rep. Wiley Nickel, who was elected Wake County district attorney on Tuesday, would consider a Senate run if state Attorney General Jeff Jackson doesn't, a source close to him told Axios. The two served together in the House. Democratic former Gov. Roy Cooper won North Carolina's other U.S. Senate seat last week in a nearly 20-percentage-point landslide over Republican Michael Whatley. Pennsylvania: A huge field of Democrats is gearing up to potentially run for the seat held by Democratic Sen. John Fetterman. Fetterman, who has morphed from a populist firebrand to an arch-centrist, has angered much of the party by siding with Republicans on key votes. Rep. Chris Deluzio (D-Pa.) told Axios in a statement: "I am thinking hard about my next steps and will be having that conversation with my family and supporters." Said former Rep. Susan Wild: "I am not ruling anything out at this time. ... I think PA is long overdue for a woman senator, and that will factor into my eventual decision." Florida: State Rep. Angie Nixon is already hinting at a 2028 run against Republican Sen. Ashley Moody after losing to her on Tuesday by three percentage points. But some in the party's centrist wing believe Nixon's left-wing politics and her affiliation with the Democratic Socialists of America may have cost her in a Democratic wave year and are looking to recruit elsewhere. Rep. Jared Moskowitz (D-Fla.), who won reelection in a district Trump carried by nine points in 2024 and is often mentioned as a potential candidate for statewide office, is in the mix, sources said. Sources also pointed to Rep. Kathy Castor (D-Fla.), who won in a district that went for Trump by 11 points, as another possible candidate. A Castor spokesperson did not respond to a request for comment.

events.title: France says Iranian hackers sabotaged supermarket refrigerators
events.summary: The French government has blamed an Iranian military hacking unit for cyberattacks that disrupted refrigeration systems at roughly 700 grocery stores and other retail locations last month, causing food losses and at least 15 fires. Why it matters: The attacks underscore how Iranian government hackers are moving beyond stealing data and disrupting websites to manipulating the physical equipment that keeps essential services running. Driving the news: France's Ministry for Europe and Foreign Affairs attributed the Oct. 11–12 attacks to Iran on Monday, calling them the country's first cyberattack campaign conducted purely for sabotage on French territory. The government's Cyber Crisis Coordination Center specifically attributed the attacks to Shahid Kaveh, a hacking unit within Iran's Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps. Hackers manipulated refrigeration equipment to raise temperatures, causing tens of millions of euros in food losses and at least 15 fires, according to French officials. The same operation also targeted equipment at small hydroelectric facilities in France, with limited effects, according to an intelligence report. Yes, but: The French government has not publicly attributed a separate wave of refrigeration attacks that occurred last week to the same hackers. Zoom in: French intelligence linked Shahid Kaveh to several online hacktivist personas, including CyberAveng3rs and Soldiers of Solomon, that publicly claim responsibility for the unit's operations. Investigators found that infrastructure used in the refrigeration attacks was also used to scan industrial equipment using techniques previously associated with Shahid Kaveh. They also found traces of Farsi in the attack infrastructure and identified a propaganda outlet linked to the unit that publicized the attack. The big picture: Iran has a history of targeting industrial equipment in cyber operations, including American water systems and Israeli refrigeration equipment. French intelligence linked Shahid Kaveh to attacks on Israeli refrigeration equipment earlier this year and a 2023 campaign targeting industrial controllers manufactured by Unitronics. What to watch: France plans to summon Iran's ambassador and propose new European Union sanctions against Iranian individuals and entities involved in the attacks.

events.title: Republican infighting escalates after election drubbing
events.summary: The News Fresh off what one senator called a “good old-fashioned shellacking,” Republicans are now turning to a more painful phase of their post-election soul-searching: the airing of grievances. Several senators are unhappy about a rush to reelect the GOP’s Senate leadership team after voters repudiated the party’s reign in Washington. A small but vocal minority is pushing to delay leadership elections beyond Tuesday, giving more time for a potential challenger to emerge against Majority Leader John Thune and his team. Thune’s allies say the move is unnecessary, won’t change the result, and will only lead to more intraparty fighting after an election that could cost the Senate GOP as many as nine seats. Either way, the party’s second-guessing of Thune and President Donald Trump — not to mention its uncertainty about its own agenda — will come to a head on Tuesday morning in the Old Senate Chamber. “I saw five signatures on a letter,” Sen. Kevin Cramer, R-N.D., told Semafor of his colleagues advocating for a delay. “I think we have to talk, but I don’t see why we’d need to change the leadership to do that.” Beneath the procedural battle are huge debates within the Republican Party about where to turn next. A party that did little to defy Trump’s unpopular war with Iran and his tariffs now must figure out what strategic adjustments to make — or, perhaps, whether to make none at all. Cramer blamed the stunning losses on “bad negotiations with Canada, tariffs, not supporting Ukraine enough to end the war” and allowing more foreign beef into the US. He said “people who are overly surprised” by the election result “probably aren’t being honest with themselves.” Retiring Sen. Joni Ernst, R-Iowa, who dubbed it a “shellacking,” said the “war in Iran is extremely unpopular. I don’t know what the secretary is briefing the president [on], but it’s not working.” “We need to have a tough, family conversation. We just lost seven Senate seats. And there may be more,” said Sen. Josh Hawley, R-Mo. “I see a lot of blame shifting going on in all of these postmortems. I think it’s probably time for people in Congress to take responsibility for what Congress did.” Hawley cited Medicaid cuts, the GOP’s closeness to data centers, its turn away from anti-abortion priorities, and its move to “abandon” poor people and the working class. He said he couldn’t pledge his vote to Thune or the rest of the leadership team right now. Sen. Ron Johnson, R-Wis., who is leading the effort to delay the leadership election, was even more harsh: “After that stunning defeat, we just can’t continue on business as usual. I mean … that kind of defeat demands change.” “You can’t come off a defeat like that and just ram through elections and just elect that leadership team by acclamation,” Johnson said. “It’s obnoxious, particularly at this moment.” Trump said on Monday that it’s up to the GOP senators to make a call on Thune, calling him a “very fine man” but lamenting that he wishes “they could get more produced.” Thune said he didn’t see how delaying the election “solves anything” but agreed the GOP needs to discuss its future. ‘Just move forward’ Johnson’s bid to delay the leadership elections means that before taking any votes on them, the GOP will have a special conference meeting beginning at 9 a.m. on Tuesday. They will then vote on whether to delay the elections of Thune and the rest of the leadership team, which includes Whip John Barrasso of Wyoming; Conference Chair Tom Cotton of Arkansas; Sen. Shelley Moore Capito, R-W.Va ., the policy chair; and Conference Vice Chair James Lankford of Oklahoma. The GOP is also expected to select Sen. Bernie Moreno, R-Ohio, a top ally of Trump, as its new campaign chair. A similar delay bid failed in 2022 after the GOP lost one Senate seat. Though the losses this month are several magnitudes greater, several Republican senators said they don’t expect the vote to prevail. Some think the effort to delay is merely a smokescreen to undercut Thune. “This is a question that will come up tomorrow: If there’s a desire for a leadership change, then let’s make the leadership change. I don’t sense that, and so I think we ought to just move forward as planned. We’ll have a vote, the majority will rule,” Capito told Semafor. She said the election was a wakeup call for Republicans to take Americans’ concerns about rising prices more seriously: “Message received.” That doesn’t mean it will necessarily translate into a binding bipartisan effort to end Trump’s tariffs or wind down the Iran war. And for either idea to clear the Senate, the GOP’s votes will be required — even with what could be a brawny 56-seat Democratic majority in the Senate and a House majority in the 250s, Trump can still wield the veto pen. “Ultimately, I think the lesson is: We needed senators to act in a more independent fashion. But even Susan Collins — who was very independent — didn’t survive it because the whole election became about Donald Trump and whether he was concerned about gas prices,” said Sen. Rand Paul, R-Ky. Voters, Paul concluded, “were just mad.” Paul said he was probably OK with a leadership vote on Tuesday after a “frank discussion.” He added that his hope coming out of the election would be more Republicans joining him in voting against the Iran war and tariffs. The View From The House Change may not come for the Senate GOP. But across the Capitol, House Republicans will see a big shakeup as they choose a new minority leader in a race between Reps. Jim Jordan, R-Ohio, and Steve Scalise, R-La. Burgess’s view Thune doesn’t even have a challenger, it’s hard to see a scenario where he isn’t reelected as leader on Tuesday. But the anger within the Republican Party is real, and perhaps a bit misdirected. Few senators beyond Paul want to blame Trump for the party’s crushing losses, but midterms are as much a referendum on the president as they are on the Congress. This is just the beginning of what’s going to be a long and painful debate within the GOP about whether Republicans are still Trump’s party — or whether they should change course, if they’re capable of it. Notable Democrats may have a leadership race of their own; Sen. Chris Van Hollen, D-Md., declined on Monday to rule out running against Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer.
