events.title: Jensen Huang’s Troubles Leave the AI Industry Reeling
events.summary: No executive has pulled the strings in the artificial intelligence era quite like Nvidia’s CEO, Jensen Huang . He parlayed the boom into incredible wealth, became a close confidant of President Donald Trump, and emerged as a prominent voice in US–China relations. That now all stands in the balance. Over the past few days, Huang’s status as an AI titan has come under scrutiny amid an admission that he had an affair with Alice Huang , an executive at a Singapore-based company whom US intelligence services concluded was a Chinese intelligence asset. Nvidia’s board of directors said the company would launch an investigation into the incident. Huang, the company said, “fully supports the review and has committed to cooperating with it.” Huang earned $36 million last year and owned about 3.5 percent of Nvidia as of March, according to a corporate filing—which also noted that Huang is an at-will employee who can be let go anytime without severance. How exactly the investigation shakes out, and what it means for Huang’s future at the company, remains to be seen. But the incident at least puts his position at risk, and raises questions about how the industry will respond. “He’s the person who decides who gets the chips and who doesn't,” says David Yoffie, a professor at Harvard Business School who tracks the chip industry. Nvidia, which Huang cofounded in 1993, controls 90 percent of the market for chips used in training frontier AI models. With those chips in short supply, Huang has the power to determine which areas of AI get a boost next. Nvidia has also bankrolled much of the AI buildout, investing billions in the very companies buying its chips, such as OpenAI and Anthropic. When Elon Musk wants to build a new data center, Yoffie says, he can put in a call to Huang. Internally, Huang closely manages even small details at Nvidia, responds to emails from any one of its roughly 60,000 staffers, and raises his voice to get points across, according to current and former employees. He’s a regular on cable TV and at tech conferences, where he’s been trying to deflate concerns about an AI market bubble and boost the positioning of his company . But Nvidia has no other executive anywhere close to Huang’s prominence, and no apparent potential successor. “We have no idea who would replace him,” Yoffie says. “You put someone new into that position, if you're a customer, who knows what that's going to mean.” Ryan Fedasiuk, a senior fellow at the think tank Foundation for American Innovation, says Huang has played such an important role—and become so close to the president—that he has become load-bearing for the entire US AI industry. “On the one hand, Huang is irreplaceable. He built Nvidia into the juggernaut it is today, and he was the visionary behind the GPU, which has sustained the intelligence revolution,” Fedasiuk says. But he says that the company, which is indispensable to the AI industry, has to come first. “He has to be replaceable as the CEO of the world's largest company, at $4 trillion in capex.” Nvidia shares fell more than 4 percent on Monday, even as broader stock market indices rose. The board’s investigation will most likely focus on whether Huang violated any company policies, Yoffie says. But the FBI could also investigate whether laws were broken, and Congress may decide to look into whether Huang’s affair influenced the US government’s policy on selling chips to China. Nvidia didn’t immediately respond to WIRED’s request for comment. The scandal also raises serious questions about whether China may have gained sensitive information about US AI companies and the government’s strategy on China, Fedasiuk says. Huang’s affair appears especially damning given how outspoken he has been in recent years against calls for more aggressive technology export controls on China. His credibility on the topic could be permanently in doubt. Both the first Trump administration and the Biden administration imposed export controls designed to limit China’s access to Nvidia’s chips, as well as to technology required to mint advanced semiconductors. In his second term, however, Trump loosened these controls, giving China access to older generations of Nvidia chips; it was better to make China reliant on US technology, the argument went. Sam Bresnick , a research fellow at Georgetown University’s Center for Security and Emerging Technology, says the Huang scandal is likely to accelerate efforts to crack down on chip exports. “There was going to be more of an impetus to control what chips are getting sent to China anyway,” he says. “I expect there to be more scrutiny on what's going on, what's getting sent to China. I think there's also going to be more scrutiny from the Commerce Department.” In your inbox: For life-tested picks, sign up for our Gear newsletters Airbnb hosts are furious they can no longer make guests do their chores big story: cool kids write in all lowercase —does that make you mad?

Bank of Canada Governor Tiff Macklem’s role as Chair of the Consultative Council for the Americas (CCA) of the BIS extended until 31 March 2027. The central bank Governors of the Global Economy Meeting (GEM) at the Bank for International Settlements (BIS) have appointed Bank of Korea Governor Hyun Song Shin as Chair of the Committee on Payments and Market Infrastructures (CPMI) for a renewable three-year term. The CPMI brings together central banks from around the world to monitor and analyse developments in payment, clearing and settlement systems and to develop international standards and guidance. Mr Shin took up his new role on 1 November 2026. He succeeds Fabio Panetta, Governor of the Bank of Italy and Chair of the BIS Board of Directors. In addition, the Board of Directors has extended the term of Tiff Macklem, Governor of the Bank of Canada, as Chair of the Consultative Council for the Americas (CCA) until 31 March 2027. The Board has also appointed Santiago Bausili, Governor of the Central Bank of Argentina, as CCA Chair starting 1 April 2027, for a two-year term. The CCA was established in May 2008 as an advisory committee to the BIS Board of Directors. It comprises the Governors of the eight BIS member central banks in the Americas: Argentina, Brazil, Canada, Chile, Colombia, Mexico, Peru and the United States. The BIS Representative Office for the Americas , located in Mexico City, provides the secretariat for the CCA.

events.title: Sex, secrets and spies: The history of suspected honey traps
events.summary: Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang's affair with a woman suspected of spying for China echoes past controversies involving prominent Americans whose romantic relationships raised national security concerns. Why it matters: Foreign intelligence operatives can use romantic relationships to gain access to political intelligence, corporate secrets and classified information — posing serious national security risks. Driving the news: Jensen Huang acknowledged an extramarital affair in a message to employees Sunday, following reports that he had a relationship with a suspected Chinese spy. Per The New York Times , U.S. authorities suspected China's Ministry of State Security of recruiting Alice Huang to seek information about Jensen Huang and influence his feelings about selling AI chips to Chinese firms. Nvidia's board says it has no reason to believe company secrets or national security were compromised. China has also denied the allegations. Zoom out: The evidence of foreign intelligence involvement varies, with some cases involving actual security breaches, while others raised concerns about possible foreign spying. Read more below. Jensen Huang State of play: Reports about Jensen Huang's relationship with Alice Huang have raised questions about whether Chinese intelligence gained access to Nvidia's secrets or sought to influence its business decisions. AFP and Reuters photos showed them together in 2024 and 2025. Employees reported seeing Jensen Huang at Megaspeed's offices, where Alice Huang worked as an executive, according to Culper Research, a short-seller that published a report on Nvidia's China business in May 2026. An employee told Culper that Jensen and Alice had a "very close" relationship. What's next: Three Republican House committee chairs have requested a briefing with Huang about his relationship with Alice Huang and Nvidia's safeguards against foreign threats. James J. Smith and Katrina Leung A 2006 DOJ report found that counterintelligence agent James J. Smith had a secret 18-year affair with Katrina Leung, an FBI informant who was suspected of passing information onto China. The investigation found that Leung had provided classified U.S. government information to China without FBI authorization, exposing major failures in the bureau's oversight of informants. A DOJ inspector general investigation also found that Leung had an affair with another FBI agent, William Cleveland. Smith and Leung were arrested in 2003. Both ultimately pleaded guilty to making false statements, rather than espionage charges. Maria Butina and Paul Erickson Russian activist-turned-politician Maria Butina pleaded guilty in 2018 to conspiring to act as an unregistered agent of the Russian government after becoming romantically involved with Republican operative Paul Erickson. Federal prosecutors withdrew the allegation that she traded sex for political access, saying they misinterpreted the evidence, per ABC News . Prosecutors maintained that Butina used her relationship with Erickson to conceal activities intended to advance Russian interests, according to ABC News. Eric Swalwell and Christine Fang FBI records declassified in August 2026 show former Congressman Eric Swalwell acknowledged having sexual encounters with a suspected Chinese operative, Christine Fang, per the Washington Post . According to the records , Swalwell said the interactions were casual and that they never formally dated. Flashback: In 2020, Axios uncovered that Fang had targeted politicians in California, including Swalwell. According to reports, Fang participated in fundraising for Swalwell's campaign and helped place an intern in his office. Intelligence officials told Axios at the time that Fang gained access to political power through fundraising, networking, personal charisma, and romantic or sexual relationships with at least two Midwestern mayors, too. The FBI never accused Swalwell of wrongdoing in connection with his relationship with Fang, per the Washington Post. Benjamin Bishop In 2014, defense contractor Benjamin Pierce Bishop pleaded guilty to disclosing classified information to a Chinese woman with whom he had a romantic relationship, according to the Department of Justice . Bishop was sentenced to more than seven years in prison for disclosing classified national defense information and unlawfully retaining classified documents. According to the DOJ , Bishop, a former Army lieutenant colonel, retrieved a classified photograph of a Chinese naval asset at his girlfriend's request.

events.title: Nvidia CEO is in Congress’ sights after spy scandal
events.summary: The News Nvidia and its embattled CEO can add Washington to their list of huge problems. Members of Congress in both parties are pushing for strengthened export controls and investigations of company chief Jensen Huang after he admitted an affair with a woman accused by US intelligence of spying for the Chinese government. Beyond the corporate governance questions raised by the furor, lawmakers are incensed by reports that Nvidia may have pushed for access to its chips by dubious Chinese companies. After Democrats’ resounding victories in the midterm elections — after campaigning on promises to investigate big corporations and CEOs — Huang is in line for especially sharp scrutiny. Huang’s future is up to his board, not Congress, but lawmakers can pass stricter export controls that would limit Nvidia’s chip sales to Beijing and drag the CEO to Capitol Hill for an investigation of the company’s dealings with China. “Nvidia says it’s going to investigate, but we need a Senate investigation, and I’m going to be chairing” the investigations arm of the Intelligence Committee next year, said Sen. Richard Blumenthal, D-Conn. “Whether it’s my subcommittee or another, there needs to be a really penetrating, comprehensive investigation of all the possible compromises of our intelligence that may have occurred, but also the reasons that Donald Trump is so high on the head of Nvidia,” Blumenthal added. “So it is not just an intelligence issue; it’s also a potential corruption issue.” Stronger export controls, which Nvidia has lobbied to kill, are a likely first consequence. The top House Democrat and future Speaker-in-waiting, Rep. Hakeem Jeffries, said Monday that he “strongly supports” the stricter chip export control provisions that the Senate has already advanced in its annual defense policy bill. “We’re going to work hard to make sure that those provisions make it into the final version,” Jeffries told reporters, adding: “We’re going to need a full briefing specifically as it relates to the Nvidia issue, so we can all get to the bottom of what happened.” The chief authors of the Senate-passed export controls plan, Sens. Elizabeth Warren, D-Mass., and Jim Banks, R-Ind., affirmed their proposal in a joint statement that said the Commerce Department also needs to immediately close any export control loopholes. Huang is poised to face Hill investigations into his knowledge of the woman at the center of the scandal, Alice Huang, as well as his relationships with the White House and Commerce. Sen. Chris Coons, D-Del., the incoming Foreign Relations Committee chair, said he wants a probe “to determine whether our national security was compromised.” “We need answers about the relationship between AI billionaires and the Trump administration, who’s making these decisions, and who’s really got their hand on the wheel,” added Coons. Huang will have some backup from President Donald Trump, who defended him on Monday as “an amazing guy.” Trump said the Nvidia CEO told him during a conversation earlier in the day, when asked, that “he had absolutely no idea that the person in question was a spy.” The Commerce Department and the White House did not respond to a request for comment. The intelligence wrinkle Republican leaders, fresh off bruising losses in the midterms, were quieter following the intelligence briefing they received in the Capitol on Monday. “We want to be responding in a serious way to anything that threatens America’s national security interests or our values,” Senate Majority Leader John Thune told reporters. Asked how Congress should respond to the Nvidia crisis, House Speaker Mike Johnson told Semafor: “They’re still gathering information on all that.” The more striking circumspection came from other lawmakers on intelligence committees, who were clearly hesitant to call for immediate action until more details were shared about Huang’s relationship with Alice Huang. “We don’t know much about anything other than [that] this gentleman had relationships. We don’t know where it went,” Sen. Ron Wyden, D-Ore., told Semafor. “I’m on the intelligence committee, and I’ll leave it at that … until we have a chance to run down more information.” Another committee member, Sen. Mike Rounds, R-S.D., said that he doesn’t expect to get more details from the Trump administration, but that “we’ll work it through Senate Intel. Most certainly we have access to that information, and I think we’ll be able to get it.” Asked if Huang should testify before Congress, the Senate intelligence panel’s top Democrat, Mark Warner of Virginia, demurred: “Lots of people have expressed concerns …. I want to get more facts before I weigh in.” Regarding the potential that sensitive information may have been compromised by Huang’s actions, given the advanced chips his company manufactures, Warner told Semafor: “I’m not going to speculate at this point in time ... We need to hear from the FBI, and they weren’t there today.” Trump also told reporters on Monday that “the FBI is looking into it,” without elaborating further. An FBI spokesperson declined to comment. Notable Coons spoke with NPR in depth about his Nvidia plans.

events.title: Trump: New Iran attacks "quite unlikely"
events.summary: President Trump said Monday that a renewed military campaign against Iran is "quite unlikely" and "doesn't seem to be necessary." Why it matters: Trump stopped short of saying the war was over, but his comments on Truth Social and at an impromptu press conference were the furthest he went in that direction since February. Trump made his comments less than a week after conceding that the war was one of the reasons Republicans lost the midterm elections. Driving the news: The president in recent days has been weighing three options: launch new strikes, continue to strangle Iran's regime economically, or cut a deal that includes significant concessions to the Iranians. Trump signaled on Monday that he's going with the strangle strategy for now. That means keeping up the "status quo" — continuing the naval blockade, in addition to a new operation dubbed "Iron Gate" to cut off land routes that Iran uses to move advanced weaponry and other technology. Trump said the war is "effectively over" militarily. But he added that he doesn't want to formally announce that before he makes sure U.S. allies in the region are safe. "We have great allies and we have to make sure they are not hurt. We want a long-term solution," Trump said. State of play: Trump made his comments hours after meeting with Qatari Prime Minister Sheikh Mohammed bin Abdul Rahman Al Thani about the negotiations with Iran. "Qatar, Saudi Arabia, UAE, Bahrain, Kuwait, and others, would prefer the status quo" to resuming the war, Trump said. The Qatari prime minister also met separately with Vice President Vance, who's been leading the Iran talks for the administration in recent weeks. Al Thani wrote on X that he discussed with Trump ways "to progress the U.S.-Iran talks." "Grateful for the positive discussions on reaching a deal and bringing peace to the region," he added. A diplomat briefed on the details of the meeting said Trump made clear to Al Thani that he wants a deal and will give negotiations a chance. But he also noted that if Iranians don't take negotiations seriously, he could reverse course, the diplomat said. What he is saying: "Should there be any change with respect to developments in the Middle East, the United States of America is locked and loaded and ready to go. At this point, however, that seems to be quite unlikely," Trump wrote on Truth Social. "We are seeing positive momentum toward an end to this Conflict, and will ensure that America's interests are at all times protected. At the conclusion of this Military Engagement, the American People, and the World, will be far safer and more secure," he added. What to watch: Trump said that Iran is "talking very politely" with the U.S. and noted that there is a "good chance that could get ended," seemingly referring to the military conflict. "Hope we are gonna be able to make a deal with them," he added. The other side: Iran's Supreme National Security Council secretary, Mohsen Rezaei, wrote on X shortly after Trump made his comments that the war "has wrecked the U.S. government." He called Trump comments about negotiations with Iran "imaginary" and called on the U.S. "to SURRENDER" to Iran's conditions for ending the war. What we're watching: Oil prices have eased in recent weeks amid optimism that combat will end. Brent crude oil futures dropped to $92 on Monday.

events.title: What we know about the mystery woman at the center of Nvidia's spy scandal
events.summary: Alice Huang, a former executive of a Singapore-based AI computing company, is at the center of a suspected Chinese espionage scandal after Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang acknowledged an extramarital affair. Why it matters: The investigation raises questions about whether Chinese intelligence sought access to Nvidia's technology and CEO through Alice Huang as the U.S. and China compete in the AI race. Driving the news: Over the weekend, Jensen Huang admitted in a letter to Nvidia employees that he had a romantic relationship with a suspected Chinese spy. Though he did not name Alice Huang, the letter came after The New York Times first reported that U.S. authorities believed she was a Chinese spy in October. Photos captured Alice and Jensen Huan g together in 2024 and 2025. Though they have the same surname, Alice and Jensen Huang are not related or married. Jensen Huang has been married to Lori Huang for 40 years. Context: Little is known about Alice Huang. She has lead a Singapore-based company called Megaspeed International, a cloud computing and data center operator that became a multibillion-dollar Nvidia customer. The New York Times reported Monday that the Commerce Department was leading the investigation into Megaspeed before it was sent to the Justice Department after Nvidia reached out about the case. Read more about Alice Huang and Megaspeed below. Who is Alice Huang? Zoom in: Huang, also known as Huang Le, is a Chinese citizen with a reported background in journalism and finance. An AFP investigation found an online profile that said she previously worked at the financial services company HSBC and the broadcasters CCTV and Hunan TV. However, AFP said it couldn't independently verify the information. Zoom out: The New York Times reports that China's Ministry of State Security recruited Alice Huang to seek information about Jensen Huang and influence his feelings about selling AI chips to Chinese firms. But it's still unclear what information she provided to Beijing and whether she obtained any from Jensen Huang. Nvidia's board says it has no reason to believe Alice Huang obtained trade secrets. China has also denied the allegations. What to know about Alice Huang's company Alice Huang is a former executive of Megaspeed International, which rents out computing power from advanced Nvidia processors, giving customers power to run AI systems without owning chips. Before it was Megaspeed, the company was known as 7Road International, a subsidiary of prominent Chinese video game developer, 7Road Holdings. Before the AI boom, Nvidia products were primarily used in the video game industry. In the 2010s, Alice worked at Shanghai Hexi Investment Management, which had investment connections to the 7Road gaming company. She also sold a cloud business to 7Road in 2019, according to documents compiled by Tesari AI, an AI startup focused on national security matters. 7Road International, the Singapore subsidiary of 7Road Holdings, became Megaspeed in March 2023, and Alice Huang became managing director, per Tesari AI's documents. Her company Huang Le Limited became the sole owner of Megaspeed. In November 2023, Megaspeed was bought by a company called Swiftdata . Alice Huang and another director, Cang Yang, soon resigned from the company. The company faced an investigation by Singapore police in October 2025 over violations of local laws, but specific offenses were not shared publicly. Employees told The Wall Street Journal that Alice Huang continued leading the business after resigning. Alice Huang is "actually still our boss," an employee told Culper Research , which published an investigation into Nvidia's China business in May 2026. How Alice Huang's Megaspeed ties to Nvidia By the numbers: Megaspeed became an official Nvidia Cloud Partner in 2023, per Bloomberg , and purchased more than $4.8 billion worth of Nvidia chips over roughly two years, per AP . Alice Huang bragged about her access to Jensen Huang and Nvidia connections to help raise funds for her businesses, according to the NYT . A Megaspeed employee told Culper that Jensen Huang would visit Megaspeed sometimes, adding that Jensen and Alice had a "very close" relationship. Follow the money: Megaspeed's balance sheet ballooned from $33 million at the end of 2023 to nearly $3 billion a year later, according to corporate records examined by Culper, a short seller with a financial interest in Nvidia's decline. Much of that growth involved approximately $2.9 billion in refundable deposits from an unidentified source, per Culper. The financing raises additional questions about Megaspeed's relationship with Chinese businesses. More recently, in early 2025, Alice Huang and business partner Kang Wei told investors they had "no problem securing GPUs" and touted Alibaba as a customer for a new data center project, according to the Financial Times . What are authorities investigating? State of play: U.S. authorities, including the Commerce Department and Justice Department, have investigated whether Megaspeed helped Chinese companies obtain advanced Nvidia processors and whether that violated export-control restrictions. The company disputed illegal chip transfers in December 2025. The company has said it plans to work with U.S. authorities over the investigation. What's next: Three Republican House committee chairs have requested a closed-door briefing with Jensen Huang on Nov. 18 about his interactions with Alice Huang and how Nvidia protects itself against foreign threats.

events.title: Hegseth faces impeachment resolution from a GOP member with little to lose
events.summary: Rep. Thomas Massie (R-KY) introduced articles of impeachment against Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth on Monday over his handling of the Iran war and other alleged misconduct. Why it matters: The coming vote could mark the first impeachment of a Cabinet secretary during the second Trump administration and signal what's to come when Democrats take control of Congress next year. What they're saying: Hegseth "will remain a threat to the Constitution if allowed to remain in office, and has acted in a manner grossly incompatible with his duties and the rule of law," Massie said Monday while reading the articles of impeachment on the House floor. "Secretary Hegseth knowingly executed and implemented unlawful orders to initiate war against a foreign nation… thereby substituting unlawful executive action for the constitutional and statutory judgment of Congress." Later, at a Monday press conference, Massie warned that "[w]hen the Democrats get in charge, they are going to be very vicious." He predicted that Democrats would hold hearings, question people who worked with Hegseth and pursue a Senate impeachment trial if he remains in office. The other side: Hegseth dismissed the impeachment push as politically motivated "noise" Monday, telling reporters that he and his team aren't worried about the push. The Department of Defense didn't immediately respond to Axios' request for comment. Catch up quick: Massie first introduced the articles of impeachment before the House went into recess so members could campaign. He reintroduced the resolution Monday, restarting a two-legislative-day clock for House leaders to act. Massie and other members of Congress accuse Hegseth of defying Congress by continuing the unpopular war in Iran despite legislative efforts to shut it down. Three of the eight articles accuse Hegseth of violating congressional war powers in Iran. The others allege misconduct involving civilian casualties, strikes on suspected drug boats, retaliation against Sen. Mark Kelly, the capture of Nicolás Maduro and military operations in Yemen. Hegseth has reportedly been among the Iran war's most ardent supporters, telling Trump the conflict would be easy to win. Eight months later, that doesn't appear to be true. Between the lines: Republicans who previously resisted reining in the administration's war effort might be more willing to impeach Hegseth now that voters have delivered a strong rebuke of the administration and its war during the 2026 midterms. And with dozens of House and Senate members retiring or leaving Congress, it's possible the YOLO caucus might decide Hegseth should be the fall guy. "If they are part of the retirement caucus, what do they have to lose?" Massie asked Monday. House GOP leaders are bracing for defections from members whose terms are ending, Axios reported Sunday . Massie acknowledged that the impeachment vote would be tough for some Republican lawmakers, but said Monday that impeaching Hegseth is "the best vote you can take right now to put some daylight between yourself and the failed policy of this war in Iran." What we're watching: Even if the House impeaches Hegseth, removing him from office would require a two-thirds vote in the Republican-controlled Senate. Go deeper: House poised to impeach Pete Hegseth after GOP midterm defeat Editor's note: This story has been updated with additional quotes from Massie.

events.title: With a weak board and no successor, Nvidia confronts a governance crisis
events.summary: The News Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang’s spy scandal shines a spotlight on thin corporate governance and opaque succession planning at what has become the world’s most important company. Huang’s chances of remaining as CEO, after admitting to an affair with a woman suspected of spying for Chinese intelligence services, are now in the hands of a board of directors that lacks the experience and stature typically found at companies of Nvidia’s size and importance. They have allowed Huang to run the company with no obvious successor and a leadership structure with little precedent in corporate America, in which he has more than 50 direct reports. Top of mind, too, is what Nvidia would be without Huang, its CEO since he co-founded the company in 1993. He has nearly single-handedly turned Nvidia from a niche maker of graphics chips for video games into the centerpiece of the world’s AI boom — and, depending on the day, its most valuable company. “It appears [Huang] did mislead the public,” said Gary Gensler, the former chair of the Securities & Exchange Commission under the Biden administration, referencing earlier denials by Huang and the company that his dealings were “all completely normal and not unusual.” “It’s really a question of is that material, and today’s stock drop will suggest to a court it was material,” Gensler said. Nvidia’s shares were down 5% in afternoon trading, slicing more than $200 billion from its market value. When asked if the SEC was going to investigate, an agency spokesperson declined to comment. For its part, Nvidia’s board has said it still has confidence in Huang. Cozy Ties, Light Resumes The average Nvidia board member has been there almost 15 years — nearly twice as long as the average S&P 500 director. Nvidia’s lead director is a 77-year-old former law-firm executive. None of the board members are current or former S&P 500 CEOs or have national-security experience. (Meta and Microsoft each have four big-company CEOs on their boards.) Huang and two other directors have been on the board since the company’s founding 33 years ago. “The board composition suggests this is… a CEO exercising effective control over the board instead of vice versa,” said Jill Fisch, a professor at The University of Pennsylvania’s Carey Law School, adding that long tenure on a board can reduce directors’ independence and breed complacency. At the same time, she said, Nvidia exemplifies how limited boards’ ability to check executives’ power can be when their CEO is known as an industry visionary: “How do you say no to someone with this track record of success?” Succession Questions Nvidia has never publicly signaled a succession plan for Huang, both of whose adult children work for the company. It also lacks a clear No. 2, with no president or chief operating officer. The word “succession” appears nowhere in its most recent annual report to shareholders, versus 25 times for Microsoft and 16 for Alphabet. The Nvidia board has for years enabled Huang’s unusual management style, in which he has more than 50 direct reports. It’s a nearly unheard-of management structure that is meant to enable Nvidia to operate at what Huang has called the “speed of light,” but leaves the company without an obvious internal replacement for Huang, should the board’s investigation unearth facts that make it untenable for him to remain CEO. It also sets up a talent drain: If Huang is ultimately fired and replaced with an insider, “you’re going to have 59 people who will all think ‘it should have been me,’” said Jason Schloetzer, a professor at Georgetown University who co-authors an annual report on CEO succession planning. “A horse race with 60 horses has no good solution.” That will likely force directors to look outside, with a short list of CEOs from seasoned chipmakers such as AMD’s Lisa Su or Broadcom’s Hock Tan. Beyond the Usual Sex Scandal Huang’s case has implications beyond those raised by “the usual sex scandal in the corporate boardroom,” said John C. Coffee Jr, a Columbia Law School professor and veteran corporate governance expert. “Other companies have fired the CEO [for infidelity] but those companies probably didn’t have quite as important a figure as CEO,” he said. “It’s possible he was at most negligent,” Coffee said, “but negligence doesn’t require that you shoot yourself in the foot by firing a well regarded CEO.” The company’s investigation, and likely congressional hearings, will help determine whether Huang did anything during the course of his extramarital relationship to compromise company secrets or US national security in an industry of intense significance to the geopolitical competition between the US and China. The board said on Sunday it had “no reason to believe that either national security or NVIDIA secrets were compromised,” and President Donald Trump expressed confidence in Huang. The company will also face questions about an earlier investigation it said it conducted into the allegations. Any suggestion that Huang misled the board, or that the company knowingly misled investors about a material issue could expose it to even more shareholder litigation. Enforcement action is another risk, though Gensler said “I think this administration does things differently. The President has already spoken on the matter.” Notable The scandal, and governance crisis, adds to the company’s list of challenges , including a Democratic Congress that threatens to slow down the AI infrastructure buildout, Semafor wrote.

events.title: Democrats' 2028 presidential auditions begin in Denver
events.summary: A who's who of Democratic power players descends on Denver this week to plot the party's future, fresh off its sweeping midterm victories . Why it matters: The gathering gives Democrats' rising stars an early stage to test their 2028 message, and explore whether Colorado's red-to- deep-blue shift could offer a national playbook. Driving the news: The three-day " What's Next " conference, starting Thursday, features dozens of Democratic heavyweights and potential presidential contenders, including House Democratic Leader Hakeem Jeffries , Pennsylvania Gov. Josh Shapiro , Texas Sen.-elect James Talarico and former Transportation Secretary Pete Buttigieg . Colorado's own Gov.-elect Phil Weiser , U.S. Sen. Michael Bennet, U.S. Rep. Joe Neguse and Denver Mayor Mike Johnston round out the lineup. Majority Democrats, a group seeking to shape the party's direction, is organizing the event. The big picture: Colorado's two-decade transformation into a Democratic powerhouse made it a natural host, spokesperson Vidhya Jeyadev told Axios. Organizers want to dissect and pinpoint what worked — and what didn't — in the midterms, and how to turn wins into lasting power. The gathering comes as Democrats debate whether they should double down on progressive policies or tack toward the center heading into 2028. Behind the scenes: Johnston, a Majority Democrats member, told Axios in a phone interview he personally lobbied to bring the conference to Denver after organizers began scouting locations about a year ago. He'll give opening and closing remarks and expects private meetings with most of the national leaders attending. He plans to pitch Denver's approaches to homelessness , housing and public safety as national models. He'll also press for more federal money for affordable housing and his universal child care plan . Between the lines: Colorado Democrats have embraced gun safety , immigration and LGBTQ rights — positions some in the party worry could cost votes elsewhere. Johnston argues Colorado proved otherwise: "Leading on those values has made our majority stronger here, not weaker." What we're watching: Denver is one of three finalists to host the 2028 Democratic National Convention, alongside Boston and Philadelphia. With a decision expected soon, Johnston sees this week as an audition. "We'd love to make the case that the '28 presidential cycle can start in Denver and end in Denver," he said.

events.title: Nvidia has no obvious successor to Jensen Huang — and that's a problem
events.summary: Nvidia is coming under fire for having no clear succession plan to replace Jensen Huang in the event that something unexpected happens — like an international incident with him at the center . Why it matters: The spotlight on Huang shows the vulnerabilities of a large company being dependent on one executive — and the risks it poses to investors and customers, corporate governance experts tell Axios. Catch up quick: Huang — who founded the chips giant, serves as its all-powerful CEO and exerts significant influence over the global AI economy — admitted to having an affair with a woman suspected of being a Chinese spy. Nvidia's board announced an independent investigation Sunday, and experts say Huang's chances of keeping his job are a coin flip . The big picture: The company, by all accounts, has no clear bench of potential replacements. Huang famously has dozens of direct reports, ensuring that no single individual — other than him — has a wide-ranging purview at the company. "The biggest issue is no human goes on forever, and this is exactly why you want a good succession plan in place if something like this were to happen," says Charles Elson, a corporate governance expert and former University of Delaware professor. "You can't base a company that big around one person. You just can't," Elson added. "What if he gets hit by a bus?" CEO succession planning is a standard practice for big public companies, and it's not clear whether Nvidia has a confidential plan. State of play: The highest-profile member of Huang's executive team is Colette Kress, Nvidia's chief financial officer, who appears alongside him during the company's earnings calls. But analysts say Kress — who has spent her career in financial roles — isn't necessarily a natural successor to Huang in his role as an innovator and visionary for the AI age. What they're saying: "It's ridiculous that they have nobody in management identified," says Jeffrey Sonnenfeld, a professor at the Yale School of Management who is one of the nation's premier CEO whisperers . And no one has been put through any kind of trial assignments to get them ready for the role, Sonnenfeld says. The lack of a clear succession plan suggests Nvidia's board was "asleep at the wheel," says Peter Jaworski, a business ethics professor at Georgetown University. Consequently, it's essential that the board now steps up and exerts its authority by ensuring that the investigation is thorough, independent, and "reveals as much as they can," Jaworski says. "Transparency is really critical." For now, Nvidia investors are anxiously awaiting results of the probe — but in general, most say they are hoping he's able to stay. "In some ways he's irreplaceable," says Michael Monaghan, partner at Founder ETFs, an Nvidia investor. Monaghan says Founder ETFs — which specializes in backing founder-led companies — will sell Nvidia shares if Huang exits. "We don't really believe there is such thing as succession in these massive founder-led companies," Monaghan says. Reality check: There are many examples of companies surviving and even thriving after a well-known headline-grabbing founder departs — think Travis Kalanick at Uber. "People thought he was so critical," says Sonnenfeld. The company did "far better when they got rid of him." Yes, but: Nvidia might not have a choice. "We always think there's no chance this person gets fired, until they do – and this might be one of those cases," Georgetown's Jaworski says. Nvidia reps had no immediate comment. What we're watching: Sonnenfeld says that he's heard former Google CEO Eric Schmidt's name come up as someone who could steer the company if Huang has to step away. "I've heard it rumored. He could step in tomorrow and do a very good job," Sonnenfeld says.

events.title: White House cautiously upbeat about Russia-Ukraine peace talks this week
events.summary: The White House is "cautiously optimistic" as peace talks between Russia and Ukraine resume in Abu Dhabi this week, U.S. officials said on Monday. Why it matters: The talks on Tuesday and Wednesday will be the first time the parties have met with U.S. mediators present since February, when they were suspended due to the war in Iran. White House envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner have worked for weeks to convince Russian President Vladimir Putin to restart negotiations. President Trump and his team hope Putin will be more willing to compromise after the U.S. lifted sanctions on Russian diesel sales and took other steps welcomed by Moscow. "The relations we have built with Putin will be instrumental in these negotiations," a U.S. official said. After the meetings in Abu Dhabi, Witkoff and Kushner may travel to Moscow and Kyiv to speak directly with Putin and Zelensky, a U.S. official said. Yes, but: The parties remain far apart, particularly over potential territorial concessions by Ukraine. Russia's escalating attacks on Ukrainian cities and Putin's refusal to agree to a ceasefire have cast doubt on prospects for meaningful progress. Behind the scenes: Over the last two weeks, Witkoff and Kushner had daily phone calls — sometimes multiple times a day — with Russian and Ukrainian officials to prepare for the upcoming talks, U.S. officials said. What they're saying: U.S. officials who briefed reporters on Monday struck a positive tone despite skepticism in Europe and Ukraine about Putin's willingness to end the war. "There is a shot to make significant progress towards a deal and to try and bridge the gaps," a U.S. official said. "Getting the parties back to the table wasn't easy to do and we see promising signs as mediators." The official added that Witkoff and Kushner want to use the talks to "crystallize" the decisions Putin and Zelensky will have to make. Driving the news: The talks in Abu Dhabi will focus on two tracks: A military working group led by the commander of U.S. European command, Gen. Alexus Grynkewich, will discuss post-war ceasefire monitoring and security arrangements. The working group made significant progress on this front during the last round of talks in February. A political working group that focuses on the most sensitive topic: territorial demands. There was no progress on this issue in February. State of play: The two sides haven't budged publicly. Russia is demanding control over the entire region of Donbas, while Ukraine insists that territory be divided based on current front lines. In private, though, U.S. officials say that both sides "have shown a little bit of flexibility" on the territorial issue in recent weeks. They say an agreement on territory won't be possible until security guarantees are reached. The big picture: Witkoff and Kushner invited senior officials from NATO, the EU and four major European powers — the UK, France, Germany and Italy — to Abu Dhabi to hold separate discussions on the sidelines of the Russia-Ukraine negotiations. Ukraine's European allies will play a key role in any post-war security arrangements. The U.S. also wants to start a third track of negotiations between European countries and Russia to create new ways of easing tensions and avoiding conflict. But many European countries are highly suspicious of the idea. They believe it endorses a Russian narrative that Europe is a security threat to Moscow and worry it will result in weakening NATO. U.S. officials stress that the proposed Europe-Russia security initiative would not replace or diminish NATO and the central role it plays in protecting Europe. But a new security agreement between Europe and Russia would help end the war in Ukraine, they say. A U.S. official said Witkoff and Kushner hope Russians will agree to include European representatives in the next round of peace talks after Abu Dhabi. What to watch: Ukrainian officials say they have three priorities for the talks: Clinching a deal to de-escalate tensions on the Black Sea and allow grain exports. Reaching an agreement to stop attacks on Ukrainian power plants and Russian oil refineries before the winter. Organizing a trilateral summit between Trump, Putin and Zelensky, possibly during the G20 summit in Miami next month.
